title: When will the Moon become a Synchronous Satellite
problem:
# Theoretical Question 1

# When will the Moon become a Synchronous Satellite?

The period of rotation of the Moon about its axis is currently the same as its period of revolution about the Earth so that the same side of the Moon always faces the Earth. The equality of these two periods presumably came about because of actions of tidal forces over the long history of the Earth-Moon system.

However, the period of rotation of the Earth about its axis is currently shorter than the period of revolution of the Moon. As a result, lunar tidal forces continue to act in a way that tends to slow down the rotational speed of the Earth and drive the Moon itself further away from the Earth.

In this question, we are interested in obtaining an estimate of how much more time it will take for the rotational period of the Earth to become equal to the period of revolution of the Moon. The Moon will then become a synchronous satellite, appearing as a fixed object in the sky and visible only to those observers on the side of the Earth facing the Moon. We also want to find out how long it will take for the Earth to complete one rotation when the said two periods are equal.

Two right-handed rectangular coordinate systems are adopted as reference frames. The third coordinate axes of these two systems are parallel to each other and normal to the orbital plane of the Moon.

(I) The first frame, called the $CM$ frame, is an inertial frame with its origin located at the center of mass $C$ of the Earth-Moon system.
(II) The second frame, called the xyz frame, has its origin fixed at the center $O$ of the Earth. Its $z$ -axis coincides with the axis of rotation of the Earth. Its $x$ -axis is along the line connecting the centers of the Moon and the Earth, and points in the direction of the unit vector $\hat{r}$ as shown in Fig.1a. The Moon remains always on the negative $x$ -axis in this frame.

Note that distances in Fig.1a are not drawn to scale. The curved arrows show the directions of the Earth's rotation and the Moon's revolution. The Earth-Moon distance is denoted by $r$ .

Fig. 1a

# The following data are given:

(a) At present, the distance between the Moon and the Earth is $r_0=3.85 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m}$ and increases at a rate of $0.038 \mathrm{~m}$ per year.
(b) The period of revolution of the Moon is currently $T_{M} =27.322$ days.
(c) The mass of the Moon is $M =7.35 \times 10^{22} \, \mathrm{kg}$ .
(d) The radius of the Moon is $R_{M} =1.74 \times 10^{6} \, \text{m}$ .
(e) The period of rotation of the Earth is currently $T_{E} =23.933$ hours.
(f) The mass of the Earth is $M_{E} =5.97 \times 10^{24} \, \mathrm{kg}$ .
(g) The radius of the Earth is $R_{E} =6.37 \times 10^{6} m$ .
(h) The universal gravitational constant is $G =6.67259 \times 10^{-11} N \cdot m^2/ kg^2$ .

# The following assumptions may be made when answering questions:

(i) The Earth-Moon system is isolated from the rest of the universe.
(ii) The orbit of the Moon about the Earth is circular.
(iii) The axis of rotation of the Earth is perpendicular to the orbital plane of the Moon.
(iv) If the Moon is absent and the Earth does not rotate, then the mass distribution of the Earth is spherically symmetric and the radius of the Earth is $R_{E}$ .
(v) For the Earth or the Moon, the moment of inertia $I$ about any axis passing through its center is that of a uniform sphere of mass $M$ and radius $R$ , i.e. $I = \frac{2}{5} MR^2$ .
(vi) The water around the Earth is stationary in the $xyz$ frame.

# Answer the following questions:

sub_problems.problem: (1) With respect to the center of mass $C$ , what is the current value of the total angular momentum $L$ of the Earth-Moon system?
sub_problems.solution:
All angular momenta are parallel to the $z$-axis, so we compute only the magnitudes of the $z$-components.
\nThe angular speed of the Moons orbit is
\[
\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_M}
=\frac{2\pi}{27.322\times 86400}
=2.6617\times 10^{-6}\ \text{rad/s}.
\]
\nThe distance from the Earths center $O$ to the center of mass $C$ is
\[\nr_{CM}=\frac{M r_0}{M+M_E}
=\frac{7.35\times 10^{22}}{7.35\times 10^{22}+5.97\times 10^{24}}(3.85\times 10^8)
=4.68\times 10^6\ \text{m}.
\]\nHence the Moons distance from $C$ is $r_0-r_{CM}$, and the Earths distance from $C$ is $r_{CM}$.
\nThe Moons orbital angular momentum about $C$ is
\[\nL_M^{\text{orb}}=M(r_0-r_{CM})^2\omega_0
=2.83\times 10^{34}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}.
\]
\nThe Moons spin angular momentum is
\[\nS_M=\frac{2}{5}MR_M^2\omega_0
=2.37\times 10^{29}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s},
\]\nwhich is negligible compared with its orbital angular momentum.
\nThe Earths orbital angular momentum about $C$ is
\[\nL_E^{\text{orb}}=M_E r_{CM}^2\omega_0
=3.48\times 10^{32}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}.
\]
\nThe Earths spin angular speed is
\[
\Omega_E=\frac{2\pi}{T_E}
=\frac{2\pi}{23.933\times 3600}
=7.2926\times 10^{-5}\ \text{rad/s},
\]\nand its spin angular momentum is
\[\nS_E=\frac{2}{5}M_E R_E^2\Omega_E
=7.07\times 10^{33}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}.
\]
\nTherefore the total angular momentum of the Earth-Moon system about the center of mass is
\[\nL=L_M^{\text{orb}}+L_E^{\text{orb}}+S_E+S_M
\approx 2.83\times 10^{34}+3.48\times 10^{32}+7.07\times 10^{33}
=3.57\times 10^{34}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}.
\]
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{3.57\times 10^{34}\ \text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{s}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
The total angular momentum about the centre of mass \(C\) is the sum of several independent contributions, all of which are parallel to the same axis (perpendicular to the Earth–Moon orbital plane).  Because the vectors are parallel, you may work with their magnitudes and add them at the end.  The key idea, directly from reference, is that the angular momentum of a system is the sum of the *orbital* angular momentum of each body about the chosen point, plus the *spin* angular momentum of each body about its own centre.  The Earth–Moon problem is the very illustration used in the “additivity of angular momentum” passage.

Follow these steps, using only the relations given in the provided passages.

1. **Find the centre of mass \(C\)**  
   Treat the Earth and Moon as two point masses separated by the centre‑to‑centre distance \(r_0\).  Place the origin at the Earth’s centre \(O\).  The position of the centre of mass is given by the two‑body centre‑of‑mass formula

sub_problems.problem: (2) When the period of rotation of the Earth and the period of revolution of the Moon become equal, what is the duration of one rotation of the Earth? Denote the answer as $T$ and express it in units of the present day. Only an approximate solution is required so that iterative methods may be used.
sub_problems.solution:
Use conservation of the total angular momentum of the isolated Earth--Moon system. When the Earths rotation rate equals the Moons orbital angular speed, let this common angular speed be \(\omega\).
\nFor a circular Earth--Moon orbit, Newtons form of Keplers third law gives
\[
\omega^2 r^3 = G(M_E+M).
\]\nHence
\[\nr = \left(\frac{G(M_E+M)}{\omega^2}\right)^{1/3}.
\]\nThe orbital angular momentum of the Earth--Moon system about the center of mass is
\[
\ell = \mu r^2\omega,
\qquad 
\mu=\frac{M_E M}{M_E+M},
\]\nso
\[
\ell = \frac{M_E M}{M_E+M}\left(\frac{G(M_E+M)}{\omega^2}\right)^{2/3}\omega
= M_E M\left(\frac{G^2}{(M_E+M)\omega}\right)^{1/3}.
\]\nThe Earths spin angular momentum is
\[\nS_E=I_E\omega=\frac{2}{5}M_E R_E^2\omega,
\]\nwhile the Moons spin is neglected.
\nTherefore the total angular momentum at the final synchronous state is
\[\nL_f = M_E M\left(\frac{G^2}{(M_E+M)\omega}\right)^{1/3} + \frac{2}{5}M_E R_E^2\omega.
\]\nThis must equal the present total angular momentum of the system. Solving this equation iteratively gives
\[
\omega \approx 1.35\times 10^{-6}\ \text{rad s}^{-1}.
\]\nThus the Earths rotation period in the synchronous state is
\[\nT=\frac{2\pi}{\omega}\approx \frac{2\pi}{1.35\times 10^{-6}}\approx 5.39\times 10^6\ \text{s}
\approx 53.9\ \text{days}.
\]\nSo the Earth will complete one rotation in \(\boxed{53.9\ \text{days}}\), which is about \(\boxed{2.25}\) times the present-day rotation period.

sub_problems.problem:
(3) Consider the Earth to be a rotating solid sphere covered with a surface layer of water and assume that, as the Moon moves around the Earth, the water layer is stationary in the xyz-frame. In one model, frictional forces between the rotating solid sphere and the water layer are taken into account. The faster spinning solid Earth is assumed to drag lunar tides along so that the line connecting the tidal bulges is at an angle $\delta$ with the $x$ -axis, as shown in Fig.1b. Consequently, lunar tidal forces acting on the Earth will exert a torque $\Gamma$ about $O$ to slow down the rotation of the Earth.

The angle $\delta$ is assumed to be constant and independent of the Earth-Moon distance $r$ until it vanishes when the Moon's revolution is synchronous with the Earth's rotation so that frictional forces no longer exist. The torque $\Gamma$ therefore

scales with the Earth-Moon distance and is proportional to $\frac{1}{r^6}$ .

According to this model, when will the rotation of the Earth and the revolution of the Moon have the same period? Denote the answer as $t_f$ and express it in units of the present year.

Fig.1b

$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{r^{2} + s^{2} +2 r x}} \approx \left(\frac{1}{r} - \frac{x}{r^{2}} + \frac{3 x^{2} - s^{2}}{2 r^{3}} + \dots\right)$$

sub_problems.solution:
Let \(n\) be the Moons orbital angular speed and \(\Omega\) the Earths spin angular speed. For a circular orbit,
\[
\ell = \mu r^2 n,\qquad \mu=\frac{M_E M}{M_E+M},\qquad n^2 r^3=G(M_E+M),
\]\nso
\[
\ell=\mu [G(M_E+M)]^{2/3}n^{-1/3}.
\]
\nThe tidal torque is assumed to scale as
\[
\Gamma=\Gamma_0\left(\frac{r_0}{r}\right)^6.
\]\nFrom \(\ell=\mu\sqrt{G(M_E+M)r}\),
\[
\dot\ell=\frac12\mu\sqrt{\frac{G(M_E+M)}{r}}\,\dot r,
\]\nso at the present time
\[
\Gamma_0=\dot\ell_0
=\frac12\mu\sqrt{\frac{G(M_E+M)}{r_0}}\,\dot r_0
\approx 4.5\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{N\,m}.
\]
\nUsing \(r=[G(M_E+M)/n^2]^{1/3}\), the torque becomes
\[
\Gamma=\Gamma_0\left(\frac{r_0}{r}\right)^6
=\Gamma_0\,\frac{r_0^6}{[G(M_E+M)]^2}n^4.
\]\nSince \(\dot\ell=-\Gamma\),
\[
-\frac13\mu [G(M_E+M)]^{2/3}n^{-4/3}\dot n
=\Gamma_0\,\frac{r_0^6}{[G(M_E+M)]^2}n^4,
\]\nwhich gives
\[
\dot n=-K n^{16/3},\qquad\nK=\frac{3\Gamma_0 r_0^6}{\mu [G(M_E+M)]^{8/3}}.
\]\nIntegrating from the present value \(n_0=2\pi/T_M\) to the final synchronous value \(n_f\),
\[
 t_f=\frac{3}{13K}\left(n_f^{-13/3}-n_0^{-13/3}\right).
\]\nThe synchronous angular speed \(n_f\) is found from conservation of total angular momentum:
\[\nI_E\Omega_0+\mu [G(M_E+M)]^{2/3}n_0^{-1/3}
=I_E n_f+\mu [G(M_E+M)]^{2/3}n_f^{-1/3},
\]\nwith \(I_E=\frac25 M_E R_E^2\) and \(\Omega_0=2\pi/T_E\). Solving gives
\[\nn_f\approx 1.35\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}},
\]\ncorresponding to a common period of about \(54\) days.
\nSubstituting \(n_0\), \(n_f\), and \(\Gamma_0\) into the time formula yields
\[\nt_f\approx 8.1\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{s}\approx 2.6\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{years}.
\]\nTherefore, the Earth and Moon will become synchronous after \(\boxed{2.6\times10^{10}\ \text{years}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the time \(t_f\) when Earth’s rotation and the Moon’s revolution become synchronous, you need to combine several ideas from your textbook passages in a careful sequence. Do not try to jump straight to a number—work through the logic step by step.

**1. Understand the two angular momenta involved.**  
The total angular momentum of the Earth–Moon system has two parts: the spin angular momentum of the Earth (a rotating solid sphere) and the orbital angular momentum of the Moon. From the textbook, the moment of inertia of a uniform solid sphere is \(I = \frac{2}{5} M R^2\) (see the sphere-and-cylinder worked example). The orbital angular momentum for a circular orbit is given by \(L_{\text{orb}} = \mu \sqrt{G M a}\), where \(\mu\) is the reduced mass and \(M\) is the total mass (see the interacting binary systems passage). Recall that \(\mu = \frac{M_E M_m}{M_E + M_m}\) and \(M = M_E + M_m\). The semi-major axis \(a\) is simply the Earth–Moon distance \(r\) for a circular orbit.

**2. Use conservation of total angular momentum.**  
The textbook explains that if no external torques act, the total angular momentum of an isolated system is conserved. Here, internal tidal torques transfer angular momentum between Earth’s spin and the Moon’s orbit, but the total remains constant. Therefore, write the total angular momentum today (using Earth’s present spin period and the Moon’s present orbital period) and set it equal to the total angular momentum at the final synchronous state (when Earth’s spin angular speed and the Moon’s orbital angular speed are the same, call that common value \(n_f\)). This gives you one equation linking \(n_f\) to known present quantities.

**3. Relate the Moon’s orbital angular speed to the distance.**  
From the general form of Kepler’s third law for a circular orbit (see the passage deriving \(P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{G(m_1+m_2)} a^3\)), you can write the orbital angular speed \(n\) (which is \(2\pi/P\)) in terms of the distance \(r\) and the total mass \(M\). Use this to express the orbital angular momentum purely in terms of \(n\), eliminating \(r\). This will be useful because the torque law is given in terms of \(r\), and you will need to convert it to a differential equation in \(n\).

**4. Set up the differential equation for \(n\) from the tidal torque.**  
The problem states that the torque scales as \(\Gamma \propto 1/r^6\). With the relation between \(r\) and \(n\) from Kepler’s third law, you can write \(\Gamma\) as a function of \(n\): \(\Gamma = C n^4\), where \(C\) is a constant you can build from present values.  

Now, the torque causes a change in the orbital angular momentum: \(dL_{\text{orb}}/dt = -\Gamma\) (the minus sign because the torque slows Earth’s spin but increases the Moon’s orbital angular momentum—check the sign carefully using the physical description in the tidal forces passage). Take the time derivative of \(L_{\text{orb}}\) expressed in terms of \(n\), and equate it to \(-\Gamma\). This yields a differential equation of the form \(\dot{n} = -K n^{16/3}\), where \(K\) is a constant involving known quantities and the present torque \(\Gamma_0\).

**5. Apply separation of variables to solve for the time.**  
The differential equation \(\dot{n} = -K n^{16/3}\) is separable. Although the textbook’s separation-of-variables examples focus on linear cases, the method extends directly: rearrange to \(\frac{dn}{n^{16/3}} = -K dt\) and integrate from the present angular speed \(n_0\) to the final synchronous speed \(n_f\). The hint (M2) in the problem is a specific integral formula for a power-law relation; you can use it with \(a = 13/3\) and \(b = -K\) to find \(t_f\) in terms of \(n_0, n_f\), and \(K\).

**6. Determine the constant \(K\) from present data.**  
To evaluate \(K\), you need the present torque \(\Gamma_0\). The textbook passage on tidal effects tells you that the Moon is receding at 3–4 cm/year today. From the orbital angular momentum expression \(L_{\text{orb}} = \mu \sqrt{G M r}\), take a time derivative and relate \(\dot{r}\) to \(\dot{L}_{\text{orb}} = \Gamma_0\). Use the present Earth–Moon distance and the observed recession rate to find \(\Gamma_0\). (Be careful with units—convert everything to SI.) Then assemble \(K\) using the known masses, \(G\), and the present distance.

**7. Put it all together.**  
Solve the angular momentum conservation equation for \(n_f\) (you will need Earth’s present spin angular speed \(\Omega_0\) and the Moon’s present orbital angular speed \(n_0\)). Substitute \(n_0, n_f\), and \(K\) into your integrated time formula. The result will be in seconds; convert to years using \(1\text{ yr} \approx 3.156\times 10^7\text{ s}\).  

At every stage, refer back to the relevant textbook ideas: Kepler’s third law for the \(n\)–\(r\) relation, the orbital angular momentum formula for a circular binary, the moment of inertia of a uniform sphere, and the conservation of total angular momentum. The calculation is lengthy, but each piece is a direct application of these concepts.

title: Motion of an Electric Dipole in a Magnetic Field
problem:
# Theoretical Question 2

# Motion of an Electric Dipole in a Magnetic Field

In the presence of a constant and uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ , the translational motion of a system of electric charges is coupled to its rotational motion. As a result, the conservation laws for the momentum and the component of the angular momentum along the direction of $\vec{B}$ are modified from the usual form. This is illustrated in this problem by considering the motion of an electric dipole made of two particles of equal mass $m$ and carrying charges $q$ and $-q$ respectively ( $q > 0$ ). The two particles are connected by a rigid insulating rod of length $\ell$ , the mass of which can be neglected. Let $\vec{r}_1$ be the position vector of the particle with charge $q$ , $\vec{r}_2$ that of the other particle and $\vec{\ell} = \vec{r}_1- \vec{r}_2$ . Denote by $\vec{\omega}$ the angular velocity of the rotation around the center of mass of the dipole. Denote by $\vec{r}_{CM}$ and $\vec{\nu}_{CM}$ the position and the velocity vectors of the center of mass respectively. Relativistic effects and effects of electromagnetic radiation can be neglected.

Note that the magnetic force acting on a particle of charge $q$ and velocity $\vec{v}$ is $q\vec{v} \times \vec{B}$ , where the cross product of two vectors $\vec{A}_1 \times \vec{A}_2$ is defined, in terms of the $x, y, z$ , components of the vectors, by

$$\begin{array}{l} (\vec{A}_{1} \times \vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{x}} = (\vec{A}_{1})_{\mathrm{y}} (\vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{z}} - (\vec{A}_{1})_{\mathrm{z}} (\vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{y}} \\ (\vec{A}_{1} \times \vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{y}} = (\vec{A}_{1})_{\mathrm{z}} (\vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{x}} - (\vec{A}_{1})_{\mathrm{x}} (\vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{z}} \\ (\vec{A}_{1} \times \vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{z}} = (\vec{A}_{1})_{\mathrm{x}} (\vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{y}} - (\vec{A}_{1})_{\mathrm{y}} (\vec{A}_{2})_{\mathrm{x}}. \\ \end{array}$$

# Part 1

sub_problems.problem: (1.1) Write down the equations of motion for the center of mass of the dipole and for the rotation around the center of mass by computing the total force and the total torque with respect to the center of mass acting on the dipole.
sub_problems.solution:
For the two charges, let
\[
\vec r_{CM}=\frac{\vec r_1+\vec r_2}{2},\qquad 
\vec v_{CM}=\frac{\vec v_1+\vec v_2}{2},\qquad
\vec\ell=\vec r_1-\vec r_2.
\]\nSince the rod is rigid, the relative velocity satisfies
\[
\dot{\vec\ell}=\vec v_1-\vec v_2=\vec\omega\times\vec\ell.
\]
\nThe magnetic forces on the two charges are
\[
\vec F_1=q\,\vec v_1\times\vec B,\qquad \vec F_2=-q\,\vec v_2\times\vec B.
\]\nHence the total force on the dipole is
\[
\vec F=\vec F_1+\vec F_2
= q(\vec v_1-\vec v_2)\times\vec B
= q\,\dot{\vec\ell}\times\vec B.
\]\nWith total mass \(M=2m\), the center-of-mass equation of motion is
\[
2m\,\dot{\vec v}_{CM}=q\,\dot{\vec\ell}\times\vec B.
\]
\nFor the torque about the center of mass, the position vectors of the two particles relative to the center are \(\pm \vec\ell/2\), so
\[
\vec\tau_{CM}=\frac{\vec\ell}{2}\times(q\vec v_1\times\vec B)
+\left(-\frac{\vec\ell}{2}\right)\times(-q\vec v_2\times\vec B).
\]\nThis simplifies to
\[
\vec\tau_{CM}=\frac{q}{2}\,\vec\ell\times\bigl[(\vec v_1+\vec v_2)\times\vec B\bigr]
= q\,\vec\ell\times(\vec v_{CM}\times\vec B).
\]\nFor a rigid rod of length \(\ell\), the moment of inertia about the center of mass is
\[\nI=2m\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^2=\frac12 m\ell^2.
\]\nTherefore the rotational equation is
\[
\frac12 m\ell^2\,\dot{\vec\omega}=q\,\vec\ell\times(\vec v_{CM}\times\vec B).
\]\nThus the equations of motion are
\[
\boxed{2m\,\dot{\vec v}_{CM}=q\,\dot{\vec\ell}\times\vec B},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac12 m\ell^2\,\dot{\vec\omega}=q\,\vec\ell\times(\vec v_{CM}\times\vec B)}.
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
To write the equations of motion for the dipole, you need to treat it as a system of two particles connected by a rigid massless rod, moving in a uniform magnetic field. The problem separates naturally into two parts: translation of the center of mass (CM) and rotation about the CM. You will use Newton’s second law for a system and the rotational equation of motion, together with the Lorentz force law.

**1. Set up the description of the system.**
From reference’s definition of the CM, for two equal masses \(m\) at positions \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2\) you have
\[
\mathbf{R} = \frac{m\mathbf{r}_1 + m\mathbf{r}_2}{2m} = \frac{\mathbf{r}_1 + \mathbf{r}_2}{2}.
\]
The same relation holds for the CM velocity \(\mathbf{V} = (\mathbf{v}_1 + \mathbf{v}_2)/2\). Define the relative position vector \(\boldsymbol{\ell} = \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2\). Because the rod is rigid and massless (as described in the rigid‑body passages), the relative velocity obeys \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\ell}} = \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \boldsymbol{\ell}\), where \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) is the angular velocity of the rod. This is the “rigid body relative velocity” relation given in reference.

**2. Find the total force on the dipole.**
The Lorentz force on a charge \(q\) moving with velocity \(\mathbf{v}\) in a magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) (with zero electric field) is \(\mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\). Apply this to the positive charge (\(+q\)) at \(\mathbf{r}_1\) and the negative charge (\(-q\)) at \(\mathbf{r}_2\) to write \(\mathbf{F}_1\) and \(\mathbf{F}_2\). Sum them to get the total external force \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}\). You should express the sum in terms of \(\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2\) and \(\mathbf{B}\), then replace \(\mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2\) with \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\ell}}\).

**3. Write the CM equation of motion.**
Newton’s second law for a system states that the total external force equals the total mass times the acceleration of the CM:
\[
\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = M \ddot{\mathbf{R}} = M \dot{\mathbf{V}},
\]
where \(M = 2m\). Substitute your expression for \(\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}\) from step 2. This gives the translational equation.

**4. Compute the torque about the CM.**
Torque is defined as \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\). The position vectors of the two charges relative to the CM are \(\boldsymbol{\ell}/2\) and \(-\boldsymbol{\ell}/2\). Compute the torque from each Lorentz force about the CM and add them. Use vector algebra to simplify the sum. You should find that the torque can be written in terms of \(\boldsymbol{\ell}\), \(\mathbf{V}\) (the CM velocity), and \(\mathbf{B}\).

**5. Relate torque to angular momentum and write the rotational equation.**
The fundamental relation for rotation is \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = d\mathbf{L}/dt\). For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis (here the instantaneous axis through the CM), the angular momentum is \(L = I\omega\), and the equation of motion becomes \(I\dot{\boldsymbol{\omega}} = \boldsymbol{\tau}\). You need the moment of inertia \(I\) of two point masses \(m\) separated by a distance \(\ell\), rotating about the CM. reference defines \(I = \sum m_j \rho_j^2\), where \(\rho_j\) is the perpendicular distance from the axis. For each mass, \(\rho = \ell/2\), so compute \(I\). Then set \(I\dot{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\) equal to the torque you found in step 4.

**6. Assemble the final equations.**
You now have two vector equations: one for \(2m \dot{\mathbf{V}}\) and one for \(I \dot{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\). They involve \(\boldsymbol{\ell}\), \(\dot{\boldsymbol{\ell}}\) (or \(\boldsymbol{\omega} \times \boldsymbol{\ell}\)), \(\mathbf{V}\), and the constant \(\mathbf{B}\). These are the equations of motion requested.

sub_problems.problem: (1.2) From the equation of motion for the center of mass, obtain the modified form of the conservation law for the total momentum. Denote the corresponding modified conserved quantity by $\vec{P}$ . Write down an expression in terms of $\vec{\nu}_{CM}$ and $\vec{\omega}$ for the conserved energy $E$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The center of mass of the dipole has total mass $M=2m$. In a uniform magnetic field, the Lorentz forces on the two charges do not cancel in the usual way, so the conserved momentum is modified by a term depending on the dipole separation:
\[
\dot{\vec P}=0,\qquad \vec P = M\vec\nu_{CM} - q\,\vec\ell\times\vec B.
\]\nHere $\vec\ell=\vec r_1-\vec r_2$ is the vector from the charge $-q$ to the charge $q$.
\nThe magnetic force does no work, so the conserved energy is just the sum of translational kinetic energy of the center of mass and rotational kinetic energy about the center of mass:
\[\nE = \frac12 M\nu_{CM}^2 + \frac12 I\omega^2,
\]\nwhere $I$ is the moment of inertia of the two-mass system about its center of mass. For two equal masses $m$ at distance $\ell$, $I=2m(\ell/2)^2=\frac{m\ell^2}{2}$.
\nTherefore the conserved quantities are
\[
\boxed{\vec P = M\vec\nu_{CM} - q\,\vec\ell\times\vec B},\qquad
\boxed{E = \frac12 M\nu_{CM}^2 + \frac12 I\omega^2}.
\]
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\vec P = M\vec\nu_{CM} - q\,\vec\ell\times\vec B}, \boxed{E = \frac12 M\nu_{CM}^2 + \frac12 I\omega^2}

sub_problems.guidance:
To solve this problem, you need to combine ideas from the conservation of momentum, the Lorentz force law, rigid-body kinematics, and the work–energy theorem for a rigid body. Work step by step, using reference passages as your foundation.

First, recall the definition of the center of mass (CM) for a system of two equal point masses \( m \). The total mass is \( M = 2m \). The equation of motion for the CM follows from Newton’s second law, as discussed in the momentum-conservation passage from Morin: the rate of change of total momentum equals the net external force. Here, the external forces are the Lorentz forces on each charge due to the uniform magnetic field \( \mathbf{B} \). Use the Lorentz force law \( \mathbf{F} = q\mathbf{E} + q\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \) (from Purcell & Morin, reference.1, reference.1). Since the problem involves only a magnetic field, set \( \mathbf{E} = 0 \), so each charge feels \( q \mathbf{v}_i \times \mathbf{B} \).

Now write the total force on the system as the sum of the forces on the two charges. You will notice that the velocities of the two charges are not equal when the dipole can rotate: they differ by a term involving the relative position and the angular velocity. The rigid-body velocity relation from Morin (reference.2.1) tells you that for a point at position \( \mathbf{r}_i \) in a body rotating with angular velocity \( \boldsymbol{\omega} \), the velocity is \( \mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{v}_{\text{CM}} + \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}_i' \), where \( \mathbf{r}_i' \) is the position relative to the CM. Apply this to express \( \mathbf{v}_1 \) and \( \mathbf{v}_2 \) in terms of \( \mathbf{v}_{\text{CM}} \), \( \boldsymbol{\omega} \), and the separation vector \( \boldsymbol{\ell} = \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2 \).

Substitute these velocities into the total Lorentz force. The terms involving \( \mathbf{v}_{\text{CM}} \times \mathbf{B} \) will cancel because the charges are opposite. The terms involving \( \boldsymbol{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}_i' \) will combine to leave a net force that can be written as the time derivative of a quantity. The idea is to recognize that the total external force is not simply \( M \, d\mathbf{v}_{\text{CM}}/dt \); an extra term appears. By moving that extra term to the left side of \( d\mathbf{P}_{\text{total}}/dt = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} \), you can define a modified conserved momentum \( \mathbf{P} \) that is constant in time. Follow the logic of momentum conservation from Morin (reference.5.1): if the sum of the forces can be expressed as a total time derivative, then the quantity whose derivative gives that force, when subtracted from the total mechanical momentum, yields a conserved vector.

For the conserved energy \( E \), note reference passage from Griffiths (reference.3) and Purcell & Morin (reference.12) that the magnetic force \( q\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \) does no work on a point charge because it is always perpendicular to the velocity. Therefore, the kinetic energy of the system is conserved. The kinetic energy of a rigid body is the sum of the translational kinetic energy of the CM and the rotational kinetic energy about the CM, as shown in Kleppner & Kolenkow (reference.9, Eqs. 7.24 and 7.25). Write the translational part as \( \frac{1}{2} M v_{\text{CM}}^2 \). For the rotational part, use \( \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2 \), where \( I \) is the moment of inertia about the CM. To find \( I \), treat the two point masses as a rigid rotor: each mass \( m \) is at a distance \( \ell/2 \) from the CM. The moment of inertia of a system of point masses about an axis is \( I = \sum m_i r_{i,\perp}^2 \) (see the parallel-axis theorem discussion in Morin, reference.1.3, where the CM moment of inertia is the starting point). Compute \( I \) for the two masses about an axis through the CM and perpendicular to the line joining them.

sub_problems.problem:
(1.3) The angular momentum consists of two parts. One part is due to the motion of the center of mass and the other is due to rotation around the center of mass. From the modified form of the conservation law for the total momentum and the equation of motion of the rotation around the center of mass, prove that the quantity $J$ as defined by

$$J = \left(\vec{r}_{C M} \times \vec{P} + I \vec{\omega}\right) \cdot \hat{B}$$

is conserved.

Note that

$$\begin{array}{l} \vec{A}_{1} \times \vec{A}_{2} = - \vec{A}_{2} \times \vec{A}_{1} \\ \vec{A}_{1} \cdot (\vec{A}_{2} \times \vec{A}_{3}) = (\vec{A}_{1} \times \vec{A}_{2}) \cdot \vec{A}_{3} \\ \vec{A}_{1} \times (\vec{A}_{2} \times \vec{A}_{3}) = (\vec{A}_{1} \cdot \vec{A}_{3}) \vec{A}_{2} - (\vec{A}_{1} \cdot \vec{A}_{2}) \vec{A}_{3} \\ \end{array}$$

for any three vectors $\vec{A}_1$ , $\vec{A}_2$ and $\vec{A}_3$ . Repeated application of the above first two formulas may be useful in deriving the conservation law in question.

In the following, let $\vec{B}$ be in the $z$ -direction.

# Part 2

Suppose initially the center of mass of the dipole is at rest at the origin, $\vec{\ell}$ points in the $x$ -direction and the initial angular velocity of the dipole is $\omega_0\hat{z}$ ( $\hat{z}$ is the unit vector in the $z$ -direction).
sub_problems.solution:
Let the total momentum of the two charges be \(\vec P\). The modified momentum equation for the dipole is
\[
\frac{d\vec P}{dt}= q\,\vec\ell\times \vec B,
\]\nand the rotational equation about the center of mass is
\[\nI\,\dot{\vec\omega}= -q\,\vec\ell\times(\vec\nu_{CM}\times \vec B).
\]\nWe now differentiate the projected angular-momentum-like quantity
\[\nJ=\bigl(\vec r_{CM}\times \vec P+I\vec\omega\bigr)\cdot \hat B.
\]\nUsing \(\dot{\vec r}_{CM}=\vec\nu_{CM}\),
\[
\frac{d}{dt}(\vec r_{CM}\times \vec P)\cdot \hat B
= (\vec\nu_{CM}\times \vec P)\cdot \hat B+\left(\vec r_{CM}\times \frac{d\vec P}{dt}\right)\cdot \hat B.
\]\nThe two terms combine, and with the momentum equation and the vector identities
\(\vec A\cdot(\vec B\times\vec C)=(\vec A\times\vec B)\cdot\vec C\) and
\(\vec A\times(\vec B\times\vec C)=(\vec A\cdot\vec C)\vec B-(\vec A\cdot\vec B)\vec C\), this becomes
\[
\frac{d}{dt}(\vec r_{CM}\times \vec P)\cdot \hat B
= q\,\vec\ell\times(\vec\nu_{CM}\times\vec B)\cdot \hat B.
\]\nTherefore
\[
\frac{dJ}{dt}
= \frac{d}{dt}(\vec r_{CM}\times \vec P)\cdot \hat B + I\dot{\vec\omega}\cdot \hat B
= q\,\vec\ell\times(\vec\nu_{CM}\times\vec B)\cdot \hat B - q\,\vec\ell\times(\vec\nu_{CM}\times\vec B)\cdot \hat B =0.
\]\nHence the quantity \(J\) is conserved:
\[
\boxed{\bigl(\vec r_{CM}\times \vec P+I\vec\omega\bigr)\cdot \hat B=\text{constant}.}
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
To prove that \(J = (\vec{r}_{CM} \times \vec{P} + I \vec{\omega})\cdot \hat{B}\) is conserved, you should show that its time derivative is zero. The problem gives you two key equations of motion to use: a modified form of the conservation law for total momentum, and the equation of motion for rotation around the center of mass. Your task is to take the time derivative of \(J\) and simplify it using these equations and the provided vector identities.

First, recall from the textbook (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 7.8) that the angular momentum of a rigid body can be decomposed into an orbital part (due to the motion of the center of mass) and a spin part (due to rotation around the center of mass). The quantity \(J\) defined here is exactly the projection of this total angular momentum vector onto the direction of \(\hat{B}\). The conservation proof follows the same general strategy as the derivation of energy conservation from a time-independent Lagrangian (Morin, Section 5.5.2): you assume the equations of motion hold and then differentiate the quantity of interest.

**Step-by-step method:**

1.  **Write down the time derivative of \(J\):**
    Since \(J\) is the dot product of \(\hat{B}\) with a vector, and \(\hat{B}\) is a constant unit vector (fixed in direction), you can write
    \[
    \frac{dJ}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\Bigl[ (\vec{r}_{CM} \times \vec{P} + I \vec{\omega}) \Bigr] \cdot \hat{B}.
    \]
    Because the derivative of a sum is the sum of derivatives, this has two main parts: the time derivative of the orbital term \((\vec{r}_{CM} \times \vec{P})\) and the time derivative of the spin term \((I \vec{\omega})\).

2.  **Differentiate the orbital term.**
    The time derivative of a cross product follows the rule given in the textbook (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 7.5):
    \[
    \frac{d}{dt}(\vec{r}_{CM} \times \vec{P}) = \left(\frac{d\vec{r}_{CM}}{dt} \times \vec{P}\right) + \left(\vec{r}_{CM} \times \frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\right).
    \]
    Recognize that \(d\vec{r}_{CM}/dt = \vec{v}_{CM}\) is the velocity of the center of mass. So the first term becomes \((\vec{v}_{CM} \times \vec{P}) \cdot \hat{B}\). The second term involves \(d\vec{P}/dt\), for which you should use the modified momentum equation provided in the problem statement. Substitute that equation for \(d\vec{P}/dt\) into the second term.

3.  **Differentiate the spin term.**
    The spin part is \(I \vec{\omega}\), where \(I\) is the moment of inertia of the rigid dipole about its center of mass. The textbook (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 7.9) gives the rotational equation of motion for fixed-axis rotation around the center of mass as \(\tau_0 = I d\omega/dt\). In vector form for this problem, the equation of motion for rotation around the center of mass relates the time derivative of the angular velocity vector (\(I d\vec{\omega}/dt\)) to a torque-like expression involving the cross product of \(\vec{\ell}\) and the magnetic force terms. You are given this rotational equation directly. So, the time derivative of the spin term dotted with \(\hat{B}\) is simply \(I d\vec{\omega}/dt \cdot \hat{B}\), and you can replace \(I d\vec{\omega}/dt\) with the right-hand side of the rotational equation provided.

4.  **Combine and simplify using vector identities.**
    Now you have an expression for \(dJ/dt\) with several cross-product terms. The problem notes that repeated application of the identities
    \[
    \vec{A}_1 \cdot (\vec{A}_2 \times \vec{A}_3) = (\vec{A}_1 \times \vec{A}_2) \cdot \vec{A}_3
    \]
    and the triple vector product expansion may be useful. Your goal is to show that all terms cancel exactly. You will find that a term arising from the derivative of the orbital part exactly cancels the term from the derivative of the spin part, leaving \(dJ/dt = 0\). The cancellation relies on manipulating the vectors using the identities so that the two terms become identical in magnitude but opposite in sign.

**Connecting to the textbook:**
This proof mirrors the logic in Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 7.8.1, where they derive the equation of rotational motion about the center of mass (\(\tau_0 = I_0 \alpha\)) by starting from \(\tau = d\mathbf{L}/dt\), decomposing the angular momentum and torque, and showing that the terms involving the center-of-mass motion cancel. Here, you are performing a similar cancellation, but for the time derivative of the projected angular momentum \(J\) using the specific force and torque laws for a moving dipole.

Now, proceed to carry out the differentiation and the algebraic simplifications yourself. Write out the expression for \(dJ/dt\) clearly, substitute the given equations of motion, and then apply the vector identities to group and cancel the terms.

sub_problems.problem: (2.1) If the magnitude of $\omega_0$ is smaller than a critical value $\omega_c$ , the dipole will not make a full turn with respect to its center of mass. Find $\omega_c$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Let the magnetic field be along the $z$-axis, and describe the orientation of the dipole by the angle $\varphi(t)$ in the $xy$-plane. Then
\[
\vec\ell=\ell\bigl(\cos\varphi\,\hat{x}+\sin\varphi\,\hat{y}\bigr),
\qquad \dot\varphi(0)=\omega_0.
\]\nSince the dipole rotates about its center of mass, its angular velocity is
\[
\vec\omega=\dot\varphi\,\hat{z}.
\]
\nFor the two charges $+q$ and $-q$, the conserved total momentum can be written as
\[\nM\vec v_{\rm CM}=\vec P+q\ell B\,\bigl(\sin\varphi\,\hat{x}-\cos\varphi\,\hat{y}\bigr),
\]\nwhere $M=2m$ is the total mass. Using the initial condition $\vec v_{\rm CM}(0)=0$ and $\varphi(0)=0$, we find
\[
\vec P=q\ell B\,\hat{y}.
\]\nHence
\[
\dot x_{\rm CM}=\frac{q\ell B}{M}\sin\varphi,\qquad
\dot y_{\rm CM}=\frac{q\ell B}{M}(1-\cos\varphi).
\]
\nThe kinetic energy of the system is conserved. With the moment of inertia of two equal masses at the ends of a rod,
\[\nI=2m\left(\frac{\ell}{2}\right)^2=\frac{m\ell^2}{2},
\]\nenergy conservation gives
\[
\frac12 I\dot\varphi^{\,2}+\frac{(q\ell B)^2}{M}(1-\cos\varphi)=\frac12 I\omega_0^2.
\]\nRewriting,
\[
\dot\varphi^{\,2}+\frac12\omega_c^2(1-\cos\varphi)=\omega_0^2,
\]\nwhere
\[
\omega_c^2=\frac{4(q\ell B)^2}{MI}.
\]\nSubstituting $M=2m$ and $I=m\ell^2/2$ yields
\[
\omega_c^2=\left(\frac{2qB}{m}\right)^2.
\]
\nTo make a full turn, $\dot\varphi$ must never vanish. Thus the initial angular speed must satisfy $|\omega_0|>\omega_c$, so the critical value is
\[
\boxed{\omega_c=\frac{2qB}{m}}.
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
1. Set up the angular coordinate: define $\varphi$ as the angle the dipole makes with, say, the $x$-axis in the plane of rotation. According to the angular parametrization (Morin 8.1.2), the angular velocity vector is $\boldsymbol{\omega} = \dot\varphi \hat{z}$, so the rotational speed is $\dot\varphi$. The rotational kinetic energy is then $\frac12 I \dot\varphi^2$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia about the center of mass.

2. Compute the moment of inertia: treat the dipole as two point masses $m$ at distance $\ell/2$ from the center. Using the idea from the dumbbell example in K&K 8.6.1, the moment of inertia about the center is $I = 2m(\ell/2)^2$. (The student can compute this directly.)

3. Apply conservation of kinetic energy: because magnetic forces do no work and there are no other non-conservative forces, the total kinetic energy is conserved (as in elastic collisions described in K&K 6.5.2). The total kinetic energy is the sum of the translational kinetic energy of the center of mass and the rotational kinetic energy about the center of mass. Initially, at $t=0$, the center of mass is at rest and the angular speed is $\omega_0$, so the initial kinetic energy is $K_i = \frac12 I \omega_0^2$.

4. Express the translational kinetic energy in terms of $\varphi$: from the earlier analysis of the system’s momentum (or given in the problem), the velocity of the center of mass has been found to depend on $\varphi$. sub_problems.problem: (2.2) For a general $\omega_0 > 0$ , what is the maximum distance $d_m$ in the $x$ -direction that the center of mass can reach?
sub_problems.solution:
The conserved quantity for this system can be written as
\[
 x_{\mathrm{CM}} P + I\omega = J,
\]\nwhere $P$ is the magnitude of the conserved generalized momentum and $I$ is the moment of inertia of the dipole about its center of mass.
\nAt $t=0$, the center of mass is at the origin and the angular velocity is $\omega_0$, so
\[\nJ = I\omega_0.
\]\nTherefore,
\[
 x_{\mathrm{CM}} P + I\omega = I\omega_0.
\]\nSince $x_{\mathrm{CM}} \ge 0$, the center of mass reaches its maximum $x$-displacement when $\omega$ is as small as possible.
\nThe allowed minimum value of $\omega$ depends on the initial angular velocity $\omega_0$:

- If $\omega_0 < \omega_c$, then the rotation can reverse and the minimum is $\omega_{\min} = -\omega_0$. Hence
\[
 d_m = \frac{I}{P}(\omega_0 - (-\omega_0)) = \frac{2I\omega_0}{P}.
\]\nUsing $I = \frac{1}{2}m\ell^2$ and $P = qB\ell$ gives
\[
 d_m = \frac{m\ell}{qB}\,\omega_0.
\]

- If $\omega_0 > \omega_c$, then the minimum angular velocity is
\[
\omega_{\min} = \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \omega_c^2},
\]\nso
\[
 d_m = \frac{I}{P}\left(\omega_0 - \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \omega_c^2}\right)
 = \frac{m\ell}{2qB}\left(\omega_0 - \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \omega_c^2}\right).
\]

- If $\omega_0 = \omega_c$, the system approaches the limiting angle only asymptotically, so the maximum distance is obtained from $\omega_{\min}=0$ in the limiting sense, giving
\[
 d_m = \frac{I}{P}\omega_c = \frac{m\ell}{2qB}\,\omega_c.
\]
\nThus the maximum distance reached by the center of mass is
\[
\boxed{
 d_m =
 \begin{cases}
 \dfrac{m\ell}{qB}\,\omega_0, & \omega_0 < \omega_c,\\[6pt]
 \dfrac{m\ell}{2qB}\left(\omega_0 - \sqrt{\omega_0^2 - \omega_c^2}\right), & \omega_0 > \omega_c,\\[6pt]
 \dfrac{m\ell}{2qB}\,\omega_c, & \omega_0 = \omega_c.
 \end{cases}}
\]

sub_problems.problem: (2.3) What is the tension on the rod? Express it as a function of the angular velocity $\omega$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For each charge, the force along the rod has three contributions.

1. **Coulomb repulsion** between the two charges tends to separate them:
\[\nF_C=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{\ell^2}.
\]\nThis contributes as compression on the rod.

2. **Rotational motion** of the dipole requires a centripetal force for each mass. Since each mass is at distance \(\ell/2\) from the center of mass,
\[\nF_{\rm rot}=m\omega^2\frac{\ell}{2}=\frac12 m\ell\omega^2,
\]\nwhich reduces the compression.

3. **Magnetic force from the center-of-mass motion** gives a contribution along the rod
\[\nF_B=q\,\vec v_{CM}\times\vec B\cdot(-\hat\ell)=q\,\vec v_{CM}\cdot(\hat\ell\times\vec B).
\]\nUsing the conserved quantity for the motion, this becomes
\[\nq\,\vec v_{CM}\cdot(\hat\ell\times\vec B)
=\frac{1}{4}m\ell\left(\omega_0^2-\omega^2\right).
\]
\nAdding the three contributions, the tension on the rod is
\[\nT=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{\ell^2}-\frac12 m\ell\omega^2+\frac14 m\ell\left(\omega_0^2-\omega^2\right).
\]\nTaking compression as positive, the final result is
\[
\boxed{T=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q^2}{\ell^2}-\frac12 m\ell\omega^2+\frac14 m\ell\left(\omega_0^2-\omega^2\right)}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Tension in a rigid rod
knowledge_points.description: The tension (or compression) in a massless rigid rod connecting two particles is the net force along the rod, with sign convention (e.g., compression positive). The total tension is the sum of all force components along the rod from electrostatic, centripetal, and magnetic effects.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the tension in the rod as a function of angular velocity \(\omega\), you need to analyze the forces acting along the rod on one of the charged masses. The rod can be under either tension (being pulled) or compression (being pushed), and your sign convention will reflect that. The net force along the rod determines what the rod must provide.

**Step 1 — Identify the three contributions along the rod.**
There are three distinct physical effects that produce forces with components along the rod. You should treat each separately, using the appropriate law from the textbook.

1. **Coulomb repulsion.** The two charges repel each other. Use *Coulomb's law* (Eq. 1.1 or Eq. 8-1) to find the magnitude of the electric force one charge exerts on the other. Because the charges are like signs, this force pushes them apart, which tends to *compress* the rod. The direction is along the line joining the charges, which is exactly the rod’s direction.  
   *Textbook grounding:* Coulomb’s law states that the force is proportional to \(q_1 q_2 / r^2\) and acts along the line joining the charges.

2. **Centripetal force requirement.** Each mass moves in a circle about the center of mass. For uniform circular motion, there must be a net inward force (centripetal force) of magnitude \(m v^2 / r\) or \(m \omega^2 r\). Identify the radius of each mass’s circular path (it is half the rod length \(\ell\)) and write the required centripetal force. This required force must be supplied by the rod (and possibly other forces), so it contributes to the tension/compression.  
   *Textbook grounding:* The principle that a net force \(m \omega^2 r\) inward causes centripetal acceleration is used in the spherical pendulum and mass-on-turntable examples.

3. **Magnetic force from center-of-mass motion.** There is an external magnetic field, and the whole system’s center of mass moves. The *Lorentz force law* (Eq. 6.1) gives the magnetic force on a moving charge: \(\mathbf{F} = q \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\). You need the component of this force along the rod. The problem statement (and the reference solution) indicates that the center-of-mass motion leads to a known relation involving \(\omega_0\) and \(\omega\). Use the Lorentz force expression and the given conserved quantity to express this component in terms of \(m, \ell, \omega, \omega_0\).  
   *Textbook grounding:* The Lorentz force law is \(\mathbf{F} = q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\). Here \(\mathbf{E}=0\) for the magnetic part, so \(\mathbf{F} = q \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}\).

**Step 2 — Determine the sign of each contribution.**
Decide what you call positive tension. For example, if you define tension as positive when the rod is being pulled (i.e., the rod is under tension and pulls inward on the masses), then forces that push the masses apart (compression) will enter with the opposite sign.  
- Coulomb repulsion pushes masses apart → contributes to compression (negative tension).  
- The centripetal force required points inward toward the center → the rod must pull inward on the masses to provide this, so it contributes to tension (positive tension, if tension is defined as pulling inward on the masses).  
- The magnetic component’s sign depends on the directions of \(\mathbf{v}_{CM}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\); evaluate it from the geometry given in your problem.

**Step 3 — Combine the contributions.**
Write the total force that the rod must exert on one mass along the rod’s direction. Since the rod is massless (implied by typical textbook treatments of tension), the net force on any segment must be zero, so the tension is uniform. The tension in the rod is equal to the force the rod exerts on a mass (by Newton’s third law, the mass exerts an equal and opposite force on the rod). Sum the three contributions with their correct signs to obtain the tension as a function of \(\omega\).

**Step 4 — Express your answer.**
Your final expression should contain only the given constants (\(q, m, \ell, \omega_0\)), the variable \(\omega\), and physical constants like \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)\). Make sure the sign convention you chose is clearly reflected in the signs of your terms.

title: Thermal Vibrations of Surface Atoms
problem:
# Theoretical Question 3

# Thermal Vibrations of Surface Atoms

This question considers the thermal vibrations of surface atoms in an elemental metallic crystal with a face-centered cubic (fcc) lattice structure. The unit cubic cell of an fcc lattice consists of one atom at each corner and one atom at the center of each face of the cubic cell, as shown in Fig. 3a. For the crystal under consideration, we use $(a,0,0)$ , $(0,a,0)$ and $(0,0,a)$ to represent the locations of the three atoms on the $x,y$ and $z$ axes of its cell. The lattice constant $a$ is equal to $3.92\AA$ (i.e..the length of each side of the cube is $3.92\AA$ ).

# Part 1

sub_problems.problem: (1.1) What is the wavelength of the matter waves of the incident electrons?
sub_problems.solution:
The wavelength of the incident electron is given by the de Broglie relation
\[
\lambda=\frac{h}{p}.
\]
For an electron accelerated through a potential difference $V$, its momentum is
\[
p=\sqrt{2meV},
\]
so
\[
\lambda=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}}.
\]
Substituting $h=6.63\times10^{-34}\,\text{J s}$, $m=9.11\times10^{-31}\,\text{kg}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\text{C}$, and $V=64.0\,\text{V}$,
\[
\lambda=\frac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2(9.11\times10^{-31})(1.60\times10^{-19})(64.0)}}
=1.53\times10^{-10}\,\text{m}.
\]
Thus the wavelength is \(\boxed{1.53\times10^{-10}\,\text{m}}\) (or \(\boxed{1.53\,\text{\AA}}\)).

knowledge_points.name: de Broglie relation
knowledge_points.description: The wavelength of a matter wave is given by λ = h/p, where h is Planck's constant and p is momentum. It is the central relation needed to find the wavelength of the incident electrons.

knowledge_points.name: kinetic energy from potential difference
knowledge_points.description: An electron accelerated through a potential difference V gains kinetic energy K = eV, where e is the elementary charge. This converts the given accelerating voltage into the electron's kinetic energy.

knowledge_points.name: non-relativistic momentum-energy relation
knowledge_points.description: For a classical (non-relativistic) particle, kinetic energy K and momentum p are related by K = p²/(2m), so p = √(2mK). This links the kinetic energy from the potential difference to the momentum needed in the de Broglie relation.

knowledge_points.name: non-relativistic electron
knowledge_points.description: The electron's speed is assumed to be much less than the speed of light (64 eV kinetic energy is well below the rest energy of 511 keV), so relativistic corrections are negligible and the classical momentum-energy relation is valid.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the kinetic energy of the incident electrons from the accelerating potential difference \( V \). The textbook passage on x-ray production states that an electron accelerated through a voltage \( V \) gains kinetic energy \( K = eV \) (Section 2-6, where \( K \) equals \( eV \) for the incident electron energy). This same idea appears in the photoelectric effect discussion (Section 2-2, \( K_{\max} = eV_0 \)). Use this to express the electron's kinetic energy in terms of the given \( V \), the elementary charge \( e \), and any needed conversion factors for energy units.

Next, recall that the de Broglie relation (Section 3-1, Equation 3-2) connects a particle's wavelength to its momentum: \( \lambda = h/p \). To find \( p \) from the known kinetic energy, use the nonrelativistic momentum–energy relation \( K = p^2/(2m) \), which gives \( p = \sqrt{2mK} \). This step is demonstrated in Example 3-1(b) of the textbook, where the de Broglie wavelength of an electron with a given kinetic energy in eV is calculated by substituting \( p = \sqrt{2mK} \) into \( \lambda = h/p \).

Combine the two ideas: replace \( K \) with \( eV \) in the expression for momentum, then substitute into the de Broglie relation. That yields \( \lambda = h/\sqrt{2meV} \). Now you can insert the values of Planck's constant \( h \), the electron mass \( m \), the elementary charge \( e \), and the given accelerating voltage \( V \) (remember to handle units consistently, converting eV to joules as shown in Example 3-1). Carry out the arithmetic to find the wavelength.

title: Satellite's orbit transfer
problem:
# Theoretical Competition

# I. Satellite's orbit transfer

In the near future we ourselves may take part in launching of a satellite which, in point of view of physics, requires only the use of simple mechanics.

sub_problems.problem: (a) A satellite of mass $m$ is presently circling the Earth of mass $M$ in a circular orbit of radius $R_0$ . What is the speed $(u_0)$ of mass $m$ in terms of $M, R_0$ and the universal gravitation constant $G$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
For a circular orbit, the gravitational force provides the required centripetal force:
\[
\frac{m u_0^2}{R_0}=\frac{GMm}{R_0^2}.
\]\nCancelling $m$ and solving for $u_0$ gives
\[
 u_0=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R_0}}.
\]\nTherefore, the satellite’s speed is \(\boxed{u_0=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R_0}}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational force between two point masses M and m separated by distance r is F = GMm/r^2. Used to express the force on the satellite.

knowledge_points.name: Centripetal force formula
knowledge_points.description: For an object in uniform circular motion, the net force towards the center is F = m v^2 / r, where v is the tangential speed and r is the radius. Used to express the required force for the circular orbit.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Identify the force acting on the satellite.**  
   The only force acting on the satellite is the Earth’s gravity. According to Newton’s law of universal gravitation (reference.11 in Carroll & Ostlie), the magnitude of this force is  
   \(F = G \frac{M m}{R_0^2}\),  
   directed toward the Earth’s center.

2. **Recall the centripetal force required for circular motion.**  
   For an object of mass \(m\) moving at constant speed \(u_0\) in a circle of radius \(R_0\), a net force toward the center (a centripetal force) is needed. The Carroll & Ostlie passage derives the same force expression when combining Kepler’s third law with circular motion: they identify the term \(m \frac{v^2}{r}\) as the centripetal force for a circular orbit.  
   Alternatively, the polar‑coordinate acceleration derivation (Kleppner & Kolenkow) shows that the radial component of acceleration is \(-r \dot{\theta}^2 \hat{\mathbf{r}}\); the magnitude of the centripetal force is therefore \(m \frac{u_0^2}{R_0}\) (since \(u_0 = R_0 \dot{\theta}\)).

3. **Equate the gravitational force to the centripetal force.**  
   Because gravity alone provides the centripetal force that keeps the satellite in its circular orbit, the two forces are equal in magnitude. Set up the equality between the gravitational force from step 1 and the centripetal force from step 2.

4. **Solve for the orbital speed \(u_0\).**  
   The satellite mass \(m\) appears on both sides and cancels out. Rearrange the equation to isolate \(u_0\) in terms of the given quantities \(G\), \(M\), and \(R_0\). No numerical substitution is needed; the answer will be a simple algebraic expression.

sub_problems.problem: (b) We are to put this satellite into a trajectory that will take it to point $\mathrm{P}$ at distance $R_{1}$ from the centre of the Earth by increasing (almost instantaneously) its velocity at point $\mathrm{Q}$ from $u_{0}$ to $u_{1}$ . What is the value of $u_{1}$ in terms of $u_{0}, R_{0}, R_{1}$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
After the impulsive increase of speed at $Q$, the satellite moves along an elliptical transfer orbit. Let its speed just after the boost be $u_1$ at radius $R_0$, and let its speed at point $P$ be $u_2$ at radius $R_1$.
\nSince the gravitational force is central, angular momentum is conserved along the transfer orbit:
\[\nm u_1 R_0 = m u_2 R_1.
\]\nHence
\[\nu_2 = u_1 \frac{R_0}{R_1}.
\]
\nMechanical energy is also conserved between $Q$ and $P$:
\[
\frac12 m u_2^2 - \frac{GMm}{R_1} = \frac12 m u_1^2 - \frac{GMm}{R_0}.
\]\nSubstitute $u_2 = u_1 R_0/R_1$:
\[
\frac12 m u_1^2 \frac{R_0^2}{R_1^2} - \frac{GMm}{R_1} = \frac12 m u_1^2 - \frac{GMm}{R_0}.
\]\nRearranging gives
\[
\left(\frac{R_0^2}{R_1^2}-1\right)u_1^2 = 2GM\left(\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_0}\right).
\]\nUsing
\[
\frac{R_0^2-R_1^2}{R_1^2}=\frac{(R_0-R_1)(R_0+R_1)}{R_1^2},
\qquad
\frac{1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{R_0}=\frac{R_0-R_1}{R_0R_1},
\]\nwe obtain
\[\nu_1^2=\frac{2GM}{R_0}\frac{R_1}{R_0+R_1}.
\]\nSince the initial circular speed satisfies $u_0^2=GM/R_0$, this becomes
\[
 u_1 = u_0\sqrt{\frac{2R_1}{R_0+R_1}}.
\]\nTherefore the required speed is \(\boxed{u_1=u_0\sqrt{\frac{2R_1}{R_0+R_1}}}\).

knowledge_points.name: impulsive tangential boost
knowledge_points.description: The velocity increase at Q is instantaneous and tangential to the original circular orbit. This places the satellite into an elliptical transfer orbit with Q as perigee (radius R0) and P as apogee (radius R1). At perigee and apogee, the velocity is perpendicular to the radius vector, so the angular momentum magnitude is simply m v r.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of angular momentum
knowledge_points.description: For a central force, angular momentum about the center is conserved. Applied at perigee (Q) and apogee (P): m u1 R0 = m u2 R1.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: The total mechanical energy (kinetic plus gravitational potential) is conserved along the orbit: (1/2) m v^2 - GMm/r = constant. Applied at Q and P: (1/2) m u1^2 - GMm/R0 = (1/2) m u2^2 - GMm/R1.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational potential energy of a point mass m at distance r from a point mass M is U = -GMm/r.

knowledge_points.name: circular orbit speed relation
knowledge_points.description: From part (a), the speed in the initial circular orbit of radius R0 is u0 = sqrt(GM/R0), so u0^2 = GM/R0. This relation is used to express the required speed u1 in terms of u0.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recognise that after the impulsive boost at point Q (where the satellite is still at distance \(R_{0}\) from Earth’s centre), the only force acting is Earth’s gravity – a central force.  This means both angular momentum and mechanical energy of the satellite are conserved during the coasting flight from Q to P.

**Angular momentum conservation:**  
From reference discussion (Palen, “Angular Momentum”, or Kleppner & Kolenkow 7.5.1), for a point mass the angular momentum about the force centre is \(L = m\,v\,r\) and remains constant when no net torque acts.  
Just after the boost at Q the satellite has speed \(u_{1}\) and radius \(R_{0}\); at the distant point P it will have some unknown speed (call it \(v_{\mathrm{P}}\)) and radius \(R_{1}\).  Write the conservation equation and solve it for \(v_{\mathrm{P}}\) in terms of \(u_{1}, R_{0}, R_{1}\).  (This is essentially Kepler’s second law.)

**Mechanical energy conservation:**  
Gravity is a conservative force.  reference passages on gravitational potential energy (Carroll & Ostlie, or Palen) give \(U = -GMm/r\).  According to the conservation of mechanical energy (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Sections 5.4 and 10.3.2), the total energy \(E = K + U\) is the same at Q and at P.  
Write down the energy at Q (kinetic \(\frac{1}{2}m u_{1}^{2}\) plus potential \(-GMm/R_{0}\)) and at P (kinetic \(\frac{1}{2}m v_{\mathrm{P}}^{2}\) plus potential \(-GMm/R_{1}\)), set them equal, and cancel the mass \(m\) where possible.

**Combine the two laws:**  
Substitute the expression you found for \(v_{\mathrm{P}}\) from angular momentum into the energy equation.  This will give you an equation that links \(u_{1}^{2}\) with \(GM, R_{0}, R_{1}\).  Rearrange it to isolate \(u_{1}^{2}\).

**Relate \(GM\) to the given circular speed \(u_{0}\):**  
Before the boost the satellite was in a circular orbit of radius \(R_{0}\) with speed \(u_{0}\).  For a circular orbit the gravitational force supplies the centripetal acceleration, so \(GMm/R_{0}^{2} = m u_{0}^{2}/R_{0}\).  This simplifies to \(GM = u_{0}^{2} R_{0}\).  Replace \(GM\) in your equation with this combination.

**Final step:**  
Simplify the resulting expression.  You will obtain \(u_{1}\) as \(u_{0}\) multiplied by a square‑root factor that depends only on \(R_{0}\) and \(R_{1}\).  Carry out the algebra carefully; the factor simplifies to a neat form involving \(R_{1}\) and the sum \(R_{0}+R_{1}\).  No external information beyond reference passages and the circular‑orbit condition is needed.

history.llm_reason: The guidance reveals the final answer by describing it as "\(u_1\) as \(u_0\) multiplied by a square-root factor involving only \(R_0\) and \(R_1\)" and instructs the student to simplify to a compact answer, which strongly implies the boxed expression.
The guidance explicitly instructs the student to carry out the algebra that leads directly to the final boxed expression, including the specific simplified form involving \(R_1\) and \(R_0+R_1\).

sub_problems.problem: (c) Deduce the minimum value of $u_{1}$ in term of $u_{0}$ that will allow the satellite to leave the Earth's influence completely.
sub_problems.solution:
To leave the Earth’s gravitational influence completely, the satellite must have just enough kinetic energy to reach infinity with zero speed.
\nUsing conservation of mechanical energy,
\[
\frac{1}{2}m u_1^2 - \frac{GMm}{R} = 0,
\]\nwhere $R$ is the launch radius. If $u_0$ is the circular orbital speed at that radius, then
\[\nu_0^2 = \frac{GM}{R}.
\]\nSubstituting this into the escape condition gives
\[
\frac{1}{2}u_1^2 = u_0^2,
\]\nso
\[\nu_1 = \sqrt{2}\,u_0.
\]\nTherefore, the minimum required speed is
\[
\boxed{u_1^{\min}=\sqrt{2}\,u_0}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: escape velocity
knowledge_points.description: The minimum speed needed for an object to escape a gravitational field completely, reaching infinity with zero kinetic energy. This is the condition used to set the satellite's total mechanical energy to zero.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: In the absence of non-conservative forces, the sum of kinetic and gravitational potential energy, (1/2)mv² - GMm/r, remains constant. The solution applies this between the impulse point and infinity to derive the escape condition.

knowledge_points.name: circular orbit velocity relation
knowledge_points.description: For a satellite in a circular orbit under Newtonian gravity, the orbital speed u₀ satisfies u₀² = GM/R. This relation is used to eliminate GM/R and express the escape speed in terms of u₀.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the minimum \(u_{1}\) (in terms of \(u_{0}\)) for the satellite to leave Earth’s influence completely, you need to combine two key ideas from your textbook: the conservation of mechanical energy and the relation for circular orbital speed.

First, consider the physical condition for just barely escaping Earth’s gravity. As shown in the escape velocity exposition (Problem 10, part a), the cutoff case is when the object reaches infinity with zero speed. Apply conservation of mechanical energy to this situation: set the total mechanical energy at the starting point (radius \(R\), speed \(u_{1}\)) equal to the total energy at infinity (zero kinetic, zero potential). This gives an equation that relates \(u_{1}\) to \(GM/R\). You are not solving for a number here—just writing the energy balance that defines the escape speed.

Second, you need to connect this to the circular orbit speed \(u_{0}\). The textbook shows in the Hohmann transfer worked example and the tunnel problem that for a circular orbit, the centripetal acceleration condition \(m(v^{c})^{2}/r = GMm/r^{2}\) leads to \((v^{c})^{2} = GM/r\). Apply this at the same radius \(R\) to express \(u_{0}^{2}\) in terms of \(GM/R\).

Finally, compare the two equations you have: one from the escape energy condition and one from the circular orbit condition. You can eliminate the common factor \(GM/R\) to find the relationship between \(u_{1}\) and \(u_{0}\). The result is the minimum \(u_{1}\) required for escape, expressed as a simple multiple of \(u_{0}\).

sub_problems.problem: (d) (Referring to part b.) What is the velocity $(u_{2})$ of the satellite at point P in terms of $u_{0}, R_{0}, R_{1}$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
From part (b), the speed at point $P$ scales as
\[
 u_2 = u_1\frac{R_0}{R_1}.
\]\nUsing the result from part (b) for $u_1$,
\[
 u_1 = u_0\sqrt{\frac{2R_1}{R_1+R_0}},
\]\nwe obtain
\[
 u_2 = u_0\frac{R_0}{R_1}\sqrt{\frac{2R_1}{R_1+R_0}}
 = u_0\sqrt{\frac{2R_0^2}{R_1(R_1+R_0)}}.
\]\nTherefore, the velocity of the satellite at point $P$ is
\[
\boxed{u_2 = u_0\frac{R_0}{R_1}\sqrt{\frac{2R_1}{R_1+R_0}}}.
\]

title: Optical Gyroscope
problem:
# II. Optical Gyroscope

In 1913 Georges Sagnac (1869-1926) considered the use of a ring resonator to search for the aether drift relative to a rotating frame. However, as often happen, his results turned out to be useful ways that Sagnac himself never dreamt of. One of those applications is the Fibre-Optic Gyroscope (FOG) which is based upon a simple phenomena, first observed by Sagnac. The essential physics associated with the Sagnac effect is due to the phase shift caused by two coherent beams of light being sent around a rotating ring of optical fibre in the opposite directions. This phase shift is also used to determine the angular speed of the ring.

As shown in a schematic diagram in Fig. 1, a light wave enters a circular optical fibre light path of radius $R$ at point $P$ on the rotating platform with a uniform angular speed $\Omega$ , in the clockwise direction. Here the light wave is split into two waves which travels in the opposite directions, clockwise (CW) and counter clockwise (CCW), through the ring. The refractive index of optical fibre material is $\mu$ . Assuming the light traveling inside the fibre-optic cable is a smooth circular path of radius $R$ .

Fig.1

sub_problems.problem: (b) Find the optical path difference, $\Delta L$ , for the CW and CCW beams to complete one round-trip of the light within the rotating ring.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the fibre loop have circumference $2\pi R$. In the lab frame, light propagates in a medium of refractive index $\mu$, so its speed relative to the fibre is $c/\mu$. Because the ring rotates, the point where the beam must return moves during the transit.
\nFor the clockwise beam, the effective speed relative to the ring is $\dfrac{c}{\mu}-\Omega R$, while for the counterclockwise beam it is $\dfrac{c}{\mu}+\Omega R$. Thus the travel times for one round trip are
\[\nt_{\rm CW}=\frac{2\pi R}{\frac{c}{\mu}-\Omega R},\qquad
 t_{\rm CCW}=\frac{2\pi R}{\frac{c}{\mu}+\Omega R}.
\]\nThe time difference is
\[
\Delta t=t_{\rm CW}-t_{\rm CCW}
=\frac{4\pi R^2\Omega}{\left(\frac{c}{\mu}\right)^2-(\Omega R)^2}.
\]\nFor ordinary gyroscope operation, $\Omega R\ll c/\mu$, so
\[
\Delta t\approx \frac{4\pi R^2\Omega\,\mu^2}{c^2}.
\]\nThe corresponding optical path difference is the distance light would travel in time $\Delta t$ inside the fibre, i.e.
\[
\Delta L=\frac{c}{\mu}\,\Delta t\approx \frac{4\pi R^2\Omega\,\mu}{c}.
\]\nTherefore, the optical path difference for the CW and CCW beams is
\[\boxed{\Delta L=\frac{4\pi R^2\Omega\,\mu}{c}}.

knowledge_points.name: speed of light in a medium
knowledge_points.description: The speed of light in a medium with refractive index μ is v = c/μ, used to determine the propagation speed of the beams in the fibre.

knowledge_points.name: Galilean velocity addition in rotating frame
knowledge_points.description: The effective speed of the light relative to the rotating ring is obtained by adding or subtracting the tangential speed ΩR to the light speed in the medium, valid for non-relativistic rotation.

knowledge_points.name: first-order approximation for small rotation
knowledge_points.description: Since ΩR ≪ c/μ, terms of order (ΩR)^2 are neglected to simplify the time difference expression.

knowledge_points.name: optical path difference
knowledge_points.description: The optical path difference ΔL is the distance light would travel in the medium during the time difference Δt, computed as ΔL = (c/μ) Δt.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the optical path difference, we need to compare the distances light would travel *in the fibre medium* for the clockwise and counterclockwise beams. The textbook explains that optical path means the equivalent distance in vacuum: a real distance *d* in a medium of refractive index *n* corresponds to an optical path *nd* (see the Fizeau experiment passage under "optical path difference"). Here, the medium is the fibre, with a given refractive index.

Start by thinking about the time each beam takes to complete one round trip. The fibre loop has a known circumference expressed in terms of its radius. Because the ring rotates, the point where a beam must return moves during the transit. For a beam co-rotating with the ring (CW), the effective speed relative to the ring is slightly less than the speed of light in the medium; for the counter-rotating beam (CCW), it is slightly greater. The speed of light in a stationary medium is *c/n* (from the "speed of light in a medium" passages, where *n* is the refractive index). You can write the effective speeds as *c/n* minus or plus the tangential speed of the ring's rim, *ΩR*, where *Ω* is the angular speed.

Using these effective speeds, write expressions for the round-trip times *t_CW* and *t_CCW* (time = distance / speed). Then find their difference, *Δt*. The expression you get will have a denominator that involves the square of *c/n* minus the square of *ΩR*.

Now apply the idea of small rotations: the problem involves a slowly rotating ring, so *ΩR* is much smaller than *c/n*. The textbook discussions on infinitesimal rotations show that to first order in small angles, higher-order terms can be neglected. Here, you can neglect (*ΩR*)² compared to (*c/n*)² in the denominator. This gives a simplified, first-order approximation for *Δt*.

Finally, relate the time difference to an optical path difference. Since the light travels inside the fibre at speed *c/n*, the extra distance it would cover in that medium during the time *Δt* is simply (*c/n*) × *Δt*. This product is the optical path difference *ΔL* you are asked to find. Substitute your approximate *Δt* to obtain the result.

kp_used: speed of light in a medium

sub_problems.problem: (c) For a circular fibre-optic of radius, $R =1 \mathrm{~m}$ , what is the maximum value of $\Delta L$ for the rotation of the earth? Given $\mu =1.5$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a Sagnac interferometer, the path-length difference between the two counter-propagating beams is
\[
\Delta L = \frac{4A\Omega}{c},
\]\nwhere $A=\pi R^2$ is the area enclosed by the ring. For maximum effect from the Earth's rotation, take the ring axis parallel to the Earth's angular velocity, so the projected area is maximal.
\nWith $R=1\,\mathrm{m}$,
\[\nA=\pi(1)^2=\pi\,\mathrm{m}^2.
\]\nUsing the Earth's angular speed
\[
\Omega_E \approx 7.29\times 10^{-5}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}},
\]\nwe get
\[
\Delta L = \frac{4\pi(7.29\times 10^{-5})}{3.0\times 10^8}
\approx 4.5\times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{m}.
\]\nThus the maximum path-length difference is \(\boxed{4.5\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Sagnac effect path difference
knowledge_points.description: For a circular loop of area A rotating with angular speed Ω, the optical path difference between counter-propagating beams is ΔL = 4AΩ/c. This formula is used directly to compute ΔL from the Earth's rotation.

knowledge_points.name: Earth's angular velocity
knowledge_points.description: The Earth rotates once per sidereal day, giving an angular speed of approximately 7.29×10^{-5} rad/s. This value is needed to evaluate the Sagnac shift for terrestrial rotation.

knowledge_points.name: speed of light in vacuum
knowledge_points.description: The speed of light in vacuum is c ≈ 3.0×10^8 m/s. It appears in the denominator of the Sagnac formula and is required to convert the product AΩ into a length difference.

knowledge_points.name: optimal ring orientation
knowledge_points.description: To obtain the maximum Sagnac path difference from Earth's rotation, the plane of the fibre ring must be perpendicular to the Earth's rotation axis, so that the area vector is parallel to the angular velocity vector and the projected area is maximal.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the Sagnac effect for a ring interferometer: when the ring rotates with angular speed \(\Omega\), the path-length difference between the two counter-propagating light beams is \(\Delta L = \frac{4A\Omega}{c}\), where \(A\) is the area enclosed by the ring and \(c\) is the speed of light in vacuum. The maximum effect is obtained when the rotation axis is parallel to the ring's axis, so the full \(\Omega\) enters the formula.

Now, gather the necessary quantities from reference passages you have studied.
- The speed of light in vacuum, \(c\), is given in the Schaum’s Outline passage: \(c = 3 \times 10^{8} \, \text{m/s}\).
- The Earth’s angular velocity, \(\Omega_e\), appears in the worked example from Kleppner & Kolenkow: \(\Omega_e = 7.27 \times 10^{-5} \, \text{rad/s}\).

The ring has radius \(R = 1 \, \text{m}\), so its area is \(A = \pi R^2\). Compute this area.

Finally, substitute the values of \(A\), \(\Omega_e\), and \(c\) into the Sagnac formula to find the maximum path-length difference \(\Delta L\). The problem also gives a refractive index \(\mu = 1.5\), but for the Sagnac effect in a vacuum interferometer the path-length difference depends only on the vacuum speed of light, so you do not need \(\mu\) in this calculation.

sub_problems.problem:
(d) In part b), the measurement could be amplified by increasing number of turns in fibre-optic coil, $N$ , find the phase difference, $\Delta \theta$ , for lights to complete the turns.

The second scheme of the Optical Gyroscope is Ring Laser Gyroscope (RLG). This could be accomplished by the inclusion of active laser cavity into an equilateral triangular ring, of total length $L$ , as illustrated in Fig.2. The laser source here will generate two amplified coherent light sources propagating in the opposite directions. In order to sustain the laser oscillation in this triangular ring resonator, the perimeter of the ring must be equal to the integer multiple of wavelength $\lambda$ . Etalon, additional component inserted into the ring, is possible to cause frequency selective losses in the ring resonator, so that the undesired modes can be damped and suppressed.

Fig.2: Schematic illustration of the Ring Laser Gyroscope

Fig. 3: Illustration of the Ring Laser Gyroscope discussed in this problem
sub_problems.solution:
For one round trip in the ring, the Sagnac phase shift is proportional to the optical path-length difference:
\[
\Delta\theta_1=\frac{2\pi\,\Delta L}{\lambda'}.
\]\nFor a circular fibre loop of radius $R$, the rotation produces the path-length difference
\[
\Delta L=\frac{4\pi R^2\Omega}{c},
\]\nso
\[
\Delta\theta_1=\frac{2\pi}{\lambda'}\cdot\frac{4\pi R^2\Omega}{c}
=\frac{8\pi^2 R^2\Omega}{c\lambda'}.
\]\nIf the fibre is wound into $N$ turns, the effective enclosed area increases by a factor of $N$, so the phase shift is multiplied by $N$:
\[
\Delta\theta=N\Delta\theta_1=\frac{8\pi^2 R^2 N\Omega}{c\lambda'}.
\]\nUsing $\lambda'=\lambda/\mu$, this can also be written as
\[
\Delta\theta=\frac{8\pi^2 \mu R^2 N\Omega}{c\lambda}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[
\boxed{\Delta\theta=\frac{8\pi^2 R^2 N\Omega}{c\lambda'}=\frac{8\pi^2 \mu R^2 N\Omega}{c\lambda}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Sagnac path-length difference for a single circular loop
knowledge_points.description: The optical path difference for one round trip in a rotating circular fiber loop is ΔL = 4πR²Ω/c, as derived in part (b).

knowledge_points.name: phase difference from optical path difference
knowledge_points.description: The phase difference Δθ between two waves is related to the optical path difference ΔL and the wavelength in the medium λ' by Δθ = 2π ΔL / λ'.

knowledge_points.name: phase shift multiplication by number of fiber turns
knowledge_points.description: When a fiber is wound into N turns, the Sagnac phase shift scales linearly with N because the effective enclosed area increases by a factor of N.

knowledge_points.name: wavelength in a medium
knowledge_points.description: The wavelength of light in a medium with refractive index μ is λ' = λ/μ, where λ is the vacuum wavelength.

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem asks you to find the phase difference after the light has made \(N\) turns in the fibre‑optic coil. You already know from part (b) how a single loop produces a phase shift. The new idea is simply that the effect of the rotation accumulates over many turns.

**Step 1 – Relate phase difference to optical path difference.**  
From reference description of Fizeau’s interferometer (French, Fig. 2‑5) you know that interference fringes are linked to the *optical path difference* between two beams:
> “A particular fringe represents a particular optical path difference between the two interfering beams.”  
> “By optical path we mean the distance in vacuum equivalent to any actual path. A distance \(d\) through a medium of refractive index \(n\) represents an optical path \(nd\); it is this that defines the number of wavelengths of the light that can be fitted into the distance.”

Thus, if the optical path difference between the two counter‑propagating beams is \(\Delta L\) (measured in vacuum‑equivalent length), the phase difference is
\[
\Delta\theta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda}\,\Delta L,
\]
where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength in vacuum.  
If you prefer to work with the wavelength in the medium \(\lambda'\) (where \(\lambda' = \lambda / \mu\) and \(\mu\) is the refractive index of the fibre), the same relation can be written using the physical path difference \(\Delta L_{\text{phys}}\) as
\[
\Delta\theta = \frac{2\pi}{\lambda'}\,\Delta L_{\text{phys}}.
\]
This is consistent with reference note (Carroll & Ostlie) that the wavelength in a medium is \(\lambda_{\text{medium}} = \lambda_{\text{vacuum}} / n\).

**Step 2 – Use the rotation‑induced path difference for one turn.**  
In part (b) you determined the phase shift for a single loop. The origin of that shift is the Sagnac effect: a rotation of the coil causes a physical path‑length difference between the two beams. Call that shift \(\Delta\theta_1\). You already have an expression for it (or for the corresponding optical path difference) from the earlier part.

**Step 3 – Multiply by the number of turns.**  
When the fibre is wound into \(N\) turns, the light travels the same loop \(N\) times. The physical path that each beam traverses is multiplied by \(N\), so the path‑length difference (and therefore the optical path difference) also scales by \(N\). Because the phase difference is directly proportional to the optical path difference, the total phase shift becomes
\[
\Delta\theta = N \times \Delta\theta_1.
\]

**Step 4 – Write the final expression.**  
Take the result you have for \(\Delta\theta_1\) from part (b) and multiply it by \(N\). Express it either in terms of the vacuum wavelength \(\lambda\) and the refractive index \(\mu\) (using \(\lambda' = \lambda/\mu\)) or directly in terms of \(\lambda'\), whichever is more convenient. That gives the phase difference after the light has completed the \(N\) turns.

Do not forget: the physical reasoning relies on the fact that the optical path difference is additive over successive loops, exactly as the Fizeau interferometer adds the optical path difference from two tube lengths. reference’s concept of optical path difference is the key to understanding why the phase shift simply scales with \(N\).
