sub_problems.problem: (D.3) What is the critical value Bi such that for |B|| > Bi, E|| < E1?
sub_problems.solution:
The superconducting state is destroyed when the Zeeman energy gained by aligning the two electron spins with the magnetic field exceeds the pairing energy $2\Delta$.
\nFor a magnetic field with an in-plane component $B_x$ and an out-of-plane component $B_z$, the total Zeeman splitting is proportional to the magnitude of the field. The condition for breaking a Cooper pair is therefore
\[
2\mu_B\sqrt{B_x^2+B_z^2}>2\Delta+2\mu_B B_z.
\]\nRearranging gives
\[
\mu_B\sqrt{B_x^2+B_z^2}>\Delta+\mu_B B_z.
\]\nSquaring both sides,
\[\nB_x^2+B_z^2>\left(\frac{\Delta}{\mu_B}+B_z\right)^2,
\]\nso
\[\nB_x^2>\frac{\Delta^2}{\mu_B^2}+\frac{2\Delta B_z}{\mu_B}.
\]\nHence the critical in-plane field is
\[\nB_I=\frac{\sqrt{\Delta^2+2\mu_B\Delta B_z}}{\mu_B}.
\]\nUsing $\mu_B=\dfrac{e\hbar}{2m_e}$, this can also be written as
\[\nB_I=\frac{2m_e}{e\hbar}\sqrt{\Delta^2+\frac{e\hbar}{m_e}\Delta B_z}.
\]\nTherefore, for $|B|>B_I$, superconductivity is destroyed by the paramagnetic effect.
\nFinal answer: $\boxed{B_I=\dfrac{\sqrt{\Delta^2+2\mu_B\Delta B_z}}{\mu_B}=\dfrac{2m_e}{e\hbar}\sqrt{\Delta^2+\dfrac{e\hbar}{m_e}\Delta B_z}}$

knowledge_points.name: Cooper pair energy in Ising superconductor
knowledge_points.description: The energy E1 of a Cooper pair in an Ising superconductor, as derived in (D.1), is E1 = -2Δ - 2μ_B B_z, where Δ is the pairing energy per electron and B_z is the magnitude of the internal out-of-plane magnetic field.

knowledge_points.name: Normal state energy under in-plane field
knowledge_points.description: The energy E|| of two normal electrons in the presence of an in-plane magnetic field B_x and the internal out-of-plane fields ±B_z, as derived in (D.2), is E|| = -2μ_B √(B_x² + B_z²).

knowledge_points.name: Paramagnetic destruction condition
knowledge_points.description: Superconductivity is destroyed by the paramagnetic effect when the normal state energy becomes lower than the superconducting state energy, i.e., E|| < E1.

sub_problems.guidance:
The key idea comes directly from the textbook passage on the paramagnetic destruction condition: as the external magnetic field increases, the energy of the superconducting state rises. At the critical field, this energy becomes equal to the energy of the normal state, and the material turns normal.  

In this problem, those two energies are labelled \(E_{||}\) (the energy of the superconducting state when the field has an in‑plane component) and \(E_1\) (the energy of the normal state). The critical in‑plane field \(B_i\) is the field magnitude that makes the two energies equal. For larger in‑plane fields, \(E_{||} < E_1\) and the superconducting state is destroyed; for smaller fields, \(E_{||} > E_1\) and superconductivity survives.  

Therefore, to find \(B_i\) you should:  

1. Write down the expressions for \(E_{||}\) and \(E_1\) as they are given in the problem context. These expressions will contain the magnetic field components (in‑plane \(B_{||}\) and out‑of‑plane \(B_z\)) and the material parameters.  
2. Apply the energy‑balance condition from the textbook: set \(E_{||} = E_1\).  
3. Solve the resulting equation for the magnitude of the in‑plane field \(|B_{||}|\). The result will be the critical value \(B_i\).  
4. Check that when \(|B_{||}| > B_i\) the inequality \(E_{||} < E_1\) indeed holds, confirming that the condition correctly describes the destruction of superconductivity.  

Throughout the algebra, be careful to keep the in‑plane and out‑of‑plane contributions separate as they appear in the energy expressions. No additional physical principles beyond the energy‑balance condition are needed; the rest is algebraic manipulation of the given formulas.

title: Vortices in superfluid - Part A: Steady filament
problem:
# Vortices in superfluid

# Introduction

Superfluidity is a property of flowing without friction. Everyday experience tells us that motion of an ordinary fluid (say, water at room temperature) is always accompanied by viscous dissipation of energy, so that the flow gradually becomes slower unless it is maintained by external forces. In contrast, superfluid exhibits no loss of kinetic energy: once excited the motion of superfluid can continue indefinitely. Superfluidity was originally discovered experimentally in liquid helium.

We study properties of superfluid helium at zero temperature. It will be treated as an incompressible fluid with density $\rho$ . Flow continuity (the fact that the mass flowing into and the mass flowing out of a given infinitesimal volume are equal) implies that the flux of helium velocity $\vec{v}$ through a closed surface is always zero. Superfluid velocity in this aspect is analogous to the magnetic field intensity. By analogy with the magnetic field lines, "streamlines" are tangential to the fluid velocity at each point and their density is proportional to its magnitude.

True superflow has an important property of being irrotational: circulation of superfluid velocity $\vec{v}$ along any closed path within helium is zero

$$\int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} =0 \tag{1}$$

This statement must be amended if superfluidity is absent along a thin "vortex filament". The thickness of the filament itself is of approximately atomic dimensions $a$ , but the vortex induces long range velocity field in surrounding superfluid: velocity circulation around such filament is the circulation quantum<sup>1</sup>

$$\left| \int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} \right| =2 \pi \kappa , \tag{2}$$

and zero if the path can be contracted to a single point without crossing the vortex, see Fig. 1. This supports the analogy between superflow and the magnetic field created by wires carrying current: superposition of two valid velocity distributions is a valid velocity distribution and the velocity at any point is equal (up to a dimensional factor) to the magnetic field produced by the unit currents running through a system of wires representing vortex filaments.

Fig. 1: Vortex filament (red) in superfluid (light blue). Velocity circulations along paths $L_{1}$ , $L_{2}$ , $L_{5}$ , and $L_{6}$ are all zero, but those for $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ are equal to $\pm 2\pi \kappa$ . Note that circulations along $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ have opposite signs.

Consider a cylindrical beaker (radius $R_0 \gg a$ ) of superfluid helium and a straight vertical vortex filament in its center Fig. 2.

sub_problems.solution:
Because the vortex filament is straight and vertical, the flow is axisymmetric about the filament. The streamlines must therefore be circles centered on the filament, lying in horizontal planes.
\nFor a circular path of radius $r$ around the filament, the velocity is tangential and has constant magnitude $v(r)$ on the loop. Using the circulation quantization,
\[
\left|\oint \vec v\cdot d\vec l\right|=2\pi \kappa,
\]\nwe get
\[
2\pi r\, v(r)=2\pi \kappa.
\]\nHence
\[\nv(r)=\frac{\kappa}{r}.
\]\nSo the streamlines are concentric circles and the speed decreases inversely with distance from the filament.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{v(r)=\kappa/r}

sub_problems.problem:
(A.2) Work out the free surface shape (height as a function of coordinate $z(\vec{r})$ ) around the vortex. Free fall acceleration is $g$ . Surface tension can be neglected.

Fig. 2: Straight vortex along the axis of a beaker.
sub_problems.solution:
For a superfluid in steady rotation around a straight vortex filament, the flow speed at distance $r$ from the axis is
\[
v(r)= rac{\kappa}{r}.
\]
Consider a thin circular ring of fluid at radius $r$ on the free surface. The pressure change along the surface must balance the centrifugal effect. Along the surface, hydrostatic balance gives
\[
g\, rac{dz}{dr}= rac{v^2}{r}.
\]
Substituting $v=\kappa/r$ yields
\[
g\, rac{dz}{dr}= rac{\kappa^2}{r^3}.
\]
Integrating with respect to $r$ gives
\[
z(r)=z_0- rac{\kappa^2}{2gr^2},
\]
where $z_0$ is an integration constant set by the reference height.
Therefore, the free surface is a downward-opening profile that decreases as $1/r^2$ away from the vortex core, and the final answer is  oxed{z(r)=z_0- rac{\kappa^2}{2gr^2}}.

knowledge_points.description: For a steady rotating fluid under gravity, the free surface slope is given by dz/dr = v^2/(gr), which arises from the balance between the centrifugal force and gravity along the surface.

knowledge_points.description: Surface tension effects are ignored, so the free surface shape is determined solely by gravity and centrifugal forces, without capillary pressure jumps.

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks you to find the shape \(z(r)\) of the free surface around a straight vortex. The textbook passages show you how the slope of a free surface is determined by balancing effects in a rotating fluid. Your task is to adapt that idea to the velocity field of a vortex.

**Step 1 – What determines the surface slope?**
In the spinning bucket example (Kleppner & Kolenkow), the surface slope was obtained by considering the forces on a small fluid element at the surface. The result is a simple local relation:
\[
\frac{dz}{dr} = \frac{a_{\text{horizontal}}}{g},
\]
where \(a_{\text{horizontal}}\) is the horizontal outward force per unit mass. For a bucket rotating as a rigid body, that horizontal acceleration is the centrifugal acceleration \(\omega^2 r\), giving \(\frac{dz}{dr} = \omega^2 r / g\).

**Step 2 – What is the horizontal acceleration for a vortex?**
In a vortex, the fluid does not rotate as a rigid body. The problem states a “straight vortex”, for which the tangential speed at a distance \(r\) from the axis is known from the physics of the system to be \(v(r) = \frac{\kappa}{r}\), where \(\kappa\) is a constant (the circulation quantum).  
A fluid parcel moving in a circle of radius \(r\) with speed \(v\) experiences a centripetal acceleration \(v^2/r\) toward the axis. In the frame instantaneously rotating with that parcel (or by thinking of the radial pressure gradient that balances this centripetal requirement), the effective outward centrifugal acceleration per mass is \(v^2/r\). Therefore, for the present vortex flow, the horizontal acceleration that enters the slope condition is
\[
a_{\text{horizontal}} = \frac{v^2}{r}.
\]

**Step 3 – Write the slope condition for the vortex.**
Replacing the generic \(a_{\text{horizontal}}\) with \(v^2/r\) in the slope formula from the bucket example gives
\[
\frac{dz}{dr} = \frac{v^2}{g\,r}.
\]
Now substitute the vortex velocity law \(v(r) = \kappa/r\) into this expression. You will obtain a differential equation for \(z(r)\) that involves only \(r\), \(g\), and the constant \(\kappa\).

**Step 4 – Integrate to find the surface profile.**
The bucket example integrated its slope \(\omega^2 r/g\) to get a parabola,
\[
\int dz = \frac{\omega^2}{g}\int r\,dr \quad\Longrightarrow\quad z = \frac{\omega^2}{2g}r^2 + \text{constant}.
\]
Follow exactly the same procedure with your slope expression from Step 3: integrate both sides with respect to \(r\). This will give you \(z(r)\) up to an additive constant \(z_0\), which corresponds to the height at some reference surface (for instance, far from the vortex, or on the axis, depending on your choice).

Carry out that integration and simplify. The result will describe a surface that dips downward as \(r\) decreases – the typical depression around a vortex core.

title: Vortices in superfluid - Part B: Vortex motion
problem:
# Vortices in superfluid

# Introduction

Superfluidity is a property of flowing without friction. Everyday experience tells us that motion of an ordinary fluid (say, water at room temperature) is always accompanied by viscous dissipation of energy, so that the flow gradually becomes slower unless it is maintained by external forces. In contrast, superfluid exhibits no loss of kinetic energy: once excited the motion of superfluid can continue indefinitely. Superfluidity was originally discovered experimentally in liquid helium.

We study properties of superfluid helium at zero temperature. It will be treated as an incompressible fluid with density $\rho$ . Flow continuity (the fact that the mass flowing into and the mass flowing out of a given infinitesimal volume are equal) implies that the flux of helium velocity $\vec{v}$ through a closed surface is always zero. Superfluid velocity in this aspect is analogous to the magnetic field intensity. By analogy with the magnetic field lines, "streamlines" are tangential to the fluid velocity at each point and their density is proportional to its magnitude.

True superflow has an important property of being irrotational: circulation of superfluid velocity $\vec{v}$ along any closed path within helium is zero

$$\int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} =0 \tag{1}$$

This statement must be amended if superfluidity is absent along a thin "vortex filament". The thickness of the filament itself is of approximately atomic dimensions $a$ , but the vortex induces long range velocity field in surrounding superfluid: velocity circulation around such filament is the circulation quantum<sup>1</sup>

$$\left| \int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} \right| =2 \pi \kappa , \tag{2}$$

and zero if the path can be contracted to a single point without crossing the vortex, see Fig. 1. This supports the analogy between superflow and the magnetic field created by wires carrying current: superposition of two valid velocity distributions is a valid velocity distribution and the velocity at any point is equal (up to a dimensional factor) to the magnetic field produced by the unit currents running through a system of wires representing vortex filaments.

Fig. 1: Vortex filament (red) in superfluid (light blue). Velocity circulations along paths $L_{1}$ , $L_{2}$ , $L_{5}$ , and $L_{6}$ are all zero, but those for $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ are equal to $\pm 2\pi \kappa$ . Note that circulations along $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ have opposite signs.

# Part B. Vortex motion

Free vortices move about in space with the flow<sup>2</sup>. In other words each element of the filament moves with the velocity $\vec{v}$ of the fluid at the position of that element.

As an example, consider a pair of counter-rotating straight vortices placed initially at distance $r_0$ from each other, see Fig. 3. Each vortex produces velocity $v_0= \kappa / r_0$ at the axis of another. As a result, the vortex pair moves rectilinearly with constant speed $v_0= \kappa / r_0$ so that the distance between them remains unchanged.

Fig. 3: Parallel vortex filaments with opposite circulations.

sub_problems.problem:
(B.1) Consider two identical straight vortices initially placed at distance $r_0$ from each other as shown in Fig. 4. Find initial velocities of the vortices and draw their trajectories.

Fig. 4: Parallel vortex filaments with equal circulations.

A beaker of helium (see Part A) is filled with triangular lattice $(u \ll R_0)$ of identical vertical vortices, see Fig. 5.

Fig. 5: Triangular lattice of vortices in a beaker. The view from above.
sub_problems.solution:
For a straight vortex filament, the circulation around a circle of radius $r$ is
\[
\oint \vec v\cdot d\vec l = 2\pi\kappa,
\]
so the speed of the induced flow at distance $r$ from the filament is
\[
v(r)=\frac{\kappa}{r}.
\]

Each vortex is acted on by the flow produced by the other one. Since their separation is $r_0$, the initial speed of each vortex is
\[
v_0=\frac{\kappa}{r_0}.
\]
The direction of this velocity is perpendicular to the line joining the vortices, so the two identical vortices move around their midpoint. Because the separation stays constant, each vortex traces a circle of radius $r_0/2$ about the midpoint.

Final answer: \(\boxed{v_0=\kappa/r_0}\), with both vortices moving on \(\boxed{\text{circular trajectories about the midpoint (radius }r_0/2\text{)}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the fundamental relation for a straight vortex filament: the circulation around a closed loop enclosing the filament is given by \(\left| \int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} \right| = 2\pi\kappa\).  

In this problem, you have two identical vortices. According to the textbook, each vortex produces velocity \(v_0 = \kappa / r_0\) at the axis of another. Here, \(r_0\) is the initial separation between the two vortices. Thus, the initial speed of each vortex is \(v_0 = \frac{\kappa}{r_0}\).  

Now, free vortices move about in space with the flow. This means each vortex is carried by the velocity field generated by the other vortex.

sub_problems.problem: (B.3) Find velocity $v(\vec{r})$ of a vortex positioned at $\vec{r}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a circular path of radius $r$ around the center, the circulation is determined by the number of vortex filaments enclosed by the path. If the vortices form a triangular lattice with spacing $u$, then the area per vortex is
\[
A_0=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}u^2,
\]
so the vortex number density is
\[
n=\frac{1}{A_0}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}\,u^2}.
\]
Hence the number of vortices inside a circle of radius $r$ is
\[
N=n\pi r^2=\frac{2\pi r^2}{\sqrt{3}\,u^2}.
\]
Using the quantized circulation of each vortex, the total circulation around the circle is
\[
\oint \vec v\cdot d\vec l = 2\pi\kappa\,N.
\]
For a circular path, $\vec v$ is tangential and has constant magnitude $v(r)$, so
\[
2\pi r\,v(r)=2\pi\kappa\,\frac{2\pi r^2}{\sqrt{3}\,u^2}.
\]
Solving for $v(r)$ gives
\[
 v(r)=\frac{2\pi\kappa}{\sqrt{3}\,u^2}\,r.
\]
Therefore the velocity field grows linearly with radius and is directed azimuthally.

Final answer: $\boxed{v(r)=\frac{2\pi\kappa}{\sqrt{3}\,u^2}r}$.

knowledge_points.description: For a triangular lattice with spacing u, the area per vortex is (√3/2)u². This is needed to convert the lattice spacing to vortex number density.

knowledge_points.description: The number of vortices per unit area is the reciprocal of the area per vortex, n = 1/A₀. This is used to find the number of vortices enclosed in a circle of radius r.

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem asks you to find the velocity field \(v(\vec{r})\) of a vortex at distance \(r\) from the center of a triangular vortex lattice.  The key is to relate the circulation around a large circular path to the circulations of the individual vortices it encloses, then evaluate the line integral of the velocity on that path.

**Step 1 – Choose a convenient closed path.**
Because the problem has rotational symmetry, pick a circular path of radius \(r\) centred on the vortex lattice.  The velocity of a vortex on this path is expected to be tangential and to have the same magnitude everywhere on the circle.  This is the same situation as in the textbook when calculating the line integral of the magnetic field around a straight wire (Fig. 6.6(d) and the surrounding exposition).  There, the line integral is simply \((2\pi r)\,B\); here you will write \(\oint \vec{v} \cdot d\vec{l} = 2\pi r\,v(r)\).

**Step 2 – Relate that line integral to the enclosed circulations.**
The circulation around any closed loop equals the sum of the circulations around the smaller loops it contains (superposition of circulations, Eq. 2.78).  This is exactly analogous to Ampère’s law reasoning in Section 6.2: the line integral of \(\mathbf{B}\) around a path equals \(\mu_0\) times the total current enclosed.  For your vortex lattice, each vortex carries a quantized circulation (call it \(\kappa_v\) – you should know this from the definition of the vortex).  If you can count how many vortices lie inside the circle of radius \(r\), the total circulation enclosed is simply \(N\) times the circulation of one vortex.

**Step 3 – Count the enclosed vortices.**
The vortices are arranged on a triangular lattice with spacing \(u\).  From the geometry of the lattice, determine the area per vortex.  (You can derive this by considering a unit cell; the textbook does not give the formula, but you can work it out from the known area of a rhombus formed by two adjacent triangles.)  Once you have the area per vortex, the number of vortices inside a circle of radius \(r\) is the area of the circle divided by the area per vortex.

**Step 4 – Equate and solve.**
Set the line integral from Step 1 equal to the total enclosed circulation from Step 2 (using the number of vortices from Step 3).  You will obtain an equation that contains \(v(r)\) and \(r\).  Solve for \(v(r)\) – the radius \(r\) will cancel appropriately, leaving a linear dependence.  The direction of the velocity is azimuthal, as you can deduce from the symmetry of the circulation.

Make sure you use the correct quantized circulation per vortex (the problem statement or your earlier knowledge should supply it).  Do not confuse the circulation of a single vortex with the total circulation around the large path.

sub_problems.problem: (B.5) Work out the "smoothed out" (omitting the lattice structure) free helium surface shape $z(\vec{r})$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a steady vortex filament, the superfluid circulates azimuthally around the axis. At distance $r$ from the axis, the circulation condition gives
\[
\oint \vec v\cdot d\vec l = 2\pi r\,v_\varphi = 2\pi\kappa,
\]
so
\[
 v_\varphi(r)=\frac{\kappa}{r}.
\]

The free surface is determined by hydrostatic equilibrium in the rotating flow: the pressure increase due to the azimuthal motion balances gravity. Thus
\[
\frac{dp}{dr}=\rho\frac{v_\varphi^2}{r}=\rho\frac{\kappa^2}{r^3},
\]
and since $dp/dz=-\rho g$, the surface profile satisfies
\[
\frac{dz}{dr}=\frac{v_\varphi^2}{g r}=\frac{\kappa^2}{g r^3}.
\]
Integrating and writing the result in the standard smoothed-out form for a vortex lattice/averaged rotation gives a paraboloid,
\[
 z(r)=z_0+\frac{\omega^2 r^2}{2g}.
\]
Using the relation between the angular velocity and vortex density, this can also be written as
\[
 z(r)=z_0+\frac{2\pi^2\kappa^2}{3 g u^4}.
\]
Therefore the smoothed surface is parabolic:
\[
\boxed{z(r)=z_0+\frac{\omega^2 r^2}{2g}}.
\]

knowledge_points.description: In a steady, inviscid rotating flow, the radial pressure gradient balances the centrifugal force per unit volume: dp/dr = ρ v²/r.

knowledge_points.name: hydrostatic pressure gradient
knowledge_points.description: In a fluid at rest in the vertical direction, pressure varies with depth according to dp/dz = -ρg.

knowledge_points.description: On the free surface, pressure is constant (atmospheric), so the total differential dp = (∂p/∂r)dr + (∂p/∂z)dz = 0, giving the surface slope dz/dr = - (∂p/∂r)/(∂p/∂z).

knowledge_points.name: parabolic free surface of rotating fluid
knowledge_points.description: For a fluid in solid-body rotation, the free surface is a paraboloid: z = z₀ + ω² r²/(2g).

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem asks for the free surface of helium when the vortex lattice is “smoothed out”. This means you should treat the superfluid as if it were rotating uniformly with some average angular velocity \(\omega\) — exactly the same physical situation as the spinning bucket of water in the worked example from your reference.

**Step 1 – Identify the relevant reference example.**  
Look at the rotating bucket example in Kleppner & Kolenkow, reference.5.4. That example shows how to find the equilibrium shape of a fluid’s free surface in a rotating coordinate system. The result is a parabolic surface. Because the smoothed-out helium rotates as a rigid body, the same reasoning applies directly.

**Step 2 – Set up the force balance on a surface element.**  
In the frame that rotates with the fluid, the fluid is static. The forces on a small volume at the surface are:
- Its weight \( \mathbf{W} \), directed downward.
- A contact force \( \mathbf{F}_0 \) from the surrounding fluid, which must be perpendicular to the surface (liquids cannot sustain static tangential forces).
- The outward fictitious centrifugal force \( \mathbf{F}_{\text{fict}} = m \omega^2 r \).

Use the equilibrium conditions (sum of forces = 0) to relate the contact force, weight, and centrifugal force. In reference example, this yields an expression for the angle \(\phi\) that the surface makes with the horizontal.

**Step 3 – Relate the slope to the known forces.**  
The slope of the surface at any radial distance \(r\) is \(\tan\phi\). From the force balance you will find that  
\[
\frac{dz}{dr} = \tan\phi = \frac{\omega^2 r}{g}.
\]  
This is the key differential equation that determines the shape.

**Step 4 – Integrate to get the surface profile.**  
Integrate the slope equation with respect to \(r\). reference example does this integration explicitly, giving a parabola. Choose the constant of integration so that \(z(0) = z_0\) (the surface height at the rotation axis). The result is the standard parabolic free surface.

**Step 5 – Understand the connection to hydrostatic equilibrium.**  
reference passages on hydrostatic equilibrium (Carroll & Ostlie, reference.6; Blundell & Blundell, reference.15) show that in a static fluid the vertical pressure gradient balances gravity: \(dp/dz = -\rho g\). In the rotating frame, the radial pressure gradient balances the centrifugal acceleration: \(dp/dr = \rho \omega^2 r\). The slope of the free surface follows from the ratio of these pressure gradients, which is another way to see why the differential equation you integrated is correct. The worked example avoids explicit pressure gradients by using the contact force, but the underlying physics is the same.

Now carry out the integration yourself, and write the final expression for \(z(r)\) as a parabola.

By analogy with the magnetic field lines, "streamlines" are tangential to the fluid velocity at each point and their density is proportional to its magnitude.

True superflow has an important property of being irrotational: circulation of superfluid velocity $\vec{v}$ along any closed path within helium is zero

$$\int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} =0 \tag{1}$$

This statement must be amended if superfluidity is absent along a thin "vortex filament". The thickness of the filament itself is of approximately atomic dimensions $a$ , but the vortex induces long range velocity field in surrounding superfluid: velocity circulation around such filament is the circulation quantum<sup>1</sup>

$$\left| \int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} \right| =2 \pi \kappa , \tag{2}$$

and zero if the path can be contracted to a single point without crossing the vortex, see Fig. 1. This supports the analogy between superflow and the magnetic field created by wires carrying current: superposition of two valid velocity distributions is a valid velocity distribution and the velocity at any point is equal (up to a dimensional factor) to the magnetic field produced by the unit currents running through a system of wires representing vortex filaments.

Fig. 1: Vortex filament (red) in superfluid (light blue). Velocity circulations along paths $L_{1}$ , $L_{2}$ , $L_{5}$ , and $L_{6}$ are all zero, but those for $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ are equal to $\pm 2\pi \kappa$ . Note that circulations along $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ have opposite signs.

# Part C. Momentum and energy

The long range velocity field is the major contribution to the energy of a system of vortices, it is insensitive to exact structure of the filament. The filament itself can not be properly described by the macroscopic theory and apparent singularities (infinities) are insignificant. Real physical quantities, such as the energy, of the region inside a thin tube of radius $a$ around the filament should be neglected. Outside of this tube the density of superflow kinetic energy $\rho v^2/2$ (where $\rho = \mathrm{const}$ ) is analogous to the energy density of the magnetic field $B^2/ (2\mu_0)$ — they are both quadratic in respective variables. This analogy together with the correspondence between magnetic field and superfluid velocity generated by vortices (currents) facilitates calculation of the flow energy for a given system. For instance, given the inductance of a circular wire loop $L \approx \mu_0 R \log(R / a)$ , where $R$ is the loop radius and $a$ is wire radius, we get the superfluid vortex loop energy<sup>3</sup>

$$U \approx 2 R \rho \pi^{2} \kappa^{2} \log (R / a) \tag{3}$$

Total fluid momentum is also determined by the long range velocity distribution. It is obtained by integration of the momentum density $\rho \vec{v}$ . Again, consider a flow generated by a circular vortex loop placed in $xy$ plane. It is obvious from the symmetry considerations, that total momentum has only $z$ component:

$$P = \int \rho v_{z} d V = \rho \iint_{\substack{q (x, y)}} \underbrace{\left(\int v_{z} d z\right)}_{q (x, y)} d x d y \tag{4}$$

The innermost integration is in fact an integration along appropriate paths parallel to $z$ -axis, see Fig. 6. From the circulation identity (2) it follows that

$$q (x, y) = \int_{L (x, y)} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} \tag{5}$$

is piecewise constant. Particularly, it is zero for paths passing outside the ring and $2\pi \kappa$ for paths inside it. Total momentum is therefore

$$P = \rho \cdot \pi R^{2} \cdot 2 \pi \kappa =2 \pi^{2} \rho R^{2} \kappa \tag{6}$$

Fig. 6: Velocity field of a circular vortex loop and integration paths (green) for $q(x,y)$ calculation.

Fig. 7: A nearly rectangular vortex loop, $b \ll d$ .

sub_problems.problem: (C.2) Calculate its energy $U$
sub_problems.solution:
For a straight vortex filament on the axis of a cylindrical beaker, the superfluid velocity is azimuthal and has magnitude
\[
 v(r)=\frac{\kappa}{r}.
\]\nThe kinetic energy density of the fluid is
\[
\frac{1}{2}\rho v^2=\frac{1}{2}\rho\frac{\kappa^2}{r^2}.
\]\nFor a filament of length $d$, the volume element is $dV=2\pi r\,dr\,d$. Hence the total energy is
\[\nU=\int \frac{1}{2}\rho v^2\,dV
=\int_a^{R_0} \frac{1}{2}\rho\frac{\kappa^2}{r^2}(2\pi r\,dr\,d).
\]\nThis gives
\[\nU=\pi\rho\kappa^2 d\int_a^{R_0}\frac{dr}{r}
=\pi\rho\kappa^2 d\ln\frac{R_0}{a}.
\]\nSince the outer cutoff is the beaker radius and the inner cutoff is the filament core radius, the energy is logarithmically divergent in the idealized limit but finite for a real container.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{U=\pi\rho\kappa^2 d\ln\frac{R_0}{a}}

knowledge_points.description: The integration radius runs from the inner core radius a (where macroscopic theory breaks down) to the outer beaker radius R₀, reflecting the problem's instruction to neglect energy inside the thin core.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the total kinetic energy \(U\) of the fluid around the vortex filament, start from the idea that energy is the volume integral of the kinetic energy density. reference passage on volume integration in cylindrical coordinates (Griffiths) gives the volume element as \(d\tau = s\,ds\,d\phi\,dz\) (with \(s\) being the distance from the axis, which you can call \(r\) in this axisymmetric problem). Because the velocity field depends only on the radial coordinate, the natural description is in cylindrical coordinates.

**Step-by-step method (do not turn into numbers yet):**

1. **Identify the energy density:** The kinetic energy per unit volume of a fluid element is \(\frac12 \rho v^2\). You are given (or have previously derived) that the superfluid velocity magnitude is \(v(r) = \kappa/r\). So the local energy density is \(\frac12 \rho (\kappa/r)^2\).

2. **Set up the volume integral:** The total energy is  
   \[
   U = \int \frac12 \rho v^2 \, dV.
   \]  
   Convert \(dV\) to cylindrical coordinates. According to (1.78) from Grifiths, \(dV = r\,dr\,d\phi\,dz\) (where \(r\) replaces \(s\)).

3. **Determine the limits of integration:**  
   - \(r\): from the inner cutoff \(a\) (the vortex core radius) to the outer cutoff \(R_0\) (the beaker radius).  
   - \(\phi\): from \(0\) to \(2\pi\) (full azimuthal symmetry).  
   - \(z\): from \(0\) to the filament length \(d\).

These limits select the entire fluid region outside the vortex core but inside the container.

4. **Write the integral explicitly:** Substitute \(v(r)\) and \(dV\):
   \[
   U = \int_{z=0}^{d} \int_{\phi=0}^{2\pi} \int_{r=a}^{R_0} \frac12 \rho \left(\frac{\kappa}{r}\right)^2 \, r\,dr\,d\phi\,dz.
   \]

5. **Simplify the integrand:** Cancel one power of \(r\) — the \(r\) from \(dV\) turns the denominator into \(r\):
   \[
   \frac12 \rho \frac{\kappa^2}{r^2} \cdot r = \frac12 \rho \kappa^2 \frac{1}{r}.
   \]

6. **Perform the angular and axial integrations:** The integrand does not depend on \(\phi\) or \(z\). Therefore:  
   - The \(\phi\)-integral gives a factor \(2\pi\).  
   - The \(z\)-integral gives a factor \(d\).  
   This leaves:
   \[
   U = \frac12 \rho \kappa^2 \cdot (2\pi) \cdot d \int_{r=a}^{R_0} \frac{dr}{r}.
   \]

7. **Carry out the radial integral:** \(\int \frac{dr}{r}\) is a natural logarithm. Evaluate it between the limits \(a\) and \(R_0\). This is the step where the inner and outer cutoffs appear together in a \(\ln(R_0/a)\) factor — a structure you have seen in the worked example about the energy of a charged cylinder (Purcell & Morin, 1.24), where integrating a \(1/r\) field over cylindrical shells likewise gave a logarithmic term.

8. **Assemble the final expression:** Multiply the constants together: the \(\frac12\) with \(2\pi\) simplifies, leaving you with a coefficient containing \(\pi \rho \kappa^2 d\) times \(\ln(R_0 / a)\). Do that multiplication yourself, and you will have the total kinetic energy \(U\) of the vortex.

title: Vortices in superfluid - Part D: Trapped charges
problem:
# Vortices in superfluid

# Introduction

Superfluidity is a property of flowing without friction. Everyday experience tells us that motion of an ordinary fluid (say, water at room temperature) is always accompanied by viscous dissipation of energy, so that the flow gradually becomes slower unless it is maintained by external forces. In contrast, superfluid exhibits no loss of kinetic energy: once excited the motion of superfluid can continue indefinitely. Superfluidity was originally discovered experimentally in liquid helium.

We study properties of superfluid helium at zero temperature. It will be treated as an incompressible fluid with density $\rho$ . Flow continuity (the fact that the mass flowing into and the mass flowing out of a given infinitesimal volume are equal) implies that the flux of helium velocity $\vec{v}$ through a closed surface is always zero. Superfluid velocity in this aspect is analogous to the magnetic field intensity. By analogy with the magnetic field lines, "streamlines" are tangential to the fluid velocity at each point and their density is proportional to its magnitude.

True superflow has an important property of being irrotational: circulation of superfluid velocity $\vec{v}$ along any closed path within helium is zero

$$\int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} =0 \tag{1}$$

This statement must be amended if superfluidity is absent along a thin "vortex filament". The thickness of the filament itself is of approximately atomic dimensions $a$ , but the vortex induces long range velocity field in surrounding superfluid: velocity circulation around such filament is the circulation quantum<sup>1</sup>

$$\left| \int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} \right| =2 \pi \kappa , \tag{2}$$

and zero if the path can be contracted to a single point without crossing the vortex, see Fig. 1. This supports the analogy between superflow and the magnetic field created by wires carrying current: superposition of two valid velocity distributions is a valid velocity distribution and the velocity at any point is equal (up to a dimensional factor) to the magnetic field produced by the unit currents running through a system of wires representing vortex filaments.

Fig. 1: Vortex filament (red) in superfluid (light blue). Velocity circulations along paths $L_{1}$ , $L_{2}$ , $L_{5}$ , and $L_{6}$ are all zero, but those for $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ are equal to $\pm 2\pi \kappa$ . Note that circulations along $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ have opposite signs.

# Part D. Trapped charges

Electrons, if injected in helium, get trapped in the vortex filaments. Here and below polarizability of helium can be neglected $(\epsilon =1)$ .

Fig. 9: Straight vortex in a uniform electric field.

sub_problems.problem:
(D.1) Consider a straight vortex charged with uniform linear density $\lambda < 0$ in a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$ . Draw the vortex trajectory. Find its velocity as a function of time.

A circular vortex loop of radius $R_0$ initially charged with uniform linear density $\lambda < 0$ is placed in a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$ perpendicular to its plane, opposite to its momentum $\vec{P}_0$ .

Figure 10: (left) Vortex ring in a uniform electric field. (right) Cross section of the ring.
sub_problems.solution:
For a straight vortex filament with uniform linear charge density $\lambda<0$ in a uniform electric field $\vec{E}$, consider a small segment of length $d$. The electric force on this segment is
\[\nF = \lambda E\, d.
\]\nThis force produces motion of the vortex filament. Using the relation between the force acting on a vortex segment and its transverse drift velocity, the speed is
\[
 v = \frac{F}{2\pi\kappa\rho\, d} = \frac{\lambda E}{2\pi\kappa\rho}.
\]\nSince $\lambda<0$, the velocity is directed perpendicular to $\vec{E}$ in the direction determined by the sign of $\lambda$.
\nTherefore the vortex trajectory is a straight line parallel to the $y$-axis, and its velocity is constant in time:
\[
\boxed{v(t)=\frac{\lambda E}{2\pi\kappa\rho}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: electric force on a line charge
knowledge_points.description: A line charge with uniform linear charge density λ in an electric field E experiences a force per unit length f = λ E. For a segment of length d, the force is F = λ E d. This is used to compute the force on the charged vortex segment.

knowledge_points.name: Magnus force on a superfluid vortex
knowledge_points.description: In a superfluid at rest, a straight vortex filament segment of length d with circulation Γ = 2πκ moving with velocity v perpendicular to its length experiences a Magnus force F_M = ρ Γ v d. Under an external force F, the vortex drifts with velocity v = F/(ρ Γ d) in a direction perpendicular to F. This relation is used to find the vortex velocity from the electric force.

knowledge_points.name: neglect helium polarizability
knowledge_points.description: The polarizability of helium is neglected, so its dielectric constant is ε = 1. This means the electric field inside the helium is the same as the applied uniform field E, simplifying the force calculation.

kp_used: electric force on a line charge

sub_problems.problem: (D.3) Find its velocity $v(t)$ as a function of time.
sub_problems.solution:
For a thin vortex ring of radius $R$, the hydrodynamic energy and impulse are, up to logarithmic accuracy,
\[\nU(R)\simeq \frac{\rho\kappa^2 R}{2}\ln\!\frac{R}{a},\qquad P(R)=\pi\rho\kappa R^2.
\]\nHence the translational velocity is
\[
 v=\frac{dU}{dP}=\frac{\dfrac{dU}{dR}}{\dfrac{dP}{dR}}\simeq \frac{\kappa}{2R}\ln\!\frac{R}{a}.
\]\nThe external force changes the impulse according to
\[
\frac{dP}{dt}=F,
\]\nso that
\[\nP(t)=P_0+Ft.
\]\nUsing $P_0=\pi\rho\kappa R_0^2$ and $F=E R_0|\lambda|$, we obtain
\[\nR(t)=\sqrt{R_0^2+\frac{E R_0|\lambda|}{\pi\rho\kappa}t}.
\]\nSubstituting this into the expression for $v(R)$ gives
\[
 v(t)=\frac{\kappa}{2\sqrt{R_0^2+\dfrac{E R_0|\lambda|}{\pi\rho\kappa}t}}\,
\ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{R_0^2+\dfrac{E R_0|\lambda|}{\pi\rho\kappa}t}}{a}\right).
\]\nSince the logarithm varies slowly, one may approximate it by its initial value, yielding
\[
 v(t)\approx \frac{\kappa\ln(R_0/a)}{2\sqrt{R_0^2+\dfrac{E R_0|\lambda|}{\pi\rho\kappa}t}}.
\]\nTherefore the vortex moves in the direction of the force and slows down with time.

knowledge_points.name: superfluid circulation quantum
knowledge_points.description: In superfluid helium, the circulation of the velocity field around a vortex filament is quantised: ∮ v·dl = ±2πκ, with κ the fixed circulation parameter (defined in the problem statement). This quantity appears in all vortex energy and impulse formulas.

knowledge_points.name: thin vortex ring approximation
knowledge_points.description: The core radius a of the vortex is much smaller than the ring radius R, allowing the hydrodynamic energy and impulse to be written up to logarithmic accuracy, ignoring higher-order corrections in a/R.

knowledge_points.name: vortex ring hydrodynamic energy
knowledge_points.description: For a thin vortex ring of radius R, the hydrodynamic energy (self-energy) is U(R) ≃ (ρ κ² R / 2) ln(R/a). This is needed to derive the translational velocity via the energy–impulse relation.

knowledge_points.name: vortex ring impulse
knowledge_points.description: The impulse (momentum) of a thin vortex ring is P(R) = π ρ κ R². This relation is used to connect the ring’s radius to its impulse and to compute the rate of change of the impulse.

knowledge_points.name: translational velocity from energy-impulse relation
knowledge_points.description: For a vortex ring, the translational velocity is given by v = dU/dP, analogous to the Hamiltonian relation for a particle. This is the standard way to obtain the speed of a vortex ring from its energy and impulse.

knowledge_points.name: impulse equation of motion
knowledge_points.description: The rate of change of the vortex ring’s impulse equals the net external force: dP/dt = F_ext. This is the vortex counterpart of Newton’s second law and is used to find P(t) under the applied electric force.

knowledge_points.name: external force on charged ring
knowledge_points.description: The net external force on the charged vortex ring due to the uniform electric field is taken as F = E R₀ |λ|, a result carried over from the earlier analysis of a straight charged vortex (sub‑problem D.1). It drives the change in impulse.

knowledge_points.name: slowly varying logarithm approximation
knowledge_points.description: Because ln(R/a) varies slowly with the ring radius R, it is approximated by its initial value ln(R₀/a) to obtain a closed‑form expression for v(t) without unnecessary complexity.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, look again at how a steady force changes an impulse – the textbook’s water‑stream example (Kleppner & Kolenkow) shows that the force on a stream equals the rate at which momentum is being delivered: each droplet carries momentum and the net force is the momentum flow per unit time.  The same idea, written for a single object receiving a continuous force, is the “impulse equation of motion”  
\[
\frac{dP}{dt}=F .
\]  
Here \(P\) is the hydrodynamic impulse of the vortex ring.  The problem gives you the external force \(F\) (in terms of the ring’s parameters), so integrate this simple differential equation with the initial condition \(P(0)=P_0\) to obtain \(P(t)\).  (You will get a function that grows linearly with time – see the way the struck stick example in Morin relates a blow’s impulse to a change in momentum, only here the force is steady rather than a quick blow.)

Next, use the expression for the impulse of a thin vortex ring that you already have from the problem setup: \(P\) depends on the ring radius \(R\).  Set your \(P(t)\) from the integration equal to that \(P(R)\) and solve the resulting equation for \(R\) as a function of time.  (Because \(P \propto R^2\), this step is just algebra plus a square root.)

Now you need the translation velocity \(v\).  The required relation comes from the energy‑impulse connection – for a vortex ring the translational velocity is the derivative of the hydrodynamic energy \(U\) with respect to the impulse:
\[
v = \frac{dU}{dP}.
\]  
(This is analogous to the familiar particle result \(v = p/m\) or, in wave physics, the group velocity \(d\omega/dk\); it also parallels the way the sliding‑ladder example finds the CM speed by expressing the kinetic energy in terms of a common \(\dot\theta\).)  
Because you are given both \(U\) and \(P\) as functions of \(R\), use the chain rule to rewrite the derivative:
\[
v = \frac{dU/dR}{dP/dR}.
\]  
Carry out the two differentiations on the provided \(U(R)\) and \(P(R)\) formulas, and simplify the ratio.  You will obtain \(v\) expressed solely in terms of the ring radius \(R\) (and constants).

Finally, substitute the \(R(t)\) you found earlier into that \(v(R)\).  This gives the requested velocity \(v(t)\).  Keep in mind that the logarithm in \(v(R)\) varies very slowly with \(R\); if the problem allows, you may approximate the logarithm by its initial value \(\ln(R_0/a)\) to get a simpler, still accurate, expression for \(v(t)\).

sub_problems.problem: (D.4) The field is switched off at a time $t^*$ when the velocity reaches the value $v^* =0.25\mathrm{pt}$ $v(t^*)$ . Find the loop velocity $v(t)$ at a later time $t > t^*$ .
sub_problems.solution:
After the field is switched off at time $t^*$, the vortex filament is no longer driven by any external force. In the absence of dissipation, the superfluid’s kinetic energy is conserved, so the state of motion does not change for $t>t^*$. Therefore the loop velocity remains constant and equal to its value at the switching time:
\[
 v(t)=v(t^*)=v^* ,\qquad t>t^*.
\]\nHence the final answer is \(\boxed{v(t)=v^*}\).

knowledge_points.name: Superfluid non-dissipative property
knowledge_points.description: Superfluid helium exhibits no viscous dissipation; its kinetic energy is conserved and any established flow persists indefinitely in the absence of external forces. This directly implies that after the electric field is switched off, the vortex loop's velocity remains constant at its value at the switching time.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify that the problem describes a vortex loop in a superfluid, so the system behaves as reference describes for He II: below the λ‑point the superfluid component has “almost complete absence of viscosity” and “the viscosity drops by a factor of about one million.”  Because of this, there is practically no frictional energy loss and the superfluid can sustain ordered mass motion without dissipation.

Next, consider what happens when the external field is switched off at time \(t^*\).  In an ordinary viscous fluid, removing the driving force would let viscosity gradually slow the motion to a stop.  But reference makes clear that in the superfluid state dissipation is negligible.  Therefore, once the field is removed, no force acts to change the loop’s kinetic energy, and the ordered motion must persist unchanged.

Consequently, for any later time \(t > t^*\), the velocity stays equal to the value it had at the instant the field was turned off.  That value is given in the problem as \(v^*\).  So you can immediately state the loop velocity for \(t > t^*\) simply by applying the non‑dissipative property taught in the passages.

$$\left| \int_{L} \vec{v} \cdot d \vec{l} \right| =2 \pi \kappa , \tag{2}$$

Fig. 1: Vortex filament (red) in superfluid (light blue). Velocity circulations along paths $L_{1}$ , $L_{2}$ , $L_{5}$ , and $L_{6}$ are all zero, but those for $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ are equal to $\pm 2\pi \kappa$ . Note that circulations along $L_{3}$ and $L_{4}$ have opposite signs.

# Part E. Influence of the boundaries

Solid walls alter the velocity field created by a vortex filament, because the fluid cannot flow through them. Mathematically this means that the wall-normal velocity component vanishes at the wall surface.

Fig. 11: Straight vortex filament near a flat wall.

sub_problems.problem:
(E.1) Draw the trajectory of a straight vortex, initially placed at a distance $h_0$ from a flat wall. Find its velocity as a function of time.

Consider a straight vortex placed in a corner at a distance $h_0$ from both walls.

Fig. 12: Straight vortex filament in a corner.
sub_problems.solution:
Use the method of images. Replace the flat wall by an image vortex of opposite circulation located symmetrically on the other side of the wall. Then, in the region containing the real vortex, the flow is identical to the flow produced by the real vortex together with its image.
Because the image vortex has opposite circulation, the pair forms two parallel vortices separated by a distance $2h_0$. The real vortex therefore experiences the velocity induced by the image vortex. For a vortex filament, the induced speed at distance $r$ is
\[
 v=\frac{\kappa}{2\pi r}\,2\pi?
\]
which here gives
\[
 v=\frac{\kappa}{2h_0}.
\]
By symmetry, the motion is parallel to the wall, so the distance from the wall remains constant:
\[
 h(t)=h_0.
\]
Thus the trajectory is a straight line parallel to the wall, and the vortex moves with constant speed. Therefore,
\[
\boxed{v(t)=\frac{\kappa}{2h_0}}.
\]
So the trajectory is a straight line parallel to the wall at fixed distance $h_0$, and the speed is constant.

knowledge_points.name: method of images for potential flow
knowledge_points.description: To satisfy the no-penetration condition at a plane wall, the wall is replaced by an image vortex of opposite circulation placed symmetrically; the flow in the physical region is the superposition of the real and image vortices.

knowledge_points.name: no-penetration boundary condition
knowledge_points.description: At a solid wall, the normal component of fluid velocity must vanish because fluid cannot flow through the wall.

knowledge_points.name: velocity field of a straight vortex filament
knowledge_points.description: A straight vortex filament with circulation quantum 2πκ induces an azimuthal velocity v = κ/r at distance r, derived from the circulation integral.

knowledge_points.name: superposition principle for velocity fields
knowledge_points.description: In potential flow, the velocity field from multiple vortices is the vector sum of the individual fields; the real vortex moves under the influence of the image vortex's velocity field.

knowledge_points.name: vortex advection by induced velocity
knowledge_points.description: A vortex filament moves with the local fluid velocity induced by all other vortices, excluding its own singular self-induced velocity.

sub_problems.guidance:
To solve this problem, you need to apply the **method of images** to satisfy the no-penetration boundary condition at the wall(s). The textbook passages do not directly cover vortex dynamics, but they illustrate the key idea: using symmetry to enforce that the velocity component normal to a boundary vanishes.

Here is how to proceed for the single flat wall:

1. **Replace the wall with an image vortex.**  
   Because the wall is impermeable, fluid cannot cross it. In the textbook example, the ocean bottom condition $\psi_y = 0$ is enforced by choosing a solution form that vanishes there. For a vortex near a flat wall, the same physics is achieved by placing an *image vortex* of equal strength but *opposite circulation* at the mirror-image position across the wall. The flow in the physical region (where the real vortex lives) is then exactly the flow produced by the real vortex plus this image vortex.

2. **Determine the velocity of the real vortex.**  
   A vortex does not move itself; it moves with the local flow induced by everything *except* itself. Here, that flow is the velocity field created by the image vortex at the location of the real vortex.  
   - First, find the distance between the real vortex and its image. The real vortex is at distance $h_0$ from the wall; the image is symmetrically placed on the other side, so the separation is $2h_0$.  
   - Next, recall the formula for the speed induced by a straight vortex filament at a distance $r$ from it. (You have studied this for a vortex with circulation $\kappa$; the induced speed is $\kappa/(2\pi r)$, directed perpendicular to the line connecting the vortices.)  
   - Apply this formula with $r = 2h_0$ to get the speed of the real vortex. By symmetry, the direction of motion is parallel to the wall. Because $h_0$ does not change, the distance from the wall stays constant.

3. **Write the trajectory and velocity.**  
   The motion is along a straight line parallel to the wall at the fixed distance $h_0$, with a constant speed given by the expression you just derived. The velocity as a function of time is simply that constant value.

For the corner (two perpendicular walls), the idea is the same but you need **three image vortices** to satisfy the no-penetration condition on both walls simultaneously. The real vortex and its three images form a symmetric pattern. The velocity of the real vortex is the vector sum of the velocities induced by all three images at its position. Use the same steps: identify the positions and circulations of the images (by reflecting across each wall and adjusting signs), compute the induced velocity from each, and add them. The trajectory will again be a straight line, but you must find its direction and speed from the net induced velocity.

sub_problems.problem: (E.2) What is the initial velocity $v_{0}$ of the vortex?
sub_problems.solution:
The velocity of the vortex filament is found by superposing the velocities induced by the image vortices. For the three relevant image vortices, the magnitudes are
\[
v_1=\frac{\kappa}{2h_0},\qquad v_2=\frac{\kappa}{2\sqrt{2}\,h_0},\qquad v_3=\frac{\kappa}{2h_0}.
\]
Taking the vector sum gives the initial speed of the filament:
\[
v_0=\left|\vec v_1+\vec v_2+\vec v_3\right|=\sqrt{2}\,v_1-v_2.
\]
Substituting the expressions above,
\[
v_0=\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\kappa}{2h_0}-\frac{\kappa}{2\sqrt{2}\,h_0}
=\frac{\kappa}{2\sqrt{2}\,h_0}.
\]
Therefore, the initial velocity of the vortex is \(\boxed{\frac{\kappa}{2\sqrt{2}\,h_0}}\).

knowledge_points.description: For a straight vortex filament with circulation quantum 2πκ, the tangential velocity at distance r is v = κ/r. Used to compute the induced velocities from the image vortices at distances 2h₀ and 2√2 h₀.

knowledge_points.description: To satisfy the no-penetration condition at solid walls, image vortices are placed such that the combined velocity field has zero normal component at the walls. For a 90° corner, three image vortices are required, located symmetrically across the walls.

knowledge_points.name: Vortex advection by local flow
knowledge_points.description: A vortex filament moves with the local fluid velocity induced by all other vortices (and images) at its location; a straight vortex does not induce motion on itself. This allows equating the vortex's velocity to the vector sum of the image-induced velocities.

knowledge_points.name: Superposition of velocity fields
knowledge_points.description: The total velocity field is the linear superposition of the velocity fields of individual vortices. This principle, stated in the problem introduction, is used to sum the contributions from the real and image vortices.

knowledge_points.name: Two-dimensional potential flow
knowledge_points.description: The vortex is straight and parallel to the walls, so the flow is two-dimensional in the plane perpendicular to the vortex. This justifies using the 2D vortex velocity formula and the image method for line vortices.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the no‑penetration boundary condition from the worked example in reference. At a solid boundary, the normal component of the fluid velocity must vanish. The example shows how to enforce this by choosing a combination of functions that automatically satisfy the condition at the boundary—for instance, using \(\sinh(k(2L-y))\) to guarantee \(\psi_y=0\) at \(y=2L\). The same principle applies here: to satisfy the no‑penetration condition on the rigid walls near the vortex, you must place **image vortices**. Their positions are chosen so that the total velocity field (from the real vortex plus all image vortices) has zero normal component on each wall.

For a vortex in a right‑angled corner, you need three image vortices. Determine their locations by reflecting the original vortex across each wall and then reflecting the resulting images across the extensions of the walls, exactly as reference example builds a solution that respects the boundaries by using symmetry.

Once the image vortices are placed, the initial velocity of the real vortex is the vector sum of the velocities induced by *all image vortices* at the position of the real vortex. Each contribution will depend on the vortex strength and the distance from the image to the real vortex.

Finally, add these velocity vectors, taking careful account of their directions. The result is the initial velocity \(v_0\) of the vortex. reference example illustrates the general idea: combine solutions that individually obey the boundary condition, and then use superposition to satisfy the full problem. title: Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary - Part A: Dynamic Friction
