# Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary

# Introduction

The concept of gravitational waves is one of the most impressive predictions of Einstein's Theory of General Relativity. Gravitational waves are the space-time ripples propagating with the speed of light similarly to electromagnetic waves. Direct detection of gravitational waves is incredibly difficult, however, the first signal was detected on September 14, 2015, by LIGO and VIRGO collaborations.

Gravitational waves are emitted during the rapid motion of massive objects. The most powerful source of gravitational waves is the merging of two Supermassive Black Holes (SBH). Black holes predicted by Theory of General Relativity represent extremely compact objects which might have very large masses. Other specific properties of black holes will not be needed in the solution of this problem.

In the generally accepted theory of galaxies' evolution, it is supposed that there is SBH with the mass ranging from $10^{5} -10^{9}$ of Solar masses in the galaxy's center. Galaxies are huge stellar systems containing $10^{10} -10^{11}$ stars. During their evolution, two galaxies can collide and merge into one. What happens to two SBHs initially located in their centers? The evolution of the SBH binary system can be divided into three main stages. At each stage SBHs approach each other, although the underlying physical phenomena differ. We will examine these phenomena separately in the first three parts of the problem. In the fourth part, we will use the obtained relations to calculate the total time of the SBH binary system evolution.

At the end of their evolution, two SBHs will eventually approach each other and merge into a single black hole. The merging process lasts about an hour and is accompanied by an intense burst of gravitational radiation. Future observatories like LISA will be able to detect this gravitational radiation. Still, the research on the SBH evolution is under way now, at the dawn of gravitational-wave astronomy.

# General information

1. Express all your numerical answers in parsecs (pc) for the distances and giga-years (Gy) for the time intervals. We will use Solar mass $(M_S)$ as a reference mass. You might need these values:

$$\begin{array}{l} 1 \mathrm{pc} =3.1 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{m}, \\ M_{s} =2.0 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{kg}, \\ \end{array}$$

$t_H =13.7$ Gy, age of the Universe,

$$\begin{array}{l} G =6.67 \times 10^{-11} N \times m^{2} / k g^{2}, \\ c =3.0 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}. \\ \end{array}$$

2. When you encounter the word "estimate", you are not demanded the exact answer. It is sufficient to obtain a result that differs from the accurate one, not more than by a factor of 10. On the contrary, when you encounter the word "find", you are supposed to achieve the exact answer. The word "calculate" asks you to bring the numerical answer.
3. Throughout the problem, assume every star in the galaxy to have the same mass $m = M_S$ .
4. Throughout the problem we will not take into account the effects of the Theory of General Relativity except gravitational waves emission. All stars and black holes are considered as point masses governed by Newton's gravitation law.

# Part A. Dynamic Friction

In this part we shall study the simplified model of the galaxy. You can ignore the velocities of the stars in the galaxy and assume the constant stellar concentration $n$ . The characteristic size of the galaxy is $R$ . The stellar concentration is small enough, so the stellar collisions are extremely rare and negligible. Let us consider a SBH with the mass $M \gg m$ moving with the velocity $v$ through the galaxy. Surprisingly, the SBH experiences nonzero average force from the stars. This force slows the motion of the SBH and is called the force of dynamical friction for this reason. This part is devoted to the determination of this force.

sub_problems.problem:
(A.1) Let us work in the SBH's reference frame and consider the transit of one star with impact parameter $b$ (fig. 1). Assume that

$$b \gg b_{1} = \frac{G M}{v^{2}}. \tag{1}$$

The angular deflection of the star $\alpha = kb_{1} / b$ , where $k$ is some coefficient. Find the value of $k$ . If you cannot find $k$ , assume $k =1$ hereafter.

Fig. 1: The deflection of a star by the SBH with mass $M$ . The impact parameter is $b$ , the minimal distance between the star and the SBH is $r_m$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a star passing the black hole with impact parameter $b \gg b_1=GM/v^2$, the deflection is small, so we may treat the trajectory as a straight line and write
\[
\alpha \simeq \tan\alpha = \frac{p_y}{p_x}.
\]\nThe transverse momentum gained by the star is
\[\np_y=\int F_y\,dt.
\]\nUsing Newton’s law, the transverse force is
\[\nF_y=\frac{GMm}{r^2}\frac{b}{r}.
\]\nWith $r^2=b^2+x^2$ and $x=b\tan\varphi$, this becomes
\[\nF_y=\frac{GMm}{b^2}\cos^3\varphi.
\]\nAlso, since $dx=v\,dt$ and $x=b\tan\varphi$,
\[\ndt=\frac{dx}{v}=\frac{b}{v}\frac{d\varphi}{\cos^2\varphi}.
\]\nTherefore
\[\np_y=\frac{GMm}{b^2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^3\varphi\,\frac{b}{v}\frac{d\varphi}{\cos^2\varphi}
=\frac{GMm}{bv}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos\varphi\,d\varphi
=\frac{2GMm}{bv}.
\]\nSince $p_x\simeq mv$, we get
\[
\alpha=\frac{p_y}{p_x}=\frac{2GM}{bv^2}=\frac{2b_1}{b}.
\]\nThus $k=2$.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{\alpha=\frac{2GM}{bv^2}=\frac{2b_1}{b}}, \boxed{k=2}$

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational force between the SBH (mass M) and a star (mass m) is F = GMm/r². Used to write the transverse force component during the star's flyby.

knowledge_points.name: impulse-momentum theorem
knowledge_points.description: The change in a particle's momentum equals the time integral of the applied force: Δp = ∫ F dt. Applied to compute the transverse momentum p_y transferred to the star.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small deflections, α ≈ tan α = p_y/p_x and the longitudinal momentum p_x ≈ mv remains essentially unchanged, giving α ≈ p_y/(mv).

knowledge_points.name: straight-line trajectory
knowledge_points.description: Because b ≫ b₁ the deflection is so small that the star's actual curved path can be replaced by a straight line, allowing r² = b² + x² with x = vt in the force integral.

sub_problems.problem: (A.2) Let Ox axis be directed along the SBH's velocity. Find the momentum component $\Delta p_{x}$ transferred from the star to the SBH.
sub_problems.solution:
For the star moving past the massive black hole, the speed far before and far after the encounter is the same, so the magnitude of its momentum is conserved:
\[\np_x^2+p_y^2=p^2.
\]\nIf the transverse component after the deflection is small, then the longitudinal component is
\[\np_x=\sqrt{p^2-p_y^2}\approx p-\frac{p_y^2}{2p}.
\]\nHence the change of the $x$-component is
\[
\Delta p_x=p_x-p=-\frac{p_y^2}{2p}.
\]\nFor a gravitational encounter at impact parameter $b$, the small deflection angle is
\[
\alpha\approx \frac{2GM}{bv^2},
\]\nand therefore
\[\np_y\approx p\alpha,
\qquad p=mv.
\]\nSubstituting gives
\[
\Delta p_x=-\frac{p\alpha^2}{2}
=-\frac{mv}{2}\left(\frac{2GM}{bv^2}\right)^2
=-\frac{2G^2M^2m}{b^2v^3}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[
\boxed{\Delta p_x=-\frac{2G^2M^2m}{b^2v^3}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: small-angle gravitational deflection
knowledge_points.description: The deflection angle for a star passing a massive object at large impact parameter b is α ≈ 2GM/(bv²), a result from part A.1. This gives the transverse momentum after the encounter.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of energy in gravitational scattering
knowledge_points.description: Because the gravitational potential vanishes at large distances, the star's kinetic energy and hence the magnitude of its velocity v (and momentum p = mv) are unchanged after the hyperbolic encounter.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For a small deflection angle α, the transverse momentum is p_y ≈ p α, and the change in the longitudinal component is Δp_x ≈ -p_y²/(2p) via a first‑order expansion of sqrt(p² – p_y²).

knowledge_points.name: momentum conservation
knowledge_points.description: The x‑component of momentum transferred from the star to the black hole equals the negative of the star's change in x‑momentum. This links the computed star‑momentum change to the required answer.

sub_problems.guidance:
Start by recalling that the star and the SBH form an isolated system, so total momentum is conserved (Spacetime Physics shows that each component of total momentum before and after an encounter is the same; Morin emphasizes that the two particles experience equal and opposite forces, so momentum is exchanged). Because the SBH is much more massive than the star, the SBH’s motion is negligible; you can therefore relate the momentum transferred **to** the SBH in the x‑direction to the change in the star’s x‑momentum: the transfer is minus the change in the star’s \(p_x\).

The star’s encounter with the SBH is a central‑force scattering. The comet example in Kleppner & Kolenkow (Section 10.4) illustrates that the gravitational force is conservative, so far from the SBH the star’s speed is the same before and after the deflection — hence the magnitude of its momentum \(p = mv\) is unchanged. Only the direction of the momentum vector is rotated by a small angle \(\alpha\).

Now decompose the star’s final momentum into components along the original direction (x) and perpendicular to it (y). Because the magnitude is conserved,
\[
p'_{x} = p\cos\alpha,\qquad p'_{y} = p\sin\alpha .
\]

The problem tells you the deflection is small. Use the small‑angle approximations from Kleppner & Kolenkow (Section 1.11.4):
\[
\sin\alpha \approx \alpha,\qquad \cos\alpha \approx 1 - \frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}.
\]
Thus
\[
p'_{x} \approx p\Bigl(1-\frac{\alpha^{2}}{2}\Bigr),\qquad p'_{y} \approx p\,\alpha .
\]

The change in the star’s x‑momentum is therefore
\[
\Delta p_{x}^{\text{(star)}} = p'_{x} - p .
\]
Carrying out the subtraction (leave the symbols for the student) gives an expression in terms of \(p\) and \(\alpha^{2}\).

The momentum transferred to the SBH is the opposite of that change:
\[
\Delta p_{x}^{\text{(transferred)}} = -\,\Delta p_{x}^{\text{(star)}} .
\]

At this stage you need the actual deflection angle \(\alpha\) for a star of mass \(m\) passing a point mass \(M\) with impact parameter \(b\) and speed \(v\). (This relation is usually derived earlier in such a problem; if it is not provided, it comes from the impulse approximation or the small‑angle scattering formula.) Substitute that expression for \(\alpha\) into the transfer formula, simplify, and you will obtain \(\Delta p_{x}^{\text{(transferred)}}\) in terms of \(G, M, m, b,\) and \(v\). The result tells you how much x‑momentum the SBH gains from the fly‑by.

kp_used: conservation of energy in gravitational scattering

sub_problems.problem: (A.3) Estimate the average force $F_{DF}$ acting on the SBH by taking the average over impact parameter $b$ . Neglect the contribution of the stars with impact parameters $b < b_1$ . Assume the SBH to reside in the central part of a galaxy. Express $F_{DF}$ in terms of $M, v, R, G$ and stellar density $\rho = mn$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a star passing the supermassive black hole (SBH) with impact parameter $b$, the momentum transfer in the direction opposite to the motion leads, after averaging over the encounter geometry, to a contribution proportional to $\mathrm{d}b/b$. The number of stars crossing an annulus between $b$ and $b+\mathrm{d}b$ in time $\Delta t$ is proportional to $2\pi b\,v\,n\,\mathrm{d}b\,\Delta t$, so the total dynamical-friction force is obtained by integrating over impact parameters:
\[\nF_{DF}=\frac{1}{\Delta t}\int \Delta p_x\,\mathrm{d}N
= -4\pi G^2 M^2 \frac{nm}{v^2}\int_{b_1}^{R}\frac{\mathrm{d}b}{b}.
\]\nUsing $\rho=mn$ and the logarithmic factor
\[
\ln\Lambda = \ln\frac{R}{b_1},
\]\nwe get
\[\nF_{DF}=-4\pi G^2 M^2 \frac{\rho}{v^2}\ln\Lambda,
\qquad \Lambda=\frac{R}{b_1}.
\]\nThus the average dynamical-friction force is
\[
\boxed{F_{DF}=-4\pi G^2 M^2 \frac{\rho}{v^2}\ln\frac{R}{b_1}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: constant stellar concentration
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the stellar number density n is uniform and constant, which allows the number of stars in an impact-parameter annulus to be written simply as n times the cylindrical shell volume.

knowledge_points.name: impact parameter cutoff
knowledge_points.description: The solution neglects stars with impact parameter b < b₁, using b₁ as a lower cutoff in the integral, and uses the galaxy size R as the upper cutoff, which is needed to avoid a divergent integral.

knowledge_points.name: flux-based rate counting
knowledge_points.description: The number of stars passing the SBH per unit time with impact parameter between b and b+db is computed as the particle flux through a cylindrical shell: dN/dt = n v 2π b db, a standard technique for collision rates in kinetic theory.

knowledge_points.name: momentum transfer from prior sub-problem
knowledge_points.description: The solution directly uses the momentum component Δp_x transferred per star, which was derived in sub-problem (A.2) and is proportional to 1/b, to build the integrand for the total force.

knowledge_points.name: dynamical friction force
knowledge_points.description: The average force F_DF is defined as the total momentum transferred to the SBH by many stellar encounters per unit time, obtained by integrating the single-encounter momentum transfer over the impact-parameter distribution.

knowledge_points.name: Coulomb logarithm
knowledge_points.description: The factor ln(R/b₁) appears naturally from integrating db/b over the impact-parameter range; it is known as the Coulomb logarithm in plasma physics and gravitational dynamics, and the solution explicitly defines Λ = R/b₁.

knowledge_points.name: stellar mass density
knowledge_points.description: The solution replaces the product of stellar number density n and individual stellar mass m with the mass density ρ = m n to express the final force in terms of ρ, as requested by the problem.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Recall the single‑encounter momentum transfer**  
   From the earlier sub‑problem you already have an expression for the impulse \(\Delta p_x(b)\) that the supermassive black hole (SBH) receives from one star passing at impact parameter \(b\). This result was obtained using the impulse concept (see Morin 8.4.1 for the definition of impulse and angular impulse) applied to a gravitational encounter. Keep that \(\Delta p_x(b)\) handy – it is the momentum transferred to the SBH in its direction of motion.

2. **Count the encounters with flux‑based rate counting**  
   To find how many stars with impact parameters in the range \([b,\, b+db]\) interact with the SBH in a time interval \(\Delta t\), use the idea from Carroll & Ostlie 10.3: the number of incident particles that hit a target of cross‑sectional area \(\sigma\) is \(dN = n\, v\, \sigma\, dt\), where \(n\) is the number density and \(v\) their relative speed.  
   Here, the “target” is the SBH, and the effective area for impact parameters between \(b\) and \(b+db\) is an annular ring of area \(dA = 2\pi b\, db\). With \(v\) as the relative speed, the number of such stars is  
   \[
   dN = n\, v\, (2\pi b\, db)\, \Delta t .
   \]  
   (Ignore stars with \(b < b_1\), as instructed.)

3. **Build the total momentum transfer**  
   The total impulse delivered to the SBH by all stars in the time \(\Delta t\) is the sum of individual contributions over impact parameters:  
   \[
   \Delta P_{\text{total}} = \int_{b_1}^{R} \Delta p_x(b)\; dN .
   \]  
   Substitute the expression for \(dN\) from step 2. Because \(\Delta t\) appears as a factor, the average force follows from the definition of impulse: \(F_{DF} = \Delta P_{\text{total}} / \Delta t\) (the average force equals the total momentum change per unit time, consistent with Morin 8.4.1).

4. **Assemble the force and recognise its form**  
   Insert your \(\Delta p_x(b)\) into the integral. After bringing all constants outside, you will be left with an integral over \(db/b\) from \(b_1\) to \(R\); this yields the familiar logarithmic (Coulomb) factor \(\ln(R/b_1)\).  
   At this stage, replace \(m n\) by the stellar mass density \(\rho\).

5. **Check the structure with dimensional analysis**

sub_problems.problem: (A.4) As you obtained in the previous task, the expression for $F_{DF}$ includes the factor $0.2\mathrm{pt}\log R / b_1$ , which we will denote further as $\log \Lambda$ . Calculate the value of $\log \Lambda$ for $M =10^{8}M_{S}$ , $R =20\mathrm{kpc} =20\times 10^{3}pc$ and velocity $v =200\mathrm{km / s}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
From the previous task, the Coulomb logarithm is defined as
\[
\log\Lambda = \log\frac{R}{b_1},
\]\nwhere
\[
 b_1 = \frac{GM}{v^2}.
\]\nFor the given values,
\[\nM=10^8 M_S,\qquad v=200\ \mathrm{km/s}.
\]\nFirst compute $b_1$:
\[
 b_1=\frac{G M}{v^2}
 =\frac{(6.67\times10^{-11})(10^8\cdot 2.0\times10^{30})}{(2.0\times10^5)^2}
 \approx 3.3\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{m}.
\]\nConverting to parsecs,
\[
 b_1\approx \frac{3.3\times10^{17}}{3.1\times10^{16}}\approx 10.7\ \mathrm{pc}.
\]\nNow with $R=20\ \mathrm{kpc}=2.0\times10^4\ \mathrm{pc}$,
\[
\log\Lambda = \log\left(\frac{R}{b_1}\right)=\log\left(\frac{2.0\times10^4}{10.7}\right)\approx \log(1.9\times10^3)\approx 7.5.
\]\nTherefore,
\[
\boxed{\log\Lambda\approx 7.5}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Coulomb logarithm (log Λ)
knowledge_points.description: The Coulomb logarithm log Λ is defined as the natural logarithm of the ratio of the maximum impact parameter (galaxy size R) to the minimum impact parameter (b_1). It appears in the dynamical friction force formula and is needed here to compute its numerical value.

knowledge_points.name: impact parameter b_1 = GM/v^2
knowledge_points.description: The characteristic minimum impact parameter for a gravitational encounter with a massive object is b_1 = GM/v^2, as derived in part A.1. This formula is required to evaluate the argument of the Coulomb logarithm.

title: Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary - Part B: Gravitational snagshot
problem:
# Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary

# Introduction

The concept of gravitational waves is one of the most impressive predictions of Einstein's Theory of General Relativity. Gravitational waves are the space-time ripples propagating with the speed of light similarly to electromagnetic waves. Direct detection of gravitational waves is incredibly difficult, however, the first signal was detected on September 14, 2015, by LIGO and VIRGO collaborations.

Gravitational waves are emitted during the rapid motion of massive objects. The most powerful source of gravitational waves is the merging of two Supermassive Black Holes (SBH). Black holes predicted by Theory of General Relativity represent extremely compact objects which might have very large masses. Other specific properties of black holes will not be needed in the solution of this problem.

In the generally accepted theory of galaxies' evolution, it is supposed that there is SBH with the mass ranging from $10^{5} -10^{9}$ of Solar masses in the galaxy's center. Galaxies are huge stellar systems containing $10^{10} -10^{11}$ stars. During their evolution, two galaxies can collide and merge into one. What happens to two SBHs initially located in their centers? The evolution of the SBH binary system can be divided into three main stages. At each stage SBHs approach each other, although the underlying physical phenomena differ. We will examine these phenomena separately in the first three parts of the problem. In the fourth part, we will use the obtained relations to calculate the total time of the SBH binary system evolution.

At the end of their evolution, two SBHs will eventually approach each other and merge into a single black hole. The merging process lasts about an hour and is accompanied by an intense burst of gravitational radiation. Future observatories like LISA will be able to detect this gravitational radiation. Still, the research on the SBH evolution is under way now, at the dawn of gravitational-wave astronomy.

# General information

1. Express all your numerical answers in parsecs (pc) for the distances and giga-years (Gy) for the time intervals. We will use Solar mass $(M_S)$ as a reference mass. You might need these values:

$$\begin{array}{l} 1 \mathrm{pc} =3.1 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{m}, \\ M_{s} =2.0 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{kg}, \\ \end{array}$$

$t_H =13.7$ Gy, age of the Universe,

$$\begin{array}{l} G =6.67 \times 10^{-11} N \times m^{2} / k g^{2}, \\ c =3.0 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}. \\ \end{array}$$

2. When you encounter the word "estimate", you are not demanded the exact answer. It is sufficient to obtain a result that differs from the accurate one, not more than by a factor of 10. On the contrary, when you encounter the word "find", you are supposed to achieve the exact answer. The word "calculate" asks you to bring the numerical answer.
3. Throughout the problem, assume every star in the galaxy to have the same mass $m = M_S$ .
4. Throughout the problem we will not take into account the effects of the Theory of General Relativity except gravitational waves emission. All stars and black holes are considered as point masses governed by Newton's gravitation law.

# Part B. Gravitational snagshot

In this part, we will consider the system of two SBHs with equal masses $M \gg m$ located in the center of the galaxy. Let's call this system a SBH binary. We will assume that there are no stars near the SBH binary, each SBH has a circular orbit of radius $a$ in the gravitational field of another SBH.

sub_problems.problem:
(B.1) Find the orbital velocity $v_{bin}$ of each SBH. Find the total energy $E$ of the SBH binary. Express it in terms of $a, G$ and $M$ .
There are a lot of stars at distances much larger than $a$ from the binary. Stars travel along complex and diverse trajectories in the gravitational field of the whole galaxy. The motion of the stars can be considered chaotic, like the motion of the molecules in an ideal gas. Let us assume that stars' velocities have equal magnitudes $\sigma \ll v_{bin}$ and their average mass density is $\rho$ . In this case dynamical friction is no longer affecting the SBH binary and energy losses are caused by other phenomenon.
sub_problems.solution:
For two identical black holes of mass $M$ moving on a circular orbit, each black hole orbits the common center of mass at radius $a$, so the distance between them is $2a$.
\nThe gravitational force acting on one black hole is
\[\nF_g=\frac{G M^2}{(2a)^2}=\frac{G M^2}{4a^2}.
\]\nThis force provides the centripetal acceleration:
\[
\frac{M v_{\rm bin}^2}{a}=\frac{G M^2}{4a^2}.
\]\nHence
\[
 v_{\rm bin}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{4a}}.
\]
\nThe total energy of the binary is the sum of the kinetic energies of both black holes and their mutual potential energy:
\[\nE=2\cdot \frac{Mv_{\rm bin}^2}{2}-\frac{GM^2}{2a}.
\]\nSubstituting $v_{\rm bin}^2=\frac{GM}{4a}$ gives
\[\nE=\frac{GM^2}{4a}-\frac{GM^2}{2a}=-\frac{GM^2}{4a}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[
\boxed{v_{\rm bin}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{4a}},\qquad E=-\frac{GM^2}{4a}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
knowledge_points.description: Used to compute the gravitational force between the two black holes as F = G M^2 / (2a)^2, where the separation is 2a.

knowledge_points.name: Centripetal force for circular motion
knowledge_points.description: Used to relate the gravitational force to the orbital velocity: M v_bin^2 / a = F, giving the condition for a circular orbit.

knowledge_points.name: Kinetic energy
knowledge_points.description: Used to compute the kinetic energy of each black hole as (1/2) M v_bin^2, and the total kinetic energy as twice that.

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational potential energy
knowledge_points.description: Used to compute the potential energy of the binary system as U = -G M^2 / (2a), where the separation is 2a.

knowledge_points.name: Center of mass for equal masses
knowledge_points.description: Needed to determine that when each black hole orbits the common center of mass at radius a, the separation between them is 2a, which appears in both the gravitational force and potential energy.

knowledge_points.name: Total mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: The total energy of the binary is the sum of the kinetic energies of both black holes and their mutual gravitational potential energy.

sub_problems.guidance:
**Understand the geometry using center of mass**  
Since the two black holes (SBHs) are identical (each of mass \( M \)), their common center of mass lies exactly halfway between them. From the center-of‑mass descriptions (Kleppner, reference.4, and Carroll & Ostlie, reference.18), the position vectors satisfy \( \mathbf{r}_1' = -\mathbf{r}_2' \), so each SBH orbits the center of mass at the same distance. You are given that distance as \( a \); therefore the separation between the two black holes is \( 2a \).

**Relate gravity to the required centripetal force**  
For one SBH moving uniformly on a circular path of radius \( a \), the inward centripetal force is  
\[
F_c = \frac{M v_{\text{bin}}^2}{a},
\]  
as derived in the circular‑motion work (Kleppner & Kolenkow, reference.8.2).  
The only force providing this centripetal pull is the gravitational attraction from the other black hole, given by Newton’s law of universal gravitation:  
\[
F_g = G\frac{M \cdot M}{(\text{separation})^2} = G\frac{M^2}{(2a)^2}.
\]  
(You can see the same type of force‑balance argument in Carroll & Ostlie’s derivation of Kepler’s third law, where they set \( m v^2/r \) equal to the gravitational force.)

**Solve for the orbital speed**  
Set \( F_c = F_g \) and solve the resulting equation for \( v_{\text{bin}} \). This requires only a simple algebraic rearrangement and taking a square root. You will obtain an expression that depends only on \( G, M \), and \( a \).

**Write the total mechanical energy**  
Total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies, as stated in the conservation‑of‑energy discussion (Kleppner, reference.6a): \( E = K + U \).

- The system has two moving SBHs, each with kinetic energy \( \frac{1}{2}M v_{\text{bin}}^2 \). Therefore the total kinetic energy is  
\[
K = 2 \times \frac{1}{2}M v_{\text{bin}}^2 = M v_{\text{bin}}^2.
\]

- The gravitational potential energy of two point masses separated by a distance \( 2a \) is (from Carroll & Ostlie, reference.14, or Palen’s summary)  
\[
U = -G\frac{M \cdot M}{2a} = -G\frac{M^2}{2a}.
\]

Thus the total energy is  
\[
E = M v_{\text{bin}}^2 - G\frac{M^2}{2a}.
\]

**Express \( E \) in the requested variables**  
Now substitute the squared speed \( v_{\text{bin}}^2 \) you found earlier into this expression for \( E \). Combine the terms over a common denominator and simplify. The result will be a negative constant (as expected for a bound circular orbit) that depends only on \( G, M \), and \( a \).

As a useful check, you may recall from the virial‑theorem remark in the gravitational‑collapse passage (Carroll & Ostlie, reference.3) that for a gravitationally bound system in equilibrium the total energy is one‑half the potential energy. Your simplified expression should satisfy that relation.

kp_used: Center of mass for equal masses

sub_problems.problem:
(B.2) Let us solve a related problem. Let a star of mass $m$ transit by a point mass $M_2 \gg m$ being at rest. The minimal distance between the star and the point during the transit is $r_m$ . The velocity of the star at large distance is $\sigma$ . Find the exact value of impact parameter $b$ .
If a star approaches the SBH binary for a distance about $a$ , it participates in a complex 3-body interaction with the binary that almost always results in a star being shot out with the velocity about $v_{bin}$ (the velocity of the star at the large distance after interaction). We will call such a strong interaction a collision of a star with the SBH binary. Acceleration and the shot of the star after the collision is called "gravitational slingshot".
sub_problems.solution:
Let the star move in the gravitational field of the point mass $M_2$ with speed $\sigma$ at infinity and minimum distance $r_m$.
\nBy conservation of angular momentum between infinity and the point of closest approach,
\[\nb\,\sigma = r_m v_0,
\]\nwhere $v_0$ is the star’s speed at distance $r_m$.
\nBy conservation of mechanical energy,
\[
\frac{\sigma^2}{2} = \frac{v_0^2}{2} - \frac{G M_2}{r_m}.
\]\nHence
\[\nv_0^2 = \sigma^2 + \frac{2GM_2}{r_m}.
\]\nSubstituting this into the angular momentum relation gives
\[\nb = r_m\frac{v_0}{\sigma}
= r_m\sqrt{1+\frac{2GM_2}{\sigma^2 r_m}}.
\]\nTherefore, the impact parameter is
\[
\boxed{b = r_m\sqrt{1+\frac{2GM_2}{\sigma^2 r_m}}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Impact parameter
knowledge_points.description: The perpendicular distance from the center of force to the initial velocity vector of an incoming particle; needed to interpret the quantity b that the problem asks for.

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of angular momentum
knowledge_points.description: For a particle moving under a central force, angular momentum about the force center is conserved; used to equate the angular momentum at infinity (m σ b) and at closest approach (m v0 r_m).

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: Total mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) is conserved for a particle in a conservative force field; used to relate the speed at infinity σ to the speed at closest approach v0 and the gravitational potential.

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational potential energy
knowledge_points.description: The gravitational potential energy of two point masses M and m separated by distance r is U = -G M m / r; needed to express the potential energy at the closest approach distance r_m.

knowledge_points.name: Distance of closest approach condition
knowledge_points.description: At the point of closest approach, the radial component of velocity is zero, so the velocity is purely tangential and angular momentum is simply m v r; used to write the angular momentum at r_m as m v0 r_m.

knowledge_points.name: Stationary massive body approximation
knowledge_points.description: Because M2 >> m, the massive body is considered at rest, providing a fixed central gravitational field; this reduces the problem to one-body motion in a static potential.

knowledge_points.name: Point mass approximation
knowledge_points.description: The star and the massive body are treated as point masses, so their gravitational fields are those of point sources and they have no internal structure; justifies using the point-mass potential and particle mechanics.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Identify the physical situation and the simplifying assumptions.**  
   The star’s mass \(m\) is much smaller than the point mass \(M_2\) (\(M_2 \gg m\)), so \(M_2\) can be treated as stationary. The star moves in the gravitational field of \(M_2\) alone, and we treat \(M_2\) as a point mass at the origin. The gravitational potential energy of the star is  
   \[
   U = -\frac{G M_2 m}{r},
   \]  
   as stated both in the Carroll & Ostlie passage (\(U = -G M m / r\)) and in Palen’s text. The force is conservative, so mechanical energy is conserved (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 5.4).

2. **Understand the meaning of “impact parameter” and the condition at large distance.**  
   At a large distance the star’s speed is \(\sigma\) and its path would miss \(M_2\) by a perpendicular distance \(b\), the impact parameter. As explained in Kleppner & Kolenkow’s section on hyperbolic orbits (10.5.1), the angular momentum about the force centre is  
   \[
   L = (\text{mass}) \times (\text{speed}) \times (\text{impact parameter}),
   \]  
   and the total mechanical energy at infinity is purely kinetic: \(E = \frac12 m \sigma^2\) (since \(U \to 0\) as \(r \to \infty\)).

   *Why this matters:* The initial angular momentum and energy are constants of the motion that link the incoming state to the state at closest approach.

3. **Write the conservation of angular momentum between infinity and the point of closest approach.**  
   At the distance of closest approach \(r_m\), the star’s velocity is purely transverse (the radial component is momentarily zero). Therefore the angular momentum there is \(m \, v_{\text{min}} \, r_m\), where \(v_{\text{min}}\) is the speed at that instant. Using the general expression for angular momentum of an orbiting object (Palen: \(L = m v r\); Kleppner & Kolenkow: \(L = \mu v_0 b\) for the reduced mass system) and equating the two values gives  
   \[
   m\, \sigma \, b = m\, v_{\text{min}} \, r_m.
   \]  
   (Recall that angular momentum is conserved because the gravitational force is central, so torque is zero; see Kleppner & Kolenkow’s discussion of conservation of angular momentum.)

4. **Write the conservation of mechanical energy between infinity and the point of closest approach.**  
   The total mechanical energy \(E = K + U\) is constant (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 5.4).  
   - At infinity: \(K = \frac12 m \sigma^2\), \(U = 0\).  
   - At \(r_m\): \(K = \frac12 m v_{\text{min}}^2\), \(U = -G M_2 m / r_m\).  

   Equate the total energies:  
   \[
   \frac12 m \sigma^2 = \frac12 m v_{\text{min}}^2 - \frac{G M_2 m}{r_m}.
   \]

5. **Combine the two conservation laws to eliminate the unknown speed \(v_{\text{min}}\).**  
   Solve the energy equation for \(v_{\text{min}}^2\). Then substitute that expression into the angular momentum equation to obtain a relation that involves only \(b\), \(r_m\), \(\sigma\), \(G\), and \(M_2\). Finally, isolate \(b\).  

   *Tip:* The step is algebraically identical to the logic used in the Kleppner & Kolenkow hyperbola discussion (10.5.1), where one eliminates the angular momentum and energy to find the orbit parameters. Here you are finding \(b\) directly instead of the eccentricity. You may also find the “energy diagram” approach of Kleppner & Kolenkow (Section 10.4) helpful for understanding why the radial kinetic energy vanishes at closest approach, which is exactly the condition you are enforcing.  

6. **Check the result.**  
   The impact parameter you obtain should depend only on the given quantities \(r_m\), \(\sigma\), \(G\), and \(M_2\). For a given star and point mass, it tells you how “off‑centre” the initial path must be to achieve a minimum separation \(r_m\).

sub_problems.problem: (B.3) Estimate the characteristic time $\Delta t$ between two successive collisions of the SBH binary with stars. Take into account that $\sigma \ll v_{bin}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The collision time is estimated from the collision rate
\[
\Delta t^{-1}=n\,\sigma\,\pi b_{\max}^2,
\]\nwhere $n$ is the stellar concentration, $\sigma$ is the relative speed at large distance, and $\pi b_{\max}^2$ is the collision cross section.
\nTo find $b_{\max}$, treat the binary from far away as a point mass $2M$. A star must reach the distance $a$ from the binary to interact strongly, so we set the periapsis to $r_m=a$. Using gravitational focusing,
\[
 b_{\max}=a\sqrt{1+\frac{4GM}{a\sigma^2}}.
\]\nBecause $\sigma^2\ll GM/a$, this simplifies to
\[
 b_{\max}\simeq \frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{GMa}.
\]\nHence
\[
\Delta t^{-1}=n\,\sigma\,\pi\left(\frac{2}{\sigma}\sqrt{GMa}\right)^2
=\frac{4\pi G M a n}{\sigma},
\]\nso
\[
\Delta t=\frac{\sigma}{4\pi G M a n}.
\]\nIf $\rho=mn$ is used for the mass density, this is equivalently
\[
\Delta t=\frac{m\sigma}{4\pi G M a\rho}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[
\boxed{\Delta t=\frac{\sigma}{4\pi G M a n}=\frac{m\sigma}{4\pi G M a\rho}}.
\]
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\Delta t=\frac{\sigma}{4\pi G M a n}=\frac{m\sigma}{4\pi G M a\rho}}

knowledge_points.name: collision rate formula
knowledge_points.description: The collision frequency of a test object moving with speed v through a field of stationary scatterers of number density n and cross-sectional area A is n v A. Here the relative speed is the stellar velocity σ.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational focusing impact parameter
knowledge_points.description: For a test particle moving in the gravitational field of a point mass M_eff, the impact parameter b and the distance of closest approach r_min satisfy b = r_min sqrt(1 + 2 G M_eff / (r_min v_∞^2)). Here this is applied to treat the binary as a point mass 2M with v_∞ = σ.

knowledge_points.name: strong-interaction distance ~ a
knowledge_points.description: A star must approach the SBH binary to a minimum distance of about a to undergo a strong gravitational slingshot (collision); this sets r_min = a in the focusing formula.

knowledge_points.name: binary treated as point mass 2M
knowledge_points.description: For distant stars, the SBH binary can be treated as a single point mass with total mass 2M, because the binary separation (∼2a) is much smaller than typical impact parameters.

knowledge_points.name: strong gravitational focusing regime
knowledge_points.description: The condition σ << v_bin implies σ^2 << GM/a, so the kinetic term 1 in the impact parameter radical is negligible, yielding b_max ≈ (2/σ) sqrt(G M a).

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks for the characteristic time between collisions of stars with a tight binary (SBH binary). The solution follows the same logic as the textbook’s worked example “aiming a spacecraft at a planet”, where gravity focuses trajectories and increases the effective target area. You will need to apply that method to a star approaching a binary, then simplify using the given condition \(\sigma \ll v_\text{bin}\).

**1. Relate collision time to a cross-section**
The mean collision time is the inverse of the collision rate per star. For a population of background stars with number density \(n\) and relative speed \(\sigma\), a standard rate estimate is \(\Delta t^{-1} = n\,\sigma\,(\text{cross-section})\). The cross-section is \(\pi b_{\max}^2\), where \(b_{\max}\) is the largest impact parameter for which a star’s orbit brings it close enough to interact strongly. The problem defines “strong interaction” as coming within a distance \(a\) (the binary semi-major axis) of the binary’s center of mass. So your task is to find \(b_{\max}\) for which the distance of closest approach \(r_{\min} = a\).

**2. Apply gravitational focusing to find \(b_{\max}\)**
At large distances the binary behaves like a point mass \(M_\text{bin} = 2M\). Treat a star as a test particle (neglect its mass compared to \(M_\text{bin}\), just as in the spacecraft–planet example). Use the conserved energy and angular momentum of the relative motion.

- **Energy:** \(\displaystyle E = \frac{1}{2}\mu\sigma^2\) (at infinity) \(=\) \(\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}\mu v_{\min}^2 - \frac{G (2M)\mu}{r_{\min}}\) (at closest approach).
- **Angular momentum:** \(L = \mu\sigma b = \mu v_{\min}r_{\min}\) (purely transverse at \(r_{\min}\)).

Here \(\mu\) is approximately the star’s mass and cancels out. Eliminate \(v_{\min}\) from these two conservation equations. You should obtain a relation that is identical in form to the spacecraft example:  
\[
b = r_{\min}\sqrt{1 + \frac{2G(2M)}{r_{\min}\,\sigma^2}} .
\]
If you are uncertain about this step, review the textbook’s “aiming a spacecraft” worked example, which derives exactly this formula for the critical impact parameter to just graze a planet of radius \(R\) with escape speed \(v_\text{esc}\).

Now set \(r_{\min}=a\) to get the maximum impact parameter for a star to reach the binary’s strong-interaction zone.

**3. Exploit the condition \(\sigma \ll v_\text{bin}\)**
The binary’s internal orbital speed is of order \(v_\text{bin} \sim \sqrt{GM/a}\). The problem states \(\sigma \ll v_\text{bin}\); therefore \(\sigma^2 \ll GM/a\). Consequently the term \(4GM/(a\sigma^2)\) inside the square root is much larger than 1. Neglect the 1 and simplify \(b_{\max}\) to an expression proportional to \(1/\sigma\).

**4. Assemble the collision time**
With the approximate \(b_{\max}\), form the cross-section \(\pi b_{\max}^2\). Plug this into the rate formula \(\Delta t^{-1} = n\,\sigma\,\pi b_{\max}^2\). Simplify the product algebraically. You will find that the \(\sigma\) dependence partly cancels, leaving \(\Delta t\) proportional to \(\sigma\) in the numerator. Express the final result in terms of the given parameters \(\sigma, G, M, a, n\). If you prefer to use the mass density \(\rho = m n\) (where \(m\) is the typical stellar mass), you may substitute \(n = \rho / m\) to obtain an equivalent form.

Self-check: Verify that the expression for \(\Delta t\) increases with \(\sigma\) and decreases as the density, mass, or binary size increase—qualitatively reasonable.

sub_problems.problem: (B.4) Estimate the SBH binary energy loss rate $dE/dt$ . Estimate the radius variation rate $da/dt$ . Express it in terms of $a, \rho, \sigma, G$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For one gravitational slingshot, the star gains on average an energy
\[
\Delta E_{\text{star}}=\frac{m v_{\text{bin}}^{2}}{2}-\frac{m\sigma^{2}}{2}.
\]\nThe binary loses the same amount of energy:
\[
\Delta E_{\text{bin}}=-\Delta E_{\text{star}}.
\]\nSince \(\sigma \ll v_{\text{bin}}\), we may neglect the initial stellar kinetic energy, giving
\[
\Delta E_{\text{bin}}\simeq -\frac{m}{2}v_{
\text{bin}}^{2}.
\]\nUsing the orbital speed scale for a binary of separation \(a\), this becomes
\[
\Delta E_{\text{bin}}=\frac{GmM}{8a}.
\]\nHence the average energy loss rate of the binary is
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{\Delta E}{\Delta t}=-\frac{\pi G^{2}M^{2}\rho}{2\sigma}.
\]\nNow write the binary orbital energy as
\[\nE=-\frac{GM^{2}}{4a}.
\]\nDifferentiating with respect to time,
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}\left(-\frac{GM^{2}}{4a}\right)=\frac{GM^{2}}{4a^{2}}\frac{da}{dt}.
\]\nEquating this with the previous expression for \(dE/dt\), we obtain
\[
\frac{GM^{2}}{4a^{2}}\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{\pi G^{2}M^{2}\rho}{2\sigma},
\]\nso
\[
\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{2\pi G\rho a^{2}}{\sigma}.
\]\nTherefore, the energy loss rate and separation shrinkage rate are
\[
\boxed{\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{\pi G^{2}M^{2}\rho}{2\sigma}},\qquad \boxed{\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{2\pi G\rho a^{2}}{\sigma}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: gravitational slingshot energy transfer
knowledge_points.description: In a strong 3-body interaction (collision) with the binary, a star is ejected with a final speed of order v_bin, so the star gains kinetic energy ~ (1/2) m v_bin^2 and the binary loses the same amount.

knowledge_points.name: neglect initial stellar kinetic energy
knowledge_points.description: Because the stellar velocity dispersion σ is much smaller than the binary orbital speed v_bin, the star's initial kinetic energy (1/2) m σ^2 is negligible compared to the energy gained during the slingshot.

knowledge_points.name: binary orbital energy
knowledge_points.description: The total mechanical energy of a binary system of two equal masses M in a circular orbit of separation 2a is E = -G M^2 / (4a). This expression is differentiated to relate dE/dt to da/dt.

knowledge_points.name: chain rule differentiation
knowledge_points.description: The rate of change of the binary separation a is obtained by differentiating the orbital energy E(a) with respect to time using the chain rule: dE/dt = (dE/da)(da/dt).

knowledge_points.name: average energy loss rate from collision frequency
knowledge_points.description: The average energy loss rate of the binary is the energy lost per slingshot event multiplied by the average collision rate 1/Δt, where Δt was estimated in the previous sub-problem.

knowledge_points.name: result from previous sub-problem for collision time
knowledge_points.description: The solution imports the characteristic time between successive star-binary collisions Δt derived in part (B.3), which depends on ρ, σ, M, and G.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, write down the orbital energy of the binary system as a function of separation \(a\). reference passage on binary orbital energy gives Eq. (18.33):
\[
E_i = -G\frac{M_1 M_2}{2a}.
\]
For a supermassive black hole binary where both components have equal mass \(M\), simplify this expression to find \(E(a)\) in terms of \(M\), \(a\), and \(G\).

Next, relate the rate of change of the orbital energy to the rate of change of the separation. Because \(E\) depends on \(a\), you can use the chain rule in the same way the central‑force passage uses it to connect \(dr/dt\) and \(d\theta/dt\): 
\[
\frac{dE}{dt} = \frac{dE}{da}\,\frac{da}{dt}.
\]
Thus, once you know \(dE/da\) and \(dE/dt\), you can isolate \(da/dt\).

Differentiate your expression for \(E(a)\) with respect to \(a\) to obtain \(dE/da\). This step is straightforward calculus; keep the result symbolic.

The energy loss rate \(dE/dt\) due to gravitational slingshots was found in the previous part (B.3). Substitute that result into the chain‑rule relation. Notice that \(dE/dt\) from the slingshot estimate contains the black hole mass \(M\); when you combine it with \(dE/da\) (which also depends on \(M\)), the mass will cancel. Rearrange the equation to solve for \(da/dt\) and express the answer solely in terms of \(a\), \(\rho\), \(\sigma\), and \(G\), as the problem requests. The sign should be negative, showing that the binary hardens over time.

sub_problems.problem: (B.5) Let us denote the initial radius of the system as $a_1$ . Estimate the time $T_{SS}$ for the radius to decrease by a factor of 2 due to "gravitational slingshot". Calculate $T_{SS}$ for $\sigma =200 \, \mathrm{km/s}$ , $a_1=1 \, \mathrm{pc}$ , $\rho =10^4 M_S / \mathrm{pc}^3$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For the radius evolution we use the differential equation
\[
\frac{d a}{a^{2}}=-\frac{2\pi G\rho}{\sigma}\,dt.
\]\nIntegrating from the initial radius $a_1$ to $a_1/2$ gives
\[
\int_{a_1}^{a_1/2}\frac{da}{a^2}=-\frac{2\pi G\rho}{\sigma}\int_0^{T_{SS}}dt.
\]\nSince
\[
\int_{a_1}^{a_1/2}\frac{da}{a^2}=\left[-\frac{1}{a}\right]_{a_1}^{a_1/2}=-\frac{2}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_1}=-\frac{1}{a_1},
\]\nwe obtain
\[\nT_{SS}=\frac{\sigma}{2\pi G\rho a_1}.
\]\nNow substitute the given values:
\[
\sigma=200\,\text{km/s},\qquad a_1=1\,\text{pc},\qquad \rho=10^4\,M_S/\text{pc}^3.
\]\nThis yields
\[\nT_{SS}\approx 7.3\times 10^{-4}\,\text{Gy}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[
\boxed{T_{SS}=\frac{\sigma}{2\pi G\rho a_1}\approx 7.3\times 10^{-4}\,\text{Gy}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: gravitational slingshot orbital decay rate
knowledge_points.description: The rate of change of the binary's semi-major axis due to energy loss from gravitational slingshot encounters with stars is da/dt = -(2π G ρ / σ) a², where ρ is the stellar mass density and σ the typical stellar velocity. This result from part B.4 is the starting point for integrating the time to halve the radius.

knowledge_points.name: separation of variables
knowledge_points.description: The differential equation da/dt = f(a) is solved by rewriting it as da/f(a) = dt and integrating both sides. Here it is applied to da/dt ∝ −a² to obtain the time to go from initial radius a₁ to a₁/2.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, write down the given differential equation for the radius \(a\) as a function of time \(t\):  
\[
\frac{da}{a^2} = -\frac{2\pi G\rho}{\sigma}\,dt .
\]  
This equation relates the infinitesimal change in \(a\) to an infinitesimal time interval. The right‑hand side is constant except for \(dt\); the left depends only on \(a\).  

To find the finite time \(T_{SS}\) it takes for the radius to halve from \(a_1\) to \(a_1/2\), you can use the separation‑of‑variables technique illustrated in the first method of Morin’s textbook (where they separate \(dx/x = a\,dt\) and integrate). Here the procedure is analogous:  

1. **Separate the variables** – they are already partially separated; just integrate both sides over their respective intervals.  
   - Integrate \(da/a^2\) from the initial radius \(a = a_1\) to the final radius \(a = a_1/2\).  
   - Integrate \(dt\) from \(t = 0\) (the start) to \(t = T_{SS}\).  

2. **Set up the definite integrals** with the constant factor pulled out:  
   \[
   \int_{a_1}^{a_1/2} \frac{da}{a^2}
   = -\frac{2\pi G\rho}{\sigma} \int_{0}^{T_{SS}} dt .
   \]

3. **Evaluate the left‑hand integral**. The function \(1/a^2\) integrates to \(-1/a\). Apply the limits \(a_1\) and \(a_1/2\) carefully. You will obtain an expression involving only \(a_1\).  

4. **Evaluate the right‑hand integral** – it simply gives \(T_{SS}\).  

5. **Solve for \(T_{SS}\)** by isolating it. You will find that \(T_{SS}\) is expressed in terms of the given quantities: \(\sigma\), \(\rho\), \(a_1\), and the gravitational constant \(G\).  

Finally, **substitute the numerical values** \(\sigma = 200\,{\rm km/s}\), \(a_1 = 1\,{\rm pc}\), \(\rho = 10^4\,M_S/{\rm pc}^3\) and the known value of \(G\) (in consistent units) into your formula. Carry out the unit conversions and arithmetic to obtain a numerical estimate.  

No further physical or algebraic steps are needed – the whole procedure mirrors the “first method” from the textbook where a differential equation is solved by separating variables and integrating with prescribed limits.

title: Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary - Part C: Emission of gravitational waves
problem:
# Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary

# Introduction

The concept of gravitational waves is one of the most impressive predictions of Einstein's Theory of General Relativity. Gravitational waves are the space-time ripples propagating with the speed of light similarly to electromagnetic waves. Direct detection of gravitational waves is incredibly difficult, however, the first signal was detected on September 14, 2015, by LIGO and VIRGO collaborations.

Gravitational waves are emitted during the rapid motion of massive objects. The most powerful source of gravitational waves is the merging of two Supermassive Black Holes (SBH). Black holes predicted by Theory of General Relativity represent extremely compact objects which might have very large masses. Other specific properties of black holes will not be needed in the solution of this problem.

In the generally accepted theory of galaxies' evolution, it is supposed that there is SBH with the mass ranging from $10^{5} -10^{9}$ of Solar masses in the galaxy's center. Galaxies are huge stellar systems containing $10^{10} -10^{11}$ stars. During their evolution, two galaxies can collide and merge into one. What happens to two SBHs initially located in their centers? The evolution of the SBH binary system can be divided into three main stages. At each stage SBHs approach each other, although the underlying physical phenomena differ. We will examine these phenomena separately in the first three parts of the problem. In the fourth part, we will use the obtained relations to calculate the total time of the SBH binary system evolution.

At the end of their evolution, two SBHs will eventually approach each other and merge into a single black hole. The merging process lasts about an hour and is accompanied by an intense burst of gravitational radiation. Future observatories like LISA will be able to detect this gravitational radiation. Still, the research on the SBH evolution is under way now, at the dawn of gravitational-wave astronomy.

# General information

1. Express all your numerical answers in parsecs (pc) for the distances and giga-years (Gy) for the time intervals. We will use Solar mass $(M_S)$ as a reference mass. You might need these values:

$$\begin{array}{l} 1 \mathrm{pc} =3.1 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{m}, \\ M_{s} =2.0 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{kg}, \\ \end{array}$$

$t_H =13.7$ Gy, age of the Universe,

$$\begin{array}{l} G =6.67 \times 10^{-11} N \times m^{2} / k g^{2}, \\ c =3.0 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}. \\ \end{array}$$

2. When you encounter the word "estimate", you are not demanded the exact answer. It is sufficient to obtain a result that differs from the accurate one, not more than by a factor of 10. On the contrary, when you encounter the word "find", you are supposed to achieve the exact answer. The word "calculate" asks you to bring the numerical answer.
3. Throughout the problem, assume every star in the galaxy to have the same mass $m = M_S$ .
4. Throughout the problem we will not take into account the effects of the Theory of General Relativity except gravitational waves emission. All stars and black holes are considered as point masses governed by Newton's gravitation law.

# Part C. Emission of gravitational waves

In this part we shall study the SBH binary with equal masses which doesn't interact with the stars. Even in this case the system loses the energy due to gravitational waves emission. The energy loss rate due to gravitational waves is

$$\frac{d E}{d t} = - \frac{1024}{5} \frac{G}{c^{5}} (\omega^{3} I)^{2}, \tag{2}$$

where $\omega$ is angular velocity of the binary, and $I =2Ma^2$ is quadrupole moment of the system.

sub_problems.problem:
(C.1) Find the SBH binary radius variation rate $da/dt$ due to the emission of gravitational waves.

When the orbit radius of the SBH binary $a$ becomes close to the gravitational radius of the black hole:

$$r_{g} = \frac{2 G M}{c^{2}}, \tag{3}$$

two SBHs quickly merge.
sub_problems.solution:
For a circular binary with two equal black holes of mass $M$, the orbital angular frequency is
\[
\omega=\frac{v_{\rm bin}}{a}=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{4a^3}}.
\]\nUsing the gravitational-wave power formula, the energy loss rate is
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{64}{5}\frac{G^4M^5}{c^5a^5}.
\]\nFor a circular binary, the orbital energy is
\[\nE=-\frac{GM^2}{2a},
\]\nso
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{GM^2}{2a^2}\frac{da}{dt}.
\]\nEquating the two expressions gives
\[
\frac{GM^2}{2a^2}\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{64}{5}\frac{G^4M^5}{c^5a^5},
\]\nhence
\[
\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{256}{5}\frac{G^3M^3}{c^5a^3}.
\]\nTherefore, the binary radius decreases as
\[
\boxed{\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{256}{5}\frac{G^3M^3}{c^5a^3}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law for binary systems
knowledge_points.description: Relates the orbital angular frequency ω to the masses and orbital radius a for a circular binary of two equal masses: ω² = GM/(4a³). Used to express ω in terms of a and M in the gravitational-wave power formula.

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational wave luminosity (quadrupole formula)
knowledge_points.description: The power radiated in gravitational waves by a binary is dE/dt = -(1024/5)(G/c⁵)(ω³ I)², with I the quadrupole moment. Provided in the problem and used directly.

knowledge_points.name: Mass quadrupole moment
knowledge_points.description: For two equal point masses M each at distance a from the center of mass, the quadrupole moment is I = 2Ma², as given in the problem. Needed to evaluate the luminosity formula.

knowledge_points.name: Orbital energy of a circular binary
knowledge_points.description: The total mechanical energy of a circular binary of two equal masses with orbital radius a is E = -GM²/(4a). Differentiating this with respect to a gives dE/da, which is used with the chain rule to relate dE/dt to da/dt.

knowledge_points.name: Circular orbit
knowledge_points.description: The binary orbit is assumed circular so that the orbital radius a is well-defined and constant over one period, and the simple relations for ω and energy hold. This is implicit in the use of a single angular frequency and the given quadrupole formula.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the binary radius variation rate \(da/dt\), you need to connect three key ideas: the orbital energy of a circular binary, the gravitational-wave luminosity (energy loss rate), and the orbital frequency from Kepler’s third law. All of these are grounded in the textbook passages.

**Step 1 – Write the orbital energy for a circular binary.**  
For a binary system of two equal masses \(M\) in a circular orbit with separation \(a\), the total mechanical energy (kinetic plus potential) is given by a formula analogous to Eq. (18.33):  
\[
E = -\frac{G M^2}{2a}.
\]  
This is your starting expression for the binary’s energy at any given separation. (The passage on “Formation of Binaries with Neutron Stars or Black Holes” shows exactly this form for an arbitrary binary, and you can adapt it to the equal‑mass case.)

**Step 2 – Relate the rate of change of the orbital energy to \(da/dt\).**  
Differentiate the expression from Step 1 with respect to time. Because \(E\) depends on \(a\), the chain rule gives  
\[
\frac{dE}{dt} = \frac{dE}{da} \frac{da}{dt}.
\]  
Carry out the derivative yourself; you will obtain a relation that links \(dE/dt\) directly to \(da/dt\).

**Step 3 – Identify the gravitational‑wave luminosity (quadrupole formula).**  
The textbook passage on “Double Neutron Star Binaries” presents the general‑relativistic quadrupole formula for the energy radiated by a binary in gravitational waves. For a circular binary (\(e=0\)) the formula simplifies because the eccentricity factor \(f(e)=1\). The same passage shows that the power radiated depends on the combination \(G^4 \mu^2 M^3 / c^5 a^5\), where \(\mu\) is the reduced mass and \(M\) the total mass. For two equal masses \(M\), the reduced mass is \(\mu = M/2\). Substitute this into the luminosity expression from the passage to find \(dE/dt\) in terms of \(M\), \(a\), \(G\), and \(c\).  
(The passage uses the orbital period \(P_{\text{orb}}\); you can convert it to the orbital frequency or directly to \(a\) using Kepler’s third law, but for the quadrupole luminosity you only need the dependence on masses and separation as given.)

**Step 4 – Use Kepler’s third law to relate orbital frequency to separation (if needed).**  
The Newtonian form of Kepler’s third law,  
\[
P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G(M_1+M_2)},
\]  
appears in the textbook under “Kepler’s Laws.” For the equal‑mass circular binary, the total mass is \(2M\). The orbital angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi/P\) then becomes  
\[
\omega^2 = \frac{G(2M)}{a^3}.
\]  
This relation may be needed to express the gravitational‑wave luminosity purely in terms of \(a\) and the constants, if your luminosity formula from Step 3 still contains the orbital period or frequency.

**Step 5 – Equate the two expressions for \(dE/dt\).**  
You now have one expression for \(dE/dt\) from differentiating the orbital energy (Step 2), and a second from the quadrupole formula (Step 3). Set them equal. This equation contains \(da/dt\) as the only unknown – all other quantities are the constant masses, \(G\), \(c\), and the instantaneous separation \(a\).

**Step 6 – Solve for \(da/dt\).**  
Isolate \(da/dt\) algebraically. The result will be a simple power‑law dependence on \(a\), along with \(G\), \(M\), and \(c\). You do not need to plug in any numbers; the problem asks for the symbolic expression.

**Why this order?**  
Starting from the energy gives you the mechanical link to \(da/dt\). The quadrupole formula supplies the energy loss rate due to gravitational radiation. Equating them is the physical statement that the orbital energy decrease is exactly what powers the gravitational waves. The textbook examples (e.g., the Hulse–Taylor pulsar discussion) follow the same logic, only there the observable is the orbital period decay \(\dot{P}_{\text{orb}}\) rather than \(da/dt\). Your task is to adapt that logic to the separation \(a\) for an equal‑mass circular binary.

For a circular binary, the separation $a$ decreases due to gravitational-wave emission according to
\[
\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{256}{5}\frac{G^3M^3}{c^5a^3}.

\[\na^3\,da=-\frac{256}{5}\frac{G^3M^3}{c^5}\,dt.
\]\nIntegrate from the initial separation $a_2$ down to the final separation of order $r_g$:
\[
\int_{a_2}^{r_g} a^3\,da=-\frac{256}{5}\frac{G^3M^3}{c^5}\int_0^{T_{GW}} dt.
\]\nThus
\[
\frac{r_g^4-a_2^4}{4}=-\frac{256}{5}\frac{G^3M^3}{c^5}T_{GW},
\]\nor
\[
\frac{a_2^4-r_g^4}{4}=\frac{256}{5}\frac{G^3M^3}{c^5}T_{GW}.

\[\nT_{GW}\approx \frac{5}{1024}\frac{a_2^4c^5}{G^3M^3}.
\]\nTherefore, the time for the binary to shrink to the scale of $r_g$ is
\[
\boxed{T_{GW}=\frac{5}{1024}\frac{a_2^4c^5}{G^3M^3}}.
\]

To estimate the time \(T_{GW}\) for the binary to shrink from an initial separation \(a_2\) down to roughly the gravitational radius \(r_g\), you need to follow a process of setting up and solving a differential equation, using the concepts and formulas found in your textbook passages.

**Step 1: Identify the rate of orbital decay.**
The problem states that the shrinkage is due to the emission of gravitational waves. Your textbook provides the formula for the orbital decay rate for a binary system. The key equation, which appears in the discussion of the Hulse–Taylor pulsar, relates the rate of change of the orbital period to the system's properties. For a circular binary, this decay can be expressed in terms of the separation \(a\). The specific form you need is a differential equation for \(da/dt\) that is proportional to \(-1/a^3\), with constants involving \(G\), \(M\), and \(c\). Locate this relation in the section on "Double Neutron Star Binaries"; it is the physical law that governs how the orbit shrinks.

**Step 2: Set up the differential equation.**
Write down the decay rate equation as \(da/dt = -K / a^3\), where \(K\) is a constant you can read directly from the textbook's expression (it involves \(G\), \(M\), \(c\), and numerical factors). The minus sign indicates that the separation decreases with time. This is a first-order ordinary differential equation for \(a(t)\).

**Step 3: Solve the differential equation using separation of variables.**
The equation you have is not linear, but it is separable. The technique of "separation of variables" is introduced in your textbook's chapter on linear differential equations, but the method applies broadly: rearrange the equation so that all terms involving \(a\) are on one side and all terms involving \(t\) are on the other. You will get something of the form \(a^3 \, da = -K \, dt\). This is exactly the type of move described in the first method of your textbook, where you separate variables and then integrate.

**Step 4: Integrate both sides with the appropriate limits.**
You know the initial condition: at time \(t=0\), the separation is \(a_2\). The final condition you want is when the separation has shrunk to the order of the gravitational radius, \(r_g\), at time \(t = T_{GW}\). So integrate the left side with respect to \(a\) from \(a_2\) to \(r_g\), and the right side with respect to \(t\) from \(0\) to \(T_{GW}\). This gives you an algebraic relation involving \(a_2^4\), \(r_g^4\), and \(T_{GW}\).

**Step 5: Apply the approximation \(a_2 \gg r_g\).**
The problem explicitly notes that the initial separation is much larger than the gravitational radius. This is an "Initial separation much larger than gravitational radius" condition, similar to the assumption \(r_i \gg r_f\) used in the textbook's estimate of luminosity from an accretion disk around Sgr A*. Because \(a_2\) is vastly larger than \(r_g\), you can neglect \(r_g^4\) compared to \(a_2^4\) in your integrated expression. This simplifies the algebra significantly.

**Step 6: Isolate \(T_{GW}\).**
Solve the simplified algebraic equation for \(T_{GW}\). Your result will be an expression in terms of \(a_2\), the constant \(K\) (which itself contains \(G\), \(M\), and \(c\)), and a numerical factor from the integration. Finally, substitute the full expression for \(K\) back in to get \(T_{GW}\) as a function of \(a_2, M, c\), and \(G\), as requested.

title: Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary - Part D: Full evolution
problem:
# Evolution of Supermassive Black Holes Binary

# Introduction

The concept of gravitational waves is one of the most impressive predictions of Einstein's Theory of General Relativity. Gravitational waves are the space-time ripples propagating with the speed of light similarly to electromagnetic waves. Direct detection of gravitational waves is incredibly difficult, however, the first signal was detected on September 14, 2015, by LIGO and VIRGO collaborations.

Gravitational waves are emitted during the rapid motion of massive objects. The most powerful source of gravitational waves is the merging of two Supermassive Black Holes (SBH). Black holes predicted by Theory of General Relativity represent extremely compact objects which might have very large masses. Other specific properties of black holes will not be needed in the solution of this problem.

In the generally accepted theory of galaxies' evolution, it is supposed that there is SBH with the mass ranging from $10^{5} -10^{9}$ of Solar masses in the galaxy's center. Galaxies are huge stellar systems containing $10^{10} -10^{11}$ stars. During their evolution, two galaxies can collide and merge into one. What happens to two SBHs initially located in their centers? The evolution of the SBH binary system can be divided into three main stages. At each stage SBHs approach each other, although the underlying physical phenomena differ. We will examine these phenomena separately in the first three parts of the problem. In the fourth part, we will use the obtained relations to calculate the total time of the SBH binary system evolution.

At the end of their evolution, two SBHs will eventually approach each other and merge into a single black hole. The merging process lasts about an hour and is accompanied by an intense burst of gravitational radiation. Future observatories like LISA will be able to detect this gravitational radiation. Still, the research on the SBH evolution is under way now, at the dawn of gravitational-wave astronomy.

# General information

1. Express all your numerical answers in parsecs (pc) for the distances and giga-years (Gy) for the time intervals. We will use Solar mass $(M_S)$ as a reference mass. You might need these values:

$$\begin{array}{l} 1 \mathrm{pc} =3.1 \times 10^{16} \mathrm{m}, \\ M_{s} =2.0 \times 10^{30} \mathrm{kg}, \\ \end{array}$$

$t_H =13.7$ Gy, age of the Universe,

$$\begin{array}{l} G =6.67 \times 10^{-11} N \times m^{2} / k g^{2}, \\ c =3.0 \times 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}. \\ \end{array}$$

2. When you encounter the word "estimate", you are not demanded the exact answer. It is sufficient to obtain a result that differs from the accurate one, not more than by a factor of 10. On the contrary, when you encounter the word "find", you are supposed to achieve the exact answer. The word "calculate" asks you to bring the numerical answer.
3. Throughout the problem, assume every star in the galaxy to have the same mass $m = M_S$ .
4. Throughout the problem we will not take into account the effects of the Theory of General Relativity except gravitational waves emission. All stars and black holes are considered as point masses governed by Newton's gravitation law.

# Part D. Full evolution

In this part we will use the results obtained above. Let us consider the real astrophysical situation. Two galaxies having SBH of mass $M =10^{8}M_{S}$ in their centers merged into a new stellar system. Let the new galaxy be spherically symmetrical with radius $R =20\mathrm{kpc} =20\times 10^3\mathrm{pc}$ . Let us assume that stellar density varies with radius $r$ to the galaxy center as

$$\rho (r) = \frac{\sigma^{2}}{4 \pi G r^{2}}, \tag{4}$$

where $\sigma =200\mathrm{km / s}$

sub_problems.problem:
(D.1) Let the body move in circular orbit of radius $a < R$ in gravitational field of the stars. Neglect the force of dynamical friction and find the velocity $v$ of the body.

Immediately after the merging of galaxies two SBHs have arbitrary positions inside the new galaxy and do not affect each other. Let's consider one SBH. We assume it moves in a circular orbit of radius $a < R$ around the galaxy center and slowly loses energy due to the dynamical friction.
sub_problems.solution:
For a spherically symmetric galaxy, the gravitational field at radius $r$ is determined only by the mass enclosed within that radius. The enclosed mass is given by
\[M(r)=\int_0^r 4\pi x^2\rho(x)\,dx=\frac{\sigma^2 r}{G}.\]
Hence the gravitational acceleration is
\[g(r)=\frac{G M(r)}{r^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{r}.\]
For a body moving in a circular orbit of radius $r=a$, the centripetal acceleration must equal the gravitational acceleration:
\[
\frac{v^2}{r}=g(r)=\frac{\sigma^2}{r}.
\]
Therefore,
\[v^2=\sigma^2 \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad v=\sigma.\]
So the orbital speed is independent of radius. Final answer: \(\boxed{v=\sigma}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the orbital speed \( v \) of a body moving in a circular orbit of radius \( a < R \) in this galaxy, follow the method outlined below. This approach uses the concepts of centripetal acceleration, Newton’s law of gravitation, the shell theorem, and the specific density profile of the galaxy.

**Step 1: Relate the orbital speed to the gravitational acceleration.**
Since the body is in uniform circular motion, its centripetal acceleration is \( v^2/r \). According to the dynamics of circular motion (see reference discussion on acceleration in polar coordinates and circular motion), this centripetal acceleration must be provided by the gravitational attraction of the galaxy. Therefore, you can equate the required centripetal acceleration to the gravitational field strength at that radius.

**Step 2: Determine the gravitational field at radius \( a \).**
The galaxy is described as spherically symmetric. reference passages on Newton’s shell theorem state that for a spherically symmetric mass distribution, the gravitational force at a distance \( r \) from the center is the same as if all the mass interior to \( r \) were concentrated at the center; mass outside \( r \) contributes nothing. Thus, you need to find the mass \( M(r) \) enclosed within a sphere of radius \( r = a \).

**Step 3: Compute the enclosed mass using the given density profile.**
The problem context and reference discussion of the Milky Way’s kinematics indicate that the galaxy follows a singular isothermal sphere density profile: \( \rho(r) \propto 1/r^2 \). Specifically, reference shows that for a flat rotation curve (constant orbital speed), the density is \( \rho(r) = V^2/(4\pi G r^2) \), where \( V \) is the constant speed. In this problem, the velocity dispersion \( \sigma \) plays the role of that constant speed. The enclosed mass is found by integrating this density over the volume interior to \( r \):
\[
M(r) = \int_0^r 4\pi x^2 \rho(x)\, dx.
\]
Carrying out this integration will yield an expression for \( M(r) \) in terms of \( \sigma \), \( r \), and \( G \). (reference example leading to reference.49 illustrates exactly this calculation.)

**Step 4: Apply Newton’s law of universal gravitation.**
With the enclosed mass \( M(a) \) known, the magnitude of the gravitational force on a body of mass \( m \) at radius \( a \) is \( F = G\, M(a)\, m / a^2 \). The gravitational acceleration (field strength) is then \( g(a) = F/m = G\, M(a) / a^2 \).

**Step 5: Equate centripetal acceleration and gravitational acceleration.**
Set the centripetal acceleration \( v^2/a \) equal to the gravitational acceleration \( g(a) \) you just found:
\[
\frac{v^2}{a} = \frac{G\, M(a)}{a^2}.
\]
Substitute your expression for \( M(a) \) from Step 3 into this equation. Notice that the radius \( a \) will cancel out, reflecting the fact that the rotation curve is flat—the orbital speed is independent of radius, as discussed in reference passage on the flat rotation curve.

**Step 6: Solve for the orbital speed \( v \).**
After the cancellation, solve the resulting equation for \( v \). You should find that \( v \) is expressed solely in terms of the velocity dispersion \( \sigma \), a quantity characterizing the galaxy’s gravitational potential. The final step is straightforward algebra.

sub_problems.problem:
(D.2) Estimate the orbit radius variation rate $da/dt$ . In part A we ignored the velocities of the stars. Although stars are moving in the real galaxy, not all of them have exactly the same speed $\sigma$ . Instead, the speed of the stars is only of the order of $\sigma$ , and so is the relative speed of SBH with respect to the stars, hence you can use the result obtained in A.3 for estimation. You should use the density $\rho(r)$ from equation (4). Assume $\log \Lambda$ to be a constant calculated in A.4.

After a certain time, two SBH will approach the center of the galaxy. Let two SBH move in a circular orbit of radius $a$ around the center galaxy in the gravitational field of the stars.
sub_problems.solution:
For a circular orbit in the galaxy potential, the orbital speed is constant and of order \(\sigma\). Hence the kinetic energy of the black hole is constant, so
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=\frac{dU}{dt}=\frac{dU}{da}\frac{da}{dt}.
\]
The gravitational field of the stellar background gives
\[
\frac{dU}{da}=Mg(a)=\frac{M\sigma^{2}}{a}.
\]
The energy loss due to dynamical friction is the power of the friction force:
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=-F_{\mathrm{df}}v.
\]
Using the result for dynamical friction from part A,
\[F_{\mathrm{df}}=4\pi G^{2}M^{2}\frac{\rho(a)}{\sigma^{2}}\ln\Lambda,
\]
and taking \(v\sim \sigma\), we obtain
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=-4\pi G^{2}M^{2}\frac{\rho(a)}{\sigma}\ln\Lambda.
\]
With the density profile \(\rho(a)=\dfrac{\sigma^{2}}{4\pi G a^{2}}\), this becomes
\[
\frac{dE}{dt}=-\frac{GM^{2}\sigma\ln\Lambda}{a^{2}}.
\]
Equating the two expressions for \(dE/dt\),
\[
\frac{M\sigma^{2}}{a}\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{GM^{2}\sigma\ln\Lambda}{a^{2}}.
\]
Solving for \(da/dt\),
\[
\boxed{\frac{da}{dt}=-\frac{GM\ln\Lambda}{a\sigma}}.
\]
