knowledge_points.name: Schwarzschild radius
knowledge_points.description: The event horizon radius of a non‑rotating black hole is given by R_s = 3 (M/M_sun) km, as supplied in the problem. This formula is needed to obtain the physical diameter of the black hole.

knowledge_points.name: Small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small angular diameters, the angular size θ is the physical size divided by the distance. The solution uses this to express the black hole's angular diameter as θ_BH = 2R_s / L.

knowledge_points.name: Rayleigh criterion
knowledge_points.description: The diffraction‑limited angular resolution of a telescope with a circular aperture of diameter D is θ = 1.22 λ / D. This sets the minimum resolvable angle for the Earth‑sized interferometer.

knowledge_points.name: Resolution condition
knowledge_points.description: To resolve an object, the instrument's angular resolution must be at most the angular size of the object. The solution adopts the marginal case θ_BH = θ_tel to find the required wavelength.

knowledge_points.name: Earth-sized VLBI aperture
knowledge_points.description: The problem states an Earth‑sized telescope using Very Long Baseline Interferometry. The solution accordingly takes the effective aperture diameter to be the Earth's diameter D = 2R_e.

knowledge_points.name: Non-rotating black hole
knowledge_points.description: The black hole is assumed to be non‑rotating (Schwarzschild metric), which justifies using the given Schwarzschild radius formula. This is explicitly stated in the problem.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the wavelength needed to resolve the event horizon, work in two parallel tracks: one for the angular size of the object (the black hole’s event horizon) and one for the angular resolution of the telescope. Then set them equal to find the required wavelength.

**Track 1 — Angular size of the event horizon.**  
The problem gives you the Schwarzschild radius for a non‑rotating black hole as \(R_s = 3(M/\mathrm{M}_\odot)\) km. From reference passage on the Schwarzschild radius (Carroll & Ostlie, reference.27 and the surrounding discussion), you know this is the radius of the event horizon. The diameter is therefore \(2R_s\). The black hole is at a distance \(L = 8.5\) kpc from the Sun. Because this distance is huge compared with the size of the black hole, the small‑angle approximation applies — the angular diameter \(\theta_{\mathrm{BH}}\) is simply the physical diameter divided by the distance. (reference passages on the small‑angle approximation show that for small angles, \(\sin x \approx x\) and the angle in radians is essentially the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side.) So you can write \(\theta_{\mathrm{BH}} = \frac{2R_s}{L}\).

**Track 2 — Angular resolution of the telescope.**  
The telescope is “Earth‑sized,” meaning its diameter \(D\) is the Earth’s diameter \(2R_e\) (use the Earth’s radius). The fundamental limit on resolution comes from diffraction. reference passage on the Rayleigh criterion (Carroll & Ostlie, reference.1) gives the condition for the first minimum of a single‑slit (or circular aperture) diffraction pattern: \(\sin\theta = \lambda/D\). For a circular aperture, the standard form is \(\theta_{\mathrm{tel}} = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}\). This is exactly the formula used in reference’s radio‑telescope example (Example 6.3.2). Apply it here with \(D = 2R_e\).

**Combining the two tracks.**  
To just resolve the event horizon, the angular size must be at least as large as the telescope’s resolution limit. The marginal case is \(\theta_{\mathrm{BH}} = \theta_{\mathrm{tel}}\). Substitute the expressions from Track 1 and Track 2 into this equality. You will get an equation where the only unknown is \(\lambda\). Rearrange it to isolate \(\lambda\) on one side. The result will involve \(R_e\), \(R_s\), and \(L\), along with the numerical factor 1.22.

**Carrying out the calculation (you do this).**  
- Compute \(R_s\) from the given mass using the formula provided in the problem.  
- Convert the distance \(L\) from kiloparsecs to kilometers (1 pc = \(3.086 \times 10^{13}\) km; you may need to look up or recall that 1 kpc = \(10^3\) pc).  
- Use the Earth’s radius \(R_e \approx 6371\) km.  
- Plug everything into your rearranged expression for \(\lambda\).

The answer will come out in kilometers; convert to millimeters to see what part of the electromagnetic spectrum is required. This approach mirrors the logic of reference’s radio‑resolution example, but applied to an astrophysical source whose size is given by the Schwarzschild radius.

title: Photon detection rate from a star
problem:
A star has a measured I-band magnitude of 22.0. How many photons per second are detected from this star by the Gemini Telescope (8m diameter)? Assume that the overall quantum efficiency is $40\%$ and the filter passband is flat.

Filter $\lambda_0(nm)$ $\Delta \lambda (nm)$ $F_{\mathrm{VEGA}}(Wm^{-2}nm^{-1})$

$I$ $8.00\times 10^{2}$ 24.0 $8.30\times 10^{-12}$
solution:
The definition of magnitude is:
$$
m_I = -2.5 \lg F_I + \text{const}
$$
where $F_I$ is the flux received from the source. Using the Vega data ($m_I=0$, $F_{\mathrm{VEGA}}=8.30\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}$):
$$
0.0 = -2.5 \lg(8.30\times10^{-12}) + \text{const}
$$
$$
\text{const} = 2.5 \lg(8.30\times10^{-12}) \approx -27.7
$$
Thus for the star with $m_I=22.0$:
$$
22.0 = -2.5 \lg F_I -27.7
$$
$$
\lg F_I = \frac{22.0+27.7}{-2.5} = -19.88
$$
$$
F_I = 10^{-19.88} \approx 1.32\times10^{-20}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}
$$
The energy of a photon at the effective wavelength $\lambda_0=800\,\mathrm{nm}$:
$$
E_\gamma = \frac{hc}{\lambda_0} = \frac{6.626\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^8}{800\times10^{-9}} \approx 2.48\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}
$$
Photon flux per unit area per unit wavelength:
$$
N_I = \frac{F_I}{E_\gamma} = \frac{1.32\times10^{-20}}{2.48\times10^{-19}} \approx 5.32\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{photons\,s^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}
$$
Total detected photons per second:
$$
N_{\text{total}} = (\text{telescope area}) \times \text{QE} \times \text{bandwidth} \times N_I
$$
$$
= (\pi\times(4\,\mathrm{m})^2) \times 0.40 \times 24\,\mathrm{nm} \times 5.32\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{photons\,s^{-1}\,m^{-2}\,nm^{-1}}
$$
$$
\approx 50.27 \times 0.40 \times 24 \times 5.32\times10^{-2} \approx 25.7\,\mathrm{photons/s}
$$
\boxed{26\,\mathrm{photons/s}}

knowledge_points.name: Pogson's magnitude equation (Vega system)
knowledge_points.description: The apparent magnitude m in the Vega system is defined as m = -2.5 log10(F/F_Vega), where F is the flux of the source and F_Vega is the flux of Vega in the same band (Vega has m=0). Used here to convert the given I-band magnitude 22.0 into a spectral energy flux density.

knowledge_points.name: Photon energy
knowledge_points.description: The energy of a single photon is E = hc/λ, with Planck's constant h and speed of light c. Needed to convert the energy flux into a photon flux.

knowledge_points.name: Photon flux from spectral energy flux
knowledge_points.description: For a source with spectral energy flux density F_λ (energy per unit time per unit area per unit wavelength) and a flat filter passband of width Δλ, the total photon flux per unit area is approximately F_λ Δλ / (hc/λ0), where λ0 is the effective wavelength. This assumes the photon energy is constant across the band.

knowledge_points.name: Telescope collecting area
knowledge_points.description: The collecting area of a telescope with diameter D is A = πD²/4. The total photon flux collected is the incident photon flux per unit area multiplied by this area.

knowledge_points.name: Quantum efficiency
knowledge_points.description: The quantum efficiency (QE) of a detector is the fraction of incident photons that are detected. The detected photon rate is the incident photon rate multiplied by the QE.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the detected photon rate, you need to combine several ideas from your reading in a specific order. Work step by step, and handle each conversion only when the quantity it provides is required next.

1. **Convert the star’s magnitude to a monochromatic flux**  
   The apparent magnitude scale (from *Carroll & Ostlie, Section 3.2*) is defined so that a difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to a factor of 100 in brightness. For a star and Vega, whose I‑band magnitude is 0.0 and whose calibrated flux is given in the table, the flux ratio satisfies  
   \[
   \frac{F_{\text{star}}}{F_{\text{Vega}}} = 100^{-(m_{\text{star}} - m_{\text{Vega}})/5}
   \]  
   or equivalently using the modern logarithmic form \( m_1 - m_2 = -2.5\log_{10}(F_1/F_2) \).  
   Using the provided Vega flux \(F_{\text{Vega}}\) (in W m⁻² nm⁻¹), calculate the monochromatic flux per unit wavelength for the star. This is the first conversion.

2. **Find the total flux per unit area in the I‑band**  
   The filter passband is flat, so the total flux at the top of the atmosphere integrated over the band is simply the monochromatic flux from step 1 multiplied by the bandwidth \(\Delta\lambda\) given in the table. You now have \(F_{\text{total}}\) in W m⁻².

3. **Compute the energy of a single I‑band photon**  
   The quantum nature of light (discussed in *Eisberg & Resnick* and in the Bohr atom section of *Kleppner & Kolenkow*) gives \(E_{\text{photon}} = h\nu = hc/\lambda_0\).  
   Use the effective wavelength \(\lambda_0\) from the table; Planck’s constant \(h\) and the speed of light \(c\) are standard. This yields joules per photon.

4. **Convert the total flux to a photon flux**  
   Divide the total flux per unit area from step 2 by the photon energy from step 3 to get the number of photons per second per square meter arriving at Earth.

5. **Account for the telescope’s light‑gathering power**  
   The amount of light collected is proportional to the collecting area (*Palen, Schaum’s Outline*, and *Carroll & Ostlie, Section 6.1*). For a circular primary mirror of diameter \(D = 8\,\text{m}\), the area is \(\pi (D/2)^2\). Multiply the photon flux from step 4 by this area to obtain the total photons per second incident on the telescope.

6. **Apply the quantum efficiency**  
   Only a fraction of the incident photons are actually detected. The problem states the overall quantum efficiency is \(40\%\). Modern CCDs can have very high QE (*Carroll & Ostlie, Section 6.2*), but here you simply multiply the incident photon rate by \(0.40\) to get the detected photon rate.

By following this sequence—magnitude → flux per unit wavelength, bandwidth → total energy flux, photon energy → photon flux, area → incident photon rate, QE → detected photon rate—you will arrive at the answer without skipping any physical reasoning.

title: Vertical exponential density profile of G-type main-sequence stars
problem: Assuming that the G-type main-sequence stars (such as the Sun) in the disc of the Milky Way obey a vertical exponential density profile with a scale height of 300pc, by what factor does the density of these stars change at 0.5 and 1.5kpc from the mid-plane relative to the density in the mid-plane?
solution:
The vertical exponential density profile is given by $n(z) = n_0 \exp(-|z|/h_z)$, where $h_z = 300\,\mathrm{pc}$ is the scale height. For $z = 0.5\,\mathrm{kpc} = 500\,\mathrm{pc}$:
$$
n(500\,\mathrm{pc}) = n_0 \exp(-500/300) = n_0 e^{-5/3} \approx 0.189\,n_0.
$$
Thus the density at 0.5 kpc is about $0.189$ times the mid-plane density, i.e., $\boxed{0.189}$.

For $z = 1.5\,\mathrm{kpc} = 1500\,\mathrm{pc}$:
$$
n(1500\,\mathrm{pc}) = n_0 \exp(-1500/300) = n_0 e^{-5} \approx 0.00674\,n_0.
$$
Thus the density at 1.5 kpc is about $0.00674$ times the mid-plane density, i.e., $\boxed{0.00674}$.

knowledge_points.name: vertical exponential density profile
knowledge_points.description: For a stellar disc obeying a vertical exponential density profile, the number density n at a distance z from the mid-plane is n(z) = n_0 exp(-|z|/h_z), where n_0 is the mid-plane density and h_z is the scale height (the vertical distance over which the density drops by a factor of e).

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem describes a vertical exponential density profile for G-type main-sequence stars, with a scale height of \(300\,\text{pc}\). This is the same mathematical form you encountered in the textbook for the thin disk component (Eq. 24.9 and Table 24.1), where the number density \(n\) at a height \(|z|\) above the mid‑plane is given by  
\[
n(z) = n_0 \, e^{-|z|/h_z},
\]  
with \(n_0\) the mid‑plane density and \(h_z\) the scale height (the distance over which the density drops by a factor of \(e^{-1}\)).  

You are asked for the *factor* by which the density changes relative to the mid‑plane, which is simply the ratio \(n(z)/n_0\). From the exponential law this ratio is \(e^{-|z|/h_z}\); you do not need to know \(n_0\) itself.

Follow these steps:

1. Write down the ratio: \(\displaystyle \frac{n(z)}{n_0} = e^{-|z|/h_z}\) with \(h_z = 300\,\text{pc}\).  
2. For each height given, first convert the distance to parsecs to match the units of \(h_z\):  
   - \(0.5\,\text{kpc} = 500\,\text{pc}\)  
   - \(1.5\,\text{kpc} = 1500\,\text{pc}\)  
3. Substitute \(z\) into the exponent \((-|z|/h_z)\) and evaluate the exponential using your calculator. That exponential value is the factor you need.  
4. Do this separately for the two heights; the result is the factor by which the density at that height differs from the mid‑plane density.

No other physics is required—just the definition of the exponential vertical profile as presented in your textbook for the disk components. Let the numerical evaluation be your own.

title: Mars Great Opposition Date Estimation
problem: Mars arrived at its great opposition at UT $17^{h}56^{m}$ Aug.28, 2003. The next great opposition of Mars will be in 2018, estimate the date of that opposition. The semi-major axis of the orbit of Mars is 1.524 AU.
solution: First, compute the orbital period of Mars using Kepler's third law: $T_M = \sqrt{\frac{R_M^3}{R_E^3}} T_E = \sqrt{1.524^3} \times 1 \text{ year} = 1.881 \text{ years}$. The synodic period $T_s$ (time between oppositions) satisfies $\frac{1}{T_s} = \frac{1}{T_E} - \frac{1}{T_M}$, so $T_s = \frac{T_E T_M}{T_M - T_E} = \frac{1.881}{0.881} \times 365.25 \text{ days} = 779.8 \text{ days}$. From Aug.28, 2003 to Aug.28, 2018 is $15 \times 365 + 4 = 5479 \text{ days}$. The number of synodic periods in this interval is $5479 / 779.8 = 7.026$, so 7 full oppositions occur before Aug.28, 2018. The remaining time is $5479 - 7 \times 779.8 = 20.4 \text{ days}$, meaning the next great opposition is 20.4 days before Aug.28, 2018, i.e., on Aug.7, 2018. \boxed{\text{Aug.7, 2018}}

sub_problems.guidance:
To estimate the date of the next great opposition, you need to find how many oppositions occur between the given date in 2003 and the target year 2018, then determine the remaining time to pinpoint the exact date. This involves three main steps: finding Mars’s orbital period, computing the time between successive oppositions (the synodic period), and counting how many synodic periods fit in the interval.

First, use Kepler’s third law to find the sidereal period of Mars. reference states that for objects orbiting the Sun, when the period is measured in years and the semi-major axis in astronomical units, the law simplifies to \(P^2 = a^3\) (see the “Kepler’s third law” passage). You are given the semi-major axis of Mars’s orbit as 1.524 AU. Apply the formula with Earth’s period as 1 year to find Mars’s period. This step mirrors the idea in reference’s Table 10.1, which shows that the ratio \(a^3 / P^2\) is constant for all planets.

Next, compute the synodic period—the time between oppositions. Since Mars is a superior planet (its orbit lies outside Earth’s), reference provides the relationship for superior planets: \(1/S = 1/P_{\oplus} - 1/P\), where \(S\) is the synodic period, \(P_{\oplus}\) is Earth’s sidereal period (1 year), and \(P\) is the planet’s sidereal period (see the “Synodic period formula for superior planet” passage). Substitute the periods you have into this formula to find \(S\). The result will be in years; convert it to days using the fact that a year is about 365.25 days long, as noted in reference’s discussion of the year (the “Year-to-day conversion” passage).

Now, determine the time interval between the given opposition date (August 28, 2003) and the same date in 2018. Count the number of days in this 15‑year span, accounting for leap years appropriately, using the 365.25‑day year as a guide. Then, divide this total number of days by the synodic period \(S\) (in days) to find how many full synodic periods fit into the interval. The integer part of this quotient tells you how many oppositions occur before August 28, 2018. Multiply that integer by \(S\) and subtract the product from the total interval to find the remaining days.

title: Ratio of radii from brightness difference and temperatures
problem: The difference in brightness between two main sequence stars in an open cluster is 2 magnitudes. Their effective temperatures are 6000K and 5000K respectively. Estimate the ratio of their radii.
solution:
Let the brighter star have radius $R_{\max}$ and temperature $T_{\max}=6000\,\mathrm{K}$, and the fainter star have radius $R_{\min}$ and temperature $T_{\min}=5000\,\mathrm{K}$. The luminosity of a star is $L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4$. The magnitude difference is $\Delta m = -2.5\lg(L_{\min}/L_{\max})$. Substituting the luminosity expressions:
$$
\Delta m = -2.5\lg\left(\frac{4\pi R_{\min}^2 \sigma T_{\min}^4}{4\pi R_{\max}^2 \sigma T_{\max}^4}\right) = -2.5\lg\left(\frac{R_{\min}^2}{R_{\max}^2}\cdot\frac{T_{\min}^4}{T_{\max}^4}\right) = -5\lg\left(\frac{R_{\min}}{R_{\max}}\right) -10\lg\left(\frac{T_{\min}}{T_{\max}}\right).
$$
Given $\Delta m = 2$, solve for $\lg(R_{\min}/R_{\max})$:
$$
\lg\left(\frac{R_{\min}}{R_{\max}}\right) = -0.2\Delta m - 2\lg\left(\frac{T_{\min}}{T_{\max}}\right) = -0.2\times 2 - 2\lg\left(\frac{5000}{6000}\right) = -0.4 - 2\lg\left(\frac{5}{6}\right).
$$
$\lg(5/6) \approx \lg 0.8333 \approx -0.07918$, so $-2\times(-0.07918)=0.15836$. Thus $\lg(R_{\min}/R_{\max}) \approx -0.4 + 0.15836 = -0.24164$. Hence
$$
\frac{R_{\min}}{R_{\max}} = 10^{-0.24164} \approx 0.573.
$$
Therefore the ratio of the smaller radius to the larger radius is approximately $0.57$.

\boxed{\frac{R_{\min}}{R_{\max}} \approx 0.57}

knowledge_points.name: Luminosity of a spherical blackbody
knowledge_points.description: The total power radiated by a star is L = 4πR²σT⁴, where R is radius and T is effective temperature. This formula relates luminosity to radius and temperature, allowing the magnitude difference to be expressed in terms of the radius ratio.

knowledge_points.name: Magnitude-luminosity relation
knowledge_points.description: The difference in apparent magnitude between two stars at the same distance is Δm = -2.5 log10(L1/L2). This converts the given 2-magnitude difference into a luminosity ratio.

knowledge_points.name: Equal distance in open cluster
knowledge_points.description: Stars in an open cluster are at approximately the same distance from Earth, so the ratio of their apparent brightness equals the ratio of their luminosities. This justifies using the magnitude difference directly to compare luminosities without distance corrections.

knowledge_points.name: Main sequence temperature-luminosity relation
knowledge_points.description: On the main sequence, a star's luminosity increases with its effective temperature. This allows identifying the 6000 K star as the brighter one and the 5000 K star as the fainter one, which is necessary to assign the temperatures correctly in the luminosity ratio and obtain a unique numerical radius ratio.

sub_problems.guidance:
**Goal:** Use the given magnitude difference and the effective temperatures to find the ratio of the radii of the two main‑sequence stars. Both stars belong to the same open cluster, so they are at essentially the same distance, which simplifies the magnitude‑luminosity relation.

**Step 1: Connect the magnitude difference to the luminosity ratio.**
- From the magnitude scale (see the discussion around Eq. 3.7 in the textbook), the difference in apparent magnitudes between two stars at the same distance is linked to their luminosity ratio. If star 1 is the brighter star (smaller magnitude) and star 2 is the fainter star, the magnitude difference \(\Delta m = m_2 - m_1\) is given as 2 magnitudes.
- In the textbook passage you studied, Eq. (3.7) alone is enough, but the key relationship is that for two stars at the same distance,  
  \( \displaystyle 100^{(m_1-m_2)/5} = \frac{L_2}{L_1} \)  
  or, equivalently, \( m_2 - m_1 = -2.5 \log_{10}(L_2/L_1) \).  
- Because the cluster stars share the same distance, the flux ratio equals the luminosity ratio. Therefore, rearrange the magnitude equation to express \(\log_{10}(L_{\text{faint}}/L_{\text{bright}})\) in terms of \(\Delta m\).

**Step 2: Express the luminosity of each star with the Stefan–Boltzmann law.**
- The textbook gives the luminosity of a spherical blackbody (a good approximation for a star) in Eq. (3.17):  
  \[
  L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T_e^4,
  \]
  where \(T_e\) is the effective temperature. Example 3.4.2 illustrates exactly this formula applied to the Sun.
- Write this expression for the brighter star (temperature 6000 K) and for the fainter star (temperature 5000 K). Form the ratio \(L_{\text{faint}} / L_{\text{bright}}\). All the constants (\(4\pi\), \(\sigma\)) cancel, leaving a combination of the radii squared and the temperatures raised to the fourth power:
  \[
  \frac{L_{\text{faint}}}{L_{\text{bright}}} = \left(\frac{R_{\text{faint}}}{R_{\text{bright}}}\right)^2 \left(\frac{T_{\text{faint}}}{T_{\text{bright}}}\right)^4.
  \]

**Step 3: Equate the two expressions for the luminosity ratio and solve for the radius ratio.**
- Set the luminosity ratio from the magnitude difference equal to the expression from the Stefan–Boltzmann law.
- Take base‑10 logarithms of both sides. Use the logarithm identities \(\log(ab) = \log a + \log b\) and \(\log(x^n) = n \log x\) to break the right‑hand side into terms containing \(\log(R_{\text{faint}}/R_{\text{bright}})\) and \(\log(T_{\text{faint}}/T_{\text{bright}})\).
- Isolate \(\log(R_{\text{faint}}/R_{\text{bright}})\). You will obtain a formula involving \(\Delta m\) and the temperatures. The general form is:
  \[
  \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{R_{\text{faint}}}{R_{\text{bright}}}\right) = -0.4\,\Delta m - 2\log_{10}\!\left(\frac{T_{\text{faint}}}{T_{\text{bright}}}\right).
  \]
  (Check the factor carefully from your own algebra; it arises because \( -2.5\log_{10}(L_2/L_1) = \Delta m \) and the squared radii give a factor 2 in the log.)

**Step 4: Insert the given numbers and compute.**
- Put \(\Delta m = 2\), \(T_{\text{bright}} = 6000\ \text{K}\), \(T_{\text{faint}} = 5000\ \text{K}\) into the formula.
- First compute the log of the temperature ratio, then multiply by \(-2\). Combine with the \(-0.4 \times 2\) term. The result is \(\log_{10}(R_{\text{faint}}/R_{\text{bright}})\).
- Finally, find the ratio by evaluating \(10^{\text{that log value}}\).

(You can also solve for the inverse ratio, if preferred, by adjusting the sign. The estimation requested is the ratio of their radii, normally expressed as a number smaller than 1 if the fainter star is the smaller one.)

**What about the “main‑sequence temperature–luminosity relation”?**  
The problem tells you that both stars are on the main sequence. The textbook passage (Sec. 8.2) discusses that main‑sequence stars follow a clear relation between luminosity and temperature, but here you do not need an extra equation because the temperatures are given directly. The Stefan–Boltzmann law and the magnitude relation alone are sufficient to find the radius ratio. The main‑sequence context mainly assures you that the effective temperatures are meaningful and that the two stars can be compared consistently.

title: Estimate the effective temperature of the photosphere of the Sun using the naked eye colour of the Sun
problem: Estimate the effective temperature of the photosphere of the Sun using the naked eye colour of the Sun.
solution:
The Wien law is

$$
\lambda_{\max} = \frac{0.29}{T} \, (\text{cm})
$$

Using the typical wavelength of visible light corresponding to the Sun's colour (yellow-green), we take \(\lambda_{\max} \approx 550 \, \text{nm} = 550 \times 10^{-9} \, \text{m}\). Then

$$
T = \frac{0.29}{550 \times 10^{-9}} = 5272 \, \text{K} \approx 5300 \, \text{K}.
$$

Alternatively, using \(\lambda_{\max} \approx 500 \, \text{nm}\) gives \(T \approx 5800 \, \text{K}\). The accepted range is 5200–6000 K.

\boxed{T \approx 5300 \, \text{K}}

sub_problems.guidance:
Your task is to estimate the Sun’s photospheric (effective) temperature from the colour you see with your unaided eye. reference passages give you all the tools you need, so let’s walk through the reasoning step by step.

**Step 1 – Identify the dominant wavelength from colour**
The problem tells you to use the “naked eye colour of the Sun.” reference passage *VISIBLE LIGHT AND COLOR* reminds you that colour is related to wavelength: longer wavelengths are redder, shorter wavelengths are bluer. You need to decide what colour the Sun appears to be (typically described as yellow-white or yellow-green) and then locate the corresponding wavelength in the visible spectrum. The same passage includes Fig. 1‑3, which maps colours to approximate wavelength ranges; for example, green light lies roughly between 491 nm and 575 nm. You should pick a representative wavelength for the Sun’s colour and convert it to metres (or keep it in nanometres, as long as you are consistent with the formula in the next step).

**Step 2 – Relate wavelength to temperature via Wien’s displacement law**
reference section *The Connection between Color and Temperature* introduces Wien’s displacement law, Eq. (3.15):

\[
\lambda_{\max} T = 0.002897755\ \text{m·K}.
\]

This law says that the wavelength at which a blackbody spectrum peaks is inversely proportional to the temperature. The Sun is approximated as a blackbody, so the colour you see (which corresponds to the peak of its continuous spectrum) can be used as \(\lambda_{\max}\) in this equation.

**Step 3 – Rearrange and estimate the temperature**
You now have a chosen \(\lambda_{\max}\) (in metres) from Step 1. Rearrange Wien’s law to solve for the temperature:

\[
T = \frac{0.002897755\ \text{m·K}}{\lambda_{\max}}.
\]

Substitute your wavelength into this expression and carry out the arithmetic. This directly yields an estimate of the Sun’s effective temperature, because the photosphere radiates roughly as a blackbody.

**Step 4 – Check consistency with reference examples**
reference already applies this exact method to the Sun in Example 3.4.2, where it uses the known effective temperature (5777 K) to find \(\lambda_{\max} \approx 501.6\ \text{nm}\) in the green region. Your calculation reverses that logic: you start with the colour/wavelength and recover a temperature. Your result should fall in the same neighbourhood (a few thousand kelvin). If you wish, you can also compare your answer with the range implied by different reasonable choices of the Sun’s colour (e.g., slightly more yellow or slightly more green) to see how the estimate varies.

By following these steps—colour → wavelength → Wien’s law → temperature—you can complete the estimate using only the concepts and formulas explicitly given in the provided reference passages.

title: Ratio of Annular to Total Solar Eclipses
problem: On average, the visual diameter of the Moon is slightly less than that of the Sun, so the frequency of annular solar eclipses is slightly higher than total solar eclipses. For an observer on the Earth, the longest total solar eclipse duration is about 7.5 minutes, and the longest annular eclipse duration is about 12.5 minutes. Here, the longest duration is the time interval from the second contact to the third contact. Suppose we count the occurrences of both types of solar eclipses for a very long time, estimate the ratio of the occurrences of annular solar eclipses and total solar eclipses. Assume the orbit of the Earth to be circular and the eccentricity of the Moon's orbit is 0.0549. Count all hybrid eclipses as annular eclipses.
solution:
Let the semi-major axis of the Moon's orbit be $a$, eccentricity $e = 0.0549$, orbital period $T$. The apparent angular radius of the Moon is $r$, of the Sun is $R$. At perigee, distance $d_1 = a(1-e)$, angular radius $r_1$, linear velocity $v_1$, angular velocity $\omega_1 = v_1/d_1$. The longest total eclipse duration (from second to third contact) is $t_1 = 2(r_1 - R)/\omega_1$. At apogee, $d_2 = a(1+e)$, $r_2$, $v_2$, $\omega_2 = v_2/d_2$, and longest annular eclipse duration $t_2 = 2(R - r_2)/\omega_2$. From conservation of angular momentum, $v_2/v_1 = d_1/d_2 = (1-e)/(1+e)$. Hence
$$
\frac{t_2}{t_1} = \frac{R - r_2}{r_1 - R} \times \left(\frac{1+e}{1-e}\right)^2.
$$

During a lunar orbit, the apparent radius $r$ varies inversely with distance $d$. Since $e$ is small, assume $r$ changes linearly with time $t$ from perigee ($t=0$):
$$
r = r_2 + \frac{2(r_1 - r_2)}{T} t, \quad 0 \le t < T/2.
$$
Set $r = R$ to find the critical time $t_R$:
$$
t_R = \frac{R - r_2}{2(r_1 - r_2)} T.
$$
For $t \in (t_R, T - t_R)$, $r > R$ and central eclipses are total; the time interval is $\Delta t_T = T - 2t_R$. For $t \in [0, t_R] \cup [T - t_R, T]$, $r \le R$ and central eclipses are annular; $\Delta t_A = 2t_R$. The probability of a central eclipse occurring at any time is uniform, so the ratio of counts is
$$
\frac{f_A}{f_T} = \frac{\Delta t_A}{\Delta t_T} = \frac{2t_R}{T - 2t_R} = \frac{R - r_2}{r_1 - R} = \frac{t_2}{t_1} \Big/ \left(\frac{1+e}{1-e}\right)^2.
$$
Substituting $t_1 = 7.5$ min, $t_2 = 12.5$ min, $e = 0.0549$:
$$
\frac{R - r_2}{r_1 - R} = \frac{12.5}{7.5} \times \left(\frac{1-0.0549}{1+0.0549}\right)^2 \approx 1.6667 \times (0.8959)^2 \approx 1.6667 \times 0.8026 \approx 1.338.
$$
Thus
$$
\frac{f_A}{f_T} \approx 1.338 \approx \frac{4}{3}.
$$

\boxed{\frac{f_A}{f_T} \approx \frac{4}{3}}

sub_problems.guidance:
Use the longest given eclipse durations, which occur at the orbital extremes (perigee and apogee), to relate the Moon’s changing angular size to the Sun’s fixed angular size \(R\).

**First, model the eclipse durations.**  
The central eclipse duration from second to third contact (reference: Carroll & Ostlie §7.3, the binary‑eclipse chord idea) gives the time for the Moon’s disk to sweep across the Sun’s disk. In angular terms, the chord length is twice the difference between the Moon’s angular radius \(r\) and the solar radius \(R\). So  
- For the longest total eclipse (perigee, \(r_1 > R\)): \(t_1 = 2(r_1-R)/\omega_1\)  
- For the longest annular eclipse (apogee, \(r_2 < R\)): \(t_2 = 2(R-r_2)/\omega_2\)

Here \(\omega_1\) and \(\omega_2\) are the Moon’s angular speeds relative to the Earth–Sun direction at those points.

**Then, bring in Kepler’s laws for elliptical motion.**  
At perigee and apogee the velocity is perpendicular to the line of sight, and angular momentum is conserved (Second Law, Morin §6.4.4: \(\mathrm{d}A/\mathrm{d}t = L/2m\) constant). From \(v_1 d_1 = v_2 d_2\) with the distances \(d_1 = a(1-e),\; d_2 = a(1+e)\), the ratio of angular speeds is  
\[
\frac{\omega_2}{\omega_1} = \frac{v_2/d_2}{v_1/d_1} = \frac{d_1}{d_2} \cdot \frac{v_2}{v_1} = \left(\frac{1-e}{1+e}\right)^2 .
\]
Form the ratio \(t_2/t_1\) from the duration formulas, substitute this speed ratio, and algebraically isolate the quantity \((R-r_2)/(r_1-R)\). You will obtain an expression that still contains the known \(t_2, t_1\), and the eccentricity factor.

**Now switch to the long‑term occurrence ratio.**  
Because the eccentricity is small, approximate that the Moon’s apparent angular radius changes linearly with time between apogee and perigee (the “linear approximation” idea applied to angular size). Over half an orbit (period \(T\)), \(r\) sweeps uniformly from \(r_2\) to \(r_1\). When a central eclipse happens at a random moment, it is annular if \(r<R\) and total if \(r>R\). Using the linear law to find the critical time when \(r=R\) lets you compute the fraction of time the Moon spends with \(r<R\) versus \(r>R\). The ratio of annular to total central‑eclipse counts then equals the ratio of the corresponding time intervals:

\[
\frac{f_A}{f_T} = \frac{2t_R}{T-2t_R} = \frac{R-r_2}{r_1-R} .
\]

**Finally, combine the two parts.**  
Notice that the ratio you just obtained is exactly the combination you separated from the duration ratio earlier. Therefore, the desired \(f_A/f_T\) can be written solely in terms of the measured longest durations \(t_1, t_2\) and the orbital eccentricity \(e\). You can now plug in the given numbers (7.5 min, 12.5 min, \(e=0.0549\)), perform the arithmetic, and get the final estimate. (Counting hybrid eclipses as annular simply matches the choice of the boundary \(r=R\).)

title: Spacecraft trajectory to Mars
problem: A spacecraft is launched from the Earth and it is quickly accelerated to its maximum velocity in the direction of the heliocentric orbit of the Earth, such that its orbit is a parabola with the Sun at its focus point, and grazes the Earth orbit. Take the orbit of the Earth and Mars as circles on the same plane, with radius of $r_E = 1AU$ and $r_M = 1.5AU$ , respectively. Make the following approximation: during most of the flight only the gravity from the Sun needs to be considered.

sub_problems.problem: (a) What is the angle $\psi$ between the path of the spacecraft and the orbit of the Mars (see Fig. 1) as it crosses the orbit of the Mars, without considering the gravity effect of the Mars?
sub_problems.solution:
The spacecraft's orbit is a parabola, so its specific energy relative to the Sun is zero: $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}v_{\max}^2 - \frac{k_{\text{sun}}}{r_E} = 0$, giving $v_{\max} = \sqrt{2k_{\text{sun}}/r_E}$. The angular momentum per unit mass is $l = r_E v_{\max} = \sqrt{2k_{\text{sun}} r_E}$. At Mars's orbit $r_M = 1.5\,\text{AU}$, the total speed is $v = \sqrt{2k_{\text{sun}}/r_M} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}v_{\max}$. The transverse component from angular momentum conservation: $r_M v_\theta = l$, so $v_\theta = \frac{r_E}{r_M}v_{\max} = \frac{2}{3}v_{\max}$. The angle $\psi$ satisfies $\cos\psi = v_\theta/v = \sqrt{r_E/r_M} = \sqrt{2/3}$. Hence $\psi = \arccos\sqrt{2/3} \approx 35.26^\circ$.

\boxed{\psi = \arccos\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}} \approx 35.26^\circ}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the angle ψ between the spacecraft’s path and Mars’s orbit at the crossing point, you need to determine the spacecraft’s velocity vector (its direction and magnitude) at the distance of Mars from the Sun. Use the following steps, grounded in reference passages.

1. **Recognize the orbit type**  
   The problem states that the spacecraft follows a parabolic trajectory relative to the Sun (ignoring Mars’s gravity). As explained in Morin (reference.4.2) and Carroll & Ostlie (reference.3), a parabolic orbit corresponds to a total mechanical energy of zero. For a body of small mass moving under the Sun’s gravity, the specific orbital energy (energy per unit mass) is  
   \[
   \varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}v^{2} - \frac{GM_{\text{sun}}}{r} = 0 .
   \]  
   This relation links the spacecraft’s speed \(v\) at any distance \(r\) from the Sun. Write it down — you will use it at two different distances.

2. **Apply conservation of specific angular momentum**  
   Both Carroll & Ostlie (reference.3) and Morin (Theorem 6.1) show that for any central force (such as the Sun’s gravity) the angular momentum \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{p}\) is constant. Per unit mass, the specific angular momentum \(h = r v_{\perp}\) (where \(v_{\perp}\) is the velocity component perpendicular to the radius vector) therefore does not change along the orbit.  
   At the starting point — Earth’s orbit — the spacecraft is at its perihelion, so the velocity is purely tangential; hence \(h = r_E \, v_{\text{max}}\), where \(v_{\text{max}}\) is its speed there. At the crossing of Mars’s orbit (distance \(r_M\)), the perpendicular component is the transverse speed \(v_\theta\), so  
   \[
   r_M v_\theta = r_E v_{\text{max}} .
   \]  
   This gives you the transverse component at the crossing in terms of \(v_{\text{max}}\) and the known distances.

3. **Find the total speed at Mars**  
   Use the zero‑energy condition again, this time at \(r = r_M\), to express the spacecraft’s total speed \(v\) at the crossing. You can relate that speed to \(v_{\text{max}}\) by combining the zero‑energy expression at \(r_E\) and at \(r_M\); eliminate \(GM_{\text{sun}}\) between the two equations.

4. **Relate the angle to velocity components**  
   The orbit of Mars is approximately circular, so its velocity is tangential. (The Newtonian condition for circular motion \(v^{2}/r = GM/r^{2}\) is given in Carroll & Ostlie, Sections 17.2 and 7.3.) The spacecraft’s velocity vector at the crossing has a radial component and a transverse component \(v_\theta\); the angle ψ between the spacecraft’s path and the tangential direction therefore satisfies \(\cos\psi = v_\theta / v\).

5. **Combine the results**  
   Substitute the expressions you obtained for \(v_\theta\) (from angular‑momentum conservation) and \(v\) (from the energy condition) into \(\cos\psi = v_\theta/v\). All quantities will cancel except the ratio of the orbital radii \(r_E/r_M\). Because the Earth–Sun distance is \(1\text{ AU}\) and Mars–Sun distance is \(1.5\text{ AU}\), you can compute ψ as the inverse cosine of that resulting expression.

Carry out each algebraic step carefully, using the laws exactly as they appear in the referenced passages, and you will obtain the numerical value of ψ.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Suppose the Mars happens to be very close to the crossing point at the time of the crossing, from the point of view of an observer on Mars, what is the approaching velocity and direction of approach (with respect to the Sun) of the spacecraft before it is significantly affected by the gravity of the Mars?
sub_problems.solution:
Mars moves on a circular orbit with speed $v_M = \sqrt{k_{\text{sun}}/r_M} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}v_E$ (where $v_E = \sqrt{k_{\text{sun}}/r_E}$). The spacecraft's velocity at crossing is $\vec{v} = v\sin\psi\,\hat{r} + v_\theta\,\hat{\theta}$ with $\sin\psi = \sqrt{1-\cos^2\psi} = 1/\sqrt{3}$, $v = \sqrt{2k_{\text{sun}}/r_M}$, $v_\theta = \frac{2}{3}v_{\max} = \frac{2}{3}\sqrt{2k_{\text{sun}}/r_E} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{k_{\text{sun}}/r_M}$. The relative velocity is $\vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{v} - \vec{v}_M = v\sin\psi\,\hat{r} + (v_\theta - v_M)\,\hat{\theta}$. Substituting: $v\sin\psi = \sqrt{\frac{2k_{\text{sun}}}{3r_M}}$, $v_\theta - v_M = \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1\right)\sqrt{\frac{k_{\text{sun}}}{r_M}}$. The magnitude is $v_{\text{rel}} = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3} + \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}-1\right)^2}\sqrt{\frac{k_{\text{sun}}}{r_M}} \approx 20.21\,\text{km/s}$. The direction angle $\theta$ from the radial direction (Sun-spacecraft line) satisfies $\tan\theta = \frac{v_\theta - v_M}{v\sin\psi} = \frac{2/\sqrt{3}-1}{\sqrt{2/3}} \approx 0.1894$, so $\theta \approx 10.72^\circ$ (i.e., the spacecraft approaches from a direction $10.72^\circ$ ahead of the radial line, as seen from Mars).

\boxed{v_{\text{rel}} \approx 20.21\,\text{km/s},\; \theta \approx 10.72^\circ}

First, recall from the **circular orbital speed** example (the Hohmann transfer worked example in Kleppner & Kolenkow) that for a circular orbit the speed is found by balancing centripetal force and gravity:  
\( \displaystyle m \frac{(v^{\text{c}})^2}{r} = \frac{G m M}{r^2}\).

Next, the spacecraft is in an elliptical transfer orbit. In the same Hohmann example you saw how to use the energy (vis‑viva) equation for an ellipse:  
\( \displaystyle \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{G m M}{r} = -\frac{G m M}{2a} \),  
where \(a\) is the semimajor axis. Use this to find the spacecraft’s total speed \(v\) at the distance of Mars’s orbit, \(r_M\). (The semimajor axis and all necessary distances should already be known from the Earth–Mars transfer geometry.)

Now invoke the **conservation of angular momentum**. According to the textbook exposition, for a planet/spacecraft the angular momentum \(L = m\, v_{\text{trans}} \, r\) is constant (Kepler’s second law). Because the spacecraft’s orbit is an ellipse that leaves Earth orbit at perihelion, you know its angular momentum per unit mass from the perihelion data (radius \(r_E\) and the transverse velocity there, which equals the total speed at perihelion). Equate \( (v_{\text{trans}}\, r) \) at perihelion to \( (v_{\theta}\, r_M) \) at the crossing point to solve for the transverse component \(v_\theta\) at Mars’s distance.

With the total speed \(v\) and the transverse component \(v_\theta\), find the radial component of the spacecraft’s velocity:  
\( v_r = \sqrt{v^2 - v_\theta^2} \).  
(This is the component along the Sun–spacecraft line, directed outward.)

Now form the **relative velocity** of the spacecraft as seen from Mars. The textbook passage on velocity addition reminds you that for ordinary speeds the classical vector difference is perfectly accurate. Mars moves only tangentially (\( \vec{v}_M = v_M\,\hat{\theta} \)), while the spacecraft’s velocity is  
\( \vec{v} = v_r\,\hat{r} + v_\theta\,\hat{\theta} \).  
Therefore the velocity relative to Mars is  
\( \vec{v}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{v} - \vec{v}_M = v_r\,\hat{r} + (v_\theta - v_M)\,\hat{\theta} \).

Finally, the **magnitude** of the approach velocity is  
\( v_{\text{rel}} = \sqrt{ v_r^2 + (v_\theta - v_M)^2 } \).  
The **direction** is the angle \(\theta\) measured from the radial line (the Sun–Mars line) toward the forward tangential direction. By looking at the relative vector components you can find  
\( \tan\theta = \frac{|v_\theta - v_M|}{v_r} \),  
and decide the sign/sense from the fact that the tangential relative component is small and positive (if the spacecraft’s transverse speed is slightly larger than Mars’s). This gives the direction of approach as seen from Mars before any significant martian gravity acts.

Obtain the numerical result by substituting the known speeds (Earth’s orbital speed, Sun’s \(GM\), and the orbit radii) into each expression in the order above.

title: The Taris System
problem:
The planet Taris is the home of the Korribian civilization. The Korribian species is a highly intelligent alien life form. They speak Korribianese language. The Korribianese-English dictionary is shown in Table 1; read it carefully! Korriban astronomers have been studying the heavens for thousands of years. Their knowledge can be summarized as follows:

$\star$ Taris orbits its host star Sola in a circular orbit, at a distance of 1 Tarislength.

$\star$ Taris orbits Sola in 1 Tarisyear.
$\star$ The inclination of Taris's equator to its orbital plane is $3^{\circ}$
$\star$ There are exactly 10 Tarisdays in 1 Tarisyear.
$\star$ Taris has two moons, named Endor and Extor. Both have circular orbits.
$\star$ The sidereal orbital period of Endor (around Taris) is exactly 0.2 Tarisdays.
$\star$ The sidereal orbital period of Extor (around Taris) is exactly 1.6 Tarisdays.
$\star$ The distance between Taris and Endor is 1 Endorlength.
$\star$ Corulus, another planet, also orbits Sola in a circular orbit. Corulus has one moon.
$\star$ The distance between Sola and Corulus is 9 Tarislengths.
$\star$ The tarisyear begins when Solaptic longitude of the Sola is zero.

sub_problems.problem: (c) What is the distance between Taris and Extor, in Endorlengths?
sub_problems.solution:
By Kepler's third law for moons of Taris: $\frac{T^2}{R^3}$ is constant. For Endor: $T_{\text{en}} = 0.2$ Tarisdays, $R_{\text{en}} = 1$ Endorlength. For Extor: $T_{\text{ex}} = 1.6$ Tarisdays. Thus:

$$
\frac{T_{\text{ex}}^2}{R_{\text{ex}}^3} = \frac{T_{\text{en}}^2}{R_{\text{en}}^3}
$$

$$
R_{\text{ex}}^3 = \frac{1.6^2 \cdot 1^3}{0.2^2} = \frac{2.56}{0.04} = 64
$$

$$
R_{\text{ex}} = \sqrt[3]{64} = 4 \text{ Endorlengths}
$$

If the orbits are circular, the semi‑major axis is simply the orbital radius.
- In this problem you have two moons (Endor and Extor) that both orbit Taris. Therefore, you can apply Kepler’s third law by equating the constant for the two moons. Write down the equality of the ratios: \(\frac{P_{\text{Endor}}^{2}}{R_{\text{Endor}}^{3}} = \frac{P_{\text{Extor}}^{2}}{R_{\text{Extor}}^{3}}\), using the periods and the orbital radii.

sub_problems.problem: (d) What is the orbital period of Corulus, in Tarisyears?
sub_problems.solution:
Using Kepler's third law for planets around Sola: $\frac{T^2}{R^3}$ is constant. For Taris: $T_T = 1$ Tarisyear, $R_T = 1$ Tarislength. For Corulus: $R_C = 9$ Tarislengths. Thus:

$$
\frac{T_C^2}{9^3} = \frac{1^2}{1^3}
$$

$$
T_C^2 = 729
$$

$$
T_C = \sqrt{729} = 27 \text{ Tarisyears}
$$

sub_problems.problem: (f) If at the beginning of a particular tarisyear, Corulus and Taris were in opposition, what would be Solaptic longitude (as observed from Taris) of Corulus $n$ tarisdays from the start of that year?
sub_problems.solution:
Let $n$ be the number of Tarisdays after opposition. The angular speed of Taris around Sola is $\frac{2\pi}{10}$ per Tarisday (since 10 Tarisdays per Tarisyear). The angular speed of Corulus around Sola is $\frac{2\pi}{270}$ per Tarisday (since 27 Tarisyears = 270 Tarisdays). At opposition, both are aligned. After $n$ days, the angle between them (as seen from Sola) is $\frac{2\pi n}{10} - \frac{2\pi n}{270} = \frac{52\pi n}{270}$. Using geometry and the sine rule in triangle Sola-Taris-Corulus, the Solaptic longitude $\lambda$ of Corulus (angle from the direction of Sola as seen from Taris) is:

$$
\lambda = \pi + \frac{2\pi n}{270} - \tan^{-1}\left[ \frac{\sin\left(\frac{52\pi n}{270}\right)}{9 - \cos\left(\frac{52\pi n}{270}\right)} \right]
$$

sub_problems.guidance:
Your goal is to find the Solaptic longitude of Corulus as seen from Taris, \(n\) Tarisdays after they are in opposition. The problem involves two key ideas: the angular speeds of the planets from their orbital periods, and the geometric configuration at and after opposition.

**Step 1: Find the angular speeds of Taris and Corulus.**
From reference discussion of uniform circular motion, the angular speed \(\omega\) is related to the period \(T\) by \(\omega = 2\pi/T\). The period here is the time for one complete orbit (a sidereal period). The problem gives the orbital periods in terms of Tarisdays and Tarisyears. Convert both periods to the same unit (Tarisdays), then calculate \(\omega_{\text{Taris}}\) and \(\omega_{\text{Corulus}}\) in radians per Tarisday. This uses the concept of angular frequency from the harmonic oscillator section, applied to circular motion.

**Step 2: Determine the angular separation between the planets as seen from Sola.**
At opposition, a superior planet and the Earth (or here, Taris and Corulus) are aligned on the same side of the central star. reference explains that for superior planets, opposition occurs when they are opposite the Sun in the sky. After \(n\) Tarisdays, both planets have moved along their orbits. The angle each has swept out from the opposition line is its angular speed multiplied by time \(n\). Since Taris moves faster (shorter period), it pulls ahead. The angular separation \(\theta\) between them, as viewed from Sola, is the difference of these swept angles: \(\theta = (\omega_{\text{Taris}} - \omega_{\text{Corulus}}) n\).

**Step 3: Relate this separation to the geometry of the Sola-Taris-Corulus triangle.**
After \(n\) days, Taris, Corulus, and Sola form a triangle. You know the distance from Sola to Taris (call it \(r_T\)) and from Sola to Corulus (call it \(r_C\)). The problem context or earlier parts should give the ratio of these distances—for instance, from the synodic/sidereal relation or given data, you may know \(r_C/r_T\) (likely 10, based on the numbers in the problem). The angle at Sola in this triangle is exactly the \(\theta\) you just computed.

**Step 4: Find the direction of Corulus as seen from Taris.**
The Solaptic longitude is the angle measured at Taris from the direction toward Sola to the direction toward Corulus. In the triangle, this is the angle between the line Taris-Sola and the line Taris-Corulus. The geometry is analogous to finding an angle in a triangle when two sides and the included angle are known. You can use the law of sines or the tangent formula for an angle in a triangle. The reference solution suggests using an arctangent expression derived from the triangle’s geometry: the angle at Taris depends on the distance ratio and the angle \(\theta\). Set up the triangle with Sola at the vertex, Taris and Corulus at the other vertices. The angle at Taris is the supplement of the angle you want, because the Solaptic longitude is measured from the anti-Sola direction. Carefully draw the triangle and apply the appropriate trigonometric relation to isolate the requested angle.

**Step 5: Assemble the final expression.**
Combine your results: the Solaptic longitude will be an initial value (at opposition, the longitude has a known value—think about what “opposition” means for the direction of Corulus in Taris’s sky) plus the change due to the orbital motion. Substitute your expressions for \(\theta\) and the triangle solution to write the longitude as a function of \(n\).

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the area of the triangle formed by Sola, Taris and Corulus at the given time, you need to compute the area using two sides of the triangle and the sine of the included angle. This approach is directly motivated by the textbook discussion of Kepler’s second law, where the area swept out by a radius vector is given by a thin triangle.  

Recall from the textbook passage on Kepler’s laws: during a short time interval, the radius vector sweeps out a small triangle of area `dA = (1/2) r (r dθ)`. The quantity `r dθ` is the base of that thin triangle, and `r` is its other side, so the area is essentially `(1/2) * side1 * side2 * sin(included angle)` for a very small angle. That same formula works for any triangle with a finite angle:  
**area = (1/2) * a * b * sin(γ)**, where `a` and `b` are the lengths of two sides and `γ` is the angle between them.  

Now, identify which lengths and which angle you have already determined from the earlier parts of the problem.  
- You know the distance from Sola to Taris (`ST`) and from Sola to Corulus (`SC`) at the moment you are considering.  
- You also know the angular separation between Taris and Corulus as seen from **Sola** (or possibly the angle at Taris, but the easiest choice is the angle at the vertex where the two known sides meet).  

If you have the distances from Sola to each of the other two bodies and the angle **at Sola** between them, then those two distances are exactly the sides that form that angle. In that case, the area of triangle Sola‑Taris‑Corulus is simply  

> area = ½ × (ST) × (SC) × sin(angle at Sola).

If instead you have the angle at Taris, then you would need the length of the side opposite that angle (i.e., the distance Taris‑Corulus) or use another relation. Check your configuration carefully: after one Tarisday, you can express the positions of Taris and Corulus relative to Sola, which gives you the two radii and the angular difference between them as measured from the central star.  

Once you have identified the correct pair of sides and the angle between them, substitute the values you obtained earlier into the area formula. The computation is a direct application of the general triangle area expression that the textbook illustrates with the thin‑triangle example in the Kepler’s‑law derivation. Perform the multiplication and the sine evaluation yourself; the result will be the requested area in square Tarislengths.

title: Mean surface temperature of Earth (blackbody with albedo)
problem: What would be the mean temperature on the Earth's surface if we ignore the greenhouse effect, assume that the Earth is a perfect black body and take into account its non-vanishing albedo? Assume that the Earth's orbit around the Sun is circular.
solution: The solar luminosity is $L_\odot = 4\pi R_\odot^2 \sigma T_\odot^4$. At Earth's distance $r_\oplus$, the solar flux (power per unit area) is $S = \frac{L_\odot}{4\pi r_\oplus^2} = \frac{R_\odot^2 \sigma T_\odot^4}{r_\oplus^2}$. The Earth intercepts this flux over its cross-sectional area $\pi R_\oplus^2$, so the total power absorbed is $P_{\text{abs}} = (1-\alpha) S \pi R_\oplus^2$, where $\alpha$ is the albedo. The Earth radiates as a blackbody over its entire surface area $4\pi R_\oplus^2$: $P_{\text{rad}} = 4\pi R_\oplus^2 \sigma T_\oplus^4$. In equilibrium, $P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{rad}}$ gives $(1-\alpha) \frac{R_\odot^2 \sigma T_\odot^4}{r_\oplus^2} \pi R_\oplus^2 = 4\pi R_\oplus^2 \sigma T_\oplus^4$. Cancelling common factors yields $T_\oplus^4 = \frac{(1-\alpha) R_\odot^2 T_\odot^4}{4 r_\oplus^2}$, so $T_\oplus = T_\odot (1-\alpha)^{1/4} \sqrt{\frac{R_\odot}{2 r_\oplus}}$. Using $T_\odot = 5778\,\text{K}$, $R_\odot = 6.96\times10^8\,\text{m}$, $r_\oplus = 1.496\times10^{11}\,\text{m}$, and $\alpha = 0.39$, we compute $T_\oplus = 5778 \times (0.61)^{1/4} \times \sqrt{\frac{6.96\times10^8}{2\times1.496\times10^{11}}} \approx 5778 \times 0.883 \times \sqrt{2.327\times10^{-3}} \approx 5778 \times 0.883 \times 0.04824 \approx 246\,\text{K}$. Converting to Celsius: $246 - 273 = -27^\circ\text{C}$. Thus the mean temperature is $\boxed{T_\oplus = 246\,\text{K}}$ or $\boxed{T_\oplus = -27^\circ\text{C}}$.

The Earth radiates as a blackbody over its entire surface area $4\pi R_\oplus^2$: $P_{\text{rad}} = 4\pi R_\oplus^2 \sigma T_\oplus^4$. In equilibrium, $P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{rad}}$ gives $(1-\alpha) \frac{R_\odot^2 \sigma T_\odot^4}{r_\oplus^2} \pi R_\oplus^2 = 4\pi R_\oplus^2 \sigma T_\oplus^4$. Cancelling common factors yields $T_\oplus^4 = \frac{(1-\alpha) R_\odot^2 T_\odot^4}{4 r_\oplus^2}$, so $T_\oplus = T_\odot (1-\alpha)^{1/4} \sqrt{\frac{R_\odot}{2 r_\oplus}}$. Using $T_\odot = 5778\,\text{K}$, $R_\odot = 6.96\times10^8\,\text{m}$, $r_\oplus = 1.496\times10^{11}\,\text{m}$, and $\alpha = 0.39$, we compute $T_\oplus = 5778 \times (0.61)^{1/4} \times \sqrt{\frac{6.96\times10^8}{2\times1.496\times10^{11}}} \approx 5778 \times 0.883 \times \sqrt{2.327\times10^{-3}} \approx 5778 \times 0.883 \times 0.04824 \approx 246\,\text{K}$. Converting to Celsius: $246 - 273 = -27^\circ\text{C}$. Thus the mean temperature is $\boxed{T_\oplus = 246\,\text{K}}$ or $\boxed{T_\oplus = -27^\circ\text{C}}$.

knowledge_points.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
knowledge_points.description: Relates the total power radiated by a blackbody to its surface area and temperature: P = σ A T^4. Needed to compute the Sun's luminosity and the Earth's radiated power.

knowledge_points.name: Inverse-square law for radiation
knowledge_points.description: The flux from an isotropic point source decreases with the square of distance: F = L/(4π d^2). Needed to determine the solar flux at Earth's orbit.

knowledge_points.name: Albedo
knowledge_points.description: The fraction of incident radiation reflected by a body; the absorbed fraction is (1 - albedo). Needed to account for Earth's reflectivity.

knowledge_points.name: Planetary energy balance geometry
knowledge_points.description: For a spherical planet, the power absorbed from a distant source is the incident flux times the cross-sectional area π R^2, while the power radiated as a blackbody is σ T^4 times the total surface area 4π R^2.

knowledge_points.name: Energy balance at thermal equilibrium
knowledge_points.description: In steady state, the total power absorbed by a body equals the total power it radiates. Needed to equate absorbed solar power and emitted terrestrial radiation.

knowledge_points.name: Blackbody radiation
knowledge_points.description: Both the Earth and the Sun are assumed to radiate as perfect blackbodies, allowing the application of the Stefan-Boltzmann law.

knowledge_points.name: Circular Earth orbit
knowledge_points.description: The Earth's orbit around the Sun is assumed circular, so the Earth-Sun distance and thus the solar flux are constant, simplifying the equilibrium calculation.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall that a planet in thermal equilibrium must re‑emit all the energy it absorbs. This balance is set up by equating the power absorbed from the Sun to the power the planet radiates as a blackbody. reference’s discussion of “The Temperatures of the Planets” (reference.3) and the worked example on Earth’s temperature directly illustrate this approach.

1. **Solar luminosity**  
   Treat the Sun as a spherical blackbody. Use the Stefan–Boltzmann law in the form  
   \[
   L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T^4 \quad(\text{reference.17}).
   \]  
   Insert the Sun’s effective temperature \(T_{\odot}\) and radius \(R_{\odot}\) (given in Example 3.4.2) to write down the solar luminosity \(L_{\odot}\).

2. **Flux at Earth’s orbit**  
   The total solar power is spread uniformly over a sphere of radius equal to the Earth–Sun distance \(D\). The inverse‑square law (reference.2, also explained with a diagram in the Schaum’s Outline passage) gives the radiant flux \(F\) at that distance:  
   \[
   F = \frac{L_{\odot}}{4\pi D^{2}}.
   \]  
   Because the orbit is assumed circular, \(D\) is constant.

3. **Power absorbed by Earth**  
   A spherical planet intercepts sunlight over its cross‑sectional area \(\pi R_{\oplus}^{2}\), so the power incident on it is \(F \pi R_{\oplus}^{2}\).  
   The albedo \(a\) (Schaum’s Outline) is the fraction of light reflected; therefore the fraction absorbed is \(1-a\). Hence the absorbed power is  
   \[
   P_{\text{abs}} = (1-a) \, F \, \pi R_{\oplus}^{2}.
   \]

4. **Power emitted by Earth**  
   The planet radiates as a blackbody from its entire surface area \(4\pi R_{\oplus}^{2}\). By the Stefan–Boltzmann law, the emitted power is  
   \[
   P_{\text{rad}} = 4\pi R_{\oplus}^{2} \, \sigma \, T_{\oplus}^{4},
   \]  
   where \(T_{\oplus}\) is the uniform surface temperature you want to find.

5. **Energy balance**  
   Set \(P_{\text{abs}} = P_{\text{rad}}\) (the condition stated in the atmospheric‑physics passage and used in the Blundell & Blundell worked example, but now including albedo). Cancel the common factors \(\pi R_{\oplus}^{2}\) and \(\sigma\). After simplifying, you will obtain the relation quoted in reference (reference.5):  
   \[
   T_{\oplus} = T_{\odot} \, (1-a)^{1/4} \sqrt{\frac{R_{\odot}}{2D}}.
   \]  
   Notice that the planet’s radius drops out entirely, so you don’t need its value.

6. **Plug in the numbers**  
   Use the solar temperature and radius (from Example 3.4.2), the Earth–Sun distance (from Example 3.2.1), and the albedo. reference’s own example (19.3.1) employs a particular albedo value; if your problem gives a different number, use that one. Substitute everything into Eq. (19.5) and calculate \(T_{\oplus}\).  
   If asked, convert kelvins to degrees Celsius by subtracting 273.

Following these steps, you are simply carrying out the equilibrium blackbody calculation that includes the effect of reflection by the planet. The only geometry you need is that of a sphere (cross‑section vs. surface area) together with the inverse‑square dilution of sunlight.

title: Telescope Resolution of Hot Jupiter
problem: Let us assume that we observe a hot Jupiter planet orbiting around a star at an average distance $d = 5$ AU. It has been found that the distance of this system from us is $r = 250$ pc. What is the minimum diameter, D, that a telescope should have to be able to resolve the two objects (star and planet)? We assume that the observation is done in the optical part of the electromagnetic spectrum ( $\lambda \sim 500$ nm), outside the Earth's atmosphere and that the telescope optics are perfect.
solution:
The angular separation between the star and the planet is approximately $\omega \approx d / r$. Convert distances to meters: $d = 5 \times 1.5 \times 10^{11} \, \text{m} = 7.5 \times 10^{11} \, \text{m}$, $r = 250 \times 3.09 \times 10^{16} \, \text{m} = 7.725 \times 10^{18} \, \text{m}$. Then $\omega = \frac{7.5 \times 10^{11}}{7.725 \times 10^{18}} = 9.71 \times 10^{-8} \, \text{rad}$. The telescope's angular resolution is given by the Rayleigh criterion: $\Delta \theta = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{D}$. Setting $\Delta \theta = \omega$ gives $D = 1.22 \frac{\lambda}{\omega} = 1.22 \times \frac{500 \times 10^{-9}}{9.71 \times 10^{-8}} \approx 6.28 \, \text{m}$. Rounding to one significant figure yields $D \approx 6 \, \text{m}$.

\boxed{D \approx 6 \, \text{m}}

knowledge_points.name: face‑on orbit / maximum angular separation
knowledge_points.description: The solution implicitly assumes the planet is observed at its maximum apparent separation from the star, so that the angular separation is simply d/r. This corresponds to an orbital plane perpendicular to the line of sight or taking the projection at maximum elongation.

knowledge_points.name: small‑angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: Because the angular separation is very small, the solution uses tan θ ≈ θ to write ω = d/r. This simplifies the calculation without trigonometric functions.

knowledge_points.name: astronomical unit (AU)
knowledge_points.description: The physical separation d = 5 AU must be converted to metres using 1 AU ≈ 1.5×10¹¹ m. This unit appears in the problem statement and is essential to obtain a consistent angular separation.

knowledge_points.name: parsec (pc)
knowledge_points.description: The distance r = 250 pc must be converted to metres using 1 pc ≈ 3.09×10¹⁶ m. The problem gives the distance in parsecs, so the conversion is required.

knowledge_points.name: Rayleigh criterion
knowledge_points.description: The angular resolution of a diffraction‑limited telescope is Δθ = 1.22 λ / D. This formula is the core physical law used to find the minimum aperture D.

knowledge_points.name: resolution threshold equating
knowledge_points.description: To obtain the minimum diameter D that just resolves the two objects, the solution sets the angular separation ω equal to the Rayleigh angular resolution, Δθ = ω. This is the standard condition for barely resolved point sources.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the minimum telescope diameter needed to resolve the star and its hot Jupiter, you will work through two main steps: determine the angular separation of the planet from the star as seen from Earth, and then apply the Rayleigh criterion that limits the telescope’s resolving power.

**1. Find the angular separation ω.**  
The planet orbits at an average distance \(d = 5\;\mathrm{AU}\) from the star, while the whole system is \(r = 250\;\mathrm{pc}\) away from us. Because the distance to the system is vastly larger than the orbital radius, the angle subtended is tiny – use the **small‑angle approximation**. The general relation is that the angle in radians equals the physical separation divided by the distance, provided both are in the same unit:

\[
\omega \approx \frac{d}{r}\;(\text{in radians}).
\]

To work in a common unit, convert the distance from parsecs to astronomical units using the definition of the parsec: \(1\;\mathrm{pc} = 206\,265\;\mathrm{AU}\) (see reference passage on parsec by Carroll & Ostlie or Palen). Then

\[
r(\mathrm{AU}) = 250 \times 206\,265\;\mathrm{AU}.
\]

Now compute \(\omega = d / r\) with both quantities in AU; the result is a pure number, which is the angle in radians. (If you prefer to work in metres, you may instead convert both distances to metres using \(1\;\mathrm{pc} = 3.0857\times10^{16}\;\mathrm{m}\) from Carroll & Ostlie and \(1\;\mathrm{AU} = \frac{1}{206\,265}\,\mathrm{pc}\). The essential point is to keep units consistent.)

**2. Use the Rayleigh criterion to connect angular resolution to telescope diameter.**  
For a perfect telescope with a circular aperture, the smallest angular separation \(\Delta\theta\) that can be resolved is given by the **Rayleigh criterion** (see Carroll & Ostlie, reference.1 and especially Example 6.3.2):

\[
\Delta\theta = 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{D},
\]

where \(\lambda\) is the wavelength of light and \(D\) is the diameter of the telescope’s primary mirror or lens.

To just split the two objects, set the telescope’s resolution limit equal to the true angular separation:

\[
\omega = 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{D}.
\]

**3. Isolate \(D\) and substitute the numbers.**  
Solve for \(D\):

\[
D = 1.22\,\frac{\lambda}{\omega}.
\]

The observation is made in the optical part of the spectrum with \(\lambda \approx 500\;\mathrm{nm} = 5.0\times10^{-7}\;\mathrm{m}\). Insert the value of \(\omega\) you obtained (in radians) and carry out the multiplication/division. Your answer will be in metres. Because the input numbers for \(d\) and \(r\) have only one or two significant figures, round your final diameter accordingly.

By following this sequence – convert distance with the parsec definition, compute the tiny angle using the small‑angle approximation, then impose the Rayleigh criterion – you solve the problem exactly as Example 6.3.2 in reference does for a radio telescope, but here adapted to optical wavelengths.

title: Main Sequence Lifetime vs. Mass
problem: It is estimated that the Sun will have spent a total of about $t_1 = 10$ billion years on the main sequence before evolving away from it. Estimate the corresponding amount of time, $t_2$ , if the Sun were 5 times more massive.
solution:
For the average luminosity of a main sequence star we have: $L \propto M^4$ (where $M$ the initial mass of the star). We assume that the total energy $E$ that the star produces is proportional to its mass $E \propto M$. Therefore the amount of time that the star spends on the main sequence is approximately $t_{MS} \approx \frac{E}{L} \propto \frac{M}{M^4} \approx M^{-3}$. Therefore, $\frac{t_1}{t_2} \approx \frac{1^{-3}}{5^{-3}} = 5^3 \rightarrow t_2 = \frac{1}{125} \times 10^{10} \mathrm{yr}$ or $t_2 = 8 \times 10^7 \mathrm{yr}$.

\boxed{t_2 = 8 \times 10^7 \text{ yr}}

knowledge_points.name: Mass-luminosity relation for main sequence stars
knowledge_points.description: The average luminosity of a main sequence star scales approximately as the fourth power of its initial mass (L ∝ M^4). This relation is needed to relate the luminosity of the hypothetical 5-solar-mass star to that of the Sun.

knowledge_points.name: Total fusion energy proportional to mass
knowledge_points.description: The total energy produced by a star over its main sequence lifetime is assumed to be proportional to its initial mass (E ∝ M), because the amount of nuclear fuel available scales with the star's mass. This assumption is used together with the luminosity relation to find how lifetime depends on mass.

knowledge_points.name: Main sequence lifetime formula
knowledge_points.description: The main sequence lifetime of a star is approximately the total available nuclear energy divided by the average luminosity (t_MS ≈ E/L). This concept is used to combine the mass-luminosity relation and the fuel assumption to derive the mass-lifetime scaling.

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks you to estimate the main-sequence lifetime of a star that is five times as massive as the Sun, given the Sun’s main-sequence lifetime of 10 billion years. reference passages give you a direct relationship between a star’s mass and its main-sequence lifetime, so you do not need to derive anything from the mass–luminosity relation.

Start by locating the appropriate formula in the section “The Main-Sequence Lifetime of Stars” (Palen). It states:

\[
\frac{t}{t_{\mathrm{Sun}}} = \left( \frac{M}{M_{\mathrm{Sun}}} \right)^{-2.5}
\]

This equation tells you how the main-sequence lifetime \(t\) scales with the star’s mass \(M\) relative to the Sun. The exponent \(-2.5\) means that more massive stars have much shorter lifetimes.

To apply this to the given problem, note that:
- The Sun’s main-sequence lifetime \(t_{\mathrm{Sun}}\) is exactly the \(t_1 = 10^{10}\) years quoted in the problem.
- The Sun’s mass is \(M_{\mathrm{Sun}}\), so the Sun represents the case \(M/M_{\mathrm{Sun}} = 1\).
- The star you are asked about has \(M = 5\,M_{\mathrm{Sun}}\), so the mass ratio is 5.

Use the formula exactly as reference’s worked example 7.13 does for a \(15\,M_{\mathrm{Sun}}\) star. That example substitutes the mass ratio directly into the equation and then simplifies the power:

\[
t = t_{\mathrm{Sun}} \cdot \left( \frac{M}{M_{\mathrm{Sun}}} \right)^{-2.5}
\]

Following that same procedure:
1. Set \(t_{\mathrm{Sun}} = t_1\) and the mass ratio \(M/M_{\mathrm{Sun}} = 5\).
2. Write \(t_2 = t_1 \cdot (5)^{-2.5}\).
3. Evaluate \((5)^{-2.5}\). You can break this into \((5^{2.5})^{-1} = \frac{1}{5^{2.5}}\). Recall that \(5^{2.5} = 5^2 \times 5^{0.5} = 25\sqrt{5}\).
4. Multiply the result by \(10^{10}\) years to obtain \(t_2\).

reference’s example 7.13 also illustrates the final step: after computing the number, express it in years (or million/billion years) to see how drastically the lifetime has shortened.

No other relations are needed. If you were to use the mass–luminosity relation and an energy argument you would arrive at a slightly different exponent (as shown in example 7.14), but the required reading provides the mass–lifetime relation directly. Stick to that given formula and work carefully with the exponent.
