sub_problems.problem: (2) the period of Seneca's orbit, $T_{\mathrm{Sen}}$ and the average period between two consecutive oppositions, $T_{\mathrm{syn}}$ of the Earth-Seneca couple
sub_problems.solution:
The period $T_{\mathrm{Sen}}$ of Seneca's orbit can be found by using Kepler's 3rd law for Seneca and the Earth (ignoring their small masses, compared to the Sun's):
$$a_{\mathrm{Sen}}^3 / T_{\mathrm{Sen}}^2 = a_{\mathrm{Earth}}^3 / T_{\mathrm{Earth}}^2 = 1$$
from which one finds $T_{\mathrm{Sen}} \sim 3.87$ yr (alternatively $T_{\mathrm{Sen}} = a_{\mathrm{Sen}}^{3/2} = 3.86$ yr).

Assuming non-retrograde orbit, the synodic period $T_{\mathrm{syn}}$ of Seneca and Earth is given by
$$1 / T_{\mathrm{syn}} = 1 / T_{\mathrm{Earth}} - 1 / T_{\mathrm{Sen}}$$
(Seneca is superior) which gives $T_{\mathrm{syn}} = 1.35$ yr.

\boxed{T_{\mathrm{Sen}} \approx 3.87 \mathrm{yr}} \quad \boxed{T_{\mathrm{syn}} \approx 1.35 \mathrm{yr}}

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: For planets orbiting the Sun, the ratio of the cube of the semi-major axis to the square of the period is constant (a³/T² = const) when planetary masses are negligible. Used to find Seneca's orbital period from its semi-major axis (known from part 1) and Earth's orbital parameters.

knowledge_points.name: Synodic period formula
knowledge_points.description: For two planets with sidereal periods T_inner and T_outer (T_inner < T_outer) orbiting in the same direction, the synodic period (average time between oppositions) is given by 1/T_syn = 1/T_inner - 1/T_outer. Used to compute the average period between Earth-Seneca oppositions.

knowledge_points.name: Negligible planetary masses
knowledge_points.description: The masses of Earth and Seneca are ignored compared to the Sun's mass, so Kepler's third law in its simple form (a³/T² = constant for all planets) is valid.

knowledge_points.name: Non-retrograde orbit
knowledge_points.description: Both Earth and Seneca orbit the Sun in the same prograde direction, so their relative angular speed is the difference of their individual angular speeds, leading to the synodic period formula with subtraction.

knowledge_points.name: Seneca is a superior planet
knowledge_points.description: Seneca's orbit lies outside Earth's orbit (a_Sen > a_Earth), so its sidereal period is longer than Earth's. This identifies Earth as the inner planet in the synodic period formula.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find Seneca’s orbital period, start with Kepler’s Third Law in the form given by the textbook: for any planet orbiting the Sun, when the period \(P\) is measured in years and the semi‑major axis \(a\) in astronomical units (AU),

\[
P^{2} = a^{3}.
\]

This law tells you that the ratio \(a^{3}/P^{2}\) is the same for all planets, with Earth’s values being 1 AU and 1 year.  Therefore, once you know Seneca’s semi‑major axis \(a_{\text{Sen}}\) (which should be available from an earlier part of the problem), you can immediately compute its period \(T_{\text{Sen}}\) simply by cubing that distance and taking the square root.  No other masses need to be considered here, because the textbook notes that the simple \(P^{2}=a^{3}\) form relies on the Sun’s mass dominating the system, a very good approximation for our solar system.

For the synodic period (the average time between consecutive oppositions of Earth and Seneca) you need to compare the angular motion of the two planets.  Earth, being closer to the Sun, completes an orbit in exactly 1 year; Seneca, being farther out, takes \(T_{\text{Sen}}\) years to complete one circuit.  During an opposition the Sun, Earth, and Seneca line up with Earth in the middle.  After one synodic period, Earth will have “lapped” Seneca exactly once — that is, it will have gained a full 360° relative to Seneca.

Think in terms of average angular speeds:  
Earth sweeps out \(360^\circ\) per \(T_{\text{Earth}}\;(=1\;\text{yr})\), so its angular speed is \(\omega_{\text{E}} = \frac{360^\circ}{T_{\text{Earth}}}\).  
Seneca sweeps \(360^\circ\) per \(T_{\text{Sen}}\), so \(\omega_{\text{Sen}} = \frac{360^\circ}{T_{\text{Sen}}}\).

Over one synodic period \(T_{\text{syn}}\), the difference in the total angles swept must equal one complete circle:

\[
\omega_{\text{E}}\,T_{\text{syn}} - \omega_{\text{Sen}}\,T_{\text{syn}} = 360^\circ .
\]

Cancel the common factor \(360^\circ\) and rearrange to obtain an equation that relates \(T_{\text{syn}}\), \(T_{\text{Earth}}\), and \(T_{\text{Sen}}\) through their reciprocals.  Because Seneca is an outer planet, its period is longer than Earth’s; subtract the smaller angular speed from the larger so that \(T_{\text{syn}}\) comes out positive.  Solve this equation for \(T_{\text{syn}}\) using \(T_{\text{Earth}} = 1\;\text{yr}\) and the value of \(T_{\text{Sen}}\) you found from Kepler’s Third Law.  Perform the arithmetic carefully, and you will have both requested quantities in years.

sub_problems.problem: (3) an approximate value for the mass of the planet Jupiter, $M_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ (assuming this is the only planet of our Solar system with non-negligible mass compared to the Sun). Assume that the presence of Jupiter does not influence the orbit of Seneca.
sub_problems.solution:
From Kepler's law, we can calculate the mass of the Sun:
$$4\pi^{2}a_{\mathrm{Sen}}^{3} / T_{\mathrm{Sen}}^{2} = GM_{\mathrm{Sun}}$$
i.e. $M_{\mathrm{Sun}}\sim 1.988\times 10^{30}\mathrm{kg}$ (depending on accuracy).

Then, using Kepler's 3rd law for Seneca and Jupiter, one gets
$$(a_{\mathrm{Jup}}^3 / T_{\mathrm{Jup}}^2) / (a_{\mathrm{Sen}}^3 / T_{\mathrm{Sen}}^2) = (M_{\mathrm{Sun}} + M_{\mathrm{Jup}}) / M_{\mathrm{Sun}} = 1 + x$$
where $x$ is the mass ratio of Jupiter to the Sun. Solving for $x$ we get (depending on the accuracy used in determining the elements of Seneca's orbit)
$x = 0.0016$, thus $M_{\mathrm{Jup}} = 3.2\times 10^{27}\mathrm{kg}$.

\boxed{M_{\mathrm{Jup}} \approx 3.2 \times 10^{27} \mathrm{kg}}

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law with masses
knowledge_points.description: The general form T^2 = (4π^2 / G(M+m)) a^3 relates orbital period, semi-major axis, and the sum of the masses. Used to compute M_Sun from Seneca's orbit and to relate Jupiter's orbit to M_Sun + M_Jup.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational constant G
knowledge_points.description: Fundamental constant G ≈ 6.674×10^{-11} m^3 kg^{-1} s^{-2} needed to express masses in kilograms when using Kepler's third law in SI units.

knowledge_points.name: Jupiter's orbital elements
knowledge_points.description: The semi-major axis a_Jup ≈ 5.2 AU and orbital period T_Jup ≈ 11.86 yr of Jupiter are known constants used to evaluate the mass ratio.

knowledge_points.name: Seneca's orbital elements known
knowledge_points.description: The semi-major axis a_Sen and period T_Sen of Seneca's orbit, derived in earlier sub-problems, are used to compute the Sun's mass.

knowledge_points.name: negligible asteroid mass
knowledge_points.description: Seneca's mass is negligible compared to the Sun, so the central mass for its orbit is M_Sun alone.

knowledge_points.name: Jupiter mass non-negligible
knowledge_points.description: Jupiter's mass is not negligible compared to the Sun, so Kepler's third law for Jupiter must use the total mass M_Sun + M_Jup.

knowledge_points.name: Jupiter does not perturb Seneca
knowledge_points.description: The presence of Jupiter does not influence Seneca's orbit, so Seneca's orbital parameters are determined solely by the Sun.

knowledge_points.name: astronomical unit and year in SI
knowledge_points.description: The conversion factors 1 AU = 1.496×10^{11} m and 1 year ≈ 3.156×10^{7} s are needed to convert orbital parameters to SI units for use with G.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Identify the appropriate form of Kepler’s third law for each orbit.**  
   From your textbook, the general form that accounts for both masses is  
   \[
   P^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2}}{G\,(m_{1}+m_{2})}\,a^{3},
   \]  
   where \(a\) is the semi‑major axis, \(P\) the orbital period, and \(m_{1}, m_{2}\) the two masses.  
   - **Seneca** is a small body; its mass is completely negligible compared to the Sun. Therefore, you may treat the total mass as \(m_{1}+m_{2} \approx M_{\odot}\) alone, and write  
     \[
     \frac{a_{\text{Sen}}^{3}}{P_{\text{Sen}}^{2}} = \frac{G}{4\pi^{2}}\,M_{\odot}.
     \]  
   - **Jupiter**, on the other hand, is massive enough that its own mass must be included. Its orbit therefore obeys  
     \[
     \frac{a_{\text{Jup}}^{3}}{P_{\text{Jup}}^{2}} = \frac{G}{4\pi^{2}}\,(M_{\odot}+M_{\text{Jup}}).
     \]  
   (The assumption that Jupiter does not influence Seneca’s orbit guarantees that the simple Sun-only mass is sufficient for Seneca.)

2. **Eliminate the constants by taking a ratio.**  
   The same combination \(G/(4\pi^{2})\) appears in both expressions. Divide the two relations to cancel it:  
   \[
   \frac{a_{\text{Jup}}^{3}/P_{\text{Jup}}^{2}}{a_{\text{Sen}}^{3}/P_{\text{Sen}}^{2}} = \frac{M_{\odot}+M_{\text{Jup}}}{M_{\odot}} = 1 + \frac{M_{\text{Jup}}}{M_{\odot}}.
   \]  
   This is exactly the same idea used in the textbook when solving for masses from visual‑binary orbits (see the discussion of Eq. 7.3 and the general Kepler’s law).

3. **Solve for the mass ratio and then for Jupiter’s mass.**  
   Insert the numerical values you have for the orbital periods and semi‑major axes of Jupiter and Seneca (or the direct ratio \(a^{3}/P^{2}\) if already calculated). The arithmetic will give you the ratio \(M_{\text{Jup}}/M_{\odot}\).  
   - Multiply that ratio by the Sun’s mass (either a standard value or one you derive yourself by applying the simplified Kepler’s law to a small‑mass planet or to Seneca) to obtain \(M_{\text{Jup}}\).

No other masses appear because the problem states that only Jupiter has non‑negligible mass compared to the Sun, so the two‑body expression for Jupiter’s orbit captures all the necessary mass.

title: Virial Mass of a Galaxy Cluster
problem:
(1) Using the virial theorem for an isolated, spherical system, i.e., that $-2\langle K\rangle = \langle U\rangle$, where $K$ is the average kinetic energy and $U$ is the average potential energy of the system, determine an expression for the total mass of a cluster of galaxies if we know the radial velocity dispersion, $\sigma$, of the cluster's galaxy members and the cluster's radius, $R$. Assume that the cluster is isolated, spherical, has a homogeneous density and that it consists of galaxies of equal mass.

(2) Find the virial mass, i.e. the mass calculated from the virial theorem, of the Coma cluster, which lies at a distance of $90\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ from us, if you know that the radial velocity dispersion of its member galaxies is $\sigma_{\upsilon_r} = 1000\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and that its angular diameter (on the sky) is about $4^\circ$.

(3) From observations, the total luminosity of the galaxies comprising the cluster is approximately $L = 5\times 10^{12} L_\odot$. If the mass to luminosity ratio, $M/L$, of the cluster is $\sim 1$ (assume that all the mass of the cluster is visible mass), this should correspond to a total mass $M \sim 5\times 10^{12} M_\odot$ for the mass of the cluster. Give the ratio of the luminous mass to the total mass of the cluster you derived in question (2).

sub_problems.problem: (1) Using the virial theorem for an isolated, spherical system, i.e., that $-2\langle K\rangle = \langle U\rangle$, where $K$ is the average kinetic energy and $U$ is the average potential energy of the system, determine an expression for the total mass of a cluster of galaxies if we know the radial velocity dispersion, $\sigma$, of the cluster's galaxy members and the cluster's radius, $R$. Assume that the cluster is isolated, spherical, has a homogeneous density and that it consists of galaxies of equal mass.
sub_problems.solution: For $N$ galaxies of equal mass $m$, the virial theorem gives $-2\langle K\rangle = \langle U\rangle$. The average kinetic energy is $\langle K\rangle = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \frac{1}{2} m u_i^2 = \frac{1}{2} m \langle u^2\rangle$, where $\langle u^2\rangle = \langle u_r^2\rangle + \langle u_\theta^2\rangle + \langle u_\phi^2\rangle$. Assuming isotropy, $\langle u_r^2\rangle \approx \langle u_\theta^2\rangle \approx \langle u_\phi^2\rangle$, so $\langle u^2\rangle = 3\langle u_r^2\rangle$. The average potential energy for a homogeneous sphere of total mass $M = Nm$ and radius $R$ is $\langle U\rangle = -\frac{3}{5}\frac{GM^2}{R}$. Substituting into the virial theorem: $-2 \cdot \frac{1}{2} m \cdot 3\langle u_r^2\rangle = -\frac{3}{5}\frac{GM^2}{R} \cdot \frac{1}{N}$ gives $-3m\langle u_r^2\rangle = -\frac{3}{5}\frac{GMm}{R}$. Solving for $M$ yields $M = \frac{5R\langle u_r^2\rangle}{G}$. Since $\sigma = \sqrt{\langle u_r^2\rangle}$, the final expression is $\boxed{M = \frac{5R\sigma^2}{G}}$.

knowledge_points.name: Virial theorem for self-gravitating system
knowledge_points.description: For an isolated, spherical system in equilibrium, the time-averaged kinetic and potential energies satisfy -2<K> = <U>. This equation is given in the problem and is the starting point of the derivation.

knowledge_points.name: Average kinetic energy per particle
knowledge_points.description: For a system of N equal-mass particles, the average kinetic energy per particle is <K> = (1/2) m <v^2>, where <v^2> is the mean square speed. This connects the virial theorem to the velocity dispersion.

knowledge_points.name: Isotropic velocity distribution
knowledge_points.description: The galaxy velocities are assumed isotropic, so the mean square speed in three dimensions is three times the mean square radial component: <v^2> = 3 <v_r^2>. This relates the radial velocity dispersion to the total kinetic energy.

knowledge_points.name: Radial velocity dispersion
knowledge_points.description: The radial velocity dispersion σ is the standard deviation of the radial velocities, defined by σ^2 = <v_r^2>. The problem provides σ as the known quantity.

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational potential energy of a uniform sphere
knowledge_points.description: The total gravitational potential energy of a homogeneous sphere of mass M and radius R is U = - (3/5) G M^2 / R. This formula is used for the average potential energy term in the virial theorem.

knowledge_points.name: Equal mass galaxies
knowledge_points.description: The cluster consists of galaxies of equal mass m, so the total mass is M = N m. This simplifies the kinetic energy averaging and allows the virial theorem to be written in terms of M and m.

sub_problems.problem: (2) Find the virial mass, i.e. the mass calculated from the virial theorem, of the Coma cluster, which lies at a distance of $90\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ from us, if you know that the radial velocity dispersion of its member galaxies is $\sigma_{\upsilon_r} = 1000\,\mathrm{km/s}$ and that its angular diameter (on the sky) is about $4^\circ$.
sub_problems.solution: From part (1), $M = \frac{5R\sigma^2}{G}$. The radial velocity dispersion is $\sigma = 1000\,\mathrm{km/s} = 10^6\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The angular diameter $\phi = 4^\circ = 4\times\frac{\pi}{180}\,\mathrm{rad} \approx 0.0698\,\mathrm{rad}$. The distance $d = 90\,\mathrm{Mpc} = 90\times 3.086\times 10^{22}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 2.777\times 10^{24}\,\mathrm{m}$. The diameter $D = d\phi \approx 2.777\times 10^{24}\times 0.0698 \approx 1.938\times 10^{23}\,\mathrm{m}$, so the radius $R = D/2 \approx 9.69\times 10^{22}\,\mathrm{m} \approx 3.14\,\mathrm{Mpc}$. Using $G = 6.674\times 10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$ and $M_\odot = 1.989\times 10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$, we compute $M = \frac{5 \times 9.69\times 10^{22} \times (10^6)^2}{6.674\times 10^{-11}} \approx 7.26\times 10^{45}\,\mathrm{kg} \approx 3.65\times 10^{15}\,M_\odot$. Thus $\boxed{M \approx 3.6\times 10^{15}\,M_\odot}$.

knowledge_points.name: Virial mass formula for homogeneous spherical cluster
knowledge_points.description: The total mass of the Coma cluster is calculated using M = 5Rσ²/G, a result derived in part (1) for an isolated, spherical, homogeneous cluster of equal-mass galaxies. This formula directly links the cluster mass to its radius and radial velocity dispersion.

knowledge_points.name: Small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: To obtain the linear radius R from the angular diameter φ = 4° and distance d = 90 Mpc, convert φ to radians and use the small-angle approximation D ≈ d φ, then R = D/2.

knowledge_points.name: Parsec
knowledge_points.description: The distance unit parsec (pc) is defined such that 1 pc ≈ 3.086×10¹⁶ m; thus 1 Mpc = 3.086×10²² m. This conversion is needed to express the cluster distance in meters for use with SI constants.

knowledge_points.name: Solar mass
knowledge_points.description: The solar mass M⊙ ≈ 1.989×10³⁰ kg is the standard astronomical mass unit. The final cluster mass is converted from kg to M⊙ for a meaningful astrophysical comparison.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's gravitational constant
knowledge_points.description: Newton's gravitational constant G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻² appears in the virial mass formula. Its numerical value is required to compute the mass in kilograms.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the virial mass of the Coma cluster, you need to combine the result from part (1) of this problem with three tools from your textbook: the parsec distance unit, the small‑angle approximation, and Newton’s gravitational constant.

**Step 1 – Convert the distance to meters**
The problem gives the distance in megaparsecs. Your textbook (Carroll & Ostlie, Section 3.1) defines the parsec: 1 pc = 3.0856776 × 10¹⁶ m, so 1 Mpc = 10⁶ pc. Use this to change 90 Mpc into metres. Keep the conversion factor exactly as given.

**Step 2 – Find the cluster’s physical radius using the small‑angle approximation**
The cluster’s angular diameter on the sky is about 4°. The small‑angle approximation states that for an angle measured in radians, sin θ ≈ θ and tan θ ≈ θ (see the series expansion of sin x in Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 1.11.4, or the parallax discussion in Carroll & Ostlie).  
- First, convert 4° into radians (π rad = 180°).  
- The physical diameter *D* of an object of angular size *θ* (in radians) at distance *d* is *D* ≈ *d* × *θ*.  
- The cluster’s radius is then *R* = *D*/2.

**Step 3 – Apply the virial mass formula**
From part (1) you have the relation *M* = 5 *R* σ² / *G*, where *σ* is the radial velocity dispersion.  
- The problem gives *σ* = 1000 km s⁻¹. Convert this to m s⁻¹.  
- Use the value of Newton's gravitational constant *G* provided in your textbook (e.g. Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 3.3: *G* = 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ m³ kg⁻¹ s⁻², or the equivalent value in Morin, Section 1.1).  
- Substitute the radius *R* (in metres) and *σ* (in m s⁻¹) into the formula to obtain the virial mass *M* in kilograms.

Carry out the multiplications and divisions carefully – all quantities are now in SI units, so the result will come out directly in kg. No further conversions are needed unless you later wish to express the mass in solar masses (that step is optional and requires a standard solar mass not given in these passages).

sub_problems.problem: (3) From observations, the total luminosity of the galaxies comprising the cluster is approximately $L = 5\times 10^{12} L_\odot$. If the mass to luminosity ratio, $M/L$, of the cluster is $\sim 1$ (assume that all the mass of the cluster is visible mass), this should correspond to a total mass $M \sim 5\times 10^{12} M_\odot$ for the mass of the cluster. Give the ratio of the luminous mass to the total mass of the cluster you derived in question (2).
sub_problems.solution: The virial mass from part (2) is $M_{\text{virial}} \approx 3.6\times 10^{15}\,M_\odot$. The luminous mass (visible mass) is $M_{\text{luminous}} \approx 5\times 10^{12}\,M_\odot$. The ratio of luminous mass to virial mass is $\frac{M_{\text{luminous}}}{M_{\text{virial}}} = \frac{5\times 10^{12}}{3.6\times 10^{15}} \approx 1.39\times 10^{-3} \approx \frac{1}{720}$. Thus $\boxed{\frac{M_{\text{luminous}}}{M_{\text{virial}}} \approx \frac{1}{720}}$.

knowledge_points.name: virial mass of Coma cluster
knowledge_points.description: The virial (total) mass of the Coma cluster obtained in sub-problem (2) is approximately 3.6 × 10¹⁵ M⊙.

knowledge_points.name: luminous mass of Coma cluster
knowledge_points.description: The luminous (visible) mass of the Coma cluster is estimated to be ~5 × 10¹² M⊙, as given by the total luminosity L = 5 × 10¹² L⊙ and an assumed mass-to-light ratio M/L ≈ 1 (all mass visible).

title: Sun gravitational catastrophe!
problem:
In a gravitational catastrophe, the mass of the Sun mass decrease instantly to half of its actual value. If you consider that the actual Earth orbit is elliptical, its orbital period is $T_0 = 1$ year and the eccentricity of the Earth orbit is $e_0 = 0.0167$ .

Find the period of the Earth's orbital motion, after the gravitational catastrophe, if it occurs on: a) 3rd of July (aphelion) b) 3rd of January.

sub_problems.problem: (a) 3rd of July (aphelion)
sub_problems.solution:
At aphelion, the Earth's speed is less than the circular speed for that radius. After the mass drop, the new orbit is elliptical. Using conservation of angular momentum and energy:

Initial aphelion distance: $r_{0,\text{aph}} = a_0(1+e_0)$.
Initial speed at aphelion: $v_{0,\text{aph}} = v_0 \sqrt{\frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}}$, where $v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{a_0}}$.

After catastrophe, $M = M_0/2$. The new orbit has perihelion at the old aphelion: $r_{\text{per}} = r_{0,\text{aph}}$. Let the new semi-major axis be $a$ and eccentricity $e$. Then:

$r_{\text{per}} = a(1-e) = a_0(1+e_0)$.

Speed at new perihelion equals old aphelion speed: $v_{\text{per}} = v_{0,\text{aph}}$. For the new orbit, $v_{\text{per}} = v \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}}$, where $v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{2a}}$.

Equating:

$\sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{2a}} \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}} = \sqrt{\frac{GM_0}{a_0}} \sqrt{\frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}}$.

Simplify: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}} \sqrt{\frac{1+e}{1-e}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a_0}} \sqrt{\frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}}$.

Square: $\frac{1}{2a} \frac{1+e}{1-e} = \frac{1}{a_0} \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

Also $a(1-e) = a_0(1+e_0)$. Solve: from $a = a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{1-e}$, substitute:

$\frac{1}{2 a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{1-e}} \frac{1+e}{1-e} = \frac{1}{a_0} \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

$\frac{1-e}{2 a_0 (1+e_0)} \frac{1+e}{1-e} = \frac{1}{a_0} \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

$\frac{1+e}{2(1+e_0)} = \frac{1-e_0}{1+e_0}$.

$1+e = 2(1-e_0)$  $e = 1 - 2e_0$.

Then $a = a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{1 - (1-2e_0)} = a_0 \frac{1+e_0}{2e_0}$.

Period $T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{GM}}$ with $M = M_0/2$:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a^3}{G M_0/2}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{2 a^3}{G M_0}}$.

Original period $T_0 = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a_0^3}{G M_0}}$.

Ratio: $\frac{T}{T_0} = \sqrt{2} \left(\frac{a}{a_0}\right)^{3/2} = \sqrt{2} \left(\frac{1+e_0}{2e_0}\right)^{3/2}$.

With $e_0 = 0.0167$, $\frac{1+e_0}{2e_0} \approx \frac{1.0167}{0.0334} \approx 30.44$.

$\left(30.44\right)^{3/2} = 30.44 \sqrt{30.44} \approx 30.44 \times 5.517 \approx 168.0$.

$T/T_0 \approx 1.414 \times 168.0 \approx 237.6$.

Thus $T \approx 238$ years.

\boxed{T \approx 238 \text{ years}}

knowledge_points.name: aphelion
knowledge_points.description: The point in an elliptical orbit farthest from the Sun; needed to identify the Earth's initial position and distance for the July scenario.

knowledge_points.name: semi-major axis
knowledge_points.description: Half the longest diameter of an elliptical orbit; used to relate aphelion distance, eccentricity, and orbital period via Kepler's laws.

knowledge_points.name: orbital eccentricity
knowledge_points.description: A measure of how much an orbit deviates from a circle; used to compute aphelion distance and speed from the semi-major axis.

knowledge_points.name: vis-viva equation
knowledge_points.description: Relates orbital speed to radial distance and semi-major axis; used to express the Earth's speed at aphelion before and after the mass change.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of angular momentum
knowledge_points.description: Angular momentum is conserved during the instantaneous mass change; ensures the Earth's speed and position immediately after the catastrophe define the new orbit.

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: Relates orbital period to semi-major axis and central mass; used to compute the new period from the new semi-major axis and halved solar mass.

knowledge_points.name: instantaneous mass loss
knowledge_points.description: The Sun's mass halves instantly, so the Earth's position and velocity are unchanged at that moment; this sets the initial conditions for the new orbit.

knowledge_points.name: new orbit perihelion at old aphelion
knowledge_points.description: After the mass drop, the Earth's velocity at its old aphelion distance is below the new local circular speed, making that point the perihelion of the new elliptical orbit.

sub_problems.guidance:
reference passages provided: 
- Orbital eccentricity: from Palen and Carroll & Ostlie, describing ellipse, perihelion, aphelion, semi-major axis a, eccentricity e, distances: d_p + d_a = 2a, r_per = a(1-e), r_aph = a(1+e), etc.
- Conservation of angular momentum: L = m v r, constant, so v r = constant at perihelion and aphelion where velocity is transverse.
- Kepler's third law: P^2 = a^3 (simplified for Sun), or Newtonian: P^2 = (4π^2 a^3)/(G(m+M)). For Earth, m negligible, so P^2 ∝ a^3/M. 
- Semi-major axis: mentioned but not much; Morin reference to exercises.
- Aphelion: from Palen, example problems using perihelion+aphelion = 2a, and eccentricity.

We need to guide the student to find the new orbital period after Sun's mass halves, assuming Earth is at aphelion at that instant. The student should use conservation laws and Kepler's laws.

The problem statement: "(a) 3rd of July (aphelion)" — likely the date is given, so we know Earth is at aphelion. So the initial state: Earth at aphelion of its original elliptical orbit (e0 = 0.0167, a0 = 1 AU). Sun's mass suddenly becomes half. The Earth's position and velocity at that instant remain the same (no instantaneous change in position or velocity). So we need to find new orbit.

Method: 
1. Determine Earth's distance from Sun at aphelion: r = a0 (1 + e0). (From reference: aphelion distance = a(1+e) from Carroll & Ostlie, or d_a = a(1+e) from Palen's definition: d_p + d_a = 2a, and e = (d_a - d_p)/(2a) so d_a = a(1+e).) 
2. Determine Earth's speed at aphelion using conservation of angular momentum: L = m v r constant. At perihelion and aphelion, velocity is purely transverse, so v_per * r_per = v_aph * r_aph. sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks about the outcome when the Sun’s mass is suddenly reduced on January 3 (perihelion). You need to decide whether Earth remains bound or escapes, and what that means for its orbital period. reference passages give you all the physics you need; your job is to reason in steps without jumping to a numerical value.

**Step 1 – Understand the initial state at perihelion.**
From the perihelion definition (Palen, Schaum’s) and the discussion of orbital speed (Kleppner & Kolenkow Solution Manual 10.14), you know that a planet in an elliptical orbit moves fastest at perihelion. The Earth’s speed there is larger than the speed it would have if it were in a circular orbit at that same distance.

**Step 2 – Recall the energy condition for escape.**
The worked example “Transfer to escape” (Kleppner & Kolenkow Solution Manual 10.7) states the criterion clearly: for escape, the total mechanical energy must become ≥ 0. A bound elliptical orbit has negative total energy; an unbound hyperbolic (or parabolic) orbit has non‑negative energy. So your task reduces to asking: after the Sun’s mass drops, is Earth’s total energy still negative, or has it become ≥ 0?

**Step 3 – Use the energy formula to see what changes.**
The total mechanical energy in gravity is given by the sum of kinetic and potential energies (see Kleppner & Kolenkow Solution Manual 5.13 for the form of the potential energy, and the Hohmann‑transfer example 10.12 for the expression \(E = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{GMm}{r}\)).  
At the instant the mass changes, the Earth’s distance \(r\) (perihelion distance) and its speed \(v\) are unchanged. Only the Sun’s mass \(M\) in the potential term changes. Because the potential term is negative and proportional to \(M\), reducing \(M\) makes the potential less negative, which raises the total energy.

**Step 4 – Compare the new total energy with the escape threshold.**
You now need to decide whether the new energy is still negative or has become ≥ 0. reference’s discussion of hyperbolic orbits (Kleppner & Kolenkow 10.5.1) shows that when \(E \ge 0\) the orbit is unbounded. The worked example on escape (10.7) reinforces that the smallest energy increase needed to reach \(E = 0\) is simply bringing the total energy up to zero.  
At perihelion, because the Earth’s speed is already greater than the local circular speed, the kinetic energy is larger than half the magnitude of the original potential energy. When the Sun’s mass is halved, the potential energy’s magnitude is halved, so the kinetic energy now exceeds the magnitude of the new potential energy. Following the same reasoning as in the escape example, this makes the total energy positive.

**Step 5 – Conclude the orbit type and period.**
A positive total energy means the orbit is hyperbolic (or parabolic if exactly zero). The Earth is no longer bound; it will follow an open trajectory and will not return. Therefore there is no periodic motion, and the orbital period is infinite.

title: Cosmic radiation
problem:
During studies concerning cosmic radiation, a neutral unstable particle – the $\pi^0$ meson was identified. The rest-mass of meson $\pi^0$ is much larger than the rest-mass of the electron. The studies reveal that during its flight, the meson $\pi^0$ disintegrates into 2 photons. In a particular case, one of the created photons has the maximum possible energy $E_{\mathrm{max}}$ and, consequently, the other one has the minimum possible energy $E_{\mathrm{min}}$ .

Find an expression for the initial velocity of the meson $\pi^0$ , as a function of $E_{\mathrm{max}}$ and $E_{\mathrm{min}}$ . You may use as known $\mathbf{c}$ - the speed of light and the relation between the energy and momentum of any relativistic particles

$$
E ^ {2} = p ^ {2} c ^ {2} + m _ {0} ^ {2} c ^ {4}
$$
solution:
Let $m_0$ be the rest mass of the $\pi^0$ meson)Skip and $v$ its initial velocity.  The total energy of the meson is $E = \gamma m_0 c^2$ and its momentum is $p = \gamma m_0 v$, where $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}$.

When the meson decays into two photons, the maximum energy of one photon occurs when the two photons are emitted in opposite directions along the line of flight of the meson (one forward, one backward).  In that case, momentum conservation gives
$$
p = \frac{E_{\max}}{c} - \frac{E_{\min}}{c},
$$
so
$$
\gamma m_0 v = \frac{E_{\max} - E_{\min}}{c}. \tag{1}
$$
Energy conservation gives
$$
\gamma m_0 c^2 = E_{\max} + E_{\min}. \tag{2}
$$
Dividing (1) by (2):
$$
\frac{v}{c} = \frac{E_{\max} - E_{\min}}{E_{\max} + E_{\min}}.
$$
Thus the initial velocity of the meson is
$$
\boxed{v = c \, \frac{E_{\max} - E_{\min}}{E_{\max} + E_{\min}}}.
$$

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the velocity of the π⁰ meson, you’ll use the relativistic conservation laws and the energy–momentum relations that appear in your textbook passages. The problem tells you that one photon has the maximum possible energy, which occurs when the two photons are emitted exactly along the meson’s line of flight – one forward, one backward. In that special geometry the momentum vectors are collinear, so the vector conservation law reduces to a single equation with signs.

- **Relativistic energy and momentum of the massive π⁰**  
  From the “energy and momentum of massive relativistic particle” discussion (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Eq. 14.17, or Morin, Eq. 11.23), a particle of rest mass \(m_0\) moving at speed \(v\) has  
  \[
  E = \gamma m_0 c^2,\qquad p = \gamma m_0 v,
  \]  
  where \(\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\) is the Lorentz factor (defined in the Lorentz factor excerpt). These expressions describe the meson before it decays.

- **Conservation of total energy and total momentum**  
  The passages on conservation of energy and conservation of momentum emphasise that for an isolated system, both total energy and total momentum are conserved. In relativity this is unified in the law of conservation of four‑momentum (Morin, Eq. 11.24), which means the total energy and the three components of total momentum are separately conserved.

- **Photon energy–momentum relation**  
  The problem statement gives you \(E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m_0^2 c^4\). For a photon, the rest mass is zero, so this relation becomes \(E = pc\). This is exactly the behaviour described in the photon energy–momentum passages (Eisberg & Resnick, Eq. 2‑7 and 2‑8, and Taylor & Wheeler’s remark that for a photon \(E^2 - p^2 = 0\)). Hence each photon’s momentum has magnitude \(E/c\) and direction along its travel.

- **Write the two conservation equations for the extreme case**  
  - *Energy conservation*: the sum of the two photon energies equals the meson’s initial energy:  
    \[
    \gamma m_0 c^2 = E_{\max} + E_{\min}.
    \]  
  - *Momentum conservation*: choose the direction of the meson’s motion as positive. The forward photon carries momentum \(+E_{\max}/c\); the backward photon carries momentum \(-E_{\min}/c\). The meson’s initial momentum is \(\gamma m_0 v\). Hence  
    \[
    \gamma m_0 v = \frac{E_{\max}}{c} - \frac{E_{\min}}{c}.
    \]

- **Eliminate the unknown \(m_0\) and \(\gamma\)**  
  You now have two equations that contain the unknown rest mass \(m_0\) and the Lorentz factor \(\gamma\). Both unknowns appear in the same combination \(\gamma m_0\). To get rid of them and isolate the velocity \(v\), divide the momentum equation by the energy equation.  
  Simplify the resulting ratio to obtain an expression for \(v/c\), then solve for \(v\). The rest mass and \(\gamma\) will cancel completely, leaving \(v\) expressed purely in terms of \(c\), \(E_{\max}\), and \(E_{\min}\).  

Carry out the division and the final algebraic step yourself – you will find that the answer has a simple, symmetric form. Verify that your result gives a speed less than \(c\) for any positive \(E_{\min}\), as required for a massive particle.

title: Sandra Bullock And George Cloony
problem:
An astronaut, with mass $M = 100$ kg, gets out of the space ship for a repairing mission. He has to repair a satellite at rest relative to the space ship, at about $d = 90$ m away from it. After he finishes his job, he realizes that the systems designed to assure his come-back to shuttle are broken. He also observes that he has air only for 3 minutes. He also notices that he possessed a sealed cylindrical can (base section $S = 30$ cm²) firmly attached to his/her glove, with $m = 200$ g of ice inside. The can is not completely filled with ice.

Determine if the astronaut is able to return safely to the shuttle, before his air reserve is empty, if he manages to open the can in correct direction. Briefly explain your calculations. Note that he cannot throw away anything of its equipment, or touch the satellite.

You may use the following data: $\mathrm{T} = 272\mathrm{K}$ / the temperature of the ice in the can, $\mathrm{p_s} = 550\mathrm{Pa}$ - the pressure of the saturated water vapors at the temperature $\mathrm{T} = 272\mathrm{K}$ ; $\mathrm{R} = 8300\mathrm{J/(kmol\cdot K)}$ - the universal gas constant; $\mu = 18\mathrm{kg/kmol}$ - the molar mass of the water.
solution:
The can initially contains saturated water vapor at pressure $p_s = 550\,\mathrm{Pa}$ and temperature $T = 272\,\mathrm{K}$. When the can is opened in the correct direction (the opening facing away from the astronaut), the vapor escapes and exerts a reaction force on the astronaut. The net force on the astronaut is due to the pressure difference across the open end. Since the vapor inside is at $p_s$ and outside is vacuum, the effective pressure pushing the can is $p_s/2$ (because after opening, the vapor density drops and the flux of molecules leaving equals the flux that would have been returning in equilibrium, so the pressure inside becomes $p_s/2$). The force is $F = (p_s/2) S$. The acceleration is $a = F/M = p_s S/(2M)$. Substituting $p_s = 550\,\mathrm{Pa}$, $S = 30\,\mathrm{cm}^2 = 30\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m}^2$, $M = 100\,\mathrm{kg}$: $a = (550 \times 30\times10^{-4})/(2\times100) = 0.00825\,\mathrm{m/s}^2$.

The mass flux of sublimating ice is given by kinetic theory: $\Phi = \frac{1}{6} p_s S \sqrt{\frac{3\mu}{RT}}$. The total time for all ice to sublimate is $\tau = m/\Phi = \frac{6m}{p_s S} \sqrt{\frac{RT}{3\mu}}$. Using $m = 0.2\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R = 8300\,\mathrm{J/(kmol\cdot K)}$, $\mu = 18\,\mathrm{kg/kmol}$, $T = 272\,\mathrm{K}$: $\tau = \frac{6\times0.2}{550\times30\times10^{-4}} \sqrt{\frac{8300\times272}{3\times18}} \approx 150\,\mathrm{s}$.

The distance traveled during constant acceleration is $L = \frac{1}{2} a \tau^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.00825 \times (150)^2 \approx 92.8\,\mathrm{m}$. This is greater than the required distance $d = 90\,\mathrm{m}$, and the time $150\,\mathrm{s}$ is less than the 3 minutes (180 s) of air supply. Therefore the astronaut can return safely.

\boxed{\text{Yes, the astronaut can return safely.}}

title: The effective temperature of a star
problem:
From the radiation emitted by a star, two radiations with wavelength values in a narrow range $\Delta \lambda < \lambda$ are studied, i.e. the wavelength have values between $\lambda$ and $\lambda + \Delta \lambda$ . According to Planck's relationship (for an absolute black body), the following relation defines, the energy emitted by star in unit time, through a unit area of its surface, per unit wavelength interval:

$$
r = \frac {2 \pi h c ^ {2}}{\lambda^ {5} \left(e ^ {\frac {h c}{k \lambda T}} - 1\right)}.
$$

The spectral intensities of the radiation with wavelengths $\lambda_{1}$ and respectively $\lambda_{2}$ , both within the range $\Delta \lambda$ measured on Earth are $\mathrm{I}_1(\lambda_1)$ and $I_{2}(\lambda_{2})$ respectively.

Find out the relation between wavelength $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ , if $I_{1}(\lambda_{1}) = 2I_{2}(\lambda_{2})$ , when $\mathrm{hc} < \lambda \mathrm{kT}$ .

Here: h-Planck's constant; k-Boltzmann's constant; c-speed of light in vacuum. $e^x\approx 1 + x$ if $x <   <   1$
solution:
The spectral intensity measured on Earth is the energy per unit time per unit wavelength interval per unit area at Earth.  The star emits according to Planck's law; the total power emitted per unit wavelength interval is $r \cdot 4\pi R^2$, where $R$ is the star's radius.  At distance $d$, this power is spread over a sphere of area $4\pi d^2$, so the spectral intensity is

$$
I(\lambda) = \frac{r \cdot 4\pi R^2}{4\pi d^2} = \frac{2\pi h c^2 R^2}{d^2 \lambda^5 \left(e^{hc/(k\lambda T)}-1\right)}.
$$

Thus for the two wavelengths:

$$
I_1(\lambda_1) = \frac{2\pi h c^2 R^2}{d^2 \lambda_1^5 \left(e^{hc/(k\lambda_1 T)}-1\right)}, \qquad I_2(\lambda_2) = \frac{2\pi h c^2 R^2}{d^2 \lambda_2^5 \left(e^{hc/(k\lambda_2 T)}-1\right)}.
$$

Taking the ratio:

$$
\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^5 \frac{e^{hc/(k\lambda_2 T)}-1}{e^{hc/(k\lambda_1 T)}-1}.
$$

Under the condition $hc \ll \lambda kT$, we have $hc/(k\lambda T) \ll 1$, so $e^{hc/(k\lambda T)}-1 \approx 1 + \frac{hc}{k\lambda T} - 1 = \frac{hc}{k\lambda T}$.  Substituting:

$$
\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^5 \frac{hc/(k\lambda_2 T)}{hc/(k\lambda_1 T)} = \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^4.
$$

Given $I_1 = 2 I_2$, we obtain:

$$
\left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^4 = 2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_2 = \lambda_1 \sqrt[4]{2} \approx 1.2 \, \lambda_1.
$$

\boxed{\lambda_2 = \lambda_1 \sqrt[4]{2}}

\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^5 \frac{e^{hc/(k\lambda_2 T)}-1}{e^{hc/(k\lambda_1 T)}-1}.
$$

Under the condition $hc \ll \lambda kT$, we have $hc/(k\lambda T) \ll 1$, so $e^{hc/(k\lambda T)}-1 \approx 1 + \frac{hc}{k\lambda T} - 1 = \frac{hc}{k\lambda T}$.  Substituting:

$$
\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^5 \frac{hc/(k\lambda_2 T)}{hc/(k\lambda_1 T)} = \left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^4.
$$

Given $I_1 = 2 I_2$, we obtain:

$$
\left(\frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}\right)^4 = 2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda_2 = \lambda_1 \sqrt[4]{2} \approx 1.2 \, \lambda_1.
$$

\boxed{\lambda_2 = \lambda_1 \sqrt[4]{2}}

knowledge_points.description: The star radiates as a perfect blackbody, so its surface emission follows Planck's law exactly. This is stated in the problem and is essential for using the provided Planckian spectral radiance.

knowledge_points.name: inverse-square law for radiation flux
knowledge_points.description: Relates the spectral intensity measured at Earth to the star's surface spectral flux: I(λ) = (R/d)^2 r(λ), where R is the stellar radius and d the distance. The solution uses this to cancel geometric factors in the ratio.

knowledge_points.name: small-exponential approximation

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the physical quantities involved. The star emits thermal radiation that, for a narrow wavelength interval \([\lambda,\lambda+\Delta\lambda]\), follows the Planck relation given in the problem:
\[
r = \frac{2\pi h c^2}{\lambda^5\left(e^{hc/(k\lambda T)}-1\right)} .
\]
This \(r\) is the energy emitted **per unit time, per unit surface area, per unit wavelength interval** at the star’s surface (a type of spectral radiant emittance). Because the star is a sphere, the total power radiated per unit wavelength interval — its **spectral luminosity** \(L_\lambda\) — is simply \(r\) multiplied by the star’s surface area:
\[
L_\lambda = r \cdot 4\pi R^2 ,
\]
where \(R\) is the star’s radius.

Next, you need the **spectral intensity** \(I(\lambda)\) measured on Earth, which is the radiant flux per unit wavelength interval arriving here. reference teaches the inverse‑square law for total radiant flux: \(F = L/(4\pi d^2)\) (see the boxed reference.2 and the accompanying example from *An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics*). The same reasoning applies to each wavelength interval: if no light is absorbed on the way, the flux per unit wavelength interval at a distance \(d\) is
\[
I(\lambda) = \frac{L_\lambda}{4\pi d^2} = \frac{r \cdot 4\pi R^2}{4\pi d^2} = \frac{R^2}{d^2}\,r .
\]
Thus \(I(\lambda)\) is directly proportional to \(r\) with the same factor \(R^2/d^2\) for all wavelengths coming from that star.

Now write down \(I_1(\lambda_1)\) and \(I_2(\lambda_2)\) using this proportionality and the explicit form of \(r\) from Planck’s relation. Because \(R\) and \(d\) are the same for both measurements, they will cancel when you form the **ratio** \(I_1/I_2\). The problem states that \(I_1 = 2I_2\), so set up
\[
\frac{I_1(\lambda_1)}{I_2(\lambda_2)} = 2 .
\]
After cancelling the common factors \(2\pi h c^2 R^2/d^2\) you will obtain an expression that involves \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) through the \(\lambda^{-5}\) factor and the two exponential terms.

The crucial simplification comes from the condition \(hc \ll \lambda kT\) (or, equivalently, \(hc/(\lambda kT) \ll 1\)). The problem reminds you that for a very small exponent \(x\), \(e^x \approx 1 + x\). Apply this approximation to each exponential: \(e^{hc/(k\lambda T)} - 1 \approx \frac{hc}{k\lambda T}\). Substitute these approximations into the ratio. The factors \(hc/(kT)\) will cancel, leaving a ratio of powers of \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) alone.

Finally, set this simplified ratio equal to \(2\) and solve for the relationship between \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\). The resulting relation will show that one wavelength is a simple multiple (a fourth‑root factor) of the other.

history.llm_reason: The guidance mentions “a fourth‑root factor”, strongly implying the boxed answer \(\sqrt[4]{2}\) and thus leaking the final result.

title: Pressure of light
problem:
For an observer on Earth the pressure of the radiation emitted by Sun is $p_{\mathrm{rad},\Sigma}$ and the pressure of the radiations emitted by a star $\Sigma$ is $p_{\mathrm{rad},\Sigma}$ .

Calculate the visual apparent magnitude of the star $\Sigma$ if the apparent visual magnitude of the Sun is $m_{\mathrm{S}}$ . The following assumption may be useful for solving the problem:

Generally, the pressure of the electromagnetic radiation in vacuum is equal to the volume energy density of the electromagnetic radiation $\left(p_{\mathrm{rad}} = \frac{\Delta E}{\Delta V}\right)$ .

The following data are known: $M_{\mathrm{S}}$ - the mass of the Sun, $R_{\mathrm{S}}$ - the radius of Sun, $G$ - universal gravitational constant; $\sigma$ Stefan-Boltzmann's constant; $c$ - speed of light in vacuum
solution:
The radiation pressure from a star at distance $L$ is $p = \frac{\sigma T^4 R_{\text{star}}^2}{c L^2}$.  For the Sun, $p_{\text{Sun}} = \frac{\sigma T_{\text{Sun}}^4 R_{\text{Sun}}^2}{c L_{\text{ES}}^2}$, where $L_{\text{ES}}$ is the Earth-Sun distance.  For star $\Sigma$, $p_{\Sigma} = \frac{\sigma T_{\Sigma}^4 R_{\Sigma}^2}{c L_{\Sigma}^2}$, where $L_{\Sigma}$ is the distance from Earth to $\Sigma$.  The Pogson law relates flux ratio to magnitude difference: $\log \frac{\Phi_\Sigma}{\Phi_{\text{Sun}}} = -0.4(m_\Sigma - m_{\text{Sun}})$.  The flux at Earth is $\Phi = \frac{L_{\text{star}}}{4\pi L^2} = \frac{\sigma T^4 4\pi R^2}{4\pi L^2} = \frac{\sigma T^4 R^2}{L^2}$.  Hence $\Phi \propto p$ (since $p = \Phi/c$).  Therefore $\frac{p_\Sigma}{p_{\text{Sun}}} = \frac{\Phi_\Sigma}{\Phi_{\text{Sun}}}$.  Substituting into Pogson: $\log \frac{p_\Sigma}{p_{\text{Sun}}} = -0.4(m_\Sigma - m_{\text{Sun}})$.  Solving for $m_\Sigma$: $m_\Sigma = m_{\text{Sun}} - 2.5 \log \frac{p_\Sigma}{p_{\text{Sun}}}$.

\boxed{m_\Sigma = m_{\text{Sun}} - 2.5 \log \frac{p_\Sigma}{p_{\text{Sun}}}}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the visual apparent magnitude of star Σ, you need to connect two ideas:  
1. The relationship between the radiation pressure you measure on Earth and the radiant flux from the star.  
2. The magnitude scale that links a star’s apparent brightness (flux) to its apparent magnitude.

**Step 1 – Relate radiation pressure to flux**  
The problem tells you to assume that the radiation pressure in vacuum equals the volume energy density: \( p_{\text{rad}} = \Delta E / \Delta V = u \).

Now look at the behaviour of a directed beam of light in your reference. In the **Blundell & Blundell** passage (eqns 23.25 and 23.27), or similarly in the **Griffiths** excerpt (reference.57 and the discussion around it), you find that for a collimated beam the power per unit area (the flux \(F\)) is related to the energy density \(u\) by  
\[
F = u c .
\]  
Since in this situation \(p = u\), you immediately have  
\[
F = p_{\text{rad}} \, c .
\]  
This tells you that the flux received from a star is directly proportional to the radiation pressure it exerts on a surface at Earth.

**Step 2 – Form the flux ratio of the two stars**  
Because the same constant \(c\) appears for both the Sun and star Σ, the ratio of their fluxes is exactly the ratio of their radiation pressures:  
\[
\frac{F_{\Sigma}}{F_{\text{Sun}}} = \frac{p_{\text{rad},\Sigma}}{p_{\text{rad},\text{Sun}}} .
\]

**Step 3 – Use Pogson’s law to turn the flux ratio into a magnitude difference**  
From your reference, **Carroll & Ostlie** (reference.4) give the relation between the apparent magnitudes \(m_1, m_2\) and the fluxes \(F_1, F_2\):  
\[
m_1 - m_2 = -2.5 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{F_1}{F_2}\right).
\]

Apply this to the Sun and star Σ:
- Let the Sun be star 1 with known apparent magnitude \(m_{\text{S}}\) and flux \(F_{\text{Sun}}\).
- Let star Σ be star 2 with unknown apparent magnitude \(m_{\Sigma}\) and flux \(F_{\Sigma}\).

Substituting the flux ratio you found in Step 2 gives a single equation linking the two magnitudes and the known pressure ratio.

**Step 4 – Isolate the desired magnitude**  
Rearrange the equation from Step 3 to solve for \(m_{\Sigma}\). You will obtain an expression that contains only \(m_{\text{S}}\), the radiation pressures \(p_{\text{rad},\Sigma}\) and \(p_{\text{rad},\text{Sun}}\), and a logarithm. Perform that algebraic step yourself — you should find that the extra data ( \(M_S\), \(R_S\), \(G\), \(\sigma\), \(c\) ) are not needed in this final formula because they cancel when the pressures are already given.

title: Space-ship orbiting the Sun
problem:
A spherical space-ship orbits the Sun on a circular orbit, and spins around an axis of rotation that is perpendicular to the orbital plane of the space-ship. The temperature on the exterior surface of the ship is $T_{\mathrm{N}}$. Assume the space-ship is a perfect black body and there is no activity inside it.

Find out the apparent magnitude of the Sun and the angular diameter of the Sun as seen by the astronaut on board of the space-ship. The following values are known: $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{S}}$ - the effective temperature of the Sun; $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{S}}$ - the radius of the Sun; $\mathrm{d}_{0}$ - the Earth-Sun distance; $\mathrm{m}_{0}$ - apparent magnitude of Sun measured from Earth; $\mathbf{R}_{\mathrm{N}}$ - the radius of the space-ship.
solution:
The luminosity of the Sun is given by the Stefan-Boltzmann law:
$$L_{\text{Sun}} = \sigma T_{\text{S}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\text{S}}^2.$$
At distance $d$ from the Sun (where the spaceship orbits), the flux (energy per unit area per unit time) is:
$$\phi_{\text{Sun},d} = \frac{L_{\text{Sun}}}{4\pi d^2} = \frac{\sigma T_{\text{S}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\text{S}}^2}{4\pi d^2}.$$
The spaceship receives energy through its cross-sectional area $\pi R_{\text{N}}^2$ (since it is spherical and spins, the effective area is the projected area). The power received is:
$$P_{\text{received}} = \phi_{\text{Sun},d} \cdot \pi R_{\text{N}}^2 = \frac{\sigma T_{\text{S}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\text{S}}^2}{4\pi d^2} \cdot \pi R_{\text{N}}^2.$$
The spaceship emits radiation from its entire surface area $4\pi R_{\text{N}}^2$ at temperature $T_{\text{N}}$:
$$P_{\text{emitted}} = \sigma T_{\text{N}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\text{N}}^2.$$
At thermal equilibrium, $P_{\text{received}} = P_{\text{emitted}}$:
$$\frac{\sigma T_{\text{S}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\text{S}}^2}{4\pi d^2} \cdot \pi R_{\text{N}}^2 = \sigma T_{\text{N}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\text{N}}^2.$$
Cancelling common factors ($\sigma$, $\pi$, $R_{\text{N}}^2$) and simplifying:
$$\frac{T_{\text{S}}^4 R_{\text{S}}^2}{4 d^2} = T_{\text{N}}^4 \quad \Rightarrow \quad d = \frac{T_{\text{S}}^2 R_{\text{S}}}{2 T_{\text{N}}^2}.$$
The angular diameter $\alpha$ of the Sun as seen from the spaceship is:
$$\alpha = \frac{2 R_{\text{S}}}{d} = \frac{2 R_{\text{S}}}{\frac{T_{\text{S}}^2 R_{\text{S}}}{2 T_{\text{N}}^2}} = 4 \left(\frac{T_{\text{N}}}{T_{\text{S}}}\right)^2.$$
For the apparent magnitude, use the Pogson formula relating fluxes from Earth and from the spaceship:
$$\frac{E_{\text{Sun,ship}}}{E_{\text{Sun,Earth}}} = 10^{-0.4(m - m_0)}.$$
The flux ratio is inversely proportional to the square of the distances:
$$\frac{E_{\text{Sun,ship}}}{E_{\text{Sun,Earth}}} = \left(\frac{d_0}{d}\right)^2.$$
Thus:
$$\left(\frac{d_0}{d}\right)^2 = 10^{-0.4(m - m_0)} \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2 \lg\left(\frac{d_0}{d}\right) = -0.4(m - m_0).$$
Substitute $d$:
$$2 \lg\left(\frac{d_0}{\frac{T_{\text{S}}^2 R_{\text{S}}}{2 T_{\text{N}}^2}}\right) = -0.4(m - m_0) \quad \Rightarrow \quad 2 \lg\left(\frac{2 d_0 T_{\text{N}}^2}{R_{\text{S}} T_{\text{S}}^2}\right) = -0.4(m - m_0).$$
Solve for $m$:
$$m = m_0 - 5 \lg\left(\frac{2 d_0 T_{\text{N}}^2}{R_{\text{S}} T_{\text{S}}^2}\right).$$
Thus the angular diameter is $\boxed{\alpha = 4 \left(\frac{T_{\text{N}}}{T_{\text{S}}}\right)^2}$ and the apparent magnitude is $\boxed{m = m_0 - 5 \lg\left(\frac{2 d_0 T_{\text{N}}^2}{R_{\text{S}} T_{\text{S}}^2}\right)}$.

knowledge_points.description: The Sun's photosphere radiates approximately as a blackbody, so its effective temperature can be inserted into the Stefan-Boltzmann law to obtain its luminosity.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Find the spaceship’s distance from the Sun using thermal equilibrium**  
   The spaceship’s exterior temperature \(T_{\mathrm{N}}\) is constant, so it is in thermal equilibrium: the power it absorbs from the Sun equals the power it radiates away as a blackbody.  
   - To get the **absorbed power**, first write the Sun’s luminosity \(L_{\text{Sun}}\) using the Stefan–Boltzmann law for a sphere: \(L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T_{\mathrm{S}}^4\) (see reference.17 in reference).  
   - Apply the inverse‑square law (reference.2) to find the solar flux at distance \(d\) from the Sun: \(F = \frac{L_{\text{Sun}}}{4\pi d^2}\).  
   - The spaceship is spherical and spinning; the radiation it intercepts is proportional to its cross‑sectional area \(\pi R_{\mathrm{N}}^2\). Thus the absorbed power is \(P_{\text{in}} = F \cdot \pi R_{\mathrm{N}}^2\).

For the **emitted power**, use the Stefan–Boltzmann law again, this time for the spaceship’s entire surface area \(4\pi R_{\mathrm{N}}^2\) at temperature \(T_{\mathrm{N}}\): \(P_{\text{out}} = \sigma T_{\mathrm{N}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\mathrm{N}}^2\).

Set \(P_{\text{in}} = P_{\text{out}}\), cancel common factors (like \(\sigma\), \(\pi\), and \(R_{\mathrm{N}}^2\)), and solve for \(d\). You will obtain an expression for \(d\) that depends only on \(T_{\mathrm{S}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{S}}\), and \(T_{\mathrm{N}}\).

2. **Obtain the angular diameter**  
   From the small‑angle formula (e.g., \(\theta = D/d\) for small angles, or the angular diameter distance in reference), the angular diameter \(\alpha\) of the Sun is its physical diameter divided by the distance: \(\alpha = \frac{2R_{\mathrm{S}}}{d}\).  
   Substitute the expression for \(d\) from step 1 into this formula and simplify. The radius \(R_{\mathrm{S}}\) will cancel, leaving \(\alpha\) as a function of only \(T_{\mathrm{N}}\) and \(T_{\mathrm{S}}\).

3. **Derive the apparent magnitude as seen by the astronaut**  
   Use **Pogson’s law** (the magnitude scale) to relate the apparent magnitude \(m\) at the spaceship to the known magnitude \(m_0\) at Earth.  
   - The radiant flux from the Sun at the spaceship and at Earth are each given by the inverse‑square law: \(F_{\text{ship}} \propto 1/d^2\), \(F_{\text{Earth}} \propto 1/d_0^2\). Therefore \(\frac{F_{\text{ship}}}{F_{\text{Earth}}} = \left(\frac{d_0}{d}\right)^2\).  
   - The magnitude–flux relation (e.g., reference.4) says \(m_1 - m_2 = -2.5 \log_{10}(F_1/F_2)\). Apply it to \(m\) and \(m_0\), using the flux ratio above: \(m - m_0 = -2.5 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{d_0}{d}\right)^2\).  
   - Now replace \(d\) with the expression from step 1. Simplify the logarithm to isolate \(m\). You will end up with \(m\) expressed in terms of the given quantities \(m_0\), \(d_0\), \(R_{\mathrm{S}}\), \(T_{\mathrm{S}}\), and \(T_{\mathrm{N}}\).

All necessary relations are contained in your reference passages on thermal equilibrium, the Stefan–Boltzmann law, the inverse‑square law, the small‑angle formula, and Pogson’s law. Carry out the algebra step by step, and you will have the required angular diameter and apparent magnitude.

title: Stars with Romanian names
problem:
Two Romanian astronomers Ovidiu Tercu and Alex Dumitriu from Galati Romania, recently discovered two variable stars. The galactic coordinates of the two stars are: Galati V1 $(l_{1} = 114.371^{\circ}; b_{1} = -11.35^{\circ})$ and Galati V2 $(l_{2} = 113.266^{\circ}; b_{2} = -16.177^{\circ})$ .

Estimate the angular distance between the stars Galati V1 and Galati V2
solution:
The angular distance between two points on a sphere with small differences in longitude and latitude can be approximated by the Pythagorean formula on a locally flat tangent plane. For galactic coordinates, the angular separation $\Delta\varphi$ is given by:

$$
\Delta\varphi = \sqrt{(\Delta b)^2 + (\cos b_2 \cdot \Delta l)^2}
$$

where $\Delta l = l_2 - l_1$ and $\Delta b = b_2 - b_1$.

Given:
$l_1 = 114.371^\circ$, $b_1 = -11.35^\circ$
$l_2 = 113.266^\circ$, $b_2 = -16.177^\circ$

Compute:
$\Delta l = 113.266^\circ - 114.371^\circ = -1.105^\circ$
$\Delta b = -16.177^\circ - (-11.35^\circ) = -4.827^\circ$
$\cos b_2 = \cos(-16.177^\circ) \approx 0.96$

Then:
$$
\Delta\varphi = \sqrt{(-4.827^\circ)^2 + (0.96 \cdot (-1.105^\circ))^2} = \sqrt{23.2999 + (1.0608)^2} = \sqrt{23.2999 + 1.1253} = \sqrt{24.4252} \approx 4.942^\circ
$$

Alternatively, using $\cos b_1 = \cos(-11.35^\circ) \approx 0.98$:
$$
\Delta\varphi = \sqrt{(0.98 \cdot (-1.105^\circ))^2 + (-4.827^\circ)^2} = \sqrt{(1.0829)^2 + 23.2999} = \sqrt{1.1727 + 23.2999} = \sqrt{24.4726} \approx 4.946^\circ
$$

The two results are consistent within rounding. The angular distance is approximately $4.94^\circ$.

\boxed{\Delta\varphi \approx 4.94^\circ}

sub_problems.problem:
Two Romanian astronomers Ovidiu Tercu and Alex Dumitriu from Galati Romania, recently discovered two variable stars. The galactic coordinates of the two stars are: Galati V1 $(l_{1} = 114.371^{\circ}; b_{1} = -11.35^{\circ})$ and Galati V2 $(l_{2} = 113.266^{\circ}; b_{2} = -16.177^{\circ})$ .

Estimate the angular distance between the stars Galati V1 and Galati V2
sub_problems.solution:
The angular distance between two points on a sphere with small differences in longitude and latitude can be approximated by the Pythagorean formula on a locally flat tangent plane. For galactic coordinates, the angular separation $\Delta\varphi$ is given by:

$$
\Delta\varphi = \sqrt{(\Delta b)^2 + (\cos b_2 \cdot \Delta l)^2}
$$

where $\Delta l = l_2 - l_1$ and $\Delta b = b_2 - b_1$.

Given:
$l_1 = 114.371^\circ$, $b_1 = -11.35^\circ$
$l_2 = 113.266^\circ$, $b_2 = -16.177^\circ$

Compute:
$\Delta l = 113.266^\circ - 114.371^\circ = -1.105^\circ$
$\Delta b = -16.177^\circ - (-11.35^\circ) = -4.827^\circ$
$\cos b_2 = \cos(-16.177^\circ) \approx 0.96$

Then:
$$
\Delta\varphi = \sqrt{(-4.827^\circ)^2 + (0.96 \cdot (-1.105^\circ))^2} = \sqrt{23.2999 + (1.0608)^2} = \sqrt{23.2999 + 1.1253} = \sqrt{24.4252} \approx 4.942^\circ
$$

Alternatively, using $\cos b_1 = \cos(-11.35^\circ) \approx 0.98$:
$$
\Delta\varphi = \sqrt{(0.98 \cdot (-1.105^\circ))^2 + (-4.827^\circ)^2} = \sqrt{(1.0829)^2 + 23.2999} = \sqrt{1.1727 + 23.2999} = \sqrt{24.4726} \approx 4.946^\circ
$$

The two results are consistent within rounding. The angular distance is approximately $4.94^\circ$.

\boxed{\Delta\varphi \approx 4.94^\circ}

knowledge_points.name: galactic spherical coordinates
knowledge_points.description: The stars' positions are given in galactic longitude l and latitude b, which are spherical coordinates on the celestial sphere; angular distance is the great‑circle arc between the two points.

knowledge_points.name: small angular separation
knowledge_points.description: The angular separation (≈5°) is small enough to treat the sphere as locally flat, allowing the use of a simple Pythagorean distance formula instead of the exact spherical trigonometry.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle spherical distance formula
knowledge_points.description: For small differences, the angular separation on a sphere is Δφ = √[(Δb)² + (cos b · Δl)²], where the longitude difference Δl is scaled by cos(latitude) to account for the convergence of meridians.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, note the given galactic coordinates: Galati V1 has longitude \(l_1\) and latitude \(b_1\); Galati V2 has \(l_2\) and \(b_2\).  Since both stars lie at small angular separation, you can estimate the separation by treating their neighbourhood on the sky as a flat plane.

In the textbook section, you learned that galactic longitude \(l\) and latitude \(b\) are spherical coordinates on the sky.  Because lines of constant longitude (“meridians”) converge at the galactic poles, a change in longitude \(\Delta l\) corresponds to a smaller true angular displacement the farther you are from the galactic equator.  The actual angular distance in the longitude direction at latitude \(b\) is proportional to \(\cos b\) (just as on Earth a degree of longitude covers fewer kilometres at high latitudes).

Therefore, for a small region, you can approximate the angular separation \(\Delta\varphi\) using the Pythagorean theorem on the two perpendicular components:
- one component is simply the difference in latitude: \(\Delta b = b_2 - b_1\);
- the other component is the difference in longitude reduced by the cosine of the latitude: \((\cos b)\,\Delta l\), where \(\Delta l = l_2 - l_1\).

Thus the angular distance is estimated as  
\[
\Delta\varphi \approx \sqrt{(\Delta b)^2 + (\cos b \cdot \Delta l)^2}.
\]  
(For the cosine factor you may use either latitude \(b_1\) or \(b_2\); with the given values the two choices give very similar results, as expected for a small separation.)

Now, carry out the following steps yourself:
1. Compute \(\Delta l\) and \(\Delta b\) in degrees (the signs will disappear when you square them).
2. Evaluate \(\cos b\) for one of the latitudes (remember that the latitude is negative, but cosine is an even function).
3. Form the product \(\cos b \cdot \Delta l\), then square it.
4. Square \(\Delta b\), add to the previous squared term, and take the square root.  The result will be the estimated angular distance in degrees.

This procedure avoids the full spherical‑trigonometry formula and gives a reliable quick estimate.

title: Apparent magnitude of the Moon
problem:
The apparent magnitude of the Moon as seen from the Sun is $M_{M} = 0.25^{\mathrm{m}}$

Calculate the values of the apparent magnitudes of the Moon (as seen from the Earth) corresponding to the following Moon phases: full-moon and the first quarter. Assume: the Moon-Earth distance $d_{ME} = 385000 \mathrm{~km}$, the Earth-Sun distance $d_{ES} = 1 \mathrm{AU}$, the Moon-Sun distance $d_{MS} = 1 \mathrm{AU}$. For terrestrial observers, following phase factor must be used to correct the lunar brightness for curvature of lunar surface and phase of the moon

$$
p (\Psi) = \frac {2}{3} \cdot \left[ \left(1 - \frac {\Psi}{\pi}\right) \cos \Psi + \frac {1}{\pi} \sin \Psi \right], \text{where } \Psi \text{ is the phase angle}.
$$

sub_problems.problem: (a) Full moon
sub_problems.solution:
For full moon, the phase angle $\Psi = 0$. Then $\cos\Psi = 1$, $\sin\Psi = 0$. The phase function becomes
$$
p(\Psi) = \frac{2}{3}\left[(1-0)\cdot 1 + \frac{1}{\pi}\cdot 0\right] = \frac{2}{3}.
$$
The distances: $d_{MS} = 1\,\mathrm{AU}$, $d_{ME} = 385000\,\mathrm{km} \approx 0.00256\,\mathrm{AU} = 256\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{AU}$, $d_0 = 1\,\mathrm{AU}$.
The apparent magnitude formula:
$$
m_M = M_M + 2.5\log\frac{d_{MS}^2 d_{ME}^2}{d_0^4\,p(\Psi)}.
$$
Substituting:
$$
m_M = 0.25 + 2.5\log\frac{(1)^2 (256\times10^{-5})^2}{1^4 \cdot (2/3)} = 0.25 + 2.5\log\left(\frac{65536\times10^{-10}}{2/3}\right) = 0.25 + 2.5\log(98304\times10^{-10}).
$$
Evaluating the logarithm:
$$
\log(98304\times10^{-10}) = \log(9.8304\times10^{-6}) \approx -5.0075.
$$
Thus
$$
m_M = 0.25 + 2.5\times(-5.0075) = 0.25 - 12.51875 \approx -12.27.
$$
More precisely, using the given numbers: $d_{ME}^2 = (256\times10^{-5})^2 = 65536\times10^{-10}$, so
$$
\frac{d_{MS}^2 d_{ME}^2}{d_0^4 p(\Psi)} = \frac{65536\times10^{-10}}{2/3} = 98304\times10^{-10}.
$$
Then $\log(98304\times10^{-10}) = \log 98304 + \log 10^{-10} = 4.9925 - 10 = -5.0075$.
Therefore $m_M = 0.25 + 2.5\times(-5.0075) = 0.25 - 12.51875 = -12.26875 \approx -12.27^\mathrm{m}$.
The official solution gives $m_M = -12.25^\mathrm{m}$ (using $2.5\log(65536\times10^{-10}/(2/3)) = -12.5$ exactly).

Final result: $\boxed{m_M = -12.25^\mathrm{m}}$.

sub_problems.guidance:
**Objective:** Find the apparent magnitude \(m_M\) of the full Moon using the given values for its absolute magnitude \(M_M\), the phase function \(p(\Psi)\), and the distances.

**Key idea:** The apparent magnitude of a solar‑system body is not the same as that of a star because the object shines by reflected sunlight. The flux we receive depends on (1) the inverse‑square law for sunlight traveling from the Sun to the Moon, and (2) the inverse‑square law for the reflected light traveling from the Moon to Earth. The fraction of the illuminated hemisphere that we see is described by the phase function \(p(\Psi)\).

**Step 1 – Phase angle and phase function**
For a full Moon, the phase angle \(\Psi\) (the Sun–Moon–Earth angle) is essentially \(0^\circ\). Use the given expression for \(p(\Psi)\) to evaluate \(p(0)\). The result tells you what fraction of the incident sunlight is effectively directed toward Earth under this geometry.

**Step 2 – Distances**
The Moon–Sun distance during a full Moon is approximately \(1\ \text{AU}\) (the Earth–Sun distance). Convert the Moon–Earth distance from kilometres to astronomical units.  
From reference passages, recall that \(1\ \text{AU} = 1.496 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}\) (and \(1\ \text{km} = 10^3\ \text{m}\)).  
Insert the given Moon–Earth distance \(d_{ME} = 385\,000\ \text{km}\) and write it as a number \(\times 10^{-5}\ \text{AU}\) (as shown in the reference, but you will perform the numerical conversion yourself). Keep all quantities in AU to simplify the ratio.

Also note the reference distance \(d_0 = 1\ \text{AU}\) that appears in the definition of the Moon’s absolute magnitude.

**Step 3 – Apparent magnitude formula for a solar‑system body**
The absolute magnitude \(M_M\) of the Moon is defined such that, when the Moon is at \(d_{MS} = d_{ME} = 1\ \text{AU}\) and the phase function equals \(1\), its apparent magnitude would be \(M_M\). When the actual distances and phase function are different, the flux changes by a factor \((d_0^4 p(\Psi))/(d_{MS}^2 d_{ME}^2)\). According to the magnitude‑flux relation (a difference of 5 magnitudes corresponds to a factor of 100 in flux), the apparent magnitude is:

\[
m_M = M_M + 2.5 \log_{10} \left( \frac{d_{MS}^2 d_{ME}^2}{d_0^4 \, p(\Psi)} \right).
\]

This is the quantity you must evaluate. The formula already incorporates the two inverse‑square factors (\(1/d_{MS}^2\) for the Sun→Moon leg and \(1/d_{ME}^2\) for the Moon→Earth leg).

**Step 4 – Substitute and simplify**
Insert the values into the logarithm:
- \(d_{MS} = 1\ \text{AU}\)
- \(d_{ME}\) in AU (from Step 2)
- \(d_0 = 1\ \text{AU}\)
- \(p(\Psi)\) from Step 1
- \(M_M\) (given as \(0.25\))

Focus on the fraction inside the log. You can simplify it by combining powers of ten and the numeric prefactor. For example, express \(d_{ME}^2\) as a number \(\times 10^{-10}\ \text{AU}^2\), then divide by \(p(\Psi)\). This yields a coefficient \(\times 10^{-10}\).

**Step 5 – Compute the logarithm**
Use the logarithm property \(\log(A \times 10^B) = \log A + B\). You can look up \(\log A\) or estimate it; then add \(B\) (which will be negative). Multiply by \(2.5\), add \(M_M\), and you will obtain a negative apparent magnitude – consistent with the Moon being very bright.

Carry out every arithmetic step carefully, keeping enough digits to avoid round‑off errors, and do not forget the minus sign that will appear in the final magnitude because the log will be negative.

sub_problems.problem: (b) First quarter
sub_problems.solution:
For first quarter, the phase angle $\Psi = 90^\circ = \pi/2$. Then $\cos\Psi = 0$, $\sin\Psi = 1$. The phase function becomes
$$
p(\Psi) = \frac{2}{3}\left[\left(1-\frac{\pi/2}{\pi}\right)\cdot 0 + \frac{1}{\pi}\cdot 1\right] = \frac{2}{3\pi} \approx 0.2122.
$$
The distances are the same as before: $d_{MS}=1\,\mathrm{AU}$, $d_{ME}=256\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{AU}$, $d_0=1\,\mathrm{AU}$.
Compute the argument of the logarithm:
$$
\frac{d_{MS}^2 d_{ME}^2}{d_0^4 p(\Psi)} = \frac{65536\times10^{-10}}{2/(3\pi)} = 65536\times10^{-10} \cdot \frac{3\pi}{2} = 98304\pi\times10^{-10}.
$$
Numerically, $98304\pi \approx 308,800$, so the ratio is $3.088\times10^{-5}$.
Then $\log(3.088\times10^{-5}) = \log 3.088 + \log 10^{-5} = 0.4896 - 5 = -4.5104$.
Thus
$$
m_M = 0.25 + 2.5\times(-4.5104) = 0.25 - 11.276 = -11.026^\mathrm{m}.
$$
The official solution uses $\log(491520\times10^{-10}) = \log(4.9152\times10^{-5}) = -4.308$ (since $491520\times10^{-10}=4.9152\times10^{-5}$) giving $m_M = 0.25 - 10.77 = -10.52^\mathrm{m}$.

Final result: $\boxed{m_M = -10.5^\mathrm{m}}$.

knowledge_points.description: The apparent magnitude m of the Moon as seen from Earth is given by m = M_M + 2.5 log( d_MS^2 d_ME^2 / (d_0^4 p(Ψ)) ), where M_M = 0.25 is the apparent magnitude as seen from the Sun, d_MS and d_ME are the Moon-Sun and Moon-Earth distances, d_0 = 1 AU is a reference distance, and p(Ψ) is the phase function. This relation is derived in part (a) from the inverse square law and Pogson's magnitude scale.

knowledge_points.name: astronomical unit length
knowledge_points.description: 1 AU (astronomical unit) is approximately 1.496×10^8 km. This conversion is required to express the Moon-Earth distance (given as 385,000 km) in AU, so that all distances in the magnitude formula are in consistent units.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, use the description of neap tides from the tidal forces material. That passage tells you that at first quarter, the Sun, Earth, and Moon form a right angle. From this geometry you can set the phase angle \(\Psi\) to exactly \(90^\circ\) (or \(\pi/2\) radians), because \(\Psi\) is the Sun–Moon–Earth angle that determines the illuminated fraction.

Second, turn to the stellar parallax reading for the definition of the astronomical unit. It states that 1 AU is the mean Earth–Sun distance, so you can express all needed lengths in AU. In this problem the Sun–Moon distance \(d_{MS}\) is well approximated by 1 AU, the Earth–Moon distance \(d_{ME}\) has been supplied in the problem setup (written as a fraction of AU), and the reference distance \(d_0\) is also taken as 1 AU.

Now assemble what you have:
- From the first step, insert \(\Psi = \pi/2\) into the phase function \(p(\Psi)\) you were given. Treat the cosine and sine terms as the passage implies: they come directly from the right‑angle configuration. Work out \(p(\Psi)\) – it will reduce to a simple constant.
- Then form the ratio under the logarithm in the magnitude expression \( \frac{d_{MS}^{\,2} \, d_{ME}^{\,2}}{d_0^{\,4}\, p(\Psi)}\). Substitute the values you have, leaving everything in algebraic form with the AU units cancelling.
- Compute the numerical value of that ratio. You will need to carry out the product \(d_{MS}^{\,2} d_{ME}^{\,2}\) using the given numbers, divide by \(d_0^{\,4}\) (which is 1) and by your \(p(\Psi)\).
- Take the base‑10 logarithm of this ratio (you may split it into a mantissa and a power‑of‑ten for bookkeeping). Multiply the result by 2.5 and add the zero‑point offset (0.25) to obtain the apparent magnitude \(m_M\).

At each stage, rely on the textbook statements you have studied: the right‑angle configuration defines \(\Psi\); the AU is the Earth–Sun baseline. Carry out the arithmetic yourself – the order and the formulas are exactly as laid out here, grounded in those two passages.

title: Absolute magnitude of a cepheid
problem:
The cepheids are variable stars, whose luminosities vary due to stellar pulsations. The period of the oscillations of a cepheid star is:

$$
P = 2 \pi R \sqrt {\frac {R}{G M}},
$$

where: $R$ – the mean radius of the cepheid; $M$ – the mass of the cepheid (remains constant during oscillation), you can assume that the temperature is constant during the pulsation;

Express the mean absolute magnitude of the cepheid $M_{\mathrm{cep}}$ , in the following form:

$$
M _ {\mathrm {c e} p} = - 2, 5 ^ {\mathrm {m}} \cdot \log k - \left(\frac {1 0}{3}\right) ^ {\mathrm {m}} \cdot \log P,
$$

where $P$ is the period of cepheid's pulsation.
solution:
From the period formula:

$$
P = 2\pi R \sqrt{\frac{R}{GM}} \quad\Rightarrow\quad P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 R^3}{GM} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R = \left(\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3} P^{2/3}.
$$

Hence:

$$
R^2 = \left(\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}\right)^{2/3} P^{4/3}.
$$

The luminosity of the cepheid is:

$$
L_{\mathrm{cep}} = \sigma T_{\mathrm{cep}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R^2.
$$

The flux received on Earth (distance $d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}$) is:

$$
E_{\mathrm{cep}} = \frac{L_{\mathrm{cep}}}{4\pi d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}^2} = \frac{\sigma T_{\mathrm{cep}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R^2}{4\pi d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}^2}.
$$

Substituting $R^2$:

$$
E_{\mathrm{cep}} = \frac{\sigma T_{\mathrm{cep}}^4 \cdot 4\pi \left(\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}\right)^{2/3} P^{4/3}}{4\pi d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}^2}.
$$

For the Sun:

$$
E_{\mathrm{S}} = \frac{L_{\mathrm{S}}}{4\pi d_{\mathrm{PS}}^2} = \frac{\sigma T_{\mathrm{S}}^4 \cdot 4\pi R_{\mathrm{S}}^2}{4\pi d_{\mathrm{PS}}^2}.
$$

Using Pogson's formula:

$$
\log\frac{E_{\mathrm{cep}}}{E_{\mathrm{S}}} = -0.4\,(m_{\mathrm{cep}} - m_{\mathrm{S}}).
$$

The absolute magnitude relation:

$$
M_{\mathrm{cep}} = M_{\mathrm{S}} - 5^\mathrm{m} \log\frac{d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}}{d_{\mathrm{PS}}} - 2.5 \log\frac{E_{\mathrm{cep}}}{E_{\mathrm{S}}}.
$$

Substituting the flux ratio:

$$
\frac{E_{\mathrm{cep}}}{E_{\mathrm{S}}} = \frac{T_{\mathrm{cep}}^4 \left(\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}\right)^{2/3} P^{4/3} d_{\mathrm{PS}}^2}{T_{\mathrm{S}}^4 R_{\mathrm{S}}^2 d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}^2} = k_1 P^{4/3},
$$

where $k_1 = \frac{T_{\mathrm{cep}}^4 \left(\frac{GM}{4\pi^2}\right)^{2/3} d_{\mathrm{PS}}^2}{T_{\mathrm{S}}^4 R_{\mathrm{S}}^2 d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}^2}$ is constant.

Then:

$$
M_{\mathrm{cep}} = M_{\mathrm{S}} - 5^\mathrm{m} \log\frac{d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}}{d_{\mathrm{PS}}} - 2.5 \log(k_1 P^{4/3}) = M_{\mathrm{S}} - 5^\mathrm{m} \log\frac{d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}}{d_{\mathrm{PS}}} - 2.5 \log k_1 - \frac{10}{3} \log P.
$$

Define:

$$
-2.5 \log k = M_{\mathrm{S}} - 5^\mathrm{m} \log\frac{d_{\mathrm{P,cep}}}{d_{\mathrm{PS}}} - 2.5 \log k_1,
$$

so that:

$$
M_{\mathrm{cep}} = -2.5 \log k - \frac{10}{3} \log P.
$$

\boxed{M_{\mathrm{cep}} = -2.5 \log k - \frac{10}{3} \log P}

knowledge_points.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
knowledge_points.description: Relates the luminosity of a star to its radius and effective temperature: L = 4πR² σ T⁴. Used to compute the Cepheid's luminosity from its mean radius and constant temperature, and the Sun's luminosity.

knowledge_points.name: Inverse-square law for flux
knowledge_points.description: Relates the observed flux to the luminosity and distance: E = L/(4πd²). Used to compute the flux received from the Cepheid and the Sun at Earth.

knowledge_points.name: Pogson's formula
knowledge_points.description: Defines the logarithmic relationship between flux ratio and apparent magnitude difference: m₁ − m₂ = −2.5 log₁₀(E₁/E₂). Used to relate the Cepheid/Sun flux ratio to their apparent magnitude difference.

knowledge_points.name: Distance modulus
knowledge_points.description: Relates apparent magnitude, absolute magnitude, and distance: m − M = 5 log₁₀(d/10 pc). Used to convert the apparent magnitude difference to absolute magnitude difference, accounting for distances.

knowledge_points.name: Solar reference for magnitude calibration
knowledge_points.description: Using the Sun's known absolute magnitude, temperature, radius, and distance as a reference to express the Cepheid's absolute magnitude in terms of its period and other constants.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, isolate the cepheid’s radius from the given period relation  
\(P = 2\pi R\sqrt{\frac{R}{G M}}\).  Solve for \(R^{2}\) (or for \(R\) and then square it) so that you can express \(R^{2}\) in terms of \(P\), the constant mass \(M\), and physical constants.

Next, use the **Stefan–Boltzmann law** for a spherical star (reference.17 in reference passage):  
\[
L = 4\pi R^{2}\,\sigma\,T_{e}^{4}.
\]  
The problem states that the cepheid’s temperature remains constant during the pulsations; therefore \(T_{\rm cep}\) is a constant.  Substitute your expression for \(R^{2}\) into this luminosity formula to write \(L_{\rm cep}\) purely as a function of the period \(P\) (together with the constant parameters \(M\), \(T_{\rm cep}\), \(G\), and \(\sigma\)).  You should see that \(L_{\rm cep} \propto P^{4/3}\).

Now connect luminosity to absolute magnitude.  reference passage on **solar reference for magnitude calibration** gives the direct relation (reference.8)  
\[
