sub_problems.guidance:
First, recognise that the proton’s kinetic energy is given, but its speed is not.  Because the kinetic energy (1 GeV) is comparable to the proton’s rest energy, the proton is relativistic – you must use relativistic mechanics, not Newtonian.

reference passage **Taylor & Wheeler, 7.5 ENERGY** teaches that total energy is \(E = \gamma m c^2\) and that rest energy is \(E_{\text{rest}} = m c^2\).  Kinetic energy \(K\) is the difference:  
\[
K = E - E_{\text{rest}} = (\gamma - 1) m c^2 .
\]  
Use this to find the Lorentz factor \(\gamma\) in terms of \(K\) and the proton rest energy \(m_p c^2\).  
Look up the proton rest energy from the constants list (e.g. **Eisberg & Resnick, Useful Constants** gives \(m_p c^2 = 938.3\ \text{MeV}\); **Morin, 11.4** also reference \(938\ \text{MeV}\)).  Be careful with units: given \(K = 1\ \text{GeV} = 1000\ \text{MeV}\) to match.

Once you have \(\gamma\), find the speed \(v\) from the definition of the Lorentz factor (see **Purcell & Morin, 5.7** or **G.2**):
\[
\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2 / c^2}} .
\]  
Rearrange to solve for \(v\) in terms of \(\gamma\) and \(c\).  The speed of light in vacuum is \(c = 3.0 \times 10^8\ \text{m/s}\) (from **Palen, 1.5**).

Now you need the distance travelled.  The problem says the proton goes from the Sun to the Earth, so the distance is 1 astronomical unit (AU).  The **astronomical unit** knowledge point (e.g. **Carroll & Ostlie, 3.1** or **Palen, Kepler’s Laws**) states that 1 AU is the average Earth‑Sun distance; you can convert it to metres using the definition \(1\ \text{AU} = 1.496 \times 10^{11}\ \text{m}\) (or derive it from \(1\ \text{pc} = 2.063 \times 10^5\ \text{AU} = 3.086 \times 10^{16}\ \text{m}\) given in the passage).

Finally, the proton’s speed is constant (magnetic field neglected), so the travel time in the Earth frame is simply  
\[
t = \frac{\text{distance}}{v} .
\]  
Substitute your value of \(v\) and the Earth‑Sun distance to obtain the travel time.  You may express it in seconds, then convert to minutes if convenient.

title: Volcanic activity on Io
problem:
13. Volcanic activity on lo, whose rotation period synchronizes with its orbital period, was proposed to be the result of tidal heating mainly from Jupiter. The resultant tidal force on a body is the difference in gravitational force experienced by the near and far sides of that body due to another body. Measurements of the surface distortion of lo via satellite radar altimeter mapping indicate that the surface rises and falls by up to 100m during one-half orbit. Only the surface layers will move by this amount. Interior layers within lo will move by a smaller amount, and thus we assume that on average the entire mass of lo is moved through 50m. Assume that lo is considered as two hemispheres each treated as a point mass. Calculate the average power of the tidal heating on lo.

Hint: you can use the following approximation $\left(1 + x\right)^n \approx 1 + nx$ for small $x$ .

The mass of lo is $m_{lo} = 8.931938 \times 10^{22} \, kg$

The perijove distance is $r_{peri} = 420000\mathrm{km}$

The apojove distance is $r_{apo} = 423400\mathrm{km}$

The orbital period of Io is 152853 s

The radius of lo is $R_{\mathrm{lo}} = 1821.6 \mathrm{~km}$ .
solution:
The tidal force on one hemisphere (mass $m_{Io}/2$) located at distance $R_{Io}/2$ from the center of Io is:

$$F_{\text{tidal}} = F\left(r - \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right) - F\left(r + \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right)$$

$$= -\frac{G M_J \frac{m_{Io}}{2}}{\left(r - \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right)^2} + \frac{G M_J \frac{m_{Io}}{2}}{\left(r + \frac{R_{Io}}{2}\right)^2}$$

$$= -\frac{G M_J m_{Io}}{2r^2} \left[ \frac{1}{\left(1 - \frac{R_{Io}}{2r}\right)^2} - \frac{1}{\left(1 + \frac{R_{Io}}{2r}\right)^2} \right]$$

Using $(1+x)^{-2} \approx 1 - 2x$ for small $x$:

$$F_{\text{tidal}} \approx -\frac{G M_J m_{Io}}{2r^2} \left[ \left(1 + \frac{R_{Io}}{r}\right) - \left(1 - \frac{R_{Io}}{r}\right) \right] = -\frac{G M_J m_{Io} R_{Io}}{r^3}$$

The difference in tidal force between perijove and apojove:

$$\Delta F = \left| F_{\text{tidal}}(r_{\text{peri}}) - F_{\text{tidal}}(r_{\text{apo}}) \right| = G M_J m_{Io} R_{Io} \left( \frac{1}{r_{\text{peri}}^3} - \frac{1}{r_{\text{apo}}^3} \right)$$

We need $M_J$. Using Kepler's third law for Io's orbit (assuming circular approximation with mean distance $a$):

$$a = \frac{r_{\text{peri}} + r_{\text{apo}}}{2} = \frac{420000 + 423400}{2} \, \text{km} = 421700 \, \text{km} = 4.217 \times 10^8 \, \text{m}$$

$$T = 152853 \, \text{s}$$

$$G M_J = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{T^2} = \frac{4\pi^2 (4.217 \times 10^8)^3}{(152853)^2} \approx 1.267 \times 10^{17} \, \text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$$

Now compute:

$$\frac{1}{r_{\text{peri}}^3} = \frac{1}{(4.20 \times 10^8)^3} = 1.350 \times 10^{-26} \, \text{m}^{-3}$$

$$\frac{1}{r_{\text{apo}}^3} = \frac{1}{(4.234 \times 10^8)^3} = 1.317 \times 10^{-26} \, \text{m}^{-3}$$

$$\Delta F = (1.267 \times 10^{17}) (8.931938 \times 10^{22}) (1.8216 \times 10^6) (1.350 \times 10^{-26} - 1.317 \times 10^{-26})$$

$$\Delta F \approx 6.65 \times 10^{18} \, \text{N}$$

The average power is work done over half an orbit divided by half the period:

$$\bar{P} = \frac{\Delta F \cdot d}{T/2} = \frac{(6.65 \times 10^{18}) (50)}{152853/2} \approx 4.35 \times 10^{15} \, \text{W}$$

\boxed{\bar{P} = 4.35 \times 10^{15} \, \text{W}}

knowledge_points.name: tidal force
knowledge_points.description: Tidal force is the difference in gravitational force on the near and far sides of a body; it is used to compute the net stretching force on Io.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of universal gravitation
knowledge_points.description: Gives the gravitational force between point masses; used to calculate forces on the two hemispheres of Io at different distances from Jupiter.

knowledge_points.name: two-hemisphere point-mass model
knowledge_points.description: Io is treated as two point masses (each half its total mass) separated by its diameter; this simplifies computing the tidal force as a difference of forces on the two points.

knowledge_points.name: average tidal displacement of Io mass
knowledge_points.description: The entire mass of Io is assumed to move on average by 50 m during one-half orbit due to tidal distortion; this value is used with the net tidal force to compute mechanical work.

knowledge_points.name: binomial approximation for small x
knowledge_points.description: The approximation (1+x)^n ≈ 1+nx for |x|≪1 simplifies the tidal force expression to a linear term in R/r, avoiding exact expansions.

knowledge_points.name: semi-major axis of elliptical orbit
knowledge_points.description: For an elliptical orbit the semi-major axis a equals (r_peri + r_apo)/2; this relation yields the mean distance needed in Kepler's third law.

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: Relates orbital period T to semi-major axis a and the gravitational parameter GM of the central body; here GM_J = 4π²a³/T² is used to obtain Jupiter's mass information from Io's orbit.

knowledge_points.name: Io mass negligible relative to Jupiter
knowledge_points.description: When applying Kepler's third law, Io's mass is neglected compared to Jupiter's mass, so the satellite is treated as a test particle.

sub_problems.guidance:
Your goal is to find the average power of tidal heating on Io, which is work done per unit time by tidal forces as Io’s shape distorts and its mass shifts during its eccentric orbit.  This requires you to determine the net tidal force, then the work it does over the displacement given, and finally average that power over half the orbital period.

**Step 1 – Find the tidal force on a hemisphere of Io at a given distance from Jupiter.**
The problem tells you to model Io as two hemispheres, each a point mass of \( m_{\text{Io}}/2 \), located at distances \( r \pm R_{\text{Io}}/2 \) from Jupiter’s centre (where \( r \) is the centre-to-centre distance).  
From the textbook’s definition, the tidal force is the *difference* in gravitational force between the near side and the far side.  
Use Newton’s law of universal gravitation, \( F = G M m / r^2 \), as given in Carroll & Ostlie Section 2.2. Write the force on the near hemisphere (\( r - R_{\text{Io}}/2 \)) and on the far hemisphere (\( r + R_{\text{Io}}/2 \)), then subtract them.

You will get an expression that looks like  
\[
F_{\text{tidal}} = \frac{G M_J (m_{\text{Io}}/2)}{(r - R_{\text{Io}}/2)^2} - \frac{G M_J (m_{\text{Io}}/2)}{(r + R_{\text{Io}}/2)^2}.
\]
Factor out \( 1/r^2 \) and rewrite the denominators as \( (1 \pm R_{\text{Io}}/(2r))^2 \). Now apply the binomial approximation for small \( x \):  
\[
(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + n x,
\]
as described in the textbook (Carroll & Ostlie §25.3 footnote, and Morin §4.4.2 when simplifying \( |\mathbf{R}+\mathbf{r}| \)). Here \( x = \pm R_{\text{Io}}/(2r) \) is tiny because \( R_{\text{Io}} \ll r \). Expand each term to first order and simplify.  You should obtain a tidy expression for the magnitude of the tidal force that varies as \( 1/r^3 \).

**Step 2 – Determine the tidal force difference between perijove and apojove.**  
Because Io’s orbit is elliptical, the centre-to-centre distance \( r \) changes. The problem gives you the perijove distance \( r_{\text{peri}} \) and apojove distance \( r_{\text{apo}} \). Substitute these into your tidal force formula. The difference in tidal force between the two extremes is  
\[
\Delta F = F_{\text{tidal}}(r_{\text{peri}}) - F_{\text{tidal}}(r_{\text{apo}})
\]
(be careful with signs – you need only the magnitude for the work calculation). This step tells you the net force that stretches Io as it moves from perijove to apojove (or back).

**Step 3 – Find \( G M_J \) using Kepler’s third law.**  
You don’t know Jupiter’s mass directly, but you can obtain the product \( G M_J \) from the orbital data. First, compute the semi‑major axis \( a \) of Io’s orbit. The textbook defines the semi‑major axis for an ellipse:  
\[
a = \frac{r_{\text{peri}} + r_{\text{apo}}}{2},
\]
as explained in Carroll & Ostlie §2.1 and Palen’s Schaum’s Outline. The given orbital period \( T \) and the semi‑major axis are related by Kepler’s third law in its Newtonian form (Palen, and Kleppner & Kolenkow §10.5.2):  
\[
T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 a^3}{G(m+M)}.
\]
Since Jupiter is much more massive than Io, you may approximate \( m+M \approx M_J \). Solve for \( G M_J \).

**Step 4 – Compute the average power.**  
The work done by the tidal force over one half‑orbit (from perijove to apojove) is \( W = \Delta F \times d \), where \( d \) is the average displacement of Io’s mass. The problem states that, on average, the entire mass of Io is moved through 50 m.  
Finally, the average power is the work divided by the time over which it occurs – half the orbital period:  
\[
\bar{P} = \frac{W}{T/2}.
\]

Carry out these steps in order:
1. Use Newton’s law and the binomial approximation to get \( F_{\text{tidal}}(r) \).  
2. Compute the semi‑major axis \( a \), then \( G M_J \) via Kepler’s third law.  
3. Evaluate \( \Delta F \) using \( r_{\text{peri}} \) and \( r_{\text{apo}} \).  
4. Multiply by the 50 m displacement and divide by \( T/2 \) to obtain the average power.

Do all algebraic manipulations yourself, and only plug in numbers at the very end, keeping careful track of units (convert km to m where needed).

title: 14. Mean free path in a static universe
problem: Suppose we live in a static and infinitely large universe where the average density of stars is $n = 10^9 \, \text{Mpc}^{-3}$ and the average stellar radius is equal to the solar radius. Assume that standard Euclidean geometry holds true in this universe. How far, on average, could you see in any direction before your line of sight strikes a star? Please write your answer in Mpc.
solution:
Consider a long cylinder of radius $R$ (the stellar radius) along the line of sight. The volume of a cylinder of length $\ell$ is $\pi R^2 \ell$. The average number of stars in that volume is $n \pi R^2 \ell$. The line of sight is blocked when this number is about 1, i.e., $n \pi R^2 \ell = 1$. Thus $\ell = 1/(\pi R^2 n)$. The solar radius is $R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^8 \, \text{m}$. Convert to Mpc: $1 \, \text{Mpc} = 3.086 \times 10^{22} \, \text{m}$, so $R = 6.96 \times 10^8 / (3.086 \times 10^{22}) \approx 2.3 \times 10^{-14} \, \text{Mpc}$. Then $\ell = 1 / [\pi (2.3 \times 10^{-14})^2 (10^9)] \approx 6.3 \times 10^{17} \, \text{Mpc}$.

\boxed{\ell \approx 6.3 \times 10^{17} \, \text{Mpc}}

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks for the average distance a straight line of sight travels through a static, infinite universe before it hits a star. The situation is essentially a mean‑free‑path problem: you are sending a “test photon” through a field of stationary “targets” (the stars). You already have the tools from the provided textbook passages.

**1. Recall the mean‑free‑path concept for stationary targets**  
In the thermal physics discussion (Blundell & Blundell, Section 8.1), the authors first consider a single moving molecule among stationary others. When the moving particle sweeps out a volume \(\sigma v \Delta t\), the probability of a collision is \(n\,\sigma\,v\,\Delta t\). From that analysis one finds that the average distance travelled between collisions is  

\[
\lambda = \frac{1}{n\,\sigma},
\]

where \(n\) is the number density of targets and \(\sigma\) is the cross‑sectional area each target presents to the projectile. Here the “projectile” is the line of sight itself (think of a photon moving at any speed), the “targets” are the stars, and \(\lambda\) will be the average distance before the sightline is blocked.

**2. Identify the cross‑sectional area of a star**  
For a spherical star of radius \(R\), the geometric cross‑section that a distant photon sees is a disk of area \(\sigma = \pi R^{2}\). The problem tells you to use the average stellar radius equal to the solar radius.

**3. Obtain the solar radius in convenient units**  
From the eclipsing binary example in Carroll & Ostlie (Section 7.3) you are given:

\[
1\,R_{\odot} = 6.96 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m}.
\]

Because the density \(n\) is given in \(\text{Mpc}^{-3}\) and the answer is wanted in Mpc, you should convert this radius to megaparsecs. Use the parsec definition from the stellar parallax passage (Carroll & Ostlie, Section 3.1):

\[
1\ \text{pc} = 3.0856776 \times 10^{16}\ \text{m},
\qquad
1\ \text{Mpc} = 10^{6}\ \text{pc} = 3.0856776 \times 10^{22}\ \text{m}.
\]

Divide the solar radius in metres by the number of metres per Mpc to express \(R\) in Mpc. (You will get a very small number; that is expected.)

**4. Apply the mean‑free‑path formula**  
Now that you have \(n = 10^{9}\ \text{Mpc}^{-3}\) and \(R\) in Mpc (hence \(\sigma = \pi R^{2}\) in \(\text{Mpc}^{2}\)), substitute them into  

\[
\ell = \frac{1}{n\,\pi\,R^{2}}.
\]

This gives the average distance \(\ell\) in Mpc before the line of sight strikes a star.  

Carry out the unit conversion carefully, square the radius, multiply by \(\pi\) and \(n\), and take the reciprocal. The final number is your answer in Mpc.

title: Southernmost point of great-circle flight path
problem: An airplane was flying from Lima, capital of Peru ( $12^{\circ}2' S$ and $77^{\circ}1' W$ ) to Yogyakarta ( $7^{\circ}47' S$ and $110^{\circ}26' E$ ), near the venue of the $9^{\text{th}}$ IOAA. The airplane chooses the shortest flight path from Lima to Yogyakarta. Find the latitude of the southernmost point of the flight path.
solution:
The shortest path between two points on a sphere is a great circle. The southernmost point on the great circle arc from Lima to Yogyakarta is the point where the great circle reaches its minimum latitude (maximum southern latitude). Using spherical trigonometry, let the colatitudes be $s_2 = 90^\circ - 12^\circ 2' = 77^\circ 58'$ and $s_3 = 90^\circ - 7^\circ 47' = 82^\circ 13'$. The difference in longitude is $A_1 = (180^\circ - 77^\circ 1') + (180^\circ - 110^\circ 26') = 172^\circ 33'$. Using the law of cosines for sides, the great-circle distance $s_1$ is given by $\cos s_1 = \cos s_2 \cos s_3 + \sin s_2 \sin s_3 \cos A_1$, yielding $s_1 = 2.7724$ rad. Then using the law of cosines for sides again, $\cos s_2 = \cos s_1 \cos s_3 + \sin s_1 \sin s_3 \cos A_2$ gives $A_2 = 0.35921$ rad, and $\cos s_3 = \cos s_1 \cos s_2 + \sin s_1 \sin s_2 \cos A_3$ gives $A_3 = 0.3642$ rad. At the southernmost point P, the angle at P is a right angle ($A_3 = \pi/2$). Using Napier's rule for right spherical triangles, $\sin s_2' = \sin s_3 \sin A_2$, where $s_2'$ is the colatitude of P. Thus $\sin s_2' = \sin(82^\circ 13') \sin(0.35921) = 0.9908 \times 0.3516 = 0.3484$, so $s_2' = 0.35576$ rad = $20^\circ 23'$. The latitude of P is $90^\circ - s_2' = 69^\circ 37'$ S. Therefore, the southernmost point is at latitude $69^\circ 37'$ S.

\boxed{69^\circ 37'\ \text{S}}

title: Moon orbit ellipse and apparent size
problem:
1. A moon is orbiting a planet such that the plane of its orbit is perpendicular to the surface of the planet where an observer is standing. After some necessary scaling, suppose the orbit satisfies the following equation:

$$
9 \left(\frac {x}{2} + \frac {\sqrt {3} y}{2} - 4\right) ^ {2} + 2 5 \left(- \frac {\sqrt {3} x}{2} + \frac {y}{2}\right) ^ {2} = 2 2 5
$$

Consider Cartesian coordinates where $x$ is on the horizontal plane and $y$ is on the zenith of the observer. Let $r$ be the radius of the moon. Assume that the period of rotation of the planet is much larger than the orbital period of the moon. Ignore the atmospheric refraction.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Calculate the semimajor and semiminor axis of the ellipse.
sub_problems.solution:
Introduce new variables:
$$x^* = \frac{x}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}y}{2} = x\cos\frac{\pi}{3} + y\sin\frac{\pi}{3}$$
$$y^* = -\frac{\sqrt{3}x}{2} + \frac{y}{2} = x\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) + y\cos\frac{\pi}{3}$$
The orbit equation becomes:
$$9(x^*-4)^2 + 25(y^*)^2 = 225$$
Divide both sides by 225:
$$\frac{(x^*-4)^2}{25} + \frac{(y^*)^2}{9} = 1$$
This is an ellipse centered at $(x^*,y^*)=(4,0)$ with semi-major axis $a=5$ along the $x^*$-axis and semi-minor axis $b=3$ along the $y^*$-axis.

Thus the semimajor axis is $\boxed{5}$ and the semiminor axis is $\boxed{3}$.

knowledge_points.name: standard ellipse equation
knowledge_points.description: The equation (x-h)^2/a^2 + (y-k)^2/b^2 = 1 represents an ellipse with semi-axes a and b. Needed to identify the semi-axes after transforming the given orbit equation into this standard form.

knowledge_points.name: semi-major and semi-minor axes
knowledge_points.description: In an ellipse, the semi-major axis is the larger of the two parameters a and b, and the semi-minor axis is the smaller. Needed to correctly assign 5 as semi-major and 3 as semi-minor.

knowledge_points.name: rotation of coordinate axes
knowledge_points.description: A rotation of the coordinate system by an angle θ can diagonalize a quadratic form representing an ellipse, aligning the axes with the coordinate axes. Here, the coefficients correspond to a rotation by π/3, transforming the given equation into standard form.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the semimajor and semiminor axes of the ellipse given by your equation, follow a systematic method that uses three key ideas from your textbook passages: the definition of the axes, the effect of rotating coordinate axes, and the standard algebraic form of an ellipse when its axes are aligned with the coordinates.

**1. Recognize why a rotation is needed**  
Your ellipse equation probably contains an \(xy\) term (a “cross term”). The passages from Kleppner & Kolenkow show that when an ellipse’s axes are not aligned with the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes, its Cartesian equation is more complicated; it is only when the axes are aligned that the equation simplifies to a symmetric form where the semi‑axes can be read off directly. To remove the cross term, you will rotate the coordinate axes.

**2. Apply the textbook rotation transformation**  
The Morin passage provides the transformation for rotating axes in the \(x\)-\(y\) plane through an angle \(\theta\) (Equation 8.93). Write new coordinates \(x', y'\) in terms of \(x, y\) as
\[
\begin{pmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Substitute these expressions into your original ellipse equation. After expanding, you will obtain an equation containing terms in \((x')^2\), \((y')^2\), and \(x'y'\), plus possibly linear terms in \(x'\) and \(y'\). The coefficient of the \(x'y'\) term will depend on \(\theta\).

**3. Choose \(\theta\) to eliminate the cross term**  
Set the coefficient of \(x'y'\) equal to zero and solve for a convenient \(\theta\). This is exactly the step that aligns the new axes with the principal axes of the ellipse. Once you find the correct angle (for example, \(\theta = \pi/3\) or another value), plug it back into the transformed equation. The cross term vanishes, leaving only terms in \((x')^2\), \((y')^2\), \(x'\), \(y'\), and constants.

**4. Reduce to the standard ellipse equation**  
Now the equation has the form described in the Kleppner & Kolenkow passages: after eliminating the cross term, the remaining terms can be rearranged by completing the square in \(x'\) and \(y'\). The result is an equation of the type
\[
\frac{(x' - h)^2}{A} + \frac{(y' - k)^2}{B} = 1,
\]
where \(h\) and \(k\) are constants (the center of the ellipse in the rotated frame) and \(A, B\) are positive numbers.  
This is the standard form for an ellipse whose major and minor axes lie along the primed coordinate directions.

**5. Identify the semi‑major and semi‑minor axes**  
In the standard form, the numbers under the \((x'-h)^2\) and \((y'-k)^2\) terms are the squares of the semi‑axes. According to the definitions in the Palen excerpt and the Carroll & Ostlie excerpt, the semi‑major axis \(a\) is half the long axis, and the semi‑minor axis \(b\) is half the short axis. Therefore, compare \(A\) and \(B\):  
- The larger denominator equals \(a^2\), so \(a = \sqrt{\text{larger denominator}}\).  
- The smaller denominator equals \(b^2\), so \(b = \sqrt{\text{smaller denominator}}\).  

Simply computing these square roots gives the values of the semi‑major and semi‑minor axes requested in the problem.

Carry out each algebraic step yourself—substitute the rotation, solve for \(\theta\), simplify, and complete the square. The procedure is exactly the same as the transformation shown in the reference solution (for your own later check), and it relies only on the concepts and formulas presented in the textbook passages above.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Calculate the zenith angle of perigee.
sub_problems.solution:
The transformation from $(x,y)$ to $(x^*,y^*)$ is a rotation by $\pi/3$ counterclockwise. In the $(x^*,y^*)$ system, the perigee (closest point to the observer at the origin) occurs when the distance from the origin is minimum. The ellipse has one focus at the origin $(x^*,y^*)=(0,0)$ (since the observer is at the origin in the original coordinates). For an ellipse $\frac{(x^*-4)^2}{25}+\frac{(y^*)^2}{9}=1$, the foci are at $(0,0)$ and $(8,0)$. The perigee is the point on the ellipse closest to the focus at $(0,0)$, which lies on the major axis at the end nearer to that focus. The major axis is along the $x^*$-axis, so the perigee in $(x^*,y^*)$ coordinates is at $x^*=0$ (the leftmost point). In polar coordinates, $x^* = R\cos(\alpha-\pi/3)$, $y^* = R\sin(\alpha-\pi/3)$. At perigee, $\alpha-\pi/3 = \pi$ (since the vector points opposite to the positive $x^*$-axis). Thus $\alpha = \pi + \pi/3 = 4\pi/3$. The zenith angle is measured from the zenith (positive $y$-axis) to the direction of the moon. In the original coordinates, the zenith angle $\phi$ satisfies $\phi = \alpha - \pi/2$ (since $\alpha$ is measured from the positive $x$-axis). Therefore:
$$\phi = \frac{4\pi}{3} - \frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{8\pi}{6} - \frac{3\pi}{6} = \frac{5\pi}{6}$$

Thus the zenith angle of perigee is $\boxed{\frac{5\pi}{6}}$.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Determine $\tan \frac{\theta}{2}$ where $\theta$ is the elevation angle (altitude of the upper tangent of the moon) when the moon looks largest to the observer.
sub_problems.solution:
The moon looks largest when it is closest to the observer while still fully visible. Since the observer is at the origin and the moon's center is at $(x_0, y_0)$, the condition for the whole moon to be seen is that the line of sight to the upper tangent just grazes the moon. For a spherical moon of radius $r$, the upper tangent from the observer touches the moon at a point where the line from the observer to the moon's center makes an angle $\theta/2$ with the horizontal, and the vertical coordinate of the moon's center equals $r$ (since the observer is on the surface of the planet at $y=0$). Thus $y_0 = r$.

Substitute $y_0 = r$ into the orbit equation:
$$9\left(\frac{x_0}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{3}r}{2} - 4\right)^2 + 25\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}x_0}{2} + \frac{r}{2}\right)^2 = 225$$
Multiply both sides by 4:
$$9(x_0 + \sqrt{3}r - 8)^2 + 25(-\sqrt{3}x_0 + r)^2 = 900$$
Expand:
$$9\left(x_0^2 + 2\sqrt{3}rx_0 - 16x_0 + 3r^2 - 16\sqrt{3}r + 64\right) + 25\left(3x_0^2 - 2\sqrt{3}rx_0 + r^2\right) = 900$$
$$9x_0^2 + 18\sqrt{3}rx_0 - 144x_0 + 27r^2 - 144\sqrt{3}r + 576 + 75x_0^2 - 50\sqrt{3}rx_0 + 25r^2 = 900$$
$$84x_0^2 + (-32\sqrt{3}r - 144)x_0 + (52r^2 - 144\sqrt{3}r + 576) = 900$$
$$84x_0^2 - (32\sqrt{3}r + 144)x_0 + (52r^2 - 144\sqrt{3}r - 324) = 0$$
Divide by 84:
$$x_0^2 - \frac{32\sqrt{3}r + 144}{84}x_0 + \frac{52r^2 - 144\sqrt{3}r - 324}{84} = 0$$
Simplify coefficients:
$$\frac{32\sqrt{3}r + 144}{84} = \frac{8\sqrt{3}r + 36}{21} = \frac{4\sqrt{3}r + 18}{21}$$
$$\frac{52r^2 - 144\sqrt{3}r - 324}{84} = \frac{13r^2 - 36\sqrt{3}r - 81}{21}$$
Solve the quadratic:
$$x_0 = \frac{4\sqrt{3}r + 18}{21} \pm \sqrt{\left(\frac{4\sqrt{3}r + 18}{21}\right)^2 - \frac{13r^2 - 36\sqrt{3}r - 81}{21}}$$
Compute the discriminant:
$$\Delta = \frac{(4\sqrt{3}r + 18)^2}{441} - \frac{13r^2 - 36\sqrt{3}r - 81}{21} = \frac{48r^2 + 144\sqrt{3}r + 324}{441} - \frac{273r^2 - 756\sqrt{3}r - 1701}{441} = \frac{-225r^2 + 900\sqrt{3}r + 2025}{441} = \frac{225(-r^2 + 4\sqrt{3}r + 9)}{441} = \frac{225}{441}(-r^2 + 4\sqrt{3}r + 9)$$
Thus
$$x_0 = \frac{4\sqrt{3}r + 18}{21} \pm \frac{15\sqrt{-r^2 + 4\sqrt{3}r + 9}}{21}$$
We choose the smaller $x_0$ (since the moon is to the left of the observer for the largest angular size):
$$x_0 = \frac{4\sqrt{3}r + 18}{21} - \frac{15\sqrt{-r^2 + 4\sqrt{3}r + 9}}{21}$$
The angle $\theta/2$ is the angle between the line from observer to moon center and the horizontal. From geometry, $\tan(\theta/2) = r/x_0$ (since $y_0 = r$ and $x_0$ is the horizontal distance). Therefore:
$$\tan\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{r}{x_0} = \frac{21r}{4\sqrt{3}r + 18 - 15\sqrt{-r^2 + 4\sqrt{3}r + 9}}$$

Thus $\boxed{\tan\frac{\theta}{2} = \frac{21r}{4\sqrt{3}r + 18 - 15\sqrt{-r^2 + 4\sqrt{3}r + 9}}}$.

title: Stellar thermodynamics and heat capacity
problem:
Suppose a static spherical star consists of $N$ neutral particles with radius $R$ (see Figure 3).

with $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$ , $0 \leq \phi \leq 2\pi$ , satisfying the following equation of states

$$
\boldsymbol {P} \boldsymbol {V} = N \boldsymbol {k} \frac {T _ {R} - T _ {0}}{\ln \left(T _ {R} / T _ {0}\right)} \tag {1}
$$

where $P$ and $V$ are the pressure inside the star and the volume of the star respectively, $k$ is the Boltzmann constant. $T_R$ and $T_0$ are the temperatures at the surface $r = R$ and the temperature at the center $r = 0$ respectively. Assume that $T_R \leq T_0$ .

sub_problems.problem: (a) Simplify the stellar equation of state (1) if $\Delta T = T_R - T_0 \approx 0$ (this is called ideal star) (Hint: Use the approximation $\ln(1 + x) \approx x$ for small $x$ )
sub_problems.solution:
Define $\Delta T = T_R - T_0$ with $\Delta T \approx 0$. Then $T_R = T_0 + \Delta T$. Equation (1) becomes
$$
PV = Nk \frac{\Delta T}{\ln\left(\frac{T_0+\Delta T}{T_0}\right)} = Nk \frac{\Delta T}{\ln\left(1+\frac{\Delta T}{T_0}\right)}.
$$
Using $\ln(1+x) \approx x$ for small $x$, we have $\ln\left(1+\frac{\Delta T}{T_0}\right) \approx \frac{\Delta T}{T_0}$. Hence
$$
PV \approx Nk \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta T/T_0} = Nk T_0.
$$
Thus the simplified equation of state is $PV = NkT_0$.

\boxed{PV = NkT_0}

knowledge_points.description: The hint and solution use the first-order approximation ln(1+x) ≈ x for small x to simplify the logarithmic denominator in the equation of state.

sub_problems.guidance:
We start from the given stellar equation of state (1). The problem states that the temperature difference \(\Delta T = T_R - T_0\) is approximately zero, which defines the “ideal star” limit. Because \(\Delta T\) is small, the ratio \(\Delta T / T_0\) is also a small number.

First, rewrite the denominator of equation (1) so that the temperature ratio appears explicitly. Express \(T_R\) as \(T_0 + \Delta T\) and then write the logarithm argument as \(1 + \frac{\Delta T}{T_0}\). This sets up the form \(\ln(1 + x)\) with a small \(x\).

Now use the approximation given in the hint, \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) for small \(x\). reference passage on the Taylor expansion of \(\ln(1+x)\) (from Blundell & Blundell) shows exactly this step when simplifying the Helmholtz function, using \(\ln(1+x) \approx x\) for \(x \ll 1\). Apply that same idea here: replace the logarithm with \(\frac{\Delta T}{T_0}\).

After this substitution, the factor \(\Delta T\) cancels, leaving an expression that no longer depends on \(\Delta T\). The result involves only the constant \(T_0\), the particle number \(N\), and Boltzmann’s constant \(k\). The final simplified equation of state has the same form as the ideal gas law presented in reference passages (either \(PV = NkT\) from Palen or \(\mathcal{P V} = N_{\text{mol}} R T\) from Kleppner & Kolenkow, depending on the notation in your original equation (1)). In the ideal-star limit, the temperature in the ideal gas law is simply \(T_0\).

To complete the problem, write the simplified equation of state with \(PV\) on the left and the constant terms on the right.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Find the heat capacity of the star at constant volume $C_v$ in term of $M$ and at constant pressure $C_p$ expressed in $C_v$ and $T$ (Hint: Use the approximation $(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ for small $x$ )
sub_problems.solution:
For an ideal star, the internal energy is $U = Mc^2$. For small changes, $C_v = \left(\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T}\right)_V = \left(\frac{\Delta M}{\Delta T}\right)_V c^2$.

For constant pressure, using the first law $\Delta Q = \Delta M c^2 + P\Delta V$, we have
$$
C_p = \left(\frac{\Delta Q}{\Delta T}\right)_P = \left(\frac{\Delta M}{\Delta T}\right)_V c^2 + P\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T} = C_v + P\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T}.
$$
From the equation of state (1), $PV = Nk \frac{T - T_0}{\ln(T/T_0)}$. For a small change $\Delta T$ from $T$ to $T+\Delta T$, we compute $P\Delta V$ and then $P\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T}$. Using the approximation $\ln\left(\frac{T+\Delta T}{T_0}\right) \approx \ln\left(\frac{T}{T_0}\right) + \frac{\Delta T}{T}$ and $(1+\frac{\Delta T}{T\ln(T/T_0)})^{-1} \approx 1 - \frac{\Delta T}{T\ln(T/T_0)}$, we obtain
$$
P\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T} = \frac{Nk}{\ln(T/T_0)}\left(1 - \frac{T - T_0}{T}\right).
$$
Thus
$$
C_p = C_v + \frac{Nk}{\ln(T/T_0)}\left(1 - \frac{T - T_0}{T}\right).
$$

\boxed{C_v = \left(\frac{\Delta M}{\Delta T}\right)_V c^2}, \quad \boxed{C_p = C_v + \frac{Nk}{\ln(T/T_0)}\left(1 - \frac{T - T_0}{T}\right)}

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Relate internal energy to mass using mass–energy equivalence.**  
   reference passages on relativistic energy (Eisberg & Resnick) and Einstein’s derivation (Kleppner & Kolenkow) establish that a body’s total energy can include its rest‑mass energy, \(E = mc^2\). For this star, the dominant contribution to the internal energy \(U\) is the rest‑mass energy, so you can write \(U = M c^2\), where \(M\) is the star’s mass.

2. **Obtain \(C_V\) from the definition of heat capacity at constant volume.**  
   According to the heat‑capacity passage (Blundell & Blundell), \(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial T}\right)_V\).  
   Because the volume is fixed, no work is done (\(dW = 0\) in the first law \(dU = dQ - dW\), or equivalently \(dU = dQ + dW\) depending on sign convention; use the form that gives \(dQ = dU\) when \(dV=0\)).  
   Therefore \(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V\). Substitute \(U = M c^2\) and note that \(c\) is constant, giving \(C_V = c^2 \left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial T}\right)_V\). This expresses \(C_V\) in terms of the mass \(M\) (through its temperature derivative).

3. **Use the first law to connect \(C_p\) and \(C_V\).**  
   For heating at constant pressure, the definition is \(C_p = \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial T}\right)_p\).  
   The first law (Carroll & Ostlie, or Blundell & Blundell) in the form \(dQ = dU + P\,dV\) (work done *by* the system) gives  
   \[
   C_p = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_p + P \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_p .
   \]  
   Assuming the mass \(M\) depends only on temperature (or that its temperature derivative is the same whether volume or pressure is held constant), the term \(\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_p\) can be replaced by \(C_V\). Hence  
   \[
   C_p = C_V + P \left(\frac{\partial V}{\partial T}\right)_p .
   \]

4. **Compute \(P\,(\partial V / \partial T)_p\) from the stellar equation of state.**  
   The problem provides an equation of state (which you have from earlier parts):  
   \[
   PV = Nk \frac{T - T_0}{\ln(T/T_0)} .
   \]  
   At constant pressure, solve for \(V\) as a function of \(T\):  
   \[
   V = \frac{Nk}{P} \frac{T - T_0}{\ln(T/T_0)} .
   \]  
   Now differentiate with respect to \(T\) (or, equivalently, consider a small change \(\Delta T\) and compute \(\Delta V/\Delta T\)). The hint tells you to use the approximation \((1+x)^n \approx 1 + nx\) for small \(x\). This will be needed when you expand \(\ln\!\bigl(\frac{T+\Delta T}{T_0}\bigr)\) around \(T\). The binomial series (Kleppner & Kolenkow) is exactly the tool for such first‑order expansions.  
   Carry out the differentiation (or the expansion of the finite difference) carefully, applying the quotient rule and the derivative of \(\ln(T/T_0)\). After simplifying, multiply the result by \(P\) to obtain \(P\,(\partial V / \partial T)_p\). The pressure \(P\) will cancel, leaving an expression that depends on \(N\), \(k\), \(T\), \(T_0\), and the logarithm.

5. **Combine to express \(C_p\) in terms of \(C_V\) and \(T\).**  
   Insert the expression for \(P\,(\partial V / \partial T)_p\) into the relation from step 3:  
   \[
   C_p = C_V + (\text{result from step 4}) .
   \]  
   The final formula will involve \(C_V\), the constants \(N\), \(k\), \(T_0\), and the temperature \(T\) through the factor \(1/\ln(T/T_0)\) and a combination of \(T\) and \(T_0\). No numerical substitution is needed; the answer remains symbolic.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Find the heat produced by the isobaric process if the initial temperature and the final temperature are $T_{i}$ and $T_{f}$ , respectively.
sub_problems.solution:
For an isobaric process, the heat produced is $Q_H = C_v (T_f - T_i) + P\Delta V$. Using the equation of state (1), $P\Delta V = Nk\left(\frac{T_f - T_0}{\ln(T_f/T_0)} - \frac{T_i - T_0}{\ln(T_i/T_0)}\right)$. Therefore
$$
Q_H = C_v (T_f - T_i) + Nk\left(\frac{T_f - T_0}{\ln(T_f/T_0)} - \frac{T_i - T_0}{\ln(T_i/T_0)}\right).
$$

\boxed{Q_H = C_v (T_f - T_i) + Nk\left(\frac{T_f - T_0}{\ln(T_f/T_0)} - \frac{T_i - T_0}{\ln(T_i/T_0)}\right)}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the heat produced in an isobaric process, you need to relate the heat added to the system to the change in internal energy and the work done.

First, recall the first law of thermodynamics as given in your reference: for a differential change, \(\mathrm{d}U = \mathrm{d}Q + \mathrm{d}W\) (eqn 11.7 in Blundell & Blundell), where \(\mathrm{d}Q\) is heat supplied to the system and \(\mathrm{d}W\) is work done *on* the system. In many physics contexts, it is more convenient to write \(\mathrm{d}Q = \mathrm{d}U + p\,\mathrm{d}V\) (eqn 11.11), where \(p\,\mathrm{d}V\) is the work done *by* the system on its surroundings. This is the form you should use here. For a finite isobaric (constant pressure) process, the total heat added is therefore
\[
Q = \Delta U + p\,\Delta V.
\]

Now, you need expressions for \(\Delta U\) and \(p\,\Delta V\) in terms of the given initial and final temperatures \(T_i\) and \(T_f\).

For the internal energy change: reference explains that for an ideal monatomic gas, the internal energy depends only on temperature, with \(\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial V}\right)_T = 0\) (eqn 11.21). It also defines the heat capacity at constant volume as \(C_V = \left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial T}\right)_V\) (eqn 11.15). For a temperature change at constant volume, \(\Delta U = C_V \Delta T\). Because \(U\) is a state function (its change is path-independent), you can use this same \(\Delta U\) even when the volume is not constant. So, for the isobaric process between \(T_i\) and \(T_f\), you have \(\Delta U = C_V (T_f - T_i)\).

For the work term \(p\,\Delta V\): since the process is isobaric, \(p\) is constant. The problem statement does not give you \(p\) or \(\Delta V\) directly, but it does imply that there is an equation of state linking pressure, volume, and temperature. You are told that the surface temperature equals the gas temperature, and the reference solution uses an equation of state numbered (1) that relates \(P\), \(V\), and \(T\) in a specific way involving a reference temperature \(T_0\) and a logarithmic dependence. You must apply that equation of state to express \(P\Delta V\) as the difference between its value at \(T_f\) and its value at \(T_i\). In other words, compute \(P V\) from the equation of state at each temperature and subtract: \(P\Delta V = (PV)_{T_f} - (PV)_{T_i}\).

Finally, combine the two contributions: substitute your expression for \(\Delta U\) and your expression for \(P\Delta V\) into \(Q = \Delta U + P\Delta V\). The result will be the heat produced, expressed in terms of \(C_V\), \(Nk\), \(T_i\), \(T_f\), and \(T_0\). Do not forget that reference’s derivation of \(C_V\) for an ideal monatomic gas (eqn 11.26) gives \(C_V = \frac{3}{2}R\) per mole, but you should keep the symbol \(C_V\) as requested in the problem unless instructed otherwise.

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem asks you to estimate the distance of a far-away observer from the star using information from part (c). To approach this, you need to connect the star’s energy output to the brightness the observer would measure.

First, recall the **inverse square law for flux**. reference explains that when a star radiates energy uniformly in all directions (isotropically), the radiant flux \( F \) at a distance \( r \) is given by \( F = \frac{L}{4\pi r^2} \), where \( L \) is the star’s luminosity (energy emitted per second). This is because the energy spreads over the surface area of a sphere of radius \( r \). The same idea appears in Example 3.2.1, where the Sun’s known luminosity and distance give the solar flux at Earth.

Now, think about the star in your problem. It radiates isotropically — the Stefan‑Boltzmann law in reference shows that a spherical star emits energy uniformly from its surface, so the inverse square law applies. To find the distance \( d \) to the observer, you would rearrange the inverse square law to \( d = \sqrt{\frac{L}{4\pi F}} \). Thus you need **two numbers**: the luminosity \( L \) of the star, and the flux \( F \) that the observer actually receives.

Look at what part (c) provided. Did it give you a luminosity \( L \) (energy per second), or did it give a total amount of heat \( Q_H \) without a time interval? If you only have a total heat, you cannot convert it to a luminosity unless you also know over what time that heat is radiated. Even if you could get \( L \), you still need the flux \( F \) at the observer’s location. The problem statement does not mention any measured flux at the observer’s telescope or detector. Without a known \( F \), the equation cannot be solved for a unique distance.

Therefore, before you try to calculate, identify what quantities are actually given. Ask yourself: Is the observer’s measured flux provided? Is the time over which the heat is emitted known? You will likely find that at least one essential piece of information is missing. In that case, you cannot compute a numerical estimate. The method reveals that you have **insufficient data** to determine the distance.

sub_problems.problem: (e) If the sunlight is monochromatic with frequency $5 \times 10^{14} \mathrm{~Hz}$ , estimate the number of photons radiated by the Sun per second.
sub_problems.solution:
The Sun's luminosity is $L_\odot = 3.96 \times 10^{26} \mathrm{~W}$. Each photon has energy $E = h\nu = 6.6261 \times 10^{-34} \times 5 \times 10^{14} = 3.31305 \times 10^{-19} \mathrm{~J}$. The number of photons per second is $N = L_\odot / (h\nu) = 3.96 \times 10^{26} / 3.31305 \times 10^{-19} = 1.195 \times 10^{45}$.

\boxed{N \approx 1.2 \times 10^{45} \text{ photons/s}}

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall from reference that the energy of a single photon is given by the Planck–Einstein relation, \( E = h\nu \) (where \( h \) is Planck's constant and \( \nu \) is the frequency). This is stated in the exposition on the Bohr atom and the photon concept, and also noted in the thermal physics chapter. You will need this to find the energy carried by one photon of the given monochromatic sunlight.

Second, you need the total power output of the Sun, its luminosity. reference provides the solar luminosity in the section on solar energy: \( L_\odot = 3.83 \times 10^{26} \,\mathrm{W} \) (a slightly different rounded value also appears in the astronomy worked example; use the value from the thermal physics passage). This luminosity is the total electromagnetic energy radiated by the Sun per second.

The number of photons emitted per second is simply the total power divided by the energy per photon. This idea appears in several reference contexts — for instance, when the intensity of a light beam is expressed as the product of the photon flux and the photon energy, or when an AGN’s photon output is estimated by dividing the monochromatic energy flux by \( h\nu \). Here, because the sunlight is monochromatic, every photon has the same energy \( h\nu \), so the photon flux \( N \) satisfies \( L_\odot = N \cdot (h\nu) \).

Therefore, the method is:  
1. Calculate the energy of one photon using \( E = h\nu \) with the given frequency \( \nu = 5 \times 10^{14} \,\mathrm{Hz} \) and Planck’s constant \( h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \,\mathrm{J\,s} \) (as used in reference).  
2. Use the solar luminosity \( L_\odot \) from reference.  
3. Divide the luminosity by the single-photon energy to obtain the number of photons per second: \( N = L_\odot / (h\nu) \).

Carry out the multiplication and division yourself; the result will be an estimate of the number of photons radiated by the Sun each second under the monochromatic assumption.

sub_problems.problem: (f) Calculate the heat capacity $C_v$ of the Sun assuming its surface temperature varies from 5500 K to 6000 K in one second.
sub_problems.solution:
The energy radiated per second is the solar luminosity $L_\odot = 3.96 \times 10^{26} \mathrm{~W}$. This energy comes from mass defect: $L_\odot = \Delta M c^2$. Then $C_v = \frac{\Delta M c^2}{\Delta T} = \frac{L_\odot}{\Delta T} = \frac{3.96 \times 10^{26}}{6000 - 5500} = 7.92 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{~J/K}$.

\boxed{C_v \approx 7.9 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{~J/K}}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the heat capacity \(C_v\) of the Sun under this temperature change, you need to connect the idea of heat capacity to the Sun’s energy output. The textbook defines heat capacity (Section 2.2) as \(C = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}T}\), where \(\mathrm{d}Q\) is the heat supplied and \(\mathrm{d}T\) is the resulting small temperature change. Here, the temperature change \(\Delta T\) is given directly (from 5500 K to 6000 K), so the main task is to determine how much “heat” the Sun loses (or radiates) during the one‑second interval.

The problem states that the surface temperature varies uniformly over one second. This suggests that the energy radiated in that second can be treated as the \(\mathrm{d}Q\) in the heat‑capacity definition. The Sun’s energy output per second is its luminosity \(L_\odot\). Your textbook passage on solar energy (Section 37.1) provides a value for the solar luminosity: \(L_\odot = 3.83 \times 10^{26}\,\mathrm{W}\). A watt is a joule per second, so this number directly gives the energy radiated by the Sun in one second.

Now apply the heat‑capacity definition in a straightforward way:
1. Identify \(\mathrm{d}Q\) as the energy radiated in one second, which is the luminosity \(L_\odot\).
2. Identify \(\mathrm{d}T\) as the given temperature change \(\Delta T\).
3. Use the relation \(C = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}T}\) to express the Sun’s heat capacity.

Thus, the method is: take the solar luminosity from the textbook passage, divide it by the difference between the two stated temperatures, and you obtain the heat capacity in joules per kelvin. No other data (such as solar radius or distance) are needed for this estimate, because the luminosity already encapsulates the total power emitted.

Carry out the substitution and arithmetic yourself to arrive at the final value.

title: True or False
problem: Determine if each of the following statements is True or False. In the Summary Answersheet, tick the correct answer (TRUE / FALSE) for each statement. No justifications are necessary for this question.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.1) In a photograph of the clear sky on a Full Moon night with a sufficiently long exposure, the colour of the sky would appear blue as in daytime.
sub_problems.solution:
The colour of the clear sky during night is the same as during daytime, since the spectrum of sunlight reflected by the Moon is almost the same as the spectrum of sunlight. Only the intensity is lower. Therefore the statement is true.
\boxed{\text{TRUE}}

knowledge_points.name: Rayleigh scattering
knowledge_points.description: The daytime sky appears blue because atmospheric molecules scatter sunlight with a strong wavelength dependence (shorter wavelengths scattered more). This same scattering process operates at night when the atmosphere is illuminated by moonlight.

knowledge_points.name: lunar spectrum matches solar spectrum
knowledge_points.description: The Moon reflects sunlight, and its reflectance in the visible range is nearly flat, so the spectrum of moonlight is essentially the same as that of sunlight, only dimmer.

knowledge_points.name: color independent of intensity
knowledge_points.description: The perceived color of scattered light depends on the spectral composition of the incident light, not its absolute intensity. A long exposure can compensate for low intensity without altering the color.

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem asks you to decide whether the night sky on a Full Moon would appear blue in a long-exposure photograph, similar to the daytime sky. To reason through this, focus on Rayleigh scattering and the source of light.

First, recall from the textbook passage on Rayleigh scattering that this process scatters light without changing its wavelength. The classical explanation describes how atomic electrons, driven by an incident electromagnetic wave, re-radiate waves of the same frequency. This is the mechanism that makes the clear daytime sky appear blue: sunlight is scattered by molecules in Earth’s atmosphere, and shorter (blue) wavelengths are scattered more efficiently.

Now, identify the light source at night. The problem states it is a Full Moon night. The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight. The textbook does not explicitly discuss the Moon’s spectrum, but you can infer from the Rayleigh scattering description that the key factor is the incident spectrum. Since the Moon reflects sunlight, the spectrum of moonlight is essentially the same as the spectrum of sunlight—just much less intense. The scattering process itself depends on the frequency of the incoming light, not its intensity.

Therefore, apply the same Rayleigh scattering logic: moonlight passing through the atmosphere will be scattered by air molecules, and the shorter (blue) wavelengths will be scattered more strongly. With a sufficiently long exposure, the camera would collect enough of this scattered blue light to make the sky appear blue, just as in daytime.

To structure your answer: state that Rayleigh scattering acts on moonlight the same way it acts on sunlight, because the spectrum is the same. Conclude whether the statement is true or false based on this reasoning. Let the textbook’s explanation of Rayleigh scattering and the analogy to the blue sky (mentioned in the reflection nebulae part) guide you, but do not introduce numbers or formulas—this is a qualitative judgment.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.2) An astronomer at Bhubaneswar marks the position of the Sun on the sky at 05:00 UT every day of the year. If the Earth's axis were perpendicular to its orbital plane, these positions would trace an arc of a great circle.
sub_problems.solution:
If the Earth's axis were perpendicular to its orbital plane, the celestial equator would coincide with the ecliptic and the Sun would remain along the celestial equator every day. However, as the Earth's orbit is elliptical, the true Sun would still lead or lag the mean Sun by a few minutes on different days of the year, so the positions would not trace a great circle. Therefore the statement is false.
\boxed{\text{FALSE}}

knowledge_points.name: celestial equator
knowledge_points.description: The projection of Earth's equator onto the celestial sphere; needed to understand that with a perpendicular axis it would coincide with the ecliptic.

knowledge_points.name: ecliptic
knowledge_points.description: The apparent path of the Sun on the celestial sphere over a year; needed to see that with zero obliquity the Sun would stay on the celestial equator.

knowledge_points.name: great circle
knowledge_points.description: A circle on the celestial sphere whose plane passes through the observer; the statement claims the Sun's positions trace one, which is contradicted by the equation of time.

knowledge_points.name: equation of time
knowledge_points.description: The difference between apparent solar time and mean solar time due to Earth's elliptical orbit and axial tilt; even with zero tilt, orbital eccentricity causes the Sun to lead or lag the mean Sun, so its daily positions do not trace a perfect great circle.

knowledge_points.name: Earth's axis perpendicular to orbital plane
knowledge_points.description: The hypothetical condition stated in the problem; sets the obliquity to zero so the celestial equator and ecliptic coincide.

knowledge_points.name: elliptical Earth orbit
knowledge_points.description: The Earth's orbit is not a perfect circle; this eccentricity remains even under the hypothetical perpendicular axis and causes the equation of time, breaking the great-circle trace.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall what “Earth’s axis perpendicular to its orbital plane” means from reference passages on the ecliptic and seasons. The ecliptic is the plane of Earth’s orbit, and the celestial equator is the projection of Earth’s equator onto the sky. Normally, Earth’s rotation axis is tilted relative to the ecliptic, so the celestial equator and ecliptic are separate great circles that intersect at the equinoxes. If the axis were perpendicular, however, the celestial equator and the ecliptic would coincide (as in the worked example in the passage about precession, where it states that if the pole were perpendicular, every day would be an equinox and the Sun would always be on the celestial equator). So, under that hypothetical condition, the Sun’s daily position at the same UT would lie along the celestial equator.

Next, consider what shape that path would take. reference explains that a great circle is the shortest-distance path on a sphere, such as the celestial equator itself. Because the Sun would always be on the celestial equator, its positions would indeed trace that great circle — provided the Sun’s motion along the equator is uniform.

Now you must check whether the Sun’s motion along that circle would be uniform enough to trace a simple arc. The problem says the Earth’s orbit is elliptical, and reference passage on elliptical orbits (Kepler’s first law) tells you that the Sun is at one focus of the ellipse, and the planet’s speed varies: it moves faster near perihelion and slower near aphelion. Even though the tilt is removed, the orbital eccentricity remains. Therefore, the true Sun would not move at a constant rate along the celestial equator; it would sometimes lead and sometimes lag the mean position.

Because the Sun’s position at exactly 05:00 UT each day is being marked, these timing irregularities mean the marks would not lie exactly on a single great circle. The statement claims they would trace an arc of a great circle, but the elliptical orbit causes deviations from that ideal path. Therefore, you should conclude that the statement is false.

kp_used: Earth's axis perpendicular to orbital plane

history.llm_reason: The guidance explicitly concludes that the statement is false, thereby revealing the answer.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.3) If the orbital period of a certain minor body around the Sun in the ecliptic plane is less than the orbital period of Uranus, then its orbit must necessarily be fully inside the orbit of Uranus.
sub_problems.solution:
The semi-major axis of the orbit of the body will be less than that of Uranus. However the minor body's orbit may have a high eccentricity, in which case it may go outside that of Uranus. Therefore the statement is false.
\boxed{\text{FALSE}}

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: Relates orbital period to semi-major axis; a shorter period than Uranus implies a smaller semi-major axis.

knowledge_points.name: orbital eccentricity
knowledge_points.description: Determines how much an orbit deviates from a circle; high eccentricity allows a body with smaller semi-major axis to cross outside Uranus's orbit at aphelion.

knowledge_points.name: Keplerian two-body motion
knowledge_points.description: The minor body and Sun are treated as a gravitationally bound two-body system obeying Kepler's laws, ignoring perturbations from other planets.

sub_problems.guidance:
To evaluate the statement, you need to relate the orbital period to the size of the orbit, and then consider whether “fully inside” is determined solely by that size.

First, recall Kepler’s third law from the textbook: for bodies orbiting the Sun, the square of the period \(P\) is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis \(a\) (in the simplified form \(P^2 = a^3\) when using years and AU). This law tells you that a shorter period implies a smaller semi-major axis. So, if the minor body’s period is less than that of Uranus, its semi-major axis must be smaller than that of Uranus.

Now, the phrase “fully inside the orbit of Uranus” means that at every point along its path, the minor body is closer to the Sun than Uranus is. However, Kepler’s first law (from the textbook passages on elliptical orbits) states that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus. The semi-major axis \(a\) gives the average size, but the actual distance from the Sun varies between perihelion (closest) and aphelion (farthest). The relationship is \(d_p + d_a = 2a\), where \(d_p\) is the perihelion distance and \(d_a\) is the aphelion distance.

The key additional factor is the orbital eccentricity \(e\), defined in the textbook as the distance between the foci divided by the major axis \(2a\). The aphelion distance can be expressed as \(a(1+e)\). Even if a body has a smaller semi-major axis than Uranus, a sufficiently high eccentricity could make its aphelion distance larger than Uranus’s distance at that same direction (or even larger than Uranus’s semi-major axis, depending on Uranus’s own eccentricity).

Therefore, you should reason in steps:
1. Use Kepler’s third law to conclude that a smaller period means a smaller semi-major axis than that of Uranus.
2. Recognize from the ellipse geometry that the maximum distance from the Sun (aphelion) is \(a(1+e)\).
3. Note that the statement requires the body to be *fully inside* Uranus’s orbit at all times, which would require its maximum distance to be less than Uranus’s minimum distance (or at least less than Uranus’s distance everywhere).
4. Consider whether a high eccentricity could allow the minor body’s aphelion distance to exceed Uranus’s orbital radius, even though its semi-major axis is smaller. The textbook passages on eccentricity and the geometry of elliptical motion provide the necessary relations for you to check this possibility.

By working through this logic, you can determine whether the “must necessarily” claim holds in all cases or if a counterexample exists.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.4) The centre of mass of the solar system is inside the Sun at all times.
sub_problems.solution:
The centre of mass of the Sun-Jupiter pair is just outside the Sun. Thus, if all gas giants are on the same side of the Sun, the centre of mass of the Solar system is definitely outside the Sun. Therefore the statement is false.
\boxed{\text{FALSE}}

knowledge_points.name: centre of mass
knowledge_points.description: The weighted average position of mass in a system; needed to evaluate whether the solar system's barycentre lies inside the Sun.

knowledge_points.name: two-body centre of mass formula
knowledge_points.description: The distance of the centre of mass from the primary is proportional to the secondary's mass times separation divided by total mass; used to estimate the Sun–Jupiter barycentre location.

knowledge_points.name: Sun–Jupiter barycentre outside Sun
knowledge_points.description: The reference solution states that the centre of mass of the Sun–Jupiter pair lies just outside the Sun, which is the key fact that makes the statement false.

knowledge_points.name: planetary alignment effect
knowledge_points.description: When all gas giants lie on the same side of the Sun, their combined mass shifts the solar system's centre of mass even farther from the Sun's centre, guaranteeing it is outside the Sun.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Recall the centre‑of‑mass definition**  
   The position of the centre of mass for a system of particles is given by the mass‑weighted average  
   \[
   \mathbf{R} = \frac{1}{M}\sum m_i \mathbf{r}_i
   \]  
   (Eq. 4.4 in Kleppner & Kolenkow, or Eq. 2.18 in Carroll & Ostlie). For two bodies, this means the centre of mass lies on the line joining them, and its distance from each body is inversely proportional to the mass of that body.

2. **Apply the formula to the Sun–Jupiter pair**  
   Place the origin at the Sun’s centre. Then the Sun’s position vector is zero, and Jupiter’s position vector is its orbital distance \(R_{\text{Jupiter}}\). Using the two‑body centre‑of‑mass expression, the distance of the barycentre from the Sun’s centre is  
   \[
   R_{\text{Sun}} = \frac{M_{\text{Jupiter}}}{M_{\text{Sun}}+M_{\text{Jupiter}}}\,R_{\text{Jupiter}} .
   \]  
   Because \(M_{\text{Jupiter}} \ll M_{\text{Sun}}\), this is approximately \(\frac{M_{\text{Jupiter}}}{M_{\text{Sun}}}R_{\text{Jupiter}}\). The textbook passage from Carroll & Ostlie notes that Jupiter’s mass is about \(1/1000\) of the Sun’s mass, placing the barycentre “near the surface of the Sun.” The worked example in the Kleppner & Kolenkow solution manual (Ex. 4.27) explicitly calculates this distance and compares it with the solar radius; you should carry out the same calculation using the known values (solar radius, Jupiter’s orbital radius, and the two masses) to see whether the barycentre lies inside or outside the Sun.

3. **Extend to the whole Solar System**  
   The centre of mass of the entire Solar System is the mass‑weighted average of the Sun and all the planets. If Jupiter alone can shift the barycentre outside the Sun when it is on one side, then when other massive planets (notably the other gas giants) are also on the same side, the centre of mass will be even farther from the Sun’s centre. Because the planets move, such configurations do occur. Hence, there are times when the centre of mass is not inside the Sun.

4. **Evaluate the statement**  
   Based on your calculation for the Sun–Jupiter pair and the reasoning about adding other planets, you can judge whether the claim “the centre of mass of the solar system is inside the Sun at all times” holds.

sub_problems.problem: (T1.5) A photon is moving in free space. As the Universe expands, its momentum decreases.
sub_problems.solution:
For photons the wavelength increases when the Universe expands. Since momentum is inversely proportional to wavelength, the momentum decreases. Therefore the statement is true.
\boxed{\text{TRUE}}

knowledge_points.name: cosmological redshift
knowledge_points.description: As the Universe expands, the wavelength of freely propagating photons stretches, increasing proportionally to the cosmic scale factor.

knowledge_points.name: photon momentum-wavelength relation
knowledge_points.description: The momentum p of a photon is inversely proportional to its wavelength λ, given by p = h/λ, so an increase in wavelength leads to a decrease in momentum.

knowledge_points.name: free space propagation
knowledge_points.description: The photon is moving in free space, meaning it experiences no interactions or scattering that would alter its momentum besides the cosmological expansion effect.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify what happens to the photon’s wavelength as the Universe expands. reference explains that cosmological redshifts are caused by the expansion of space itself: the wavelength of light is stretched in proportion to the growth of the scale factor \(R\) (see Sections 28.1 and 29.4). The observed wavelength \(\lambda_{\text{obs}}\) is larger than the emitted wavelength \(\lambda_{\text{emitted}}\), with \(\lambda_{\text{obs}}/\lambda_{\text{emitted}} = 1+z > 1\). So, as the Universe expands, the photon’s wavelength increases.

Next, recall the relationship between a photon’s momentum and its wavelength. In the discussion of the Compton effect (reference.5) and the de Broglie relations (reference.16), reference states that for a photon \(E = pc = hc/\lambda\), which gives \(p = h/\lambda\). This tells you that momentum is inversely proportional to wavelength: if the wavelength gets larger, the momentum gets smaller.

Now link the two ideas. You know the expansion stretches the wavelength; using \(p = h/\lambda\), determine what that stretching implies for the momentum. The direction of change will allow you to decide whether the statement “its momentum decreases” is correct.

history.llm_reason: The guidance explicitly concludes that the photon's momentum must decrease, directly revealing the answer to the true/false statement.

The guidance explicitly states the inverse relationship p = h/λ and instructs the student to use it to determine the momentum change, effectively performing the key reasoning step that directly leads to the answer.

title: Gases on Titan
problem:
Gas particles in a planetary atmosphere have a wide distribution of speeds. If the r.m.s. (root mean square) thermal speed of particles of a particular gas exceeds $1/6$ of the escape speed, then most of that gas will escape from the planet. What is the minimum atomic weight (relative atomic mass), $A_{\mathrm{min}}$ , of an ideal monatomic gas so that it remains in the atmosphere of Titan?

Given, mass of Titan $M_{\mathrm{T}} = 1.23 \times 10^{23} \mathrm{~kg}$ , radius of Titan $R_{\mathrm{T}} = 2575 \mathrm{~km}$ , surface temperature of Titan $T_{\mathrm{T}} = 93.7 \mathrm{~K}$ .
solution:
For a monatomic ideal gas, the rms speed is given by $\frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T = \frac{1}{2} m v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$, so $v_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T}{m}}$. The escape speed from Titan is $v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 G M_{\mathrm{T}}}{R_{\mathrm{T}}}}$. The condition for the gas to remain is $v_{\mathrm{rms}} < \frac{1}{6} v_{\mathrm{esc}}$. Substituting:

$$
\sqrt{\frac{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T_{\mathrm{T}}}{m}} < \frac{1}{6} \sqrt{\frac{2 G M_{\mathrm{T}}}{R_{\mathrm{T}}}}
$$

Squaring both sides:

$$
\frac{3 k_{\mathrm{B}} T_{\mathrm{T}}}{m} < \frac{2 G M_{\mathrm{T}}}{36 R_{\mathrm{T}}} = \frac{G M_{\mathrm{T}}}{18 R_{\mathrm{T}}}
$$

Thus:

$$
m > \frac{54 k_{\mathrm{B}} T_{\mathrm{T}} R_{\mathrm{T}}}{G M_{\mathrm{T}}}
$$

Using $k_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.381 \times 10^{-23} \, \mathrm{J/K}$, $G = 6.6741 \times 10^{-11} \, \mathrm{m^3 kg^{-1} s^{-2}}$, $R_{\mathrm{T}} = 2575 \times 10^3 \, \mathrm{m}$, $M_{\mathrm{T}} = 1.23 \times 10^{23} \, \mathrm{kg}$, $T_{\mathrm{T}} = 93.7 \, \mathrm{K}$:

$$
m > \frac{54 \times 1.381 \times 10^{-23} \times 93.7 \times 2.575 \times 10^6}{6.6741 \times 10^{-11} \times 1.23 \times 10^{23}} \, \mathrm{kg} \approx 2.19 \times 10^{-26} \, \mathrm{kg}
$$

The atomic mass unit is $1.66 \times 10^{-27} \, \mathrm{kg}$, so:

$$
A_{\mathrm{min}} = \frac{2.19 \times 10^{-26}}{1.66 \times 10^{-27}} \approx 13.2
$$

Thus the minimum atomic weight is $\boxed{A_{\mathrm{min}} = 13.2}$.

knowledge_points.name: Equipartition theorem for ideal gas
knowledge_points.description: For a monatomic ideal gas, the average translational kinetic energy per particle is (3/2) k_B T, giving the rms speed v_rms = sqrt(3 k_B T / m). Necessary to relate temperature to particle speed.

knowledge_points.name: Escape speed
knowledge_points.description: The minimum speed to escape a planet's gravity is v_esc = sqrt(2 G M / R). Used here to define the threshold for atmospheric retention.

knowledge_points.name: Escape condition threshold
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that a gas is retained if v_rms < (1/6) v_esc. This numerical criterion sets the inequality for atmospheric escape.

knowledge_points.name: Atomic mass unit
knowledge_points.description: Relative atomic mass (atomic weight) is the particle mass divided by the unified atomic mass unit u ≈ 1.66×10^{−27} kg. Needed to convert the critical mass from kg to atomic weight.

knowledge_points.name: Ideal monatomic gas
knowledge_points.description: The gas is ideal and monatomic, permitting the use of the equipartition theorem to obtain the rms speed from temperature.

sub_problems.guidance:
First identify the two speeds that must be compared. From the passage on escape velocity, the escape speed from a spherical body of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) is  
\(v_{\mathrm{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}}\)  
where \(G\) is the gravitational constant. Use the given mass \(M_{\mathrm{T}}\) and radius \(R_{\mathrm{T}}\) of Titan (convert the radius to meters) to write an expression for Titan's escape speed. Do not insert numbers yet.

Next, relate the thermal motion of the gas particles to the surface temperature of Titan. For a monatomic ideal gas, the equipartition theorem (see the passage from Kleppner & Kolenkow) tells you that the translational kinetic energy is equally shared among the three independent directions, so the average kinetic energy per particle is \(\frac{3}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T\). This gives  
\(\frac{1}{2}m v_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 = \frac{3}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T\)  
and therefore the r.m.s. speed is  
\(v_{\mathrm{rms}} = \sqrt{\frac{3k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{m}}\),  
where \(k_{\mathrm{B}}\) is Boltzmann's constant, \(T\) is Titan's surface temperature, and \(m\) is the mass of a single gas particle.

The problem states that the gas will remain if \(v_{\mathrm{rms}} < \frac{1}{6} v_{\mathrm{esc}}\). Substitute the expressions you have written for \(v_{\mathrm{rms}}\) and \(v_{\mathrm{esc}}\) into this inequality. To isolate \(m\), square both sides (all quantities are positive) and then solve for \(m\). This yields a minimum particle mass: the gas remains only if the particle mass is greater than some value that depends on \(T_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(R_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(M_{\mathrm{T}}\), \(k_{\mathrm{B}}\), and \(G\).

Now you must turn that minimum particle mass into an atomic weight (relative atomic mass). The atomic mass unit \(u\) is defined in the nuclear‑masses passage; note particularly that the mass equivalent is given as \(u c^2 = 931.5\ \mathrm{MeV}\). You can convert this into kilograms by using \(1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}\) and the speed of light \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), or simply use the standard value \(1\ u \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}\). The atomic weight \(A_{\mathrm{min}}\) is the ratio of the minimum single‑particle mass to the atomic mass unit:  
\(A_{\mathrm{min}} = \frac{m_{\mathrm{min}}}{u}\).

Carry out the arithmetic carefully, keeping track of units (convert Titan’s radius to metres, use Kelvin for temperature, etc.). The final result is the smallest integer‑like atomic weight that satisfies the condition; you should round appropriately.

title: Early Universe
problem: Cosmological models indicate that radiation energy density, $\rho_{\mathrm{r}}$ , in the Universe is proportional to $(1 + z)^4$ , and the matter energy density, $\rho_{\mathrm{m}}$ , is proportional to $(1 + z)^3$ , where $z$ is the redshift. The dimensionless density parameter, $\Omega$ , is given as $\Omega = \rho / \rho_{\mathrm{c}}$ , where $\rho_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the critical energy density of the Universe. In the present Universe, the density parameters corresponding to radiation and matter, are $\Omega_{\mathrm{r_0}} = 10^{-4}$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{m_0}} = 0.3$ , respectively.

sub_problems.problem: (T3.1) Calculate the redshift, $z_{\mathrm{e}}$ , at which radiation and matter energy densities were equal.
sub_problems.solution: At equality, $\rho_{\mathrm{r}} = \rho_{\mathrm{m}}$. Using $\rho_{\mathrm{r}} = \rho_{\mathrm{r_0}}(1+z)^4$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{m}} = \rho_{\mathrm{m_0}}(1+z)^3$, we have $\rho_{\mathrm{r_0}}(1+z_{\mathrm{e}})^4 = \rho_{\mathrm{m_0}}(1+z_{\mathrm{e}})^3$. Thus $1+z_{\mathrm{e}} = \rho_{\mathrm{m_0}}/\rho_{\mathrm{r_0}} = \Omega_{\mathrm{m_0}}/\Omega_{\mathrm{r_0}} = 0.3/10^{-4} = 3000$. Therefore $z_{\mathrm{e}} \simeq \boxed{3000}$.

knowledge_points.name: Redshift evolution of energy densities
knowledge_points.description: In the standard cosmological model, radiation energy density scales as (1+z)^4 and matter energy density scales as (1+z)^3, where z is the redshift. This relation is given in the problem and is used to express the densities at any redshift in terms of their present-day values.

knowledge_points.name: Density parameter Ω
knowledge_points.description: The dimensionless density parameter is defined as Ω = ρ/ρ_c, where ρ_c is the critical energy density. The problem gives present-day values Ω_r0 and Ω_m0, which are proportional to the present-day energy densities, allowing their ratio to be used directly without knowing ρ_c.

knowledge_points.name: Equality of radiation and matter densities
knowledge_points.description: The sub-problem asks for the redshift at which radiation and matter energy densities were equal, so the condition ρ_r = ρ_m is imposed. This yields the equation that is solved for z_e.

sub_problems.guidance:
The key is to use the scaling laws for energy densities and the definition of the redshift to find when radiation and matter contributed equally. Here is a step‑by‑step method grounded entirely in your textbook.

1. **Write the evolution of each density with scale factor.**  
   From the chapter you know:
   * Relativistic/radiation energy density: \(R^4 \rho_{\text{rel}} = \rho_{\text{rel},0}\)  (Eq. 29.81).
   * Matter (dust) density: \(R^3 \rho_{m} = \rho_{m,0}\)  (Eq. 29.82).  

   Because the scale factor \(R\) and redshift \(z\) are related by \(R = 1/(1+z)\) (Eq. 29.4), you can re‑express these laws as functions of redshift:
   \[
   \rho_{\text{rel}}(z) = \rho_{\text{rel},0}\,(1+z)^4, \qquad
   \rho_{m}(z) = \rho_{m,0}\,(1+z)^3.
   \]

2. **Set up the equality condition at the transition redshift \(z_e\).**  
   At the moment when radiation and matter densities are equal,
   \[
   \rho_{\text{rel}}(z_e) = \rho_{m}(z_e).
   \]
   Substitute the redshift expressions from step 1. You will get an equation involving today’s densities \(\rho_{\text{rel},0}\) and \(\rho_{m,0}\) and powers of \((1+z_e)\).

3. **Simplify to isolate \(1+z_e\).**  
   Cancel the common factor \((1+z_e)^3\) on both sides (it is positive, so this is allowed). The result gives \(1+z_e\) directly in terms of the present‑day density ratio:
   \[
   1+z_e = \frac{\rho_{m,0}}{\rho_{\text{rel},0}}.
   \]

4. **Introduce the density parameter \(\Omega\).**  
   The textbook defines the density parameter for any component as \(\Omega_{i,0} = \rho_{i,0}/\rho_{c,0}\), where \(\rho_{c,0}\) is today’s critical density. Because the same critical density appears in both numerator and denominator, the ratio of the densities equals the ratio of the corresponding \(\Omega\) values:
   \[
   \frac{\rho_{m,0}}{\rho_{\text{rel},0}} = \frac{\Omega_{m,0}}{\Omega_{\text{rel},0}}.
   \]
   Thus,
   \[
   1+z_e = \frac{\Omega_{m,0}}{\Omega_{\text{rel},0}}.
   \]

5. **Find \(z_e\) from this expression.**  
   Once you have \(1+z_e\), the redshift itself is simply \(z_e = (1+z_e) - 1\).  
   To obtain a numerical answer, insert the values of \(\Omega_{m,0}\) and \(\Omega_{\text{rel},0}\) that are appropriate for your problem (e.g. the WMAP‑based numbers discussed in the “Transition from the Radiation Era to the Matter Era” section, or any values given in your assignment). The procedure mirrors exactly the textbook’s own derivation of \(z_{r,m}\) in that section, so you can follow that worked example as a model – just keep the numbers symbolic until the very end.

By working through these steps you will arrive at the redshift where the universe switched from radiation‑dominated to matter‑dominated.

sub_problems.problem: (T3.2) Assuming that the radiation from the early Universe has a blackbody spectrum with a temperature of $2.732 \, \text{K}$ , estimate the temperature, $T_{\mathrm{e}}$ , of the radiation at redshift $z_{\mathrm{e}}$ .
sub_problems.solution: For a blackbody, the radiation energy density is proportional to $T^4$. Hence $(T_{\mathrm{e}}/T_0)^4 = \rho_{\mathrm{r e}}/\rho_{\mathrm{r 0}} = (1+z_{\mathrm{e}})^4$. Thus $T_{\mathrm{e}}/T_0 = 1+z_{\mathrm{e}} = 3000$, so $T_{\mathrm{e}} = 3000 \times 2.732 \, \text{K} = 8196 \, \text{K} \approx \boxed{8200 \, \text{K}}$.

knowledge_points.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law (energy density)
knowledge_points.description: For blackbody radiation, the energy density u is proportional to the fourth power of the temperature: u ∝ T⁴. This relates the temperature ratio to the energy density ratio.

knowledge_points.name: matter-radiation equality redshift
knowledge_points.description: From part T3.1, the redshift at which radiation and matter energy densities were equal is zₑ = 3000 (so 1+zₑ = 3000). This value is used to compute the temperature Tₑ.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall how a blackbody radiation field changes as the Universe expands. The textbook shows that the energy density for blackbody radiation follows \(u = a T^{4}\) (Eq. 9.7). Under thermodynamic equilibrium, the fluid equation with \(w_{\mathrm{rad}} = 1/3\) gives the scaling \(R^{4} u_{\mathrm{rad}} = u_{\mathrm{rad},0}\) (Eq. 29.57), where \(R\) is the scale factor, normalized to \(R(t_0)=1\) today.

Substitute the blackbody energy density into this scaling law: \(R^{4} (a T^{4}) = a T_{0}^{4}\). The constants \(a\) cancel, leading directly to Eq. (29.58):

\[
R \, T = T_0 .
\]

Thus the product of scale factor and blackbody temperature is constant. When the Universe was smaller (earlier), the radiation was hotter.

To connect this with redshift, use the definition of cosmological redshift: \(1+z = 1/R\) (since \(R(t_0)=1\)). Then Eq. (29.58) becomes

\[
T = T_0 (1+z).
\]

Now you can estimate the temperature at redshift \(z_{\mathrm{e}}\). You are given today’s CMB temperature \(T_0 = 2.732\;\mathrm{K}\). If the problem provides a value for \(z_{\mathrm{e}}\) (e.g. from an earlier part of the exercise), simply plug it into \(T_{\mathrm{e}} = T_0\,(1+z_{\mathrm{e}})\). Carry out the multiplication to find \(T_{\mathrm{e}}\); no further physical steps are needed.

sub_problems.problem: (T3.3) Estimate the typical photon energy, $E_{\nu}$ (in eV), of the radiation as emitted at redshift $z_{\mathrm{e}}$ .
