knowledge_points.description: The electronvolt is a unit of energy equal to 1.602×10^{-19} J, commonly used for photon energies. Conversion is needed to express the answer in eV.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Recall the radiation temperature at emission** — from earlier steps (not repeated here) you should already have the temperature \( T_{\mathrm{e}} \) of the radiation at the given redshift \( z_{\mathrm{e}} \). The radiation is roughly blackbody, so you can use thermal laws to estimate a “typical” photon energy.

2. **Get a characteristic wavelength via Wien’s displacement law**  
   Wien’s law, Eq. (3.15), says \(\lambda_{\max}T = 0.002898\ \text{m K}\). Solve for \(\lambda_{\max}\) by dividing the constant by \(T_{\mathrm{e}}\).  
   The numerical procedure is exactly the same as in **Example 3.4.1**, where Betelgeuse’s \(\lambda_{\max}\) was found from its surface temperature.  
   (Note: you may also encounter the form used in Section 18.2, \(\lambda_{\max} = \frac{(500\ \text{nm})(5800\ \text{K})}{T}\); both forms are equivalent.)

3. **Convert that wavelength to photon energy**  
   The photon energy–wavelength relation is given in Eq. (5.5): \(E = h\nu = hc/\lambda\).  
   Insert the \(\lambda_{\max}\) you just found, together with Planck’s constant \(h\) and the speed of light \(c\), to obtain the energy in joules.

4. **Express the result in electronvolts (eV)**  
   Use the conversion factor derived in the textbook: \(1\ \text{eV} = 1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}\) (Eq. 11.39). Divide your joule-scale energy by this number to get the energy in eV.

5. **Alternative thermal estimate (also acceptable)**  
   A coarser but simpler estimate comes from the classical equipartition idea that each mode of the radiation field carries an energy of order \(k_{\mathrm{B}}T\), where \(k_{\mathrm{B}} = 1.38065 \times 10^{-23}\ \text{J K}^{-1}\) (see the Rayleigh–Jeans discussion in Section 3.5). Thus you can obtain a typical photon energy via \(E \approx k_{\mathrm{B}} T_{\mathrm{e}}\). This value will differ from the Wien‑based result; both are reasonable estimates of the “typical” photon energy at emission.

title: Shadows
problem:
An observer in the northern hemisphere noticed that the length of the shortest shadow of a $1.000\mathrm{m}$ vertical stick on a day was $1.732\mathrm{m}$ . On the same day, the length of the longest shadow of the same vertical stick was measured to be $5.671\mathrm{m}$ .

Find the latitude, $\phi$ , of the observer and declination of the Sun, $\delta_{\odot}$ , on that day. Assume the Sun to be a point source and ignore atmospheric refraction.
solution:
Let $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ be the solar altitudes at the times of shortest and longest shadow, respectively. For a vertical stick of height $h = 1.000\,\mathrm{m}$ and shadow length $s$, we have $\tan\theta = h/s$, so $\cot\theta = s$ (in metres).

For a circumpolar Sun in the northern hemisphere, the shortest shadow occurs at the upper culmination (solar altitude $\theta_1 = 90^\circ - \phi + \delta_\odot$) and the longest shadow at the lower culmination (solar altitude $\theta_2 = \phi - 90^\circ + \delta_\odot$).

From the shortest shadow: $\cot(90^\circ - \phi + \delta_\odot) = 1.732$  $\Rightarrow$ $\tan(\phi - \delta_\odot) = 1.732$  $\Rightarrow$ $\phi - \delta_\odot = \tan^{-1}(1.732) = 60^\circ$.

From the longest shadow: $\cot(\phi - 90^\circ + \delta_\odot) = 5.671$  $\Rightarrow$ $\tan(\phi - 90^\circ + \delta_\odot) = 1/5.671$  $\Rightarrow$ $\phi + \delta_\odot = \tan^{-1}(1/5.671) + 90^\circ = 100^\circ$.

Solving the two equations: $\phi = (60^\circ + 100^\circ)/2 = 80^\circ$, $\delta_\odot = (100^\circ - 60^\circ)/2 = 20^\circ$.

Thus the latitude is $\boxed{\phi = 80^\circ}$ and the solar declination is $\boxed{\delta_\odot = 20^\circ}$.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Find the two solar altitudes from the shadow data.**  
   The *altitude* is the angle of the Sun above the horizon (see reference passage: “altitude … angle from the horizon to the object”). For a vertical stick of height \(h = 1.000\,\text{m}\) and shadow length \(s\), simple trigonometry gives \(\tan(\text{altitude}) = h/s\).

title: GMRT beam transit
problem:
Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT), one of the world's largest radio telescopes at metre wavelengths, is located in western India (latitude: $19^{\circ}6'$ N, longitude: $74^{\circ}3'$ E). GMRT consists of 30 dish antennas, each with a diameter of $45.0\mathrm{m}$ . A single dish of GMRT was held fixed with its axis pointing at a zenith angle of $39^{\circ}42'$ along the northern meridian such that a radio point source would pass along a diameter of the beam, when it is transiting the meridian.

What is the duration $T_{\mathrm{transit}}$ for which this source would be within the FWHM (full width at half maximum) of the beam of a single GMRT dish observing at 200 MHz?

Hint: The FWHM size of the beam of a radio dish operating at a given frequency corresponds to the angular resolution of the dish. Assume uniform illumination.
solution:
The altitude of the beam centre is $a = 90^\circ - z = 90^\circ - 39.70^\circ = 50.30^\circ$.  The declination of the source is $\delta = 90^\circ - a + \phi = 90^\circ - 50.30^\circ + 19.10^\circ = 58.80^\circ$ (also $\delta = z + \phi$).  The FWHM beam size for uniform illumination is $\theta = 1.22 \lambda / D = 1.22 c / (D \nu) = 1.22 \times 2.998 \times 10^8 / (45.0 \times 2 \times 10^8) = 0.0406\,\mathrm{rad} = 2.33^\circ$.  The transit duration is $T_{\mathrm{transit}} = \theta \times (3.99\,\mathrm{min}/^\circ) / \cos\delta = 2.33 \times 3.99 / \cos 58.8^\circ = 17.9\,\mathrm{min}$.

\boxed{T_{\mathrm{transit}} = 17.9\,\mathrm{min}}

title: Cepheid Pulsations
problem: The star $\beta$ -Doradius is a Cepheid variable star with a pulsation period of 9.84 days. We make a simplifying assumption that the star is brightest when it is most contracted (radius being $R_{1}$ ) and it is faintest when it is most expanded (radius being $R_{2}$ ). For simplicity, assume that the star maintains its spherical shape and behaves as a perfect black body at every instant during the entire cycle. The bolometric magnitude of the star varies from 3.46 to 4.08. From Doppler measurements, we know that during pulsation the stellar surface expands or contracts at an average radial speed of $12.8\mathrm{km~s}^{-1}$ . Over the period of pulsation, the peak of thermal radiation (intrinsic) of the star varies from 531.0 nm to 649.1 nm.

sub_problems.problem: (T6.1) Find the ratio of radii of the star in its most contracted and most expanded states $(R_{1} / R_{2})$ .
sub_problems.solution:
We first find flux ratio and then use Stefan's law to compare the fluxes.

$$m_1 - m_2 = -2.5 \log\left(\frac{F_1}{F_2}\right)$$
$$\therefore \frac{F_1}{F_2} = 10^{-0.4(m_1 - m_2)} = 10^{-0.4(3.46 - 4.08)} = 1.77$$

$$L_i = 4\pi R_i^2 \sigma T_i^4$$
$$\therefore F_1 = \frac{4\pi R_1^2 \sigma T_1^4}{4\pi D^2}, \quad F_2 = \frac{4\pi R_2^2 \sigma T_2^4}{4\pi D^2}$$

$$\frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{R_1^2}{R_2^2} \times \frac{T_1^4}{T_2^4}$$
$$\frac{R_1}{R_2} = \sqrt{\frac{F_1}{F_2}} \times \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)^2$$

From Wien's displacement law, $\frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}$.

$$\therefore \frac{R_1}{R_2} = \sqrt{\frac{F_1}{F_2}} \times \left(\frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}\right)^2 = \sqrt{1.77} \times \left(\frac{531.0}{649.1}\right)^2$$

$$\boxed{\frac{R_1}{R_2} = 0.890}$$

knowledge_points.name: relation between magnitude and flux
knowledge_points.description: Converts the given bolometric magnitudes into a flux ratio using m1 - m2 = -2.5 log(F1/F2).

knowledge_points.name: Stefan-Boltzmann law
knowledge_points.description: Relates luminosity L to radius R and effective temperature T via L = 4πR²σT⁴, and flux F at distance D via F = L/(4πD²).

knowledge_points.name: Wien's displacement law
knowledge_points.description: Relates the peak wavelength of blackbody radiation to temperature, λ_max ∝ 1/T, allowing the temperature ratio to be found from the given peak wavelengths.

knowledge_points.name: perfect blackbody radiation
knowledge_points.description: The star radiates as a perfect blackbody at every instant, justifying the use of Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien's laws.

knowledge_points.name: spherical star shape
knowledge_points.description: The star maintains a spherical shape throughout pulsation, so surface area is 4πR².

knowledge_points.name: same distance for both states
knowledge_points.description: The distance D from Earth to the star is effectively constant during the pulsation cycle, so it cancels in the flux ratio.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the ratio of radii \( R_1 / R_2 \) for the star in its most contracted (state 1) and most expanded (state 2) states, you will need to connect the observed magnitudes to the fluxes, then connect the fluxes to the stellar radii and temperatures, and finally relate the temperatures to the observed wavelengths using blackbody laws. The problem states that the distance to the star is the same in both states, which simplifies the flux comparison.

**Step 1: Relate the given apparent magnitudes to the flux ratio.**
The problem provides the apparent magnitudes \( m_1 \) and \( m_2 \) for the two states. From the textbook’s magnitude scale (Eq. 3.4), a difference in apparent magnitude is directly tied to the logarithm of the flux ratio:
\[
m_1 - m_2 = -2.5 \log_{10}\left(\frac{F_1}{F_2}\right).
\]
Use this equation to find the ratio of the fluxes \( F_1 / F_2 \) received at Earth. This step is analogous to the logic behind the absolute magnitude definition, where a magnitude difference corresponds to a flux ratio.

**Step 2: Express the observed flux in terms of the star’s radius and temperature.**
The star is treated as a spherical blackbody. The Stefan–Boltzmann equation for a spherical star (Eq. 3.17) gives its total luminosity as \( L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T_e^4 \). Because both states are observed from the same distance \( D \), the flux received at Earth for each state is the luminosity spread over a sphere of radius \( D \):
\[
F = \frac{L}{4\pi D^2} = \frac{4\pi R^2 \sigma T_e^4}{4\pi D^2} = \left(\frac{R^2}{D^2}\right) \sigma T_e^4.
\]
Write this expression for \( F_1 \) and \( F_2 \). Then form the ratio \( F_1 / F_2 \). Notice that the distance \( D \) and the Stefan–Boltzmann constant \( \sigma \) cancel out, leaving a relationship involving the ratio of radii and the ratio of effective temperatures.

**Step 3: Replace the temperature ratio with a wavelength ratio using Wien’s displacement law.**
You are given the wavelengths of peak emission, \( \lambda_1 \) and \( \lambda_2 \), for the two states. Wien’s displacement law (Eq. 3.15) states that \( \lambda_{\text{max}} T \) is a constant (approximately \( 0.0029 \, \text{m K} \)). Therefore, for the two states:
\[
\lambda_1 T_1 = \lambda_2 T_2 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{T_2}{T_1} = \frac{\lambda_1}{\lambda_2}.
\]
Substitute this temperature ratio into the expression you obtained for \( F_1 / F_2 \) in Step 2.

**Step 4: Combine the equations to isolate \( R_1 / R_2 \).**
Now you have two expressions for \( F_1 / F_2 \): one from the magnitude difference (Step 1) and one from the radii and wavelengths (Steps 2 and 3). Set them equal. The only unknown will be the ratio \( R_1 / R_2 \). Solve for it algebraically; the result will involve the square root of the flux ratio and the square of the wavelength ratio. Once you have the symbolic expression, plug in the numerical values for \( m_1, m_2, \lambda_1, \lambda_2 \) and carry out the arithmetic to obtain the final dimensionless ratio.

sub_problems.problem: (T6.2) Find the radii of the star (in metres) in its most contracted and most expanded states $(R_{1}$ and $R_{2})$ .
sub_problems.solution:
$$R_2 - R_1 = v \times P/2$$
$$R_2 - R_1 = 12.8 \times 10^3 \times 86400 \times \frac{9.84}{2} \mathrm{m} = 5.441 \times 10^9 \mathrm{m}$$
$$(1 - 0.890) R_2 = 5.441 \times 10^9 \mathrm{m}$$
$$\therefore R_2 = 4.95 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{m}$$
$$R_1 = 4.41 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{m}$$

$$\boxed{R_1 = 4.41 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{m}}, \quad \boxed{R_2 = 4.95 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{m}}$$

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks for two radii, \(R_1\) and \(R_2\), of a star in its most contracted and most expanded states. You already know some information from the context of the problem (a pulsation period \(P\), a radial velocity \(v\), and a fractional radius change). Your task is to combine these pieces using the physics of constant-speed motion and simple algebra.

**Step 1 – Find the total change in radius over half a pulsation cycle.**  
The star expands from its smallest radius \(R_1\) to its largest radius \(R_2\) during half of its pulsation period. The radial motion happens at a constant average speed \(v\). The textbook passage on supernova remnants (Palen, Schaum’s Outline) shows exactly this idea: to find a linear expansion \(D\) from a constant speed and a time interval, you multiply the speed by the time, \(D = v \cdot t\). Apply that same principle here. The time for half a cycle is \(P/2\), so the difference \(R_2 - R_1\) is obtained from \(v\) and \(P/2\). (Be careful with units: the period is given in days, so you will need to convert days into seconds. The textbook passage from Taylor & Wheeler reminds you that time can be converted using a known conversion factor—here, use the number of seconds in one day.)

**Step 2 – Relate the radius difference to the radii themselves.**  
You are also told that the fractional change in radius is \(1 - 0.890\); that is, the difference \(R_2 - R_1\) is equal to \((1 - 0.890)R_2\). This gives you a direct linear relationship between the two unknown radii.

**Step 3 – Solve the two linear equations.**  
Now you have two simple linear equations involving \(R_1\) and \(R_2\):
- One from Step 1: \(R_2 - R_1 = \text{(the distance you computed)}\).
- One from Step 2: \(R_2 - R_1 = (1 - 0.890)R_2\).

The textbook passage from Morin (the moving plane problem) demonstrates how to handle two linear equations in two unknowns: you can use substitution or elimination. Here it is easiest to equate the right-hand sides of the two expressions for \(R_2 - R_1\) to solve for \(R_2\) first. Once you have \(R_2\), subtract the difference found in Step 1 to get \(R_1\).

Carry out the unit conversion, the multiplication, and the algebraic steps yourself. You will end up with the two radii in metres.

sub_problems.problem: (T6.3) Calculate the flux of the star, $F_{2}$ , when it is in its most expanded state.
sub_problems.solution:
To get the absolute value of flux $(F_2)$ we must compare it with observed flux of the Sun.

$$m_2 - m_\odot = -2.5 \log\left(\frac{F_2}{F_\odot}\right)$$
$$\therefore F_2 = F_\odot \, 10^{-0.4(m_2 - m_\odot)}$$
$$= \frac{L_\odot}{4\pi a_\oplus^2} \times 10^{-0.4(4.08 + 26.72)}$$
$$= \frac{3.826 \times 10^{26} \times 4.7863 \times 10^{-13}}{4\pi (1.496 \times 10^{11})^2} \mathrm{W m}^{-2}$$

$$\boxed{F_2 = 6.51 \times 10^{-10} \mathrm{W m}^{-2}}$$

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the flux of the star at its most expanded state, you need to compare the star’s brightness to the Sun’s brightness using the magnitude scale. The approach has two main steps: first determine the solar flux at Earth, and then relate that to the star’s flux through the apparent magnitude difference.

1. **Use the inverse‑square law to get the solar flux at Earth**  
   The Sun’s luminosity \(L_\odot\) and the Earth–Sun distance (1 AU) give the radiant flux from the Sun received at the top of Earth’s atmosphere.  
   - The inverse‑square law (Eq. 3.2 in Carroll & Ostlie) is \(F = \frac{L}{4\pi r^2}\).  
   - Example 3.2.1 in the textbook applies this exact formula with \(L_\odot = 3.839\times10^{26}\,\text{W}\) and \(1\,\text{AU}=1.496\times10^{11}\,\text{m}\) to obtain the solar constant (the solar flux at Earth). You may carry out that calculation yourself.  
   - The result is the solar flux \(F_\odot\) that you will use as a reference.

2. **Apply Pogson’s equation to connect the star’s flux to the solar flux**  
   The magnitude system relates a difference in apparent magnitudes to a ratio of fluxes.  
   - From Carroll & Ostlie, Eq. (3.4): \(m_1 - m_2 = -2.5\log_{10}(F_1/F_2)\).  
   - Let \(m_2\) be the star’s apparent magnitude in its most expanded state (which you should already have from the earlier parts of the problem), and let \(m_\odot\) be the Sun’s apparent magnitude. The textbook lists the solar bolometric magnitude as \(m_\odot = -26.83\).  
   - Rearranging Eq. (3.4) to isolate the star’s flux gives  
     \[
     F_2 = F_\odot \times 10^{-0.4\,(m_2 - m_\odot)} .
     \]

3. **Substitute the numbers**  
   - Insert the solar flux \(F_\odot\) you computed in step 1.  
   - Insert the known magnitudes \(m_2\) and \(m_\odot\).  
   - Perform the exponentiation and multiplication to obtain \(F_2\) in \(\text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}\).

This method follows exactly the logic of the worked example in the Schaum’s Outline passage (Problem 7.15), where the solar flux is first found from the inverse‑square law and then used to compare fluxes, except here the comparison is made via the magnitude difference rather than a direct luminosity ratio.

sub_problems.problem: (T6.4) Find the distance to the star, $D_{\mathrm{star}}$ , in parsecs.
sub_problems.solution:
$$D_{\mathrm{star}} = \sqrt{\frac{L_2}{4\pi F_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{R_2^2 \sigma T_2^4}{F_2}} = R_2 T_2^2 \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{F_2}}$$

Wien's law: $T_2 = \frac{2.898 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{mK}}{\lambda_2}$

$$D_{\mathrm{star}} = 4.95 \times 10^{10} \times \left(\frac{2.898 \times 10^{-3}}{649.1 \times 10^{-9}}\right)^2 \sqrt{\frac{5.670 \times 10^{-8}}{6.51 \times 10^{-10}}}$$

$$\therefore \boxed{D_{\mathrm{star}} = 9.208 \times 10^{18} \mathrm{m} = 298 \mathrm{pc}}$$

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the distance to the star, you need to work step by step, combining several laws of blackbody radiation and the inverse-square law for light. Here is the logical order to follow, grounded in your reference passages.

First, determine the star’s effective temperature. You are given a wavelength that is presumably the peak wavelength of its blackbody spectrum. Use **Wien’s displacement law** to relate this peak wavelength to the star’s surface temperature. reference states this law as \(\lambda_{\max} T = 0.002897755 \, \text{m K}\) (reference.15), and the Schaum’s outline gives it in the form \(\lambda_{\max} = \frac{0.0029 \, \text{m} \cdot \text{K}}{T}\). Solve this relation for temperature \(T\). This step is directly analogous to Example 3.4.1 in reference, where the surface temperature of Betelgeuse is found from its peak wavelength.

Next, you must find the star’s luminosity. reference explains that for a spherical star, the **Stefan–Boltzmann law** takes the form \(L = 4\pi R^2 \sigma T_e^4\) (reference.17), where \(R\) is the star’s radius and \(\sigma\) is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant. You should know the star’s radius (likely given in the problem or deducible from other context) and you have just found its temperature. Substitute these values into reference.17 to obtain the luminosity \(L\). The worked example for the Sun in the same section (Example 3.4.2) shows exactly this calculation in reverse: given the Sun’s luminosity and radius, its effective temperature is computed.

Finally, relate the luminosity to the distance using the **inverse-square law for flux**. reference defines the radiant flux \(F\) received at a distance \(r\) from a star of luminosity \(L\) as \(F = \frac{L}{4\pi r^2}\) (reference.2). You are given a measured flux \(F\) from the star. You now know \(L\) from the previous step. Rearrange reference.2 to solve for the distance \(r\) (here called \(D_{\text{star}}\)). This is the same principle used in Example 3.2.1, where the solar flux at Earth’s distance is calculated from the Sun’s luminosity.

Carry out these three stages in sequence: Wien’s law to get temperature, Stefan–Boltzmann to get luminosity, and the inverse-square law to get distance. The final step will ask you to express the distance in parsecs; you will need the conversion factor between meters and parsecs, which is standard knowledge but not explicitly in these passages. Perform all substitutions and algebraic manipulations yourself to arrive at the answer.

title: Telescope optics
problem: In a particular ideal refracting telescope of focal ratio $f / 5$ , the focal length of the objective lens is $100\mathrm{cm}$ and that of the eyepiece is $1\mathrm{cm}$ .

sub_problems.problem: (T7.1) What is the angular magnification, $m_0$ , of the telescope? What is the length of the telescope, $L_0$ , i.e. the distance between its objective and eyepiece?
sub_problems.solution:
The magnification is given by $m_0 = \frac{f_o}{f_e} = \frac{100}{1} = 100$. The length of the telescope is $L_0 = f_o + f_e = 100 + 1 = 101\mathrm{cm}$.

\boxed{m_0 = 100}, \boxed{L_0 = 101\mathrm{cm}}

knowledge_points.name: angular magnification
knowledge_points.description: The angular magnification of a telescope is the factor by which the apparent angular size of a distant object is increased when viewed through the instrument. The problem explicitly asks for this quantity.

knowledge_points.name: telescope angular magnification formula
knowledge_points.description: For a simple refracting telescope in normal adjustment, the angular magnification equals the ratio of the objective focal length to the eyepiece focal length: m = f_o / f_e. This formula is directly applied in the solution.

knowledge_points.name: telescope tube length in normal adjustment
knowledge_points.description: In normal adjustment (final image at infinity), the distance between the objective and the eyepiece is the sum of their focal lengths: L = f_o + f_e. The solution uses this to compute the length of the telescope.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the angular magnification, use the formula given in your textbook for a simple refracting telescope in normal adjustment (object at infinity, final image at infinity). From Carroll & Ostlie, Eq. (6.9) states \( m = \frac{f_{\text{obj}}}{f_{\text{eye}}} \) (see also Georgi, Eq. 11.158). This direct ratio arises because the objective lens brings the distant light to a focus in its focal plane, and the eyepiece then acts as a magnifying glass to view that real image; the resulting angular size is magnified by the factor of the focal lengths. Identify the objective focal length \( f_{\text{obj}} \) and the eyepiece focal length \( f_{\text{eye}} \) given in the problem, and simply divide the former by the latter to obtain \( m_0 \).

For the telescope length, recall the arrangement described in the passage: the objective forms a real image at its focal plane, located a distance \( f_{\text{obj}} \) behind the objective lens. To view the final image at infinity (normal adjustment), the eyepiece is placed so that its own focal point lies exactly at that focal plane—thus the distance from the eyepiece to the focal plane is its focal length \( f_{\text{eye}} \). The total separation between objective and eyepiece is therefore the sum of these two distances. Use the relation \( L_0 = f_{\text{obj}} + f_{\text{eye}} \) (implicit in the text’s description of the eyepiece placement and the diagrams in Figure 6.15 and Figure 11.48). Substitute the same two focal lengths you used for the magnification and add them to find the tube length \( L_0 \).

sub_problems.problem: (T7.2) At what distance, $d_{\mathrm{B}}$ , from the prime focus must the Barlow lens be kept in order to obtain this desired double magnification?
sub_problems.solution:
Use sign convention: lens is origin, direction of light positive. Lens formula $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u}$ with $f$ positive for convex, negative for concave. For Barlow lens $f_B = -1\mathrm{cm}$. Object distance $u = d_B$ (distance before prime focus). Magnification $m_B = 2 = \frac{v}{u} = \frac{v}{d_B}$, so $v = 2 d_B$. Substitute into lens formula: $\frac{1}{-1} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{d_B} = \frac{1}{2d_B} - \frac{1}{d_B} = -\frac{1}{2d_B}$. Thus $-1 = -\frac{1}{2d_B}$, giving $d_B = 0.5\mathrm{cm}$.

\boxed{d_{\mathrm{B}} = 0.5\mathrm{cm}}

knowledge_points.name: Thin lens equation (Gaussian form)
knowledge_points.description: The equation 1/f = 1/v - 1/u relates focal length f, image distance v, and object distance u for a thin lens. It is applied to the Barlow lens with the given sign convention.

knowledge_points.name: Lateral magnification formula
knowledge_points.description: For a lens, lateral magnification m = v/u. Used to relate object and image distances knowing the desired magnification of 2 for the Barlow lens.

knowledge_points.name: Lens sign convention
knowledge_points.description: Sign convention adopted: lens at origin, direction of incident light positive. Object distance u is positive when measured in this direction, and focal length f is negative for a diverging lens. This sets f = -1 cm and u = d_B.

knowledge_points.name: Barlow lens properties
knowledge_points.description: The Barlow lens is a diverging (concave) lens with focal length f = -1 cm, placed between the objective and its prime focus to increase effective magnification. Its focal length is taken as given in the problem.

knowledge_points.name: Prime focus of objective
knowledge_points.description: The prime focus is the point where the objective lens forms an image without the Barlow lens. The Barlow lens is positioned a distance d_B from this focus, so the object for the Barlow lies at the prime focus.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the distance \( d_{\mathrm{B}} \), you need to apply the thin lens equation and the lateral magnification formula to the Barlow lens. The Barlow lens is a diverging lens, so its focal length is negative (see Fig. 6.2(b) in the Carroll & Ostlie passage: diverging lenses have \( f_{\lambda} < 0 \)).

First, think about where the “object” for the Barlow lens is. The objective lens of the telescope brings light to a focus at the **prime focus** (described in the “Reflecting Telescopes” excerpt). The Barlow lens is placed before that focus, so it intercepts the converging beam. For the Barlow lens, the prime focus acts as a virtual object because the rays are converging toward a point that lies on the opposite side of the lens. Therefore, in the thin lens formula

\]
from Georgi, the object distance \( d_{1} \) will be **negative** (the sign convention for virtual objects is the natural extension of the one mentioned there for virtual images). Since the physical separation between the lens and the prime focus is what you are looking for, set \( d_{1} = -d_{\mathrm{B}} \).

Next, the problem states that the overall effect should be a **double magnification**. The lateral magnification relates image size to object size (Eq. 11.154 in Georgi):

sub_problems.problem: (T7.3) What is the increase, $\Delta L$ , in the length of the telescope?
sub_problems.solution:
The increase in length is $\Delta L = v - d_B = 1.0 - 0.5 = 0.5\mathrm{cm}$.

\boxed{\Delta L = 0.5\mathrm{cm}}

knowledge_points.name: telescope tube length
knowledge_points.description: The length of a refracting telescope is the distance between the objective lens and the eyepiece. In normal infinity-focus configuration the eyepiece is placed so that its focal plane coincides with the prime focus of the objective, making the length equal to the sum of the objective and eyepiece focal lengths. Inserting optical elements shifts the final focus and requires a length adjustment.

knowledge_points.name: Barlow lens focal shift
knowledge_points.description: A Barlow lens inserted between the objective and its prime focus shifts the final focal plane further back. If the Barlow lens is placed at a distance d_B from the original prime focus and the new real image is formed at a distance v from the Barlow lens, the eyepiece must be moved back by ΔL = v − d_B to intercept the new focal plane.

knowledge_points.description: The specific numerical values for d_B (0.5 cm) and v (1.0 cm) are taken from the solution of sub-problem T7.2, where they were calculated for the 2x Barlow lens configuration.

sub_problems.problem: (T7.4) What will be the distance in pixels between the centroids of the images of the two stars, $n_{\mathrm{p}}$ , on the CCD, if they are $20^{\prime \prime}$ apart on the sky?
sub_problems.solution:
Plate scale at prime focus: $s = \frac{1}{f_o} = \frac{1\mathrm{rad}}{1\mathrm{m}} = 0.206265\mathrm{arcsec}/\mu\mathrm{m}$. Each pixel is $10\mu\mathrm{m}$, so $s_p = 10 \times 0.206265 \approx 2.06\mathrm{arcsec/pixel}$. Separation: $n_p = \frac{20^{\prime\prime}}{2.06^{\prime\prime}} \approx 9.7$ pixels. Acceptable range 9.5 to 10.5 pixels.

\boxed{n_{\mathrm{p}} \approx 10\text{ pixels}}

knowledge_points.name: prime focus configuration
knowledge_points.description: The CCD is placed at the prime focus of the objective lens, so the plate scale is determined solely by the objective focal length without any additional optics (eyepiece or Barlow lens). This justifies using the objective focal length directly.

knowledge_points.name: plate scale
knowledge_points.description: At the focal plane of a telescope, the relation between angular size on the sky (in radians) and linear size on the detector is s = 1/f rad per unit length, where f is the focal length. This converts the given stellar separation (20 arcsec) to a linear distance on the CCD.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For sufficiently small angles, sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ (in radians), yielding the linear relation y = fθ. This underlies the plate scale formula and justifies using radian measure for the angular separation.

knowledge_points.name: radian–arcsecond conversion
knowledge_points.description: 1 radian equals 206265 arcseconds. This conversion factor is needed to express the plate scale in practical units of arcsec per micrometre and to relate the given angular separation in arcseconds to radians.

knowledge_points.name: CCD pixel size
knowledge_points.description: The CCD camera has square pixels of 10 μm size. This value is used to convert the linear separation on the detector into a number of pixels.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, express the given angular separation between the stars (20″) in radians. The textbook’s discussion of stellar parallax provides the needed conversion: 1 radian ≈ 206 265 arcseconds. Use this to write the angle θ in radians.

Next, because 20″ is a very small angle, the small‑angle approximation tan θ ≈ θ holds (this is the same approximation used in the plate‑scale derivation of Fig. 6.6 and Eq. 6.3). The telescope’s focal plane relationship then becomes y = f θ, where y is the linear separation between the star images on the detector and f is the focal length of the telescope. (The problem should give you f and the pixel size — if not, they are part of the telescope/setup described earlier.) With θ in radians and f in the same length units as your detector dimensions, calculate y.

Finally, convert this linear separation into a distance in pixels. The CCD pixel size tells you the width of one pixel (for example, in μm). Divide the linear separation y by the pixel size to obtain the number of pixels nₚ between the centroids. Make sure the units cancel correctly.

The method therefore follows three steps directly supported by the passages:  
(1) convert arcseconds → radians using 1 rad ≈ 2.06×10⁵ arcsec,  
(2) find the image separation on the focal plane via y = f θ (plate scale, Eq. 6.3),  
(3) divide that linear distance by the pixel size to get nₚ.  
Carry out the arithmetic yourself to arrive at the result.

title: U-Band photometry
problem:
A star has an apparent magnitude $m_{\mathrm{U}} = 15.0$ in the $U$ -band. The $U$ -band filter is ideal, i.e., it has perfect (100%) transmission within the band and is completely opaque (0% transmission) outside the band. The filter is centered at $360 \mathrm{~nm}$ , and has a width of $80 \mathrm{~nm}$ . It is assumed that the star also has a flat energy spectrum with respect to frequency. The conversion between magnitude, $m$ , in any band and flux density, $f$ , of a star in Jansky (1 Jy = 1 × $10^{-26}$ W Hz $^{-1}$ m $^{-2}$ ) is given by

$$
f = 3 6 3 1 \times 1 0 ^ {- 0. 4 m} J y
$$

sub_problems.problem: (T8.1) Approximately how many $U$ -band photons, $N_0$ , from this star will be incident normally on a $1\mathrm{m}^2$ area at the top of the Earth's atmosphere every second?
sub_problems.solution:
The $U$-band is $(360 \pm 40)\mathrm{nm}$. Thus:
\[
\nu_{\max} = \frac{c}{\lambda_{\min}} = \frac{3\times10^8\mathrm{m/s}}{320\times10^{-9}\mathrm{m}} = 9.369\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz}
\]
\[
\nu_{\min} = \frac{c}{\lambda_{\max}} = \frac{3\times10^8\mathrm{m/s}}{400\times10^{-9}\mathrm{m}} = 7.495\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz}
\]
\[
\nu_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{\nu_{\max}+\nu_{\min}}{2} = 8.432\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz}
\]
\[
\Delta\nu = \nu_{\max}-\nu_{\min} = 1.874\times10^{14}\mathrm{Hz}
\]
Flux density from magnitude:
\[
f_{\mathrm{st1}} = 3631\times10^{-0.4\times15.0} = 3.631\times10^{-29}\mathrm{W\,Hz^{-1}\,m^{-2}}
\]
Energy per second per $1\mathrm{m}^2$: $\Delta\nu\,f_{\mathrm{st1}}\times1\mathrm{m}^2\times1\mathrm{s}$.
Number of photons:
\[
N_0 = \frac{\Delta\nu\,f_{\mathrm{st1}}}{h\nu_{\mathrm{avg}}} = \frac{1.874\times10^{14}\times3.631\times10^{-29}}{6.626\times10^{-34}\times8.432\times10^{14}} \approx \boxed{12180}
\]

knowledge_points.name: ideal rectangular bandpass filter
knowledge_points.description: The U-band filter has 100% transmission between 320 nm and 400 nm (center 360 nm ± 40 nm half-width), and 0% outside, as implied by the given center and full width.

knowledge_points.name: wave speed equation c = λν
knowledge_points.description: Converts the wavelength limits (320 nm, 400 nm) to frequency limits (ν_max, ν_min) using the speed of light c.

knowledge_points.name: photon energy E = hν
knowledge_points.description: Used to convert the total energy per second in the U-band to the number of photons, by dividing total power by the energy per photon at the average frequency.

knowledge_points.name: magnitude to flux density conversion
knowledge_points.description: Given formula f = 3631 × 10^{-0.4 m} Jy directly relates U-band apparent magnitude m to flux density in Jansky.

knowledge_points.name: flat frequency spectrum
knowledge_points.description: The star's energy spectrum is flat with respect to frequency, i.e., flux density f_ν is constant across the U-band, so total flux is simply f_ν × Δν.

knowledge_points.name: arithmetic mean approximation for average frequency
knowledge_points.description: Approximates the typical photon frequency by the arithmetic mean of the band edges, (ν_min + ν_max)/2, to simplify the photon number calculation instead of integrating 1/ν across the band.

knowledge_points.name: Jansky unit conversion
knowledge_points.description: 1 Jy = 1 × 10^{-26} W Hz^{-1} m^{-2}, needed to convert the flux density obtained from the magnitude formula into SI units for compatibility with Planck's constant h.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, turn the U‑band wavelength range into a frequency interval.  
Use the wave speed relation from your reference: \(c = \lambda \nu\) (or \(v = \lambda f\)).  For light in a vacuum, \(c = 3\times 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}\).  From the given \(\lambda_{\min}\) and \(\lambda_{\max}\) (320 nm and 400 nm) compute the corresponding \(\nu_{\max}\) and \(\nu_{\min}\) via \(\nu = c/\lambda\).  The bandwidth is then \(\Delta\nu = \nu_{\max} - \nu_{\min}\), and you can approximate the typical photon frequency by the midpoint \(\nu_{\text{avg}} = (\nu_{\max}+\nu_{\min})/2\).  This step follows directly from reference’s statement that frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional.

Next, convert the star’s U‑band magnitude into a physical flux density.  
Your reference shows that a magnitude difference relates to a flux ratio as

\[
\frac{F_2}{F_1} = 100^{(m_1-m_2)/5}.
\]

You are given the U‑band flux density for a zero‑magnitude star (e.g., 3631 Jy).  Treat that star as \(m_1=0\) and your star as \(m_2=m\); then the star’s flux density in janskys is \(F_{\text{star}} = F_0 \times 100^{-m/5}\).  reference’s discussion of jansky units tells you that \(1\ \text{Jy} = 10^{-26}\ \text{W}\,\text{m}^{-2}\,\text{Hz}^{-1}\); apply that conversion to get the spectral flux density \(S\) in SI units.

Now find the power received per unit area in the whole U‑band.  
The radio‑telescope passage explains that for a constant spectral flux density over a bandwidth \(\Delta\nu\), the detected power is \(P = S A \Delta\nu\).  Here the collecting area is \(1\ \text{m}^2\), so the power (energy per second) falling on that area is simply \(P = S \times 1\,\text{m}^2 \times \Delta\nu\).

Finally, turn that energy flow into a photon count.  
The quantization‑of‑energy passage tells you that a photon has energy \(E = h\nu\).  Take the average frequency \(\nu_{\text{avg}}\) you found and multiply by Planck’s constant \(h = 6.626\times 10^{-34}\ \text{J}\,\text{s}\).  The number of photons per second, \(N_0\), is then the total power divided by the energy of one average photon:

\[
N_0 = \frac{S\,\Delta\nu}{h\,\nu_{\text{avg}}}.
\]

Now carry out the substitutions and arithmetic yourself; this step‑by‑step chain of reasoning gives you the route without handing you the numerical answer.

sub_problems.problem: (T8.2) What is the ratio, $R$ , of number of photons received per second from the star to that received from the sky, when measured over a circular aperture of diameter $2^{\prime\prime}$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
Sky surface brightness $22.0\,\mathrm{mag/arcsec^2}$. For a circular aperture of radius $1''$, area $A = \pi\,\mathrm{arcsec^2}$. The total sky magnitude over that area:
\[
m_{\mathrm{sky}} = 22.0 - 2.5\log_{10}(\pi) \approx 20.76
\]
Atmospheric extinction reduces star flux by $50\%$, so effective star flux $\phi_{\mathrm{st2}} = 0.5\,\phi_{\mathrm{st1}}$.
Ratio:
\[
R = \frac{\phi_{\mathrm{st2}}}{\phi_{\mathrm{sky}}} = 0.5\times10^{(20.76-15.0)/2.5} \approx \boxed{100}
\]

knowledge_points.name: Surface brightness
knowledge_points.description: The flux per unit solid angle from an extended source, expressed in magnitudes per square arcsecond. Needed to understand that the sky contribution scales with aperture area and to compute the total sky flux.

knowledge_points.name: Pogson's law (magnitude-flux relation)
knowledge_points.description: The logarithmic relation m = -2.5 log10(f) + constant, or equivalently f ∝ 10^{-0.4 m}. Used to convert the magnitude difference between star and sky into a flux ratio.

knowledge_points.name: Integrated magnitude from surface brightness
knowledge_points.description: For a uniform extended source with surface brightness μ per unit solid angle, the total magnitude over an area A is m_total = μ - 2.5 log10(A). Applied to find the sky magnitude within the circular aperture.

knowledge_points.name: Atmospheric extinction factor
knowledge_points.description: The Earth's atmosphere reduces the star's flux by 50% (transmission factor 0.5). This factor is applied to the star's flux before computing the photon ratio.

knowledge_points.name: Photon count ratio equals flux ratio
knowledge_points.description: For the same U-band filter, the ratio of detected photon numbers is taken to be equal to the ratio of energy fluxes, allowing the magnitude-derived flux ratio to directly give the photon count ratio R.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the given quantities you have from previous parts: the sky’s surface brightness in mag arcsec⁻², the star’s apparent magnitude above the atmosphere, and the factor by which the atmosphere reduces the star’s flux.

The key is to compare the total flux from the sky inside the aperture with the (atmospherically dimmed) flux from the star, and express this ratio using magnitudes.

**1.  Compute the total sky magnitude inside the aperture**  
The sky is an extended source with a constant surface brightness. For a uniform surface brightness μ (in mag arcsec⁻²), the total flux collected from an area *A* arcsec² is simply the product of the flux per unit solid angle and *A*.  
Because of how the magnitude scale works (see the apparent magnitude exposition in reference.2), adding area is like adding identical patches of light: each doubling of area adds a constant amount of flux, which corresponds to a specific change in magnitude.  
Therefore the total magnitude of the sky within the aperture is  
\[
m_{\text{sky}} = \mu_{\text{sky}} - 2.5 \log_{10} A,
\]  
where the area *A* is that of a circle of diameter 2″ (so radius 1″). Use the given surface brightness and compute *A* (in arcsec²), then find \(m_{\text{sky}}\).

**2.  Account for atmospheric extinction on the star**  
The star’s flux is reduced by the atmosphere. If you know the fraction of light transmitted (e.g., 50 %, meaning a factor of 0.5 in flux), the corresponding increase in the star’s apparent magnitude is  
\[
\Delta m = -2.5 \log_{10}(\text{transmission}).
\]  
Apply this to the star’s original apparent magnitude to obtain the effective magnitude \(m_{\text{star,eff}}\) that would be measured.

**3.  Convert the magnitude difference into a flux ratio**  
Pogson’s law (reference.2) tells us that a difference of 5 magnitudes equals a factor of [final result intentionally omitted] in brightness. Therefore a magnitude difference \(\Delta m\) corresponds to a flux ratio  
\[
\frac{F_2}{F_1} = 10^{0.4\,\Delta m}.
\]  
Here you want the ratio *R* of the star’s (extincted) flux to the sky’s flux in the aperture. Since photon count rates are proportional to flux, *R* is simply  
\[
R = 10^{0.4\,(m_{\text{sky}} - m_{\text{star,eff}})}.
\]  
Use your result from step 1 for \(m_{\text{sky}}\) and the extinction‑corrected star magnitude from step 2.

Carry out the arithmetic with the numbers provided—you will find the magnitude difference and then the ratio *R*, which is the answer.

sub_problems.problem: (T8.3) In practice, only $20\%$ of U-band photons falling on the primary mirror are detected. How many photons, $N_{\mathrm{t}}$ , from the star are detected per second?
sub_problems.solution:
Telescope area: $A_{\mathrm{t}} = \pi(1.0\,\mathrm{m})^2 = \pi\,\mathrm{m}^2$.
Photons incident on mirror per second: $N_0\times A_{\mathrm{t}}$ (since $N_0$ is per $1\mathrm{m}^2$).
After atmospheric extinction ($50\%$) and detection efficiency ($20\%$):
\[
N_{\mathrm{t}} = N_0 \times 0.5 \times 0.2 \times A_{\mathrm{t}} = 12180 \times 0.5 \times 0.2 \times \pi \approx 12180 \times 0.1 \times \pi = 1218\pi \approx \boxed{3813}
\]

knowledge_points.name: photon flux N0 from star
knowledge_points.description: The number of U‑band photons per second per square metre incident at the top of the atmosphere, N0 ≈ 12180, was calculated in part T8.1 and is used directly as the starting flux density.

knowledge_points.name: telescope primary mirror area
knowledge_points.description: The collecting area of the telescope primary mirror is π m² (radius 1.0 m); this value is needed to convert the photon flux per unit area into the total number of photons incident on the mirror.

knowledge_points.name: atmospheric extinction factor
knowledge_points.description: A 50% reduction in photon flux (transmission factor 0.5) in the U‑band due to atmospheric extinction is applied to the flux reaching the ground.

knowledge_points.name: detection efficiency
knowledge_points.description: Only 20% of the U‑band photons falling on the primary mirror are actually detected; this efficiency factor is multiplied with the incident photon rate to obtain the detected count rate.

title: Mars Orbiter Mission
problem:
India's Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) was launched using the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) on 5 November 2013. The dry mass of MOM (body + instruments) was $500\mathrm{kg}$ and it carried fuel of mass $852\mathrm{kg}$ . It was initially placed in an elliptical orbit around the Earth with perigee at a height of $264.1\mathrm{km}$ and apogee at a height of $23903.6\mathrm{km}$ , above the surface of the Earth. After raising the orbit six times, MOM was transferred to a trans-Mars injection orbit (Hohmann orbit).

The first such orbit-raising was performed by firing the engines for a very short time near the perigee. The engines were fired to change the orbit without changing the plane of the orbit and without changing its perigee. This gave a net impulse of $1.73 \times 10^{5} \, \mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ to the satellite. Ignore the change in mass due to burning of fuel.

sub_problems.problem: (T9.1) What is the height of the new apogee, $h_{\mathrm{a}}$ above the surface of the Earth, after this engine burn?
sub_problems.solution:
Let apogee and perigee distances be $r_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $r_{\mathrm{p}}$ respectively.

$$\begin{array}{l} r _ {\mathrm {p}} = R _ {\oplus} + h _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {i} = (6371 + 264) \mathrm {k m} = 6635 \mathrm {k m} \\ r _ {\mathrm {a}} = R _ {\oplus} + h _ {\mathrm {a}} ^ {i} = (6371 + 23904) \mathrm {k m} = 30275 \mathrm {k m} \end{array}$$

Conservation of energy and angular momentum gives

$$E = - \frac {G m M _ {\oplus}}{r _ {\mathrm {p}} + r _ {\mathrm {a}}}$$

Total energy at perigee

$$\frac {1}{2} m v _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {2} - \frac {G m M _ {\oplus}}{r _ {\mathrm {p}}} = E = - \frac {G m M _ {\oplus}}{r _ {\mathrm {p}} + r _ {\mathrm {a}}}$$

$$\frac {1}{2} v _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {2} = \frac {G M _ {\oplus}}{r _ {\mathrm {p}}} \left(1 - \frac {r _ {\mathrm {p}}}{r _ {\mathrm {p}} + r _ {\mathrm {a}}}\right)$$

$$\begin{array}{l} \therefore v _ {\mathrm {p}} = \sqrt {2 \frac {G M _ {\oplus}}{r _ {\mathrm {a}} + r _ {\mathrm {p}}} \frac {r _ {\mathrm {a}}}{r _ {\mathrm {p}}}} \\ = \sqrt {\frac {2 \times 6.674 \times 10 ^ {-11} \times 5.972 \times 10 ^ {24} \times 3.0275 \times 10 ^ {7}}{6.635 \times 10 ^ {6} \times (3.0275 + 6.635 \times 10 ^ {6})}} \\ = 9.929 \mathrm {k m} \mathrm {s} ^ {-1} \end{array}$$

As the engine burn is just $41.6\mathrm{s}$ , we assume that the entire impulse is applied instantaneously at perigee. The impulse is $J = 1.73 \times 10^{5}\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{ms}^{-1}$ . Note that the total mass of MOM must include the fuel, so we have to use

$$m = 500 + 852 = 1352 \mathrm {k g}.$$

Change in velocity due to impulse at perigee is

$$\Delta v = \frac {J}{m} = \frac {1.73 \times 10 ^ {5}}{1352} = 128.0 \mathrm {m s} ^ {-1}$$

The new velocity will be given by (we use ' symbol to denote quantities after the first orbit-raising maneuver)

$$v _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime} = v _ {\mathrm {p}} + \Delta v = 10.06 \mathrm {k m s} ^ {-1}$$

The perigee remains unchanged. So we get $r_{\mathrm{p}}^{\prime} = r_{\mathrm{p}}$

Since the satellite is moving faster, the new apogee will be higher.

$$v _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime} = \sqrt {2 G M _ {\oplus} \frac {r _ {\mathrm {a}} ^ {\prime}}{r _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime} (r _ {\mathrm {a}} ^ {\prime} + r _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime})}}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} \therefore 1 + \frac {r _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime}}{r _ {\mathrm {a}} ^ {\prime}} = \frac {2 G M _ {\oplus}}{(v _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime}) ^ {2} \times r _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime}} \\ = \frac {2 \times 6.674 \times 10 ^ {-11} \times 5.972 \times 10 ^ {24}}{(10.06 \times 10 ^ {3}) ^ {2} \times 6.635 \times 10 ^ {6}} = 1.188 \\ r _ {\mathrm {a}} ^ {\prime} = \frac {6635}{0.188} = 35380 \mathrm {k m} \\ h _ {\mathrm {a}} = 35380 - 6371 \\ = \boxed {29009 \mathrm {k m}} \end{array}$$

knowledge_points.name: Perigee and apogee
knowledge_points.description: The perigee is the point of closest approach to Earth, apogee the farthest point. Their distances from Earth's center (r_p, r_a) are used in the vis-viva equation to describe the initial elliptical orbit and to compute the new apogee.

knowledge_points.name: Altitude to orbital radius
knowledge_points.description: The distance from Earth's center is r = R_earth + h. This conversion is needed because the problem gives perigee and apogee heights above the surface, but orbital equations require radial distances from the center.

knowledge_points.name: Vis-viva equation
knowledge_points.description: For an elliptical orbit, v^2 = GM(2/r - 1/a). It is used to compute the initial velocity at perigee from r_p and r_a, and to find the new apogee distance from the new velocity after the burn.

knowledge_points.name: Semi-major axis of ellipse
knowledge_points.description: The semi-major axis a = (r_p + r_a)/2. This relation is needed to apply the vis-viva equation using the given perigee and apogee distances.

knowledge_points.name: Impulse-momentum theorem
knowledge_points.description: The change in velocity Δv = J/m, where J is the impulse and m is the mass. It is used to calculate the new velocity after the engine burn from the given impulse and spacecraft mass.

knowledge_points.name: Impulsive burn approximation
knowledge_points.description: The engine burn is treated as instantaneous, so the spacecraft's position does not change during the burn. This allows simply adding Δv to the perigee velocity.

knowledge_points.name: Perigee unchanged after tangential burn
knowledge_points.description: A tangential burn at perigee changes only the velocity magnitude, leaving the perigee distance unchanged (r_p' = r_p). This is given in the problem and simplifies finding the new orbit.

knowledge_points.name: Constant mass during burn
knowledge_points.description: The mass of the spacecraft is treated as constant, ignoring the small change due to expelled fuel. This simplifies the Δv calculation by using the initial total mass.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the new apogee height after the engine burn, follow these steps using only the concepts and formulas from your reference passages. You will carry out all numerical substitutions and algebraic steps yourself.

**1. Convert altitudes to orbital radii**  
The apogee and perigee are given as heights above Earth's surface. Use the relation from the exposition on altitude to orbital radius: the distance from Earth’s center is \(R_e + h\). Apply this to the initial perigee and apogee altitudes using the provided value of Earth’s radius \(R_e\).

**2. Find the initial perigee speed**  
The orbit before the burn is an ellipse. As shown in the perigee/apogee worked example (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Sec. 10.5.2), the semi-major axis of an ellipse is \(A = r_p + r_a\). The fastest speed (at perigee) follows from the energy relation they derive:  
\[
v_p^2 = 2GM_e\left( \frac{1}{r_p} - \frac{1}{A} \right).
\]  
Equivalently, you may combine this into the form \(v_p = \sqrt{2GM_e \frac{r_a}{r_p(r_p+r_a)}}\). Use the value of \(GM_e\) for Earth. (If needed, you can obtain \(GM_e = gR_e^2\) from the gravity acceleration exposition, where \(g=9.80\,\text{m/s}^2\).) Carry out this calculation to obtain \(v_p\).

**3. Compute the velocity change from the impulse**  
The engine burn occurs at perigee and is treated as an instantaneous impulse. The impulse-momentum theorem (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Sec. 4.6) states that the impulse \(J = \int F\,dt\) equals the change in momentum: \(\Delta p = J\). For a constant mass \(m\) (including fuel, as the problem indicates), the change in velocity is \(\Delta v = J/m\). Apply this to the given impulse and total mass.

**4. New perigee speed**  
The burn is tangential, so the new perigee velocity is simply \(v_p' = v_p + \Delta v\). The perigee distance remains unchanged because the burn is applied at that point.

**5. Determine the new apogee distance**  
The new orbit is again an ellipse, so the same perigee-speed–geometry relation holds, but now with unknown \(r_a'\):  
\[
v_p'^2 = 2GM_e\frac{r_a'}{r_p(r_a' + r_p)}.
\]  
Solve this equation for \(r_a'\). A convenient rearrangement is  
\[
1 + \frac{r_p}{r_a'} = \frac{2GM_e}{v_p'^2\,r_p},
\]  
from which you can isolate \(r_a'\). Perform the algebra and substitution yourself.

**6. Convert to height above the surface**  
Finally, obtain the new apogee altitude by subtracting Earth’s radius: \(h_a = r_a' - R_e\). This is the requested quantity.

history.llm_reason: The guidance explicitly instructs the student to compute \(v_p\) and later to solve for \(r_a'\), which are key intermediate numeric calculations that the student should perform themselves.

sub_problems.problem: (T9.2) Find the eccentricity $(e)$ of the new orbit after the burn and the new orbital period $(P)$ of MOM in hours.
sub_problems.solution:
As seen above,

$$\frac {r _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime}}{r _ {\mathrm {a}} ^ {\prime}} = 0.188 = \frac {1 - e}{1 + e}$$

$$\therefore e = \frac {1 - 0.188}{1 + 0.188} = \boxed {0.683}$$

The new orbital semi-major axis and orbital period will be,

$$\begin{array}{l} a ^ {\prime} = \frac {r _ {\mathrm {a}} ^ {\prime} + r _ {\mathrm {p}} ^ {\prime}}{2} \\ = \frac {35380 + 6635}{2} = 20933 \mathrm {k m} \end{array}$$

$$\begin{array}{l} P = 2 \pi \sqrt {\frac {a ^ {\prime 3}}{G M _ {\oplus}}} \\ = 2 \pi \sqrt {\frac {(2.0933 \times 10 ^ {7}) ^ {3}}{6.674 \times 10 ^ {-11} \times 5.972 \times 10 ^ {24}}} = \boxed {30136 \mathrm {s} = 8.37 \mathrm {h}} \end{array}$$

knowledge_points.name: Eccentricity-apsides relation
knowledge_points.description: For an elliptical orbit, the ratio of perigee distance (r_p) to apogee distance (r_a) is related to eccentricity e by r_p/r_a = (1-e)/(1+e). Needed to compute e from the apsidal ratio obtained in T9.1.

knowledge_points.name: Semi-major axis of ellipse
knowledge_points.description: The semi-major axis a of an ellipse is the average of the periapsis and apoapsis distances from the focus: a = (r_p + r_a)/2. Used to find a for the new orbit to apply Kepler's third law.

knowledge_points.name: Kepler's third law
knowledge_points.description: The orbital period P is given by P = 2π √(a³/(GM)), where M is the mass of the central body. Applied to Earth to find the period of the new orbit.

knowledge_points.name: Earth's gravitational parameter
knowledge_points.description: The product GM for Earth is a known constant (approx. 3.986×10¹⁴ m³/s², or G = 6.674×10⁻¹¹ m³/kg/s² and M = 5.972×10²⁴ kg). The numerical evaluation of the period requires this value.

knowledge_points.name: New apsidal distances from T9.1
knowledge_points.description: The perigee and apogee distances after the first orbit-raising burn are r_p' = 6635 km and r_a' = 35380 km (or their ratio 0.188) as determined in the previous sub-problem. These numbers are used directly to compute e and a.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the eccentricity and the new orbital period, proceed step by step using the relations you’ve studied.

**1. Eccentricity from the periapsis/apoapsis ratio**  
From the problem’s earlier part you already have the periapsis distance \(r'_p\) and the apoapsis distance \(r'_a\) of the post‑burn orbit.  
In the worked example in the Kleppner & Kolenkow solution manual you find the expressions for periapse and apoapse:  
\(r_{\text{periapse}} = \frac{r_0}{1+\epsilon},\quad r_{\text{apoapse}} = \frac{r_0}{1-\epsilon}\).  
Take the ratio \(r'_p / r'_a\) and use these formulas to eliminate \(r_0\); this gives a relation that contains only the eccentricity \(e\) (the textbook uses \(\epsilon\)). Solve that equation for \(e\).  
*(Equivalently, you may recall that for any ellipse \(r_p/r_a = (1-e)/(1+e)\).)*  
Keep the value of \(e\); you will not need it for the period calculation, but it is part of the answer.

**2. Semi‑major axis of the new orbit**  
The semi‑major axis \(a'\) is simply the average of the two apsidal distances, because the sum of them equals twice the major axis. This is illustrated in the Palen example for Halley’s comet, where  
\(\text{perihelion} + \text{aphelion} = 2a\).  
So compute  
\(a' = (r'_a + r'_p)/2\).

**3. Orbital period via Kepler’s Third Law**  
The Newtonian form of Kepler’s Third Law (given in the Palen exposition) is  

\[
P^{2} = \frac{4\pi^{2} a^{3}}{G(m+M)} .
\]

Because the spacecraft MOM has negligible mass compared to Earth, \(m+M \approx M_{\oplus}\).  
Substitute your \(a'\) and the known values of \(G\) and \(M_{\oplus}\) into  

\[
P = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{a'^{\,3}}{G M_{\oplus}}}\, .
\]

The result will be in seconds. Finally, convert it to hours.

title: Gravitational Lensing Telescope
problem:
Einstein's General Theory of Relativity predicts bending of light around massive bodies. For simplicity, we assume that the bending of light happens at a single point for each light ray, as shown in the figure. The angle of bending, $\theta_{\mathrm{b}}$ , is given by

$$
\theta_ {\mathrm {b}} = \frac {2 R _ {\mathrm {s c h}}}{r}
$$

where $R_{\mathrm{sch}}$ is the Schwarzschild radius associated with that gravitational body. We call $r$ , the distance of the incoming light ray from the parallel $x$ -axis passing through the centre of the body, as the "impact parameter".

A massive body thus behaves somewhat like a focusing lens. The light rays coming from infinite distance beyond a massive body, and having the same impact parameter $r$ , converge at a point along the axis, at a distance $f_{r}$ from the centre of the massive body. An observer at that point will benefit from huge amplification due to this gravitational focusing. The massive body in this case is being used as a Gravitational Lensing Telescope for amplification of distant signals.

sub_problems.problem: (T10.1) Consider the possibility of our Sun as a gravitational lensing telescope. Calculate the shortest distance, $f_{\mathrm{min}}$ , from the centre of the Sun (in A.U.) at which the light rays can get focused.
sub_problems.solution: The rays travelling closest to the Sun (grazing the solar surface) will bend the most and converge at the shortest distance. For a ray with impact parameter $r = R_\odot$, the bending angle is $\theta_\mathrm{b} = 2R_\mathrm{sch}/R_\odot$. From geometry, $\theta_\mathrm{b} \approx R_\odot / f_\min$. Equating: $2R_\mathrm{sch}/R_\odot = R_\odot/f_\min$, so $f_\min = R_\odot^2/(2R_\mathrm{sch})$. Using $R_\mathrm{sch} = 2GM_\odot/c^2$, we get $f_\min = R_\odot^2 c^2/(4GM_\odot)$. Substituting $R_\odot = 6.955\times10^8$ m, $c = 2.998\times10^8$ m/s, $G = 6.674\times10^{-11}$ m$^3$ kg$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $M_\odot = 1.989\times10^{30}$ kg gives $f_\min = 8.188\times10^{13}$ m = $8.188\times10^{13} / 1.496\times10^{11}$ AU = 547.3 AU. Therefore $\boxed{f_\min = 547.3\ \mathrm{AU}}$.

knowledge_points.name: Schwarzschild radius formula
knowledge_points.description: The Schwarzschild radius of a mass M is $R_{\mathrm{sch}} = \frac{2GM}{c^2}$. Used to express the bending angle in terms of the Sun's mass and fundamental constants, and then to eliminate $R_{\mathrm{sch}}$ from the focal length expression.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small bending angles, $\theta_b \approx \tan\theta_b$, allowing the geometry of the deflected ray to be expressed as $\theta_b \approx r / f$, where $r$ is the impact parameter and $f$ is the distance to the focus.

knowledge_points.name: minimum impact parameter equals solar radius
knowledge_points.description: The shortest focal length is achieved for rays that just graze the solar surface, because the impact parameter cannot be smaller than the Sun's radius. Thus $r_{\min} = R_\odot$.

knowledge_points.name: astronomical unit (AU)
knowledge_points.description: The astronomical unit is the mean Earth–Sun distance, 1 AU = 1.496×10¹¹ m. Needed to convert the focal length from metres to the requested unit of AU.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, set up the geometry of the lens using the **small‑angle approximation** from your reference.  
For a ray that arrives parallel to the axis and passes at a distance \(b\) (the impact parameter) from the centre of the Sun, the deflection angle \(\theta\) is very small.  
Under the approximation \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) and \(\tan\theta \approx \theta\) (see the series expansions in Kleppner & Kolenkow, Sec. 1.11.4, or the pendulum derivation in Sec. 7.7.1), the ray will cross the optical axis at a distance  
\[
f \approx \frac{b}{\theta}.
\]  
The *shortest* focal length occurs for the ray that is bent the most. That ray just grazes the solar surface, so its impact parameter is the solar radius \(R_\odot\), and its deflection angle is the maximum possible, \(\theta_{\rm b}\).

Second, express \(\theta_{\rm b}\) in terms of the **Schwarzschild radius**.  
From your black‑hole passage (Palen, Sec. 9.9, and Carroll & Ostlie, Sec. 24.4) you know that the Schwarzschild radius of a mass \(M\) is  
\[
R_{\rm s} = \frac{2GM}{c^2}.
\]  
In gravitational lensing, the bending angle for light that passes at distance \(b\) from the centre of a spherical mass is \(\theta = 4GM/(c^2 b) = 2R_{\rm s}/b\).  
Applying this to the ray that just grazes the Sun (\(b = R_\odot\)) gives \(\theta_{\rm b} = 2R_{\rm s}/R_\odot\).  
Thus the shortest focal distance becomes  
\[
f_{\rm min} = \frac{R_\odot}{\theta_{\rm b}} = \frac{R_\odot^2}{2R_{\rm s}}.
\]

Third, combine the expressions to relate \(f_{\rm min}\) to the fundamental constants.  
Substitute the Schwarzschild radius formula into the result above:  
\[
f_{\rm min} = \frac{R_\odot^2}{2\bigl(2GM_\odot/c^2\bigr)} = \frac{R_\odot^2 c^2}{4GM_\odot}.
\]

Finally, obtain the numerical value and convert it to **astronomical units (AU)**.  
Look up the solar radius, the gravitational constant, the speed of light, and the solar mass. Plug them into the expression for \(f_{\rm min}\) to get the distance in metres.  
To convert to AU, use the relationship given in the stellar‑parallax passage:  
\[
1\ \text{pc} = 2.06264806\times 10^{5}\ \text{AU} = 3.0856776\times 10^{16}\ \text{m},
\]  
which implies \(1\ \text{AU} = 1.496\times 10^{11}\ \text{m}\).  
Divide your metre‑result by the length of an AU to find the focal distance in astronomical units.

sub_problems.problem: (T10.2) Consider a small circular detector of radius $a$ , kept at a distance $f_{\mathrm{min}}$ centered on the $x$ -axis and perpendicular to it. Note that only the light rays which pass within a certain annulus (ring) of width $h$ (where $h \ll R_{\odot}$ ) around the Sun would encounter the detector. The amplification factor at the detector is defined as the ratio of the intensity of the light incident on the detector in the presence of the Sun and the intensity in the absence of the Sun. Express the amplification factor, $A_{\mathrm{m}}$ , at the detector in terms of $R_{\odot}$ and $a$.
sub_problems.solution: The ray grazing the Sun at $r=R_\odot$ focuses at $f_\min$ and hits the detector center. A ray with impact parameter $r=R_\odot+h$ focuses at $f_2 = (R_\odot+h)^2/(2R_\mathrm{sch})$. For small angles, the detector radius $a$ is related to the difference in focal lengths and the bending angle $\theta_2 = 2R_\mathrm{sch}/(R_\odot+h)$: $a = (f_2 - f_\min)\theta_2 = \left[\frac{(R_\odot+h)^2}{2R_\mathrm{sch}} - \frac{R_\odot^2}{2R_\mathrm{sch}}\right]\frac{2R_\mathrm{sch}}{R_\odot+h} = \frac{2R_\odot h + h^2}{R_\odot+h} \approx 2h$ (since $h\ll R_\odot$). Hence $h \approx a/2$. The flux in the presence of the Sun is $\Phi_\odot = I_0 \cdot 2\pi R_\odot h$, where $I_0$ is the original intensity. Without the Sun, the flux on the detector is $\Phi_0 = I_0 \pi a^2$. The amplification is $A_\mathrm{m} = \Phi_\odot/\Phi_0 = (I_0 2\pi R_\odot h)/(I_0 \pi a^2) = 2R_\odot h / a^2 = 2R_\odot (a/2)/a^2 = R_\odot/a$. Therefore $\boxed{A_\mathrm{m} = \frac{R_\odot}{a}}$.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational bending angle formula
knowledge_points.description: The bending angle of a light ray passing a massive body at impact parameter r is θ_b = 2R_sch / r, used directly to compute the angle for the ray at R_sun + h and to relate focal length to r.

knowledge_points.name: focal length formula for gravitational lens
knowledge_points.description: From small‑angle geometry and the bending angle, the focal distance for impact parameter r is f = r / θ_b = r²/(2R_sch). This gives f_min = R_sun²/(2R_sch) and f_2 = (R_sun + h)²/(2R_sch), both required to relate h to the detector radius a.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For very small bending angles, tan θ ≈ θ, allowing the detector radius to be written as a ≈ (f_2 – f_min) θ_2 without trigonometric complexity.

knowledge_points.name: thin annulus (h ≪ R_sun)
knowledge_points.description: The problem states h ≪ R_sun, which is used to drop h² terms and simplify a to 2h, and to approximate the annulus area as 2πR_sun h.

knowledge_points.name: radiative flux (intensity)
knowledge_points.description: Intensity I₀ is power per unit area. The total power collected by a detector of area A is I₀ A. The amplification factor is the ratio of the power on the detector with the lens (collected from an annulus) to that without the lens (collected from the detector area alone).

knowledge_points.name: area of a thin annulus
knowledge_points.description: For a thin annulus of width h around a circle of radius R, the area is approximately 2πR h. This gives the effective collecting area of the Sun’s lens for rays that reach the detector.
