sub_problems.problem: (T10.3) Consider a spherical mass distribution, such as dark matter in a galaxy cluster, through which light rays can pass while undergoing gravitational bending. Assume for simplicity that for the gravitational bending with impact parameter, $r$ , only the mass $M(r)$ enclosed inside the radius $r$ is relevant. What should be the mass distribution, $M(r)$ , such that the gravitational lens behaves like an ideal optical convex lens?
sub_problems.solution: For an ideal convex lens, all rays (with different impact parameters) must focus at the same point. For a ray with impact parameter $r$, the focal distance is $f = r^2/(2R_\mathrm{sch}(r))$, where $R_\mathrm{sch}(r) = 2GM(r)/c^2$. Thus $f = r^2 c^2/(4GM(r))$. For two different impact parameters $r_1$ and $r_2$ to have the same $f$, we require $r_1^2/M(r_1) = r_2^2/M(r_2)$. Hence $M(r) \propto r^2$. Therefore $\boxed{M(r) \propto r^2}$.

knowledge_points.name: Ideal convex lens
knowledge_points.description: An ideal convex lens focuses all incoming parallel rays to a single focal point, independent of their distance from the optical axis. This property defines the behavior that the gravitational lens must mimic.

knowledge_points.name: Schwarzschild radius formula
knowledge_points.description: The Schwarzschild radius of a mass M is R_sch = 2GM/c^2. The solution uses this to express the focal length in terms of the enclosed mass M(r).

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational lens focal length formula
knowledge_points.description: For a gravitational lens, a ray with impact parameter r focuses at a distance f = r^2/(2R_sch(r)) from the lens. This result from earlier parts (T10.1) is used directly to relate f and M(r).

knowledge_points.name: Enclosed mass assumption
knowledge_points.description: For a spherical mass distribution, only the mass M(r) enclosed within radius r contributes to gravitational bending. This assumption, stated in the problem, allows the use of M(r) in the bending formula.

knowledge_points.name: Constant focal length condition
knowledge_points.description: To behave as an ideal lens, the focal length must be the same for all impact parameters. Setting f(r) = constant yields the required mass distribution M(r) ∝ r^2.

title: AstroSat
problem:
India astronomy satellite, AstroSat, launched in September 2015, has five different instruments.

In this question, we will discuss three of these instruments (SXT, LAXPC, CZTI), which point in the same direction and observe in X-ray wavelengths. The details of these instruments are given in the table below.

| Instrument | Band [keV] | Collecting Area [m2] | Effective Photon Detection Efficiency | Saturation level [counts] | No. of Pixels |
|------------|------------|----------------------|---------------------------------------|---------------------------|---------------|
| SXT        | 0.3 – 80   | 0.067                | 60%                                   | 15000 (total)             | 512 x 512     |
| LAXPC      | 3 – 80     | 1.5                  | 40%                                   | 50000 (in any one counter) or 200000 (total) | --- |
| CZTI       | 10 – 150   | 0.09                 | 50%                                   | ---                       | 4 x 4096      |

You should note that LAXPC energy range is divided into 8 different energy band counters of equal bandwidth with no overlap.

These instruments were used to observe an X-ray source (assumed to be a point source), whose energy spectrum followed the power law,

$$F(E) = K E^{-2/3} \quad [\text{in units of counts/keV/m}^2/\text{s}]$$

where $E$ is the energy in keV, $K$ is a constant and $F(E)$ is photon flux density at that energy. Photon flux density, by definition, is given for per unit collecting area (m$^2$) per unit bandwidth (keV) and per unit time (seconds). From prior observations, we know that the source has a flux density of 10 counts/keV/m$^2$ s at 1 keV, when measured by a detector with 100% photon detection efficiency. The "counts" here mean the number of photons reported by the detector.

As the source flux follows the power law given above, we know that for a given energy range from $E_1$ (lower energy) to $E_2$ (higher energy) the total photon flux $(F_{\mathrm{T}})$ will be given by

$$F_{\mathrm{T}} = 3K \left(E_2^{1/3} - E_1^{1/3}\right) \quad [\text{in units of counts/m}^2/\text{s}]$$

sub_problems.problem: (T12.1) Some X-ray sources like Cas A have a prominent emission line at $0.01825\mathrm{nm}$ corresponding to a radioactive transition of $^{44}\mathrm{Ti}$. Suppose there exists a source which emits only one bright emission line corresponding to this transition. What should be the minimum relative velocity $(v)$ of the source, which will make the observed peak of this line to get registered in a different energy band counter of LAXPC as compared to a source at rest?
sub_problems.solution:
The rest wavelength is $\lambda_0 = 0.01825\,\mathrm{nm}$. The energy is $E_0 = hc/\lambda_0$. Using $hc = 1240\,\mathrm{eV\,nm}$, $E_0 = 1240/0.01825 \approx 67945\,\mathrm{eV} \approx 67.945\,\mathrm{keV}$. LAXPC band is 3–80 keV, divided into 8 equal bandwidth counters. Bandwidth per counter = (80-3)/8 = 9.625 keV. The counters are: 3–12.625, 12.625–22.25, 22.25–31.875, 31.875–41.5, 41.5–51.125, 51.125–60.75, 60.75–70.375, 70.375–80 keV. The rest line at 67.945 keV lies in counter 7 (60.75–70.375 keV). To move to a different counter, the observed energy must shift to counter 6 (51.125–60.75 keV) or counter 8 (70.375–80 keV). The minimum shift is to counter 8, requiring observed energy $E_{\text{obs}} \ge 70.375\,\mathrm{keV}$. For a source moving towards the observer, relativistic Doppler: $E_{\text{obs}} = E_0 \sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}}$, where $\beta = v/c$. Setting $E_{\text{obs}} = 70.375\,\mathrm{keV}$ gives $\sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}} = 70.375/67.945 \approx 1.03576$. Squaring: $\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta} = 1.0728$. Solve: $1+\beta = 1.0728(1-\beta) \Rightarrow 1+\beta = 1.0728 - 1.0728\beta \Rightarrow \beta + 1.0728\beta = 1.0728 - 1 \Rightarrow 2.0728\beta = 0.0728 \Rightarrow \beta \approx 0.03512$. Thus $v \approx 0.03512c \approx 1.053\times 10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}$.

\boxed{v \approx 1.05 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}}

knowledge_points.name: Photon energy-wavelength relation
knowledge_points.description: Converts the rest wavelength 0.01825 nm to rest energy ~67.945 keV using E = hc/λ, with hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm, to locate the line within the LAXPC energy counters.

knowledge_points.name: Relativistic Doppler effect for light
knowledge_points.description: Relates observed photon energy to rest energy and radial velocity via E_obs = E_0 √((1+β)/(1-β)) for a source moving directly towards the observer; used to compute the velocity needed to shift the line into the adjacent counter.

knowledge_points.name: Source approaching observer (blueshift)
knowledge_points.description: The solution assumes the source moves towards the observer because the nearest LAXPC counter boundary is at higher energy; a blueshift requires less speed than the redshift to the lower edge, giving the minimum relative velocity.

sub_problems.guidance:
To solve this problem, you first need to find the energy of the emission line when the source is at rest. Use the photon energy–wavelength relation from Eq. (5.5) in Carroll & Ostlie: \( E = hc/\lambda \). The textbook gives a useful form \( E_{\text{photon}} = h\nu = hc/\lambda \), and you can use \( hc = 1240 \, \text{eV} \cdot \text{nm} \) for convenience. Compute the rest energy \( E_0 \) from the given rest wavelength \( \lambda_0 = 0.01825 \, \text{nm} \).  

Next, determine which energy band counter of LAXPC this rest energy falls into. The LAXPC covers 3–80 keV, and you are told it is divided into 8 equal bandwidth counters. Calculate the width of one counter, then list the energy ranges of all 8 counters. Identify which counter contains \( E_0 \).  

The goal is to find the minimum relative velocity that shifts the observed line into a *different* energy band counter. The smallest shift that accomplishes this will be to move the observed energy just across the boundary into an adjacent counter. Determine the threshold observed energy \( E_{\text{obs}} \) required to enter the nearest counter above or below the current one.  

Now relate this energy shift to the source velocity. The problem involves a source moving toward the observer (a blueshift), because that increases the observed energy. For radial motion toward the observer, use the relativistic Doppler formula from Eq. (4.33) in Carroll & Ostlie:  

\[
\nu_{\text{obs}} = \nu_{\text{rest}} \sqrt{\frac{1 - v_r/c}{1 + v_r/c}} .
\]

Since \( \nu \propto E \), this becomes \( E_{\text{obs}} = E_0 \sqrt{\frac{1 + \beta}{1 - \beta}} \) when the source moves toward you (\( v_r = -u \), so \( v_r/c = -\beta \)).  

Solve this equation for \( \beta = v/c \) using your threshold \( E_{\text{obs}} \) and the rest energy \( E_0 \). The algebra involves squaring both sides and isolating \( \beta \). The result gives the minimum relative velocity as a fraction of the speed of light. This approach mirrors the reasoning in the Morin passage, where the longitudinal Doppler effect is derived by combining time dilation and the changing distance light must travel.

sub_problems.problem: (T12.2) Estimate the incident flux density from the source at $1\,\mathrm{keV}$, $5\,\mathrm{keV}$, $40\,\mathrm{keV}$ and $100\,\mathrm{keV}$. Also estimate what will be the total count per unit bandwidth recorded by each of the instruments at these energies for an exposure time of 200 seconds.
sub_problems.solution:
Given $F(E) = K E^{-2/3}$ and $F(1\,\mathrm{keV}) = 10$ counts/keV/m$^2$/s, so $K = 10$. Then $F(1) = 10$, $F(5) = 10 \times 5^{-2/3} = 10 \times 5^{-0.6667} \approx 10 \times 0.342 = 3.42$ counts/keV/m$^2$/s, $F(40) = 10 \times 40^{-2/3} = 10 \times 40^{-0.6667} \approx 10 \times 0.085 = 0.85$ counts/keV/m$^2$/s, $F(100) = 10 \times 100^{-2/3} = 10 \times 100^{-0.6667} = 10 \times 0.0464 = 0.464$ counts/keV/m$^2$/s.

For each instrument, the recorded count per unit bandwidth (counts/keV) for exposure time $t=200$ s is: $C = F(E) \times A \times \epsilon \times t$, where $A$ is collecting area, $\epsilon$ is efficiency.

SXT: $A=0.067\,\mathrm{m}^2$, $\epsilon=0.6$. At 1 keV: $C = 10 \times 0.067 \times 0.6 \times 200 = 80.4$ counts/keV. At 5 keV: $3.42 \times 0.067 \times 0.6 \times 200 \approx 27.5$ counts/keV. At 40 keV: $0.85 \times 0.067 \times 0.6 \times 200 \approx 6.83$ counts/keV. At 100 keV: $0.464 \times 0.067 \times 0.6 \times 200 \approx 3.73$ counts/keV.

LAXPC: $A=1.5\,\mathrm{m}^2$, $\epsilon=0.4$. At 1 keV: not in band (3–80 keV), so 0. At 5 keV: $3.42 \times 1.5 \times 0.4 \times 200 = 410.4$ counts/keV. At 40 keV: $0.85 \times 1.5 \times 0.4 \times 200 = 102$ counts/keV. At 100 keV: not in band, 0.

CZTI: $A=0.09\,\mathrm{m}^2$, $\epsilon=0.5$. At 1 keV: not in band (10–150 keV), 0. At 5 keV: not in band, 0. At 40 keV: $0.85 \times 0.09 \times 0.5 \times 200 = 7.65$ counts/keV. At 100 keV: $0.464 \times 0.09 \times 0.5 \times 200 = 4.176$ counts/keV.

\boxed{F(1)=10,\,F(5)\approx3.42,\,F(40)\approx0.85,\,F(100)\approx0.464\,\text{counts/keV/m}^2/\text{s}} \\ \boxed{\text{SXT: }80.4,\,27.5,\,6.83,\,3.73\,\text{counts/keV}} \\ \boxed{\text{LAXPC: }0,\,410.4,\,102,\,0\,\text{counts/keV}} \\ \boxed{\text{CZTI: }0,\,0,\,7.65,\,4.176\,\text{counts/keV}}

knowledge_points.name: photon flux density
knowledge_points.description: Photon flux density F(E) is the number of photons per unit area, per unit time, per unit energy bandwidth. It is needed to interpret the given source spectrum and to compute the incident flux at the requested energies.

knowledge_points.name: detected count calculation
knowledge_points.description: For a given instrument, the total detected counts per unit energy bandwidth over an exposure time t is the product of the incident photon flux density F(E), the collecting area A, the detection efficiency ε, and the exposure time t: C = F(E) A ε t. This formula is used to compute the recorded counts for each instrument.

knowledge_points.name: instrument energy band limits
knowledge_points.description: Each instrument is sensitive only within a specified energy range. Photons with energies outside this range are not detected, so the recorded count is zero for those energies. This is used to determine when an instrument records zero counts.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, use the concept of **photon flux density** from your textbook (e.g., the intensity expressed as the average number of photons crossing unit area per unit time). In this problem the incident flux density is given differentially in energy: \(F(E) = K E^{-2/3}\) with the normalisation \(F(1\ \text{keV}) = 10\ \text{counts}\ \text{keV}^{-1}\ \text{m}^{-2}\ \text{s}^{-1}\). From these you can find the flux at any energy using the scaling relation  
\[
F(E) = F(1\ \text{keV}) \times \left(\frac{E}{1\ \text{keV}}\right)^{-2/3}.
\]  
Simply substitute each requested energy (1, 5, 40, 100 keV) into this expression to obtain the corresponding incident flux density. (No further physical law is needed; the power‑law index and normalisation are taken directly from the problem.)

Next, to obtain the **total count per unit bandwidth** recorded by each instrument, turn to the detection‑count logic illustrated in the nuclear‑reactions example (Eisberg & Resnick, Section 16‑7). There, the number of detected events per second is the product of the incident particle flux, the effective detection area, and the number of target nuclei per unit area. Here the analogue is:

- The incident flux per unit energy, per unit area, per unit time is \(F(E)\).
- Each instrument has a geometric collecting area \(A\) and an efficiency \(\epsilon\) (so the effective area is \(A\epsilon\)).
- Multiplying \(F(E)\) by \(A\epsilon\) gives the detection rate per unit energy (counts per keV per second).
- Multiplying by the exposure time \(t = 200\ \text{s}\) converts the rate into the total recorded counts per unit bandwidth (counts per keV).

Thus, for a given energy that lies **inside** an instrument’s operating band, the expected count per keV is  
\[
C = F(E) \times A \times \epsilon \times t .
\]  
(The textbook’s event‑rate calculation \(dN = I\,d\sigma\,n\) is the same idea: flux times effective area times number of targets, here the “target” being the detector itself with effective area \(A\epsilon\).)

Before calculating for a particular instrument, check its energy range (given in the instrument specifications). If the energy falls **outside** the band, no photo-events are expected; simply set \(C = 0\) for that energy.

Finally, use the flux densities you obtained in the first step, together with the \(A\), \(\epsilon\), and band limits for SXT, LAXPC, and CZTI, to compute the recorded counts per keV at each of the four energies. Carry out all numerical evaluations yourself—the recipe above tells you what to multiply and in what order.

sub_problems.problem: (T12.3) For this source, calculate the maximum exposure time $(t_{\mathrm{S}})$, without suffering from saturation, for the CCD of SXT.
sub_problems.solution:
SXT saturation level is 15000 counts total. The total count rate for SXT over its full band (0.3–80 keV) is: $R = \int_{0.3}^{80} F(E) \, A \, \epsilon \, dE = A \epsilon \int_{0.3}^{80} K E^{-2/3} dE = A \epsilon \cdot 3K (80^{1/3} - 0.3^{1/3})$. $80^{1/3} \approx 4.3089$, $0.3^{1/3} \approx 0.6694$, difference $\approx 3.6395$. $K=10$, $A=0.067$, $\epsilon=0.6$. So $R = 0.067 \times 0.6 \times 3 \times 10 \times 3.6395 \approx 0.067 \times 0.6 \times 109.185 \approx 0.067 \times 65.511 \approx 4.389$ counts/s. Maximum exposure $t_S = 15000 / 4.389 \approx 3417$ s.

\boxed{t_{\mathrm{S}} \approx 3.42 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{s}}

knowledge_points.name: Detector saturation
knowledge_points.description: A detector has a maximum number of counts it can record before saturating; the maximum exposure time is obtained by dividing this saturation count by the total count rate.

knowledge_points.name: Count rate from total flux
knowledge_points.description: The detected count rate R is the product of the total photon flux F_T (counts/m²/s), the effective collecting area A (m²), and the photon detection efficiency ε: R = F_T · A · ε.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the concept of detector saturation from the photoelectric effect described in the textbook (the saturation current in Figure 2-2 is the limiting value where all photoelectrons are collected, and it is directly proportional to light intensity). In our CCD, this translates to a maximum total number of counts the detector can accumulate before saturating — a fixed number \(N_{\text{sat}}\) (you should identify this value from the problem’s instrument information). The exposure time \(t_S\) that avoids saturation is then simply the saturation count divided by the total count rate \(R\):

\[
t_S = \frac{N_{\text{sat}}}{R}.
\]

Your first step is to find the total count rate \(R\) for the SXT over its full energy band (0.3–80 keV).

The count rate is the number of photons detected per unit time. The incident photon flux is given as a spectrum \(F(E) = K E^{-2/3}\) (with \(K=10\)) — this is a photon number flux per unit area per unit time per unit energy. The textbook’s discussion of the wave–particle duality tells us that intensity can be written as \(I = Nh\nu\), where \(N\) is the average number of photons crossing unit area per unit time; so \(F(E)\) appropriately describes a photon number flux. To obtain the total photon number flux \(\Phi\) arriving at the detector (photons per unit area per unit time), integrate the spectrum over the energy band:

\[
\Phi = \int_{0.3}^{80} F(E) \, dE .
\]

You can carry out this integral using the rule \(\int E^{-2/3} dE = 3 E^{1/3}\).

To convert the incident flux into a count rate, use the multiplicative logic seen in the nuclear reaction rate passage. There, reaction rate equals incident particle flux times cross‑sectional area (and times target number). For our detector, the analogous “cross‑section” is the product of the effective collecting area \(A\) (in cm²) and the detection efficiency \(\epsilon\) (the fraction of photons that actually give a count). Therefore the count rate is

\[
R = A \,\epsilon \,\Phi = A \,\epsilon \int_{0.3}^{80} F(E) \, dE .
\]

Insert the given values for \(A\) and \(\epsilon\) along with your integrated result to obtain \(R\) (in counts per second). Watch units: the flux integral yields photons cm⁻² s⁻¹, so multiplying by area (cm²) gives photons s⁻¹.

Finally, combine this count rate with the saturation limit using \(t_S = N_{\text{sat}} / R\) to find the maximum exposure time in seconds. All numerical steps — the integral, the multiplications, and the final division — are left for you to perform.

sub_problems.problem: (T12.4) If the source became 3500 times brighter, calculate the expected counts per second in LAXPC counter 1, counter 8 as well as total counts across the entire energy range. If we observe for longer period, will the counter saturate due to any individual counter or due to the total count? Tick the appropriate box in the Summary Answersheet.
sub_problems.solution:
The source becomes 3500 times brighter, so $K' = 3500 \times 10 = 35000$. LAXPC band 3–80 keV, 8 counters each of width 9.625 keV. Counter 1: 3–12.625 keV, counter 8: 70.375–80 keV. Count rate per counter: $R_i = A \epsilon \int_{E_{1,i}}^{E_{2,i}} K' E^{-2/3} dE = A \epsilon \cdot 3K' (E_{2,i}^{1/3} - E_{1,i}^{1/3})$. $A=1.5$, $\epsilon=0.4$, $3K'=105000$.

Counter 1: $E_{1}=3$, $E_{2}=12.625$. $3^{1/3}\approx1.442$, $12.625^{1/3}\approx2.329$, difference $\approx0.887$. $R_1 = 1.5 \times 0.4 \times 105000 \times 0.887 \approx 0.6 \times 105000 \times 0.887 = 63000 \times 0.887 \approx 55881$ counts/s.

Counter 8: $E_{1}=70.375$, $E_{2}=80$. $70.375^{1/3}\approx4.128$, $80^{1/3}\approx4.309$, difference $\approx0.181$. $R_8 = 0.6 \times 105000 \times 0.181 = 63000 \times 0.181 \approx 11403$ counts/s.

Total count rate over entire band: $R_{\text{total}} = A \epsilon \cdot 3K' (80^{1/3} - 3^{1/3}) = 0.6 \times 105000 \times (4.309 - 1.442) = 63000 \times 2.867 \approx 180621$ counts/s.

Saturation limits: per counter 50000 counts, total 200000 counts. For 1 second, counter 1 already exceeds 50000, so it saturates immediately. Thus saturation is due to an individual counter.

\boxed{R_1 \approx 5.59 \times 10^4\,\text{counts/s},\, R_8 \approx 1.14 \times 10^4\,\text{counts/s},\, R_{\text{total}} \approx 1.81 \times 10^5\,\text{counts/s}} \\ \boxed{\text{Saturation due to individual counter}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{R_1 \approx 5.59 \times 10^4\,\text{counts/s},\, R_8 \approx 1.14 \times 10^4\,\text{counts/s},\, R_{\text{total}} \approx 1.81 \times 10^5\,\text{counts/s}} \\ \boxed{\text{Saturation due to individual counter}}

knowledge_points.name: source brightness scaling factor
knowledge_points.description: If the source becomes 3500 times brighter, the flux density constant K scales by the same factor, so K' = 3500 × 10 = 35000 counts/keV/m²/s.

knowledge_points.name: X-ray source spectral normalization
knowledge_points.description: The source has a flux density of 10 counts/keV/m²/s at 1 keV for a 100% efficient detector, fixing K=10 for the power law F(E)=K E^{-2/3}.

knowledge_points.name: detector count rate from photon flux
knowledge_points.description: The count rate (counts/s) in a detector is the product of collecting area, photon detection efficiency, and the energy-integrated photon flux: R = A × ε × ∫ F(E) dE.

knowledge_points.name: integrated power-law flux formula
knowledge_points.description: For the given spectrum F(E)=K E^{-2/3}, the total photon flux over an energy band [E1, E2] is F_T = 3K (E2^{1/3} - E1^{1/3}) counts/m²/s.

knowledge_points.name: equal bandwidth LAXPC energy channels
knowledge_points.description: LAXPC's 3–80 keV range is divided into 8 equal‑width counters (ΔE = 9.625 keV); counter 1 covers 3–12.625 keV, counter 8 covers 70.375–80 keV.

knowledge_points.name: LAXPC saturation limits
knowledge_points.description: Saturation occurs if any individual counter exceeds 50000 counts or the total LAXPC count exceeds 200000 counts.

sub_problems.guidance:
First identify how the brightness increase changes the source normalization.  
The problem states the source became 3500 times brighter; from earlier work (or the original problem setup) the original normalization constant was \(K = 10\). Therefore the new normalization is \(K' = 3500 \times 10\). You will use this value in every count‑rate calculation.

Next recall the photon number spectrum of the source. The integrated power‑law flux method from reference (reference.2) shows that the energy received in a frequency/energy interval is obtained by integrating the flux over that interval. For this AGN source the photon number per unit energy follows a power law \(N(E) \propto E^{-\Gamma}\) with spectral index \(\Gamma = 2/3\) (as used in this problem set). The count rate in an energy band \([E_1, E_2]\) is therefore proportional to  
\[
\int_{E_1}^{E_2} E^{-2/3}\,dE \;=\; 3\,(E_2^{1/3} - E_1^{1/3}) .
\]  
You will combine this integral with the effective area \(A = 1.5\) cm², efficiency \(\epsilon = 0.4\), and the source normalization \(K'\).

Now determine the energy bands. LAXPC has 8 counters each of width \(9.625\) keV covering 3–80 keV.  
- Counter 1 covers the lowest energies: \(E_1 = 3\) keV, \(E_2 = 12.625\) keV.  
- Counter 8 covers the highest energies: \(E_1 = 70.375\) keV, \(E_2 = 80\) keV.  
- The total band is simply 3–80 keV.

**For Counter 1:**  
Compute the rates using  
\[
R_1 = A\,\epsilon\,K' \times \bigl[ 3\,(E_2^{1/3} - E_1^{1/3}) \bigr]_{\text{for counter 1}} .
\]  
Evaluate the cube roots, find the difference, multiply by \(3K'\) and then by \(A\epsilon\) (which is \(0.6\)). Leave all numerical evaluation for yourself; just follow the order: cube roots → subtraction → multiplication by \(3K'\) → multiplication by \(0.6\).

**For Counter 8:**  
Use the same expression with \(E_1 = 70.375\) keV and \(E_2 = 80\) keV.  
\[
R_8 = 0.6 \times (3K') \times (80^{1/3} - 70.375^{1/3}) .
\]

**Total count rate:**  
Integrate over the full band 3–80 keV:  
\[
R_{\text{total}} = 0.6 \times (3K') \times (80^{1/3} - 3^{1/3}) .
\]

Once you obtain the three count rates (in counts per second), compare them with the instrumental saturation limits:
- Per individual counter: \(5 \times 10^4\) counts/s
- Total over all counters: \(2 \times 10^5\) counts/s

If any single counter’s rate already exceeds the per‑counter limit, then that counter saturates immediately during the observation; the saturation is due to an **individual counter**. If all individual rates are below \(5 \times 10^4\) counts/s but the sum exceeds \(2 \times 10^5\) counts/s, saturation is due to the **total count**. Tick the appropriate box on your answer sheet according to your computed rates.

sub_problems.problem: (T12.5) Assume that the counts reported by CZTI due to random fluctuations in electronics are about 0.00014 counts per pixel per keV per second at all energy levels. Any source is considered as "detected" when the SNR (signal to noise ratio) is at least 3. What is minimum exposure time, $t_c$, needed for the source above to be detected in CZTI? Note that the "noise" in a detector is equal to the square root of the counts due to random fluctuations.
sub_problems.solution:
CZTI has 4 x 4096 = 16384 pixels. Noise rate per pixel per keV: $r_n = 0.00014$ counts/pixel/keV/s. Total noise rate over all pixels and over the CZTI band (10–150 keV) is: $R_n = r_n \times N_{\text{pixels}} \times \Delta E = 0.00014 \times 16384 \times 140 \approx 0.00014 \times 2293760 \approx 321.1264$ counts/s. Noise counts in time $t$: $N_n = R_n t$. Noise (standard deviation) $\sigma = \sqrt{N_n} = \sqrt{R_n t}$.

Signal count rate from source: $R_s = A \epsilon \int_{10}^{150} K E^{-2/3} dE = A \epsilon \cdot 3K (150^{1/3} - 10^{1/3})$. $A=0.09$, $\epsilon=0.5$, $K=10$. $150^{1/3}\approx5.313$, $10^{1/3}\approx2.154$, difference $\approx3.159$. $R_s = 0.09 \times 0.5 \times 3 \times 10 \times 3.159 = 0.045 \times 30 \times 3.159 = 1.35 \times 3.159 \approx 4.265$ counts/s. Signal counts in time $t$: $N_s = R_s t$.

SNR = $N_s / \sigma = R_s t / \sqrt{R_n t} = R_s \sqrt{t} / \sqrt{R_n} \ge 3$. So $\sqrt{t} \ge 3 \sqrt{R_n} / R_s$. $\sqrt{R_n} \approx \sqrt{321.1264} \approx 17.92$. $R_s \approx 4.265$. Then $\sqrt{t} \ge 3 \times 17.92 / 4.265 \approx 53.76 / 4.265 \approx 12.60$. Thus $t \ge (12.60)^2 \approx 158.8$ s.

\boxed{t_c \approx 159\,\mathrm{s}}

knowledge_points.name: Signal-to-noise ratio
knowledge_points.description: The signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is defined as the ratio of the mean signal counts to the standard deviation of the noise (here the square root of the background counts). The solution uses this definition to set up the detection condition.

knowledge_points.name: Poisson noise (shot noise)
knowledge_points.description: For random counting events such as detector noise fluctuations, the noise (standard deviation) equals the square root of the mean number of counts. This is used to relate the noise counts to the noise rate and exposure time.

knowledge_points.name: Detector count rate equation
knowledge_points.description: The count rate measured by an instrument equals the product of its effective collecting area, its photon detection efficiency, and the incident photon flux. The solution applies this to convert the source photon flux into a signal count rate in CZTI.

knowledge_points.name: Detection criterion
knowledge_points.description: A source is considered detected if the signal-to-noise ratio meets or exceeds a prescribed minimum threshold (here SNR >= 3). This sets the inequality that determines the minimum exposure time.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Total noise count rate.**  
   The problem gives a per-pixel, per-keV, per-second random‑fluctuation rate.  
   - Identify the total number of CZTI pixels (4 × 4096) and the energy bandwidth (10–150 keV, so ΔE = 140 keV).  
   - Multiply these three quantities to obtain the average total noise rate \(R_n\) (counts/s).  
   This step simply uses the fact that independent random events add linearly in rate.

2. **Signal count rate from the source.**  
   - Use the counting‑rate idea from the nuclear‑reaction example (Eisberg & Resnick, §16‑7): detected events per second are proportional to the effective area (here given by \(A\) and efficiency \(\epsilon\)) times the incident photon flux.  
   - The source spectrum is \(K E^{-2/3}\) from 10 to 150 keV. The flux (photons per second) is the integral \(\int E^{-2/3} dE\) times the constants \(K\), \(A\), and \(\epsilon\). Integrate analytically to obtain \(R_s\) (counts/s).  
   You are essentially applying the cross‑section / probability approach:  
   \[
   \text{rate} = (\text{effective area}) \times (\text{photon flux}).
   \]

3. **Signal and noise counts in time \(t\).**  
   - Signal counts: \(N_s = R_s t\).  
   - Noise counts (average): \(N_n = R_n t\).  
   - According to the Poisson (shot‑noise) behaviour described in Purcell & Morin, the standard deviation of the noise counts equals \(\sqrt{N_n}\) (the square root of the mean). Therefore the “noise” for SNR purposes is \(\sigma = \sqrt{R_n t}\).

4. **Set up the SNR condition.**  
   - The signal‑to‑noise ratio is  
     \[
     \mathrm{SNR} = \frac{N_s}{\sigma} = \frac{R_s t}{\sqrt{R_n t}} = \frac{R_s \sqrt{t}}{\sqrt{R_n}}.
     \]
   - The detection criterion is \(\mathrm{SNR} \ge 3\).  
   - Solve the inequality for \(\sqrt{t}\), then square to get the minimum exposure time \(t_c\).  

5. **What you will obtain.**  
   Carry out the integration, the multiplications, and the square‑root algebra yourself. The result gives the minimum time in seconds. The approach exactly parallels the event‑rate calculation in the Eisberg & Resnick example and the noise scaling of the Purcell & Morin shot‑noise discussion.

sub_problems.problem: (T12.6) Let us consider the situation where the source shows variability in number flux, so that the factor $K$ increases by $20\%$. AstroSat observed this source for 1 second before the change and 1 second after this change in brightness. Calculate the counts measured by SXT, LAXPC and CZTI in both the observations. Which instrument is best suited to detect this change? Tick the appropriate box in the Summary Answersheet.
sub_problems.solution:
Before change: $K=10$. After change: $K' = 12$. Counts in 1 second for each instrument:

SXT: $C = A \epsilon \int_{0.3}^{80} K E^{-2/3} dE = A \epsilon \cdot 3K (80^{1/3} - 0.3^{1/3})$. $A=0.067$, $\epsilon=0.6$, $3(80^{1/3}-0.3^{1/3}) \approx 3 \times 3.6395 = 10.9185$. Before: $C_{\text{SXT,before}} = 0.067 \times 0.6 \times 10 \times 10.9185 \approx 0.0402 \times 109.185 \approx 4.389$ counts. After: $C_{\text{SXT,after}} = 4.389 \times 1.2 = 5.267$ counts.

LAXPC: $C = A \epsilon \int_{3}^{80} K E^{-2/3} dE = A \epsilon \cdot 3K (80^{1/3} - 3^{1/3})$. $A=1.5$, $\epsilon=0.4$, $3(80^{1/3}-3^{1/3}) \approx 3 \times 2.867 = 8.601$. Before: $C_{\text{LAXPC,before}} = 1.5 \times 0.4 \times 10 \times 8.601 = 0.6 \times 86.01 = 51.606$ counts. After: $C_{\text{LAXPC,after}} = 51.606 \times 1.2 = 61.927$ counts.

CZTI: $C = A \epsilon \int_{10}^{150} K E^{-2/3} dE = A \epsilon \cdot 3K (150^{1/3} - 10^{1/3})$. $A=0.09$, $\epsilon=0.5$, $3(150^{1/3}-10^{1/3}) \approx 3 \times 3.159 = 9.477$. Before: $C_{\text{CZTI,before}} = 0.09 \times 0.5 \times 10 \times 9.477 = 0.045 \times 94.77 = 4.265$ counts. After: $C_{\text{CZTI,after}} = 4.265 \times 1.2 = 5.118$ counts.

To detect the change, we need the fractional change relative to noise. The noise for each instrument in 1 second: SXT: $\sqrt{C_{\text{before}}} \approx \sqrt{4.389} \approx 2.095$, fractional change $\Delta C / \sigma = (5.267-4.389)/2.095 \approx 0.878/2.095 \approx 0.419$. LAXPC: $\sqrt{51.606} \approx 7.184$, $\Delta C/\sigma = (61.927-51.606)/7.184 \approx 10.321/7.184 \approx 1.436$. CZTI: $\sqrt{4.265} \approx 2.065$, $\Delta C/\sigma = (5.118-4.265)/2.065 \approx 0.853/2.065 \approx 0.413$. LAXPC has the highest significance, so it is best suited.

\boxed{\text{SXT: }4.39,\,5.27\,\text{counts}} \\ \boxed{\text{LAXPC: }51.6,\,61.9\,\text{counts}} \\ \boxed{\text{CZTI: }4.27,\,5.12\,\text{counts}} \\ \boxed{\text{Best: LAXPC}}

knowledge_points.name: Photon count rate equation
knowledge_points.description: The total detected counts equals the product of collecting area, effective photon detection efficiency, exposure time, and the integral of the incident photon flux density over the energy band. Used to compute the counts for SXT, LAXPC, and CZTI before and after the change.

knowledge_points.name: Poisson noise
knowledge_points.description: For a Poisson-distributed count, the standard deviation (noise) is the square root of the expected count. Used to estimate the noise σ = √C_before for each instrument.

knowledge_points.name: Signal-to-noise ratio for variability detection
knowledge_points.description: The detectability of a change in signal is assessed by the ratio of the change ΔC to the noise σ. The instrument with the highest SNR is best suited to detect the change.

knowledge_points.name: Poisson-limited noise
knowledge_points.description: The solution assumes that background and instrumental noise are negligible, so the only noise is the Poisson fluctuation of the source counts themselves.

sub_problems.guidance:
The core idea comes from the cross‑section concept in the passage: the number of detected interactions is proportional to the incident photon number \(I\) and the number of target atoms (or effective area) times an efficiency factor. For your instruments, that means the counts \(C\) you measure in a time \(\Delta t\) depend on the instrument’s effective area \(A\), its quantum efficiency \(\epsilon\), and the total photon number flux that reaches the detector within its energy band.

1. **Source flux and its change**  
   The source has a photon number flux per unit energy of the form \(K E^{-2/3}\). You are told that \(K\) increases by 20%: initially \(K=10\), afterwards \(K' = 12\). The observation time is \(\Delta t = 1\ \text{s}\) for both the “before” and “after” measurements.

2. **Counts from the flux integral**  
   For each instrument, the counts in \(1\ \text{s}\) are given by  
   \[
   C = A\,\epsilon \int_{E_{\min}}^{E_{\max}} K E^{-2/3}\,dE .
   \]  
   Use the elementary integral \(\int E^{-2/3}dE = 3E^{1/3}\) to evaluate the definite integral. This produces a numerical factor  
   \[
   I_{\text{band}} = 3\bigl(E_{\max}^{1/3} - E_{\min}^{1/3}\bigr),
   \]  
   which is different for each instrument because the energy limits differ. Now multiply: \(C = A\,\epsilon\,K\,I_{\text{band}}\).

3. **Calculating the two observations**  
   *Before change:* set \(K=10\) and compute \(C_{\text{before}}\) for SXT, LAXPC, and CZTI using their own \(A\), \(\epsilon\), and energy limits.  
   *After change:* because only \(K\) changes, the after‑counts are simply \(C_{\text{after}} = 1.2\,C_{\text{before}}\). (The factor 1.2 comes from \(12/10\).)

Leave the number crunching to yourself – plug in the values from the instrument table, compute each integral factor, and get the counts.

4. **Which instrument best detects the change?**  
   A useful measure is the statistical significance of the change. In photon counting, the uncertainty in a measured number \(C\) is approximately \(\sqrt{C}\) (Poisson counting statistics). Therefore, the signal (the change in counts) relative to the noise (the uncertainty on the before count) is:
   \[
   \frac{\Delta C}{\sigma} = \frac{C_{\text{after}} - C_{\text{before}}}{\sqrt{C_{\text{before}}}}.
   \]  
   Compute this ratio for each of the three instruments. The instrument that yields the largest ratio gives the most reliable detection of the brightness change.

After you have performed the integrals and the comparisons, you will be able to fill in the count tables and tick the box in the Summary Answersheet for the instrument with the highest significance.

title: The Large Magellanic Cloud in Phuket
problem: The coordinates of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) are R.A. = 5h 24min and Dec = -70°00'. The latitude and longitude of Phuket are $7^{\circ}53'$ N and $98^{\circ}24'$ E, respectively. What is the date when the LMC culminates at 9pm as seen from Phuket in the same year? You may note that the Greenwich Sidereal Time, GST, at 00h UT $1^{\text{st}}$ January is about 6h 43min, and Phuket is in the UT+7 time zone.
solution: When the LMC culminates, its Local Hour Angle (LHA) is 0, so the Local Sidereal Time (LST) equals the Right Ascension (RA) of the LMC: LST = RA = 5h 24min.  The LST is related to Greenwich Sidereal Time (GST) and the longitude L of Phuket (east longitude positive) by LST = GST + L (in time units).  Phuket's longitude is 98°24' E, which in hours is 98°24' / 15° per hour = 6h 33.6min ≈ 6h 34min.  Thus GST = LST - L = 5h 24min - 6h 34min = -1h 10min.  Adding 24h gives GST = 22h 50min.  Phuket time 9pm (21:00) is UT+7, so UT = 21:00 - 7h = 14:00.  The GST at a given UT and day of year is: GST = GST_0 + (days since Jan 1) × (24h / 365.2422 days) + UT × (24h / 23.9344h).  Here GST_0 = 6h 43min.  So 22h 50min = 6h 43min + (days × 24h / 365.2422) + (14h × 24h / 23.9344h).  Compute the UT term: 14h × (24/23.9344) ≈ 14h × 1.0027379 ≈ 14h 2.3min ≈ 14h 2min.  Then days × (24h / 365.2422) = 22h 50min - 6h 43min - 14h 2min = 22h 50min - 20h 45min = 2h 5min.  Convert to days: days = (2h 5min) × (365.2422 days / 24h) = (2.08333 h) × (365.2422 / 24) ≈ 2.08333 × 15.2184 ≈ 31.7 days.  So the date is about 31.7 days after January 1, which is February 1 or 2.  Since the calculation is approximate, the answer is February 2.  \boxed{\text{February 2}}

knowledge_points.name: Culmination (transit)
knowledge_points.description: When a celestial object culminates, its Local Hour Angle is zero, so the Local Sidereal Time (LST) equals the object's Right Ascension (RA). Used here to set LST = 5h 24min for the LMC.

knowledge_points.description: Local Sidereal Time (LST) = Greenwich Sidereal Time (GST) + observer's east longitude (in time units). Essential to relate LMC's culmination LST to the given GST reference.

title: The Milky Way's Distant Outer Arm
problem: In 2011, Dame and Thaddeus found a new part of the outer arm of the Milky Way by studying the CO line using the CfA $1.2\mathrm{m}$ telescope. They found that the CO line was detected at galactic longitude $\ell = 13.25^{\circ}$ (marked A in the figure) where it had a radial velocity of $20.9\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$ towards the Sun. Assume that the galactic rotation curve is flat beyond $5\mathrm{kpc}$ from the Galactic centre. The distance between the Sun and the Galactic centre is $8.5\mathrm{kpc}$ . The velocity of the Sun around the Galactic centre is $220\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$ .

sub_problems.problem: (a) Find the distance from the start of the arm (point $\mathbf{A}$ ) to the Galactic centre.
sub_problems.solution:
For a flat rotation curve, the orbital velocity of the Sun and the start of the arm are both $v_{\mathrm{LSR}} = 220\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.  Using the sine law in triangle AGS: $\frac{\sin(\ell)}{d} = \frac{\sin(\alpha)}{R_0}$.  The radial velocity is $v_r = -v_{\mathrm{LSR}}\sin(\ell) + v_{\mathrm{LSR}}\sin(\alpha) = -v_{\mathrm{LSR}}\sin(\ell) + v_{\mathrm{LSR}} R_0 \frac{\sin(\ell)}{d}$.  Substituting $v_r = 20.9\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, $\ell = 13.25^\circ$, $R_0 = 8.5\,\mathrm{kpc}$: $20.9 = 220\sin(13.25^\circ) - 220 \cdot 8.5 \frac{\sin(13.25^\circ)}{d}$.  Solving gives $d = 14.5\,\mathrm{kpc}$.

\boxed{d = 14.5\,\mathrm{kpc}}

knowledge_points.name: flat rotation curve
knowledge_points.description: The Galactic rotation curve is flat beyond 5 kpc, so orbital speed is constant (220 km/s) for both the Sun and the outer arm; this allows setting equal tangential speeds in the radial velocity formula.

knowledge_points.name: circular orbits
knowledge_points.description: Both the Sun and the arm follow circular orbits around the Galactic centre, so their velocity vectors are purely tangential and the geometry of radial velocity projection uses sine of angles.

knowledge_points.name: galactic longitude
knowledge_points.description: Galactic longitude l is the angle measured at the Sun in the Galactic plane between the line to the Galactic centre and the line to the object; needed to define the triangle AGS and to use l=13.25° in the sine law.

knowledge_points.name: radial velocity formula for flat rotation
knowledge_points.description: For a flat Galactic rotation curve, the relative radial velocity of an object at longitude l and distance d is v_r = v_circ (R0 sin l / d - sin l); this equation links the observed radial velocity to the unknown distance.

knowledge_points.name: sine law in triangle
knowledge_points.description: Applying the law of sines to triangle AGS (Arm–Galactic centre–Sun) relates the distance d to the baseline R0 and angles l and alpha, enabling elimination of the unknown angle.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Find the distance from the start of the arm (point $\mathbf{A}$ ) to the Sun.
sub_problems.solution:
Using the cosine law in triangle AGS: $d^2 = x^2 + R_0^2 - 2 x R_0 \cos(\ell)$.  Substitute $d = 14.5\,\mathrm{kpc}$, $R_0 = 8.5\,\mathrm{kpc}$, $\ell = 13.25^\circ$: $14.5^2 = x^2 + 8.5^2 - 2 \cdot 8.5 x \cos(13.25^\circ)$.  Solve the quadratic: $x = \frac{17\cos(13.25^\circ) + \sqrt{17^2\cos^2(13.25^\circ) - 4(8.5^2 - 14.5^2)}}{2} = 22.6\,\mathrm{kpc}$.

\boxed{x = 22.6\,\mathrm{kpc}}

knowledge_points.name: Galactic longitude geometry
knowledge_points.description: Galactic longitude l = 13.25° is the angle at the Sun between the direction to the Galactic centre and the line-of-sight to point A, defining the included angle in the law of cosines triangle.

knowledge_points.name: Law of cosines
knowledge_points.description: A planar triangle relation used to solve for the unknown side x (distance from Sun to A) when the other two sides (R0, d) and the included angle (l) are known.

knowledge_points.name: Galactic plane approximation
knowledge_points.description: The Sun, the Galactic centre, and point A lie sufficiently close to the Galactic plane that the triangle geometry is Euclidean and the given longitude accurately represents the planar angle.

knowledge_points.name: Known distance from A to Galactic centre
knowledge_points.description: The distance d = 14.5 kpc from point A to the Galactic centre was derived in sub-problem (a) and is taken as a given side for this sub-problem's geometry.

sub_problems.guidance:
You know three quantities that form a triangle with vertices at the Sun, the Galactic centre, and the start of the arm (point A).  
- The Sun–Galactic centre distance \(R_0\) is a standard value from Galactic structure (given in your earlier work).  
- The Galactic centre–point A distance (let’s call it \(d\)) should already be known from a previous part of the problem.  
- The direction to point A is specified by its Galactic longitude \(\ell\); according to Fig. 24.17, this is the angle at the Sun measured from the direction toward the Galactic centre.

Your target is the distance from the Sun to point A. This is the third side of the triangle, and it lies opposite the angle at the Sun? No – look at the triangle: the side opposite the Sun is the Galactic centre–point A side. That side appears in the law of cosines with the angle at the Sun.

Take the triangle with sides:  
 \(S\) (Sun) to \(G\) (Galactic centre) = \(R_0\),  
 \(S\) to \(A\) = unknown, call it \(x\),  
 \(G\) to \(A\) = known \(d\).  
The angle at the Sun between the line to the Galactic centre and the line to point A is exactly the Galactic longitude \(\ell\) (see the definition in the galactic coordinate system passage and Fig. 24.17).

Now use the **law of cosines** exactly as presented in the textbook ( \(C^2 = A^2 + B^2 - 2AB\cos\phi\) ) from the vector-dot‑product derivation. Apply it to the side \(GA\) (our \(d\)), which is opposite the angle at the Sun. This gives an equation that relates \(d\), \(R_0\), \(x\), and \(\cos\ell\):

\[
\text{(GA)}^2 = \text{(SA)}^2 + \text{(SG)}^2 - 2\,(\text{SA})(\text{SG})\cos\ell .
\]

In that equation, only the Sun–A distance \(x\) is unknown. Substitute the known numbers for \(d\), \(R_0\), and \(\ell\). You will obtain a quadratic equation in \(x\). Solve it with the quadratic formula; of the two roots, choose the one that is positive and physically meaningful for the distance to the arm.  

Be careful with the order: the cosine term subtracts, and the known side \(d\) sits on the left-hand side. After bringing all terms to one side, the standard form \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\) will emerge, and you can solve for \(x\).

title: 21-cm HI galaxy survey
problem:
A radio telescope is equipped with a receiver which can observe in a frequency range from 1.32 to $1.52\mathrm{GHz}$ . Its detection limit is $0.5\mathrm{mJy}$ per beam for a 1-minute integration time. In a galaxy survey, the luminosity of the HI spectral line of a typical target galaxy is $10^{28}\mathrm{W}$ with a linewidth of $1\mathrm{MHz}$ . For a large beam, the HI emitting region from a far-away galaxy can be approximated as a point source. The HI spin-flip spectral line has a rest-frame frequency of $1.42\mathrm{GHz}$ .

What is the highest redshift, $z$ , of a typical HI galaxy that can be detected by a survey carried out with this radio telescope, using 1-minute integration time? You may assume in your calculation that the redshift is small and the non-relativistic approximation can be used. Note that $1\mathrm{Jy} = 10^{-26}\mathrm{Wm}^{-2}\mathrm{Hz}^{-1}$ .

What is the highest redshift, $z$ , of a typical HI galaxy that can be detected by a survey carried out with this radio telescope, using 1-minute integration time? knowledge_points.name: Small redshift approximation
knowledge_points.description: The redshift is small (z ≪ 1), so non-relativistic formulas apply and the observed linewidth is approximately equal to the rest linewidth. This simplifies the Doppler formula and the flux density calculation.

knowledge_points.name: Point source approximation
knowledge_points.description: The galaxy is far enough that its angular size is smaller than the telescope beam, so it can be treated as an unresolved point source. This justifies using the inverse-square law without beam dilution.

knowledge_points.name: Spectral flux density
knowledge_points.description: Flux density is the power received per unit area per unit frequency, measured in Jansky (1 Jy = 10⁻²⁶ W m⁻² Hz⁻¹). Understanding this unit is necessary to apply the detection limit.

knowledge_points.name: Parsec
knowledge_points.description: An astronomical distance unit: 1 pc ≈ 3.086×10¹⁶ m, 1 Mpc = 10⁶ pc. Needed to convert the Hubble constant from km/s/Mpc to SI units for the flux calculation.

knowledge_points.name: Non-relativistic redshift formula
knowledge_points.description: For small redshifts, the observed frequency f_obs is related to the rest frequency f_rest by z ≈ (f_rest - f_obs)/f_rest, and the recessional velocity v ≈ cz. Used to compute z from the receiver's frequency range and to convert distance to redshift.

knowledge_points.name: Hubble's law
knowledge_points.description: v = H₀ d relates the recessional velocity of a galaxy to its distance. For small z, combining with v ≈ cz gives d ≈ cz/H₀. Used to find the redshift corresponding to the flux-limited distance.

knowledge_points.name: Inverse-square law for spectral flux density
knowledge_points.description: For a point source emitting a total line luminosity L over a bandwidth Δf, the observed flux density at distance d is S = L/(4π d² Δf). Used to determine the maximum distance from the detection limit.

sub_problems.guidance:
Your task is to find the highest redshift at which a typical HI galaxy can be detected in 1 minute of integration. Two independent conditions must both be satisfied: (1) the redshifted 21‑cm line must fall inside the receiver’s frequency band, and (2) the flux density arriving from the galaxy must be at least the detection limit of the instrument. The highest redshift allowed by both constraints together is the **smaller** of the two limiting redshifts.

**Step 1 – Frequency‑band limit**  
As the problem states, you may use the non‑relativistic Doppler formula. In this approximation the observed frequency \(f_{\text{obs}}\) is related to the rest frequency \(f_0 = 1.42\ \text{GHz}\) and the recession velocity \(v\) by \(f_{\text{obs}} \approx f_0 (1 - v/c)\). Since \(z = v/c\) for small \(z\), you immediately have \(z \approx (f_0 - f_{\text{obs}})/f_0\).

The receiver accepts frequencies from 1.32 GHz to 1.52 GHz. The redshift lowers the observed frequency, so the largest redshift corresponds to the **lowest** frequency that can still be received, i.e. \(f_{\text{obs}} = 1.32\ \text{GHz}\). Plug this value into the formula for \(z\) above; the result is the highest redshift limited only by the receiver band. *(At this point leave the number as an expression — you will compute it when you have both candidates.)*

**Step 2 – Flux‑sensitivity limit**  
The detection limit is given as a spectral flux density \(S_{\lim} = 0.5\ \text{mJy}\).  
From reference passage on **spectral flux density** (§6.3), the jansky is defined as \(1\ \text{Jy}=10^{-26}\ \text{W m}^{-2}\ \text{Hz}^{-1}\). Convert \(S_{\lim}\) to those SI units (you will need it for the computation later).

A galaxy radiates its HI line with a total power \(L=10^{28}\ \text{W}\) spread over a line width \(\Delta f = 1\ \text{MHz}\) (\(10^6\ \text{Hz}\)). For a far‑away, point‑like source the **inverse‑square law** for the radiant flux \(F\) (reference.2) tells you that the power per unit area at a distance \(d\) is \(F = L/(4\pi d^2)\).  
Since \(F\) is a bolometric flux (power per unit area) and \(\Delta f\) is the frequency interval over which that power is distributed, the average spectral flux density at Earth is \(S = F/\Delta f = L/(4\pi d^2 \Delta f)\). This follows directly from the way spectral flux density is introduced in the radio‑telescope discussion (§6.3): for a constant \(S\) over a bandwidth \(\Delta\nu\), the power collected is \(P = S A \Delta\nu\), and the flux density itself is the power per unit area per unit frequency.

Set the observed spectral flux density equal to the detection limit: \(S = S_{\lim}\). Solve that equation for the distance \(d\) that makes the galaxy just detectable. (You will obtain \(d = \sqrt{L / (4\pi \Delta f S_{\lim})}\).)

Now relate distance to redshift. **Hubble’s law** (§27.2 or the Palen exposition) gives \(v = H_0 d\), and with the non‑relativistic approximation \(z \approx v/c\) you have \(z \approx H_0 d / c\). Substitute the expression for \(d\) into this relation to obtain the redshift that results from the flux‑sensitivity constraint.

For the value of \(H_0\) you may adopt the typical figure mentioned in reference, around \(65\ \text{km s}^{-1}\ \text{Mpc}^{-1}\). Be careful with units: you will need to convert megaparsecs to metres using the definition of a parsec (1 pc = 3.0856776 × 10\(^{16}\) m from §3.1), so that \(H_0\) in s\(^{-1}\) correctly cancels with \(c\) in m s\(^{-1}\) and the square‑root factor. The conversion steps for \(H_0\) are illustrated in Example 3.2.1 (where AU are converted to metres) and in the parsec passage itself; the process is identical in spirit.

You should now have an expression (or a numerical value) for the flux‑limited redshift.

title: A Synchronous Satellite
problem: A synchronous satellite is a satellite which orbits the Earth with its period exactly equal to the period of rotation of the Earth. The height of these satellites is $35786\mathrm{km}$ above the surface of the Earth. A satellite is put in an inclined synchronous orbit with an inclination of $\theta = 6.69^{\circ}$ to the equatorial plane. Calculate the precise value of the maximum possible altitude of the satellite for an observer at latitude of $\phi = 51.49^{\circ}$ . Ignore the effect of refraction due to the Earth's atmosphere.
solution:
The maximum altitude occurs when the satellite is at the observer's meridian. The geometry gives the relation:
\[
\tan(90^{\circ} - (\phi - \theta) - h) = \frac{R\sin(\phi - \theta)}{H + R - R\cos(\phi - \theta)}
\]
where $R = 6.38 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{km}$ is the Earth's radius and $H = 35786\,\mathrm{km}$ is the satellite's height above the equator. Solving for $h$:
\[
h = 90^{\circ} - (\phi - \theta) - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{R\sin(\phi - \theta)}{H + R - R\cos(\phi - \theta)}\right)
\]
Substituting $\phi = 51.49^{\circ}$, $\theta = 6.69^{\circ}$, $R = 6.38 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{km}$, $H = 35786\,\mathrm{km}$:
\[
h = 90^{\circ} - (51.49^{\circ} - 6.69^{\circ}) - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin(51.49^{\circ} - 6.69^{\circ})}{\frac{35786}{6.38 \times 10^3} + 1 - \cos(51.49^{\circ} - 6.69^{\circ})}\right)
\]
\[
h = 90^{\circ} - 44.80^{\circ} - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin 44.80^{\circ}}{5.609 + 1 - \cos 44.80^{\circ}}\right)
\]
\[
h = 45.20^{\circ} - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{0.7046}{5.609 + 1 - 0.7096}\right) = 45.20^{\circ} - \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{0.7046}{5.8994}\right)
\]
\[
h = 45.20^{\circ} - \tan^{-1}(0.1194) = 45.20^{\circ} - 6.81^{\circ} = 38.39^{\circ}
\]
Thus the maximum altitude is $\boxed{38.4^{\circ}}$.

title: Supernova 1987A
problem: Supernova SN 1987A was at its brightest with an apparent magnitude of $+3$ on about $15^{\mathrm{th}}$ May 1987 and then faded, finally becoming invisible to the naked eye by $4^{\mathrm{th}}$ February 1988. It is assumed that brightness $B$ varied with time $t$ as an exponential decline, $B = B_{0}e^{-t / \tau}$ , where $B_{0}$ and $\tau$ are constant. The maximum apparent magnitude which can be seen by the naked eye is $+6$ .

sub_problems.problem: (a) Determine the value of $\tau$ in days.
sub_problems.solution:
The magnitude difference is given by $m - m_0 = -2.5 \log_{10} \left(\frac{B}{B_0}\right)$. Substituting $B = B_0 e^{-t/\tau}$ gives $m - m_0 = 2.5 \frac{t}{\tau} \log_{10} e$. The time from 15 May 1987 to 4 February 1988 is 265 days. With $m_0 = +3$, $m = +6$, we have $6 - 3 = 2.5 \frac{265}{\tau} \log_{10} e$. Solving for $\tau$ yields $\tau = \frac{2.5 \times 265 \times \log_{10} e}{3} = 95.9$ days.

\boxed{\tau = 95.9 \text{ days}}

knowledge_points.name: Pogson's equation
knowledge_points.description: Relates the difference in apparent magnitudes to the logarithm of the brightness ratio: m - m0 = -2.5 log10(B/B0). This is the fundamental equation connecting the given magnitudes to the exponential brightness model.

knowledge_points.name: exponential brightness decay
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that brightness varies as B = B0 e^{-t/tau}. The solution directly substitutes this into Pogson's equation to relate magnitude change to time.

knowledge_points.name: base-10 logarithm manipulation
knowledge_points.description: The solution uses the identity log10(e^{-t/tau}) = -(t/tau) log10(e) to linearize the exponential inside the logarithm, converting the magnitude difference into a linear equation in t.

knowledge_points.name: naked-eye limiting magnitude
knowledge_points.description: The problem gives the maximum apparent magnitude visible to the naked eye as +6. This value is used as the final magnitude m when the supernova becomes invisible, defining the time interval for the decay.

knowledge_points.name: time interval between observations
knowledge_points.description: The solution calculates the number of days between 15 May 1987 and 4 February 1988 as 265 days. This specific time interval is required to solve for tau.

sub_problems.guidance:
Your goal is to find the decay timescale τ (in days) for the supernova’s brightness, using two observed apparent magnitudes and the time between those observations.

**Step 1 – Understand the brightness decay model**
From reference passage on exponential brightness decay (reference.3), the light curve of SN 1987A follows the radioactive decay of isotopes such as cobalt‑56. The brightness \(B\) decreases with time \(t\) according to an exponential law: \(B = B_0 e^{-t/\tau}\). Here \(B_0\) is the brightness at some starting time, and \(\tau\) is the e‑folding timescale you need to find.

**Step 2 – Connect brightness to magnitude**
reference explains Pogson’s equation (reference.2). For two measurements of the same object with brightnesses \(B_0\) and \(B\), the apparent magnitudes \(m_0\) and \(m\) are related by:
\[
m - m_0 = -2.5 \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{B}{B_0}\right).
\]
This formula is the only link you have between the observed magnitudes and the physical brightness ratio.

**Step 3 – Combine the exponential decay with Pogson’s equation**
Substitute the exponential decay expression \(B/B_0 = e^{-t/\tau}\) into Pogson’s equation. This will give you a relationship that connects the magnitude difference \(m - m_0\) directly to the elapsed time \(t\) and the unknown \(\tau\).

**Step 4 – Determine the elapsed time between observations**
The problem states the observations were made on 15 May 1987 and 4 February 1988. You need the number of days between these two dates. reference (reference.3) discusses time intervals in astronomy and the use of Julian dates for precise timing, but for this problem a simple day count within a non‑leap year (1987–1988) is sufficient. Count carefully the days remaining in May 1987, the full months between, and the days in February 1988. This gives you the value of \(t\) to use.

**Step 5 – Identify the magnitude values**
reference notes that Hipparchus assigned \(m = 1\) to the brightest naked‑eye stars and \(m = 6\) to the dimmest. The problem gives \(m_0 = +3\) (brighter) and \(m = +6\) (dimmer). The magnitude difference \(m - m_0\) is therefore a positive number you can compute directly.

**Step 6 – Solve for τ**

**Step 7 – Check consistency**
Verify that your calculated τ is physically reasonable for a supernova light curve decay timescale (comparable to the slopes seen in Figure 15.12). This does not require any new formulas—just a quick sanity check.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Find the last day that observers could have seen the supernova if they had a 6-inch (15.24-cm) telescope with transmission efficiency $T = 70\%$ . Assume that the average diameter of the human pupil is $0.6 \, \text{cm}$.
sub_problems.solution:
The energy collected by the telescope is proportional to its area times transmission, and by the eye to the pupil area. For the same perceived brightness, $B_e d^2 = T B_T D^2$, where $d=0.6$ cm is pupil diameter, $D=15.24$ cm is telescope diameter, and $B_e$, $B_T$ are the brightnesses as seen by eye and telescope respectively. Thus $\frac{B_e}{B_T} = T \frac{D^2}{d^2}$. The limiting magnitude for the telescope is $m_{\lim} = m_e + 2.5 \log_{10} T + 5 \log_{10} \left(\frac{D}{d}\right)$, where $m_e = +6$ is the naked-eye limit. Substituting: $m_{\lim} = 6 + 2.5 \log_{10} 0.7 + 5 \log_{10} \left(\frac{15.24}{0.6}\right) = 12.64$. Using $m - m_0 = 2.5 \frac{t}{\tau} \log_{10} e$ with $m_0 = +3$, $\tau = 95.9$ days, we get $12.64 - 3 = 2.5 \frac{t}{95.9} \log_{10} e$, so $t = 851.5$ days after 15 May 1987. Adding 851.5 days gives 12 September 1989 (1113 September 1989 acceptable).

\boxed{12^{\text{th}} \text{ September 1989}}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the last day the supernova could be seen with the telescope, we need to combine two separate ideas from your textbook: how a telescope’s light-gathering power changes the faintest magnitude you can detect, and how the supernova’s brightness faded with time due to radioactive decay.

**Step 1 – Find the telescope’s limiting magnitude.**
First, recall from the magnitude scale (Pogson’s law) that the ratio of fluxes for two sources is related to the difference in their magnitudes by Eq. (3.4). When comparing the light collected by the telescope to that collected by the unaided eye, the flux collected is proportional to the area of the aperture times the transmission efficiency. The textbook explains in the “Telescopes” section that the amount of light collected scales with the collecting area, and in “The Brightness of an Image” section that the illumination is proportional to the area of the aperture (∝ D²). Therefore, for a point source (the supernova is unresolved), the ratio of fluxes reaching the detector through the telescope versus the eye is T (D/d)², where D is the telescope diameter, d is the pupil diameter, and T is the transmission factor.
Use the magnitude–flux relation (Eq. 3.4) to express how many magnitudes fainter the telescope can see compared to the naked‑eye limit (mₑ = +6, as stated in the apparent magnitude passage). Set up the difference between the limiting magnitude m_lim and mₑ using that flux ratio. This will give you an expression like the one used in the reference solution, but you should write it out yourself and compute m_lim.

**Step 2 – Relate the magnitude change to the time since the explosion.**
The supernova’s light curve (Fig. 15.12 and the surrounding text) shows that after the initial peak the brightness decayed exponentially, driven by the radioactive decay of cobalt‑56. The problem implies the decay can be described by a linear magnitude increase with time. From the exponential decay law and Pogson’s law, the magnitude increases at a constant rate related to the mean lifetime (or half‑life). The textbook gives the slope in terms of the half‑life via Eq. (15.11) and the associated discussion. For SN 1987A, you are given that the magnitude m₀ at the reference time (15 May 1987) was +3, and the decay time constant τ = 95.9 days. The relation between magnitude and time is of the form m – m₀ ∝ t / τ, with the proportionality constant coming from the conversion between exponential decay and the magnitude scale (involving log₁₀ e).

**Step 3 – Solve for the time and add it to the reference date.**
Set the limiting magnitude you found in Step 1 equal to the magnitude expression from Step 2, and solve for the elapsed time t in days. Then add that number of days to 15 May 1987 to find the calendar date when the supernova faded to the telescope’s detection limit. Be careful with the calendar arithmetic (remember leap years if the interval crosses February 1988).

By following these steps, you will carry out the same logic as Example 6.1.2 (using aperture areas) and the light‑curve analysis of Fig. 15.12, but applied to the specific numbers given in this problem.

title: Life on Other Planets
problem:
One place to search for life is on planets orbiting main sequence stars. A good starting point is the planets that have an Earth-like temperature range and a small temperature fluctuation. Assume that for a main sequence star, the relation between the luminosity $L$ and the mass $M$ is given by $$ L \propto M ^ {3.5}. $$ You may assume that the total energy $E$ released over the lifetime of the star is proportional to the mass $M$ of the star. For the Sun, it will have a main sequence lifetime of about 10 billion years. The stellar spectral types are given in the table below. Assume that the spectral subclasses of stars (0-9) are assigned on a scale that is linear in $\log M$.
Spectral ClassO5VB0VA0VF0VG0VK0VM0V
Mass (M⊙)6017.52.91.61.050.790.51

sub_problems.problem: (a) If it takes at least $4 \times 10^{9}$ years for an intelligent life form to evolve, what is the spectral type (accurate to the subclass level) of the most massive star in the main sequence around which astronomers should look for intelligent life?
sub_problems.solution:
Since $E \propto M$ and $L \propto M^{3.5}$, the main-sequence lifetime $\tau \propto E/L \propto M/M^{3.5} = M^{-2.5}$.  Using the Sun's lifetime $\tau_\odot = 10^{10}$ yr, we have

$$
\tau = \tau_\odot \left(\frac{M_\odot}{M}\right)^{2.5}.
$$

Setting $\tau = 4 \times 10^9$ yr gives

$$
M = M_\odot \left(\frac{\tau_\odot}{\tau}\right)^{1/2.5} = M_\odot \left(\frac{10^{10}}{4 \times 10^9}\right)^{1/2.5} = 1.44\,M_\odot.
$$

The spectral subclasses are linear in $\log M$.  From the table, $\log 1.6 - \log 1.05$ corresponds to 10 subclasses (F0V to G0V).  The difference from F0V ($M=1.6\,M_\odot$) to $M=1.44\,M_\odot$ is

$$
\frac{10}{\log 1.6 - \log 1.05} \times (\log 1.6 - \log 1.44) \approx 2.5,
$$

so the spectral type is F2.5V, i.e., between F2V and F3V.

\boxed{\text{F2V to F3V}}

sub_problems.guidance:
The core of this problem is to find the maximum mass a main-sequence star can have while still providing at least \(4 \times 10^9\) years for life to evolve. Your reference explains that the time a star spends on the main sequence depends on mass according to  
\[
\frac{t}{t_{\text{Sun}}} = \left(\frac{M}{M_{\text{Sun}}}\right)^{-2.5},
\]  
and that the Sun’s main-sequence lifetime is \(t_{\text{Sun}} = 10^{10}\) years.

**Step 1 – Relate the required time to the mass**  
Since high-mass stars burn out faster, a *minimum* required time translates into an *upper limit* on the mass: the most massive star we should look at is the one whose main-sequence lifetime is exactly \(4 \times 10^9\) years. Set \(t\) equal to that value in the formula above, and keep \(t_{\text{Sun}} = 10^{10}\) yr.

**Step 2 – Solve for the mass**  
You now have an equation with one unknown, \(M/M_{\text{Sun}}\). To isolate the mass, rewrite the proportion so the mass term is on one side – this will involve taking the reciprocal and raising to the power \(1/2.5\) (or alternatively, writing \(M/M_{\text{Sun}} = \left(t_{\text{Sun}}/t\right)^{1/2.5}\)). Carry out the arithmetic carefully (you may leave the ratio in terms of powers of 10). Do **not** approximate prematurely; keep the exact value from your calculation.

**Step 3 – Convert the mass to a spectral type**  
You have now found the star’s mass in solar units. To assign a spectral subclass, you need the table of main-sequence masses for different spectral types (this table appears in your reference — likely in a chapter on stellar classification or the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram). Locate the two spectral entries that *bracket* your computed mass.  
Your reference teaches that spectral subclasses are spaced linearly in \(\log M\). Therefore, you can interpolate between the bracketing masses. Determine the logarithmic difference between your mass and one of the bounding masses, compare it with the total logarithmic interval between the two bounding spectral types, and then distribute the 10 subclasses proportionally. This will give you the precise subclass (e.g., F2.5V).

Throughout, remember the physical logic: you first use the lifetime–mass relation to set the limit, then turn the mass into a classification using tabulated stellar data. All substitutions and algebraic steps are yours to perform — apply the law, set up the proportion, and interpolate using the table at hand.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Assume that the target planet has the same emissivity $\varepsilon$ and albedo $a$ as the Earth. In order to have the same temperature as the Earth, express the distance $d$, in au, of the planet to its parent main sequence star, of mass $M$.
sub_problems.solution:
The power received by the planet is

$$
P_{\text{input}} = (1-a) \frac{\pi r^2 L}{4\pi d^2} = (1-a) \frac{r^2 L}{4 d^2}.
$$

The power radiated by the planet (blackbody) is

$$
P_{\text{output}} = 4\pi r^2 \varepsilon \sigma T^4.
$$

Equating for thermal equilibrium:

$$
(1-a) \frac{r^2 L}{4 d^2} = 4\pi r^2 \varepsilon \sigma T^4.
$$

For the same temperature as Earth, $T$ is the same, and $a$, $\varepsilon$ are the same.  Hence

$$
\frac{L}{d^2} = \frac{L_\odot}{d_\odot^2}.
$$

Using $L \propto M^{3.5}$ and $d_\odot = 1$ au,

$$
\left(\frac{d}{1\,\text{au}}\right)^2 = \frac{L}{L_\odot} = \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^{3.5},
$$

so

$$
d = \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^{3.5/2}\,\text{au}.
$$

\boxed{d = \left(\frac{M}{M_\odot}\right)^{1.75}\,\text{au}}

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Set up thermal equilibrium** — According to the textbook passage on the temperatures of the planets, a planet’s total energy content stays constant only if the power it absorbs equals the power it radiates. So write  
   \[
   P_{\text{absorbed}} = P_{\text{radiated}} .
   \]

2. **Express the absorbed power** — The star radiates its luminosity \(L\) uniformly in all directions. The inverse square law (e.g., Eq. 3.2 in Carroll & Ostlie) tells you that the flux at distance \(d\) is \(F = L/(4\pi d^2)\). The planet presents a cross‑sectional area \(\pi r^{2}\) to this flux. A fraction \(a\) (the albedo; see the Palen passage) is reflected, so the absorbed power is  
   \[
   P_{\text{absorbed}} = (1-a)\, \pi r^{2} \, \frac{L}{4\pi d^{2}} = \frac{(1-a)\, r^{2} L}{4 d^{2}} .
   \]

3. **Express the radiated power** — The planet is not a perfect blackbody; its emission is reduced by an efficiency factor \(\varepsilon\) (emissivity). The passage from Carroll & Ostlie 12.2 shows that a radiating body’s luminosity can be written as \(L_{\text{rad}} = 4\pi R^{2} e \sigma T^{4}\) (where \(e\) is the same efficiency factor). Here the planet’s total emitting area is \(4\pi r^{2}\), so  
   \[
   P_{\text{radiated}} = 4\pi r^{2} \varepsilon \sigma T^{4}.
   \]

4. **Equate and simplify** — Set \(P_{\text{absorbed}} = P_{\text{radiated}}\) and cancel the common factor \(r^{2}\) (the planet radius disappears). You obtain  
   \[
   \frac{(1-a)L}{4 d^{2}} = 4\varepsilon \sigma T^{4}.
   \]

5. **Use the Earth as a reference** — The problem states that the target planet has the *same* \(a\), \(\varepsilon\), and temperature \(T\) as Earth. Earth orbits the Sun at \(d_{\oplus}=1\ \text{au}\) and the Sun has luminosity \(L_{\odot}\). Because the right‑hand side of the equation above is identical for both planets, the left‑hand sides must be equal:  
   \[
   \frac{L}{d^{2}} = \frac{L_{\odot}}{(1\ \text{au})^{2}} .
   \]  
   Solve this for \(d\):  
   \[
   d = 1\ \text{au} \times \sqrt{\frac{L}{L_{\odot}}}.
   \]

6. **Bring in the stellar mass** — The star is on the main sequence, so its luminosity is determined by its mass \(M\). Look up the main‑sequence mass–luminosity relation from your course (it is often \(L \propto M^{\alpha}\) with a specific exponent \(\alpha\)). Replace \(L/L_{\odot}\) by \((M/M_{\odot})^{\alpha}\) in the expression for \(d\). Then carry out the square root to get the distance in astronomical units as a function of \(M/M_{\odot}\).

By following these steps, you will derive a formula that gives the orbital distance \(d\) (in au) for a planet around a main‑sequence star of mass \(M\) such that the planet’s

sub_problems.problem: (c) The existence of a planet around a star can be shown by the variation in the radial velocity of the star about the star-planet system centre of mass. If the smallest Doppler shift in the wavelength detectable by the observer is $(\Delta \lambda / \lambda) = 10^{-10}$, calculate the lowest mass of such a planet in b), in units of Earth masses, that can be detected by this method, around the main sequence star in a).
sub_problems.solution:
From Kepler's third law for the star-planet system (circular orbit):

$$
T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 d^3}{G(M+m)} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \omega = \sqrt{\frac{G(M+m)}{d^3}}.
$$

Centre of mass: $M d_s = m d$, so $d_s = \frac{m}{M} d$.  The star's orbital speed is

$$
v = \omega d_s = \frac{m}{M} \sqrt{\frac{G(M+m)}{d}} \approx m \sqrt{\frac{G}{M d}} \quad (m \ll M).
$$

The Doppler shift gives $\frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{v}{c}$, so

$$
m = \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} c \sqrt{\frac{M d}{G}}.
$$

From part (a), $M = 1.44\,M_\odot$.  From part (b), $d = (M/M_\odot)^{1.75}\,\text{au} = (1.44)^{1.75}\,\text{au}$.  Using $M_\odot = 1.99\times10^{30}\,\text{kg}$, $1\,\text{au} = 1.50\times10^{11}\,\text{m}$, $G = 6.67\times10^{-11}\,\text{m}^3\text{kg}^{-1}\text{s}^{-2}$, $c = 2.99792458\times10^8\,\text{m/s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m &= 10^{-10} \times 2.99792458\times10^8 \\
&\quad \times \sqrt{\frac{1.44\times1.99\times10^{30} \times (1.44)^{1.75} \times 1.50\times10^{11}}{6.67\times10^{-11}}} \\
&\approx 3.31\times10^{24}\,\text{kg}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Earth mass $M_\oplus = 5.97\times10^{24}\,\text{kg}$, so

$$
m = \frac{3.31\times10^{24}}{5.97\times10^{24}} M_\oplus \approx 0.554\,M_\oplus.
$$

\boxed{m \approx 0.554\,M_\oplus}

sub_problems.guidance:
Your task is to find the minimum planet mass (in Earth masses) that produces a stellar radial velocity just at the detection limit. The problem gives you that limit as \(\Delta\lambda/\lambda = 10^{-10}\), and you have already determined the star’s mass \(M\) from part (a) and the star–planet separation \(d\) from part (b). You will combine several ideas from the readings, in the following order.

1. **Radial velocity from the Doppler shift** — The non‑relativistic Doppler formula (Palen, “The Doppler Effect”; or Carroll & Ostlie, Eq. 4.39) is  
   \(\displaystyle \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{v_r}{c}\), valid when \(v_r \ll c\).  
   Use this to express the star’s orbital speed \(v\) (taken as the radial velocity amplitude, which for the lowest detectable mass is \(v = c\,(\Delta\lambda/\lambda)\)).  
   This gives you a numerical value for \(v\) once you substitute the given \(\Delta\lambda/\lambda\) and the speed of light.

2. **Centre of mass and orbital speed of the star** — The star and planet orbit their common centre of mass (CM). From the two‑body CM definition (Kleppner & Kolenkow, “Center of Mass”, Eq. 4.4 or the baton example), the star’s distance from the CM is  
   \(\displaystyle r_* = \frac{m}{M+m}\,d\), where \(m\) is the planet mass and \(d\) is the total separation.  
   Because the orbit is (or is assumed) circular, the star’s speed is simply the tangential speed of a point moving on a circle: \(v = \omega r_*\) (Kleppner & Kolenkow, polar‑coordinate “Case 2”; see also the circular‑orbit relation used in Carroll & Ostlie, Example 7.4.1).

3. **Angular frequency from Kepler’s third law** — The two bodies share the same orbital period. The general Newtonian form of Kepler’s third law (Palen: \(P^2 = 4\pi^2 a^3/[G(m+M)]\); Carroll & Ostlie, Eq. 2.37) gives  
   \(\displaystyle \omega = \frac{2\pi}{P} = \sqrt{\frac{G(M+m)}{d^3}}\).  

4. **Combine to relate \(v\) and \(m\)** — Substitute the expressions for \(r_*\) and \(\omega\) into \(v = \omega r_*\):  
   \(\displaystyle v = \sqrt{\frac{G(M+m)}{d^3}} \cdot \frac{m}{M+m}\,d = m \sqrt{\frac{G}{(M+m)d}}\).  
   For a planet whose mass is much smaller than the star’s (\(m \ll M\)), this simplifies to  
   \(\displaystyle v \approx m \sqrt{\frac{G}{M d}}\),  
   exactly as justified by the approximation noted in Carroll & Ostlie’s Ex. 23.1.1 and the discussion after Eq. 2.37. (You can first write the exact expression and then neglect \(m\) relative to \(M\); the error is tiny.)

5. **Solve for the planet mass** — Rearrange the approximate relation to isolate \(m\):  
   \(\displaystyle m \approx v \sqrt{\frac{M d}{G}}\).  
   Now replace \(v\) with \(c\,(\Delta\lambda/\lambda)\) from step 1, and insert the values of \(M\) and \(d\) you obtained in earlier parts (use consistent SI units: kg, m, s). Carry out the arithmetic to get \(m\) in kilograms.

6. **Convert to Earth masses** — The problem asks for the mass in Earth masses. Use the standard Earth mass (you may look it up; typical value \(M_\oplus = 5.97 \times 10^{24}\,\text{kg}\)) to find \(m/M_\oplus\).

By following this chain – Doppler shift → star’s orbital speed → centre‑of‑mass relation → Kepler’s third law → circular motion – you have used all the required knowledge in the same logical order as the textbook examples, without ever needing to guess a missing step.

title: The Star of Bethlehem
problem:
A great conjunction is a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn for observers on Earth. Assume that Jupiter and Saturn have circular orbits in the ecliptic plane.

The time between successive conjunctions may vary slightly as viewed from the Earth. However, the average time period of the great conjunctions is the same as that of an observer at the centre of the Solar system.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Find the average great conjunction period (in years) and average heliocentric angle between two successive great conjunctions (in degrees).
sub_problems.solution:
Assume that the average Earth's orbit is at the Sun. Therefore, average great conjunction period equals to the synodic period between Jupiter and Saturn.
$$
\frac{1}{P_{\text{Synodic}}} = \frac{1}{P_{\text{Jupiter}}} - \frac{1}{P_{\text{Saturn}}}
$$
$$
\frac{1}{P_{\text{Synodic}}} = \frac{1}{11.86} - \frac{1}{29.45}
$$
$$
P_{\text{Synodic}} = 19.86 \text{ years}
$$
From average great conjunction period, in 19.86 years Jupiter and Saturn move
Heliocentric angle $= \frac{19.86}{11.86} \times 360^{\circ} = 602.7^{\circ} = 242.7^{\circ}$
in an eastward direction through the zodiac, or $360^{\circ} - 242.7^{\circ} = 117.3^{\circ}$ in a westward direction through the zodiac.
\boxed{P = 19.86\text{ years}, \theta = 242.7^{\circ}}

knowledge_points.description: For two planets orbiting the Sun, the synodic period P_syn satisfies 1/P_syn = 1/P_inner - 1/P_outer, where P_inner and P_outer are the sidereal orbital periods.
