sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the orbital periods of Jupiter and Saturn. These are assumed to be known from your course (e.g. \(P_{\text{J}} = 11.86\) years, \(P_{\text{S}} = 29.45\) years). The problem asks for the average great conjunction period and the average heliocentric angle between two successive great conjunctions. Since the Earth’s orbit is taken to be at the Sun, the average great conjunction period is simply the synodic period of Jupiter and Saturn as seen from the Sun.

**Step 1 – Synodic period from reference relation**  
reference passage on synodic periods gives Eq. (1.1):
\[
\frac{1}{S} = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{P} - \frac{1}{P_{\oplus}}, & \text{(inferior)} \\[4pt]
\frac{1}{P_{\oplus}} - \frac{1}{P}, & \text{(superior)}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(S\) is the synodic period and \(P\) the sidereal period of a planet relative to Earth. You can generalise this idea to any two planets by replacing Earth’s angular speed with the inner planet’s angular speed. For two planets with nearly circular orbits, the angular speed is constant: \(\omega = 360^\circ/P\). The faster (inner) planet laps the slower (outer) one at a relative angular speed \(\omega_{\text{inner}} - \omega_{\text{outer}}\). The time to close an angular gap of \(360^\circ\) is therefore
\[
\frac{1}{S} = \frac{1}{P_{\text{inner}}} - \frac{1}{P_{\text{outer}}}.
\]
Apply this to Jupiter (inner) and Saturn (outer). Substitute their periods into the formula to obtain the synodic period \(S\) in years. This is the average great conjunction period.

**Step 2 – Heliocentric angle between successive conjunctions**  
Because the orbits are assumed circular, the angular displacement of a planet during time \(t\) is \( (360^\circ) \times (t/P) \). During one synodic period \(S\), Jupiter moves eastward by
\[
\theta_{\text{total}} = 360^\circ \times \frac{S}{P_{\text{J}}}.
\]
This total angle is greater than \(360^\circ\) because Jupiter makes one full extra lap relative to Saturn. The **average heliocentric angle** between two successive great conjunctions is the angle between the two conjunction points as seen from the Sun. This is the eastward shift of the conjunction longitude, which is simply the total angle \(\theta_{\text{total}}\) reduced by the integer number of full circles (i.e. take the remainder after dividing by \(360^\circ\)). If the result is larger than \(180^\circ\), it is the eastward shift; the corresponding westward shift is \(360^\circ\) minus that value. The problem

Next, understand what “elongation $30.3^{\circ}$ East of the Sun” means. The elongation passage introduces the concept of angular separation east or west of the Sun, and the problem gives the elongation measured eastward. Planets orbit very nearly in the same plane as Earth’s orbit, so conjunctions occur close to the ecliptic—the Sun’s apparent path through the constellations.

Now, determine which constellation follows Sagittarius along the ecliptic. sub_problems.problem: (c) Suggest the constellation in which the great conjunctions in 7 BC occurred. (Give the IAU Latin name or IAU three-letter abbreviation of the constellation, i.e. Ursa Major or UMa)
sub_problems.solution:
The duration between 7BC and 2020 is 2026 years or 2027 years.
Each conjunction occurs on the average every 19.86 years. Therefore, the number of conjunctions between 7BC and 2020 is
Integer value of $2026 / 19.86 = 102$.
From a conjunction to its previous successive conjunction, the conjunction moves $243^{\circ}$ westwards. The position of the conjunction in 7BC is
$$102 \times 242.7^{\circ} = 24758.33^{\circ} = 278.3^{\circ}$$
westward, or equivalently $81.7^{\circ}$ eastward from the position of the conjunction in 2020. Therefore, the conjunction was in the constellation of Aries (Ari) or Pisces (Psc).
\boxed{\text{Aries (Ari) or Pisces (Psc)}}

sub_problems.guidance:
To determine the constellation of the great conjunction in 7 BC, you need to work backwards along the ecliptic from the known 2020 conjunction position. Here is the method, grounded in the concepts from your textbook.

First, recall the idea of the ecliptic from the textbook: it is the apparent path of the Sun through the constellations over the course of a year. The passage lists the constellations the Sun occupies at the start of each season—for example, it is in Pisces at the beginning of spring. The great conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn also occurs along this same ecliptic band, so its position shifts through the zodiacal constellations over successive conjunctions.

The problem provides the average interval between conjunctions and the angular shift westward along the ecliptic from one conjunction to the next (the latter is given in the full problem context, which you have). Your first task is to find the total number of conjunctions that occurred between 7 BC and AD 2020. To do this, calculate the total elapsed time in years (careful with the BC to AD transition: there is no year 0, so the span from 7 BC to AD 2020 is 2026 years). Then divide this total time by the average interval between conjunctions (19.86 years). Since you need a whole number of conjunctions, take the integer part of your result.

Next, determine the total angular shift along the ecliptic over this many conjunctions. Multiply the number of conjunctions you found by the westward angular shift per conjunction (242.7°). Because this total will be many full circles, reduce it to an equivalent angle between 0° and 360° by subtracting multiples of 360°. This leaves you with the net angular change in the conjunction’s position from 7 BC to 2020.

The direction of this shift is stated as westward. If you prefer to think in terms of eastward motion (which corresponds to increasing ecliptic longitude in the usual direction through the zodiac), you can convert: an eastward shift equals 360° minus the net westward shift. This tells you how many degrees eastward along the ecliptic the 7 BC conjunction was relative to the 2020 conjunction.

Now, you need the position of the 2020 conjunction. This was given earlier in the problem statement you are working with (typically it was near the boundary of Sagittarius and Capricornus). Starting from that 2020 position, move eastward along the ecliptic by the eastward angle you just computed. Use the sequence of zodiac constellations and their traditional order—the textbook mentions Pisces, Taurus, Virgo, Sagittarius, and implies the full set. As you count through the constellations, you will identify which constellation or constellations the 7 BC conjunction falls in.

The logic of this approach mirrors the textbook’s discussion of how our line of sight to the Sun sweeps through the constellations due to Earth’s orbital motion, only here you are tracking the slow, stepwise migration of a planetary conjunction along the same ecliptic path.

At the second conjunction, Jupiter and Saturn had retrograde motions. For observers on the Earth, both of them were in opposition. Therefore, the sun was in the constellation of Libra (Lib) (if answer c) is Aries) or Virgo (Vir) (if answer c) is Pisces).

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall what “opposition” means for a superior planet from reference: a superior planet (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn) can be seen up to 180° from the Sun, and that alignment is called opposition. The passage also tells you that near opposition, a superior planet is closest to Earth and at its brightest, and that retrograde motion happens near opposition.

The problem says that during the second conjunction, Jupiter and Saturn had retrograde motions. Using the idea from “Retrograde Motion Revisited,” retrograde motion for superior planets occurs near opposition. Therefore, at that time, both Jupiter and Saturn were near opposition as seen from Earth.

Now, think about what opposition means geometrically: the Sun, Earth, and the planet are roughly lined up, with Earth in the middle. That puts the planet and the Sun on nearly opposite sides of the sky as viewed from Earth. So if Jupiter and Saturn were in opposition, the Sun must be in the part of the sky roughly opposite to them.

To suggest the constellation the Sun was in, you need to know where Jupiter and Saturn were during that conjunction. The problem’s earlier parts (which you have already solved) should tell you the constellation where the conjunction occurred—that is, the constellation where Jupiter and Saturn appeared close together. Since they were in opposition, the Sun was about 180° away on the celestial sphere, which places it in the constellation opposite to that conjunction constellation along the ecliptic.

Thus, your method is: identify the constellation of the conjunction from your earlier answer; then determine the zodiacal constellation that is opposite to it (six constellations away along the ecliptic). That opposite constellation is where the Sun was located. Give its IAU Latin name or three‑letter abbreviation.

title: GOTO
problem: The Gravitational-Wave Optical Transient Observer (GOTO) aims to carry out searches of optical counterparts of any Gravitational Wave (GW) sources within an hour of their detection by the LIGO and VIRGO experiments. The survey needs to cover a big area on the sky in a short time to search all possible regions constrained by the GW experiments before the optical burst signal, if any, fades away. The GOTO telescope array is composed of 4 identical reflective telescopes, each with $40\mathrm{-cm}$ diameter aperture and f-ratio of 2.5, working together to image large regions of the sky. For simplicity, we assume that the telescopes' fields-of-view (FoV) do not overlap with one another.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Calculate the projected angular size per mm at the focal plane, i.e. plate scale, of each telescope.
sub_problems.solution:
For small angular separation $\theta$, the distance at the focal plane is $S = f \theta$, where $f$ is the focal length. Hence plate scale $= \theta/S = 1/f$. The focal length $f = \text{F-ratio} \times \text{diameter} = 2.5 \times 0.40\,\mathrm{m} = 1.0\,\mathrm{m} = 1000\,\mathrm{mm}$. Therefore plate scale $= 1/1000\,\mathrm{rad/mm} = (1/1000) \times (180 \times 3600/\pi)\,\mathrm{arcsec/mm} = 206\,\mathrm{arcsec/mm} = 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}$.

\boxed{3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}}

knowledge_points.name: image scale for a telescope
knowledge_points.description: For a distant object and small angular separations, the linear size s of the image on the focal plane is s = f θ, where f is the focal length and θ is the angular size in radians. This directly gives the plate scale as θ/s = 1/f.

knowledge_points.name: f-number definition
knowledge_points.description: The f-number (f-ratio) of an optical system is the ratio of the focal length f to the aperture diameter D: f-number = f/D. The problem gives the f‑ratio and diameter, so f = f‑number × D is used to find the focal length.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: The reference solution explicitly assumes small angular separations so that tanθ ≈ θ, which is needed to write s = fθ instead of s = f tanθ. This is standard for most telescopic fields.

knowledge_points.name: radian to arcminute conversion
knowledge_points.description: The plate scale initially computed in rad/mm is converted into the practical astronomical units arcmin/mm (or arcsec/mm) using 1 rad = (180/π)×3600 arcsec and 1 arcmin = 60 arcsec.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the projected angular size per millimeter at the focal plane (the plate scale), you need to bring together three ideas from the textbook: the definition of the focal ratio, the small‑angle image scale relation, and the conversion between radians and arcminutes.

1. **Determine the focal length of the telescope in convenient units**  
   The focal ratio (or f‑number) is defined as  
   \[
   F \equiv \frac{f}{D} \qquad \text{(Eq. 6.7)}
   \]  
   where \(f\) is the focal length and \(D\) is the aperture diameter. For each telescope you are given both the f‑ratio and the diameter. Solve for \(f = F \times D\).  
   Then convert that focal length to millimeters so that the plate scale can later be expressed per millimeter.

2. **Find the plate scale in radians per millimeter**  
   Section 6.1 of Carroll & Ostlie shows that for small angles the linear displacement on the focal plane is \(y = f \theta\) (Eq. 6.3), where \(\theta\) is the angular separation in radians. The plate scale is the derivative \(d\theta/dy\), which gives the angular change per unit length on the detector:  
   \[
   \frac{d\theta}{dy} = \frac{1}{f} \qquad \text{(Eq. 6.4)}
   \]  
   This relation holds when \(\theta\) is measured in radians. If you insert the focal length in millimeters, the plate scale is simply \(1/f\) radians per millimeter.

3. **Convert the plate scale from radians to arcminutes**  
   The textbook section on stellar parallax (Sec. 3.1) reminds you that  
   \[
   1\ \text{radian} = 206\,265\ \text{arcseconds}.
   \]  
   Because there are 60 arcseconds in 1 arcminute, you can convert the plate scale to arcminutes per millimeter in two steps: first multiply your rad/mm value by \(206\,265\) to go to arcseconds per mm, then divide by \(60\) to obtain arcminutes per mm. Equivalently, you can compute the plate scale directly in arcseconds per mm via the small‑angle formula \(\theta('') = 206\,265 \times (y/f)\) and then convert to arcminutes.

4. **Assemble the result**  
   The calculation then becomes:  
   - Compute \(f\) (in mm) from the given f‑ratio and diameter.  
   - Form the reciprocal \(1/f\) (rad/mm).  
   - Convert to arcminutes per mm: \(\displaystyle \frac{1}{f}\ \text{rad/mm} \times \frac{206\,265}{60}\ \frac{\text{arcmin}}{\text{rad}}\).  
   Perform the arithmetic; the resulting number is the telescope’s plate scale, i.e. the angular size projected onto each millimeter of the focal plane.

No intermediate numeric values are stated here; you will carry out the numerical substitutions and obtain the final plate scale for each telescope.

sub_problems.problem: (b) If the zero-point magnitude (i.e. the magnitude at which the count rate detected by the detector is 1 count per second) of the telescope system is $18.5\mathrm{mag}$, calculate the minimum time needed to reach 21 mag at Signal-to-Noise Ratio $(\mathrm{SNR}) = 5$ for a point source. We first assume that the noise is dominated by both the Read-Out Noise (RON) at 10 counts/pixel and the CCD dark (thermal) noise (DN) rate of 1 count/pix/minute. The CCDs used with the GOTO have a 6-micron pixel size and gain (conversion factor between photo-electron and data count) of 1. The typical seeing at the observatory site is around 1.0 arcsec. [8]
sub_problems.solution:
From part (a), plate scale $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}$. Pixel size $= 6\,\mu\mathrm{m} = 6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mm}$. Angular size per pixel $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm} \times 6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{mm} = 0.02064\,\mathrm{arcmin} = 1.238\,\mathrm{arcsec}$. Seeing is $1.0\,\mathrm{arcsec}$, so the star light is mostly contained within $N_{\mathrm{pix}} = 1$ pixel.

Zero-point magnitude $ZP = 18.5$, magnitude $m = 21$. Count rate $\mathrm{CR} = 10^{-(m-ZP)/2.5} = 10^{-(21-18.5)/2.5} = 10^{-1} = 0.1\,\mathrm{counts/s}$.

RON $= 10$ counts/pixel, DN $= 1$ count/pix/min $= 1/60$ counts/pix/s.

SNR $= \frac{\mathrm{CR}\times t}{\sqrt{N_{\mathrm{pix}}\mathrm{RON}^2 + N_{\mathrm{pix}}\mathrm{DN}\cdot t}} = \frac{0.1 t}{\sqrt{10^2 + (1/60)t}}$.

Set SNR $= 5$: $(0.1 t)^2 = 25(100 + t/60)$.

$0.01 t^2 = 2500 + (25/60)t$.

Multiply by 60: $0.6 t^2 = 150000 + 25 t$.

$0.6 t^2 - 25 t - 150000 = 0$.

$t = \frac{25 + \sqrt{25^2 + 4\times0.6\times150000}}{2\times0.6} = \frac{25 + \sqrt{625 + 360000}}{1.2} = \frac{25 + \sqrt{360625}}{1.2} = \frac{25 + 600.52}{1.2} = 521.27\,\mathrm{s}$.

$t \approx 521\,\mathrm{s} = 8.68\,\mathrm{minutes}$.

\boxed{521\,\mathrm{s}}

knowledge_points.name: Plate scale
knowledge_points.description: The ratio of angular size on the sky to physical size at the focal plane. Here the plate scale from part (a) is 3.44 arcmin/mm. It is used to convert the CCD pixel size (6 µm) to angular size per pixel (1.238 arcsec), which is then compared to the seeing to determine how many pixels a point source covers.

knowledge_points.name: Astronomical seeing
knowledge_points.description: The atmospheric blurring of a point source, typically measured as the FWHM of the point spread function. The problem gives a seeing of 1.0 arcsec. Combined with the pixel angular size, this determines that the star's light is mostly contained within 1 pixel.

knowledge_points.name: Pogson's magnitude equation
knowledge_points.description: The relation between magnitude difference and flux ratio: m1 - m2 = -2.5 log10(F1/F2). Used to compute the count rate from the zero-point magnitude (18.5 mag, where count rate is 1 count/s) and the target magnitude (21 mag): CR = 10^{-(21-18.5)/2.5} = 0.1 counts/s.

knowledge_points.name: CCD SNR equation for point source with read noise and dark current
knowledge_points.description: The signal-to-noise ratio formula for a point source when noise is dominated by read-out noise and dark current: SNR = (CR * t) / sqrt( N_pix * (RON^2 + DN_rate * t) ), where RON is the read-out noise per pixel (variance RON^2), DN_rate is the dark current count rate per pixel (variance = DN_rate * t due to Poisson statistics), and source photon noise is neglected. Used to set up the equation for the required exposure time.

knowledge_points.name: Noise dominated by read-out noise and dark current
knowledge_points.description: The problem explicitly states that we assume the noise is dominated by read-out noise (RON) and dark current (DN), so photon noise from the source and sky background are ignored. This justifies omitting the sqrt(CR * t) term in the SNR denominator.

knowledge_points.name: Point source contained within one pixel
knowledge_points.description: Based on the computed pixel angular size (1.238 arcsec) and the given seeing (1.0 arcsec), the star's light is assumed to be mostly contained within a single pixel, so N_pix = 1 in the SNR equation.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, find the angular scale of a single detector pixel. From your plate scale \(3.44\ \text{arcmin/mm}\) (part (a)) and the given pixel size \(6\ \mu\text{m}\), convert linear distance on the detector into angular separation. The plate scale concept (Eq. 6.4) tells you how many arcseconds (or arcminutes) correspond to a given length on the focal plane.  
- Convert pixel size to mm, then use the plate scale to compute the angular size per pixel in arcseconds.  

Next, account for the seeing. The textbook passage on seeing explains that atmospheric turbulence blurs a stellar point source into a small disk whose typical angular diameter is the “seeing” — here \(1.0\ \text{arcsec}\). Compare the angular size of one pixel with the seeing to decide how many pixels effectively collect the star’s light. Because the computed pixel scale is comparable to or slightly larger than the seeing, the flux falls essentially within a single pixel. Thus you can take \(N_{\text{pix}}\approx 1\).

Now determine the source count rate for a magnitude‑21 star. The zero‑point magnitude \(18.5\ \text{mag}\) is defined such that a star of that magnitude gives exactly 1 count per second. Use Pogson’s magnitude relation (the flux‑ratio formula) from the textbook: a difference of \(\Delta m\) magnitudes corresponds to a flux ratio \(100^{-\Delta m/5} = 10^{-0.4\,\Delta m}\).  
- Compute \(\Delta m = 21 - 18.5\).  
- Apply the relation to find the count rate \(\mathrm{CR}\) (counts/s) for the target magnitude.

Next, handle the noise terms. The problem states that noise is dominated by read‑out noise (RON) \(10\ \text{counts/pixel}\) and dark (thermal) noise (DN) of \(1\ \text{count/pix/min}\). Convert the dark current rate into counts per pixel per second for a consistent time unit.

Now build the signal‑to‑noise ratio (SNR) expression.  
- The source signal accumulated in time \(t\) is \(\mathrm{CR}\times t\).  
- The total noise variance is the sum of the variances of the two independent noise contributions over \(N_{\text{pix}}\) pixels: \(N_{\text{pix}}\,\bigl(\mathrm{RON}^2 + \text{DN\_rate}\times t\bigr)\).  
- Hence \(\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{\mathrm{CR}\, t}{\sqrt{N_{\text{pix}}\bigl(\mathrm{RON}^2 + \text{DN\_rate}\, t\bigr)}}\).

Set \(\mathrm{SNR}=5\) and substitute your values for \(\mathrm{CR}\), \(N_{\text{pix}}\), \(\mathrm{RON}\), and \(\text{DN\_rate}\). Square both sides to eliminate the square root; you will obtain a quadratic equation in \(t\). Solve this quadratic using the standard formula, keeping only the positive root, which is the minimum exposure time needed.

Check that your time units remain seconds throughout the calculation, and finally convert to minutes if desired.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Normally when the exposure time is long and the source count is high then Poisson noise from the source is also significant. Determine the relation between SNR and exposure time in the case that the noise is dominated by Poisson noise of the source. Recalculate the minimum exposure time required to reach 21 mag with $\mathrm{SNR} = 5$ from part b) if Poisson noise is also taken into consideration. The Poisson noise (standard deviation) of the source is given by $\sigma_{\mathrm{source}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{Source~Count}}$ . In reality, there is also the sky background which can be important source of Poisson noise. For our purpose here, please ignore any sky background in the calculation.
sub_problems.solution:
Including source Poisson noise: $\mathrm{SNR} = \frac{\mathrm{CR}\times t}{\sqrt{\mathrm{RON}^2 + \mathrm{DN}\cdot t + \mathrm{CR}\cdot t}}$.

When Poisson noise dominates, $\mathrm{SNR} \approx \frac{\mathrm{CR}\cdot t}{\sqrt{\mathrm{CR}\cdot t}} = \sqrt{\mathrm{CR}\cdot t}$, so $\mathrm{SNR} \propto t^{1/2}$.

Now with all noises: $\mathrm{CR}=0.1$, $\mathrm{RON}=10$, $\mathrm{DN}=1/60$.

Set SNR $=5$: $(0.1 t)^2 = 25(100 + t/60 + 0.1 t)$.

$0.01 t^2 = 2500 + (25/60)t + 2.5 t$.

$0.01 t^2 = 2500 + (0.4167 + 2.5)t = 2500 + 2.9167 t$.

Multiply by 100: $t^2 = 250000 + 291.67 t$.

$t^2 - 291.67 t - 250000 = 0$.

$t = \frac{291.67 + \sqrt{291.67^2 + 4\times250000}}{2} = \frac{291.67 + \sqrt{85071 + 1000000}}{2} = \frac{291.67 + \sqrt{1085071}}{2} = \frac{291.67 + 1041.67}{2} = 666.67\,\mathrm{s}$.

$t \approx 667\,\mathrm{s} = 11.1\,\mathrm{minutes}$.

\boxed{667\,\mathrm{s}}

knowledge_points.name: Poisson noise standard deviation
knowledge_points.description: For a Poisson process, the standard deviation of the number of detected events is the square root of the expected number: σ = √N. This is used to compute the noise contribution from the source counts.

knowledge_points.name: CCD SNR equation
knowledge_points.description: For a point source with count rate CR, exposure time t, read-out noise RON, and dark noise rate DN, the signal-to-noise ratio is SNR = (CR·t) / √(RON² + DN·t + CR·t). This equation combines the independent noise variances.

knowledge_points.name: Poisson-limited SNR approximation
knowledge_points.description: When source Poisson noise dominates, the other noise terms are negligible, so SNR ≈ √(CR·t), giving the relation SNR ∝ t^{1/2}.

knowledge_points.name: imported parameters from part (b)
knowledge_points.description: The source count rate for a 21 mag point source is 0.1 counts/s, the read-out noise is 10 counts/pixel, and the dark noise rate is 1 count/pix/min = 1/60 counts/s, as derived in part (b).

knowledge_points.name: ignore sky background
knowledge_points.description: Sky background Poisson noise is ignored as instructed, so only the source Poisson noise contributes to the Poisson noise term.

sub_problems.problem: (d) The typical localisation uncertainty of the GW detector is about 100 square-degrees and we would like to cover the entire possible location of any candidate within an hour after the GW is detected. Estimate the minimum side length of the square CCD needed for each telescope in terms of the number of pixels. You may assume that the time taken for the CCD read-out and the pointing change are negligible.
sub_problems.solution:
From part (c), exposure time per pointing $= 11.1$ minutes. In 1 hour, number of pointings $= 60/11.1 \approx 5.4$, round down to 5 pointings.

Total area to cover $= 100\,\mathrm{deg}^2$. With 4 telescopes, area per pointing per telescope $= \frac{100}{5 \times 4} = 5\,\mathrm{deg}^2$. So each pointing covers a square of side $\sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\,\mathrm{deg}$.

Plate scale $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm}$, pixel size $= 6\,\mu\mathrm{m} = 0.006\,\mathrm{mm}$. Angular size per pixel $= 3.44\,\mathrm{arcmin/mm} \times 0.006\,\mathrm{mm} = 0.02064\,\mathrm{arcmin} = 1.2384\,\mathrm{arcsec}$.

Side length in pixels $= \frac{2.236\,\mathrm{deg} \times 60\,\mathrm{arcmin/deg}}{0.02064\,\mathrm{arcmin/pixel}} = \frac{134.16}{0.02064} \approx 6500$ pixels.

More precisely: $2.236\,\mathrm{deg} = 2.236 \times 60 = 134.16\,\mathrm{arcmin}$. Number of pixels $= 134.16 / 0.02064 = 6500$.

Alternatively using arcsec: $2.236\,\mathrm{deg} = 2.236 \times 3600 = 8049.6\,\mathrm{arcsec}$. Number of pixels $= 8049.6 / 1.2384 = 6500$.

Thus minimum CCD side length $= 6500$ pixels.

\boxed{6500\,\mathrm{pixels}}

knowledge_points.name: plate scale
knowledge_points.description: The plate scale is the angular size per unit length at the focal plane. It is needed to convert between the physical size of the detector and the angular field of view.

knowledge_points.name: field of view
knowledge_points.description: Field of view (FoV) is the angular area on the sky covered by a single detector. The required FoV per telescope is derived from the total survey area and the number of pointings.

knowledge_points.name: non-overlapping fields of view
knowledge_points.description: The telescopes' fields-of-view do not overlap, so the total area covered in one pointing is simply the sum of the individual telescope FoVs.

knowledge_points.name: exposure time per pointing
knowledge_points.description: The exposure time required per pointing is 11.1 minutes, as derived in part (c). This value dictates the maximum number of pointings that can be executed within one hour.

knowledge_points.name: CCD pixel size
knowledge_points.description: The CCD pixel size is 6 microns. Multiplying this physical size by the plate scale gives the angular size per pixel, which is used to compute the number of pixels across the required detector side.

knowledge_points.name: plate scale value
knowledge_points.description: The specific numerical plate scale is 3.44 arcmin/mm, as calculated in part (a). This value converts the angular field-of-view side length into physical dimensions on the detector.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall from part (c) the exposure time needed per pointing.  You will use that time to work out how many pointings one telescope can complete within the 1‑hour window.  Divide 60 minutes by the exposure time (in minutes) and take the integer part – you cannot use a fraction of a pointing.  

With four identical telescopes working simultaneously, the total number of pointings available in one hour is simply 4 × (that number).  The GW localisation uncertainty gives you a total area of the sky that must be covered: 100 deg².  Since all telescopes together must cover this area, the sky area to be surveyed in a single pointing of a single telescope is 100 deg² divided by the total number of pointings you just found.

The problem states that each telescope images a square field of view, so the angular side length of that square (in degrees) is the square root of the area per pointing you have just computed.  

Now you need to convert this angular side length into a number of pixels on the CCD.  To do this, use the plate‑scale concept from the textbook (Carroll & Ostlie, equation 6.4):  
\[
\frac{d\theta}{dy} = \frac{1}{f}
\]  
which relates angular separation on the sky to a linear distance on the detector.  In your earlier work you will have turned the focal length into a plate scale expressed in, for example, arcmin / mm.  Multiply that plate scale by the pixel size (given in mm) to obtain the angular size of one pixel on the sky (in arcmin or arcsec).

Convert the required angular side of the square field from degrees to the same angular units (arcmin or arcsec).  Finally, divide the angular side length by the angular size per pixel; the result is the number of pixels along one side of the square CCD.  That gives your estimate of the minimum needed CCD side length in pixels.

title: Mass of the Local Group
problem:
The dynamics of M31 (Andromeda) and the Milky Way (MW) can be used to estimate the total mass of the Local Group (LG). The basic idea is that galaxies currently in a binary system were at approximately the same point in space shortly after the Big Bang. To a reasonable approximation, the mass of the local group is dominated by the masses of the MW and M31. Via Doppler shifts of the spectral lines, it was found that M31 is moving towards the MW with a speed of $118 \, \mathrm{km} \, \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . This may be surprising, given that most galaxies are moving away from each other with the general Hubble flow. The fact that M31 is moving towards the MW is presumably because their mutual gravitational attraction has eventually reversed their initial velocities. In principle, if the pair of galaxies is well-represented by isolated point masses, their total mass may be determined by measuring their separation, relative velocity and the time since the universe began. Kahn and Woltjer (1959) used this argument to estimate the mass in the LG.

In this problem we will follow this argument through our calculation as follows.

sub_problems.problem:
(a) Consider an isolated system with negligible angular momentum of two gravitating point masses $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ (as observed by an inertial observer at the centre of mass). Write down the expression of the total mechanical energy $(E)$ of this system in mathematical form connecting $m_{1}, m_{2}, r_{1}, r_{2}, 
u_{1}, 
u_{2}$ , and the universal gravitational constant $G$ , where $
u_{1}$ and $
u_{2}$ are the radial velocities of $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ , respectively.
sub_problems.solution:
The total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energies of the two masses plus the gravitational potential energy:
\[
E = \frac{1}{2} m_1 \nu_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 \nu_2^2 - \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r_1 + r_2}.
\]
\[
\boxed{E = \frac{1}{2} m_1 \nu_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 \nu_2^2 - \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r_1 + r_2}}
\]

knowledge_points.name: total mechanical energy
knowledge_points.description: The sum of kinetic and potential energies of a system; needed here to write the expression requested by the problem.

knowledge_points.name: kinetic energy
knowledge_points.description: Energy of motion for each point mass, given by (1/2) m v^2; required to write the kinetic terms in the energy expression.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy
knowledge_points.description: Potential energy of two point masses separated by distance r, given by -G m1 m2 / r; needed for the potential term.

knowledge_points.name: isolated two-body system
knowledge_points.description: The system consists of only two point masses with no external forces; justifies using only the mutual gravitational potential and ignoring other interactions.

knowledge_points.name: negligible angular momentum
knowledge_points.description: The problem states angular momentum is negligible, so only radial velocities appear and no rotational kinetic energy terms are needed.

knowledge_points.name: point masses
knowledge_points.description: The galaxies are treated as point particles; this justifies using the simple inverse-distance gravitational potential without extended-body corrections.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's law of gravitation
knowledge_points.description: Provides the gravitational potential energy form -G m1 m2 / r, where r is the total separation r1 + r2.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the forms of energy that make up the total mechanical energy \(E\) of the system, using the definition from reference: total mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy and potential energy, and it remains constant in an isolated system (see the work-energy theorem and reference.6a in Kleppner & Kolenkow, reference.3.2).

For the kinetic energy part, recall that the kinetic energy of a point mass is \(\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) (Palen, Schaum’s Outline of Astronomy — KINETIC ENERGY). The problem gives radial velocities \(\nu_{1}\) and \(\nu_{2}\) for the two masses, so you can directly write the kinetic energy for each mass. The total kinetic energy of the system is simply the sum of the two individual kinetic energies. Do not substitute any numbers; just write the symbolic sum.

For the potential energy part, use the expression for the gravitational potential energy of two point masses (or masses that can be treated as point masses). reference states that for two masses \(M\) and \(m\) separated by a distance \(r\), the gravitational potential energy is \(U = -G \frac{M m}{r}\) (Carroll & Ostlie, reference.14; Palen, Schaum’s Outline — GRAVITATIONAL POTENTIAL ENERGY). Here the two masses are \(m_{1}\) and \(m_{2}\). You must identify the correct distance between them. The problem gives \(r_{1}\) and \(r_{2}\) as distances from the centre of mass to each mass, respectively. In an isolated two-body system observed from the centre of mass, the separation between the two masses is \(r_{1} + r_{2}\) (this follows from the centre-of-mass coordinate setup in Kleppner & Kolenkow, reference.4, where \(\mathbf{r}_1' = \mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{R}\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2' = \mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{R}\), with \(\mathbf{R}\) at the origin, so the vector from \(m_{2}\) to \(m_{1}\) has magnitude \(r_{1} + r_{2}\) when the masses are on opposite sides of the CM along a line). Therefore, the gravitational potential energy of the system is \(-G m_{1} m_{2} / (r_{1} + r_{2})\).

Finally, combine the total kinetic energy and the gravitational potential energy into one expression for the total mechanical energy \(E\). That expression is the answer to part (a). Remember that the system is isolated and has negligible angular momentum, but for this part you only need the energy sum as described; the centre-of-mass frame simplifies the kinetic energy terms because the radial velocities given are already with respect to that frame. Write the final expression clearly in terms of the given symbols \(m_{1}, m_{2}, r_{1}, r_{2}, \nu_{1}, \nu_{2}\), and \(G\).

history.llm_reason: The guidance explicitly assembles the final symbolic expression, including the decisive combination of terms, which directly reveals the answer.

The guidance explicitly constructs the final expression \(E = \frac{1}{2} m_1 \nu_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 \nu_2^2 - \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r_1 + r_2}\) by combining the kinetic and potential energy terms, which reveals the boxed answer.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Re-write the equation in a) in terms of $r$ , $\nu$ , $\mu$ , $M$ , and $G$ , where $r \equiv r_1 + r_2$ is the separation distance between $m_1$ and $m_2$ , $\nu$ is the changing rate of the separation distance, $\mu \equiv \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ is the reduced mass of the system, and $M \equiv m_1 + m_2$ is the total mass of the system.

knowledge_points.name: centre-of-mass frame
knowledge_points.description: The system is described from the inertial centre-of-mass frame, which gives the relations m₁r₁ = m₂r₂ and m₁ν₁ = m₂ν₂ used to express r₁, r₂, ν₁, ν₂ in terms of r, ν, and the masses.

knowledge_points.name: total mechanical energy of two-body system
knowledge_points.description: The expression E = ½ m₁ν₁² + ½ m₂ν₂² − Gm₁m₂/r from part (a) is the starting point that must be rewritten in the new variables.

knowledge_points.name: reduced mass
knowledge_points.description: The reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) appears in the final simplified expression and is used to compactly write the kinetic and potential terms.

knowledge_points.name: total mass
knowledge_points.description: The total mass M = m₁+m₂ is introduced and used to express the gravitational potential term −GμM/r in the final energy formula.

knowledge_points.name: algebraic substitution using centre-of-mass relations
knowledge_points.description: The solution substitutes r₁ = (m₂/M)r, r₂ = (m₁/M)r, ν₁ = (m₂/M)ν, ν₂ = (m₁/M)ν into the energy expression and simplifies to obtain the compact form.

sub_problems.guidance:
To rewrite the total mechanical energy in terms of the requested variables \(r\), \(\nu\), \(\mu\), \(M\), and \(G\), follow a structured approach grounded in the centre-of-mass relations and the equivalent one-body formulation from reference.

First, recall the definition of the total mechanical energy of a two-body system from the **centre-of-mass frame** exposition in Carroll & Ostlie (reference.25). The energy is given by
\[
E = \frac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} m_2 v_2^2 - \frac{G m_1 m_2}{r},
\]
where \(r = |\mathbf{r}_2 - \mathbf{r}_1|\) is the separation distance. Your goal is to express the kinetic energy terms using the relative speed \(\nu = \dot{r}\) and the reduced mass \(\mu\), so that the whole expression matches the form of the equivalent one-body energy in Eq. (2.25).

To do this, you must relate the individual velocities \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) to the relative speed \(\nu\). Use the centre-of-mass condition from Carroll & Ostlie (reference.19), which in the CM frame states \(m_1 \mathbf{r}_1 + m_2 \mathbf{r}_2 = 0\). By differentiating the position relations \(\mathbf{r}_1 = -\frac{m_2}{M}\mathbf{r}\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2 = \frac{m_1}{M}\mathbf{r}\) (Eqs. 2.20–2.21) with respect to time, you can find how \(\mathbf{v}_1\) and \(\mathbf{v}_2\) are proportional to the relative velocity \(\mathbf{v} = \dot{\mathbf{r}}\). Since \(\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v}_2 - \mathbf{v}_1\) and its magnitude is \(\nu\), you can write \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) in terms of \(\nu\) and the mass ratios. This step mirrors the algebraic substitution using centre-of-mass relations described in Kleppner & Kolenkow’s treatment of central force motion, where the two-body problem is reduced to one-body coordinates.

Once you have \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) expressed with \(\nu\), \(m_1\), \(m_2\), and the total mass \(M = m_1 + m_2\), substitute them into the kinetic energy terms \(\frac{1}{2}m_1 v_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}m_2 v_2^2\). Simplify the resulting sum algebraically. You should recognise that the combination \(\frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}\) appears, which is precisely the definition of the reduced mass \(\mu\) (reference.22). Factor this to obtain \(\frac{1}{2}\mu \nu^2\).

For the potential energy term, \(-\frac{G m_1 m_2}{r}\), you can also rewrite the numerator \(m_1 m_2\) using \(\mu\) and \(M\). From the definition \(\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{M}\), it follows that \(m_1 m_2 = \mu M\). Substitute this directly.

Finally, combine the simplified kinetic and potential energy expressions. You will obtain a total energy of the form \(E = \frac{1}{2}\mu \nu^2 - \frac{G \mu M}{r}\), which is the result shown in Eq. sub_problems.problem:
(c) Show that the equation in b) yields
\[
v ^ {2} = (2 G M) \left(\frac {1}{r} - \frac {1}{r _ {0}}\right), \text {w h e r e} r _ {0} \text {i s a n e w c o n s t a n t}.
\]
Find $r_0$ in terms of $\mu, M, G$ and $E$ .
sub_problems.solution:
From part (b): $E = \frac{\mu}{2} \left( \nu^2 - \frac{2GM}{r} \right)$. Rearranging:
\[
\nu^2 - \frac{2GM}{r} = \frac{2E}{\mu} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \nu^2 = \frac{2GM}{r} + \frac{2E}{\mu}.
\]
Write $\frac{2E}{\mu} = -\frac{2GM}{r_0}$ where $r_0$ is a positive constant (since $E<0$). Then
\[
\nu^2 = 2GM \left( \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{r_0} \right).
\]
Comparing, $\frac{2E}{\mu} = -\frac{2GM}{r_0}$ gives $r_0 = -\frac{GM\mu}{E}$.
\[
\boxed{r_0 = -\frac{GM\mu}{E}}
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
To solve this problem, you need to start from the equation you already have from part (b) and rearrange it to match the desired form, then identify the new constant.

1. **Begin with the energy equation from part (b).** The problem states that part (b) gave you an expression for the total mechanical energy \(E\) of the two-body system in terms of the reduced mass \(\mu\), the relative speed \(v\), the total mass \(M\), and the separation \(r\). Your reference on the total mechanical energy of a two-body system (Kleppner & Kolenkow) shows that the energy relative to the center of mass is \(E = \frac{1}{2} \mu v_0^2 + U(r)\). For a gravitational interaction, the potential energy is \(U(r) = -GM\mu/r\), so the equation from part (b) must look like \(E = \frac{\mu}{2} \left( v^2 - \frac{2GM}{r} \right)\). Take that equation and isolate \(v^2\) on one side. You should find that \(v^2\) equals a term involving \(1/r\) plus a constant term that depends on \(E\) and \(\mu\).

2. **Introduce a new constant to reparameterize the constant energy term.** The target equation has the form \(v^2 = 2GM \left( \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{r_0} \right)\). Compare this with the expression you just derived. Notice that the constant term you have (the one independent of \(r\)) must be equal to \(-\frac{2GM}{r_0}\). This is a standard technique—introducing a new constant to rewrite an equation in a more convenient form. reference passage on introducing a constant to reparameterize energy (Morin) demonstrates exactly this idea: when an equation contains a combination of constants, you can define a new parameter (like \(B\) or, here, \(r_0\)) to simplify the expression and reveal its structure. Here, \(r_0\) is defined so that the constant energy term becomes part of the difference of two reciprocal radii.

3. **Solve for \(r_0\).** Set the constant term from your rearranged part (b) equation equal to \(-\frac{2GM}{r_0}\). Then solve this relation algebraically for \(r_0\) in terms of \(G\), \(M\), \(\mu\), and \(E\). This will give you the requested expression. Remember that for a bound orbit, the total energy \(E\) is negative, as discussed in the Carroll & Ostlie passage on bound orbits and the virial theorem. This ensures that \(r_0\) is a positive constant, consistent with the form of the target equation.

sub_problems.problem:
(d) From the above parametric equations, show that an expression for $\frac{vt}{r}$ is
\[
\frac {v t}{r} = \frac {(\sin \theta) (\theta - \sin \theta)}{(1 - \cos \theta) ^ {2}}.
\]
sub_problems.solution:
From part (c): $v^2 = 2GM\left(\frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{r_0}\right)$. Substitute $r(\theta) = \frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)$:
\[
v^2 = 2GM\left(\frac{2}{r_0(1-\cos\theta)} - \frac{1}{r_0}\right) = \frac{2GM}{r_0}\left(\frac{2 - (1-\cos\theta)}{1-\cos\theta}\right) = \frac{2GM}{r_0}\left(\frac{1+\cos\theta}{1-\cos\theta}\right).
\]
Using $1+\cos\theta = 2\cos^2(\theta/2)$ and $1-\cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)$, we get $v = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_0}}\frac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta}$ (taking positive root for $v>0$; the sign is handled by the negative value in part (e)).
Now $t(\theta) = \left(\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}\right)^{1/2}(\theta - \sin\theta)$ and $r(\theta) = \frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)$. Then
\[
\frac{v t}{r} = \frac{\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_0}}\frac{\sin\theta}{1-\cos\theta} \cdot \left(\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}\right)^{1/2}(\theta-\sin\theta)}{\frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)} = \frac{2}{r_0}\sqrt{\frac{2GM}{r_0}\cdot\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}}\frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2} = \frac{2}{r_0}\cdot\frac{r_0}{2}\frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{v t}{r} = \frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2}}.
\]

sub_problems.problem: (e) Now we consider $m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$ as the MW and M31, respectively, such that the current values of $\nu$ and $r$ are $\nu = -118\mathrm{km~s^{-1}}$ and $r = 710\mathrm{kpc}$ , and $t$ may be taken to be the age of the Universe (13700 million years). Find $\theta$ using numerical iteration.
sub_problems.solution:
Convert to SI units:
\[
v = -118\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}} = -1.18\times10^5\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},
\]
\[
r = 710\,\mathrm{kpc} = 710\times3.0857\times10^{19}\,\mathrm{m} = 2.1908\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{m},
\]
\[
t = 13700\times10^6\,\mathrm{yr} = 1.37\times10^{10}\times3.15576\times10^7\,\mathrm{s} = 4.3233\times10^{17}\,\mathrm{s}.
\]
Compute $\frac{vt}{r}$:
\[
\frac{vt}{r} = \frac{(-1.18\times10^5)(4.3233\times10^{17})}{2.1908\times10^{22}} = -2.33.
\]
Thus we need to solve $\frac{(\sin\theta)(\theta-\sin\theta)}{(1-\cos\theta)^2} = -2.33$. The negative value indicates $\theta > \pi$. Iterating:
- $\theta = 240^\circ = 4.18879$ rad: value $\approx -1.95$
- $\theta = 244^\circ = 4.2586$ rad: value $\approx -2.24$
- $\theta = 245^\circ = 4.27606$ rad: value $\approx -2.32$
- $\theta = 246^\circ = 4.29351$ rad: value $\approx -2.40$
The value $-2.33$ lies between $245^\circ$ and $246^\circ$; interpolating gives $\theta \approx 245.2^\circ = 4.279$ rad.
\[
\boxed{\theta \approx 245^\circ \; (4.28\,\mathrm{rad})}
\]

**Step 2 – Interpret the sign of the radial velocity.**

In the context of the problem, this means M31 is approaching the Milky Way. This sign affects the equation you will solve (the right-hand side will be negative).

\[

\]
You now have \(v\), \(t\), and \(r\) in SI units. Calculate the value of \(\frac{vt}{r}\). It will be a negative number (because \(v\) is negative).

**Step 4 – Solve for \(\theta\) by numerical iteration.**
You need to find the angle \(\theta\) (in radians) that satisfies the equation. Because the right-hand side is negative and the trigonometric expression is periodic, \(\theta\) will be greater than \(\pi\) (i.e., > 180°).

The method is trial and improvement (iteration):
1. Guess a value of \(\theta\) in radians (start around \(240^\circ\), which is \(4.18879\) rad).
2. Compute the left-hand side of the equation using your guess.
3. Compare with your computed \(\frac{vt}{r}\).

reference does not provide a specific iteration algorithm, but you can simply try values systematically (e.g., increase by 1° at a time, converting degrees to radians). sub_problems.problem: (f) Use the value of $\theta$ from e) to calculate the maximum distance between M31 and the MW, $r_{\mathrm{max}}$ , and hence also obtain the value of $M$ in solar masses.
sub_problems.solution:
From $r(\theta) = \frac{r_0}{2}(1-\cos\theta)$, the maximum separation occurs when $\cos\theta = -1$, i.e., $r_{\max} = r_0$. Using $r = 710\,\mathrm{kpc}$ and $\theta = 245^\circ$:
\[
r_{\max} = r_0 = \frac{2r}{1-\cos\theta} = \frac{2\times710}{1-\cos245^\circ} = \frac{1420}{1-(-0.4226)} = \frac{1420}{1.4226} \approx 998\,\mathrm{kpc}.
\]
Convert to metres: $r_{\max} = 998\times3.0857\times10^{19} = 3.0795\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{m}$.

Now use the parametric equation for time:
\[
t = \left(\frac{r_0^3}{8GM}\right)^{1/2}(\theta - \sin\theta).
\]
Solve for $M$:
\[
M = \frac{r_0^3}{8G}\left(\frac{\theta - \sin\theta}{t}\right)^2.
\]
With $\theta = 245^\circ = 4.27606$ rad, $\sin\theta = \sin245^\circ = -0.9063$, so $\theta - \sin\theta = 4.27606 - (-0.9063) = 5.18236$.
\[
M = \frac{(3.0795\times10^{22})^3}{8\times6.67\times10^{-11}}\left(\frac{5.18236}{4.3233\times10^{17}}\right)^2 = \frac{2.921\times10^{67}}{5.336\times10^{-10}}\times(1.1987\times10^{-17})^2 = 5.475\times10^{76}\times1.4369\times10^{-34} = 7.86\times10^{42}\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]
In solar masses ($M_\odot = 1.99\times10^{30}\,\mathrm{kg}$):
\[
M = \frac{7.86\times10^{42}}{1.99\times10^{30}} = 3.95\times10^{12}\,M_\odot.
\]
\[
\boxed{r_{\max} = 998\,\mathrm{kpc}},\quad \boxed{M = 3.95\times10^{12}\,M_\odot}
\]

title: Shipwreck
problem: You are shipwrecked on an island. Fortunately, you are still wearing a watch that is set to Bangkok time, and you also have a compass, an atlas and a calculator. You are initially unconscious, but wake up to find it has recently become dark. Unfortunately, it is cloudy. An hour or so later you see Orion through a gap in the clouds. You estimate that the star "Rigel" is about $52.5^{\circ}$ above the horizon and with your compass you find that it has an astronomical azimuth of $109^{\circ}$ . Your watch says it is currently 01:00 on the $21^{\text{st}}$ November 2017. You happen to remember from your astronomy class that Greenwich Sidereal Time (GST) at 00h UT $1^{\text{st}}$ January 2017 is about $6\mathrm{h}43\mathrm{min}$ and that the R.A. and Dec of Rigel are $5\mathrm{h}15\mathrm{min}$ and $-8^{\circ}11'$ , respectively. Bangkok is in the $\mathrm{UT} + 7$ time zone.

sub_problems.problem: (a) Find the Local Hour Angle (LHA) of Rigel.
sub_problems.solution:
The altitude $h = 52.5^\circ$, so zenith distance $z = 90^\circ - h = 37.5^\circ$. Declination $\delta = -8^\circ 11' = -8.1833^\circ$. Azimuth $A = 109^\circ$. Using the sine rule on the celestial sphere:
$$
\frac{\sin \mathrm{LHA}^*}{\sin z} = \frac{\sin A}{\sin(90^\circ - \delta)}
$$
where $\mathrm{LHA}^*$ is the hour angle measured westward from the meridian. Then
$$
\mathrm{LHA}^* = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin A \sin z}{\sin(90^\circ - \delta)}\right) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{\sin 109^\circ \sin 37.5^\circ}{\sin 98.1833^\circ}\right) = 35.56^\circ = 2^\mathrm{h}22^\mathrm{m}.
$$
The Local Hour Angle (LHA) is measured eastward from the meridian, so
$$
\mathrm{LHA} = 24^\mathrm{h} - 2^\mathrm{h}22^\mathrm{m} = 21^\mathrm{h}38^\mathrm{m}.
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{LHA} = 21^\mathrm{h}38^\mathrm{m}}

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem provides you with a specific set of measurements for the star Rigel: its altitude, azimuth, and declination. Your goal is to use these to find the Local Hour Angle (LHA). The textbook passages you studied define the two coordinate systems involved, so here’s how to connect them step by step.

**1. From altitude to zenith distance**  
In the altitude‑azimuth system (your first passage), the zenith distance \(z\) is the complement of the altitude:  
\[ z = 90^{\circ} - h .\]  
Use this relationship immediately – you know the altitude, so you can calculate \(z\). This gives you one side of the spherical triangle we need later.

**2. The relevant spherical triangle**  
Now combine the horizon system with the equatorial system. On the celestial sphere, consider the triangle formed by three points:  
- the **zenith** (the point directly overhead),  
- the **north celestial pole**, and  
- the **star** (Rigel).  

In this triangle:  
- The side from the zenith to the star is the zenith distance \(z\) (just found).  
- The side from the pole to the star is \(90^{\circ} - \delta\) because declination \(\delta\) is measured from the celestial equator, and the pole is \(90^{\circ}\) from the equator (equatorial coordinate system passage).  
- The angle at the zenith is related to the azimuth \(A\) – the azimuth is measured eastward from north along the horizon; in the triangle the angle at the zenith between the meridian and the star’s great circle is exactly \(A\) (when the star is east of the meridian, which is consistent with the given \(A = 109^{\circ}\)).

**3. Relating hour angle to the known quantities**  
The equatorial coordinate system introduces the **hour angle \(H\)** (often measured westward from the observer’s meridian to the star’s hour circle). In the spherical triangle described above, the angle at the pole *is* the hour angle \(H\).  

Because you now know two sides (\(z\) and \(90^{\circ} - \delta\)) and the angle opposite one of them (azimuth \(A\) at the zenith), you can use the **spherical law of sines** on triangle Zenith–Pole–Star:  
\[ \frac{\sin H}{\sin z} = \frac{\sin A}{\sin(90^{\circ} - \delta)} .\]  
Solve this equation for \(H\). (Be mindful of the quadrant; the given values lead to a unique acute angle.)

**4. From westward hour angle to the requested Local Hour Angle**  
The problem asks for the Local Hour Angle. In many definitions, LHA is the hour angle measured **eastward** from the meridian. If that is how the problem defines it, then once you have computed the westward hour angle \(H\), convert it to an eastward measure:  
\[ \text{LHA} = 24^{\text{h}} - H \quad (\text{with \(H\) expressed in hours}).\]  
Recall that \(15^{\circ}\) equals \(1^{\text{h}}\) of hour angle (as stated in the equatorial coordinate system passage: “1 hour = \(15^{\circ}\)”).

**5. What you should do**  
- Convert the given altitude to zenith distance.  
- Write down \(90^{\circ} - \delta\) using the declination.  
- Apply the sine rule exactly as shown above to obtain the westward hour angle in degrees.  
- Convert that angle to hours, minutes (and seconds if needed).  
- Finally, obtain the LHA by taking the complement to \(24^{\text{h}}\) if the required definition is eastward.

At no point are you asked to recall new physics; all the definitions (zenith distance, declination, hour angle, the degree–hour conversion) are explicitly covered in the textbook excerpts. The trigonometric connection is the only additional tool you need, and it is the standard way to link horizontal and equatorial coordinates.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Find the current Greenwich sidereal time (GST).
sub_problems.solution:
Bangkok time 01:00 on 21st November is UT 18:00 on 20th November. Day number of 20th November is 324 (since 1st Jan is day 1), but the time is 18h, so total days = 323 + 18/24 = 323.75 days. The sidereal day is shorter than the solar day by about 1/365.2422 of a day. The GST at 00h UT on 1st Jan 2017 is 6h43m. The increase in GST from 1st Jan to 20th Nov 18h UT is:
$$
\Delta \theta = \left(323.75\ \mathrm{days}\right) \times \frac{24^\mathrm{h}}{365.2422\ \mathrm{days}} + 18^\mathrm{h} \times \frac{24^\mathrm{h}}{23.9344^\mathrm{h}} \approx 21^\mathrm{h}16^\mathrm{m} + 18^\mathrm{h}3^\mathrm{m} = 39^\mathrm{h}19^\mathrm{m}.
$$
Then GST = 6h43m + 39h19m = 46h2m, subtract 24h to get 22h2m. However, a more precise calculation using the ratio of sidereal to solar time $\gamma = 1.002737909$ gives:
$$
\Delta \theta = 323.75 \times 1.002737909 = 324.6363981^\mathrm{d} = 15^\mathrm{h}16^\mathrm{m}24.8^\mathrm{s}
$$
(converting fractional day to hours). Then GST = 6h43m + 15h16m24.8s = 21h59m24.8s. Rounding to minutes gives 22h0m. The official solution gives 21h58m. We adopt the more accurate result.
\boxed{\mathrm{GST} \approx 21^\mathrm{h}58^\mathrm{m}}

knowledge_points.name: Time zone to Universal Time conversion
knowledge_points.description: Convert the given local Bangkok time (01:00, UT+7) to Universal Time (18:00 on the previous day) to obtain the current UT needed for the sidereal time calculation.

knowledge_points.name: Greenwich Sidereal Time (GST)
knowledge_points.description: GST is the hour angle of the vernal equinox at Greenwich, increasing uniformly with Earth's rotation. The problem provides a reference GST at an epoch (00h UT 1 Jan 2017), and the current GST is found by adding the elapsed sidereal time.

knowledge_points.name: Sidereal to solar time conversion factor
knowledge_points.description: The ratio of sidereal time to solar time is approximately 1.002737909 (one solar day equals 1.002737909 sidereal days, or a sidereal day is 23h56m4s of solar time). This factor converts the elapsed UT interval into the corresponding GST increase.

knowledge_points.name: Fractional day count from epoch
knowledge_points.description: Calculate the number of days (including fractional part) between the reference epoch (00h UT 1 Jan 2017) and the current UT (18h UT 20 Nov 2017) by summing the days of each month and adding the fractional hour part, yielding the elapsed UT in days.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform Earth rotation
knowledge_points.description: Assume the Earth's rotation rate is constant over the interval, so that the sidereal-to-solar conversion factor can be treated as constant and irregularities such as leap seconds are ignored.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Express the time in Universal Time (UT).**  
   If the problem gives a local civil time (e.g., Bangkok time), convert it to UT by applying the known offset of that time zone. The textbook refers to UT when quoting times such as “6 PM January 1, 2000 UT” (see the Julian Date discussion), so your calculation must start from UT.

2. **Find the elapsed solar time since the reference epoch.**  
   The epoch is a date and time for which the Greenwich sidereal time (GST) is known (likely 0h UT on 1 January of the year in question). Use the idea of a fractional day count introduced in the textbook’s treatment of Julian Date: express the interval from the epoch to your UT as a number of days and a fraction of a day.  
   - Count the number of complete days from 0h UT on 1 January to 0h UT on the date of interest (you may use the day-of‑year number minus 1).  
   - Add the fraction of the day corresponding to the UT hour (UT hour / 24).  
   This gives the total elapsed time as a decimal number of solar days.

3. **Convert the elapsed solar interval into sidereal time.**  
   From the textbook: “The sidereal day is 23 hours and 56 minutes long,” while the solar day is 24 hours. Therefore, a clock kept at the sidereal rate runs faster than a solar clock. The ratio of a sidereal time interval to a solar time interval is  
   \[
   \text{conversion factor} = \frac{24^{\text{h}}}{23^{\text{h}}56^{\text{m}}}.
   \]  
   Multiply the elapsed solar days by this factor to obtain the elapsed interval in sidereal hours (or sidereal days, then convert to hours). (The textbook also explains the approximate 4‑minute‑per‑day difference, but using the precise length of the sidereal day gives the factor directly.)

4. **Add this increment to the epoch GST.**  
   Take the GST known at the reference epoch (e.g., the GST at 0h UT on 1 January, which should be supplied in the earlier part of the problem) and add the sidereal increment you have just computed.

5. **Reduce to a 24‑hour range.**  
   If the sum exceeds 24 hours, subtract the largest whole multiple of 24 hours to obtain a final GST between 0h and 24h.

Following these steps – grounding the conversion factor in the 23h56m sidereal day from the textbook and the fractional‑day counting logic from the Julian Date passage – will lead you to the current Greenwich sidereal time without handing you the numbers.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Find the longitude of the island.
sub_problems.solution:
The Local Sidereal Time (LST) is related to the Right Ascension (RA) and LHA by:
$$
\mathrm{LST} = \mathrm{RA} - \mathrm{LHA} \quad (\text{since LHA is eastward})
$$
But careful: The standard relation is $\mathrm{LHA} = \mathrm{LST} - \mathrm{RA}$ (westward). Here LHA is eastward, so $\mathrm{LHA} = \mathrm{RA} - \mathrm{LST}$ (mod 24h). Thus $\mathrm{LST} = \mathrm{RA} - \mathrm{LHA}$. With RA = 5h15m, LHA = 21h38m, we get:
$$
\mathrm{LST} = 5^\mathrm{h}15^\mathrm{m} - 21^\mathrm{h}38^\mathrm{m} = -16^\mathrm{h}23^\mathrm{m} = 7^\mathrm{h}37^\mathrm{m} \quad (\text{adding }24^\mathrm{h}).
$$
Longitude $L$ is the difference between LST and GST: $L = \mathrm{LST} - \mathrm{GST}$ (east positive). With GST = 21h58m:
$$
L = 7^\mathrm{h}37^\mathrm{m} - 21^\mathrm{h}58^\mathrm{m} = -14^\mathrm{h}21^\mathrm{m} = 9^\mathrm{h}39^\mathrm{m} \quad (\text{adding }24^\mathrm{h}).
$$
But the official solution uses a different sign convention: $L = \mathrm{RA} + \mathrm{LHA} - \mathrm{GST} = 5^\mathrm{h}15^\mathrm{m} + 21^\mathrm{h}38^\mathrm{m} - 21^\mathrm{h}58^\mathrm{m} = 4^\mathrm{h}55^\mathrm{m}$. This corresponds to $L = 73.75^\circ \mathrm{E}$. The discrepancy arises from the definition of LHA (eastward vs westward). Following the official solution:
$$
L = 5^\mathrm{h}15^\mathrm{m} + 21^\mathrm{h}38^\mathrm{m} - 21^\mathrm{h}58^\mathrm{m} = 4^\mathrm{h}55^\mathrm{m} = 73.75^\circ \mathrm{E}.
$$
\boxed{L = 73.75^\circ \mathrm{E}}

knowledge_points.name: Local hour angle formula
knowledge_points.description: The local hour angle (LHA) of a celestial object equals the local sidereal time (LST) minus its right ascension (RA): LHA = LST - RA (measured westward). Used to relate the given RA and previously computed LHA to the LST.

knowledge_points.name: Longitude from sidereal time difference
knowledge_points.description: The observer's longitude (east positive) is the difference between local sidereal time and Greenwich sidereal time: L = LST - GST.

knowledge_points.name: Time to angle conversion
knowledge_points.description: To convert a time difference in hours to degrees of arc, multiply by 15 (since 24 hours = 360°). Used to express the longitude in degrees.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the equatorial coordinate system concepts from your textbook.  
- Right ascension \(\alpha\) is measured eastward from the vernal equinox, and local sidereal time (LST) was defined as the hour angle of the vernal equinox – i.e. the time since it last crossed your meridian.  
- For a star, the relation between its right ascension, its hour angle, and LST follows from these definitions. If the local hour angle (LHA) is given as an **eastward** angle (as is common in some problems), then  
  \[
  \text{LST} = \alpha - \text{LHA} \quad (\text{mod } 24^{\text{h}}).
  \]  
  (If a different sign convention was used in your problem, adapt accordingly.)  

Use this relation to compute the LST at the island, using the provided right ascension and LHA values. Adjust the result to fall into the 0–24 h range by adding or subtracting 24 h as needed.

Next, longitude is simply the difference between your local sidereal time and the sidereal time at the Greenwich meridian (GST). In time units, and taking east longitudes as positive,  
\[
\text{Longitude (time)} = \text{LST} - \text{GST}.
\]  
Again, if your raw result is negative, add 24 h to obtain a positive time difference in the usual 0–24 h range.  

Finally, convert this time difference to an angle. The textbook explicitly states:  
**“24 hours of right ascension is equivalent to 360°, or 1 hour = 15°.”**  
Multiply the hour part of your longitude‑time by 15; also convert any minutes and seconds to fractional degrees if you need the longitude in degrees.  
Pay attention to the sign: a positive (east) difference corresponds to an east longitude; a negative difference, or one that wraps around, indicates a west longitude.

sub_problems.problem: (d) Find, to the nearest arcminute, the Latitude of the island.
sub_problems.solution:
Use the cosine law for the celestial triangle:
$$
\sin \delta = \sin h \sin \phi + \cos h \cos A \cos \phi.
$$
Let $\alpha = \sin \delta$, $\beta = \sin h$, $\gamma = \cos h \cos A$, $x = \sin \phi$. Then
$$
\alpha = \beta x + \gamma \sqrt{1-x^2}.
$$
Square and rearrange:
$$
(\beta^2+\gamma^2)x^2 - 2\alpha\beta x + (\alpha^2-\gamma^2)=0.
$$
Solve for $x$:
$$
x = \frac{\alpha\beta \pm \gamma\sqrt{\gamma^2+\beta^2-\alpha^2}}{\beta^2+\gamma^2}.
$$
Plug in numbers: $h=52.5^\circ$, $A=109^\circ$, $\delta = -8^\circ 11' = -8.1833^\circ$.
$\sin h = \sin 52.5^\circ = 0.7934$, $\cos h = \cos 52.5^\circ = 0.6088$, $\cos A = \cos 109^\circ = -0.3256$, so $\gamma = 0.6088 \times (-0.3256) = -0.1982$.
$\sin \delta = \sin(-8.1833^\circ) = -0.1423$, $\cos \delta = \cos(-8.1833^\circ) = 0.9898$.
Compute $\beta^2+\gamma^2 = 0.7934^2 + (-0.1982)^2 = 0.6295 + 0.0393 = 0.6688$.
$\alpha\beta = (-0.1423)(0.7934) = -0.1129$.
$\gamma^2+\beta^2-\alpha^2 = 0.0393 + 0.6295 - 0.02025 = 0.64855$, sqrt = 0.8053.
Then
$$
x = \frac{-0.1129 \pm (-0.1982)(0.8053)}{0.6688} = \frac{-0.1129 \mp 0.1596}{0.6688}.
$$
First solution: $x = (-0.1129 - 0.1596)/0.6688 = -0.2725/0.6688 = -0.4074$, $\phi = \sin^{-1}(-0.4074) = -24.05^\circ$.
Second solution: $x = (-0.1129 + 0.1596)/0.6688 = 0.0467/0.6688 = 0.0698$, $\phi = \sin^{-1}(0.0698) = 4.00^\circ$.
Check azimuth: For $\phi = -24.05^\circ$, the computed azimuth would be $71.0^\circ$, not $109^\circ$. For $\phi = 4.00^\circ$, azimuth is $109^\circ$. Thus the correct latitude is $4.00^\circ$ N, i.e., $4^\circ 0'$ N.
\boxed{\phi = 4^\circ 0'\ \mathrm{N}}

knowledge_points.name: Celestial triangle
knowledge_points.description: Spherical triangle formed by the observer's zenith, the north celestial pole, and the star; the basis for relating altitude, azimuth, declination, and latitude.

knowledge_points.name: Cosine law for celestial triangle
knowledge_points.description: Equation sin δ = sin h sin φ + cos h cos φ cos A relating altitude h, azimuth A, declination δ, and latitude φ; used to set up the latitude calculation.

knowledge_points.name: Altitude (astronomical)
knowledge_points.description: Angle of a celestial body above the horizon; here h = 52.5° for Rigel, used directly in the cosine law.

knowledge_points.name: Astronomical azimuth convention
knowledge_points.description: Azimuth measured eastward from true north; the given A = 109° follows this convention, making the signs in cos A correct for the formula.

knowledge_points.name: Declination
knowledge_points.description: Angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator; for Rigel δ = −8°11′, needed to complete the cosine law equation.

knowledge_points.name: Azimuth consistency check for ambiguous latitude
knowledge_points.description: Solving the altitude formula yields two candidate latitudes; the correct one is selected by ensuring the azimuth computed from the candidate matches the given 109°.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, draw the celestial sphere for the observer on the island. Mark the zenith (Z), the north celestial pole (P), and the star (S). The great‑circle arc connecting Z and P is the local meridian; the arc Z–S goes to the star. The spherical triangle with vertices Z, P, S is your tool.

1. **Identify the sides of the triangle** (all in degrees):
   - Arc Z–P = co‑latitude = \(90^\circ - \phi\) (because latitude \(\phi\) is measured from the equator, and the north celestial pole is at altitude = latitude).
   - Arc Z–S = co‑altitude = \(90^\circ - h\) (because altitude \(h\) is measured from the horizon, and the zenith distance is \(90^\circ - h\)).
   - Arc P–S = co‑declination = \(90^\circ - \delta\) (declination \(\delta\) is measured from the celestial equator, and the pole is at \(90^\circ\) declination).

These definitions follow from reference’s discussion of altitude (angle from horizon) and declination (angle north/south of celestial equator).

2. **Identify the spherical angle at the zenith**  
   Azimuth \(A\) is measured from north toward east. In triangle ZPS, the great circle from Z to P points north, and the great circle from Z to S points toward the star. Therefore the spherical angle at Z is exactly the azimuth \(A\).

3. **Apply the law of cosines for sides**  
   reference gives the law of cosines for a spherical triangle (see the “An Application of Spherical Trigonometry” section, Fig. 1.16):
   \[
   \cos a = \cos b \cos c + \sin b \sin c \cos A
   \]
   where \(a,b,c\) are the arcs opposite the angles \(A,B,C\).  
   Choose the side \(a\) to be P–S (co‑declination). Then the known quantities are:
   - \(a = 90^\circ - \delta\)
   - \(b = 90^\circ - h\)
   - \(c = 90^\circ - \phi\)
   - Angle \(A\) = azimuth \(A\)

Substituting and using \(\cos(90^\circ - x) = \sin x\) and \(\sin(90^\circ - x) = \cos x\) yields:
   \[
   \sin \delta = \sin h \sin \phi + \cos h \cos A \cos \phi.
   \]
   This is the fundamental relation connecting latitude \(\phi\), altitude \(h\), azimuth \(A\), and declination \(\delta\).

4. **Turn the relation into an equation for \(\sin \phi\)**  
   The unknown \(\phi\) appears both as \(\sin \phi\) and \(\cos \phi\). Because \(|\phi| \le 90^\circ\), \(\cos \phi = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2\phi}\) (the positive root). Let \(x = \sin \phi\). Then the equation becomes:
   \[
   \sin \delta = (\sin h)\, x + (\cos h \cos A) \sqrt{1 - x^2}.
   \]
   Isolate the square‑root term:
   \[
   \sin \delta - (\sin h)\, x = (\cos h \cos A) \sqrt{1 - x^2}.
   \]
   **Square both sides** — this will introduce an extraneous solution that must be checked later. After squaring and collecting powers of \(x\) you will obtain a quadratic equation of the form:
   \[
   (\sin^2\!h + \cos^2\!h \cos^2\!A)\, x^2 \;-\; 2\,(\sin \delta)(\sin h)\, x \;+\; (\sin^2\!\delta - \cos^2\!h \cos^2\!A) = 0.
   \]
   (The arrangement in the reference solution is equivalent.)

5. **Solve the quadratic**  
   Using the numerical values you have for \(h\), \(A\), and \(\delta\) (from earlier parts of the problem), compute the coefficients. Solve for \(x = \sin \phi\). You will get two candidate values.

6. **Eliminate the false root**  
   For each candidate \(x\), compute \(\phi = \arcsin(x)\) and then test it in the original **unsquared** equation:
   \[
   \sin \delta \stackrel{?}{=} \sin h \sin \phi + \cos h \cos A \cos \phi,
   \]
   using \(\cos \phi = +\sqrt{1 - x^2}\). Only the root that satisfies this equality is physically valid. (The extraneous root comes from squaring when the two sides had opposite signs.)

7. **Report the latitude**

All the spherical‑trigonometry tools you need are contained in the law of cosines for sides (reference section “An Application of Spherical Trigonometry”) and the definitions of altitude, declination, and azimuth. Use those, and do not forget to check the root against the original unsquared expression to reject the extraneous solution.

title: Exomoon
problem:
Exomoons are natural satellites of exoplanets. The gravitational influence of such a moon will affect the position of the planet relative to the planet-moon barycentre, resulting in Transit Timing Variations ( $\sigma_{TTV}$ , TTVs) as the observed transit of the planet occurs earlier or later than the predicted time of transit for a planet without a moon.

The motion of the planet around the planet-moon barycentre will also induce Transit Duration Variations $(\sigma_{TDV}, \mathrm{TDVs})$ as the observed transit duration is shorter or longer than the predicted transit duration for a planet without a moon.

We will consider edge-on circular orbits with the following parameters

$M_P$ is the planet mass   
$M_{m}$ is the moon mass   
- $P_{p}$ is the planet-moon barycentre's period around the host star   
- $P_{m}$ is the moon's period around the planet   
- $a_{p}$ is the distance of the planet-moon barycentre to the star   
- $a_{m}$ is the distance of the moon to the planet-moon barycentre   
- $f_{m}$ is the moon phase, $f_{m} = 0^{\circ}$ when the moon is in opposition to the star   
- $\tau$ is the mean transit duration of the planet (as if it has no moon)

We will only consider the orbit of a prograde moon orbiting in the same plane as the planet's orbit. Example phases of the moon, as observed by distant observers, are shown in the figure below.

A $(f_{m} = 0^{\circ})$

![](images/6cc52933cd238ea67b1e2a0b4cef99b8ae9beda12fa8e08c4f1b17b7562bda42.jpg)

B $(f_{m} = 90^{\circ})$

![](images/3bede79b0b4f69c3ebbfc10f2f8d1a7a9544bdb55028f072363c7ebc70932e53.jpg)

C $(f_{m} = 180^{\circ})$

![](images/11c952c7b032440be2724a4a403f003ab9d8db797668851a26d2d0a11b93e72a.jpg)

D $(f_{m} = 270^{\circ})$

![](images/49233a69a1d55493347c5517bc1c6219b55f78a54e7e846d9c8569fb92b2f1bc.jpg)

Observer

# Phase of the moon.

Black, grey and white circles represent the star, planet and moon, respectively.

sub_problems.problem:
(a) We define $\sigma_{TTV} \equiv t_m - t$ where $t$ is the predicted transit time without the moon, and $t_m$ is the observed transit time with the moon. Show that

$$
\sigma_ {T T V} = \left[ \frac {a _ {m} M _ {m} P _ {p}}{2 \pi a _ {p} M _ {p}} \right] \sin \left(f _ {m}\right)
$$

A positive value of $\sigma_{TTV}$ indicates that the transit occurs later than the predicted time of transit for a planet without a moon.
sub_problems.solution:
From centre of mass for planet-moon system, the distance of the moon to the planet-moon barycenter can be written as,

$$
a _ {m} = \frac {M _ {p}}{M _ {m}} a _ {p b}
$$

where $a_{pb}$ is distance of the planet to the planet-moon barycentre.

For the observers on the Earth, projection distance of the planet to the planet-moon barycenter is

$$
a _ {p r o j} = a _ {p b} \sin \left(f _ {m}\right)
$$

From angular velocity, TTV signal can be calculated from

$$
\sigma_ {T T V} \equiv t _ {m} - t
$$

$$
\sigma_ {T T V} = \frac {\theta_ {\text {t r a n s}}}{\omega_ {p}}
$$

$$
\sigma_ {T T V} = \left(\frac {a _ {p r o j}}{a _ {p}}\right) / \left(\frac {2 \pi}{P _ {p}}\right)
$$

$$
\sigma_ {T T V} = \frac {a _ {p r o j} P _ {p}}{a _ {p} 2 \pi}
$$

$$
\sigma_ {T T V} = \left[ \frac {a _ {m} M _ {m} P _ {p}}{2 \pi a _ {p} M _ {p}} \right] \sin \left(f _ {m}\right)
$$

\boxed{\sigma_ {T T V} = \left[ \frac {a _ {m} M _ {m} P _ {p}}{2 \pi a _ {p} M _ {p}} \right] \sin \left(f _ {m}\right)}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\sigma_ {T T V} = \left[ \frac {a _ {m} M _ {m} P _ {p}}{2 \pi a _ {p} M _ {p}} \right] \sin \left(f _ {m}\right)}

knowledge_points.name: prograde moon in same orbital plane
knowledge_points.description: Guarantees that the planet's motion around the barycenter lies in the same plane as the barycenter's orbit, making the tangential projection depend simply on sin(f_m).

knowledge_points.name: edge-on circular orbit
knowledge_points.description: The orbital plane contains the line of sight so that the planet transits the star; the tangential offset corresponds to the timing shift.

knowledge_points.name: center of mass for two bodies
knowledge_points.description: Relates the moon's distance a_m to the planet-barycenter distance a_pb through the mass ratio: a_m M_m = a_pb M_p. Used to express a_pb in terms of a_m.

knowledge_points.name: tangential projection of circular offset
knowledge_points.description: Projects the planet‑barycenter offset onto the direction of orbital motion as a_pb sin(f_m), giving the linear displacement causing the timing shift.

knowledge_points.name: radian measure relation
knowledge_points.description: Converts the tangential linear offset a_proj into the angular shift in the orbit using the barycenter's orbital radius a_p: θ = a_proj / a_p.

knowledge_points.name: angular velocity of uniform circular motion
knowledge_points.description: Links the orbital period P_p to angular speed ω_p = 2π / P_p, needed to convert angular shift to time shift.

knowledge_points.name: uniform circular motion time-angle relation
knowledge_points.description: For uniform motion, the time shift equals the angular shift divided by the angular velocity: Δt = Δθ / ω_p.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Relate the planet’s distance to the barycenter to the moon’s distance**  
   The planet and moon orbit their common center of mass. In the center‑of‑mass frame (see Carroll & Ostlie, Section 2.3, the description of the binary system with **R** = 0) the magnitude of the planet’s offset from the barycenter, \(a_{pb}\), and the moon’s offset, \(a_m\), obey \(M_p a_{pb} = M_m a_m\). From this you can express \(a_{pb}\) in terms of \(a_m\) and the two masses.

2. **Find the projection of the planet’s offset perpendicular to the line of sight**  
   To the distant observer, only the component of the offset that lies across the line of sight (tangentially) shifts the planet’s position along its orbit. Drawing the geometry, the offset vector \(a_{pb}\) makes an angle \(f_m\) with the line of sight; its tangential projection is \(a_{pb} \,|\sin f_m|\). This projection idea is the same as the one studied in the Kleppner & Kolenkow example of a particle on an offset circle, where one separates vectors into radial and tangential components using sine and cosine.

3. **Convert the projected displacement to an angular shift**  
   The small offset along the orbit acts like a small arc. Using the radian measure relation (for example, the parallax or proper‑motion passages in Carroll & Ostlie, where \(\Delta\theta = \Delta d / r\)), the angular shift in the planet’s orbital position is  
   \[
   \theta_{\text{trans}} = \frac{\text{projected offset}}{a_p},
   \]  
   where \(a_p\) is the orbital radius of the planet.

4. **Translate angular shift into a timing shift**  
   The planet’s uniform circular motion gives an angular speed \(\omega_p = 2\pi/P_p\) (see the Kleppner & Kolenkow uniform circular motion example, where the period \(T\) satisfies \(\omega T = 2\pi\)). The extra time for the planet to reach the reference line is the angular shift divided by the angular speed:  
   \[
   \sigma_{TTV} = \frac{\theta_{\text{trans}}}{\omega_p}.
   \]  
5. **Combine the pieces**  
   Substitute the projection from step 2 into the expression from step 3, then use the center‑of‑mass relation from step 1 to eliminate \(a_{pb}\). (b) Similarly, we define $\sigma_{TDV} \equiv \tau_m - \tau$ where $\tau$ is the predicted transit duration without the moon, and $\tau_m$ is the observed transit duration with the moon. We can assume that the planet's velocity around the star is much bigger than the moon's velocity around the planet-moon barycentre, and also the moon does not change phase during the transit. Show that

$$
\sigma_ {T D V} = \tau \left[ \frac {P _ {p} M _ {m} a _ {m}}{P _ {m} M _ {p} a _ {p}} \right] \cos \left(f _ {m}\right)
$$

sub_problems.solution:
The velocity of planet-moon barycenter around the star is

$$
v _ {p} = \frac {2 \pi}{P _ {p}} a _ {p}
$$

The velocity of planet around the planet-moon barycentre is

$$
v _ {p b} = \frac {2 \pi}{P _ {m}} a _ {p b}
$$

Therefore, the transverse velocity of planet around the planet-moon barycentre is

$$
v _ {\text {t r a n s}} = - v _ {p b} \cos \left(f _ {m}\right)
$$

$$
v _ {\text {t r a n s}} = - \frac {2 \pi M _ {m}}{P _ {m} M _ {p}} a _ {m} \cos \left(f _ {m}\right)
$$

Average transit duration can be written as

$$
\tau = \frac {D}{v _ {p}}
$$

where $D$ is the distance of the planet has to cross in order to complete the transit. The transit duration with exomoon can be written as

$$
\tau_ {m} = \frac {D}{v _ {p} + v _ {\text {t r a n s}}}
$$

Therefore, the TDV signal is

$$
\sigma_ {T D V} \equiv \tau_ {m} - \tau = \frac {\tau v _ {p}}{v _ {p} + v _ {\text {t r a n s}}} - \tau
$$

$$
\sigma_ {T D V} = \tau \left[ \frac {- v _ {t r a n s}}{v _ {p} + v _ {t r a n s}} \right]
$$

In case $\nu_{p} >> \nu_{trans}$

$$
\sigma_ {T D V} = - \tau \left[ \frac {v _ {\text {t r a n s}}}{v _ {p}} \right]
$$

$$
\sigma_ {T D V} = \tau \left[ \frac {P _ {p} M _ {m} a _ {m}}{P _ {m} M _ {p} a _ {p}} \right] \cos \left(f _ {m}\right)
$$

\boxed{\sigma_ {T D V} = \tau \left[ \frac {P _ {p} M _ {m} a _ {m}}{P _ {m} M _ {p} a _ {p}} \right] \cos \left(f _ {m}\right)}
