sub_problems.problem: 3) Calculate and sketch the pattern of impacts (i.e., the intensity distribution) on the viewing screen that classical physics predicts.
sub_problems.solution:
Most of the bending of the trajectory occurs within a distance from the wire of order $b$. On the scale of $L$, order $b$ is very small indeed. Therefore we may approximate the trajectory by two straight lines with a kink near the wire. Thus, at the viewing surface, the transverse displacement of each trajectory is

$$
\text{transverse displacement} = \theta_{\text{final}} L = 6.21 \times 10^{-5} \times 0.3 = 1.86 \times 10^{-5} \text{ meter} \cong 19 r_0 \gg r_0.
$$

Thus the portions of the beam that pass on opposite sides of the wire have a region of overlap, as shown in the sketch.

The full width of the overlap region is

$$
\text{full width} = 2 \times (\theta_{\text{final}} L - r_0) \cong 36 r_0 = 36 \times 10^{-6} \text{ meter}.
$$

The density of impacts is constant within each region and doubled in the overlap region.

\boxed{\text{Intensity distribution: constant in each single-pass region, doubled in the overlap region of width } 36 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{Intensity distribution: constant in each single-pass region, doubled in the overlap region of width } 36 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}}

knowledge_points.name: Uniform electron beam
knowledge_points.description: The initial beam has a constant number of electrons per unit transverse distance (impact parameter b), which is necessary to determine that the intensity on the screen is uniform in regions where the mapping does not compress or expand.

knowledge_points.name: Wire obstruction
knowledge_points.description: Electrons with impact parameter |b| less than the wire radius r0 strike the wire and are removed from the beam, creating a gap that defines the inner edges of the two deflected beam halves and thus the width of the overlap region.

knowledge_points.name: Constant angular deflection
knowledge_points.description: The angular deflection θ_final of electrons that miss the wire is independent of impact parameter b (as derived in part 2 from the impulse due to the line charge), so each half of the beam is shifted by a constant amount, simplifying the mapping to a pure translation.

knowledge_points.name: Small-angle deflection displacement
knowledge_points.description: For small deflection angles and a localized scattering event, the transverse displacement on a screen at distance L is approximately L θ_final (using tan θ ≈ θ), allowing conversion of angular deflection to spatial shift.

knowledge_points.name: Impact parameter intensity mapping
knowledge_points.description: The intensity distribution on the screen is obtained from the initial uniform distribution via I(x) = I0 Σ |db/dx|^{-1} over all branches; because the mapping is a constant shift, dx/db = 1, giving constant intensity in single-pass regions and doubled intensity where branches overlap.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, you need to translate the small angular deflection into a linear shift on the screen. In the textbook, the small‑angle relation appears as \(D = d\,\theta\) (when the angle is in radians) – for example, the way the diameter of a tennis ball is related to its distance and the small angular size it subtends. Here the role of the angle is played by the deflection angle \(\theta_{\text{final}}\) that you already have, the distance is the screen distance \(L\), and the transverse displacement of a particle is the unknown linear distance. Because \(\theta_{\text{final}}\) is very small, \(\tan\theta \approx \theta\), so the displacement of a particle that grazes the wire surface is simply \(L \, \theta_{\text{final}}\). Be sure \(\theta_{\text{final}}\) is expressed in radians when you multiply.

Now compare that displacement to the wire radius \(r_0\). The wire would cast a geometric shadow of width \(2r_0\) if the particles were not deflected. If \(L\,\theta_{\text{final}} > r_0\), particles that pass on one side of the wire will cross into the region that would otherwise be shadowed, and similarly for the other side. The overlap region is the interval where trajectories from both sides of the wire land. Its half‑width is the amount by which the displacement exceeds the half‑shadow (\(L\,\theta_{\text{final}} - r_0\)), so the full overlap width is \(2\,(L\,\theta_{\text{final}} - r_0)\).

Finally, the intensity distribution on the screen follows directly from counting how many beam portions reach each point. Where particles from only one side of the wire arrive, the intensity is the same as the original beam (constant). Inside the overlap band, both sides contribute, so the intensity is doubled. Sketch a graph of intensity versus position: a uniform background level, with a central rectangular plateau of twice that level, centered on the wire, of width equal to the overlap width you computed. Label the horizontal axis with the appropriate positions and mark the single‑intensity and double‑intensity regions clearly.

sub_problems.problem: 4) Quantum physics predicts a major difference in the intensity distribution (relative to what classical physics predicts). Sketch the pattern for the quantum prediction and provide quantitative detail.
sub_problems.solution:
Associated with the electron beam is a quantum wave pattern whose de Broglie wavelength is

$$
\lambda = \frac{h}{m v_0} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2 m e V_0}} = 8.68 \times 10^{-12} \text{ meter}.
$$

The de Broglie wavelength is so much smaller than the beam width $2b_{\max}$ that one may ignore "single slit diffraction" effects. Rather, to the right of the wire, two plane waves that travel at a fixed angle relative to each other (an angle $2\theta_{\text{final}}$) overlap and interfere. In the region where, classically, the two halves of the original beam overlap, there will be interference maxima and minima.

Reference to the sketch indicates that

$$
\text{Interval between adjacent constructive interference locations} = \text{step in } y = \frac{\lambda/2}{\sin\theta_{\text{final}}} \cong \frac{\lambda/2}{\theta_{\text{final}}} \cong \frac{\frac{1}{2} \times 8.68 \times 10^{-12}}{6.21 \times 10^{-5}} = 7.00 \times 10^{-8} \text{ meter}.
$$

Because the region of overlap has a full width of $\cong 36 \times 10^{-6}$ meter, there will be roughly 500 interference maxima. Note that the interval between adjacent maxima does not depend on either $b$ or $b_{\max}$ (unlike the situation with ordinary "double slit interference").

\boxed{\text{The quantum intensity distribution shows interference fringes with spacing } 7.00 \times 10^{-8} \text{ m, and about 500 maxima within the overlap region.}}

knowledge_points.name: de Broglie wavelength of accelerated electron
knowledge_points.description: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a voltage V0 is λ = h/√(2meV0). This wavelength determines the scale of the quantum interference pattern.

knowledge_points.name: two-beam interference
knowledge_points.description: When two coherent plane waves overlap, they produce an interference pattern of alternating maxima and minima. The electron wave after the wire is modeled as two such plane waves intersecting at angle 2θ_final.

knowledge_points.name: fringe spacing for two intersecting plane waves
knowledge_points.description: For two plane waves of wavelength λ intersecting at angle α, the spacing between adjacent interference maxima on a screen perpendicular to the bisector is Δy = λ/(2 sin(α/2)). With α = 2θ_final, this gives Δy = λ/(2 sin θ_final).

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small angles θ (in radians), sin θ ≈ θ. Applied to simplify the fringe spacing to Δy ≈ λ/(2θ_final) because θ_final ≈ 6.21×10⁻⁵ rad is very small.

knowledge_points.name: neglect single-slit diffraction
knowledge_points.description: Because the de Broglie wavelength (≈ 8.7×10⁻¹² m) is much smaller than the beam width 2b_max (2×10⁻⁴ m), the single-slit diffraction envelope is very broad and can be ignored; the pattern is essentially two-beam interference without a modulating envelope.

knowledge_points.name: classical deflection angle as interference half-angle
knowledge_points.description: The half-angle θ_final between the two interfering plane waves is taken to be the classical deflection angle of an electron passing the charged wire, as calculated in part (2) (6.21×10⁻⁵ rad). This semi-classical link determines the fringe spacing.

knowledge_points.name: interference confined to classical overlap region
knowledge_points.description: The interference pattern occurs only in the region where the two deflected halves of the beam overlap on the screen. The full width of this overlap region is taken from the classical prediction in part (3) (≈ 36×10⁻⁶ m), and is used to estimate the number of interference maxima (≈ 500).

sub_problems.guidance:
First, determine the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons. Use the de Broglie relation \(\lambda = h/p\) (Eq. 3-2 in Eisberg & Resnick). For an electron accelerated through a known potential difference, its kinetic energy \(K\) is given by \(K = eV_0\). The momentum can then be expressed as \(p = \sqrt{2mK}\), which is exactly the procedure followed in Example 3-1(b) of that same textbook section. Compute \(\lambda\) from these expressions. You will find that it is many orders of magnitude smaller than the width of the beam (\(2b_{\max}\)). Because of this, single‑slit diffraction effects are negligible; you may think of the two parts of the beam that are deflected as ideal plane waves that intersect at a small, fixed angle \(2\theta_{\text{final}}\).

Next, analyze the superposition of these two plane waves. In the region where they overlap, the total wave is the sum of the two coherent contributions, just as in the Michelson interferometer described by Georgi or in Young’s double‑slit experiment (Carroll & Ostlie, Fig. 3.3). The intensity pattern arises from constructive and destructive interference. For two plane waves intersecting symmetrically at an angle \(2\theta\), the path difference between waves arriving at a point displaced by \(y\) from the central axis is \(2y \sin\theta\). Constructive interference (bright fringes) occurs when

\[
2y \sin\theta = m\lambda \qquad (m = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots)
\]

Thus, the spacing between adjacent maxima is

\[
\Delta y = \frac{\lambda}{2 \sin\theta}.
\]

Because \(\theta\) is very small, you may use the small‑angle approximation \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) (as justified by the power‑series discussion in Kleppner & Kolenkow, or the simple pendulum analysis where \(\sin\phi \approx \phi\)). This simplifies the fringe spacing to \(\Delta y \approx \lambda/(2\theta)\).

Finally, identify the total width of the overlap region where the two beams interfere. Divide that width by the fringe spacing \(\Delta y\) to obtain the number of interference maxima that appear. The calculation will show a large number of very closely spaced fringes—the characteristic signature of the quantum prediction that differs dramatically from the classical smooth distribution. Carry out the substitutions with your numerical values to obtain the quantitative details.

title: Relativistic Particle
problem:
In the theory of special relativity the relation between energy E and momentum P or a free particle with rest mass $m_{0}$ is

$$
E = \sqrt {p ^ {2} c ^ {2} + m _ {0} ^ {2} c ^ {4}} = m c ^ {2}
$$

When such a particle is subject to a conservative force, the total energy of the particle, which is the sum of $\sqrt{p^{2}c^{2}+m_{0}^{2}c^{4}}$ and the potential energy, is conserved. If the energy of the particle is very high, the rest energy of the particle can be ignored (such a particle is called an ultra relativistic particle).

sub_problems.problem:
1) Consider the one dimensional motion of a very high energy particle (in which rest energy can be neglected) subject to an attractive central force of constant magnitude $f$. Suppose the particle is located at the centre of force with initial momentum $p_{0}$ at time $t=0$. Describe the motion of the particle by separately plotting, for at least one period of the motion: $x$ against time $t$, and momentum $p$ against space coordinate $x$. Specify the coordinates of the turning points in terms of given parameters $p_{0}$ and $f$. Indicate, with arrows, the direction of the progress of the motion in the $(p, x)$ diagram. There may be short intervals of time during which the particle is not ultrarelativistic. However, these should be neglected.

Use Answer Sheet 1.
sub_problems.solution:
Taking the force center as the origin of the space coordinate $x$ and the zero potential point, the potential energy of the particle is

$$
U(x) = f |x|.
$$

The total energy is

$$
W = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m_0^2 c^4} + f |x|.
$$

Neglecting the rest energy, we get

$$
W = |p| c + f |x|.
$$

Since $W$ is conserved throughout the motion, we have

$$
W = |p| c + f |x| = p_0 c.
$$

Let the $x$ axis be in the direction of the initial momentum of the particle. Then

$$
\begin{cases}
p c + f x = p_0 c, & x > 0,\; p > 0; \\
-p c + f x = p_0 c, & x > 0,\; p < 0; \\
p c - f x = p_0 c, & x < 0,\; p > 0; \\
-p c - f x = p_0 c, & x < 0,\; p < 0.
\end{cases}
$$

The maximum distance of the particle from the origin, denoted by $L$, corresponds to $p = 0$. It is

$$
L = \frac{p_0 c}{f}.
$$

From the energy equation and Newton's law

$$
\frac{dp}{dt} = F = \begin{cases}
-f, & x > 0; \\
f, & x < 0,
\end{cases}
$$

we can get the speed of the particle as

$$
\left|\frac{dx}{dt}\right| = \frac{c}{f} \left|\frac{dp}{dt}\right| = c,
$$

i.e., the particle with very high energy always moves with the speed of light except in the region extremely close to the points $x = \pm L$. The time for the particle to move from the origin to the point $x = L$, denoted by $\tau$, is

$$
\tau = \frac{L}{c} = \frac{p_0}{f}.
$$

So the particle moves to and fro between $x = L$ and $x = -L$ with speed $c$ and period $4\tau = 4p_0/f$. The relation between $x$ and $t$ is

$$
\begin{cases}
x = c t, & 0 \leq t \leq \tau; \\
x = 2L - c t, & \tau \leq t \leq 2\tau; \\
x = -2L + c t, & 2\tau \leq t \leq 3\tau; \\
x = c t - 4L, & 3\tau \leq t \leq 4\tau.
\end{cases}
$$

The required plots are shown in Fig. 1 and Fig. 2. In the $(p, x)$ diagram, the motion follows straight line segments: from $(p_0, 0)$ to $(0, L)$ (with $p>0$, $x>0$), then to $(-p_0, 0)$ (with $p<0$, $x>0$), then to $(0, -L)$ (with $p<0$, $x<0$), and back to $(p_0, 0)$ (with $p>0$, $x<0$). The turning points are at $(0, L)$ and $(0, -L)$.

\boxed{L = \frac{p_0 c}{f}, \quad \tau = \frac{p_0}{f}, \quad \text{period} = \frac{4p_0}{f}}

knowledge_points.name: Ultra-relativistic energy-momentum relation
knowledge_points.description: For a particle with negligible rest mass, energy and momentum are related by E = pc. This is used to simplify the total energy to |p|c + f|x|.

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of total energy
knowledge_points.description: The total energy (kinetic plus potential) of a particle subject to a conservative force is constant. Used to equate the initial energy p0 c to the sum |p|c + f|x|.

knowledge_points.name: Potential energy of constant force
knowledge_points.description: For a constant-magnitude attractive central force, the potential energy is U = f|x|. This is needed to write the total energy expression.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law
knowledge_points.description: The time derivative of momentum equals the net force: dp/dt = F. Used to relate the constant force magnitude to the rate of change of momentum.

knowledge_points.name: Speed of ultra-relativistic particle
knowledge_points.description: A particle with negligible rest mass moves at the speed of light, v = c. This gives |dx/dt| = c and determines the linear x–t relation.

knowledge_points.name: Turning point condition
knowledge_points.description: At the turning points of one-dimensional motion the momentum (and kinetic energy) vanishes. Used to find the maximum displacement L by setting p = 0.

knowledge_points.name: Direction of central force
knowledge_points.description: The attractive central force always points toward the origin, so F = -f for x > 0 and F = f for x < 0. This sets the sign of dp/dt in each region.

sub_problems.guidance:
To describe the motion, you need to combine the ultra-relativistic energy relation with the conservation of total energy, then use Newton’s second law to find the speed and the turning points. Here is a step‑by‑step method grounded in your textbook passages.

1. **Set up the potential energy of the constant force.**  
   The problem states an attractive central force of constant magnitude \( f \). From the worked example on the potential energy of a constant force in the textbook, you know that for a force \( F = -f \) (taking the force center as origin and the force pointing toward it), the potential energy is \( U(x) = f |x| \) if you choose \( U(0)=0 \). This absolute value appears because the force always points toward the origin, so the sign of the work integral depends on which side of the origin you are on.

2. **Write the total relativistic energy and apply the ultra‑relativistic limit.**  
   According to the textbook, the total energy of a particle is \( E_{\text{total}} = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4} + U(x) \).  
   The problem says the rest energy can be neglected (the particle is ultra‑relativistic). The textbook teaches that in this limit \( E = pc \). Therefore, the total conserved energy simplifies to  
   \[
   W = |p| c + f |x|.
   \]

3. **Use conservation of total energy to relate momentum and position.**  
   The textbook emphasizes that total energy is conserved. At \( t=0 \) the particle is at the centre \( x=0 \) with momentum \( p_0 \). Hence  
   \[
   |p| c + f |x| = p_0 c.
   \]  
   This equation is the key to drawing the \( (p, x) \) diagram. Because the absolute values appear, you must treat the four sign combinations of \( x \) and \( p \) separately, just as the reference solution does. The result is a set of straight‑line segments in the \( (p, x) \) plane.

4. **Find the turning points from the energy diagram.**  
   The textbook explains that turning points occur where kinetic energy is zero, i.e. where the particle comes momentarily to rest. For an ultra‑relativistic particle, kinetic energy is essentially \( |p|c \), so a turning point corresponds to \( p=0 \).  
   Set \( p=0 \) in the energy conservation equation to find the maximum distance \( L \) from the origin in terms of \( p_0 \) and \( f \). (You will get a simple expression involving \( c \).)

5. **Find the speed using Newton’s second law.**  
   The force is constant in magnitude and always directed toward the origin: \( F = -f \,\text{sgn}(x) \).  
   Newton’s second law says \( dp/dt = F \). The textbook also provides the relation for the speed of an ultra‑relativistic particle: from \( p/E \approx v/c^2 \) and \( E \approx pc \) you can deduce that the particle moves at speed \( c \).  
   Another route: differentiate the energy equation \( |p| c + f |x| = p_0 c \) with respect to time and use \( dp/dt = F \) to find \( |dx/dt| = c \). Thus, except extremely close to the turning points (which the problem allows you to neglect), the particle moves at the speed of light.

6. **Construct the \( x \)‑\( t \) plot.**  
   Because the speed is constant in magnitude and the motion is one‑dimensional between two turning points, the particle simply moves back and forth with speed \( c \).  
   You can compute the time \( \tau \) to travel from the centre to a turning point using \( \tau = (\text{distance})/c \), with the distance obtained in step 4. The period of the full cycle is then \( 4\tau \).  
   On Answer Sheet 1, sketch \( x \) vs. \( t \) as a sawtooth (piecewise linear) function, with slopes \( \pm c \), and mark the turning points’ coordinates on both axes.

7. **Draw the \( p \)‑\( x \) diagram and indicate the direction.**  
   Using the four linear relations from step 3, plot the closed quadrilateral in the \( (p, x) \) plane. The vertices are at \( (p_0, 0) \), \( (0, L) \), \( (-p_0, 0) \), and \( (0, -L) \), where \( L \) is the turning‑point distance you found.  
   Add arrows along the segments to show the direction of motion. For instance, when \( x>0 \) and \( p>0 \), the particle moves away from the origin; when \( x>0 \) and \( p<0 \), it moves back toward the origin, and so on. The arrows should follow a clockwise or anticlockwise loop (you can decide which by tracking the sign of the velocity).

By following this sequence, you use the conservation of total energy, the ultra‑relativistic energy–momentum relation, Newton’s second law, and the turning‑point condition exactly as taught in the provided passages. Carry out the algebraic steps yourself to obtain the explicit coordinates and the period.

sub_problems.problem:
2) A meson is a particle made up of two quarks. The rest mass M of the meson is equal to the total energy of the two-quark system divided by $c^{2}$.

Consider a one-dimensional model for a meson at rest, in which the two quarks are assumed to move along the x-axis and attract each other with a force of constant magnitude f. It is assumed they can pass through each other freely. For analysis of the high energy motion of the quarks the rest mass of the quarks can be neglected. At time t=0 the two quarks are both at x=0. Show separately the motion of the two quarks graphically by a $(x, t)$ diagram and a $(p, x)$ diagram, specify the coordinates of the turning points in terms of M and f, indicate the direction of the process in your $(p, x)$ diagram, and determine the maximum distance between the two quarks.

Use Answer Sheet 2.
sub_problems.solution:
The total energy of the two-quark system is

$$
M c^{2} = |p_1| c + |p_2| c + f |x_1 - x_2|,
$$

where $x_1, x_2$ are the positions and $p_1, p_2$ the momenta of quark 1 and quark 2. For a meson at rest, the total momentum is zero and the quarks move symmetrically in opposite directions:

$$
p = p_1 + p_2 = 0, \quad p_1 = -p_2, \quad x_1 = -x_2.
$$

Let $p_0$ be the momentum of quark 1 when it is at $x=0$. Then

$$
M c^{2} = 2 p_0 c \quad \text{or} \quad p_0 = \frac{M c}{2}.
$$

Using the symmetry, the energy of quark 1 alone satisfies

$$
p_0 c = |p_1| c + f |x_1|,
$$

which is identical to the one-particle problem of part 1 with initial momentum $p_0 = M c/2$. Hence the $(x,t)$ and $(p,x)$ diagrams for quark 1 are as shown in Figs. 3 and 4. For quark 2 the signs of both $x$ and $p$ are reversed; its diagrams are also shown in the same figures.

The maximum distance between the two quarks is twice the maximum displacement of one quark, $L = p_0 c / f$, so

$$
d = 2L = \frac{2 p_0 c}{f} = \frac{M c^{2}}{f}.
$$

\boxed{d = \frac{M c^{2}}{f}}

knowledge_points.description: The rest mass M of a bound system equals the total energy in the rest frame divided by c^2. Used to set M c^2 equal to the sum of quark energies.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of momentum

knowledge_points.name: symmetric motion in two-body system
knowledge_points.description: For two identical particles with zero total momentum under mutual forces, the motion is symmetric: p1 = -p2, x1 = -x2. Used to reduce the two-quark problem to a one-particle problem.

knowledge_points.name: turning point distance from part 1
knowledge_points.description: From part 1, for an ultra-relativistic particle under constant force f with initial momentum p0 at x=0, the maximum displacement is L = p0 c / f. Used to find the maximum distance between quarks.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Identify the total energy of the system in the meson rest frame.**  
   The textbook passage on invariant mass (Taylor & Wheeler) explains that the mass of a system is the magnitude of its total momenergy 4‑vector, and in the zero‑total‑momentum frame the total energy is the rest energy of the system. Therefore the meson’s rest energy is \(M c^{2}\).

2. **Use conservation of momentum.**  
   The problem states the meson is at rest, so its total momentum is zero. As shown in the conservation of momentum passage (Morin, §4.5.1), the total momentum of an isolated system does not change. Here the two quarks are the only particles, so \(p_{1}+p_{2}=0\).

3. **Exploit symmetry of the two‑body motion.**  
   The two quarks are identical, start at the same point, and experience equal and opposite forces. The center‑of‑mass discussion (Kleppner & Kolenkow, §4.4) shows that in an isolated two‑body system the particles move symmetrically about the center of mass. Because the center of mass is at rest, the motion satisfies  
   \(x_{1} = -x_{2}\) and \(p_{1} = -p_{2}\).  
   This allows you to reduce the problem to the motion of one quark.

4. **Apply the ultra‑relativistic energy–momentum relation.**  
   The rest mass of the quarks is neglected, so they are massless. The textbook passages on the ultra‑relativistic limit (Blundell & Blundell, §25.2; Morin, eq. 11.11) state that for massless particles \(E = pc\). Hence the kinetic energy of each quark is \(|p|c\).

5. **Write the potential energy for a constant force.**  
   The force between the quarks has constant magnitude \(f\) and is attractive. The worked example of a constant force in the Kleppner & Kolenkow solution manual shows that for a constant force \(F = -B\) the potential energy is \(Bx\) (up to an additive constant). By the same work‑integral argument, the potential energy of the two‑quark interaction is \(f\) times the distance between them, i.e. \(f|x_{1}-x_{2}|\).

6. **Form the constant total energy.**  
   The total energy of the system is the sum of the kinetic energies and the potential energy:  
   \[
   M c^{2} = |p_1|c + |p_2|c + f|x_1 - x_2|.
   \]  
   Using the symmetry relations from step 3, express this energy entirely in terms of the variables of one quark (say quark 1). You will obtain a relation that is constant throughout the motion.

7. **Determine the initial momentum scale.**  
   At \(t=0\) both quarks are at \(x=0\), so the potential energy is zero. Substitute the initial condition into the total energy expression to find the initial momentum magnitude of each quark. This gives the connection between the initial momentum and the meson mass \(M\).

8. **Find the turning points and the maximum distance.**  
   At a turning point the quark momentarily stops, so its momentum is zero. Set \(p=0\) in the constant‑energy relation you derived, and solve for the maximum displacement of one quark. The maximum distance between the two quarks is twice that displacement. The result will be expressed in terms of \(M\) and \(f\) only.

9. **Sketch the required diagrams.**  
   - **\((x,t)\) diagram:** For one quark, the force is constant in magnitude and always directed toward the origin. This gives a constant acceleration (in magnitude) that reverses sign each time the quark passes through the origin. The resulting motion is a sequence of parabolic arcs. Draw the parabola for quark 1; for quark 2 the sign of \(x\) is reversed, so its graph is the mirror image about the \(t\)‑axis.
   - **\((p,x)\) diagram:** From the energy relation you can see that \(|p|\) decreases linearly with \(|x|\). Therefore the trajectory in the \((p,x)\) plane is a closed linear loop (a diamond shape). Mark the turning points on the \(x\)‑axis at the coordinates you found in step 8. Indicate the direction of the process: starting from the origin with positive momentum, moving to the right while momentum decreases to zero, then reversing direction and returning through the origin with negative momentum, and so on. Draw the curve for quark 1; the curve for quark 2 is obtained by reversing both \(p\) and \(x\) (rotate by 180° about the origin).

sub_problems.problem:
3) The reference frame used in part 2 will be referred to as frame S, the Lab frame, referred to as S', moves in the negative x-direction with a constant velocity v=0.6c. The coordinates in the two reference frames are so chosen that the point x=0 in S coincides with the point $x'=0$ in $S'$ at time $t=t'=0$. Plot the motion of the two quarks graphically in a $(x', t')$ diagram. Specify the coordinates of the turning points in terms of M, f and c, and determine the maximum distance between the two quarks observed in Lab frame $S'$.

Use Answer Sheet 3.

The coordinates of particle observed in reference frames S and $S'$ are related by the Lorentz transformation

$$
\left\{ \begin{array}{l} x' = \gamma (x + \beta c t) \\ t' = \gamma (t + \beta \frac{x}{c}) \end{array} \right.
$$

where $\beta = v/c$, $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta^{2}}$ and v is the velocity of frame S moving relative to the frame $S'$.
sub_problems.solution:
The reference frame S moves with constant velocity $v=0.6c$ relative to the Lab frame $S'$ in the negative $x'$ direction. The Lorentz transformation between S and $S'$ is

$$
\begin{cases}
x' = \gamma (x + \beta c t) \\
t' = \gamma (t + \beta x / c)
\end{cases}
$$

where $\beta = v/c = 0.6$, $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 5/4$. Since the transformation is linear, straight lines in $(x,t)$ map to straight lines in $(x',t')$. It suffices to transform the turning points of the quarks.

For quark 1, the turning points in S are $(x_1, t_1) = (0,0),\ (L,\tau),\ (0,2\tau),\ (-L,3\tau),\ (0,4\tau)$ where $L = p_0 c / f = Mc^2/(2f)$ and $\tau = p_0/f = Mc/(2f)$. Transforming to $S'$:

- $(0,0) \to (0,0)$
- $(L,\tau) \to (\gamma(1+\beta)L = 2L,\; \gamma(1+\beta)\tau = 2\tau)$
- $(0,2\tau) \to (2\gamma\beta L = \frac{3}{2}L,\; 2\gamma\tau = \frac{5}{2}\tau)$
- $(-L,3\tau) \to (\gamma(3\beta-1)L = L,\; \gamma(3-\beta)\tau = 3\tau)$
- $(0,4\tau) \to (4\gamma\beta L = 3L,\; 4\gamma\tau = 5\tau)$

For quark 2, the turning points in S are $(x_2, t_2) = (0,0),\ (-L,\tau),\ (0,2\tau),\ (L,3\tau),\ (0,4\tau)$. Transforming:

- $(0,0) \to (0,0)$
- $(-L,\tau) \to (-\gamma(1-\beta)L = -\frac{1}{2}L,\; \gamma(1-\beta)\tau = \frac{1}{2}\tau)$
- $(0,2\tau) \to (2\gamma\beta L = \frac{3}{2}L,\; 2\gamma\tau = \frac{5}{2}\tau)$
- $(L,3\tau) \to (\gamma(3\beta+1)L = \frac{7}{2}L,\; \gamma(3+\beta)\tau = \frac{9}{2}\tau)$
- $(0,4\tau) \to (4\gamma\beta L = 3L,\; 4\gamma\tau = 5\tau)$

Plot these points in the $(x',t')$ diagram. The first segments of the worldlines are straight lines:

- Quark 1: $x'_1(t') = c t'$ for $0 \le t' \le \gamma(1+\beta)\tau = 2\tau$
- Quark 2: $x'_2(t') = -c t'$ for $0 \le t' \le \gamma(1-\beta)\tau = \frac{1}{2}\tau$

The distance between the quarks is $d'(t') = x'_1(t') - x'_2(t') = 2c t'$ for $0 \le t' \le \frac{1}{2}\tau$, which increases linearly. The maximum occurs at $t' = \frac{1}{2}\tau$:

$$
d'_{\text{max}} = 2c \cdot \frac{1}{2}\tau = c\tau = c \cdot \frac{Mc}{2f} = \frac{Mc^2}{2f}.
$$

Alternatively, using the transformed coordinates: $d'_{\text{max}} = 2c \gamma (1-\beta) \tau = 2\gamma(1-\beta)L = \frac{Mc^2}{2f}$.

\boxed{d'_{\text{max}} = \frac{Mc^2}{2f}}

sub_problems.problem: 4) For a meson with rest energy $Mc^{2}=140$ MeV and velocity 0.60c relative to the Lab frame $S''$, determine its energy $E'$ in the Lab Frame $S''$.
sub_problems.solution:
The meson has rest energy $Mc^{2}=140$ MeV and moves with velocity $v=0.60c$ relative to the Lab frame $S''$. Its energy in the Lab frame is given by the relativistic energy formula:

$$
E' = \frac{Mc^{2}}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}}},
$$

where $\beta = v/c = 0.60$. Then $\sqrt{1 - \beta^{2}} = \sqrt{1 - 0.36} = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8$. Substituting the values:

$$
E' = \frac{140 \text{ MeV}}{0.8} = 175 \text{ MeV}.
$$

\boxed{E' = 175 \text{ MeV}}

knowledge_points.name: relativistic energy formula
knowledge_points.description: The total energy of a particle with rest mass M moving at speed v is E = Mc^2 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2). This formula is directly applied to compute the meson's energy in the lab frame.

knowledge_points.name: given rest energy
knowledge_points.description: The meson's rest energy Mc^2 is given as 140 MeV. This numerical value is required as input to the energy formula.

knowledge_points.name: given lab velocity
knowledge_points.description: The meson's velocity relative to the lab frame S'' is given as 0.60c. This determines the Lorentz factor used in the energy calculation.

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem gives you the rest energy of a meson (\(Mc^2 = 140\) MeV) and its speed relative to the Lab frame (\(v = 0.60c\)). You are asked for its total energy in the Lab frame.

1. **Identify the relevant formula from the textbook.**  
   The textbook passages provide the relativistic total energy formula in two equivalent forms. For a particle of rest mass \(m_0\) moving at speed \(U\),  
   \[
   E = \frac{m_0 c^2}{\sqrt{1 - U^2/c^2}} = m(U)c^2,
   \]  
   as shown in Eq. (6-13) of French’s *Special Relativity*. The same expression appears in Taylor & Wheeler’s Eq. (7-11) as \(E = m\gamma\). Here, the rest energy is already given as \(Mc^2\), so you do not need to separate mass and \(c^2\).

2. **Interpret the given data in terms of the formula.**  
   The rest energy \(Mc^2\) plays the role of \(m_0 c^2\) in Eq. (6-13). The speed \(v = 0.60c\) gives the ratio \(\beta = v/c = 0.60\). The total energy in the Lab frame is then  
   \[
   E' = \frac{Mc^2}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^2}}.
   \]

3. **Why this formula applies.**  
   The passages explain that the relativistic energy has two parts: rest energy plus kinetic energy. At zero speed the formula reduces to the rest energy (Taylor & Wheeler Eq. 7-13). At any speed, the factor \(1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}\) accounts for the motion. Since you already have the rest energy, you use the total-energy form directly, as in the worked logic surrounding Eq. (6-13).

4. **Carry out the steps (you will do this yourself).**  
   - Compute \(\beta = 0.60\).  
   - Compute \(\beta^2\).  
   - Compute \(1 - \beta^2\).  
   - Take the square root to get the denominator.  
   - Divide the given rest energy (140 MeV) by that denominator.  

   The result is the meson’s total energy in the Lab frame. This is exactly the procedure illustrated in the derivation of Eq. (6-13) and the surrounding examples in the textbook.

title: Collision of Discs with Surface Friction
problem: A homogeneous disc A of mass m and radius $R_{A}$ moves translationally on a smooth horizontal x-y plane in the x direction with a velocity V (see the figure on the next page). The center of the disk is at a distance b from the x-axis. It collides with a stationary homogeneous disc B whose center is initially located at the origin of the coordinate system. The disc B has the same mass and the same thickness as A, but its radius is $R_{B}$ . It is assumed that the velocities of the discs at their point of contact, in the direction perpendicular to the line joining their centers, are equal after the collision. It is also assumed that the magnitudes of the relative velocities of the discs along the line joining their centers are the same before and after the collision.

sub_problems.problem: 1) For such a collision determine the $X$ and $Y$ components of the velocities of the two discs after the collision, i.e. $V_{AX}^{\prime}$, $V_{AY}^{\prime}$, $V_{BX}^{\prime}$ and $V_{BY}^{\prime}$ in terms of $m$, $R_A$, $R_B$, $V$ and $b$.
sub_problems.solution:
Let $\mathbf{n}$ be the unit vector along the normal to the surfaces at the point of contact and $\mathbf{t}$ the tangential unit vector. Let $\varphi$ be the angle between $\mathbf{n}$ and the $x$-axis. Then

$$
b = (R_A + R_B) \sin \varphi.
$$

The momentum components of A and B along $\mathbf{n}$ and $\mathbf{t}$ before collision are:

$$
m V_{An} = m V \cos \varphi, \quad m V_{Bn} = 0,
$$

$$
m V_{At} = m V \sin \varphi, \quad m V_{Bt} = 0.
$$

Denote the corresponding momentum components after collision by $m V_{An}'$, $m V_{Bn}'$, $m V_{At}'$, $m V_{Bt}'$. Let $\omega_A$ and $\omega_B$ be the angular velocities of A and B about their centers after collision, and $I_A$, $I_B$ their moments of inertia:

$$
I_A = \frac{1}{2} m R_A^2, \quad I_B = \frac{1}{2} m R_B^2.
$$

Conservation of linear momentum gives:

$$
m V \cos \varphi = m V_{An}' + m V_{Bn}', \tag{1}
$$

$$
m V \sin \varphi = m V_{At}' + m V_{Bt}'. \tag{2}
$$

Conservation of angular momentum about the axis through O gives:

$$
m V b = m V_{At}' (R_A + R_B) + I_A \omega_A + I_B \omega_B. \tag{3}
$$

The impulse of the friction force on B relates tangential momentum change and angular momentum:

$$
m V_{Bt}' R_B = I_B \omega_B. \tag{4}
$$

During the collision, the tangential velocities at the point of contact are equal:

$$
V_{At}' - \omega_A R_A = V_{Bt}' - \omega_B R_B. \tag{5}
$$

The magnitudes of the relative normal velocities before and after collision are equal:

$$
V \cos \varphi = V_{Bn}' - V_{An}'. \tag{6}
$$

From Eqs. (1) and (6):

$$
V_{An}' = 0, \quad V_{Bn}' = V \cos \varphi.
$$

From Eqs. (2) to (5):

$$
V_{At}' = \frac{5}{6} V \sin \varphi, \quad V_{Bt}' = \frac{1}{6} V \sin \varphi,
$$

$$
\omega_A = \frac{V \sin \varphi}{3 R_A}, \quad \omega_B = \frac{V \sin \varphi}{3 R_B}.
$$

Using $\sin \varphi = b/(R_A+R_B)$ and $\cos \varphi = \sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2 - b^2}/(R_A+R_B)$, the $x$ and $y$ components after collision are:

$$
V_{Ax}' = V_{An}' \cos \varphi + V_{At}' \sin \varphi = \frac{5 V b^2}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2},
$$

$$
V_{Ay}' = -V_{An}' \sin \varphi + V_{At}' \cos \varphi = \frac{5 V b \sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2 - b^2}}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2},
$$

$$
V_{Bx}' = V_{Bn}' \cos \varphi + V_{Bt}' \sin \varphi = V \left[ 1 - \frac{5 b^2}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2} \right],
$$

$$
V_{By}' = -V_{Bn}' \sin \varphi + V_{Bt}' \cos \varphi = - \frac{5 V b \sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2 - b^2}}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2}.
$$

\boxed{V_{Ax}' = \frac{5 V b^2}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2}} \\
\boxed{V_{Ay}' = \frac{5 V b \sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2 - b^2}}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2}} \\
\boxed{V_{Bx}' = V \left[ 1 - \frac{5 b^2}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2} \right]} \\
\boxed{V_{By}' = - \frac{5 V b \sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2 - b^2}}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{V_{Ax}' = \frac{5 V b^2}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2}} \\ \boxed{V_{Ay}' = \frac{5 V b \sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2 - b^2}}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2}} \\ \boxed{V_{Bx}' = V \left[ 1 - \frac{5 b^2}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2} \right]} \\ \boxed{V_{By}' = - \frac{5 V b \sqrt{(R_A+R_B)^2 - b^2}}{6 (R_A+R_B)^2}}

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of linear momentum
knowledge_points.description: The two-disc system experiences no external horizontal forces during the collision, so the total linear momentum vector is conserved. This yields two scalar equations for the normal and tangential components (Eqs. 1 and 2 in the solution).

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of angular momentum
knowledge_points.description: About the origin O, the total angular momentum of the system is conserved because there are no external torques in the horizontal plane. This gives Eq. (3), relating the initial angular momentum of disc A to the final orbital and spin angular momenta of both discs.

knowledge_points.name: Moment of inertia of a solid disc
knowledge_points.description: For a homogeneous disc of mass m and radius R, the moment of inertia about its central axis is I = (1/2) m R^2. This formula is required to express the spin angular momentum of discs A and B in Eqs. (3) and (4).

knowledge_points.name: Angular impulse-momentum theorem
knowledge_points.description: For a rigid body, the angular impulse (torque integrated over time) equals the change in angular momentum. Applied to disc B, the tangential impulse at the contact point creates a torque R_B F_t, leading to the relation m V_{Bt}' R_B = I_B ω_B (Eq. 4).

knowledge_points.name: Post-collision tangential velocity equality at contact point
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that after the collision, the velocities of the discs at the point of contact in the direction perpendicular to the line of centers are equal. This no-slip condition gives Eq. (5): V_{At}' - ω_A R_A = V_{Bt}' - ω_B R_B.

knowledge_points.name: Normal restitution coefficient equal to 1
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the magnitudes of the relative velocities of the discs along the line joining their centers are the same before and after the collision. This perfectly elastic normal collision condition gives Eq. (6): V cos φ = V_{Bn}' - V_{An}'.

knowledge_points.name: Impact parameter geometry for two discs
knowledge_points.description: The impact parameter b is related to the collision angle φ by sin φ = b/(R_A+R_B). This geometric relation, derived from the fact that at contact the center-to-center distance is R_A+R_B and the y-coordinate of A's center is b, is used to express the final velocity components in terms of the given parameters.

sub_problems.problem: 2) Determine the kinetic energies $E_A'$ for disc A and $E_B'$ for disc B after the collision in terms of $m, R_A, R_B, V$ and $b$.
sub_problems.solution:
After the collision, the kinetic energy of disc A is

$$
E_A' = \frac{1}{2} m (V_{Ax}'^2 + V_{Ay}'^2) + \frac{1}{2} I_A \omega_A^2 = \frac{3 m V^2 b^2}{8 (R_A + R_B)^2}
$$

while the kinetic energy of disc B is

$$
E_B' = \frac{1}{2} m (V_{Bx}'^2 + V_{By}'^2) + \frac{1}{2} I_B \omega_B^2 = \frac{1}{2} m V^2 \left[ 1 - \frac{11 b^2}{12 (R_A + R_B)^2} \right]
$$

\boxed{E_A' = \frac{3 m V^2 b^2}{8 (R_A + R_B)^2}} \\
\boxed{E_B' = \frac{1}{2} m V^2 \left[ 1 - \frac{11 b^2}{12 (R_A + R_B)^2} \right]}
sub_problems.answer:
\boxed{E_A' = \frac{3 m V^2 b^2}{8 (R_A + R_B)^2}} \\
\boxed{E_B' = \frac{1}{2} m V^2 \left[ 1 - \frac{11 b^2}{12 (R_A + R_B)^2} \right]}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the post‑collision kinetic energies of the discs, use the fact that a rigid body’s total kinetic energy is the sum of the translational kinetic energy of its centre of mass and its rotational kinetic energy about the centre of mass. This separation is derived in the textbook (see the discussion around Eq. (8.15) in Section 8.6.3):  

\[
K = \frac{1}{2} M V^{2} + \frac{1}{2} I_{0}\,\omega^{2}
\]

where \(V\) is the speed of the centre of mass and \(I_{0}\) is the moment of inertia about the rotation axis through the centre of mass. Since both discs are moving in the plane, you can treat the translational part with the two velocity components you have already determined from the collision analysis.

1. **Translational kinetic energy** – For disc A, the speed squared is \(V_{Ax}'^{2} + V_{Ay}'^{2}\). By definition (Section 5.3.3), the translational kinetic energy is \(\frac{1}{2} m (V_{Ax}'^{2} + V_{Ay}'^{2})\). Do the same for disc B with its own post‑collision velocity components.

2. **Rotational kinetic energy** – Each disc is uniform, and the textbook’s worked‑out drum example (Section 7.8.1) tells you that the moment of inertia of a uniform disc about its symmetry axis is \(\frac{1}{2} m R^{2}\). Therefore, for disc A,  

   \[
   I_{A} = \frac{1}{2} m R_{A}^{2},
   \qquad
   K_{\text{rot},A} = \frac{1}{2} I_{A} \,\omega_{A}^{2}
   \]

   and similarly for disc B, \(I_{B} = \frac{1}{2} m R_{B}^{2}\) and \(K_{\text{rot},B} = \frac{1}{2} I_{B} \,\omega_{B}^{2}\).

3. **Total kinetic energy** – For each disc, simply add the translational and rotational contributions:

   \[
   E_{A}' = \frac{1}{2} m \bigl(V_{Ax}'^{2} + V_{Ay}'^{2}\bigr) + \frac{1}{2} \Bigl(\frac{1}{2} m R_{A}^{2}\Bigr) \omega_{A}^{2},
   \qquad
   E_{B}' = \frac{1}{2} m \bigl(V_{Bx}'^{2} + V_{By}'^{2}\bigr) + \frac{1}{2} \Bigl(\frac{1}{2} m R_{B}^{2}\Bigr) \omega_{B}^{2}.
   \]

4. **Insert the known kinematics** – In your previous steps of the problem you should have expressed the post‑collision velocity components \(V_{Ax}', V_{Ay}'\), etc., and the angular speeds \(\omega_{A}, \omega_{B}\) in terms of \(m, R_{A}, R_{B}, V,\) and \(b\). Substitute those expressions into the formulas above.

5. **Simplify** – Combine the terms algebraically. The final result will be a compact expression depending only on the required parameters. For the algebra, remember to keep the squares and to treat the fractions carefully. No further physical principles are needed beyond the kinetic‑energy formulas shown here.

title: Gravitational Red Shift and the Measurement of Stellar Mass
problem:
(a) A photon of frequency $f$ possesses an effective inertial mass $m$ determined by its energy. Assume that it has a gravitational mass equal to this inertial mass. Accordingly, a photon emitted at the surface of a star will lose energy when it escapes from the star's gravitational field. Show that the frequency shift $\Delta f$ of the photon when it escapes from the surface of the star to infinity is given by

$$
\frac{\Delta f}{f} \simeq - \frac{G M}{R c^{2}}
$$

for $\Delta f\ll f$ where:

- $G =$ gravitational constant
- $R =$ radius of the star
- $c =$ velocity of light
- $M =$ mass of the star.

sub_problems.problem:
(a) A photon of frequency $f$ possesses an effective inertial mass $m$ determined by its energy. Assume that it has a gravitational mass equal to this inertial mass. Accordingly, a photon emitted at the surface of a star will lose energy when it escapes from the star's gravitational field. Show that the frequency shift $\Delta f$ of the photon when it escapes from the surface of the star to infinity is given by

$$
\frac{\Delta f}{f} \simeq - \frac{G M}{R c^{2}}
$$

for $\Delta f\ll f$ where:

- $G =$ gravitational constant   
- $R =$ radius of the star   
- $c =$ velocity of light   
- $M =$ mass of the star.

Thus, the red-shift of a known spectral line measured a long way from the star can be used to measure the ratio M/R. Knowledge of R will allow the mass of the star to be determined.
sub_problems.solution:
A photon of energy $E = hf$ has an effective inertial mass $m = E/c^2 = hf/c^2$.  Assuming gravitational mass equals inertial mass, the photon emitted from the surface of a star loses energy as it escapes the gravitational field.  By conservation of energy, the change in photon energy equals the change in gravitational potential energy:

$$h f_i - h f_f = -\frac{GM m_f}{\infty} - \left(-\frac{GM m_i}{R}\right) = \frac{GM m_i}{R}.$$

Since the frequency shift is small ($\Delta f \ll f$), we approximate $m_f \approx m_i = h f_i / c^2$.  Substituting:

$$h f_f = h f_i - \frac{GM}{R} \cdot \frac{h f_i}{c^2} = h f_i \left(1 - \frac{GM}{R c^2}\right).$$

Thus,

$$\frac{f_f}{f_i} = 1 - \frac{GM}{R c^2},$$

and the fractional frequency shift is

$$\frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{f_f - f_i}{f_i} = -\frac{GM}{R c^2}.$$

The negative sign indicates a red-shift.  Therefore,

$$\boxed{\frac{\Delta f}{f} \simeq -\frac{GM}{R c^2}}.$$

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Photon energy and effective mass.**  
   From the photon energy–frequency relation in reference (Eisberg & Resnick: \(E = h\nu\)), write the energy of the photon before it leaves the star’s surface as \(E = hf\).  
   Using the inertia of energy (A. P. French: a photon’s energy contributes an inertial mass \(m = E/c^2\)), assign the photon an effective inertial mass \(m = hf/c^2\).

2. **Gravitational mass equals inertial mass.**  
   The equivalence principle (Carroll & Ostlie; Kleppner & Kolenkow) tells us that gravitational mass is proportional to inertial mass and, by choice of units, is numerically equal to it. Therefore, treat the photon’s gravitational mass as the same \(m\) you just found.

3. **Gravitational potential energy at the star’s surface.**  
   Newtonian gravitational potential energy for a point mass \(m\) at distance \(r\) from a star of mass \(M\) is given in the textbooks (Morin, reference.41; Kleppner & Kolenkow, contour-line example) as \(U = -GMm/r\).  
   At the surface, \(r = R\), so the photon’s potential energy is \(U_{\text{surface}} = -GMm/R\), with \(m\) evaluated at the surface.

4. **Conservation of energy.**  
   The total energy of an isolated system is conserved (Kleppner & Kolenkow, 5.10; Eisberg & Resnick, relativistic energy). Apply this to the photon + star system: the photon’s energy plus its gravitational potential energy at the surface must equal its energy plus potential energy at infinity. At infinity, the potential energy vanishes (distance → ∞), so  
   \[
   hf_i + \left(-\frac{GMm_i}{R}\right) = hf_f + 0,
   \]  
   where \(f_i\) is the frequency at emission, \(f_f\) the frequency at infinity, and \(m_i = hf_i/c^2\).

5. **Small‑shift approximation.**  
   Because the problem states \(\Delta f \ll f\), the photon’s mass changes very little. The small‑shift (or low‑velocity) approximation discussed in Taylor & Wheeler (series expansions, §7.5) and A. P. French (Doppler‑shift expansions) justifies neglecting the tiny difference between \(m_i\) and \(m_f\) in the potential‑energy term. Hence you may use \(m_i\) in the potential energy without introducing a significant error.

6. **Combine and isolate the frequency shift.**  
   Substitute \(m_i = hf_i/c^2\) into the conservation‑of‑energy equation. You will obtain an equation that relates \(f_f\) to \(f_i\). Solve for the ratio \(f_f/f_i\) and then compute the fractional shift \(\Delta f/f = (f_f - f_i)/f_i\).  
   The algebra is straightforward; carry it out step by step. When you simplify, you will obtain the expression for the redshift that the problem asks you to show. The minus sign tells you that the frequency decreases (the photon is red‑shifted).

sub_problems.solution:
For the emitted photon, conservation of energy and momentum in the laboratory frame gives:

Let $m_0$ be the rest mass of the atom before decay, $m_0'$ after decay, and $hf$ the photon energy.  The internal energy change is
\[
\Delta E = (m_0 - m_0')c^2.
\]

Before decay, the total energy is $E = m_0 c^2$ (atom at rest).  After decay, the atom recoils with momentum $p$ and the photon has momentum $hf/c$.  By conservation of momentum, $p = hf/c$.  The total energy after decay is
\[
E = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m_0'^2 c^4} + hf.
\]

Equating the energies:
\[
m_0 c^2 = \sqrt{(hf)^2 + m_0'^2 c^4} + hf.
\]

Rearrange and square:
\[
(m_0 c^2 - hf)^2 = (hf)^2 + m_0'^2 c^4,
\]
\[
m_0^2 c^4 - 2 hf m_0 c^2 = m_0'^2 c^4.
\]

Using $m_0^2 - m_0'^2 = (m_0 - m_0')(m_0 + m_0')$ and $\Delta E = (m_0 - m_0')c^2$, we obtain
\[
2 hf m_0 c^2 = (m_0^2 - m_0'^2)c^4 = \Delta E\,(m_0 + m_0')c^2.
\]

Since $m_0 + m_0' = 2m_0 - (m_0 - m_0') = 2m_0 - \frac{\Delta E}{c^2}$, we have
\[
2 hf m_0 c^2 = \Delta E\left(2m_0 c^2 - \Delta E\right),
\]
\[
hf = \Delta E\left(1 - \frac{\Delta E}{2 m_0 c^2}\right).
\]

If recoil is ignored, $hf_0 = \Delta E$.  Hence the fractional frequency shift due to recoil is
\[
\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} = \frac{f - f_0}{f_0} = -\frac{\Delta E}{2 m_0 c^2}.
\]

For the $He^+$ transition $n=2\to1$, using Bohr theory for a hydrogen-like ion with $Z=2$:
\[
\Delta E = 13.6\,\text{eV} \times 2^2 \times \left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right) = 40.8\,\text{eV}.
\]
The rest energy of the $He^+$ ion is $m_0 c^2 = 3.752 \times 10^6\,\text{eV}$.  Thus
\[
\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} = \frac{40.8}{2 \times 3.752 \times 10^6} \approx 5.44 \times 10^{-12}.
\]

This is negligible compared to the gravitational red-shift of order $10^{-5}$.

\[
\boxed{\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} = \frac{\Delta E}{2 m_0 c^2}}
\]
\[
\boxed{\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} \approx 5.44 \times 10^{-12}}
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the frequency correction due to recoil, follow a step-by-step derivation that mirrors the “Emission” example in French’s *Special Relativity* (reference). That example shows how to combine conservation of energy, conservation of momentum, and the relativistic energy–momentum relation for a stationary atom emitting a photon. Your task is to apply the same reasoning to the He⁺ ion.

**1. Set up conservation of momentum**  
The atom is initially at rest, so its total momentum is zero. After emission, the photon carries momentum \(p_\gamma = hf/c = E_\gamma/c\) (as explained in Taylor & Wheeler, reference.4, or Eisberg & Resnick, reference‑4). The recoiling atom has momentum \(\mathbf{p}\). Conservation of momentum (Morin, reference.5.1) gives \(0 = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{p}_\gamma\), so the magnitudes are equal: \(p = E_\gamma/c\).

**2. Set up conservation of total relativistic energy**  
Before decay: total energy is just the rest energy of the initial atom, \(m_0c^2\).  
After decay: total energy is the photon energy \(E_\gamma\) plus the total relativistic energy of the recoiling atom. The atom’s total energy is given by the relativistic energy–momentum relation (see Griffiths, Example 12.9, or French, reference‑19): \(E_{\text{atom}} = \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m_0'^2c^4}\), where \(m_0'\) is the rest mass of the atom after emission.  
Thus, conservation of energy reads  
\[
m_0c^2 = \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m_0'^2c^4} + E_\gamma .
\]

**3. Combine the conservation equations**  
Substitute \(p = E_\gamma/c\) into the energy equation. You will obtain an equation that involves only \(E_\gamma\), the initial rest mass \(m_0\), and the final rest mass \(m_0'\).

Now introduce the internal energy release of the transition, \(Q_0 = m_0c^2 - m_0'c^2\) (the energy that would be given to the photon if the atom did not recoil). Follow the algebraic manipulation exactly as in the French emission example:  
- Rearrange the energy equation to isolate the square root.  
- Square both sides and simplify.  
- Express \(m_0'^2c^4\) in terms of \(m_0c^2\) and \(Q_0\) using \((m_0'c^2)^2 = (m_0c^2 - Q_0)^2\).  
- Solve for \(E_\gamma\).

You should arrive at an expression of the form \(E_\gamma = Q_0\left(1 - \frac{Q_0}{2m_0c^2}\right)\). Since photon energy is proportional to frequency, the fractional frequency shift relative to the recoil‑free case is  
\[
\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} = \frac{E_\gamma - Q_0}{Q_0} = -\frac{Q_0}{2m_0c^2}.
\]

**4. Find the internal energy release \(Q_0\) for the He⁺ transition**  
Use the Bohr energy formula for hydrogen‑like ions (Carroll & Ostlie, reference.14, and the surrounding discussion of nuclear‑mass corrections). For a nucleus of charge \(Z\), the energy levels are \(E_n = -13.6\,\text{eV} \times Z^2 / n^2\). For He⁺, \(Z=2\). The transition from \(n=2\) to \(n=1\) releases  
\[
Q_0 = \Delta E = E_2 - E_1 = 13.6\,\text{eV} \times 2^2 \times \left(\frac{1}{1^2} - \frac{1}{2^2}\right).
\]
Compute this value.

**5. Determine the rest energy of the He⁺ ion**  
The problem context provides the mass of the He⁺ ion (or you can derive it from the atomic mass minus one electron mass). Convert that mass to an energy using \(m_0c^2\). (Leave the substitution and arithmetic to yourself.)

**6. Compute the fractional shift**  
Plug your \(Q_0\) and \(m_0c^2\) into \(\Delta f / f_0 = -Q_0/(2m_0c^2)\). Then compare the magnitude of this recoil shift with the gravitational red‑shift of order \(10^{-5}\) to see that the thermal‑broadening assumption is justified.

sub_problems.problem: (i) Assume that the atom decays at rest, producing a photon and a recoiling atom. Obtain the relativistic expression for the energy $hf$ of a photon emitted in terms of $\Delta E$ (the difference in rest energy between the two atomic levels) and the initial rest mass $m_{0}$ of the atom.
sub_problems.solution:
For the photon, momentum is $p = \frac{hf}{c}$ and energy is $E = hf$.  The internal energy change of the atom is related to the rest-mass change by

$$
\Delta E = (m_0 - m_0') c^2 \tag{1}
$$

In the laboratory frame, the energy before emission is

$$
E = m_0 c^2 \tag{2}
$$

After emission of a photon, the total energy is

$$
E = \sqrt{p^2 c^2 + m_0'^2 c^4} + hf \tag{3}
$$

where $p = hf/c$ by conservation of momentum.  Conservation of energy requires (2) = (3), so

$$
m_0 c^2 - hf = \sqrt{(hf)^2 + m_0'^2 c^4}
$$

Squaring both sides:

$$
(m_0 c^2 - hf)^2 = (hf)^2 + m_0'^2 c^4
$$

Expanding:

$$
m_0^2 c^4 - 2 hf m_0 c^2 + (hf)^2 = (hf)^2 + m_0'^2 c^4
$$

Cancelling $(hf)^2$ and rearranging:

$$
2 hf m_0 c^2 = (m_0^2 - m_0'^2) c^4
$$

Factor the right-hand side:

$$
2 hf m_0 c^2 = (m_0 - m_0') c^2 \cdot (m_0 + m_0') c^2
$$

Using (1) and writing $m_0 + m_0' = 2m_0 - (m_0 - m_0')$:

$$
2 hf m_0 c^2 = \Delta E \left[ 2m_0 c^2 - \Delta E \right]
$$

Solving for $hf$:

$$
hf = \Delta E \left( 1 - \frac{\Delta E}{2 m_0 c^2} \right)
$$

\boxed{hf = \Delta E \left( 1 - \frac{\Delta E}{2 m_0 c^2} \right)}

sub_problems.guidance:
You are studying the decay of a stationary atom that emits a photon and recoils.  The system is isolated, so both total relativistic energy and total momentum are conserved.  Your reference passages give you all the tools you need; the problem is essentially the same as the emission example worked out in the **French** passage, so you can follow that pattern.

**Step 1 – Write the initial state.**  
The atom is at rest, so its momentum is zero and its total energy is just its rest energy.  From the **Taylor & Wheeler** passage on rest energy, and the **Eisberg & Resnick** discussion of rest mass energy, the initial energy is \(m_0 c^2\).

**Step 2 – Write the final state after the photon is emitted.**  
The photon carries energy \(hf\) and, according to the **Taylor & Wheeler** (or **Eisberg & Resnick**) photon momentum passages, its momentum magnitude is \(p_{\text{photon}} = hf/c\).  
The atom recoils with a new rest mass \(m_0'\) (smaller than \(m_0\)) and momentum \(\mathbf{p}_{\text{atom}}\).

**Step 3 – Apply conservation of momentum.**  
Because the atom was initially at rest, the total momentum after the emission must be zero (**Morin** and **Taylor & Wheeler** on momentum conservation).  Therefore the recoiling atom’s momentum must exactly balance the photon’s momentum in magnitude:  
\[
p_{\text{atom}} = \frac{hf}{c}
\]
(directions opposite, but you only need the magnitude for the energy equation).

**Step 4 – Apply conservation of total relativistic energy.**  
The total energy before equals the total energy after.  The atom’s final energy is given by the relativistic energy–momentum relation you saw in the **Griffiths** Compton example and in the **French** emission derivation:  
\[
E_{\text{atom}} = \sqrt{p_{\text{atom}}^2 c^2 + m_0'^2 c^4}.
\]
Thus energy conservation says  
\[
m_0 c^2 = \sqrt{\left(\frac{hf}{c}\right)^2 c^2 + m_0'^2 c^4} \;+\; hf .
\]

**Step 5 – Relate the rest masses to the given energy difference \(\Delta E\).**  
The quantity \(\Delta E\) is the difference in rest energy between the two atomic levels.  From the **French** passage (and the **Eisberg & Resnick** principle that rest‑mass changes are compensated by other energy changes), the change in rest energy is  
\[
\Delta E = (m_0 - m_0') c^2 .
\]
This is exactly the \(Q_0\) introduced in the French derivation.

**Step 6 – Solve for \(hf\) in terms of \(\Delta E\) and \(m_0\).**  
Now you have an equation that contains \(hf\), \(m_0\), and \(m_0'\).  The algebraic steps are exactly those shown in the **French** emission example:  
- Isolate the square root, square both sides to eliminate it.  
- Simplify, using the identity \((m_0' c^2)^2 = (m_0 c^2 - hf)^2 - (hf)^2\) (which follows from conservation of energy and momentum, as in the French passage).  
- Replace \(m_0'\) by \(m_0 - \Delta E/c^2\) (or, following the French method, directly substitute the definitions of \(\Delta E\) and \(m_0\) to get the final expression).

Carry out the algebra yourself, keeping the quantities symbolic.  The result will be the photon energy \(hf\) expressed as a simple function of \(\Delta E\) and \(m_0\).  No numerical values are needed; the derivation is identical in structure to the one that leads to equation (6‑25) in the **French** reference passage.

To estimate the relativistic frequency shift for the He⁺ ion, you need to combine the recoil formula from special relativity with the Bohr model for hydrogen-like ions. Here is the logical path.

First, recall from reference derivation leading to Eq. (6‑25) that when a stationary atom emits a photon, the actual photon energy \( Q \) is slightly less than the nominal energy release \( Q_0 \) (the difference in rest energies between the initial and final atomic states). The relationship is  
\[
Q = Q_0 \left(1 - \frac{Q_0}{2 M_0 c^2}\right),
\]  
and the text explicitly states that “the photon energy is proportional to the frequency.” Therefore, the fractional frequency shift due to recoil, relative to the frequency that would be emitted if there were no recoil, is simply  
\[
\frac{\Delta f}{f_0} = \frac{Q_0}{2 M_0 c^2}.
\]  
This small‑recoil approximation is the key formula you will evaluate.

Now you need two quantities: \( Q_0 \), the energy difference between the two atomic levels involved, and \( M_0 c^2 \), the rest energy of the emitting ion. The problem asks for the case of He⁺, which is a hydrogen‑like ion (one electron, nuclear charge \( Z = 2 \)). The Bohr model, as described in the passages, gives the energy levels as  
\[
E_n = -\frac{13.6 \, Z^2}{n^2} \text{ eV}.
\]  
The photon is emitted in a transition from a higher level to a lower one, so \( Q_0 = E_{\text{high}} - E_{\text{low}} \). You must decide which transition to use; the problem statement implies a specific one (look back at part (c)(i) of the original question). Apply the Bohr formula with \( Z = 2 \) and the appropriate initial and final \( n \) to find \( Q_0 \) in eV.

The rest energy of the He⁺ ion is given in the data as \( m_0 c^2 = 4 \times 938 \) MeV. Convert this to eV so that the units match \( Q_0 \).

Finally, substitute your values of \( Q_0 \) and \( M_0 c^2 \) into the fractional shift expression \( \frac{Q_0}{2 M_0 c^2} \). Compare your result with the gravitational red shift from part (b) to verify that it is much smaller, as the problem states it should be.

title: Sound Propagation
problem:
The speed of propagation of sound in the ocean varies with depth, temperature and salinity. Figure 1(a) below shows the variation of sound speed c with depth z for a case where a minimum speed value $c_{0}$ occurs midway between the ocean surface and the sea bed. Note that for convenience z = 0 at the depth of this sound speed minimum, $z = z_{S}$ at the surface and $z = -z_{b}$ at the sea bed. Above z = 0, c is given by

$$
c = c _ {0} + b z.
$$

Below $z = 0$ , $c$ is given by

$$
c = c _ {0} - b z.
$$

In each case $b = \left|\frac{dc}{dz}\right|$ , that is, $b$ is the magnitude of the sound speed gradient with depth; $b$ is assumed constant.

Figure 1 (a)

Figure 1 (b)

Figure 1(b) shows a section of the z-x plane through the ocean, where x is a horizontal direction. The variation of c with respect to z is shown in figure 1(a). At the position z=0, x=0, a sound source S is located. A sound ray is emitted from S at an angle $\theta_{0}$ as shown. Because of the variation of c with z, the ray will be refracted.

sub_problems.problem:
(a) Show that the trajectory of the ray, leaving the source S and constrained to the z-x plane forms an arc of a circle with radius R where

$$
R = \frac{c_{0}}{b \sin \theta_{0}} \text{ for } 0 \leq \theta_{0} < \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$
sub_problems.solution:
Snell's law may be expressed as

$$
\frac{\sin \theta}{\sin \theta_0} = \frac{c}{c_0},
$$

where $c$ is the speed of sound. Consider an element of the ray path $ds$ and treat it as, locally, an arc of a circle of radius $R$. In the diagram, $ds = R\,d\theta$, or $\frac{ds}{d\theta} = R$.

From the equation above, for a small change in speed $dc$,

$$
\cos\theta\,d\theta = \frac{\sin\theta_0}{c_0}\,dc.
$$

For the upwardly directed ray, $c = c_0 + bz$, so $dc = b\,dz$ and

$$
\frac{\sin\theta_0}{c_0}\,b\,dz = \cos\theta\,d\theta,
\quad\text{hence}\quad
dz = \frac{c_0}{\sin\theta_0}\frac{1}{b}\cos\theta\,d\theta.
$$

We may also write (treating $ds$ as straight) $dz = ds\cos\theta$. Thus

$$
ds = \frac{c_0}{\sin\theta_0}\frac{1}{b}\,d\theta,
$$

and therefore

$$
\frac{ds}{d\theta} = R = \frac{c_0}{\sin\theta_0}\frac{1}{b}.
$$

This result strictly applies to small arc segments $ds$. However, from the equation (1) it also applies for all $\theta$, i.e., for all points along the trajectory, which therefore forms an arc of a circle with radius $R$ until the ray enters the region $z < 0$.

\boxed{R = \frac{c_{0}}{b \sin \theta_{0}}}

sub_problems.guidance:
To show that the ray follows a circular arc, you need to combine Snell’s law in a medium with varying sound speed, the description of a ray in a plane, and the local circular-arc approximation.  Follow these steps, using only the concepts and formulas from reference passages.

1. **Snell’s law along the ray**  
   The passage on Snell’s law for sound (11.2.1) states that across a boundary, \(k \sin\theta = k' \sin\theta'\).  For a wave of fixed angular frequency \(\omega\), the wave number is \(k = \omega/c\).  Because \(\omega\) is unchanged, the boundary condition implies that \(\frac{\sin\theta}{c}\) is the same on both sides.  In a medium where the sound speed \(c\) varies **continuously** with height \(z\) (here \(c = c_0 + bz\)), you can think of the ray as crossing many thin layers.  Therefore, the quantity \(\frac{\sin\theta}{c}\) stays constant along the entire ray.  At the source, the speed is \(c_0\) and the ray angle (measured from the vertical) is \(\theta_0\).  Write down the relation that equates \(\frac{\sin\theta}{c}\) at any point to its value at the source.  This gives you a connection between the local angle \(\theta\) and the local sound speed \(c\).

2. **Ray angle in the vertical plane**  
   The passage on ray angles (13.3.5) describes a plane wave whose wave-vector components are \(k_z = k\cos\theta\) and \(k_x = k\sin\theta\); the ray direction is at angle \(\theta\) from the vertical.  In the same way, the ray in your problem is confined to the \(z\)-\(x\) plane, and \(\theta\) is the angle the ray makes with the \(z\)-axis.  This is the same \(\theta\) that appears in the Snell’s law relation above.

3. **Local circular-arc approximation**  
   The worked example in the local circular-arc passage (Kleppner & Kolenkow) shows that a short segment of a curve can be treated as an arc of a circle:  \(\Delta s = R\,\Delta\theta\), where \(R\) is the local radius of curvature.  For an infinitesimal segment, this becomes \(ds = R\,d\theta\).  You will use this to find the radius of curvature of the ray path.

4. **Differentiate the Snell’s law relation**  
   Take the relation from step 1 and **differentiate** it with respect to the variable that changes along the ray.  Because the sound speed is \(c = c_0 + bz\), a small change in \(c\) is \(dc = b\,dz\).  Use the chain rule to relate \(d\theta\) and \(dz\).  You will get an equation that involves \(\cos\theta\,d\theta\) and \(dz\).

5. **Geometric relation between \(dz\) and the path length \(ds\)**  
   From the ray geometry (the same angle \(\theta\) defined in step 2), a small vertical displacement \(dz\) along the ray is related to the small path length \(ds\) by \(dz = ds \cos\theta\).  Equate this expression for \(dz\) with the one you obtained from differentiating Snell’s law.  Cancel the common factor \(\cos\theta\) (note that \(\theta < \pi/2\) so \(\cos\theta \neq 0\)) to find an expression for \(ds\) in terms of \(d\theta\).

6. **Identify the radius of curvature**  
   The result from step 5 gives you \(ds/d\theta\).  According to the local circular-arc approximation, \(ds/d\theta\) is exactly the local radius of curvature \(R\) of the trajectory.  Because the right‑hand side of your expression for \(ds/d\theta\) involves only constants (\(c_0\), \(b\), \(\sin\theta_0\)), the radius of curvature does **not** depend on position – it is constant.  A curve with constant radius of curvature is an arc of a circle.  Thus you have shown that the ray path is a circular arc, and you can read off the radius \(R\) in terms of the given parameters.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Derive an expression involving $z_{S}$, $c_{0}$ and $b$ to give the smallest value of the angle $\theta_{0}$ for upwardly directed rays which can be transmitted without the sound wave reflecting from the sea surface.
sub_problems.solution:
The smallest angle for upwardly directed rays that can be transmitted without reflection from the sea surface occurs when the ray just grazes the surface. At the surface, the sound speed is $c_0$ and the ray's turning point is at depth $z_S$. Using the relation for a linear sound speed profile $c(z) = c_0 + b z$, Snell's law gives $\frac{\cos \theta}{c} = \text{constant}$. For a ray starting at the surface with angle $\theta_0$ (measured from the horizontal), at depth $z$ the angle satisfies $\frac{\cos \theta(z)}{c(z)} = \frac{\cos \theta_0}{c_0}$. At the turning point where the ray becomes horizontal ($\theta = 0$), we have $\frac{1}{c(z_S)} = \frac{\cos \theta_0}{c_0}$, so $c(z_S) = \frac{c_0}{\cos \theta_0}$. But $c(z_S) = c_0 + b z_S$, hence $c_0 + b z_S = \frac{c_0}{\cos \theta_0}$. Solving for $\theta_0$: $\cos \theta_0 = \frac{c_0}{c_0 + b z_S}$, so $\sin \theta_0 = \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{c_0}{c_0 + b z_S}\right)^2} = \frac{\sqrt{(c_0 + b z_S)^2 - c_0^2}}{c_0 + b z_S} = \frac{\sqrt{b z_S (2 c_0 + b z_S)}}{c_0 + b z_S}$. Alternatively, from the geometry of the circular ray path, the radius of curvature is $R = c_0 / (b \sin \theta_0)$, and the depth $z_S = R - R \sin \theta_0 = R(1 - \sin \theta_0) = \frac{c_0}{b \sin \theta_0} (1 - \sin \theta_0)$. Solving for $\sin \theta_0$: $b z_S \sin \theta_0 = c_0 (1 - \sin \theta_0)$, so $b z_S \sin \theta_0 + c_0 \sin \theta_0 = c_0$, $\sin \theta_0 (b z_S + c_0) = c_0$, hence $\sin \theta_0 = \frac{c_0}{b z_S + c_0}$. Therefore the smallest angle is $\theta_0 = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{c_0}{b z_S + c_0} \right)$.

\boxed{\theta_0 = \sin^{-1} \left( \frac{c_0}{b z_S + c_0} \right)}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the smallest angle \(\theta_0\) for an upward ray that avoids reflection from the sea surface, you need to analyze the ray’s path using the concepts from your textbook, specifically Snell’s law and the condition for a ray just grazing a boundary (like total internal reflection, but applied here to a continuous medium).

Here’s how to proceed step by step:

1. **Identify the condition for “transmitted without reflection” at the sea surface.**  
   In your textbook (see Problem 9.39 and Fig. 9.28), when light goes from a denser to a less dense medium, there is a critical angle where the transmitted ray just grazes the surface. For the sound ray in this problem, the smallest upward angle that is not reflected corresponds to the ray that just grazes the sea surface at its highest point. That point is a **turning point**, where the ray becomes horizontal (the angle relative to the horizontal is \(0^\circ\)).

2. **Apply Snell’s law to relate angles and sound speeds.**  
   The textbook shows that Snell’s law gives a constant ratio along the ray: for example, with light, \(\frac{\cos\theta}{c}\) is constant when the sound speed varies only with depth. Here, the sound speed profile is linear: \(c(z) = c_0 + b z\), where \(c_0\) is the speed at the surface (\(z=0\)) and \(b\) is a constant.  
   For a ray starting at the surface with angle \(\theta_0\) (measured from the horizontal), the constant is \(\frac{\cos\theta_0}{c_0}\). At the turning point, the ray is horizontal (\(\theta = 0\)) and the depth is \(z_S\), so the sound speed there is \(c(z_S) = c_0 + b z_S\).  
   Therefore, Snell’s law gives:  
   \[
   \frac{\cos 0}{c(z_S)} = \frac{\cos\theta_0}{c_0}.
   \]

3. **Use the condition at the turning point.**  
   The ray just grazes the surface, so the turning point (where \(\theta = 0\)) is exactly at the sea surface. In this problem, however, the ray is upwardly directed and the turning point is at depth \(z_S\) (below the surface). Wait—careful: For an upward ray that *does not* reflect, its turning point must be at or below the surface. The smallest initial angle corresponds to the turning point being exactly at the surface? The problem asks for the smallest \(\theta_0\) for transmission *without* reflection, given the source is at depth \(z_S\). So: The ray originates at depth \(z_S\), travels upward, and just grazes the surface. That means at the surface (\(z=0\)), the ray becomes horizontal (\(\theta=0\)). Apply Snell’s law between the source depth \(z_S\) and the surface.

4. **Set up the equation.**  
   At the source depth \(z_S\), the angle is \(\theta_0\) (measured from horizontal). At the surface (\(z=0\)), the ray is horizontal (\(\theta = 0\)). Snell’s law says the quantity \(\frac{\cos\theta}{c(z)}\) is constant along the ray. So:  
   \[
   \frac{\cos\theta_0}{c(z_S)} = \frac{\cos 0}{c(0)}.
   \]  
   Substitute \(c(z_S) = c_0 + b z_S\) and \(c(0) = c_0\).

5. **Solve for \(\theta_0\).**  
   The equation becomes \(\frac{\cos\theta_0}{c_0 + b z_S} = \frac{1}{c_0}\).  
   From this, you can isolate \(\cos\theta_0\), and then find \(\theta_0\) using an inverse trigonometric function. The final expression will involve \(z_S\), \(c_0\), and \(b\). This is analogous to the critical angle formula in Eq. 9.200 of your textbook, but applied to the varying sound speed profile.

Follow these steps carefully, and you will derive the required expression. Remember: the key is recognizing that “transmitted without reflection” means the ray just grazes the surface, so the turning point is at \(z=0\). Then Snell’s law connects the angle at the source to the angle at the surface.

sub_problems.guidance:
Your goal is to find the smallest four launch angles \(\theta_0\) (measured relative to the horizontal) for which a sound ray emitted from a source S reaches a receiver H, given the horizontal separation \(X = 10000\ \mathrm{m}\), the surface sound speed \(c_0 = 1500\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\), and the sound-speed gradient constant \(b = 0.02000\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\).

The textbook passages describe how, in a medium where the sound speed increases linearly with depth (or height), the ray paths are arcs of circles. The relation that connects the horizontal range \(X\), the launch angle \(\theta_0\), and the medium parameters comes from the geometry of a circular ray path. Specifically, the textbook derives that the horizontal range for a ray that leaves the source at angle \(\theta_0\) and returns to the same depth is given by an expression involving \(c_0\), \(b\), and \(\cos\theta_0\). Because the ray may undergo multiple complete cycles (loops) before reaching the receiver, the general condition for the ray to hit the receiver at horizontal distance \(X\) is that \(X\) equals an integer multiple of the range of one full cycle.

Here is how to proceed methodically:

1. **Identify the relevant formula from the textbook.**  
   Look for the equation that gives the horizontal distance a ray travels in one complete cycle (a full "loop") as a function of \(c_0\), \(b\), and \(\cos\theta_0\). This formula comes directly from the circular-path geometry discussed in the text. Call one-cycle range \(R\). Then the condition for the ray to arrive at the receiver is \(X = n\,R\), where \(n\) is a positive integer representing the number of half-cycles or full cycles, depending on how the textbook defines the cycle. Check the derivation carefully: does the formula for the range of one full cycle correspond to the ray returning to its original depth after one complete loop? Adjust \(n\) accordingly.

2. **Relate the range condition to \(\theta_0\).**  
   Substitute the given \(X\), \(c_0\), and \(b\) into the condition \(X = n\,R\). This will give you an equation that involves \(\cos\theta_0\) and the integer \(n\). Rearrange the equation to isolate \(\cos\theta_0\) on one side.

3. **Solve for \(\theta_0\) for successive integers.**  
   For each integer \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\), compute the value of \(\cos\theta_0\) from the rearranged formula. Then find \(\theta_0 = \arccos(\text{that value})\). Make sure your calculator is in degree mode. The problem asks for the smallest four values of \(\theta_0\). Because \(\theta_0\) increases as \(n\) increases (check the trend from your equation), the smallest four angles will correspond to the four largest allowed values of \(n\) that still give a valid \(\cos\theta_0\) (i.e., a value between \(-1\) and \(1\)). Start from the largest possible \(n\) and work downward, or find the smallest \(n\) that yields a valid angle and then list the next three.

4. **Order the results.**  
   Once you have the angles for the appropriate four consecutive \(n\) values, list them in increasing order. These are your smallest four \(\theta_0\).

Remember, the textbook’s worked examples follow exactly this pattern: they take the ray-path range formula, set it equal to the given horizontal distance times a loop-count factor, solve for the cosine of the launch angle, and then compute the angle. Do the algebra step by step, and check that your \(\cos\theta_0\) values lie in the physically meaningful range.

sub_problems.problem:
(e) Derive an expression to give the time taken for sound to travel from S to H following the ray path associated with the smallest value of angle $\theta_{0}$, as determined in part (c). Calculate the value of this transit time for the conditions given in part (d). The following result may be of assistance:

$$
\int \frac{dx}{\sin x} = \ln \tan \left(\frac{x}{2}\right)
$$

Calculate the time taken for the direct ray to travel from S to H along z = 0. Which of the two rays will arrive first, the ray for which $\theta_{0} = \pi/2$, or the ray with the smallest value of $\theta_{0}$ as calculated for part (d)?
sub_problems.solution:
The ray path associated with the smallest launch angle consists of a single arc. The time taken is

$$
t = \int_{1}^{3} dt = \int_{1}^{3} \frac{ds}{c}.
$$

First consider the segment from point 1 to point 2:

$$
t_{12} = \int_{1}^{2} \frac{ds}{c} = \int_{\theta_{0}}^{\pi/2} \frac{R d\theta}{c}.
$$

Using $R = \frac{c}{b \sin \theta}$ gives

$$
t_{12} = \frac{1}{b} \int_{\theta_{0}}^{\pi/2} \frac{d\theta}{\sin \theta}.
$$

Evaluating the integral,

$$
t_{12} = \frac{1}{b} \left[ \ln \tan \frac{\theta}{2} \right]_{\theta_{0}}^{\pi/2} = -\frac{1}{b} \ln \tan \frac{\theta_{0}}{2}.
$$

Since the path is symmetric, $t_{13} = 2t_{12}$, so

$$
t_{13} = -\frac{2}{b} \ln \tan \frac{\theta_{0}}{2}.
$$

For the conditions given in part (d), this yields

$$
t_{13} = 6.6546\ \mathrm{s}.
$$

The direct ray along $z=0$ travels at constant speed $c_{0}$, so its travel time is

$$
t = \frac{X}{c_{0}} = 6.6666\ \mathrm{s}.
$$

Comparing the two, the ray with the smallest $\theta_{0}$ arrives first.

\boxed{t_{13} = 6.6546\ \mathrm{s}}
