title: Rising Balloon
problem: A rubber balloon filled with helium gas goes up high into the sky where the pressure and temperature decrease with height. In the following questions, assume that the shape of the balloon remains spherical regardless of the payload, and neglect the payload volume. Also assume that the temperature of the helium gas inside of the balloon is always the same as that of the ambient air, and treat all gases as ideal gases. The universal gas constant is $R=8.31\ J/mol\cdot K$ and the molar masses of helium and air are $M_{H}=4.00\times10^{-3}\ kg/mol$ and $M_{A}=28.9\times10^{-3}\ kg/mol$ , respectively. The gravitational acceleration is $g=9.8\ m/s^{2}$ .

sub_problems.problem: (a) Let the pressure of the ambient air be $P$ and the temperature be $T$. The pressure inside of the balloon is higher than that of outside due to the surface tension of the balloon. The balloon contains $n$ moles of helium gas and the pressure inside is $P + \Delta P$. Find the buoyant force $F_{B}$ acting on the balloon as a function of $P$ and $\Delta P$.
sub_problems.solution:
Using the ideal gas equation of state, the volume of the helium gas of $n$ moles at pressure $P + \Delta P$ and temperature $T$ is

$$
V = \frac{n R T}{P + \Delta P} \tag{a1}
$$

while the volume of $n'$ moles of air at pressure $P$ and temperature $T$ is

$$
V = \frac{n' R T}{P}. \tag{a2}
$$

Thus the balloon displaces $n' = n \frac{P}{P + \Delta P}$ moles of air, whose weight is $M_A n' g$. This displaced air weight is the buoyant force, i.e.,

$$
F_B = M_A n g \frac{P}{P + \Delta P}. \tag{a3}
$$

knowledge_points.name: ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: Relates pressure, volume, temperature and number of moles (PV = nRT); used for helium at P+ΔP and T to get its volume, and for ambient air at P and T to find moles of displaced air.

knowledge_points.name: Archimedes' principle
knowledge_points.description: Buoyant force on a fully submerged object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces; here F_B = (mass of displaced air) × g.

knowledge_points.name: molar mass
knowledge_points.description: Mass of one mole of a substance; used to convert the number of moles of displaced air to its mass (mass = n × M_A) for the weight calculation.

knowledge_points.name: helium temperature equals ambient temperature
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the helium gas inside the balloon always has the same temperature T as the outside air; this allows using the same T in the ideal gas law for both gases.

knowledge_points.name: balloon interior volume equals displaced air volume
knowledge_points.description: The volume calculated from the helium gas is taken to be exactly the volume of air displaced; implicitly assumes the balloon material has negligible volume (the problem neglects payload volume, and here we extend to skin).

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the buoyant force \(F_B\) as a function of \(P\) and \(\Delta P\), you need to combine the ideal gas law with Archimedes' principle and the concept of molar mass.

First, consider the helium inside the balloon. It is at pressure \(P + \Delta P\) and temperature \(T\), and contains \(n\) moles. Use the ideal gas law from your textbook, \(\mathcal{PV} = N_{\mathrm{mol}} R T\) (equation 5.24), to express the volume \(V\) of the balloon in terms of \(n\), \(R\), \(T\), \(P\), and \(\Delta P\). This step is directly analogous to how the textbook uses the ideal gas law to relate pressure, volume, and temperature for a given quantity of gas.

Next, think about the air displaced by the balloon. According to Archimedes' principle, as described in your textbook, the buoyant force on a submerged object equals the weight of the fluid it displaces. Here, the displaced fluid is the ambient air at pressure \(P\) and temperature \(T\). You need to find how many moles of air, call it \(n'\), would occupy that same volume \(V\) at pressure \(P\). Apply the ideal gas law again, but this time for the displaced air. Set up the equation for \(n'\) moles of air at pressure \(P\) and temperature \(T\) occupying volume \(V\). By comparing this with the expression for the helium volume, you can relate \(n'\) to \(n\), \(P\), and \(\Delta P\). This mirrors the idea in the textbook where the ideal gas law is applied to different conditions for the same gas; here you are applying it to two different gases at the same temperature and volume but different pressures.

Finally, the buoyant force is the weight of this displaced air. The mass of the displaced air is its number of moles \(n'\) multiplied by its molar mass \(M_A\) (the mass per mole, as defined in the molar mass discussion from your textbook). The weight is then \(M_A n' g\). Substitute your expression for \(n'\) in terms of \(n\), \(P\), and \(\Delta P\) to obtain \(F_B\) as requested.

sub_problems.problem:
(b) On a particular summer day in Korea, the air temperature $T$ at the height $z$ from the sea level was found to be $T(z) = T_0(1 - z / z_0)$ in the range of $0 < z < 15$ km with $z_0 = 49$ km and $T_0 = 303$ K. The pressure and density at the sea level were $P_0 = 1.0$ atm = $1.01 \times 10^5$ Pa and $\rho_0 = 1.16$ kg/m$^3$, respectively. For this height range, the pressure takes the form

$$
P(z) = P_0 (1 - z / z_0)^{\eta}. \tag{2.1}
$$

Express $\eta$ in terms of $z_0$, $\rho_0$, $P_0$, and $g$, and find its numerical value to the two significant digits. Treat the gravitational acceleration as a constant, independent of height.
sub_problems.solution:
The pressure difference due to a height change $dz$ is $dP = -\rho g\,dz$. Using the ideal gas law $\rho T / P = \rho_0 T_0 / P_0$, we have $\rho = \frac{P}{T} \frac{\rho_0 T_0}{P_0}$. Substituting into the hydrostatic equation:

$$
\frac{dP}{dz} = -\rho g = -\frac{\rho_0 T_0}{P_0} \frac{P}{T} g.
$$

Given $P(z) = P_0 (1 - z/z_0)^\eta$ and $T(z) = T_0 (1 - z/z_0)$, we compute $dP/dz = -\eta \frac{P_0}{z_0} (1 - z/z_0)^{\eta-1}$. Substituting into the hydrostatic equation:

$$
-\eta \frac{P_0}{z_0} (1 - z/z_0)^{\eta-1} = -\frac{\rho_0 T_0}{P_0} \frac{P_0 (1 - z/z_0)^\eta}{T_0 (1 - z/z_0)} g = -\frac{\rho_0 g}{P_0} P_0 (1 - z/z_0)^{\eta-1}.
$$

Cancelling common factors, we obtain:

$$
\eta = \frac{\rho_0 z_0 g}{P_0}.
$$

Numerically, $\rho_0 = 1.16$ kg/m$^3$, $z_0 = 49$ km $= 4.9 \times 10^4$ m, $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$, $P_0 = 1.01 \times 10^5$ Pa:

$$
\eta = \frac{1.16 \times 4.9 \times 10^4 \times 9.8}{1.01 \times 10^5} = 5.52 \approx 5.5.
$$

Thus, $\eta = \rho_0 z_0 g / P_0$ and its numerical value to two significant digits is $5.5$.

\boxed{\eta = \frac{\rho_0 z_0 g}{P_0} = 5.5}

knowledge_points.name: Hydrostatic equilibrium equation
knowledge_points.description: Relates the vertical pressure gradient in a fluid to its density and gravity: dP/dz = -ρ g. Used to set up the differential equation for atmospheric pressure variation.

knowledge_points.name: Ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: PV = nRT, which for a gas of constant composition implies density ρ = PM/(RT) and thus ρT/P = constant. Used to express air density in terms of pressure and temperature, with the constant evaluated from sea-level reference values.

knowledge_points.name: Constant gravitational acceleration
knowledge_points.description: The problem states to treat g as constant, independent of height, so it does not vary with z in the hydrostatic equation.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Start with the hydrostatic equilibrium condition**  
   From your reference (Carroll & Ostlie, reference.6), for a static fluid with constant gravitational acceleration \(g\), the pressure gradient is  
   \[
   \frac{dP}{dz} = -\rho g .
   \]  
   Here \(z\) is height, \(\rho\) is mass density. Since you are told to treat \(g\) as constant, take \(g = 9.8\ \text{m/s}^2\) (as given in the Kleppner & Kolenkow passage).

2. **Use the ideal gas law to replace density**  
   The problem gives sea‑level values \(P_0, T_0, \rho_0\). For a gas of fixed composition, the ideal gas law (\(P = n k T\) or \(\mathcal{P V} = N_{\text{mol}} R T\)) tells you that number density \(n\) is proportional to \(P/T\). Mass density is \(\rho = (\text{average particle mass}) \times n\), so it is also proportional to \(P/T\).  
   With the constants at sea level:  
   \[
   \rho(z) = \frac{\rho_0 T_0}{P_0}\, \frac{P(z)}{T(z)} .
   \]  
   (You obtain this by noting that \(\rho_0 T_0 / P_0\) is constant because the gas composition doesn’t change.)

3. **Write the given profiles**  
   \[
   T(z) = T_0 \left(1 - \frac{z}{z_0}\right), \qquad
   P(z) = P_0 \left(1 - \frac{z}{z_0}\right)^{\eta}.
   \]  
   These are valid for \(0 < z < 15\ \text{km}\) with \(z_0 = 49\ \text{km}\).

4. **Compute \(\frac{dP}{dz}\) from the given \(P(z)\)**  
   Differentiate the power‑law form:  
   \[
   \frac{dP}{dz} = -\frac{\eta P_0}{z_0} \left(1 - \frac{z}{z_0}\right)^{\eta-1}.
   \]

5. **Assemble the hydrostatic equation**  
   Substitute \(\rho(z)\) from step 2 and \(T(z)\) into \(-\rho g\):  
   \[
   -\rho g = -\frac{\rho_0 T_0}{P_0}\, \frac{P_0 (1 - z/z_0)^\eta}{T_0 (1 - z/z_0)}\, g
          = -\frac{\rho_0 g}{P_0}\, P_0 (1 - z/z_0)^{\eta-1}.
   \]  
   Set this equal to the expression from step 4:  
   \[
   -\frac{\eta P_0}{z_0} (1 - z/z_0)^{\eta-1} = -\frac{\rho_0 g}{P_0}\, P_0 (1 - z/z_0)^{\eta-1}.
   \]  
   Compare the two sides: the factors \((1 - z/z_0)^{\eta-1}\) cancel, as do the minus signs. You are left with an equation independent of \(z\); solve it for \(\eta\). You should obtain  
   \[
   \eta = \frac{\rho_0 z_0 g}{P_0}.
   \]

6. **Evaluate \(\eta\) numerically**

By following these steps you will derive \(\eta\) purely from the hydrostatic equilibrium condition, the ideal gas law, and the given atmospheric profiles — exactly as reference sections describe.

sub_problems.problem: (d) The constant $\kappa$ can be determined from the amount of the gas needed to inflate the balloon. At $T_{0}=303~K$ and $P_{0}=1.0~atm=1.01\times10^{5}~Pa$, an un-stretched balloon ($\lambda=1$) contains $n_{0}=12.5$ moles of helium. It takes $n=3.6~n_{0}=45$ moles in total to inflate the balloon to $\lambda=1.5$ at the same $T_{0}$ and $P_{0}$. Express the balloon parameter $a$, defined as $a=\kappa/\kappa_{0}$, in terms of $n$, $n_{0}$, and $\lambda$, where $\kappa_{0}\equiv\frac{r_{0}P_{0}}{4RT_{0}}$. Evaluate $a$ to the two significant digits.
sub_problems.solution:
From the ideal gas law,

$$
P_0 V_0 = n_0 R T_0 \tag{d1}
$$

where $V_0$ is the unstretched volume.  At volume $V = \lambda^3 V_0$ containing $n$ moles, the ideal gas law applied to the gas inside at $T = T_0$ gives the inside pressure $P_{\mathrm{in}}$ as

$$
P_{\mathrm{in}} = \frac{n R T_0}{V} = \frac{n}{n_0 \lambda^3} P_0. \tag{d2}
$$

On the other hand, the result of part (c) at $T = T_0$ gives

$$
P_{\mathrm{in}} = P_0 + \Delta P = P_0 + \frac{4 \kappa R T_0}{r_0} \left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda^7}\right) = \left(1 + a \left(\frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda^7}\right)\right) P_0, \tag{d3}
$$

where $a = \kappa / \kappa_0$ and $\kappa_0 \equiv \frac{r_0 P_0}{4 R T_0}$.  Equating (d2) and (d3) to solve for $a$,

$$
a = \frac{\frac{n}{n_0 \lambda^3} - 1}{\lambda^{-1} - \lambda^{-7}}. \tag{d5}
$$

Inserting $n/n_0 = 3.6$ and $\lambda = 1.5$,

$$
a = \frac{3.6 / (1.5^3) - 1}{1/1.5 - 1/1.5^7} = \frac{3.6 / 3.375 - 1}{2/3 - 1/ (1.5^7)}.
$$

Compute $1.5^3 = 3.375$, so $3.6 / 3.375 = 1.06666\ldots$, and $3.6 / 3.375 - 1 = 0.06666\ldots$.  $1.5^7 = (3/2)^7 = 2187/128 \approx 17.0859$, so $1/1.5^7 \approx 0.05853$.  Then $\lambda^{-1} - \lambda^{-7} = 2/3 - 0.05853 \approx 0.66667 - 0.05853 = 0.60814$.  Thus

$$
a \approx \frac{0.06667}{0.60814} \approx 0.1096 \approx 0.11.
$$

To two significant digits, $a = 0.11$.

\boxed{a = 0.11}

knowledge_points.name: Ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: PV = nRT is applied twice: once to find the unstretched volume V0 from n0, P0, T0, and once to express the inside pressure Pin in terms of n, V = λ³V0, and T0.

knowledge_points.name: Volume scaling for a sphere
knowledge_points.description: For a spherical balloon, volume is proportional to radius cubed; if the radius is stretched by a factor λ, V = λ³V0. This is used to relate the volume containing n moles to the unstretched volume.

knowledge_points.name: Pressure difference from surface tension
knowledge_points.description: The solution imports the result of part (c): at temperature T0 the pressure inside the balloon is P_in = P0 + (4κRT0/r0)(1/λ - 1/λ⁷). This relation, which accounts for the balloon's elastic surface tension, is needed to equate with the ideal-gas expression for P_in.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, use the ideal gas law to relate the unstretched balloon’s internal conditions. From reference passage on the ideal gas law, you have  
\[
\mathcal{P V} = N_{\mathrm{mol}} R T \quad (\text{Kleppner \& Kolenkow, reference.24})
\]  
or equivalently \(P V = N k T\) (Palen). For the un‑stretched state (\(\lambda = 1\)) you know the temperature \(T_0\), the outside pressure \(P_0\) (which equals the inside pressure when the balloon is flaccid), and the number of moles \(n_0\). Apply the ideal gas law to find the unstretched volume \(V_0\) in terms of \(n_0, R, T_0, P_0\).

Now the balloon is inflated to a stretch factor \(\lambda\). The radius of a sphere scales with \(\lambda\), so the volume scales as the cube of the radius. As reference on volume scaling points out, the volume of a sphere is \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\), so when the radius is multiplied by \(\lambda\), the volume multiplies by \(\lambda^3\). Thus the stretched volume is \(V = \lambda^3 V_0\).

The gas inside the stretched balloon is the same helium, but now \(n\) moles are inside, still at the same temperature \(T_0\). The pressure inside, \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\), is no longer simply \(P_0\) because the stretched skin exerts an extra pressure. Apply the ideal gas law to this stretched state:  
\[
P_{\mathrm{in}} V = n R T_0.
\]  
Substitute \(V = \lambda^3 V_0\) and use the expression for \(V_0\) you obtained from the un‑stretched case. Simplify to get an expression for \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\) as a multiple of \(P_0\) that involves only \(n, n_0, \lambda\).

The problem introduces the dimensionless balloon parameter \(a = \kappa / \kappa_0\) with \(\kappa_0 \equiv \frac{r_0 P_0}{4 R T_0}\). From part (c) of the problem (which you have already worked out) you know how the required pressure difference \(\Delta P\) depends on \(\kappa\) and \(\lambda\). Written in terms of \(a\) and \(\lambda\), that result gives \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\) in the form  
\[
P_{\mathrm{in}} = P_0 \left[ 1 + a \left( \frac{1}{\lambda} - \frac{1}{\lambda^7} \right) \right].
\]

Now you have two independent expressions for \(P_{\mathrm{in}}\): one from the ideal gas law (involving \(n, n_0, \lambda\)) and one from the mechanics of the stretched balloon (involving \(a\) and \(\lambda\)). Set them equal. Because \(P_0\) cancels, you obtain an equation that you can solve for \(a\). Isolate \(a\) algebraically to find a formula in terms of \(n, n_0,\) and \(\lambda\).

Finally, substitute the given numbers \(n/n_0 = 3.6\) and \(\lambda = 1.5\) into that expression. Evaluate the powers (\(\lambda^3\) and \(\lambda^7\)) carefully, carry out the subtraction and division, and round the result to two significant digits. This step is straightforward arithmetic — just follow your derived formula.

sub_problems.problem: (e) Suppose that the balloon eventually stops at the height $z_{f}$ where the buoyant force balances the total weight. Find $z_{f}$ and the inflation ratio $\lambda_{f}$ at that height. Give the answers in two significant digits. Assume there are no drift effect and no gas leakage during the upward flight.
sub_problems.solution:
The buoyant force derived in part (a) balances the total mass $M_T = 1.12$ kg. From Eq. (a3), at weight balance:

$$
\frac{P}{P + \Delta P} = \frac{M_T}{M_A n}. \tag{e1}
$$

Applying the ideal gas law to the helium inside the volume $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \lambda^3 \frac{4}{3}\pi r_0^3 = \lambda^3 V_0$, for arbitrary ambient $P$ and $T$:

$$
(P + \Delta P) \lambda^3 = \frac{n R T}{V_0} = P_0 \frac{T}{T_0} \frac{n}{n_0}. \tag{e2}
$$

Using Eq. (e2) in Eq. (e1) gives an alternative condition for weight balance:

$$
\frac{P}{P_0} \frac{T_0}{T} \lambda^3 = \frac{M_T}{M_A n_0}. \tag{e3}
$$

Using the expression for $\Delta P$ from part (c) in Eq. (e2):

$$
P \lambda^3 + \frac{4 \kappa R T}{r_0} \lambda^2 (1 - \lambda^{-6}) = P_0 \frac{T}{T_0} \frac{n}{n_0},
$$

or rearranging:

$$
\frac{P}{P_0} \frac{T_0}{T} \lambda^3 = \frac{n}{n_0} - a \lambda^2 (1 - \lambda^{-6}), \tag{e4}
$$

where $a$ is defined as before. Equating the right-hand sides of Eqs. (e3) and (e4) yields the equation for $\lambda$:

$$
\lambda^2 (1 - \lambda^{-6}) = \frac{1}{a n_0} \left( n - \frac{M_T}{M_A} \right) = 4.54. \tag{e5}
$$

Solving for $\lambda$:

$$
\lambda^2 \approx \frac{4.54}{1 - 4.54^{-3}} \approx 4.54, \quad \lambda_f \approx 2.13. \tag{e6}
$$

To find the height, replace $(P/P_0)/(T/T_0)$ on the left-hand side of Eq. (e3) using the height dependence from part (b):

$$
\frac{P}{P_0} \frac{T_0}{T} \lambda^3 = (1 - z_f / z_0)^{\gamma - 1} \lambda_f^3 = \frac{M_T}{M_A n_0} = 3.10. \tag{e7}
$$

Solving Eq. (e7) for $z_f$ with $\lambda_f = 2.13$ and $\gamma - 1 = 4.5$:

$$
z_f = 49 \times \left(1 - \left(\frac{3.10}{2.13^3}\right)^{1/4.5}\right) = 10.9 \text{ km}. \tag{e8}
$$

The required answers are $\lambda_f = 2.1$ and $z_f = 11$ km.

\boxed{\lambda_f = 2.1}, \boxed{z_f = 11 \text{ km}}

knowledge_points.name: Ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: Relates pressure, volume, temperature, and moles for the helium gas: PV = nRT. Used to derive Eq. (e2) connecting (P+ΔP), λ, T, and n, and to express V_0 in terms of reference conditions.

knowledge_points.name: Inflation ratio
knowledge_points.description: Defined as λ = r/r_0, the ratio of current radius to unstretched radius. Since the balloon remains spherical, volume scales as V = λ^3 V_0. Needed to express the helium volume in terms of λ.

knowledge_points.name: Helium-ambient temperature equality
knowledge_points.description: The helium gas inside the balloon is at the same temperature T as the ambient air. This allows using the ambient T in the ideal gas law for the helium and in the atmospheric profiles.

knowledge_points.name: Surface tension pressure difference
knowledge_points.description: The pressure difference ΔP between inside and outside of the balloon due to surface tension is given by the expression from part (c): ΔP = (4κRT/r_0)(λ^{-1} - λ^{-7}). Used to substitute ΔP in Eq. (e2).

knowledge_points.name: Balloon parameter a
knowledge_points.description: The dimensionless parameter a = κ/κ_0, with κ_0 = r_0 P_0/(4RT_0), is known from part (d). Used to simplify the equation combining ideal gas law and ΔP into Eq. (e4).

knowledge_points.name: Atmospheric profiles
knowledge_points.description: The ambient pressure and temperature as functions of height z are given by part (b): T(z) = T_0(1 - z/z_0) and P(z) = P_0(1 - z/z_0)^η, with known η. Used to express P/P_0 and T/T_0 in terms of z_f in Eq. (e7).

knowledge_points.name: Buoyant force formula
knowledge_points.description: The buoyant force on the balloon was derived in part (a) as F_B = (P/(P+ΔP)) M_A n g. At weight balance, this yields Eq. (e1): P/(P+ΔP) = M_T/(M_A n).

knowledge_points.name: Small-term approximation
knowledge_points.description: When solving λ^2 (1 - λ^{-6}) = constant, for large λ the term λ^{-6} is negligible compared to 1, allowing the approximation λ^2 ≈ constant. Used to quickly estimate λ_f.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Locate the equilibrium condition.**  
   The balloon stops rising when the buoyant force balances the total weight. Use the buoyant‑force result you obtained in part (a); set it equal to the total weight \(M_T g\). This gives an equation that links the local ambient pressure \(P\), the pressure difference \(\Delta P\) across the skin, and the known total mass \(M_T\).

2. **Introduce the inflation ratio \(\lambda\) through the ideal gas law.**  
   The helium inside the balloon obeys the ideal gas law (reference: \(\mathcal{PV} = N_{\text{mol}}RT\), or \(PV = NkT\) in the Palen passage). The volume of the balloon is \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\). Because the radius is related to the initial radius \(r_0\) by \(r = \lambda r_0\) (the definition of the inflation ratio, \(\lambda = r/r_0\)), the volume scales as \(\lambda^3 V_0\). The pressure of the helium is \(P + \Delta P\) (inside pressure exceeds ambient by \(\Delta P\)). Thus,
   \[
   (P+\Delta P)\,\lambda^3 V_0 = n R T,
   \]
   where \(n\) is the number of moles of helium.  You can normalize this relation by the initial state (ground level) values \(P_0, T_0, n_0\) to make later algebra tidier.

3. **Combine weight balance with the gas law to eliminate \(P+\Delta P\).**  
   From the weight‑balance equation, express \(P/(P+\Delta P)\) in terms of \(M_T\) and the mass of displaced air (derived in part (a)). Then use the gas‑law relation for \((P+\Delta P)\lambda^3\) to replace \(P+\Delta P\). After some algebra you will find a compact relation that links the ambient conditions, \(\lambda\), and the constant mass ratio:
   \[
   \frac{P}{P_0}\frac{T_0}{T}\,\lambda^3 = \frac{M_T}{M_A n_0},
   \]
   where \(M_A\) is the molar mass of air.  This is your “weight‑balance in terms of \(\lambda\)” equation.

4. **Incorporate the skin‑pressure relation to isolate \(\lambda\).**  
   In part (c) you derived an expression for \(\Delta P\) as a function of \(\lambda\) (it involves the surface tension/elastic constant \(\kappa\) and the radius). Substitute that \(\Delta P(\lambda)\) into the ideal‑gas law form \((P+\Delta P)\lambda^3 = \text{known constants}\). Combine this with the weight‑balance equation from step 3 to eliminate the quantities that depend on height (\(P\) and \(T\)). You will arrive at a single equation that contains only \(\lambda\) and known constants. Physically, it will have a structure like
   \[
   \lambda^2\bigl(1 - \lambda^{-6}\bigr) = \text{constant}.
   \]

5. **Apply a small‑term approximation to solve for \(\lambda\).**  
   Because the balloon inflates substantially, \(\lambda\) is expected to be several times unity, so \(\lambda^{-6}\) is very small. reference passage on differentials (Note 1.4, or the linearization logic in Example 14.3.1) tells you that for a small change, you may neglect higher‑order terms. Here, treat \(\lambda^{-6}\) as a small parameter: the factor \((1 - \lambda^{-6})\) is nearly 1. Take the approximation \(\lambda^2 \approx \text{constant}\) first, solve for \(\lambda\), then (if you wish) compute the full expression with that provisional \(\lambda\) to check that the correction is negligible. This yields \(\lambda_f\) — the equilibrium inflation ratio.

6. **Use the atmospheric profile to find the height \(z_f\).**  
   Go back to the height‑dependent weight‑balance equation from step 3:
   \[
   \frac{P}{P_0}\frac{T_0}{T}\,\lambda_f^3 = \frac{M_T}{M_A n_0}.
   \]

Throughout, rely on the ideal gas law as stated in reference to relate pressure, volume, and temperature, and on the concept of linear approximation to justify neglecting the tiny term \(\lambda^{-6}\). This systematic, step‑by‑step use of the earlier parts (a)–(c) with these core physics ideas will lead you to \(\lambda_f\) and \(z_f\).

title: Atomic Probe Microscope
problem:
Atomic probe microscopes (APMs) are powerful tools in the field of nano-science. The motion of a cantilever in APM can be detected by a photo-detector monitoring the reflected laser beam, as shown in Fig. 3.1. The cantilever can move only in the vertical direction and its displacement z as a function of time t can be described by the equation

$$
m \frac {d ^ {2} z}{d t ^ {2}} + b \frac {d z}{d t} + k z = F, \tag {3.1}
$$

where m is the cantilever mass, $k = m\omega_{0}^{2}$ is the spring constant of the cantilever, b is a small damping coefficient satisfying $\omega_{0} >> (b/m) > 0$ , and finally F is an external driving force of the piezoelectric tube.

Figure 3.1 A schematic diagram for a scanning probe microscope (SPM).

The inset in the lower right corner represents a simplified mechanical model to describe the coupling of the piezotube with the cantilever.

sub_problems.problem: (a) When $F = F_{0} \sin \omega t$, $z(t)$ satisfying Eq. (3.1) can be written as $z(t) = A \sin (\omega t - \phi)$, where $A > 0$ and $0 \leq \phi \leq \pi$. Find the expression of the amplitude A and $\tan\phi$ in terms of $F_{0}$, m, $\omega$, $\omega_{0}$, and b. Obtain A and the phase $\phi$ at the resonance frequency $\omega=\omega_{0}$.
sub_problems.solution:
Substitute $z(t) = A \sin(\omega t - \phi)$ into the equation of motion

$$
m \frac{d^{2}z}{dt^{2}} + b \frac{dz}{dt} + m \omega_{0}^{2}z = F_{0} \sin \omega t.
$$

This gives

$$
- m \omega^{2} \sin(\omega t - \phi) + b \omega \cos(\omega t - \phi) + m \omega_{0}^{2} \sin(\omega t - \phi) = \frac{F_{0}}{A} \sin \omega t.
$$

Expand $\sin(\omega t - \phi)$ and $\cos(\omega t - \phi)$ and collect coefficients of $\sin \omega t$ and $\cos \omega t$:

$$
\left[ m(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2}) \cos \phi + b \omega \sin \phi - \frac{F_{0}}{A} \right] \sin \omega t + \left[ -m(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2}) \sin \phi + b \omega \cos \phi \right] \cos \omega t = 0.
$$

For this to hold for all $t$, each bracket must vanish.  From the coefficient of $\cos \omega t$:

$$
- m(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2}) \sin \phi + b \omega \cos \phi = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \tan \phi = \frac{b \omega}{m(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2})}.
$$

From the coefficient of $\sin \omega t$:

$$
m(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2}) \cos \phi + b \omega \sin \phi = \frac{F_{0}}{A}.
$$

Using $\cos \phi = \frac{m(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2})}{\sqrt{m^{2}(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2})^{2} + b^{2} \omega^{2}}}$ and $\sin \phi = \frac{b \omega}{\sqrt{m^{2}(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2})^{2} + b^{2} \omega^{2}}}$, we obtain

$$
A = \frac{F_{0}}{\sqrt{m^{2}(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2})^{2} + b^{2} \omega^{2}}}.
$$

At resonance $\omega = \omega_{0}$:

$$
A = \frac{F_{0}}{b \omega_{0}}, \qquad \phi = \frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

\boxed{A = \frac{F_{0}}{\sqrt{m^{2}(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2})^{2} + b^{2} \omega^{2}}}, \quad \tan \phi = \frac{b \omega}{m(\omega_{0}^{2} - \omega^{2})}} \\
\boxed{\text{At } \omega = \omega_{0}: \; A = \frac{F_{0}}{b \omega_{0}}, \; \phi = \frac{\pi}{2}}

knowledge_points.name: Driven damped harmonic oscillator
knowledge_points.description: The physical system is a mass m on a spring of constant k = m ω0² with viscous damping b, driven by an external sinusoidal force F0 sin ωt. The student must recognize the equation of motion m d²z/dt² + b dz/dt + m ω0² z = F0 sin ωt and the roles of its parameters to work with the given ODE.

knowledge_points.name: Sinusoidal steady-state response
knowledge_points.description: The problem states that the solution can be written as z(t) = A sin(ωt - φ). The student must adopt this ansatz with amplitude A and phase lag φ to find the requested expressions.

knowledge_points.name: Harmonic balance (trigonometric method)
knowledge_points.description: To determine A and tan φ, substitute the trial solution into the ODE, expand sin(ωt - φ) and cos(ωt - φ) using trigonometric addition formulas, collect coefficients of sin ωt and cos ωt, and set each coefficient to zero. This yields algebraic equations for the unknowns.

knowledge_points.name: Resonance condition
knowledge_points.description: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, ω = ω0. The problem explicitly asks for A and φ at ω = ω0, so the student must evaluate the derived general formulas at that frequency.

sub_problems.guidance:
Start by identifying the equation of motion from the problem.  Eq. (3.1) is a driven damped harmonic oscillator:
\[
m \frac{d^{2}z}{dt^{2}} + b \frac{dz}{dt} + m\omega_{0}^{2}z = F_{0}\sin\omega t .
\]
This has the same structure as the standard form in the textbook (Eq. 11.25), except that here the driving term is \(\sin\omega t\) instead of \(\cos\omega t\).  Keep in mind that the constants are related by \(\gamma = b/m\).

The problem proposes the trial solution \(z(t)=A\sin(\omega t-\phi)\), with \(A>0\) and \(0\le\phi\le\pi\).  This is completely analogous to the guess used for the cosine‑driven case in the textbook (Eq. 11.26), but written in terms of sine to match the driving.  

Now use the “trigonometric method” (harmonic balance) described in the Purcell & Morin passage.  The steps are:
1. **Substitute the trial solution into the equation of motion.**  You will need the first and second derivatives of \(A\sin(\omega t-\phi)\).  
2. **Expand \(\sin(\omega t-\phi)\) and \(\cos(\omega t-\phi)\)** using the trig sum formulas, so that everything is expressed in terms of \(\sin\omega t\) and \(\cos\omega t\).  
3. **Collect coefficients of \(\sin\omega t\) and \(\cos\omega t\).**  Since the right‑hand side contains only a \(\sin\omega t\) term, the total coefficient of \(\cos\omega t\) must be zero, and the coefficient of \(\sin\omega t\) must equal \(F_{0}\).

This procedure yields two simultaneous equations.  
- The equation from the \(\cos\omega t\) coefficient will involve \(\phi\) but not \(A\).  Solve it for \(\tan\phi\).  (You should see a ratio that depends on \(\omega\), \(\omega_{0}\), \(b\), and \(m\).)  
- The equation from the \(\sin\omega t\) coefficient contains both \(A\) and \(\phi\).  Express \(\sin\phi\) and \(\cos\phi\) in terms of \(\tan\phi\) (for instance, by drawing a right triangle from your \(\tan\phi\) expression) and then solve for \(A\) as a function of \(F_{0}, m, \omega, \omega_{0}, b\).

You can follow the same logical flow as the textbook derivation that leads to Eqs. (11.27) and (11.28); the only difference is the driving function (\(\sin\) instead of \(\cos\)), which shifts the phase but leaves the amplitude form unchanged.

Finally, use the **resonance condition** discussed in the Eisberg & Resnick passage: For a driven oscillator, resonance occurs when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, i.e. \(\omega = \omega_{0}\).  Substitute \(\omega = \omega_{0}\) into your general expressions for \(A\) and \(\phi\).  At resonance you will find a simplified amplitude and a phase shift that is characteristic of a resonantly driven system.  Carry out each algebraic step carefully; the result will give you the requested amplitude and phase both off‑ and at resonance.

sub_problems.problem: (b) A lock-in amplifier shown in Fig.3.1 multiplies an input signal by the lock-in reference signal, $V_{R} = V_{R0} \sin \omega t$, and then passes only the dc (direct current) component of the multiplied signal. Assume that the input signal is given by $V_{i} = V_{i0} \sin (\omega_{i} t - \phi_{i})$. Here $V_{R0}$, $V_{i0}$, $\omega_{i}$, and $\phi_{i}$ are all positive given constants. Find the condition on $\omega (>0)$ for a non-vanishing output signal. What is the expression for the magnitude of the non-vanishing dc output signal at this frequency?
sub_problems.solution:
The multiplied signal is

$$
V_{i0} \sin(\omega_i t - \phi_i) \, V_{R0} \sin(\omega t) = \frac{1}{2} V_{i0} V_{R0} \left[ \cos\left((\omega_i - \omega) t - \phi_i\right) - \cos\left((\omega_i + \omega) t - \phi_i\right) \right].
$$

A non-vanishing dc component exists only when $\omega = \omega_i$. In this case the magnitude of the dc output signal is

$$
\frac{1}{2} V_{i0} V_{R0} \cos \phi_i.
$$

knowledge_points.name: lock-in amplifier
knowledge_points.description: Understand that the lock-in amplifier multiplies the input signal by a reference sinusoid and then retains only the dc (time-averaged) component of the product.

knowledge_points.name: product-to-sum trigonometric identity
knowledge_points.description: Apply the identity sin α sin β = ½[cos(α − β) − cos(α + β)] to rewrite the product of the two sinusoidal signals as a sum of cosine terms.

knowledge_points.name: time-average of sinusoidal signal
knowledge_points.description: Recognise that the dc component is the constant term in the expansion; any cos(Ωt + θ) term with Ω ≠ 0 averages to zero, so a non‑vanishing dc signal requires Ω = 0, i.e. ω = ωᵢ.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, write down the product of the input signal \(V_i = V_{i0}\sin(\omega_i t - \phi_i)\) and the reference signal \(V_R = V_{R0}\sin\omega t\). This is the multiplied signal that enters the lock‑in amplifier.

To see which frequency components are present, convert this product into a sum of two trigonometric terms. Use a product‑to‑sum identity—just as reference uses angle‑addition formulas to combine two sine waves into a product form when deriving the standing wave (reference.31 → reference.32). The identity you need here is  
\[
\sin A \sin B = \tfrac12[\cos(A-B) - \cos(A+B)],
\]  
with \(A = \omega_i t - \phi_i\) and \(B = \omega t\).

Applying this identity will give you two cosine terms: one containing \((\omega_i - \omega)t\) and the other containing \((\omega_i + \omega)t\). The lock‑in amplifier passes only the **dc** (direct current) component of the multiplied signal. A dc component means a term that is strictly constant in time—no oscillatory \(t\) dependence.

Therefore, examine the two cosine terms. The second term, with frequency \(\omega_i+\omega\), can never be constant because \(\omega\) and \(\omega_i\) are positive constants. The first term, however, becomes time‑independent precisely when its argument does not depend on \(t\). This occurs when the coefficient of \(t\) vanishes, i.e. when \(\omega_i - \omega = 0\). From this you immediately obtain the condition on \(\omega\) (in terms of \(\omega_i\)) for a non‑vanishing output.

With that condition satisfied, substitute \([final result intentionally omitted]\) back into the product‑to‑sum result. The constant term will be the cosine with no \(t\) dependence, and its argument simplifies to a constant phase \(-\phi_i\) (recall \(\cos(-\theta) = \cos\theta\)). The magnitude of the dc output signal is then simply the amplitude (absolute value) of that surviving constant term. Extract that amplitude from the coefficient of the cosine, remembering the factor \(1/2\) that came from the identity.

sub_problems.problem: (c) Passing through the phase shifter, the lock-in reference voltage $V_{R} = V_{R0} \sin \omega t$ changes to $V'_{R} = V_{R0} \sin (\omega t + \pi / 2)$. $V'_{R}$, applied to the piezoelectric tube, drives the cantilever with a force $F = c_{1} V'_{R}$. Then, the photo-detector converts the displacement of the cantilever, $z$, into a voltage $V_{i} = c_{2} z$. Here $c_{1}$ and $c_{2}$ are constants. Find the expression for the magnitude of the dc output signal at $\omega = \omega_{0}$.
sub_problems.solution:
At resonance, the amplitude of the cantilever displacement is $z_0 = \frac{F_0}{b \omega_0}$, where $F_0 = c_1 V_{R0}$ is the amplitude of the driving force. The photo-detector converts displacement to voltage: $V_i = c_2 z$, so the amplitude of the input signal is

$$
V_{i0} = c_2 \frac{F_0}{b \omega_0} = \frac{c_1 c_2 V_{R0}}{b \omega_0}.
$$

At resonance, the phase of the displacement relative to the driving force is $-\pi/2$. The reference voltage after the phase shifter is $V'_R = V_{R0} \sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$, so the phase of the input signal relative to the reference is $\phi_i = -\pi/2 + \pi/2 = 0$. The lock-in amplifier output is the dc component of the product $V_i V'_R$, given by

$$
\frac{1}{2} V_{i0} V_{R0} \cos \phi_i = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{c_1 c_2 V_{R0}}{b \omega_0} \cdot V_{R0} \cdot 1 = \frac{c_1 c_2}{2} \frac{V_{R0}^2}{b \omega_0}.
$$

\boxed{\frac{c_1 c_2}{2} \frac{V_{R0}^2}{b \omega_0}}

knowledge_points.name: Resonance amplitude of forced damped harmonic oscillator
knowledge_points.description: For a forced damped harmonic oscillator, the steady-state amplitude at resonance (ω = ω0) is A = F0/(b ω0), where F0 is the driving force amplitude and b is the damping coefficient.

knowledge_points.name: Phase lag at resonance for forced oscillator
knowledge_points.description: At resonance, the displacement of a forced damped harmonic oscillator lags the driving force by a phase of π/2.

knowledge_points.name: Lock-in amplifier output formula
knowledge_points.description: The dc output of a lock-in amplifier with input V_i = V_i0 sin(ω t - φ_i) and reference V_R = V_R0 sin ωt is (1/2) V_i0 V_R0 cos φ_i, as derived in part (b).

knowledge_points.name: Phase shift propagation
knowledge_points.description: The overall phase difference between two signals in a system with multiple phase-shifting elements is the sum of the individual phase shifts along the signal path.

sub_problems.problem: (d) The small change $\Delta m$ of the cantilever mass shifts the resonance frequency by $\Delta\omega_0$ . As a result, the phase $\phi$ at the original resonance frequency $\omega_0$ shifts by $\Delta\phi$ . Find the mass change $\Delta m$ corresponding to the phase shift $\Delta\phi = \pi/1800$ , which is a typical resolution in phase measurements. The physical parameters of the cantilever are given by $m = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}$ kg, $k = 1.0$ N/m, and $(b/m) = 1.0 \times 10^{3}$ s $^{-1}$ . Use the approximations $(1+x)^{a} \approx 1+ax$ and $\tan(\pi/2+x) \approx -1/x$ when $|x|<<1$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The original resonance frequency is

$$
\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}.
$$

When the mass changes by $\Delta m$, the new resonance frequency becomes

$$
\sqrt{\frac{k}{m + \Delta m}} = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \left(1 + \frac{\Delta m}{m}\right)^{-1/2} \approx \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} \left(1 - \frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta m}{m}\right) = \omega_0 \left(1 - \frac{1}{2} \frac{\Delta m}{m}\right).
$$

Thus the shift in resonance frequency is

$$
\Delta \omega_0 = -\frac{1}{2} \omega_0 \frac{\Delta m}{m}. \tag{1}
$$

Near resonance, the phase $\phi$ at the original resonance frequency $\omega_0$ shifts by $\Delta\phi$ due to the change in $\omega_0$. Substituting $\phi = \pi/2 + \Delta\phi$ and $\omega_0 \to \omega_0 + \Delta\omega_0$ into the phase expression (from part (a3)), we obtain

$$
\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + \Delta\phi\right) = -\frac{1}{\tan\Delta\phi} = \frac{b}{2m \Delta\omega_0}.
$$

For small $\Delta\phi$, $\tan\Delta\phi \approx \Delta\phi$, so

$$
\Delta\phi \approx -\frac{2m \Delta\omega_0}{b}. \tag{2}
$$

Combining (1) and (2) gives

$$
\Delta m = \frac{b}{\omega_0} \Delta\phi.
$$

Using the given values $m = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}$ kg, $k = 1.0$ N/m, and $b/m = 1.0 \times 10^3$ s$^{-1}$, we compute

$$
\omega_0 = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.0}{1.0 \times 10^{-12}}} = 1.0 \times 10^6 \text{ rad/s},
$$

and $b = (b/m) \cdot m = (1.0 \times 10^3) \cdot (1.0 \times 10^{-12}) = 1.0 \times 10^{-9}$ kg/s. With $\Delta\phi = \pi/1800$,

$$
\Delta m = \frac{1.0 \times 10^{-9}}{1.0 \times 10^6} \cdot \frac{\pi}{1800} = \frac{\pi}{1.8} \times 10^{-18} \text{ kg} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-18} \text{ kg}.
$$

\boxed{\Delta m = \frac{\pi}{1.8} \times 10^{-18} \text{ kg} \approx 1.7 \times 10^{-18} \text{ kg}}

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the resonance frequency of a mass–spring oscillator from the textbook (Kleppner & Kolenkow, 6.2.1): the angular frequency is given by  
\( \omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m} \).  
Use the given values of \(k\) and \(m\) to compute the original resonance frequency \(\omega_0\) of the cantilever when its mass is unchanged.

When a small mass change \(\Delta m\) occurs, the new resonance frequency is  
\( \omega_0' = \sqrt{\frac{k}{m+\Delta m}} \).  
To find the shift \(\Delta\omega_0 = \omega_0' - \omega_0\), rewrite the square‑root using the binomial approximation that was introduced in Kleppner & Kolenkow (1.11.4):  
\[
(1+x)^n \approx 1 + n x \quad\text{for small }x.
\]
Apply this with \(x = \Delta m/m\) and \(n = -1/2\). You will obtain an approximate linear relation between \(\Delta\omega_0\) and \(\Delta m\). This step gives you equation (1) connecting the resonance‑frequency shift to the mass change.

Now turn to the phase behaviour of a driven damped oscillator. At the original (unperturbed) resonance, you know from the textbook (Georgi, 2.3.3 and Figure 2.8) that the phase lag between the drive and the response is \(\pi/2\). The problem states that when the resonance frequency shifts by \(\Delta\omega_0\), the phase at the original driving frequency \(\omega_0\) changes by a small amount \(\Delta\phi\). From your earlier derivation of the phase \(\phi\) (e.g. in part (a3) of this problem), you can substitute \(\phi = \pi/2 + \Delta\phi\) and the shifted resonance frequency. Near resonance and for small shifts, the expression simplifies dramatically when you use the given approximation  
\[
\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} + x\right) \approx -\frac{1}{x} \quad\text{for }|x|\ll 1,
\]
and also \(\tan\Delta\phi \approx \Delta\phi\). Carry out this substitution to obtain a relation that links \(\Delta\phi\) to \(\Delta\omega_0\) and the damping constant \(b\) and mass \(m\). This step gives you equation (2).

Finally, combine the two relations: eliminate \(\Delta\omega_0\) between the equation from the binomial‑expansion step and the equation from the phase‑shift step. Solve the resulting formula for \(\Delta m\) in terms of \(\Delta\phi\), \(\omega_0\), and \(b\). To evaluate it numerically, use the given \(b/m\) ratio and the mass \(m\) to find \(b\), then insert \(\omega_0\) (from the first step) and \(\Delta\phi = \pi/1800\). All approximations are justified because \(\Delta m \ll m\) and \(\Delta\phi\) is very small. Carry out the algebra yourself — the final expression is simple, and the arithmetic will yield the requested mass change.

sub_problems.problem: (e) Assuming that the additional force $f(h)$ depends only on the distance $h$ between the cantilever and the sample surface, one can find a new equilibrium position $h_0$. Near $h = h_0$, we can write $f(h) \approx f(h_0) + c_3(h - h_0)$, where $c_3$ is a constant in $h$. Find the new resonance frequency $\omega'_0$ in terms of $\omega_0$, $m$, and $c_3$.
sub_problems.solution:
In the presence of interaction, the equation of motion near the new equilibrium position $h_0$ becomes

$$
m \frac{d^2 z}{dt^2} + b \frac{dz}{dt} + m \omega_0^2 z - c_3 z = F_0 \sin \omega t
$$

where $z = h - h_0$ is the displacement from the new equilibrium position $h_0$, and we used $f(h) \approx f(h_0) + c_3 z$. The constant term $f(h_0)$ is cancelled at the new equilibrium.

Thus the original resonance frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}$ is shifted to

$$
\omega_0' = \sqrt{\frac{k - c_3}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{m \omega_0^2 - c_3}{m}} = \omega_0 \sqrt{1 - \frac{c_3}{m \omega_0^2}}.
$$

Hence the new resonance frequency is

$$
\boxed{\omega_0' = \omega_0 \sqrt{1 - \frac{c_3}{m \omega_0^2}}}.
$$

The constant term cancels with the static spring force at equilibrium, leaving a linear term that modifies the restoring force.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall that without the additional force, the cantilever behaves as a damped, driven harmonic oscillator.  The resonance frequency \(\omega_0\) is the natural frequency of that oscillator, and from reference discussion of resonance (see the expositions that identify the resonant angular frequency \(\omega_0\) and its connection to the spring constant) you know that \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}\), where \(k\) is the original spring constant and \(m\) is the mass.  Therefore you can immediately express \(k\) in terms of \(m\) and \(\omega_0\): \(k = m\omega_0^2\).

Now introduce the additional force \(f(h)\) that depends only on the tip–sample distance \(h\).  The total force on the cantilever at any position \(h\) is the sum of the original spring restoring force (Hooke’s‑law form, directed toward its own equilibrium position) and \(f(h)\).  A **new equilibrium position** \(h_0\) is reached when the total force is zero.  To analyze the motion near this new equilibrium, define the small displacement \(z = h - h_0\).

Next, **linearize the total force** around \(h_0\).  The problem gives you the linear expansion of \(f(h)\): \(f(h) \approx f(h_0) + c_3 z\).  Combine this with the original spring force written in terms of \(z\).  The key idea – which is the same as reference discussion of Hooke’s law (Kleppner & Kolenkow, reference.7) and the effective spring‑constant examples (e.g., the diatomic molecule, or the bead between gravitating masses) – is that **for small oscillations, the force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium**, and the constant of proportionality is the effective spring constant.  Because \(h_0\) is an equilibrium point, the constant force terms cancel when you express the total force in terms of \(z\).  You are left with a linear term whose coefficient gives the effective spring constant \(k_{\text{eff}}\).

Inspect the signs carefully: the original spring supplies a term proportional to \(-k z\), while the expansion of \(f\) contributes a term proportional to \(+c_3 z\).  The total linear restoring force is therefore \(-(k - c_3)z\), so the effective spring constant is \(k_{\text{eff}} = k - c_3\).

Finally, the new resonance frequency \(\omega_0'\) is just the natural frequency of a harmonic oscillator with this effective spring constant: \(\omega_0' = \sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}/m}\).  Substituting \(k = m\omega_0^2\) will let you write \(\omega_0'\) entirely in terms of \(\omega_0\), \(m\), and \(c_3\).  This is exactly the procedure used in the worked example of the bead between two masses (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Solution Manual 6.1), where an effective spring constant is extracted from a Taylor expansion and then the oscillation frequency is found via \(\sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}/m}\).

Carry out those steps: write the total force, identify the coefficient of \(z\), obtain \(k_{\text{eff}} = k - c_3\), replace \(k\) with \(m\omega_0^2\), and finally construct \(\omega_0' = \sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}/m}\).

sub_problems.problem:
(f) While scanning the surface by moving the sample horizontally, the tip of the cantilever charged with $Q = 6e$ encounters an electron of charge $q = e$ trapped (localized in space) at some distance below the surface. During the scanning around the electron, the maximum shift of the resonance frequency $\Delta\omega_{0}(=\omega'_{0}-\omega_{0})$ is observed to be much smaller than $\omega_{0}$. Express the distance $d_{0}$ from the cantilever to the trapped electron at the maximum shift in terms of $m$, $q$, $Q$, $\omega_{0}$, $\Delta\omega_{0}$, and the Coulomb constant $k_{e}$. Evaluate $d_{0}$ in nm (1 nm = $1\times10^{-9}$ m) for $\Delta\omega_{0}=20\ \mathrm{s}^{-1}$.

The physical parameters of the cantilever are $m=1.0\times10^{-12}$ kg and $k=1.0$ N/m. Disregard any polarization effect in both the cantilever tip and the surface. Note that $k_{e}=1/4\pi\varepsilon_{0}=9.0\times10^{9}$ N·m$^{2}$/C$^{2}$ and $e=-1.6\times10^{-19}$ C.
sub_problems.solution:
The maximum shift occurs when the cantilever is directly above the trapped charge. The interaction force is Coulomb's law:

$$
f(h) = k_e \frac{qQ}{h^2}.
$$

The effective spring constant change is given by the derivative of the force with respect to height, evaluated at the equilibrium distance $d_0$:

$$
c_3 = \left. \frac{df}{dh} \right|_{h=d_0} = -2k_e \frac{qQ}{d_0^3}.
$$

Since $\Delta\omega_0 \ll \omega_0$, the frequency shift can be approximated as:

$$
\Delta\omega_0 \approx -\frac{c_3}{2m\omega_0}.
$$

Substituting $c_3$:

$$
\Delta\omega_0 = -\frac{1}{2m\omega_0}\left(-2k_e \frac{qQ}{d_0^3}\right) = k_e \frac{qQ}{m\omega_0 d_0^3}.
$$

Solving for $d_0$:

$$
d_0 = \left( k_e \frac{qQ}{m\omega_0 \Delta\omega_0} \right)^{1/3}.
$$

Now evaluate numerically. Given $q = e = -1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, $Q = 6e = -9.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$, $m = 1.0 \times 10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}$, $k = 1.0\,\mathrm{N/m}$, so $\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m} = \sqrt{1.0 / 1.0\times10^{-12}} = 1.0 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\Delta\omega_0 = 20\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $k_e = 9.0 \times 10^9\,\mathrm{N\cdot m^2/C^2}$. Note that $qQ = (-1.6\times10^{-19})(-9.6\times10^{-19}) = 1.536 \times 10^{-37}\,\mathrm{C^2}$.

$$
d_0 = \left( 9.0\times10^9 \times \frac{1.536\times10^{-37}}{(1.0\times10^{-12})(1.0\times10^6)(20)} \right)^{1/3} = \left( \frac{9.0\times10^9 \times 1.536\times10^{-37}}{2.0\times10^{-5}} \right)^{1/3} = \left( 6.912 \times 10^{-23} \right)^{1/3} = 4.1 \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{m} = 41\,\mathrm{nm}.
$$

\boxed{d_0 = 41\,\mathrm{nm}}

title: An Ill Fated Satellite
problem:
The most frequent orbital manoeuvres performed by spacecraft consist of velocity variations along the direction of flight, namely accelerations to reach higher orbits or brakings done to initiate re-entering in the atmosphere. In this problem we will study the orbital variations when the engine thrust is applied in a radial direction.

To obtain numerical values use: Earth radius $R_{T} = 6.37 \cdot 10^{6}$ m, Earth surface gravity $g = 9.81 \, m/s^{2}$ , and take the length of the sidereal day to be $T_{0} = 24.0 \, h$ .

We consider a geosynchronous $^{1}$ communications satellite of mass m placed in an equatorial circular orbit of radius $r_{0}$ . These satellites have an apogee engine which provides the tangential thrusts needed to reach the final orbit.

Image: ESA

Marks are indicated at the beginning of each subquestion, in parenthesis.

Once this geosynchronous circular orbit has been reached (see Figure F-1), the satellite has been stabilised in the desired location, and is being readied to do its work, an error by the ground controllers causes the apogee engine to be fired again. The thrust happens to be directed towards the Earth and, despite the quick reaction of the ground crew to shut the engine off, an unwanted velocity variation $\Delta v$ is imparted on the satellite. We characterize this boost by the parameter $\beta = \Delta v / v_{0}$ . The duration of the engine burn is always negligible with respect to any other orbital times, so that it can be considered as instantaneous.

F-1

Under the action of central forces obeying the inverse-square law, bodies follow trajectories described by ellipses, parabolas or hyperbolas. In the approximation $m \ll M$ the gravitating mass M is at one of the focuses. Taking the origin at this focus, the general polar equation of these curves can be written as (see Figure F-3)

$$
r (\theta) = \frac {l}{1 - \varepsilon \cos \theta}
$$

where l is a positive constant named the semi-latus-rectum and $\varepsilon$ is the eccentricity of the curve. In terms of constants of motion:

$$
l = \frac {L ^ {2}}{G M m ^ {2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \varepsilon = \left(1 + \frac {2 E L ^ {2}}{G ^ {2} M ^ {2} m ^ {3}}\right) ^ {1 / 2}
$$

F-3

where G is the Newton constant, L is the modulus of the angular momentum of the orbiting mass, with respect to the origin, and E is its mechanical energy, with zero potential energy at infinity.

We may have the following cases:

i) If $0 \leq \varepsilon < 1$ , the curve is an ellipse (circumference for $\varepsilon = 0$ ).   
ii) If $\varepsilon = 1$ , the curve is a parabola.   
iii) If $\varepsilon > 1$ , the curve is a hyperbola.

sub_problems.problem: 1.1 Compute the numerical value of $r_0$.
sub_problems.solution:
The gravitational force provides the centripetal acceleration:

\[
G \frac{M_T m}{r_0^2} = m \frac{v_0^2}{r_0}
\]

The orbital speed is related to the period:

\[
v_0 = \frac{2 \pi r_0}{T_0}
\]

The surface gravity is:

\[
g = \frac{G M_T}{R_T^2}
\]

Combining these equations yields:

\[
r_0 = \left( \frac{g R_T^2 T_0^2}{4 \pi^2} \right)^{1/3}
\]

Substituting the known values gives:

\[
\boxed{r_0 = 4.22 \times 10^7 \, \mathrm{m}}
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the numerical value of \(r_0\), you need to combine several relations that are all covered in your reference passages. Think of it as building the answer step by step from principles you already know.

**Step 1 — Identify the physical situation and the key condition.**  
The problem involves a satellite in a **geosynchronous orbit** (often called geostationary when equatorial). From reference passage on *Geosynchronous orbit period*, a satellite in such an orbit has an angular speed \(\Omega_e\) equal to the Earth’s rotation rate, so its orbital period is \(T_0 = 24\) hours (or approximately \(86\,400\) seconds). This is the starting constraint.

**Step 2 — Relate orbital speed, radius, and period.**  
For uniform circular motion, the orbital speed \(v_0\) is connected to the orbital radius \(r_0\) and the period \(T_0\) by  
\[
v_0 = \frac{2\pi r_0}{T_0}.
\]  
This is exactly the relation derived in the *Orbital speed-period relation* passage, where the period \(T\) is the time to traverse the circumference at constant speed. You will use this to replace \(v_0\) later.

**Step 3 — Apply Newton’s second law for a circular orbit.**  
The satellite is kept in its circular orbit by the gravitational force, which provides the necessary centripetal acceleration. From the *Newton’s law of universal gravitation* passage, the gravitational force between Earth (mass \(M_T\)) and the satellite (mass \(m\)) at separation \(r_0\) is  
\[
F = G\frac{M_T m}{r_0^2}.
\]  
From the *Circular orbit* discussion (and the centripetal acceleration concept), for a circular orbit we equate this force to \(m a_c = m\frac{v_0^2}{r_0}\):  
\[
G\frac{M_T m}{r_0^2} = m\frac{v_0^2}{r_0}.
\]  
Cancel the satellite mass \(m\) and simplify to obtain a relation among \(G, M_T, r_0, v_0\).

**Step 4 — Eliminate the unknown Earth mass \(M_T\) using surface gravity.**  
You do not have \(M_T\) given directly, but you know the acceleration due to gravity at Earth’s surface, \(g\), and Earth’s radius \(R_T\). The *Surface gravity relation* passage gives  
\[
g = \frac{G M_T}{R_T^2}.
\]  
Rearrange this to express the product \(G M_T\) as \(g R_T^2\). This lets you replace \(G M_T\) wherever it appears.

**Step 5 — Combine everything to isolate \(r_0\).**  
Take the equation from Step 3 and substitute both the expression for \(v_0\) from Step 2 and the product \(G M_T = g R_T^2\) from Step 4. You will get an equation where the only unknown is \(r_0\). Solve that equation for \(r_0\) — the algebra will lead to a cube root.

**Step 6 — Insert the numerical values and compute.**  
Now you can put in the numbers:  
- \(g \approx 9.80\ \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}\) (from the surface gravity passage),  
- \(R_T\) (Earth’s radius; use the value given in your problem or a standard value such as \(6.37\times10^6\ \text{m}\) or \(6400\ \text{km}\) as referenced in the geosynchronous orbit worked example),  
- \(T_0 = 24\ \text{h} = 86\,400\ \text{s}\).

Carry out the calculation carefully, watching your units. The result will be the orbital radius \(r_0\) in meters. (If you also need the altitude above Earth’s surface, subtract \(R_T\) afterward, just as shown in the geosynchronous orbit example.)

This layered approach — using period to get speed, Newton’s law and centripetal acceleration to link force and motion, and surface gravity to eliminate the planet’s mass — is exactly the reasoning behind the worked example for a geostationary orbit in your reference. Follow that logical flow, and you will arrive at the correct numerical value.

sub_problems.problem: 1.2 Give the analytical expression of the velocity $v_{0}$ of the satellite as a function of $g$, $R_{T}$, and $r_{0}$, and calculate its numerical value.
sub_problems.solution:
The centripetal force is provided by the gravitational force:

\[
G \frac{M_T m}{r_0^2} = m \frac{v_0^2}{r_0}
\]

Using the relation for gravitational acceleration at the Earth's surface:

\[
g = \frac{G M_T}{R_T^2}
\]

Eliminate \(G M_T\) to obtain:

\[
v_0 = R_T \sqrt{\frac{g}{r_0}}
\]

This is the analytical expression for the velocity \(v_0\) as a function of \(g\), \(R_T\), and \(r_0\).

To calculate the numerical value, substitute \(R_T = 6.37 \times 10^6\,\mathrm{m}\), \(g = 9.81\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), and \(r_0 = 4.22 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{m}\):

\[
v_0 = 6.37 \times 10^6 \sqrt{\frac{9.81}{4.22 \times 10^7}} \approx 3.07 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}
\]

\[
\boxed{v_0 = R_T \sqrt{\frac{g}{r_0}}}, \quad \boxed{v_0 = 3.07 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{m/s}}
\]

To find the velocity \(v_{0}\) of the satellite, you will use the fact that it is in a circular orbit around Earth. The satellite’s mass is negligible compared to Earth’s mass, so you can treat Earth as fixed, just as in the textbook examples on geostationary orbits (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 10.5.2) and small satellites (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 10.4).

**Step 1 – Relate forces for circular motion**  
Newton’s second law for circular motion tells you that the centripetal force needed to keep the satellite in a circular path of radius \(r_{0}\) at speed \(v_{0}\) is \(m v_{0}^{2}/r_{0}\) (see the discussion of centripetal acceleration in Carroll & Ostlie, Section 17.2, where they equate centripetal and gravitational accelerations for a satellite).  
This centripetal force is provided entirely by Earth’s gravitational pull. According to Newton’s law of universal gravitation (Carroll & Ostlie, Eq. 2.11), the magnitude of that force is \(G M_{T} m / r_{0}^{2}\), where \(M_{T}\) is Earth’s mass.  
Set these two forces equal to each other. Because the satellite mass \(m\) appears on both sides, it cancels out – a consequence of the fact that the gravitational acceleration is independent of the small mass, as discussed in the surface‑gravity passages.

**Step 2 – Introduce the surface gravity \(g\)**  
You now have an equation that involves \(G M_{T}\). To replace this product with the known surface gravity \(g\), use the relation from the textbook: at Earth’s surface, the gravitational acceleration is  
\[
g = \frac{G M_{T}}{R_{T}^{2}}
\]  
(see Kleppner & Kolenkow, Section 3.3.2, or Morin, Section 1.1, where this is derived). Solve this relation for \(G M_{T}\) and substitute into your force equation. This eliminates the gravitational constant and Earth’s mass, leaving an expression that contains only \(g\), \(R_{T}\), and \(r_{0}\).

**Step 3 – Solve for \(v_{0}\) analytically**  
Rearrange the resulting equation to isolate \(v_{0}\). You will obtain a formula that expresses \(v_{0}\) in terms of \(g\), \(R_{T}\), and \(r_{0}\). Do not plug in numbers yet.

**Step 4 – Numerical evaluation**  
You already have the value of \(r_{0}\) from the geostationary orbit condition; it appears in the worked example of Kleppner & Kolenkow (Section 10.5.2) as the orbital radius for a satellite that stays above a fixed point on the equator. Use that numerical value together with the standard values \(R_{T} = 6.37 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m}\) and \(g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^{2}\) (given in the surface‑gravity passages). Substitute all three numbers into your analytical expression and carry out the arithmetic to find the numerical speed of the satellite.

sub_problems.problem: 1.3 Obtain the expressions of its angular momentum $L_0$ and mechanical energy $E_0$, as functions of $v_0, m, g$ and $R_T$.
sub_problems.solution:
The angular momentum about the center of the Earth is

$$
L_0 = r_0 m v_0 = \frac{g R_T^2}{v_0^2} m v_0 = \frac{m g R_T^2}{v_0}.
$$

The mechanical energy is

$$
E_0 = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - G \frac{M_T m}{r_0} = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - \frac{g R_T^2 m}{r_0} = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 - m v_0^2 = -\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2.
$$

\boxed{L_0 = \frac{m g R_T^2}{v_0}} \quad \boxed{E_0 = -\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2}

sub_problems.problem: 2.1 Determine the parameters of the new orbit, semi-latus-rectum $l$ and eccentricity $\varepsilon$, in terms of $r_{0}$ and $\beta$.
sub_problems.solution:
The semi-latus-rectum $l$ is obtained from the conservation of orbital angular momentum. The angular momentum is the same in both orbits, so

$$
l = \frac{L_0^2}{G M_T m^2} = \frac{m^2 g^2 R_T^4}{v_0^2} \frac{1}{g R_T^2 m^2} = \frac{g R_T^2}{v_0^2} = r_0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{l = r_0}
$$

The eccentricity is given by

$$
\varepsilon^2 = 1 + \frac{2 E L_0^2}{G^2 M_T^2 m^3}
$$

where $E$ is the new mechanical energy of the satellite:

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m (v_0^2 + \Delta v^2) - G \frac{M_T m}{r_0} = \frac{1}{2} m \Delta v^2 + E_0 = \frac{1}{2} m \Delta v^2 - \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2
$$

that is

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 \left( \frac{\Delta v^2}{v_0^2} - 1 \right) = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 (\beta^2 - 1)
$$

Combining both, one gets $\varepsilon = \beta$. This is an elliptical trajectory because $\varepsilon = \beta < 1$.

\boxed{\varepsilon = \beta}

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the parameters of the new orbit after a radial impulse, follow these steps using the concepts from your reference.

**1. Find the semi-latus rectum \(l\) using conservation of angular momentum.**
The impulse is radial (along the direction of \( \mathbf{r} \)), so it exerts no torque about the center of the Earth. As explained in reference section on conservation of angular momentum, if torque is zero, angular momentum \(L\) is conserved. For an orbiting object, \( L = m v r \), where \( v \) is the transverse velocity and \( r \) is the distance from the center.
- Before the impulse, the satellite was in a circular orbit of radius \( r_0 \). From the circular velocity example, the speed in that orbit is \( v_c = \sqrt{GM/r_0} \), so the initial angular momentum is \( L_0 = m v_c r_0 \).
- After the radial impulse, the transverse velocity is unchanged (the impulse adds no transverse component), and the distance is still \( r_0 \) instantaneously. Therefore, the angular momentum \( L \) after the impulse is exactly the same as \( L_0 \).
- The semi-latus rectum \(l\) of any orbit is related to the angular momentum by the formula given in the elliptic orbits section: \( [final result intentionally omitted] = L^2/(\mu C) \), where \( C = GMm \) and \( \mu \approx m \) for a satellite much lighter than Earth. Because \( L \) is unchanged, \( l \) equals the initial circular radius. Relate this to the given \( r_0 \).

**2. Find the eccentricity \(\varepsilon\) using the new mechanical energy and the conserved angular momentum.**
reference section on elliptic orbits gives the eccentricity formula: \( \varepsilon^2 = 1 + \frac{2 E L^2}{\mu C^2} \). You already know \( L \) (or can express it in terms of \( r_0 \) and the circular speed) and \( C \). You now need the new total mechanical energy \( E \) after the impulse.
- The mechanical energy in a gravitational field is \( E = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 - \frac{GMm}{r} \), as shown in the Hohmann transfer worked example.
- Before the impulse, the satellite had energy \( E_0 = -\frac{1}{2} m v_c^2 \) (the energy of a circular orbit, also derived in the Hohmann example).
- The impulse instantaneously changes the velocity. The radial impulse adds a component \( \Delta v \) perpendicular to the original circular velocity \( v_0 \). The new speed squared is \( v_0^2 + \Delta v^2 \), because the two components are perpendicular. The problem defines \( \beta = \Delta v / v_0 \).
- Write the new kinetic energy using this speed, and subtract the unchanged potential energy at radius \( r_0 \). Express the new total energy \( E \) in terms of \( E_0 \) and \( \Delta v \), then in terms of \( v_0 \) and \( \beta \).

**3. Combine the expressions.**
Insert the expressions for \( E \) and \( L \) (in terms of \( v_0, r_0, m, GM \)) into the eccentricity formula. Simplify using the relation for circular orbits: \( v_0^2 = GM/r_0 \). Most terms cancel, leaving \( \varepsilon \) expressed solely in terms of \( \beta \). The result shows that the new orbit is an ellipse because \( \beta < 1 \) implies \( \varepsilon < 1 \), consistent with the elliptic orbits section’s condition for elliptical motion.

sub_problems.problem: 2.4 Determine the period of the new orbit, $T$, as a function of $T_0$ and $\beta$, and calculate its numerical value for $\beta = 1/4$.
sub_problems.solution:
By Kepler's third law, the period $T$ in the new orbit satisfies

$$
\frac{T^2}{a^3} = \frac{T_0^2}{r_0^3}
$$

where $a$, the semi-major axis of the ellipse, is given by

$$
a = \frac{r_{\text{max}} + r_{\text{min}}}{2} = \frac{r_0}{1 - \beta^2}
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{T = T_0 \left(1 - \beta^2\right)^{-3/2}}
$$

For $\beta = 1/4$

$$
\boxed{T = T_0 \left(\frac{15}{16}\right)^{-3/2} = 26.4\,\mathrm{h}}
$$

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the period \(T\) of the new orbit, you will need to connect the geometry of the ellipse to the orbital period, using the reference circular geosynchronous orbit as a baseline.

**1. Recall the relationship between period and semi-major axis**
From your reference, Kepler’s third law (in its Newtonian form) states that the square of the period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis. For two orbits around the same central body, the ratio \(P^2/a^3\) is constant. In this problem, you have a known circular geosynchronous orbit with period \(T_0\) and radius \(r_0\). The new orbit is an ellipse with semi-major axis \(a\) and period \(T\). Because the central body is the same, you can write:
\[
\frac{T^2}{a^3} = \frac{T_0^2}{r_0^3}
\]
This step is analogous to the comparison of planetary orbits shown in Table 10.1 of Kleppner & Kolenkow, where \(A^3/T^2\) is constant for all planets orbiting the Sun.

**2. Find the semi-major axis \(a\) of the new elliptical orbit**
The ellipse is described by the parameter \(\beta\) (which plays the role of eccentricity \(\epsilon\) in reference passages). You have already determined the perigee \(r_{\min}\) and apogee \(r_{\max}\) in a previous part of the problem. The semi-major axis \(a\) is half the major axis \(A\), and the major axis is the sum of the maximum and minimum distances from the focus:
\[
a = \frac{r_{\max} + r_{\min}}{2}
\]
Use the expressions for \(r_{\max}\) and \(r_{\min}\) in terms of \(r_0\) and \(\beta\) that you derived earlier. reference section “Properties of the Ellipse” (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Note 10.2) gives exactly this relationship: \(r_{\max} = r_0/(1-\epsilon)\), \(r_{\min} = r_0/(1+\epsilon)\), and \(a = r_0/(1-\epsilon^2)\). With \(\beta\) in place of \(\epsilon\), you can write \(a\) directly as a function of \(r_0\) and \(\beta\).

**3. Combine to express \(T\) in terms of \(T_0\) and \(\beta\)**
Substitute your expression for \(a\) into the Kepler’s law ratio from step 1. Isolate \(T\) algebraically. You should obtain a formula that involves only \(T_0\) and \(\beta\). No numerical values are needed yet.

**4. Numerical evaluation for \(\beta = 1/4\)**

sub_problems.problem: 3.1 Calculate the minimum boost parameter, $\beta_{esc}$, needed for the satellite to escape Earth gravity.
sub_problems.solution:
The satellite escapes Earth gravity if its trajectory is open, i.e., the orbit eccentricity is at least one. The minimum boost corresponds to a parabolic trajectory with eccentricity $\varepsilon = 1$. Since $\varepsilon = \beta$, we obtain

$$
\beta_{\mathrm{esc}} = 1.
$$

Equivalently, the total energy of the satellite must be zero to reach infinity with zero residual kinetic energy:

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 (\beta_{\mathrm{esc}}^2 - 1) = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \beta_{\mathrm{esc}} = 1.
$$

This also follows from requiring the orbital period $T \to \infty$ or the maximum distance $r_{\max} \to \infty$.

\boxed{\beta_{\mathrm{esc}} = 1}

knowledge_points.description: Escape occurs when total mechanical energy E = 0, so the satellite reaches infinity with zero residual kinetic energy; used as an alternative derivation.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the condition that distinguishes a bound orbit from an escape trajectory. According to the textbook (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Solution Manual 10.7), the mechanical energy in an elliptical orbit is negative; for escape, the energy must be increased to be at least zero. The minimum energy for escape is therefore exactly zero. In terms of the orbit’s shape, the same boundary is described in Morin (Section 6.4.3): the eccentricity \(\varepsilon\) determines the type of conic section, and the case \(\varepsilon = 1\) corresponds to a parabola — the “barely escapes” trajectory.

Now, the problem introduces a boost parameter \(\beta\). You have an expression for the satellite’s total mechanical energy written in terms of \(\beta\) (this comes from the problem’s earlier setup). To find the minimum \(\beta\) required for escape, set that total energy equal to zero, because that is the threshold condition you just identified. Solve the resulting equation for \(\beta_{\text{esc}}\) — no further physical conditions are needed. If you have also derived a relation between \(\beta\) and the eccentricity \(\varepsilon\), you can alternatively set \(\varepsilon = 1\) and solve for \(\beta_{\text{esc}}\); the result must be the same.

sub_problems.problem: 3.2 Determine in this case the closest approach of the satellite to the Earth centre in the new trajectory, $r_{min}'$, as a function of $r_0$.
sub_problems.solution:
For $\varepsilon = \beta_{\text{esc}} = 1$, the polar equation of the parabolic trajectory is

$$
r = \frac{l}{1 - \cos \theta}
$$

where the semi-latus rectum is $l = r_0$. The minimum distance from the Earth's centre occurs at $\theta = \pi$, giving

$$
\boxed{r_{\min}' = \frac{r_0}{2}}
$$

This result also follows from energy conservation (total energy $E = 0$) and the equality of angular momentum $L_0$ at the initial point $P$ and at the point of closest approach, where $\vec{r}$ and $\vec{v}$ are perpendicular.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall from reference discussion of parabolic orbits that a parabolic trajectory occurs when the total mechanical energy is zero, corresponding to the escape condition. The polar equation for such a trajectory is given in the problem statement and matches the form used in the “Parabola L” exercise: the distance from the focus (here the Earth’s centre) is expressed in terms of the angle measured from the direction of closest approach.

To find the closest approach distance \( r_{\min}' \), you need to identify the angle at which the radial distance \( r \) is minimised in that polar equation. Look at the denominator: \( 1 - \cos\theta \). The smallest value of \( r \) corresponds to the largest value of the denominator, which occurs when \( \cos\theta \) takes its minimum (\(-1\)). That gives you the angle \( \theta \) at closest approach — the same idea as in “Skimming a planet,” where the particle is at its nearest point to the planet’s centre.

Next, you need the constant \( l \) (the semi-latus rectum) in terms of the given initial distance \( r_0 \). The problem states that the satellite’s initial position is at distance \( r_0 \) with the escape speed \( \beta_{\text{esc}} \). At that initial point, you can relate \( r_0 \) to \( l \) by evaluating the polar equation at the corresponding angle (think about what \( \theta \) represents at the initial point \( P \) — it is not the closest-approach angle). Since the angular momentum is conserved (as emphasised in the “Parabola L” exercise), you can also connect \( l \) to \( r_0 \) using the fact that at the initial point the velocity is purely tangential with the escape speed, and at closest approach the velocity is again perpendicular to the radius vector. This lets you equate the angular momentum expressions at those two points, which will directly give you \( r_{\min}' \) as a fraction of \( r_0 \) without needing to work through the polar equation in detail.

Either method — evaluating the polar equation at the angle you found, or applying conservation of angular momentum between the initial point and closest approach (where \( \vec{r} \) and \( \vec{v} \) are perpendicular) — leads to the same result. Pick one, carry out the substitution of the angle and the relation between \( l \) and \( r_0 \), and solve for \( r_{\min}' \) as a function of \( r_0 \).

sub_problems.problem: 4.1 Determine the residual velocity at the infinity, $v_{\infty}$, as a function of $v_{0}$ and $\beta$.
sub_problems.solution:
By energy conservation, the total energy of the satellite is

$$
E = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 (\beta^2 - 1) = \frac{1}{2} m v_\infty^2
$$

Thus,

$$
\boxed{v_\infty = v_0 \left(\beta^2 - 1\right)^{1/2}}
$$

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the residual velocity at infinity \(v_{\infty}\) in terms of \(v_{0}\) and \(\beta\), follow this method, grounded in the conservation of mechanical energy.

**Step 1: Identify the total energy before the impulse.**
The problem states that a radial impulse has been given to the satellite. From reference passage on *total energy after radial impulse* (Kleppner & Kolenkow, reference.4), firing an engine radially changes the total mechanical energy \(E\) but does not change the angular momentum \(L\). The worked example there describes how a radial blow increases the energy. In your case, the energy after the impulse is expressed in terms of the initial speed \(v_{0}\) and a factor \(\beta\). You need to write the total mechanical energy \(E\) just after the impulse. According to the general form of mechanical energy for orbital motion (reference.3.2), \(E = K + U(r)\). However, the problem statement and reference solution indicate that the post-impulse energy is given directly as \(E = \frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 (\beta^2 - 1)\). Use this expression as the total energy of the satellite after the radial burn.

**Step 2: Apply conservation of mechanical energy.**
The satellite travels from its post-impulse position out to infinity. The gravitational force is conservative (reference.4), so the total mechanical energy \(E\) remains constant along its path. Write the conservation equation equating the energy at the post-impulse state (from Step 1) to the energy when the satellite is at infinity.

**Step 3: Determine the energy at infinity.**
At infinity, the satellite is on a hyperbolic escape trajectory (reference.5.1). reference passage on *zero potential energy at infinity* (Morin, reference.11) states that the potential energy is taken as zero at infinity: \(U(\infty) = 0\). The kinetic energy at infinity is \(\frac{1}{2} m v_{\infty}^2\). Therefore, the total energy at infinity is simply \(\frac{1}{2} m v_{\infty}^2\).

**Step 4: Equate and isolate \(v_{\infty}\).**
Set the total energy from Step 1 equal to the total energy at infinity from Step 3. This is the same logical structure used in the escape velocity derivation (Morin, reference.128), where initial kinetic plus potential energy equals energy at infinity (zero). In your case, the potential energy terms are already accounted for in the given post-impulse energy expression. Solve the resulting equation for \(v_{\infty}\) by isolating it algebraically. You will obtain \(v_{\infty}\) as a function of \(v_{0}\) and \(\beta\).

sub_problems.problem: 4.3 Determine the angle $\phi$ of the asymptotic escape direction in terms of $\beta$. Calculate its numerical value for $\beta = \frac{3}{2}\beta_{esc}$.
sub_problems.solution:
The angle between each asymptote and the hyperbola axis is that appearing in its polar equation in the limit $r \to \infty$. This is the angle for which the equation denominator vanishes

$$
1 - \beta \cos \theta_{\text{asym}} = 0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad \theta_{\text{asym}} = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\right)
$$

According to Figure 5

$$
\phi = \frac{\pi}{2} + \theta_{\text{asym}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{\phi = \frac{\pi}{2} + \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\right)}
$$

For $\beta = \frac{3}{2}\beta_{\text{esc}} = \frac{3}{2}$, one gets $\boxed{\phi = 138^\circ = 2.41\,\text{rad}}$

First, recall the polar equation of a conic section (the orbit equation), which you studied in the proof of conic orbits. In that derivation, the orbit shape is given by a relation involving the eccentricity \(\epsilon\) and the constant \(k\), and the origin (the force center) is at a focus. The problem asks for the asymptotic escape direction — that is, the direction of the hyperbola’s asymptotes. For a hyperbola, the asymptotes correspond to the directions where the radius \(r\) goes to infinity. In the standard polar form of a conic, \(r \to \infty\) occurs when the denominator vanishes. So your first step is to write down the denominator condition from the orbit equation and set it to zero to find the angle(s) that make \(r\) infinite. Because reference’s cartesian treatment ultimately comes from the same polar equation, you can use the fact that the polar equation denominator contains \(1 - \epsilon \cos\theta\) (the eccentricity here is the parameter \(\beta\) given in the problem). Setting that denominator to zero will give you the asymptotic polar angle \(\theta_{\text{asym}}\) in terms of \(\beta\).

Next, interpret this angle geometrically. Look at Figure 5 (or the geometry of a hyperbola relative to its axis). The problem defines \(\phi\) as the angle measured from some reference direction to the asymptote. From the figure, you can see that \(\phi\) is not simply \(\theta_{\text{asym}}\); it is shifted by \(\pi/2\) because of how the coordinate axes are oriented relative to the hyperbola’s symmetry axis. So combine the geometric relation \(\phi = \frac{\pi}{2} + \theta_{\text{asym}}\) with your expression for \(\theta_{\text{asym}}\) to obtain the formula for \(\phi\) in terms of \(\beta\).

Finally, the problem asks for a numerical value when \(\beta = \frac{3}{2}\beta_{\text{esc}}\). The escape condition is a separate idea: for a given central force, there is a critical eccentricity (or energy) that makes the orbit parabolic and just barely unbound. reference example on radial thrust illustrates how one can change the energy without changing angular momentum, and it introduces the parameter \(\beta\) (there it’s a radial oscillation frequency, but the same symbol appears in your problem as the eccentricity). From the context of conic sections, \(\beta_{\text{esc}}\) corresponds to the parabolic case \(\beta = 1\). So \(\frac{3}{2}\beta_{\text{esc}} = \frac{3}{2}\). title: Absolute Measurements of Electrical Quantities
problem: The technological and scientific transformations underwent during the XIX century produced a compelling need of universally accepted standards for the electrical quantities. It was thought the new absolute units should only rely on the standards of length, mass and time established after the French Revolution. An intensive experimental work to settle the values of these units was developed from 1861 until 1912. We propose here three case studies.

sub_problems.problem: 1. Compute the electromotive force $\varepsilon$ induced in the coil, and also the mean power $\langle P \rangle$ required for maintaining the coil in motion. Neglect the coil self inductance.
sub_problems.solution:
After some time $t$, the normal to the coil plane makes an angle $\omega t$ with the magnetic field $\vec{B}_0 = B_0\vec{i}$. The magnetic flux through the coil is

$$
\phi = N \vec{B}_0 \cdot \vec{S}
$$

where the vector surface $\vec{S}$ is given by $\vec{S} = \pi a^2 (\cos \omega t \, \vec{i} + \sin \omega t \, \vec{j})$. Therefore,

$$
\phi = N \pi a^2 B_0 \cos \omega t.
$$

The induced electromotive force is

$$
\mathcal{E} = -\frac{d\phi}{dt} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \boxed{\mathcal{E} = N \pi a^2 B_0 \omega \sin \omega t}.
$$

The instantaneous power is $P = \mathcal{E}^2 / R$, so the mean power is

$$
\langle P \rangle = \frac{(N \pi a^2 B_0 \omega)^2}{R} \langle \sin^2 \omega t \rangle = \frac{(N \pi a^2 B_0 \omega)^2}{2R},
$$

where $\langle \sin^2 \omega t \rangle = \frac{1}{T} \int_0^T \sin^2 \omega t \, dt = \frac{1}{2}$. Thus,

$$
\boxed{\langle P \rangle = \frac{(N \pi a^2 B_0 \omega)^2}{2R}}.
$$
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\mathcal{E} = N \pi a^2 B_0 \omega \sin \omega t}, \boxed{\langle P \rangle = \frac{(N \pi a^2 B_0 \omega)^2}{2R}}
