knowledge_points.name: force balance on a differential string element
knowledge_points.description: For a curved string under tension, the net tension force on a small element dl is T d n, where n is the unit tangent vector. Equating this to external forces yields the differential equation T d n/dl + I n × B = 0.

knowledge_points.name: constant pitch angle from magnetic force
knowledge_points.description: Because the magnetic force I n × B is perpendicular to B, the scalar product n·B is constant along the wire. Thus the wire maintains a constant angle α with the vertical magnetic field, leading to a helical shape.

knowledge_points.name: cylindrical helix geometry
knowledge_points.description: A cylindrical helix is a curve with constant pitch angle. Its unrolled length L, vertical height H, and horizontal arc length s satisfy L^2 = H^2 + s^2, with cos α = H/L and sin α = s/L. Used to relate L, H, R, and α.

knowledge_points.name: half-turn helix configuration
knowledge_points.description: Each half of the wire loop makes exactly a half-turn, so the horizontal arc length for one half is s = πR, where R is the cylinder radius. This is the simplest shape satisfying the condition that the suspension points are not on the same vertical.

knowledge_points.name: horizontal force balance on a helix
knowledge_points.description: Projecting the force balance equation onto the horizontal plane (or using the curvature of the helix) gives the relation between the helix radius, tension, current, magnetic field, and pitch angle: R = (T/(IB)) sin α. Used to solve for T.

knowledge_points.name: static equilibrium of a point particle
knowledge_points.description: For a point particle in static equilibrium, the vector sum of all forces is zero. Applied at the weight, the vertical components of the two tension forces balance the weight: P = 2T cos α.

title: Rod in magnetic field
problem:
# Part C. Rod in magnetic field

A weightless rod of a length $2 R$ is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field $\breve{\vec{B}} .$ . Two identical small balls of mass $m$ and charge $q$ each are attached at the rod ends. Let us direct $z$ -axis along the magnetic field and place the origin at the rod center. The balls are given the same initial velocity $v$ but in opposite directions so that one of the velocities is precisely in the $z$ -direction. What are the maximum coordinates $z_{\mathsf{m a x}}$ of the balls? Express your answer in terms of $q , B , m , v ,$ and $R$ . Find the magnitude of the ball accelerations at this moment and express your answer in terms of $q , B , m , v , R ,$ and $z_{\mathsf{m a x}}$ .
solution:
The total magnetic force on the two balls is
\[q(\vec v_1+\vec v_2)\times \vec B = 2q\,\vec v_C\times \vec B,
\]
so if the centre of mass starts from rest, it remains at rest. Therefore the rod stays centred at the origin and each ball always lies on a sphere of radius \(R\).

Now consider the angular momentum of one ball about the origin. Its \(z\)-component satisfies
\[
\frac{dL_z}{dt}= q\bigl[\vec R\times(\vec v\times \vec B)\bigr]_z.
\]
Using \(\vec B\parallel z\), this becomes
\[
\frac{dL_z}{dt}= qB\,z\,\dot z.
\]
Integrating and using that initially \(z=0\) and \(L_z=0\), we get
\[
L_z=\frac{qB}{2}z^2.
\]

At the moment when the coordinate \(z\) is maximal, \(\dot z=0\). The speed is unchanged because neither the Lorentz force nor the rod force does work, so the speed is still \(v\). At this instant the distance from the \(z\)-axis is
\[
r=\sqrt{R^2-z_{\max}^2},
\]
so the angular momentum is also
\[
L_z=mvr=m v\sqrt{R^2-z_{\max}^2}.
\]
Equating the two expressions for \(L_z\) gives
\[
\frac{qB}{2}z_{\max}^2=m v\sqrt{R^2-z_{\max}^2}.
\]
Squaring and solving for \(z_{\max}\) yields
\[
\left(\frac{qB}{2mv}\right)^2 z_{\max}^4+z_{\max}^2-R^2=0,
\]
so
\[
z_{\max}=\frac{\sqrt{2}mv}{|q|B}\sqrt{\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{qBR}{mv}\right)^2}-1}.
\]

To find the acceleration at this moment, decompose it into three mutually perpendicular components: along the velocity, toward the centre of the sphere, and the third orthogonal direction. The speed is constant, so the component along the velocity is zero. The normal component has magnitude \(v^2/R\). The magnetic force contributes the third component, whose magnitude is
\[
\frac{|q|vB}{m}\frac{z_{\max}}{R}.
\]
Therefore the acceleration magnitude is
\[
a=\sqrt{\left(\frac{v^2}{R}\right)^2+\left(\frac{qBv\,z_{\max}}{mR}\right)^2}.
\]

Therefore, \(\boxed{z_{\max}=\frac{\sqrt{2}mv}{|q|B}\sqrt{\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{qBR}{mv}\right)^2}-1}}\) and \(\boxed{a=\sqrt{\left(\frac{v^2}{R}\right)^2+\left(\frac{qBv\,z_{\max}}{mR}\right)^2}}\).

title: Motion on a horizontal surface
problem:
Force of friction is not always isotropic. Often the magnitude and direction of a friction force depend on the direction of body motion. For example, friction anisotropy can arise in the presence of "grooves" of a certain orientation on the contact surface of bodies (it is known that the coefficient of friction of oak against oak along and across the grain is equal to 0.48 and 0.34, respectively). Friction anisotropy can lead to unusual properties of motion which are studied in this problem.

# What you need to know about anisotropic friction

Suppose that a surface is made of an anisotropic material. One of the most popular models of anisotropic friction suggests that there are perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ (they are called primary) so that the friction force $\vec{F}$ acting on a body will depend on the direction of the body motion as

$$F_{x} = - \frac{| N |}{\left| v \right|} \mu_{x} v_{x} \tag{1}$$

$$F_{y} = - \frac{\frac{| v |}{| N |}}{| v |} \mu_{y} v_{y}$$

where $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ are the friction force components, $N$ is a normal reaction force acting on the body, $v_{x}$ and $v_{y}$ are components of the velocity vector $\vec{v} ,$ , and $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ are the friction coefficients along the primary axes.

Hereinafter, it is understood that the coordinate axes on the plane coincide with the primary axes. The friction coefficients are $\mu_{x} =0,75$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 5$ unless otherwise stated.

In parts A and B a body can be considered as point-like. The plane, on which the bodies move, is horizontal in all parts of the problem.

Provide a numerical answer wherever possible.

# Part A. Motion on a horizontal surface

sub_problems.problem: (1) At what angle $\alpha_{1}$ to the $X$ axis should the body velocity vector be for the absolute value of the power of the friction force be at maximum?
sub_problems.solution:
For motion with velocity making an angle \(\alpha\) to the \(X\)-axis, we have
\[v_x = v\cos\alpha, \qquad v_y = v\sin\alpha.
\]
The friction force does negative work, so its power is
\[
P = \vec F\cdot \vec v = -mg\left(\mu_x\cos^2\alpha + \mu_y\sin^2\alpha\right)v.
\]
Hence the absolute value of the power is
\[
|P| = mgv\left(\mu_x\cos^2\alpha + \mu_y\sin^2\alpha\right).
\]
Since \(\mu_x=0.75 > \mu_y=0.5\), this expression is maximal when \(\cos^2\alpha=1\), i.e. when the velocity is directed along the \(X\)-axis.

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{\alpha_1 = 0}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Anisotropic friction model
knowledge_points.description: Friction force components along primary axes are given by F_x = -μ_x |N| v_x/|v|, F_y = -μ_y |N| v_y/|v|; this model is applied to compute the friction power.

knowledge_points.name: Normal force on horizontal surface
knowledge_points.description: On a horizontal plane the normal force magnitude equals the weight mg, allowing replacement of |N| in the friction law with mg.

knowledge_points.name: Power as dot product
knowledge_points.description: Instantaneous mechanical power of a force is P = F·v, used to compute the rate of work done by friction and its magnitude.

knowledge_points.name: Velocity component decomposition
knowledge_points.description: Resolve velocity into components v_x = v cosα, v_y = v sinα to express the friction force components and power in terms of the angle α to the X‑axis.

sub_problems.guidance:
The key to answering this question lies in the idea of breaking a velocity vector into its perpendicular components — exactly as you saw in the textbook passages.  
In the French excerpt, particle A’s velocity is described by its y‑component \(u_0\) (and its zero x‑component), and the analysis explicitly uses these components. The Eisberg & Resnick argument similarly makes use of the component of velocity transverse to the relative motion. Both passages remind us that a velocity can be represented by its projections onto two mutually perpendicular axes.

Apply that same decomposition to the moving body here.
1. Draw the body’s velocity vector, call its magnitude \(v\), and let \(\alpha\) be the angle the vector makes with the positive \(X\)‑axis.  
2. Write the \(X\) and \(Y\) components of the velocity as  
   \[
   v_x = v\cos\alpha, \qquad v_y = v\sin\alpha .
   \]

Now recall that the power delivered by a force is the scalar product of the force vector and the velocity vector. The problem tells you that the friction force has different coefficients along the two directions, \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\), and the normal force is \(mg\). Because the friction opposes the motion, its components are \(-\mu_x mg\) along \(X\) and \(-\mu_y mg\) along \(Y\).  
Take the dot product:  
\[
P = (-\mu_x mg)\,v_x + (-\mu_y mg)\,v_y .
\]
When you substitute the velocity components from step 2, you will obtain an expression for the power whose absolute value is proportional to  
\[
\mu_x\cos^2\alpha + \mu_y\sin^2\alpha .
\]

Since \(v\) and \(mg\) are positive constants (the body is sliding), maximizing the absolute power is equivalent to maximizing this combination of the friction coefficients with \(\cos^2\alpha\) and \(\sin^2\alpha\).

The combination is a weighted average of \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\). To make it as large as possible, you want to give all the weight to the **larger** of the two coefficients. That happens when the trigonometric factor that multiplies the larger coefficient is set equal to 1, and the other factor becomes 0.  
Look at the numerical values of \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\) that are given in the full problem statement. Decide which one is larger, and then choose the angle \(\alpha\) that accomplishes this (for example, if \(\mu_x\) is larger, you would need \(\cos^2\alpha=1\) and \(\sin^2\alpha=0\); if \(\mu_y\) were larger, you would need \(\sin^2\alpha=1\) and \(\cos^2\alpha=0\)). This will give you the required angle \(\alpha_1\).

Complete that final step yourself using the actual numbers; the reasoning above will lead you straight to the answer.

sub_problems.problem: (2) At what angle $\alpha_{2}$ to the $X$ axis should the body velocity vector be for the absolute value of the power of the friction force be 1.2 times less than maximum?
sub_problems.solution:
The power of the friction force is
\[
P=\vec F\cdot \vec v.
\]
For a velocity making an angle \(\alpha\) with the \(X\)-axis, \(v_x=v\cos\alpha\) and \(v_y=v\sin\alpha\). Hence the magnitude of the friction power is
\[
|P|=mgv\bigl(\mu_x\cos^2\alpha+\mu_y\sin^2\alpha\bigr).
\]
Since \(\mu_x>\mu_y\), the maximum occurs when the motion is along the \(X\)-axis:
\[
|P|_{\max}=mgv\mu_x.
\]
We need the power to be 1.2 times less than the maximum, i.e.
\[
|P|=\frac{1}{1.2}|P|_{\max}=\frac56\,mgv\mu_x.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mu_x\cos^2\alpha+\mu_y\sin^2\alpha=\frac56\mu_x.
\]
Substitute \(\mu_x=0.75\) and \(\mu_y=0.5\):
\[
0.75\cos^2\alpha+0.5\sin^2\alpha=0.625.
\]
Using \(\sin^2\alpha=1-\cos^2\alpha\),
\[
0.75\cos^2\alpha+0.5(1-\cos^2\alpha)=0.625,
\]
\[
0.25\cos^2\alpha=0.125,
\]
\[
\cos^2\alpha=\frac12.
\]
Thus
\[
\cos\alpha=\pm\frac1{\sqrt2},
\]
so the possible angles are
\[
\alpha_2=\pm\frac\pi4,\ \pm\frac{3\pi}{4}.
\]
Final answer: \(\boxed{\alpha_2=\pm\frac\pi4,\ \pm\frac{3\pi}{4}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks you to find the direction of the velocity (angle \( \alpha_2 \) with the \( X \)-axis) such that the magnitude of the friction force’s power is a specified fraction of its maximum. To solve it, you will combine the concepts of vector components, power as a dot product, and the normal force on a horizontal surface.

**Step 1: Resolve the velocity into components**  
Choose a coordinate system where the body moves in the \( x-y \) plane. If the velocity vector \( \mathbf{v} \) makes an angle \( \alpha \) with the \( X \)-axis, use the method from reference.5 “Components of a Vector” to write its components:  
\[
v_x = v \cos\alpha, \qquad v_y = v \sin\alpha,
\]  
where \( v = |\mathbf{v}| \) is the speed.

**Step 2: Express the friction force**  
On a horizontal surface, the normal force \( N \) equals the weight \( mg \) (reference.4.3). The kinetic friction force opposes motion and its magnitude is proportional to \( N \). Because the surface has different friction coefficients \( \mu_x \) and \( \mu_y \) along the axes, the force components are  
\[
F_x = -\mu_x N \frac{v_x}{v}, \qquad F_y = -\mu_y N \frac{v_y}{v}.
\]  
(These follow from the idea that friction is opposite to the instantaneous velocity direction, with direction‑dependent proportionality.)

**Step 3: Write the power of the friction force**  
Power is the dot product of force and velocity, \( P = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{v} \) (reference.3.4). Substituting the components, the power (a negative quantity whose absolute value you need) is  
\[
|P| = mg\,v \bigl( \mu_x \cos^2\alpha + \mu_y \sin^2\alpha \bigr).
\]

**Step 4: Find the maximum power**  
Because \( \mu_x > \mu_y \), the expression \( \mu_x \cos^2\alpha + \mu_y \sin^2\alpha \) is greatest when \( \cos^2\alpha = 1 \) (motion purely along the \( X \)-axis). Thus  
\[
|P|_{\max} = mg\,v\,\mu_x.
\]

**Step 5: Set up the condition for the required angle**  
The problem states that the absolute value of the power should be \( 1.2 \) times less than the maximum, i.e.  
\[
|P| = \frac{1}{1.2}\, |P|_{\max}.
\]  
Divide both sides by \( mg\,v \) to obtain an equation involving only the friction coefficients and the angle:  
\[
\mu_x \cos^2\alpha + \mu_y \sin^2\alpha = \frac{\mu_x}{1.2}.
\]

**Step 6: Solve for the angle**  
Replace \( \sin^2\alpha \) by \( 1 - \cos^2\alpha \) and solve for \( \cos^2\alpha \). Use the numerical values of \( \mu_x \) and \( \mu_y \) that are given in the full problem statement (but not repeated here). Then find \( \cos\alpha \) (note the ± sign) and finally the possible angles \( \alpha \) in the range \( [0, 2\pi) \). The result will include angles in all four quadrants where the direction satisfies the equation.

Proceed step by step, carrying out the algebra carefully. You are now ready to do the substitution and solve.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Let the initial velocity have components $v_{0 x} =1 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ and $v_{0 y} =1 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ . After some time the velocity component along the $Y$ axis equals $v_{1 y} = \mathrm{0,25 m / s}$ . What is the velocity magnitude at this moment?
sub_problems.solution:
Newton’s equations for the velocity components are

\[
\begin{cases}
 m\dfrac{d v_x}{dt} = -\mu_x m g \dfrac{v_x}{v}, \\
 m\dfrac{d v_y}{dt} = -\mu_y m g \dfrac{v_y}{v},
\end{cases}
\]
where \(v=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\).

Dividing the first equation by the second gives

\[
\frac{d v_x}{d v_y} = \frac{\mu_x v_x}{\mu_y v_y}.
\]

Integrating, we obtain the invariant

\[
\frac{v_x^{\mu_y}}{v_y^{\mu_x}}=\text{const}.
\]

Using the initial conditions \(v_{0x}=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and \(v_{0y}=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\), we get

\[
\frac{v_x^{0.5}}{v_y^{0.75}}=1,
\]
so

\[
 v_x = v_y^{\mu_x/\mu_y}=v_y^{3/2}.
\]

At the moment when \(v_y=0.25\,\mathrm{m/s}\),

\[
 v_x = (0.25)^{3/2} = 0.125\,\mathrm{m/s}.
\]

Therefore the speed is

\[
 v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2} = \sqrt{0.125^2+0.25^2} \approx 0.28\,\mathrm{m/s}.
\]

Final answer: \(\boxed{0.28\,\mathrm{m/s}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law
knowledge_points.description: The net force on a particle equals mass times acceleration. Used in component form m dv_x/dt = F_x and m dv_y/dt = F_y to obtain the differential equations for the velocity components.

knowledge_points.name: normal force equals weight on horizontal plane
knowledge_points.description: On a horizontal surface with no vertical acceleration, the magnitude of the normal reaction force N equals mg. This replaces N in the friction force expressions.

knowledge_points.name: eliminating time by dividing differential equations
knowledge_points.description: Dividing the two autonomous equations of motion for v_x and v_y eliminates dt, yielding dv_x/dv_y = F_x/F_y. This transforms the system into a single relation between velocity components that can be integrated without solving for time evolution.

knowledge_points.name: constant of motion (invariant)
knowledge_points.description: A function of dynamical variables that remains constant during motion. Integration gives the invariant v_x^{μ_y} / v_y^{μ_x} = const, enabling one velocity component to be found from the other without solving the full time dependence.

knowledge_points.name: separation of variables for first-order ODE
knowledge_points.description: The ODE dv_x/dv_y = (μ_x/μ_y)(v_x/v_y) is separable. Integrating dv_x/v_x = (μ_x/μ_y) dv_y/v_y gives the logarithmic solution and the power‑law relation v_x = v_y^{μ_x/μ_y}.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, set up the equations of motion for both velocity components. Because the object moves on a horizontal plane, the normal force equals its weight (from the principle that in the perpendicular direction, N balances gravity when there is no vertical acceleration; see Kleppner & Kolenkow 3.4.3 and 2.9). The friction force is therefore proportional to the weight, directed opposite to the velocity, with different coefficients along X and Y. Write Newton’s second law for each component (Kleppner & Kolenkow 2.9, 2.5.2), expressing the acceleration as the time derivative of the velocity component and the friction force in terms of the speed magnitude \(v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\). That gives two first‑order differential equations.

Now you want to find a relation between \(v_x\) and \(v_y\) that does not involve time. To eliminate time, divide the left‑hand side of the \(v_x\) equation by the left‑hand side of the \(v_y\) equation. The idea of dividing differential equations to remove the time variable is a standard trick (discussed in Kleppner & Kolenkow 5.2 and Morin 2.3, where rewriting derivatives and separating variables is illustrated). The result is an expression containing \(dv_x/dv_y\) and the ratio \(v_x/v_y\), multiplied by the ratio of the friction coefficients.

You then have a first‑order ordinary differential equation that can be solved by separation of variables (Morin 3.1). Rearrange so that all \(v_x\)‑terms are on one side and all \(v_y\)‑terms on the other, and integrate. The integration yields an invariant (a constant of motion) that relates powers of the two velocity components. This is a conserved quantity, analogous to the idea that symmetries lead to constants of motion (Morin’s discussion of Noether’s theorem, though here you find the invariant directly).

Apply the initial conditions \(v_{0x}=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\) and \(v_{0y}=1\,\mathrm{m/s}\) to determine the constant of motion. With that constant fixed, you obtain a formula linking \(v_x\) to \(v_y\) at all later times.

At the moment when \(v_{y} = 0.25\,\mathrm{m/s}\), use that invariant relation to find the corresponding \(v_x\). Finally, compute the speed magnitude from its Pythagorean definition \(v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}\). Perform all algebraic and arithmetic steps yourself – the textbook passages equip you with the method, but the substitution and calculation are yours to carry out.

sub_problems.problem: (4) Let the velocity be $v_{2} =1.0 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s}$ . At what angle $\alpha_{3}$ to the $X$ axis should the velocity vector be for the radius of curvature of the trajectory be minimum? What is this radius equal to? The free fall acceleration is $\dot{g} =9,8 \mathrm{{m} / \mathrm{{s}^{2}}}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The radius of curvature is determined by the component of the friction force perpendicular to the velocity. For a velocity making an angle \(\alpha\) with the \(X\)-axis, this component is

\[
F_n = mg(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin\alpha\cos\alpha.
\]

Using Newton’s second law in the normal direction to the trajectory,

\[
\frac{mv^2}{R}=mg(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin\alpha\cos\alpha.
\]

Hence

\[
R=\frac{v^2}{g(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}
=\frac{2v^2}{g(\mu_x-\mu_y)\sin 2\alpha}.
\]

The radius is minimal when \(\sin 2\alpha\) is maximal, i.e. when

\[
2\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad \alpha=\frac{\pi}{4}.
\]

Then

\[
R_{\min}=\frac{2v^2}{g(\mu_x-\mu_y)}.
\]

With \(v=1.0\,\mathrm{m/s}\), \(g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\), \(\mu_x=0.75\), and \(\mu_y=0.50\),

\[
R_{\min}=\frac{2\cdot 1.0^2}{9.8\cdot(0.75-0.50)}\approx 0.82\,\mathrm{m}.
\]

Thus the minimum radius occurs for \(\alpha_3=\frac{\pi}{4}\), and the minimum radius is \(0.82\,\mathrm{m}\).

sub_problems.problem: (5) In a single diagram on the $X Y$ plane, sketch the trajectories of the body launched at the angles $\alpha_{4} = \pi /6$ and $\alpha_{5} = \pi /3$ for the friction coefficients specified above. The magnitudes of initial velocities are the same. Solve the same problem for the friction coefficients $\mu_{x} =0,4$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 7$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For anisotropic friction, the decelerations along the coordinate axes are determined separately by the coefficients \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\). The trajectory is straight only in the special isotropic case \(\mu_x=\mu_y\), because then both velocity components decrease in the same proportion.

For the given coefficients \(\mu_x=0.75\) and \(\mu_y=0.5\), we have \(\mu_x>\mu_y\). Therefore the \(x\)-component of velocity decreases faster than the \(y\)-component, so the trajectory bends away from the straight line in the same sense for both launch angles \(\alpha_4=\pi/6\) and \(\alpha_5=\pi/3\). In a single \(XY\)-diagram, both paths should start from the origin with the corresponding initial directions, and then curve so that the motion becomes progressively more aligned with the \(y\)-axis.

For the second set \(\mu_x=0.4\) and \(\mu_y=0.7\), we have \(\mu_x<\mu_y\). The bending is then in the opposite sense: the \(y\)-component decreases faster than the \(x\)-component, so both trajectories curve toward the \(x\)-axis. Again, the direction of deflection does not depend on the initial launch angle, only on whether \(\mu_x\) is greater or smaller than \(\mu_y\).

Final answer: \(\boxed{\text{For }\mu_x>\mu_y\text{ both trajectories bend toward the }y\text{-axis; for }\mu_x<\mu_y\text{ both bend toward the }x\text{-axis.}}\)

sub_problems.guidance:
First, ground the problem in the physics from reference.  
- The body moves on a horizontal plane, so the normal force is perpendicular to the surface. Because the motion is purely horizontal and there is no vertical acceleration, the normal force exactly balances the weight: \(N = mg\). (This follows directly from the discussion of the normal force in equilibrium in the Kleppner & Kolenkow passage.)  
- The body is treated as a **point particle**, so we ignore any rotation or size effects; its motion is completely described by the translation of its center of mass.

Now set up the equations of motion.  
- For anisotropic friction, the friction force in each direction is determined by the corresponding coefficient and the **same** normal force \(N\), because the normal force is a single scalar. That is, \(f_x = \mu_x N\) and \(f_y = \mu_y N\), each opposing the respective velocity component.  
- Apply Newton’s second law in component form (as done in the block‑on‑table example in reference). For the \(x\)- and \(y\)-directions you get constant decelerations:  
  \[
  a_x = -\mu_x g, \qquad a_y = -\mu_y g.
  \]  
  (The mass cancels because \(N = mg\).)

**Why the trajectory bends**  
- Because the decelerations are different when \(\mu_x \neq \mu_y\), the two velocity components do not decrease at the same rate. The component with the **larger** coefficient of friction decays faster.  
- To decide which way the path curves, compare \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\). If, for instance, \(\mu_x > \mu_y\), the \(x\)-component of the velocity shrinks more quickly than the \(y\)-component. Over time, the velocity vector (and thus the tangent to the trajectory) becomes more aligned with the \(y\)-axis. The opposite holds when \(\mu_y > \mu_x\).

**How to sketch**  
- You are given two launch angles: \(\alpha_4 = \pi/6\) and \(\alpha_5 = \pi/3\). The initial speed is the same for both, so the starting velocity vectors have the same length and point along the given angles.  
- In a single \(XY\) diagram, mark the origin and draw the initial velocity directions: a short straight segment at \(30^\circ\) and another at \(60^\circ\) from the \(x\)-axis.  
- For the first set of coefficients (\(\mu_x=0.75,\mu_y=0.5\)), determine which deceleration is larger. Then sketch both trajectories smoothly curving toward the axis of the component that decays more slowly. Because the bending arises from the inequality of the coefficients, both launch angles will curve in the **same sense** (same general direction of turning).  
- Repeat for the second set (\(\mu_x=0.4,\mu_y=0.7\)), now with the inequality reversed. Again, both trajectories curve toward the axis of the slower‑decaying component.  
- Label the axes, the angles, and indicate which coefficient set corresponds to which sketch.

Remember: the crucial step is comparing \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\) to see which velocity component survives longer; that determines the asymptotic direction of the motion and therefore the bending of the entire trajectory. Use that reasoning, and you will draw the correct qualitative shapes without needing to calculate any numbers.

title: Conditions for the beginning of body movement
problem:
Force of friction is not always isotropic. Often the magnitude and direction of a friction force depend on the direction of body motion. For example, friction anisotropy can arise in the presence of "grooves" of a certain orientation on the contact surface of bodies (it is known that the coefficient of friction of oak against oak along and across the grain is equal to 0.48 and 0.34, respectively). Friction anisotropy can lead to unusual properties of motion which are studied in this problem.

# What you need to know about anisotropic friction

Suppose that a surface is made of an anisotropic material. One of the most popular models of anisotropic friction suggests that there are perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ (they are called primary) so that the friction force $\vec{F}$ acting on a body will depend on the direction of the body motion as

$$F_{x} = - \frac{| N |}{\left| v \right|} \mu_{x} v_{x} \tag{1}$$

$$F_{y} = - \frac{\frac{| v |}{| N |}}{| v |} \mu_{y} v_{y}$$

where $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ are the friction force components, $N$ is a normal reaction force acting on the body, $v_{x}$ and $v_{y}$ are components of the velocity vector $\vec{v} ,$ , and $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ are the friction coefficients along the primary axes.

Hereinafter, it is understood that the coordinate axes on the plane coincide with the primary axes. The friction coefficients are $\mu_{x} =0,75$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 5$ unless otherwise stated.

In parts A and B a body can be considered as point-like. The plane, on which the bodies move, is horizontal in all parts of the problem.

Provide a numerical answer wherever possible.

# Part B. Conditions for the beginning of body movement

A body of mass $m$ is at rest at the origin. A force has been applied to it at an angle $\alpha$ to the $X$ axis. The force magnitude $F ( t ) = \gamma t$ linearly grows with time. Find the dependence of the moment the body starts moving on $\alpha$ . Ignore the stagnation phenomenon.
solution:
At the instant the body is just about to start moving, the applied force balances the maximal static friction force in the direction of impending motion. Since the body may start moving in a direction making an angle \(\varphi\neq \alpha\) with the \(X\)-axis, the friction components at threshold satisfy
\[
\left\{
\begin{array}{l}F_{\mathrm{fr},x}=\mu_x m g\cos\varphi=\gamma t\cos\alpha,\\ F_{\mathrm{fr},y}=\mu_y m g\sin\varphi=\gamma t\sin\alpha.
\end{array}
\right.
\]
Divide the first equation by \(\mu_x m g\) and the second by \(\mu_y m g\), then square and add:
\[
\left(\frac{\gamma t\cos\alpha}{\mu_x m g}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\gamma t\sin\alpha}{\mu_y m g}\right)^2=1.
\]
Hence
\[
(mg)^2=(\gamma t)^2\left[\left(\frac{\cos\alpha}{\mu_x}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\mu_y}\right)^2\right],
\]
so the time when motion starts is
\[
\boxed{t(\alpha)=\frac{\mu_x\mu_y\,mg}{\gamma\sqrt{\mu_y^2\cos^2\alpha+\mu_x^2\sin^2\alpha}}}.
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Determine the normal force.** Since the plane is horizontal and the body is in vertical equilibrium, the normal force simply equals the weight: \(N = m g\). This is directly from the textbook discussion of the normal force as balancing perpendicular forces, just as in the worked example where a block rests on a horizontal table.

2. **Understand the impending‑motion condition for anisotropic friction.** The friction model given in the problem defines how the friction force depends on the direction of motion. At the instant the body is about to start moving, static friction reaches its maximum possible magnitude *for that direction*. You can convert the given component relations into a single condition that doesn’t involve the unknown motion direction: from \(F_x = -\mu_x N v_x/|v|\) and \(F_y = -\mu_y N v_y/|v|\), square and add the components to obtain
\[
\left(\frac{F_{\text{fr},x}}{\mu_x}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{F_{\text{fr},y}}{\mu_y}\right)^2 = N^2 .
\]
This is the anisotropic analogue of the familiar static‑friction limit \(F_{\text{max}} = \mu_s N\) from the textbook passages on friction (see also the block‑on‑wedge example where the friction force is replaced by its maximum value \(\mu N\) at the threshold of sliding).

3. **Set up force equilibrium just before motion.** The body is still at rest, so the net force in each horizontal direction is zero. The applied force components are \(F_x(t) = \gamma t \cos\alpha\) and \(F_y(t) = \gamma t \sin\alpha\). Because friction opposes the impending motion, the friction components must exactly balance the applied force at the threshold:
\[
F_{\text{fr},x} = -\gamma t \cos\alpha, \qquad
F_{\text{fr},y} = -\gamma t \sin\alpha .
\]
This is the same idea used in the textbook examples: when an object is just about to slide, the friction force attains its maximum possible value and the acceleration is still zero (e.g., the wedge example sets \(\ddot{x}=0\) and \(f=\mu N\)).

4. **Combine the equilibrium with the friction‑limit condition.** Insert the friction components from step 3 (with the signs squared away) into the ellipse relation from step 2. You will get an equation that contains the unknown time \(t\), the known coefficients \(\mu_x,\mu_y\), the weight \(mg\), the rate \(\gamma\), and the angle \(\alpha\).

5. **Solve for the critical time.** The resulting equation contains only \(t\) and known parameters. Isolate \(t\) to find the dependence \(t(\alpha)\)—the moment the body starts moving as a function of the force direction. No further physical laws are needed; it is now an algebraic step. (For a concrete parallel, look at the turning‑car worked example: after writing the horizontal and vertical equations, the friction limit \(\mu N\) is introduced, and the equations are combined to solve for the limiting speed.) Carry out the algebra yourself, substituting the numbers for \(\mu_x\) and \(\mu_y\) only if you are asked for a numerical final expression.

# What you need to know about anisotropic friction

One of the most popular models of anisotropic friction suggests that there are perpendicular axes $X$ and $Y$ (they are called primary) so that the friction force $\vec{F}$ acting on a body will depend on the direction of the body motion as

$$F_{x} = - \frac{| N |}{\left| v \right|} \mu_{x} v_{x} \tag{1}$$

$$F_{y} = - \frac{\frac{| v |}{| N |}}{| v |} \mu_{y} v_{y}$$

where $F_{x}$ and $F_{y}$ are the friction force components, $N$ is a normal reaction force acting on the body, $v_{x}$ and $v_{y}$ are components of the velocity vector $\vec{v} ,$ , and $\mu_{x}$ and $\mu_{y}$ are the friction coefficients along the primary axes.

Hereinafter, it is understood that the coordinate axes on the plane coincide with the primary axes. The friction coefficients are $\mu_{x} =0,75$ and $\mu_{y} =0 {,} 5$ unless otherwise stated.

In parts A and B a body can be considered as point-like. The plane, on which the bodies move, is horizontal in all parts of the problem.

Provide a numerical answer wherever possible.

# Part C. Circular motion

Two identical point-like masses $m$ are connected with a weightless inextensible rod of length $L =1 \mathrm{m}_{\iota}$ the system lies on a surface with anisotropic friction. The rod is aligned with the $Y$ axis and does not touch the surface. One of the masses is given an initial velocity perpendicular to the rod.

sub_problems.problem: (1) For a given initial velocity $v_{0}$ find the dependence of its velocity $v$ on the angle of rotation of the rod $\varphi$ assuming that the other body remains at rest.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the moving mass have velocity magnitude $v$. The rod makes an angle $\varphi$ with the $X$ axis, so the velocity components are proportional to the instantaneous direction of motion. The friction force components are therefore

$$F_x=-mg\,\mu_x\frac{v_x}{v},\qquad F_y=-mg\,\mu_y\frac{v_y}{v}.$$
\nProjecting Newton’s second law onto the direction of motion gives

$$m\frac{dv}{dt}=-mg\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right).$$
\nSince the moving mass is constrained by the rigid rod, its speed is related to the angular velocity by

$$v=L\dot\varphi.$$
\nHence

$$L\ddot\varphi=-g\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right).$$
\nMultiply by $\dot\varphi$:

$$L\dot\varphi\,\ddot\varphi=-g\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right)\dot\varphi.$$
\nUsing $v=L\dot\varphi$, this becomes

$$v\,dv=-gL\left(\mu_x\cos^2\varphi+\mu_y\sin^2\varphi\right)d\varphi.$$
\nIntegrating from the initial state $(v_0,\varphi=0)$ to $(v,\varphi)$,

$$\frac{v^2-v_0^2}{2}=-gL\int_0^{\varphi}\left(\mu_x\cos^2\phi+\mu_y\sin^2\phi\right)d\phi.$$
\nEvaluating the integral,

$$v^2=v_0^2-gL\left[(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi+(\mu_x-\mu_y)\frac{\sin 2\varphi}{2}\right].$$
\nTherefore the dependence of the speed on the rotation angle is

$$\boxed{v(\varphi)=\sqrt{\,v_0^2-gL\left[(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi+(\mu_x-\mu_y)\frac{\sin 2\varphi}{2}\right]\,}}.$$

Let the tension in the rod be $T$. For the moving mass, the component of Newton’s second law along the rod gives

$$T + F_{\mathrm{fr}}\sin\beta = m\dot{\varphi}^{2}L,$$

sub_problems.guidance:
You already have from earlier parts (C1 and B1) two key expressions:  
- the tension \(T\) in the rod as a function of the angular position \(\varphi\) and the initial speed \(v_0\);  
- the condition for the other body to stay at rest, which involves a maximum static friction force that depends on \(\varphi\) and the friction coefficients.

Now you need to find the largest \(v_0\) that still satisfies the “other body at rest” condition everywhere along the motion.

1. **Relate the tension to centripetal force**  
   For the moving body, the component of the net force along the rod is what keeps it going in a circle. In classical mechanics, an object of mass \(m\) moving at speed \(v\) in a circle of radius \(L\) requires a net inward force of magnitude \(mv^2/L\). This is the centripetal force equation, illustrated in the textbook passages (e.g. the classical limit of Example 12.11 where \(F=mu^2/R\), or the inward force \(m\omega^2 r\) in the rotating‑frame discussion of Morin).  
   → In this problem, the forces along the rod are the tension \(T\) and a component of the friction force on the moving body. Write the centripetal condition (sum of forces along the rod) for the moving body and identify how the expression you already have for \(T\) follows from it.

2. **Write the inequality for the other body**  
   The rod pulls on the second body with the same tension \(T\). For that body to remain at rest, \(T\) must not exceed the maximum static friction force it can experience. You derived this limit in part B1; it is a function of \(\varphi\), \(m\), \(g\) and the friction coefficients.

3. **Set up the combined inequality**  
   Substitute your expression for \(T\) (from C1) into the static‑friction inequality. You obtain an inequality that relates \(v_0^2\) to \(\varphi\) and the known parameters. The maximum allowed \(v_0\) is the largest value for which this inequality holds for all \(\varphi\) that the moving body actually reaches.

4. **Find the limiting \(\varphi\)**  
   Study how each side of the inequality depends on \(\varphi\). Notice that as \(\varphi\) grows, the left‑hand side (which contains the tension) decreases, while the right‑hand side (the friction limit) increases. Therefore, if the inequality holds at \(\varphi = 0\), it will hold for any later \(\varphi\). The most restrictive condition is at the very beginning of the motion, \(\varphi = 0\).

5. **Determine \(v_{0\max}\)**  
   Set \(\varphi = 0\) in the inequality and turn it into an equality to find the maximum initial speed. You will get an expression involving \(g\), \(L\) and the friction coefficient \(\mu_y\) (the other coefficient cancels or is not needed at this angle). Then plug in the given values (\(\mu_y = 0.5\), \(L = 1\,\mathrm{m}\), and use \(g = 9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\) if that is standard in your course) and perform the arithmetic to obtain the numerical result. Remember to take the square root.

Follow these steps in order, and you will arrive at the answer without needing any concepts beyond those you have already used in parts C1 and B1.

sub_problems.problem: (3) What distance will the body travel until it stops completely if the initial velocity is $v_{0\mathrm{max}}$?
sub_problems.solution:
Substituting the value of \(v_{0\max}\) found in the previous part into the stopping condition from part C1, we obtain an equation for the angle \(\varphi\) at which the motion ends:\
\[\ngL\left[(\mu_x+\mu_y)\varphi + (\mu_x-\mu_y)\frac{\sin 2\varphi}{2}\right]=\mu_y gL.
\]\nWith \(\mu_x=0.75\) and \(\mu_y=0.5\), this becomes
\[
1.25\,\varphi + 0.125\,\sin 2\varphi = 0.5.
\]\nSolving numerically gives \(\varphi \approx 0.34\,\text{rad}\).
\nThe travelled distance is the arc length
\[\ns=L\varphi.
\]\nSince \(L=1\,\text{m}\),
\[\ns\approx 0.34\,\text{m}.
\]\nTherefore, the body travels \(\boxed{0.34\,\text{m}}\) before stopping completely.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall the relationship between arc length, radius, and angular displacement. As shown in the textbook examples (e.g., the rolling drum where the distance advanced is \(x = R\theta\), or the spinning loop where a short arc is \(\Delta S = R\Delta\theta\)), the distance \(s\) traveled along a circular path of radius \(L\) is simply  
\[
s = L \varphi,
\]  
where \(\varphi\) (in radians) is the total angle the body sweeps out before stopping. Therefore, finding the distance reduces to finding the stopping angle \(\varphi\).

To obtain an equation for \(\varphi\), return to the stopping condition you derived in part C1 and substitute the value of \(v_{0\max}\) you just found in the previous part. This will give a single equation that determines the angle at which the body comes to rest. Because friction forces with different coefficients are involved, the equation typically contains both \(\varphi\) and a term like \(\sin 2\varphi\); it is transcendental and has no simple algebraic solution.

When an equation cannot be solved exactly, the textbook passages on numerical methods (such as Morin’s discussion of discretising differential equations when an exact solution is impossible, or the universal numerical procedure in Eisberg & Resnick) point the way: you can find the root \(\varphi\) numerically. Choose a sensible numerical approach—graphical estimation, bisection, or a short iterative program/calculator routine—that locates the angle satisfying the equation to the desired accuracy.

Once you have the numerical value of \(\varphi\) (in radians), apply the arc length formula \(s = L \varphi\) to obtain the distance the body travels until it stops completely.

title: Classical superradiance model
problem:
When solving the problem, use the following values of the physical constants:

the speed of light in vacuum $c =3.00 \cdot 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} ;$

Planck's constant $\hbar =1.055 \cdot 10^{-34} \rfloor .$ s;

constant in Coulomb's law and electric constant $\begin{array} {r} {k = {\frac{1} {4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}} =8.99 \cdot 10^{9} ~ {\frac{\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{2}} {\mathrm{C}^{2}}}} \end{array}$;

elementary charge $e =1.60 \cdot 10^{-19} \textsf{C}$ .

# Part A. Classical superradiance model

A laser is a source of coherent optical radiation. Laser radiation is generated when a large number of atoms transferred to an excited state by external action (pumping) emit photons with the same phase and polarization. A consistent theory of laser radiation is based on quantum mechanics but some aspects of this phenomenon can be understood by means of classical electrodynamics.

Let us first consider emission of a photon by a single atom. According to classical electrodynamics, an atom can be regarded as dipole emitter. In this model an electric dipole is associated with an atom comprised of an immobile atomic nucleus with a positive charge $+ q$ and a negative charge $- q$ oscillating harmonically around it (the negative charge is located at the center of the charge distribution of electron cloud).

Here the atomic dipole moment oscillates according to the law $\vec{p} ( t ) = \vec{p}_{m} \cos ( \omega t + \varphi )$ . The cyclic oscillation frequency is related to the energy of emitted photons by the Planck relation $E_{\gamma} = \hbar \omega$ . Hereinafter the frequency of photons means cyclic frequency. The radiation power of a classical system with a variable dipole moment $\vec{P} ( t )$ is given by the formula

$$W = \frac{2 k}{3 c^{3}} \left\langle \left(\frac{d^{2} \vec{P}}{d t^{2}}\right)^{2} \right\rangle , \tag{1}$$

where the angle brackets stand for the averaging over the oscillation period.

sub_problems.problem:
(1) An atom emits light with a wavelength $\lambda_{0} =300 \mathsf{n m}$ . Using the classical model estimate an emission time $\tau$ (that is, the period of time it takes the atom to emit the energy equal to that of a single photon). This time coincides with the characteristic time, during which the atom emits a photon, by the order of magnitude. All radiation is due to a single electron located at a distance about $a_{0} =0.1$ nm from the nucleus. Express your answer in terms of the physical constants, $\lambda_{0} ,$ and $a_{0}$ .

Suppose $N$ atoms in a certain volume are transferred to an excited state by a short-term pumping action. It is known that one atom emits a photon with a frequency $\omega$ for a characteristic time $\tau$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The radiated power of a dipole with moment \(\vec p(t)=\vec p_m\cos(\omega t+\varphi)\) is
\[\nW=\frac{2k}{3c^3}\left\langle \left(\frac{d^2\vec p}{dt^2}\right)^2\right\rangle .
\]\nSince
\[
\frac{d^2\vec p}{dt^2}=-\omega^2\vec p_m\cos(\omega t+\varphi),
\]\nwe get
\[\nW=\frac{2k}{3c^3}\left\langle \omega^4 p_m^2\cos^2(\omega t+\varphi)\right\rangle
=\frac{2k}{3c^3}\cdot \omega^4 p_m^2\cdot \frac12
=\frac{k\omega^4 p_m^2}{3c^3}.
\]\nFor a single electron at a distance of order \(a_0\) from the nucleus, the dipole moment amplitude is
\[\np_m\approx ea_0.
\]\nThe characteristic emission time is the time needed to radiate one photon energy \(\hbar\omega\):
\[
\tau\sim \frac{\hbar\omega}{W}
=\frac{3\hbar c^3}{k\omega^3 e^2 a_0^2}.
\]\nUsing \(\omega=2\pi c/\lambda_0\), this becomes
\[
\tau \approx \frac{3\hbar}{k e^2 a_0^2}\left(\frac{\lambda_0}{2\pi}\right)^3.
\]\nSubstituting \(\lambda_0=300\,\mathrm{nm}\) and \(a_0=0.1\,\mathrm{nm}\) gives
\[
\tau \approx 1.5\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}.
\]\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{1.5\times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{s}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
Start by connecting the emitted wavelength to the oscillation frequency of the classical dipole. Use the relation between angular frequency, wavelength, and speed of light that you learned when studying sinusoidal waves: \(\omega = 2\pi c / \lambda_0\). This gives the frequency at which the electron must oscillate to produce the observed light.

Next, estimate the strength of the electric dipole moment. From the microscopic picture of an atom (as in Purcell & Morin’s hydrogen‑atom description), the dipole moment magnitude is roughly the product of the electron’s charge \(e\) and its distance from the nucleus. The problem tells you that this distance is about \(a_0\), so take \(p_0 \approx e a_0\). Because the electron oscillates, the dipole moment varies harmonically with amplitude \(p_0\).

Now, to find how fast energy is radiated, use the formula for the total power radiated by an oscillating electric dipole. In the Griffiths passage you studied, Eq. (11.22) gives the time‑averaged power (the factor \(1/2\) from the average of \(\cos^2\) is already included):
\[
\langle P \rangle = \frac{\mu_0 \, p_0^2 \, \omega^4}{12\pi c}.
\]
This expression is what you need; Example 11.1 in the same section even emphasises the strong \(\omega^4\) dependence.

Then bring in the quantum nature of the emitted light. From the Planck relation (discussed in your thermal physics texts), a photon of angular frequency \(\omega\) carries energy \(E = \hbar\omega\) (or equivalently \(E = h\nu\)). The characteristic emission time \(\tau\) is the time required for the radiating electron to deliver exactly this one‑photon energy to the radiation field. Because we only need an order‑of‑magnitude estimate, we can write
\[
\tau \sim \frac{\text{energy of one photon}}{\text{radiated power}} = \frac{\hbar\omega}{\langle P \rangle}.
\]
Substitute the expression for \(\langle P \rangle\) and the dipole amplitude \(p_0 \approx e a_0\) to obtain \(\tau\) in terms of physical constants, \(a_0\), and \(\omega\).

sub_problems.problem: (2) Estimate the power $W_{s}$ of electromagnetic radiation of all $N$ atoms in the spon- taneous emission mode, i.e. when the direction of atomic dipole and the phase of its oscillations randomly change from atom to atom. In your answer write down the formula for the power in terms of $N , \omega ,$ and $\tau$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a system of \(N\) atoms, the total dipole moment can be written as
\[
\vec{P}(t)=\sum_i \vec{p}_{mi}\cos(\omega t+\varphi_i).
\]
\nThe radiated power is
\[\nW=\frac{2k}{3c^3}\left\langle \left(\frac{d^2\vec{P}}{dt^2}\right)^2 \right\rangle.
\]\nSubstituting the sum over atoms gives
\[\nW=\frac{k\omega^4}{3c^3}\sum_i p_{mi}^2+\frac{k\omega^4}{3c^3}\sum_{i\ne j}(\vec p_{mi}\cdot \vec p_{mj})\cos(\varphi_i-\varphi_j).
\]
\nIn spontaneous emission the dipole orientations and phases are random and uncorrelated, so the cross terms average to zero. Since all atoms have the same dipole magnitude \(p_m\), the first sum gives \(N\) identical terms:
\[\nW_s=N\frac{k\omega^4}{3c^3}p_m^2.
\]
\nFor one atom, the spontaneous emission rate is related to the radiated power by
\[
\frac{k\omega^4 p_m^2}{3c^3}=\frac{\hbar\omega}{\tau}.
\]\nTherefore,
\[\nW_s=N\frac{\hbar\omega}{\tau}.
\]
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{W_s=N\frac{\hbar\omega}{\tau}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall from reference passages how to compute the **radiated power of a single oscillating electric dipole**. In the worked example from Griffiths reference.1.4 and the detailed derivation of Problem 11.35, you saw that an oscillating dipole  
 p(t) = p₀ cos(ωt)  
has a second time derivative   p̈(t) = –ω² p₀ cos(ωt). The time‑averaged power radiated by such a dipole is proportional to the mean square of p̈, giving  
 P₁ = (μ₀/(6πc)) ⟨p̈²⟩.  
When you substitute the harmonic form and take the average over a period, you obtain an explicit expression for P₁ in terms of p₀ and ω. (You will not need the exact numerical coefficient from reference here, because it will cancel in a later step.)

Next, extend to **N atoms radiating together**. Use the **superposition principle for dipole moments** described in the Purcell & Morin passage and the discussion of multiple oscillating dipoles in Griffiths reference.1.2: the total dipole moment of the collection is the vector sum of the individual atomic dipole moments, each with its own orientation and phase φᵢ,  
 P(t) = Σᵢ pₘᵢ cos(ωt + φᵢ).  
Now, because the problem asks for **spontaneous emission** — where atomic dipoles and phases vary randomly from atom to atom — these individual terms are uncorrelated. When you compute the total radiated power (which depends on ⟨(d²P/dt²)²⟩), the cross terms between different atoms will average to zero, as the random phases cause the average of cos(φᵢ – φⱼ) to vanish. Consequently, the total time‑averaged power is simply the sum of the powers from each atom individually, and if all atoms have the same dipole magnitude pₘ, then  
 W_s = N · P₁.

Finally, **relate the single‑atom power P₁ to the spontaneous‑emission lifetime τ**. An excited atom stores an energy ≈ ħω, and this energy is radiated away with a time constant τ, so the atom’s average radiated power is essentially  
 P₁ = ħω / τ.  
(This step uses the physical meaning of τ as the characteristic decay time; it is consistent with the Larmor‑formula expression for P₁, allowing you to eliminate the unknown dipole amplitude p₀.)

Now combine everything:  
1. Write P₁ from the Larmor formula applied to a single oscillator.  
2. Use the superposition argument to multiply that single‑atom power by N (thanks to the random phases and orientations, the total power adds incoherently).  
3. Replace the single‑atom power by ħω / τ to obtain the final formula for W_s that only involves N, ω, and τ.

Carry out the substitution and simplify — the remaining constants from the Larmor formula will cancel with those implicit in the ħω/τ relation, leaving you with a clean expression for W_s.

sub_problems.problem: (3) Estimate the duration of the spontaneous emission pulse of this system of atoms. Express your answer in terms of the same quantities.
sub_problems.solution:
The total energy emitted by the system is the sum of the photon energies from all atoms:
\[\nE = N\hbar\omega.
\]\nIf the atoms emit independently, the total spontaneous radiation power is the spontaneous power of the system, denoted by \(W_s\). The emission pulse duration is then estimated by energy conservation as
\[
\Delta t_s = \frac{E}{W_s}.
\]\nFor independent spontaneous emission, this timescale is just the characteristic lifetime \(\tau\) of an excited atom, so
\[
\Delta t_s \approx \tau.
\]\nTherefore, the spontaneous emission pulse duration is
\[
\boxed{\Delta t_s = \tau}.
\]

sub_problems.problem: (4) Estimate the power $W_{i}$ of electromagnetic radiation of all $N$ atoms in the su- perradiance mode, i.e. when the direction of atomic dipoles and the phases of their oscillations are the same for all atoms in the excited state. sub_problems.solution:
In the superradiance mode, all atomic dipoles are parallel and oscillate in phase, so for any pair of atoms the dipole contributions add coherently.
\nThus, in the total radiated power, the terms corresponding to individual atoms contribute as $N$ identical terms, and the interference terms contribute as $N(N-1)$ identical terms. Therefore the total power scales as
\[\nW_i=(N+N(N-1))\,\frac{k\omega^4}{3c^3}p_m^2 = N^2\frac{\hbar\omega}{\tau}.
\]\nHence the radiation power in the superradiance mode is
\[
\boxed{W_i = N^2\frac{\hbar\omega}{\tau}}.
\]

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall from the Planck relation (as in the Carroll & Ostlie passage) that a photon carries a quantum of energy \(E = h\nu = \hbar\omega\), where \(\omega\) is the angular frequency of the emitted radiation.  
In reference problem context, a single excited atom is given the spontaneous emission lifetime \(\tau\) — the characteristic time it takes to radiate away its excitation energy. Therefore, the average power radiated by **one** such atom is the energy of the emitted photon divided by that lifetime: \(P_{\text{one atom}} = \frac{\hbar\omega}{\tau}\). (Think of it as the energy released per decay event, occurring with an average rate \(1/\tau\).)

Next, you need to understand what happens when all \(N\) atoms are in the **superradiance mode**: the atomic dipoles are parallel and oscillate in phase. The textbooks on coherent emission teach you that when sources radiate **in phase**, the electric fields (amplitudes) add directly. From the laser discussion (Eisberg & Resnick) you see that the resulting intensity is the square of the constructively combined amplitudes. Moreover, Problem 11.18 in Griffiths explicitly shows that two identical oscillators placed exactly on top of each other radiate **four** times the power of a single one — power is proportional to the square of the total charge oscillation amplitude, i.e., to \(N^{2}\) when \(N\) identical dipoles act coherently.

Thus, for \(N\) atoms in the superradiance mode, the total radiated power scales as \(N^{2}\) times the single‑atom power. Simply combine this \(N^{2}\) factor with the expression you already have for one atom’s power.

No explicit use of the full Larmor formula is required here because the lifetime \(\tau\) already encapsulates all the dipole‑strength and frequency factors for a spontaneous emitter.

sub_problems.problem: (5) Estimate the duration of the radiation pulse of the system of atoms in the su- perradiance mode. Express your answer in terms of the same quantities.
sub_problems.solution:
In the superradiance mode, the total emitted energy is the same as in part A3, but the radiation power is enhanced by a factor of $N$ compared with a single atom. Therefore the pulse duration is

$$\Delta t_i = \frac{E}{W_i} \approx \frac{\tau}{N}.$$
\nSo the duration of the radiation pulse is

$$\boxed{\Delta t_i \approx \frac{\tau}{N}}.$$

knowledge_points.description: The average power P of a radiative process is the total energy E divided by the duration Δt: P = E/Δt, so Δt = E/P. This relation is used to compute the superradiance pulse duration from the total energy and power.

knowledge_points.name: Total energy of N excited atoms
knowledge_points.description: In both spontaneous and superradiance modes, the total emitted energy is the sum of the energies of the individual atoms, equal to N times the energy of a single photon (E = Nℏω). This result is imported from part A3.

knowledge_points.name: Superradiance power enhancement
knowledge_points.description: In superradiance mode, where all atomic dipoles oscillate in phase, the total radiated power is N^2 times the power of a single atom (W_i ∝ N^2 ℏω/τ). This coherent enhancement is derived in part A4 and used to express the power in terms of τ.

sub_problems.guidance:
To estimate the superradiance pulse duration, start by linking time, energy, and average power. reference defines average power as the energy delivered per unit time—for example, in reference.6.1 you find that the power density $S$ is the mean rate of energy flow through an area, and in reference.6 the average power in an AC circuit is given by $\overline{P} = V_{\mathrm{rms}} I_{\mathrm{rms}} \cos \phi$, which is also energy per unit time. From this general relation, the duration $\Delta t$ of an energy pulse is simply the total radiated energy $E$ divided by the average radiated power $P$:

\[
\Delta t = \frac{E}{P}.
\]

Now apply this to the superradiance system. From earlier parts of the problem (specifically part A3), you already know the total energy emitted during a spontaneous emission pulse of a single atom, and that this total energy remains unchanged when $N$ atoms cooperate in the superradiance mode. The key difference for superradiance is that the radiation power is enhanced by a factor of $N$ compared with a single isolated atom. Therefore, if the single-atom average power is $P_1$, the average power for the $N$-atom system in the superradiance mode is $P_i = N P_1$.

Finally, combine these ideas in the expression for pulse duration:

1.  Write the superradiance pulse duration $\Delta t_i$ as $E / P_i$.
2.  Replace $P_i$ with $N P_1$.
3.  Recognize that the ratio $E / P_1$ is precisely the single-atom spontaneous emission pulse duration, which you have encountered as the lifetime $\tau$ (or a closely related quantity) in the earlier analysis.

Carry out this substitution and simplify to obtain $\Delta t_i$ expressed in terms of $\tau$ and $N$. The result shows how the cooperative emission dramatically shortens the pulse.

title: Nonlinear optics and pulse compression
problem:
When solving the problem, use the following values of the physical constants:

the speed of light in vacuum $c =3.00 \cdot 10^{8} \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} ;$

Planck's constant $\hbar =1.055 \cdot 10^{-34} \rfloor .$ s;

constant in Coulomb's law and electric constant $\begin{array} {r} {k = {\frac{1} {4 \pi \varepsilon_{0}}} =8.99 \cdot 10^{9} ~ {\frac{\mathrm{N} \cdot \mathrm{m}^{2}} {\mathrm{C}^{2}}}} \end{array}$;

elementary charge $e =1.60 \cdot 10^{-19} \textsf{C}$ .

# Part B. Nonlinear optics and pulse compression

Pulses of even shorter duration can be obtained by reducing the duration of already generated laser pulses. A pulse duration $\Delta t$ and a dispersion of frequency of pulse oscillations $\Delta \omega$ (spectral width) are related by the inequality $\Delta \omega \Delta t \geq 2 \pi$ . Laser pulses generated in the superradiance mode already have the shortest possible duration for the given dispersion of frequencies, $\begin{array} {r} {\Delta t_{0} \approx \frac{2 \pi} {\Delta \omega_{0}}} \end{array}$ . Therefore, the pulse duration can be reduced in two steps: first, increase the spectral width of the pulse (without changing the duration) and second, compress the pulse in time.

One of the most common ways to solve the first problem is pulse chirping. This method is based on the use of nonlinearity of a medium, i.e. dependence of the refractive index of the medium $n$ on the amplitude of oscillations of the electric field $E_{m}$ of the wave. The dependence is of the form $n = n_{0} {+} n_{2} E_{m}^{2} ,$ , where $n_{0}$ and $n_{2}$ are some constants specific for the medium. Nonlinear effects are small, e.g. in quartz at a light intensity $I_{1} =10^{9} \mathsf{W} / \mathsf{c m}^{2}$ the refractive index increases only by $n_{2} E_{m 1}^{2} \approx 3.2 \cdot 10^{-7}$ . The intensity of an electromagnetic wave in a medium is determined by the formula $I = \frac{\varepsilon_{0} n_{0} c} {2} E_{m}^{2}$ .

Consider a pulse of duration $\Delta t_{0}$ with a small dispersion of frequencies $\begin{array} {r} {\Delta \omega_{0} \approx \frac{2 \pi} {\Delta t_{0}}} \end{array}$ , the average pulse frequency is $\omega_{0}$ . An approximate dependence of the electric field on time in such a pulse is shown in the Figure. The speed of the wave maxima is the same at the pulse edges and in the central part it decreases due to the nonlinearity effects. Because of that the total pulse duration does not change, the frequency increases at the rear part of the pulse and decreases at the front. Such a pulse is called "chirped".

sub_problems.problem: (1) Let the amplitudes of two wave maxima be $E_{m 1}$ and $E_{m 2}$ . Find the difference in their propagation speeds $\Delta v$ . Express your answer in terms of $n_{0} , n_{2} , c , E_{m 1}$ , and $E_{m 2}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
The phase velocity of the wave in the medium is
\[v=\frac{c}{n}=\frac{c}{n_0+n_2E_m^2}.\]
Since the nonlinear correction is small, expand to first order in \(n_2E_m^2\):
\[v\approx \frac{c}{n_0}\left(1-\frac{n_2E_m^2}{n_0}\right).\]
For two wave maxima with amplitudes \(E_{m1}\) and \(E_{m2}\), their speeds are
\[v_1\approx \frac{c}{n_0}\left(1-\frac{n_2E_{m1}^2}{n_0}\right),\qquad v_2\approx \frac{c}{n_0}\left(1-\frac{n_2E_{m2}^2}{n_0}\right).\]
Therefore, the difference in propagation speeds is
\[
\Delta v=v_1-v_2=\frac{c n_2}{n_0^2}\left(E_{m2}^2-E_{m1}^2\right).
\]
Final answer: \(\boxed{\Delta v=\dfrac{c n_2}{n_0^2}\left(E_{m2}^2-E_{m1}^2\right)}\).

knowledge_points.name: phase velocity in a medium
knowledge_points.description: The phase velocity of an electromagnetic wave in a medium with refractive index n is v = c/n. This relates the propagation speed of wave maxima to the given nonlinear refractive index.

knowledge_points.name: nonlinear refractive index
knowledge_points.description: The refractive index depends on the electric field amplitude as n = n0 + n2 E_m^2, as stated in the problem. This nonlinearity causes the amplitude-dependent propagation speeds.

knowledge_points.name: small nonlinear index change
knowledge_points.description: The nonlinear correction n2 E_m^2 is much smaller than n0, so the fractional change in refractive index is tiny. This justifies a first-order expansion of the phase velocity.

knowledge_points.name: binomial expansion for small parameter
knowledge_points.description: For |x| << 1, (1+x)^{-1} ≈ 1 - x. Applied to v = c/(n0 + n2 E_m^2) = (c/n0)(1 + n2 E_m^2 / n0)^{-1} to obtain the linearized form v ≈ (c/n0)(1 - n2 E_m^2 / n0).

sub_problems.guidance:
First, write the phase velocity for each wave from the given amplitude‑dependent refractive index. The problem context tells you that the index is \(n = n_0 + n_2 E_m^2\), so the velocity is \(v = c/n = \frac{c}{n_0 + n_2 E_m^2}\).

Because the nonlinear correction is small, you can separate the dominant part by factoring out \(n_0\) in the denominator:  
\[
v = \frac{c}{n_0\left(1 + \frac{n_2}{n_0}E_m^2\right)} = \frac{c}{n_0}\left(1 + \frac{n_2}{n_0}E_m^2\right)^{-1}.
\]

Now you have something that looks like \((1 + \delta)^n\) with a small \(\delta = \frac{n_2}{n_0}E_m^2\) and \(n = -1\). The binomial series from your reference (Kleppner & Kolenkow, §1.11.4) gives  
\[
(1 + x)^n = 1 + n x + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 + \dots,
\]
valid for \(|x| < 1\). Since \(\delta \ll 1\), you may approximate \((1+\delta)^{-1} \approx 1 - \delta\) by keeping only the linear term. (This is exactly the same idea you saw in Purcell & Morin when they expanded \((1+\delta)^{-1/2} \approx 1 - \delta/2\) in Eq. (10.7); here the exponent is simply \(-1\).)

Apply this expansion to your velocity expression. You will obtain a linearised form:  
\[
v \approx \frac{c}{n_0}\bigl(1 - \text{[something involving } E_m^2]\bigr).
\]

Next, write this approximation for the two amplitudes \(E_{m1}\) and \(E_{m2}\) separately, giving you \(v_1\) and \(v_2\). The requested difference is \(\Delta v = v_1 - v_2\). Subtract the two expressions and simplify. All terms that do not depend on \(E_m\) will cancel; what remains will be proportional to \(E_{m2}^2 - E_{m1}^2\). Carefully combine the constants (\(c, n_0, n_2\)) and you will arrive at \(\Delta v\) expressed entirely in the given parameters.

sub_problems.problem:
(2) A light pulse with a wavelength in vacuum of $\lambda_{0} ~ = ~ 300 ~ \mathsf{n m}$ and a maximum intensity of $I_{0} =3 \cdot 10^{9} \mathsf{W} / \mathsf{c m}^{\overline{{2}}}$ propagates along the axis of a quartz fiber. Assume the envelope of a time dependence of the electric field squared $E_{m}^{2} ( t )$ of the wave to be a parabola. How far (find the distance $s$) does the pulse propagate along the fiber before its spectral width increases by the factor of $K =200 ?$ Express your answer in terms of $K , \lambda_{0} , n_{2} , E_{m}$ and calculate the numerical value (in meters, rounded to an integer).

To compress a chirped pulse in time one can pass it through a medium in which the group velocity of the wave depends on its frequency. For the medium under consideration, the dependence of wavenumber on frequency in the vicinity of the mean frequency $\omega_{0}$ can be represented as $k ( \omega ) = k_{0} + \beta_{1} ( \omega - \omega_{0} ) +$ $\frac{\beta_{2}} {2} ( \omega - \dot{\omega}_{0} )^{2}$ , where $\beta_{1} =5 \mathsf{n s / m}$ and $| \beta_{2} | =20$ fs2/mm.
sub_problems.solution:
In a Kerr medium the nonlinear part of the refractive index is \(n-n_0=n_2E_m^2(t)\), so after propagating a distance \(z\) the pulse acquires the nonlinear phase shift
\[
\delta\varphi(t,z)=\frac{\omega_0}{c}\,n_2E_m^2(t)\,z.
\]
For the parabolic envelope
\[E_m^2(t)=E_0^2\left(1-\frac{4(t-t_0)^2}{\Delta t_0^2}\right),\]
the time-dependent part of the phase is quadratic in \(t\), hence the instantaneous frequency shift is
\[
\delta\omega(t,z)=-\frac{\partial\,\delta\varphi}{\partial t}
=\frac{8\omega_0 n_2E_0^2}{c\,\Delta t_0^2}(t-t_0)z.
\]
At the pulse edges, \(t-t_0=\pm\Delta t_0/2\), so the total spectral broadening is
\[
\Delta\omega=\frac{8\omega_0 n_2E_0^2}{c\,\Delta t_0}z.
\]
Using \(\Delta\omega_0\approx\frac{2\pi}{\Delta t_0}\), the broadening factor is
\[K=\frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta\omega_0}
=\frac{4\omega_0 n_2E_0^2}{\pi c}z.\]
Since \(\omega_0=\frac{2\pi c}{\lambda_0}\), this gives
\[K=\frac{8n_2E_m^2}{\lambda_0}z,
\qquad s=\frac{K\lambda_0}{8n_2E_m^2}.\]
For the numerical value, the intensity is three times the reference value, so
\[
 n_2E_m^2=3\times 3.2\times10^{-7}=9.6\times10^{-7}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 s=\frac{200\cdot 300\times10^{-9}}{8\cdot 9.6\times10^{-7}}\approx 7.8\,\text{m}\approx 8\,\text{m}.
\]
Final answer: \(\boxed{s=\frac{K\lambda_0}{8n_2E_m^2}}\), \(\boxed{8\ \text{m}}\).

knowledge_points.name: self-phase modulation in Kerr medium
knowledge_points.description: In a Kerr medium, the intensity-dependent refractive index n = n0 + n2 E_m^2 produces a nonlinear phase shift δφ = (ω0/c) n2 E_m^2 z, which chirps the pulse and broadens its spectrum.

knowledge_points.name: instantaneous frequency
knowledge_points.description: The instantaneous frequency shift is the negative time derivative of the phase, δω = -∂(δφ)/∂t, turning the time-dependent nonlinear phase into a frequency chirp.

knowledge_points.name: parabolic intensity envelope
knowledge_points.description: The time dependence of E_m^2(t) is assumed to be a parabola, yielding a quadratic phase and a linear chirp, which allows simple calculation of the spectral broadening.

knowledge_points.name: time-bandwidth product limit
knowledge_points.description: The initial pulse satisfies Δt0 ≈ 2π/Δω0, relating its duration to its spectral width; this is used to express the broadening factor K in terms of the chirp parameters.

knowledge_points.name: angular frequency-wavelength relation
knowledge_points.description: ω0 = 2πc/λ0 connects the central angular frequency to the vacuum wavelength, needed to rewrite the answer in terms of λ0.

knowledge_points.name: intensity scaling of nonlinear index change
knowledge_points.description: Because I ∝ E_m^2, the nonlinear index change n2 E_m^2 scales linearly with intensity; using the given reference values, one finds n2 E_m^2 at the pulse intensity by simple proportion.
