title: MUSIC
problem: — Lasse Frantti. A band consisting of three physicists is on tour. The band plays progressive world music and is equipped with an electric guitar, pipe organ and tubular bells made of steel. Their first gig is at Tavastiaclub in Helsinki, where they tune their instruments before the show. The air is comfortably dry and the temperature is 25 degrees Celsius.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Their second gig is in Libya, where the temperature is 45 degrees Celsius. Their instruments are out of tune because of the scorching heat but all the tuning equipment has been left home. How badly out of tune are they? Estimate the audible change in the original $330\mathrm{Hz}$ tuning in all of the three instruments.
sub_problems.solution:
We estimate the change in pitch for each instrument when the temperature rises from $25^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $45^\circ\mathrm{C}$, so $\Delta T = 20\,\mathrm{K}$.
\nFor the tubular bells, the resonance frequency scales as
\[
 f \propto \frac{v}{\lambda}.
\]\nFor a steel bell, the wave speed scales like
\[
 v \propto \sqrt{\frac{E}{\rho}},
\]\nand since both $E$ and $\rho$ are essentially unchanged by temperature here, the main effect is thermal expansion of the bell. The characteristic length scales as
\[\nL \to L(1+\alpha\Delta T),
\]\nso the frequency changes as
\[
 f = f_0\sqrt{1+\alpha\Delta T}.
\]\nWith $\alpha\Delta T$ very small, this gives approximately
\[
 f \approx 330.04\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]\nSo the change is negligible.
\nFor the pipe organ, the pitch comes from a standing wave in an air column, so
\[
 f \propto \frac{v}{L}.
\]\nThe pipe length change from thermal expansion is tiny compared with the change in sound speed, so we ignore it. The speed of sound scales as the square root of absolute temperature, hence
\[
 f = f_0\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}.
\]\nUsing $T_1=25+273.15\,\mathrm{K}$ and $T_2=45+273.15\,\mathrm{K}$,
\[
 f \approx 330\sqrt{\frac{318.15}{298.15}} \approx 341\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]\nSo the organ is noticeably sharp.
\nFor the guitar string, the fundamental frequency is
\[
 f = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}},
\]\nwhere $T$ is the string tension and $\mu$ is the linear mass density. Heating mainly changes the string length, which reduces the tension. Using Hooke’s law for the stretched string, the fractional change in tension is approximately proportional to the fractional thermal expansion, leading to a small decrease in frequency. The estimate from the given data is
\[
 f \approx 325\,\mathrm{Hz}.
\]\nSo the guitar becomes slightly flat.
\nThus the audible tuning changes are: tubular bells essentially unchanged, pipe organ about $341\,\mathrm{Hz}$, and guitar about $325\,\mathrm{Hz}$. The final answer is \boxed{330.04\,\mathrm{Hz},\ 341\,\mathrm{Hz},\ 325\,\mathrm{Hz}}.

knowledge_points.name: Linear thermal expansion
knowledge_points.description: The change in length of a solid is ΔL = α L ΔT. Used to estimate how the dimensions of the bells, pipes, and strings change with temperature.

knowledge_points.name: Standing wave resonance
knowledge_points.description: The frequency of a standing wave in a resonator is f = v/λ, where v is the wave speed and λ is the wavelength determined by the geometry. Used to relate frequency to wave speed and size for all three instruments.

knowledge_points.name: Elastic wave speed in solids
knowledge_points.description: The speed of elastic waves in a solid is v = √(E/ρ), where E is Young's modulus and ρ is density. Used to argue that the wave speed in the steel bell is essentially constant.

knowledge_points.name: Speed of sound in ideal gas
knowledge_points.description: The speed of sound in an ideal gas is v = √(γRT/M) ∝ √(T), with T in Kelvin. Used to compute the change in pitch for the pipe organ due to temperature.

knowledge_points.name: String fundamental frequency
knowledge_points.description: The fundamental frequency of a stretched string is f = (1/(2L))√(T/μ), where L is length, T is tension, and μ is linear mass density. Used to estimate the tuning change of the guitar.

knowledge_points.name: Hooke's law for elastic materials
knowledge_points.description: Stress is proportional to strain (σ = E ε). For a stretched string, tension T = E A (ΔL/L0). Used to relate the thermal expansion of the string to the resulting change in tension.

knowledge_points.name: Order-of-magnitude estimation
knowledge_points.description: Comparing the relative sizes of different physical effects (e.g., thermal expansion vs. sound speed change) to identify the dominant effect. Used to justify ignoring pipe expansion, assuming constant E and ρ, and focusing on tension change for the guitar.

knowledge_points.name: Binomial approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small x, (1+x)^n ≈ 1+nx. Used to quickly estimate the small frequency change for the bell.

sub_problems.guidance:
Begin by recalling that each instrument’s pitch is set by a standing‑wave resonance, so the fundamental frequency obeys \(f \propto v/\lambda\) (or an equivalent relation from the textbook’s discussion of standing waves in cavities and on strings).  
A temperature rise from \(25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) to \(45^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) will change several physical quantities; you need to decide, for each instrument, which change dominates.

**1. Tubular bells (solid metal)**  
- The relevant wave speed is the elastic wave speed in a solid. The textbook’s Debye‑model section indicates that this speed is proportional to \(\sqrt{E/\rho}\), where \(E\) and \(\rho\) (Young’s modulus and density) change very little over this small temperature interval, so you may treat the wave speed as constant.  
- The resonance wavelength is set by the dimensions of the bell. Thermal expansion (linear expansion, covered in the “Approximation Methods” note) makes the characteristic length scale as \(L \to L(1+\alpha\Delta T)\).  
- Combine these: \(f \propto v/L\) gives \(f_{\text{new}} = f_0 / (1+\alpha\Delta T)\). Because \(\alpha\Delta T\) is tiny, apply the binomial approximation (the first‑order expansion \((1+x)^n \approx 1+nx\) from the series shown in the textbook) to obtain a simple shift.  
- This shift will be extremely small; the example of the pendulum period in the Approximation Methods note shows how to handle such a fractional change.

**2. Pipe organ (air column)**  
- The pitch of a flue pipe depends on standing waves in air. The length of the pipe changes by thermal expansion, but that effect is negligible compared with the change in the speed of sound.  
- Use the worked example from Sec. 31.2: under adiabatic conditions the speed of sound in an ideal gas is \(v_s \propto \sqrt{T}\), where \(T\) is the absolute temperature.  
- Because the wavelength is fixed by the pipe length (which stays nearly constant), \(f \propto v_s\). Therefore the new frequency is \(f = f_0 \sqrt{T_2/T_1}\), with \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) in kelvin.  
- This only requires plugging the given Celsius temperatures converted to kelvin, then taking the square root – a straightforward application of the worked example. You will find a noticeable upward shift.

**3. Guitar string**  
- The textbook gives the fundamental frequency of a fixed‑end string:  
  \[
  f = \frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T}{\mu}},
  \]
  where \(T\) is the tension and \(\mu\) the linear mass density.  
- Heating the string produces thermal expansion, which increases the length \(L\) slightly. Because the string is stretched, this expansion reduces the tension.  
- Relate the change in tension to the change in length using Hooke’s law (linear restoring force: \(F = -k\,\Delta L\)) and the thermal strain \(\Delta L/L_0 = \alpha\Delta T\).  
- Since the fractional changes are small, again employ the binomial approximation to separate the effects of length and tension on the frequency.  
- The combined effect yields a small decrease in pitch.

**4. Audibility**  
- After you have computed the three new frequencies (or at least the fractional changes) relative to the original \(330\,\mathrm{Hz}\), compare the shifts.  
- The organ and guitar shifts are large enough to be heard; the bell shift is essentially negligible. The textbook’s order‑of‑magnitude approach helps you judge what “audible” means without needing precise psychoacoustic data.

Throughout, let the textbook’s “Approximation Methods” example guide you: isolate the small parameter, write the exact expression, then expand to first order using the binomial series. That will give you a clear, numerical estimate for each instrument without getting lost in messy algebra.

sub_problems.problem:
(2) The tour ends with a private gig at a pulmonary clinic. The temperature in the treatment room is 25 degrees, but instead of air the room is filled with a mixture of helium and air (heliox). How does this affect the audible sound produced by the three instruments?

Speed of sound in air

$$v_{a} =331.3 \mathrm{m} / \mathrm{s} \sqrt{1+ \frac{t^{\left(^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)}}{273.15}}$$

Speed of sound in heliox $v_{t} =1.7v_{a}$

Heat capacity of steel $450\mathrm{J / kg}\cdot \mathrm{K}$

Density of steel $7900\mathrm{kg / m^3}$

Melting point of steel $1540^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$

Heat conductivity of steel $50\mathrm{W / mK}$

Young modulus of steel $200\mathrm{GPa}$

Coefficient of thermal expansion (steel) $12.0 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$

Power of the guitar amplifier 500 W

Diameter of the guitar E string $0.30\mathrm{mm}$

Free length of the E string $65\mathrm{cm}$

Frequency of the E string $330\mathrm{Hz}$

You can neglect the effects of temperature on the guitar body. The guitar string pitch is determined by the transverse standing wave frequency on the guitar string. The pipe organ pitch is determined by the longitudinal standing wave frequency of air in the pipe. The tubular bell pitch is determined by the transverse standing wave of the (steel) tube. You may use dimensional analysis where possible. Assume that the Young modulus of steel is constant in temperature.
sub_problems.solution:
The audible frequency of each instrument is determined by the vibrating object that creates the sound, not by the surrounding gas, except for the pipe organ where the air column itself is the vibrating system.

- **Electric guitar:** The string vibrations set the pitch. Since the string properties are unchanged and the guitar body is neglected, the emitted note stays the same.
- **Tubular bells:** Their pitch is set by the transverse vibrations of the steel tube. The surrounding gas does not significantly affect the natural frequency, so the pitch stays the same.
- **Pipe organ:** The pitch comes from a longitudinal standing wave in the air column. Replacing air by heliox changes the sound speed to
  \[
  v_t = 1.7\,v_a.
  \]
  For a fixed pipe length, the wavelength is unchanged, so the frequency scales with the sound speed:
  \[
  f_t = \frac{v_t}{v_a} f_a = 1.7 f_a.
  \]
  Thus the organ note becomes 70% higher in frequency, corresponding to about
  \[
  1.7\times 330\,\text{Hz} \approx 561\,\text{Hz}.
  \]\nTherefore, only the pipe organ changes pitch; the electric guitar and tubular bells sound the same, while the organ note is raised by a factor of 1.7 to about \(\boxed{561\,\text{Hz}}\).
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{Electric guitar: unchanged}}, \boxed{\text{tubular bells: unchanged}}, \boxed{\text{pipe organ: pitch increases by }1.7\text{ to }\approx 561\,\text{Hz}}

knowledge_points.name: Transverse standing wave on a string
knowledge_points.description: The guitar's audible pitch is set by the frequency of transverse standing waves on the string, which depends solely on the string's length, tension, and linear density.

knowledge_points.name: Transverse standing wave in a solid tube
knowledge_points.description: The pitch of tubular bells is determined by the transverse vibrational modes of the steel tube, a solid-body resonance whose frequency depends on the tube's geometry and material properties.

knowledge_points.name: Longitudinal standing wave in a pipe
knowledge_points.description: The pipe organ's pitch is set by a longitudinal standing wave in the air column inside the pipe, where the wavelength is fixed by the pipe's length and boundary conditions.

knowledge_points.name: Solid resonator frequency independent of ambient gas
knowledge_points.description: The natural frequencies of solid vibrating elements (strings, tubes) are negligibly affected by the acoustic properties of the surrounding gas; thus changing from air to heliox does not alter the pitch of the electric guitar or tubular bells.

knowledge_points.name: Wave equation v = fλ
knowledge_points.description: Relates wave speed, frequency, and wavelength. For the organ pipe, the wavelength is fixed by geometry, so the frequency scales directly with the speed of sound in the gas: f ∝ v.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the **vibrating object** that produces the sound for each instrument. The problem tells you directly:  
- electric guitar: transverse standing wave on the string  
- tubular bells: transverse standing wave on the steel tube  
- pipe organ: longitudinal standing wave of the air inside the pipe

For any standing wave, the relationship between wave speed \(v\), wavelength \(\lambda\), and frequency \(f\) is the same—this is the wave equation you have studied (e.g., \(v = \lambda f\) from the passage on wavelength, frequency, and speed; or \(\nu = v/\lambda\) in the sinusoidal‑waves discussion). In a standing wave, the **wavelength is fixed by the length of the vibrating object and the boundary conditions** (as you saw for strings with fixed ends in the Figures 5.7–5.10, and for organ pipes in the section on longitudinal standing waves). Therefore, once the length is set, the **frequency is proportional to the wave speed**:  
\[ f = \frac{v}{\lambda} \]

Now consider each instrument separately, asking: does changing the surrounding gas (air → heliox) affect the **wave speed** \(v\) of the vibrating object?

- **Electric guitar string** – The wave speed on a stretched string is determined by its tension and linear mass density (reference discusses transverse standing waves on a string, showing how \(k = \omega / v_\phi\) where \(v_\phi = \sqrt{T/\rho}\)). The tension and the string itself are unchanged when the room gas is changed, so \(v\) for the string stays the same. With \(\lambda\) also fixed by the string length, \(f\) does not change.

- **Tubular bells (steel tube)** – The transverse vibrations of the tube are governed by the material’s stiffness (Young’s modulus) and density, and by the tube’s dimensions. All of these remain constant; the surrounding gas does not alter the tube’s wave speed. Hence the standing‑wave frequency is unaffected.

- **Pipe organ** – Here the vibrating medium **is** the gas itself. The organ pipe supports a longitudinal standing wave in the air column, as modelled in the organ‑pipe section (where the air column is compared to a massive spring). The wave speed **is** the speed of sound in the gas. You are given the speed in air, \(v_a\), and a direct relation: the speed in heliox is \(v_t = 1.7\,v_a\). The pipe length does not change, so the wavelength of the standing wave pattern remains the same. Apply \(f = v/\lambda\) to air and to heliox, keeping \(\lambda\) constant; you will find that the frequency scales by the same factor as the sound speed.

Finally, combine these observations. Only the pipe organ’s pitch is affected: its frequency shifts in proportion to the faster sound speed in heliox, while the guitar and bells keep their original pitch. Using the given relation between the two sound speeds and the original frequency, you can work out the new organ frequency yourself—just be careful to keep \(\lambda\) unchanged and use the proportionality \(f \propto v\).

A diac is a component whose behaviour is determined by the voltage-current diagram shown above. A triac, on the other hand, can be thought of as a switch controlled by currentlook at the following equivalent schematics.

sub_problems.problem:
(1) Assume that the resistance $R_{t}$ is large enough that the charge moving through the diac can be neglected. Let the sinusoidal supply

voltage have a maximum value of $U$ and a frequency of $f$ ; the rheostat be set to the resistance $R$ and the capacitor's capacitance be $C$ . Find the maximum value of the voltage $U_{C}$ on the capacitor, and its phase shift $\varphi$ with respect to the supply voltage.
sub_problems.solution:
Denote \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Since the diac current is neglected, the circuit reduces to a series resistor \(R\) and capacitor \(C\) driven by a sinusoidal voltage of amplitude \(U\).
\nWrite the supply voltage and capacitor voltage in complex form:
\[\nu = U e^{j\omega t}, \qquad u_C = U_C e^{j(\omega t + \varphi)}.
\]\nThe capacitor impedance is
\[\nz_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}.
\]\nUsing the voltage divider relation,
\[\nu_C = \nu \frac{z_C}{R+z_C}.
\]\nHence the transfer factor is
\[\nk=\frac{z_C}{R+z_C}=\frac{1}{1+j\omega RC}.
\]\nIts magnitude and argument are
\[
|k|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+(\omega RC)^2}}, \qquad \arg k = -\arctan(\omega RC).
\]\nTherefore the maximum capacitor voltage is
\[\nU_C = U|k| = \frac{U}{\sqrt{1+(2\pi fRC)^2}},
\]\nand the phase shift of the capacitor voltage relative to the supply voltage is
\[
\varphi = -\arctan(2\pi fRC).
\]\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{U_C=\dfrac{U}{\sqrt{1+(2\pi fRC)^2}},\ \varphi=-\arctan(2\pi fRC)}\).

knowledge_points.name: negligible diac current
knowledge_points.description: The diac branch is effectively open because R_t is large, reducing the circuit to a simple series RC circuit driven by the supply.

knowledge_points.name: angular frequency
knowledge_points.description: Converts the given frequency f to angular frequency ω = 2πf, needed for impedance and phasor calculations.

knowledge_points.name: capacitive impedance
knowledge_points.description: The impedance of a capacitor is Z_C = 1/(jωC), used to write the voltage divider in the frequency domain.

knowledge_points.name: voltage divider for impedances
knowledge_points.description: In a series circuit, the voltage across an element is the total voltage times the ratio of its impedance to the total impedance; here V_C = V_supply * Z_C/(R+Z_C).

knowledge_points.name: phasor analysis
knowledge_points.description: Represent sinusoidal voltages as complex exponentials (phasors) to compute amplitude and phase using complex algebra; the transfer function magnitude gives the amplitude ratio, its argument gives the phase shift.

knowledge_points.name: phase shift
knowledge_points.description: The phase shift φ is the argument of the complex transfer function, representing the time lag of the capacitor voltage relative to the supply voltage.

sub_problems.guidance:
First convert the given supply frequency \(f\) to angular frequency \(\omega = 2\pi f\). This conversion is standard when working with sinusoidal signals, as explained in reference (Griffiths, reference.1.2).

Because the diac current is negligible (the problem states its resistance is large enough to ignore), the circuit reduces to a simple series combination of the resistor \(R\) and capacitor \(C\) driven by the sinusoidal supply. This is analogous to reference example where a very large resistor is neglected, leaving only the main series loop (Purcell, worked example 8.19).

Next, adopt the complex‑exponential (phasor) method described in the alternating‑current circuits overview (Purcell, Chapter 8). Represent the supply voltage and the capacitor voltage as complex quantities:
\[
\tilde{V} = U e^{i\omega t}, \qquad \tilde{V}_C = U_C e^{i(\omega t + \varphi)},
\]
where \(U\) is the given amplitude, and \(U_C\), \(\varphi\) are the unknowns you need to find. The actual physical voltages are the real parts of these complex expressions.

Now find the impedance of the capacitor. reference (Purcell, reference.5) gives the admittance of a capacitor as \(Y = i\omega C\); therefore the capacitive impedance is
\[
Z_C = \frac{1}{i\omega C}.
\]
The resistor’s impedance is simply \(R\).

Since the resistor and capacitor are in series, the same complex current flows through both. You can therefore use the voltage‑divider relation for impedances, exactly as done in the worked example for a high‑pass filter (Purcell, example 8.36). The complex voltage across the capacitor is
\[
\tilde{V}_C = \tilde{V} \frac{Z_C}{R + Z_C}.
\]
Substitute \(Z_C\) and form the complex ratio
\[
k = \frac{\tilde{V}_C}{\tilde{V}} = \frac{Z_C}{R + Z_C} = \frac{1}{1 + i\omega RC}.
\]

The magnitude \(|k|\) gives the ratio of the amplitude of the capacitor voltage to the supply amplitude, so \(U_C = U |k|\). The argument \(\arg(k)\) is the phase shift \(\varphi\) of the capacitor voltage relative to the supply (a negative argument means the capacitor voltage lags the supply). This connection between complex ratios and amplitude/phase is the central idea of the phasor method outlined in reference.

All that remains is to compute \(|k|\) and \(\arg(k)\) from the complex number \(1/(1 + i\omega RC)\). Use the properties of complex numbers: the magnitude of a reciprocal is the reciprocal of the magnitude, and the argument of a reciprocal is the negative of the argument. The magnitude of the denominator is \(\sqrt{1 + (\omega RC)^2}\), and its argument is \(\arctan(\omega RC)\). Carry out these steps yourself to obtain expressions for \(|k|\) and \(\arg(k)\). Finally, replace \(\omega\) with \(2\pi f\) to write \(U_C\) and \(\varphi\) in terms of the given quantities \(U, f, R, C\).

sub_problems.problem: (4) Express through $t_0$ and $f$ , how many times the average power of the lamp is lower than the one of a lamp without a dimmer, assuming that the resistance of the lamp is unchanged.
sub_problems.solution:
The lamp conducts from phase $2\pi f t_0$ until the end of the half-cycle at phase $\pi$. Since the lamp resistance is unchanged, the average power is proportional to the time average of $U^2$, and for a sinusoidal voltage this means proportional to the average of $\sin^2\alpha$ over the conducting interval.
\nThus the ratio of the power without a dimmer to the power with a dimmer is
\[\nr=\frac{\int_0^{\pi}\sin^2\alpha\,d\alpha}{\int_{2\pi f t_0}^{\pi}\sin^2\alpha\,d\alpha}.
\]\nUsing
\[
\int \sin^2\alpha\,d\alpha=\frac{\alpha}{2}-\frac{\sin(2\alpha)}{4},
\]\nwe find
\[
\int_0^{\pi}\sin^2\alpha\,d\alpha=\frac{\pi}{2},
\]\nand
\[
\int_{2\pi f t_0}^{\pi}\sin^2\alpha\,d\alpha
=\frac{\pi}{2}-\pi f t_0+\frac{\sin(4\pi f t_0)}{4}.
\]\nTherefore
\[\nr=\frac{\pi/2}{\pi/2-\pi f t_0+\sin(4\pi f t_0)/4}
=\frac{1}{1-2ft_0+\frac{\sin(4\pi f t_0)}{2\pi}}.
\]\nSo the lamps average power is lower by a factor of \(\boxed{\frac{1}{1-2ft_0+\frac{\sin(4\pi f t_0)}{2\pi}}}\) compared with a lamp without a dimmer.

knowledge_points.name: triac turn-off at zero crossing
knowledge_points.description: The triac stops conducting when the current through it reaches zero, which for a resistive load occurs at the voltage zero crossing (phase π for a half-cycle). This defines the end of the conduction interval.

knowledge_points.name: average power in AC circuit
knowledge_points.description: For a resistive load, average power is proportional to the time average of the square of the voltage: P_avg = (1/T) ∫ (v²/R) dt. With constant R, the power ratio reduces to the ratio of the integrals of v² over the respective intervals.

knowledge_points.name: angular frequency
knowledge_points.description: The angular frequency ω relates to frequency f by ω = 2π f, so the phase of the sinusoidal voltage at time t is 2π f t.

knowledge_points.name: sinusoidal supply voltage
knowledge_points.description: The supply voltage is sinusoidal with maximum value U and frequency f, so v(t) = U sin(2π f t).

knowledge_points.name: constant lamp resistance
knowledge_points.description: The lamp resistance is assumed unchanged, so the power is directly proportional to the square of the voltage, allowing the power ratio to be computed from voltage integrals alone.

sub_problems.guidance:
Your goal is to compare the average power of the lamp with the dimmer to the average power it would have without the dimmer, assuming the lamp’s resistance stays the same.

**Step 1 – Relate average power to voltage and resistance.**
From the textbook, when a resistor \(R\) is connected directly to a sinusoidal voltage, the average power is \(\overline{P}_R = V_{\mathrm{rms}}^2 / R\) (Eq. 8.81). Because the resistance is unchanged in both scenarios, the ratio of average powers will equal the ratio of the mean-squared voltages. So you need to compare the time-average of \(V^2\) over a full cycle without the dimmer to the time-average of \(V^2\) over the conducting portion of the cycle with the dimmer.

**Step 2 – Set up the voltage waveform.**
The supply is a sinusoidal ac voltage, so you can write the instantaneous voltage as proportional to \(\sin(\omega t)\) (or \(\cos(\omega t)\); the average of the square will be the same). The angular frequency is \(\omega = 2\pi f\), as given by Eq. (9.11). Without the dimmer, the lamp conducts during the entire positive half-cycle (and the same pattern repeats for the negative half-cycle; because the square of the voltage is used, you can just consider one half-cycle from phase \(0\) to \(\pi\)).

**Step 3 – Identify the conducting interval with the dimmer.**
The dimmer delays the turn-on until a time \(t_0\) after each zero crossing. In terms of phase angle, the conduction starts at \(\alpha = \omega t_0 = 2\pi f t_0\) and continues until the end of the half-cycle at \(\alpha = \pi\). During the rest of the cycle the voltage across the lamp is zero, so it contributes nothing to the average of \(V^2\).

**Step 4 – Write the ratio of average powers as a ratio of integrals.**
Since the resistance cancels, the factor by which the average power is lowered is the ratio:
\[
\frac{\overline{P}_{\text{no dimmer}}}{\overline{P}_{\text{dimmer}}}
= \frac{\text{average of } \sin^2\alpha \text{ over } [0,\pi]}{\text{average of } \sin^2\alpha \text{ over } [2\pi f t_0, \pi]}.
\]
The denominator is the average over the whole half-cycle, but the numerator is the average only over the conduction window. Equivalently, you can compare the integrals of \(\sin^2\alpha\) over the respective intervals (the length of the interval is handled automatically if you form the ratio of the averages directly, but it is simpler to set up the ratio of the integrals and then divide each by its own interval length, or directly use the fact that the average over \([0,\pi]\) is \(1/2\), as stated in the textbook just before Eq. (8.80)).

**Step 5 – Carry out the integrations yourself.**
You will need the integral of \(\sin^2\alpha\). A standard result (which you can derive using \(\sin^2\alpha = \frac{1-\cos 2\alpha}{2}\)) is:
\[
\int \sin^2\alpha\, d\alpha = \frac{\alpha}{2} - \frac{\sin 2\alpha}{4}.
\]
Apply the limits for the full half-cycle \([0,\pi]\) to confirm the textbook’s statement that the average of \(\sin^2\) is \(1/2\). Then apply the limits for the dimmer case \([2\pi f t_0, \pi]\). Subtract the value at the lower limit from the value at the upper limit.

**Step 6 – Form the ratio and simplify.**
Write the ratio of the two integrals (the full-half-cycle integral in the numerator, the dimmer integral in the denominator). The textbook’s worked example on light bulbs (Solution Manual 4.38) uses the same principle that power is \(V^2/R\), so the resistance cancels when comparing powers. Your final expression should contain only \(f\) and \(t_0\), with no other variables. Simplify the fraction to obtain the factor by which the dimmer reduces the average power.

title: CANDY WRAPPER
problem: — Eero Uustalu. Measure the thickness $d$ of the candy wrapper, estimate the uncertainty. Equipment: Candy, two hexagonal pencils, rubber bands, green $\lambda =532$ nm laser, measuring tape, screen, stand. Warning: do not look into the laser beam and do not direct it to the eyes of others!
solution:
The candy wrapper is cut into strips and wrapped \(A\) times around one hexagonal pencil, then placed against the other pencil. This creates a slit of width \(Ad\), where \(d\) is the thickness of one layer of wrapper.
\nA laser beam is sent through the slit and a diffraction pattern appears on the screen. For small angles, the angular separation between successive maxima or minima is
\[
\theta \approx \frac{a}{L},
\]\nwhere \(a\) is the distance between the first and last counted fringe and \(L\) is the screen distance.
\nFor diffraction from a slit of width \(Ad\), the condition for maxima/minima spacing gives
\[\nAd\,\theta = N\lambda,
\]\nso the wrapper thickness is
\[
 d = \frac{N\lambda}{A\theta} = \frac{N\lambda L}{Aa}.
\]
\nUsing the table values gives three estimates:
\[\nd_1 \approx 20\,\mu\text{m},\qquad d_2 \approx 29\,\mu\text{m},\qquad d_3 \approx 23\,\mu\text{m}.
\]\nA reasonable average is
\[
 d \approx 25\,\mu\text{m}.
\]
\nThe uncertainty is estimated from the spread caused mainly by the roughness and unevenness of the pencil surface. Taking half the range,
\[
\Delta d \approx \frac{d_{\max}-d_{\min}}{2} = \frac{29-20}{2}\,\mu\text{m} = 4.5\,\mu\text{m}.
\]
\nTherefore the thickness of the candy wrapper is
\[
\boxed{d = (25 \pm 5)\,\mu\text{m}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: single-slit diffraction
knowledge_points.description: A coherent beam passing through a narrow slit produces a pattern of bright and dark fringes on a screen; the geometry of the pattern depends on the slit width and light wavelength.

knowledge_points.name: single-slit diffraction minima condition
knowledge_points.description: The condition for a minimum in the single-slit diffraction pattern is a sin θ = mλ (or, in small-angle form, a θ ≈ mλ), where a is slit width, θ the angular position of the m‑th minimum, and λ the wavelength.

knowledge_points.name: small-angle approximation
knowledge_points.description: For small diffraction angles, sin θ ≈ tan θ ≈ θ ≈ y/L, where y is the linear distance from the central maximum on the screen and L the slit‑to‑screen distance; this linearises the relation between fringe position and angle.

knowledge_points.name: ideal single slit from layered wrapper
knowledge_points.description: Wrapping the candy wrapper A times around a pencil and placing it against a second pencil creates a slit whose width equals Ad (total thickness), assuming uniform layer thickness, no air gaps, and straight parallel edges.

knowledge_points.name: coherent monochromatic light source
knowledge_points.description: The green laser provides light of a single, known wavelength (532 nm) with stable phase (coherence), which is required to form a clear, stable single‑slit diffraction pattern.

knowledge_points.name: uncertainty estimation from range
knowledge_points.description: When several independent measurements of the same quantity are available, a simple estimate of the uncertainty can be obtained as half the difference between the maximum and minimum measured values.

sub_problems.guidance:
The experiment turns the candy wrapper into a slit that is many layers thick, then uses the laser to produce a single‑slit diffraction pattern. You have studied the small‑angle approximation and the far‑field pattern of a single slit. Here is the step‑by‑step method to find the thickness \(d\) and estimate its uncertainty.

1. **Create the slit of known total thickness**  
   Cut the wrapper into strips and wrap \(A\) turns around one hexagonal pencil. Press the second pencil against it, so that the gap between the two flat faces acts as a slit. The width of this slit is \(A \times d\) because each layer adds its thickness \(d\).  
   *Why:* We need a slit whose width is a multiple of the unknown thickness, so that the diffraction pattern reveals that multiple.

2. **Observe the diffraction pattern**  
   Place the slit in front of the laser and project the transmitted light onto a screen at a large distance \(L\). Adjust until you see a clear row of bright and dark bands (the single‑slit diffraction pattern) as shown in Figure 13.5 of the textbook (Georgi, *The Physics of Waves*, 13.4.1).  
   Because the screen is far away, the angles are small enough to use the small‑angle approximation later.

3. **Link the pattern to the slit width**  
   The textbook analysis of a slit of total width \(Ad\) (the passage considers a slit from \(-a\) to \(a\), where the full width is \(2a\); adapt that to \(Ad\)) tells you that the intensity has zeros – dark fringes – at angles \(\theta\) satisfying  
   \[
   Ad \sin\theta = m\lambda \qquad (m = \pm1, \pm2, \dots)
   \]  
   (see the condition for the periodic zeros in (13.54)).  
   *Apply the small‑angle approximation* \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) (from the mechanics textbook, small‑angle expansion) because \(L\) is large compared with the extent of the pattern. Then the angular position of the \(m\)-th minimum is  
   \[
   \theta \approx \frac{x_m}{L},
   \]  
   where \(x_m\) is the distance from the centre of the pattern to that minimum on the screen.

   Combining these gives  
   \[
   Ad \, \frac{x_m}{L} \approx m\lambda .
   \]

4. **Measure a convenient angular span to improve accuracy**  
   – Instead of measuring just one fringe position, count a total number \(N\) of fringe intervals (e.g., from one dark fringe to the \(N\)-th dark fringe on one side, or entirely across the central maximum out to the \(N\)-th fringe).  
   – Measure the corresponding linear distance \(a\) on the screen between the chosen outer fringes.  
   The angular separation between them is \(a/L\).  
   For such a span the path‑difference condition becomes  
   \[
   Ad \, \frac{a}{L} \approx N\lambda .
   \]  
   (The precise meaning of \(N\) depends on how you count the fringes; be consistent – e.g., if you measure from one first‑order minimum to the symmetric first‑order minimum on the other side, the total distance corresponds to \(N=2\).)

5. **Solve for the wrapper thickness**  
   From the relation above,  
   \[
   d = \frac{N\lambda \, L}{A \, a}.
   \]  
   Here \(\lambda = 532\ \text{nm}\) is the laser wavelength (given), \(A\) is the number of wrapper layers, \(L\) is the slit‑to‑screen distance, \(a\) is the measured fringe‑span distance, and \(N\) is the number of fringe intervals spanned.  
   *Do not substitute numbers yet – this is the formula you will evaluate after taking measurements.*

6. **Estimate the uncertainty**  
   The dominant source of error in this setup is the roughness and unevenness of the pencil surface, which makes the slit width slightly irregular along its length. This causes the measured fringe positions to vary from place to place.  
   – Take several independent measurements: for example, use different numbers of turns \(A\), repeat the experiment with a fresh wrapping, or record fringe distances for different stretches of the slit.  
   – Obtain three (or more) estimates of \(d\).  
   – A reasonable estimate of the uncertainty is half the spread of these values:  
     \[
     \Delta d \approx \frac{d_{\text{max}} - d_{\text{min}}}{2}.
     \]  
   Then report the final result as \(d \pm \Delta d\).

7. **Final check**  
   Verify that your measured angles are indeed small (so \(\sin\theta \approx \theta\) holds) and that the pattern you see matches the textbook description – a broad central maximum and equally spaced zeros on either side. This confirms that you are in the far‑field regime and the single‑slit formulas apply.

title: CHARGE ON A RING
problem:
—Andreas Isacsson. A pointlike particle with mass $m$ and charge $q$ is free to slide without friction along a fixed horizontal circular ring with radius $r$ . In the plane of the ring, another charge $Q$ is placed in a fixed position, at a distance $d$ from the center of the ring, with $d < r$ (see figure).

ization of helium is $\lambda =22\mathrm{kJkg}^{-1}$ , which you can take to be constant. The specific heat of the liquid $c(T)$ is shown on the graph (a larger copy is on an extra sheet). What fraction of the liquid helium has to vaporize to cool the remaining liquid from $T_{0} =4.1\mathrm{K}$ to $T_{1} =2.3\mathrm{K}$ ?

sub_problems.problem: (2) How large is the force from the ring on the particle, as a function of the angle $\phi$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
The force from the ring is the normal force that keeps the particle on the circular path. Since the particle moves on a circle of radius $r$, the net radial force must supply the centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$ toward the center.
\nThe force from the fixed charge $Q$ has magnitude
\[\nF_Q=\frac{mC}{2\bigl(r^2+d^2+2rd\sin\phi\bigr)}
\]
(where the constant $C$ absorbs the Coulomb parameters and the sign of the interaction). Its component normal to the ring is obtained by multiplying by the cosine of the angle between the line joining $Q$ to the particle and the local radial direction. From the geometry of the triangle formed by the center, $Q$, and the particle,
\[
\cos\alpha=\frac{r+d\sin\phi}{\sqrt{r^2+d^2+2rd\sin\phi}}.
\]\nTherefore the normal component of the electric force is
\[\nF_{Q,\perp}=\frac{mC(r+d\sin\phi)}{2\bigl(r^2+d^2+2rd\sin\phi\bigr)^{3/2}}.
\]\nAdding this to the centripetal requirement gives the force from the ring:
\[\nF_n=\frac{mv^2}{r}+\frac{mC(r+d\sin\phi)}{2\bigl(r^2+d^2+2rd\sin\phi\bigr)^{3/2}}.
\]\nIn the repulsive case this force is directed inward; if the interaction is attractive, the second term changes sign.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{F_n=\frac{mv^2}{r}+\frac{mC(r+d\sin\phi)}{2\bigl(r^2+d^2+2rd\sin\phi\bigr)^{3/2}}}

knowledge_points.name: Centripetal force equation
knowledge_points.description: For a particle of mass m moving with instantaneous speed v on a circular path of radius r, the net radial component of all forces must equal mv^2/r, directed toward the center of the circle.

knowledge_points.name: Normal force from a constraint
knowledge_points.description: A constraint that confines a particle to a given path (e.g., a ring) exerts a force perpendicular to the path (normal force) whose magnitude is determined by the dynamics.

knowledge_points.name: Electrostatic force from part (1)
knowledge_points.description: The electrostatic force on the particle due to the fixed charge Q has magnitude F_Q = mC/(2(r^2+d^2+2rd sinφ)) and is directed along the line joining the particle and Q. The constant C encapsulates the charge magnitudes and Coulomb constant.

sub_problems.guidance:
First identify all forces acting on the particle. There is the electric force from the fixed charge (its magnitude and direction were found earlier in the problem), and there is the force from the ring. According to the textbook, the force that a surface applies perpendicular to itself is called the **normal force**; it arises because the surface compresses a tiny bit until the restoring force balances the push. Here the ring acts like a constraint surface for the particle, so the force from the ring on the particle is a normal force pointing radially (either inward or outward depending on how the particle presses against the ring).

Because the particle is moving on a circle of constant radius \( r \), its acceleration has a radial component inward: the **centripetal acceleration**. For classical mechanics, the net inward radial force must equal \( m v^2 / r \) (as noted in the textbook, the centripetal force is \( m u^2 / R \) classically). Thus, by Newton's second law in the radial direction, the sum of the radial components of all forces must supply this centripetal requirement.

Now break the known electric force into its radial component. Use the geometry already established (the triangle formed by the ring center, the fixed charge, and the particle) to find the cosine of the angle between the electric force vector and the local radial direction. Only this radial component participates in the radial force balance; the tangential component does not affect the normal force.

Write the radial force equation:  
\[
\text{radial component of electric force} \; \pm \; \text{normal force from ring} = m \frac{v^2}{r},
\]  
with signs chosen according to the directions (the normal force can be inward or outward, but the net result must point toward the center). Isolate the normal force from this equation, substituting the expression for the electric force magnitude and the geometric factor. The resulting expression gives the force from the ring as a function of the angle \( \phi \). If the sign of the electric interaction changes (attractive instead of repulsive), the radial component’s sign changes accordingly, so the normal force adjusts.

title: OSCILLATIONS
problem: —Lasse Frantti.

sub_problems.problem: (1) A steel ball (mass $m =1 \, \mathrm{kg}$ ) is attached to an ideal vertical spring. This causes the spring to lengthen by $x =5 \, \mathrm{cm}$ . The ball is then pulled down by $s =10 \, \mathrm{cm}$ from its equilibrium point and released, which leads to an oscillation. What should be the length of a point mass pendulum in order to have the same small oscillations period as this system?
sub_problems.solution:
For the vertical spring, the equilibrium condition is
\[mg=kx,\]
so the spring constant is
\[k=\frac{mg}{x}.\]
The period of small vertical oscillations of a mass on a spring is
\[T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}.\]
A simple pendulum of length $l$ has small-oscillation period
\[T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}.\]
For the periods to be the same, we set these equal:
\[
2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}.
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{m}{k}=\frac{l}{g}\quad \Rightarrow\quad l=\frac{mg}{k}.
\]
Using $k=mg/x$, we get
\[
l=x=5\,\mathrm{cm}.
\]
Therefore the equivalent pendulum length is \(\boxed{5\,\mathrm{cm}}\).

knowledge_points.name: vertical spring static equilibrium
knowledge_points.description: For a mass hanging on a vertical ideal spring in equilibrium, the spring force balances gravity: k x = m g. This relation allows determining the spring constant from the given static extension x.

knowledge_points.name: period of mass-spring oscillator
knowledge_points.description: The period of small oscillations of a mass m on an ideal spring of constant k is T = 2π√(m/k), independent of the oscillation amplitude.

knowledge_points.name: period of a simple pendulum (small oscillations)
knowledge_points.description: A point-mass pendulum of length l undergoing small angular oscillations has a period T = 2π√(l/g); this formula is valid only for small amplitudes, as specified in the problem statement.

sub_problems.guidance:
- Start by analyzing the vertical spring in static equilibrium. The weight of the ball stretches the spring by a known amount \(x\). Use force balance – the upward spring force equals the downward weight – to express the spring constant \(k\) in terms of \(m\), \(g\), and \(x\).
- Once you have \(k\), recall that a vertical spring oscillates about its new equilibrium with the same dynamics as a horizontal spring. As shown in the hanging‑mass solution from Morin (Chapter 4), the net force relative to equilibrium is simply \(-k\,y_{r}\), so gravity only shifts the equilibrium point. The period is still given by the standard mass–spring formula from Kleppner & Kolenkow reference.7: \(T_{\text{spring}} = 2\pi \sqrt{m/k}\).
- Substitute the expression for \(k\) (obtained from the equilibrium condition) into that period formula. Simplify the result; you should see that the mass cancels and \(T_{\text{spring}}\) becomes a function solely of \(x\) and \(g\).
- For the simple pendulum, the small‑oscillation period is derived in your reference

sub_problems.problem: (2) A hole is drilled diametrically through a spherical asteroid. An astronaut drops a stone into the hole to see what happens. Show that the stone starts to oscillate harmonically back and forth in the hole.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the asteroid be a uniform sphere of radius $R$ and density $\varrho$. Consider a point inside the sphere at distance $r$ from the center.
By spherical symmetry, the gravitational field has the same magnitude everywhere on a sphere of radius $r$ and points radially inward. Using Gauss’s law for gravity,
\[
\oint \mathbf g\cdot d\mathbf A=-4\pi G M_{\text{enc}}.
\]
The left-hand side is
\[
-4\pi r^2 g,
\]
and the enclosed mass is
\[
M_{\text{enc}}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\varrho.
\]
Thus
\[
-4\pi r^2 g=-4\pi G\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\varrho\right),
\]
so
\[
g=\frac{4}{3}\pi G\varrho\, r.
\]
Since $M=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3\varrho$, this can also be written as
\[
g=\frac{GM}{R^3}r.
\]
If $x$ is the displacement of the stone along the drilled hole measured from the center, the acceleration is directed toward the center:
\[
\ddot x=-\frac{GM}{R^3}x.
\]
This is the equation of simple harmonic motion, with angular frequency
\[
\omega=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R^3}}=\sqrt{\frac{4\pi G\varrho}{3}}.
\]
Therefore the stone oscillates harmonically back and forth in the hole.
Final answer: \boxed{\ddot x+\frac{GM}{R^3}x=0\;\text{, so the motion is simple harmonic with }\omega=\sqrt{\frac{GM}{R^3}}}

knowledge_points.name: Spherical asteroid
knowledge_points.description: The asteroid is spherical, which provides spherical symmetry to apply Gauss's law for gravity and ensures the gravitational field is radial.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform asteroid density
knowledge_points.description: The asteroid has constant density, so the enclosed mass inside a radius r is proportional to r^3, leading to a linear gravitational restoring force.

knowledge_points.name: Gauss's law for gravity
knowledge_points.description: Relates the gravitational flux through a closed surface to the enclosed mass: ∮ g·dA = -4πG M_enc. Used to derive the gravitational field inside the asteroid.

knowledge_points.name: Simple harmonic motion equation
knowledge_points.description: The differential equation d²x/dt² = -ω²x defines simple harmonic oscillation. The derived equation of motion for the stone matches this form, proving harmonic motion.

sub_problems.guidance:
Your goal is to show that the stone’s motion satisfies the equation for simple harmonic motion (SHM).  You will build that equation step by step, using the gravitational force law and the shell theorem, then compare with reference’s definition of SHM.

1. **Set up the coordinate and identify the key distance.**  
   Take the centre of the asteroid as the origin and let the hole lie along the \(x\)-axis. When the stone is at a displacement \(x\) from the centre, its distance from the centre is \(r = |x|\). Because the hole is diametric, the stone moves along a straight line through the centre, so the gravitational force on it always points toward the centre.

2. **Find the gravitational force on the stone inside the sphere.**  
   reference passage from Morin shows that a spherically symmetric sphere (or a thin spherical shell) acts like a point mass for points *outside* it.  For a point *inside* a uniform sphere the situation is different: the shell theorem (which you are proving in that section) tells us that the part of the asteroid **outside** the stone’s current radius \(r\) exerts **no net gravitational force** on the stone.  Consequently, only the mass **inside** the radius \(r\) contributes.  
   - Use Newton’s law of gravitation (\(F = GMm/d^2\), as stated in Schaum’s and Morin) to write the force that this inner mass exerts on the stone.  Treat that inner mass as if it were a point mass at the centre.  
   - Express the inner mass \(M(r)\) in terms of the total mass \(M\) of the asteroid and the total radius \(R\): because the asteroid is uniform, \(M(r) = M \left( \frac{r}{R} \right)^3\) (this is just the ratio of volumes).  
   - The force is attractive, so it points toward the centre.  In our \(x\)-coordinate, that means \(F = -\,\frac{G\,m\,M(r)}{r^2}\).

3. **Simplify the force expression to show it is linear in displacement.**  
   Substitute the expression for \(M(r)\) into the force law.  After cancelling factors you should find that the force is proportional to \(r\), i.e. proportional to \(|x|\).  Because the force always points toward the centre (opposite to the displacement), the result takes the form \(F = -\,k_{\text{eff}}\, x\), where \(k_{\text{eff}}\) is a constant that depends on \(G\), \(M\), \(m\), and \(R\).  (Carry out the algebra yourself — you should obtain a neat linear restoring force.)

4. **Write Newton’s second law and compare with the SHM equation.**  
   Apply Newton’s second law: \(m\,\frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} = F\).  
   Using the linear force you just derived, the mass \(m\) cancels and you get an equation of the form
   \[
   \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2} + \omega_0^2\, x = 0,
   \]
   with a specific \(\omega_0\) that you can read off from the coefficient.

Now turn to reference passages on simple harmonic motion.  Kleppner & Kolenkow define SHM precisely by the equation
   \[
   \ddot{x} + \omega_0^2\,x = 0,
   \]
   where \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}\) for a spring.  Any system whose equation of motion reduces to this form is a harmonic oscillator.  Compare your derived equation with this standard form; identify what plays the role of \(\omega_0\) in your expression.  (No arithmetic is needed — just read the constant coefficient.)

5. **Conclude that the motion is simple harmonic.**  
   Because the equation you obtained is exactly the SHM equation, the stone’s motion is a simple harmonic oscillation back and forth through the hole.  The period can be found from \(\omega_0\) if required, but the problem only asks you to show the harmonic nature.

**What you should do next:**  
- Write the force expression carefully, substituting \(M(r)\) and cancelling \(r^2\).  
- Derive the equation of motion and identify \(\omega_0\) symbolically.  
- Check that your final equation matches \(\ddot{x} + (\text{positive constant})\, x = 0\), which is the hallmark of SHM as defined in reference.

sub_problems.problem:
(3) You want to send a parcel to your friend at the other end of the drilled hole. You can either throw the parcel horizontally (around

the asteroid) or drop it into the hole. Which way is faster?
sub_problems.solution:
Identify the asteroid’s gravitational acceleration at the surface with the centripetal acceleration of a circular orbit just above the surface:
\[
\frac{GM}{R^2}=\omega_o^2 R \quad \Rightarrow \quad \omega_o^2=\frac{GM}{R^3},
\]\nwhere \(\omega_o\) is the orbital angular speed.
\nIf the parcel is thrown horizontally around the asteroid, it needs half an orbit to reach the friend on the opposite side of the hole:
\[
 t_o=\frac{T_o}{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2\pi}{\omega_o}=\frac{\pi}{\omega_o}.
\]
\nIf the parcel is dropped into the hole, the motion inside a uniform-density asteroid is harmonic. It is equivalent to a spring oscillation with effective stiffness
\[
 k=\frac{GMm}{R^3}.
\]\nThus
\[
\omega_h^2=\frac{k}{m}=\frac{GM}{R^3}=\omega_o^2,
\]\nso the half-period for going from one end of the hole to the other is
\[
 t_h=\frac{\pi}{\omega_h}.
\]\nSince \(\omega_h=\omega_o\), we get
\[
 t_h=t_o.
\]\nTherefore, neither way is faster: both take the same time, \(\boxed{t_o=t_h}\).

knowledge_points.name: Circular orbit condition (gravitational)
knowledge_points.description: For a circular orbit of radius R around a mass M, the centripetal acceleration equals the gravitational acceleration: ω²R = GM/R², yielding ω² = GM/R³. Used to find the orbital angular speed.

knowledge_points.name: Gravitational force inside a uniform sphere
knowledge_points.description: Inside a uniform solid sphere of mass M and radius R, the gravitational force on a mass m at distance r from the center is F = -(GMm/R³) r, a linear restoring force. Used to model the motion through the hole as simple harmonic.

knowledge_points.name: Simple harmonic oscillator frequency
knowledge_points.description: For a mass-spring system with stiffness k, the angular frequency is ω = √(k/m). Used to find the angular frequency of the parcel oscillating through the hole.

knowledge_points.name: Period and angular frequency relation
knowledge_points.description: The period T of a periodic motion with angular frequency ω is T = 2π/ω. Used to compute the half-periods for both the orbit and the oscillation.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform solid sphere asteroid
knowledge_points.description: The asteroid is assumed to be a uniform solid sphere, which is necessary for the harmonic motion inside and for the orbital mechanics to be consistent.

knowledge_points.name: Surface-level circular orbit
knowledge_points.description: The parcel thrown horizontally is assumed to be in a circular orbit exactly at the asteroid's surface, so the orbital radius equals the asteroid's radius R.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Horizontal throw (orbital motion):**  
   The problem asks you to compare the time it takes the parcel to reach the opposite side if it is thrown horizontally just above the asteroid’s surface. This is a circular orbit problem.  
   *Use the circular orbit condition:* as derived in your reference (cf. the reasoning that for a satellite in a circular orbit of radius \(r\), centripetal acceleration equals gravitational acceleration: \(v^2/r = GM/r^2\)). Apply this to an orbit right at the surface, \(r=R\). Express the result in terms of an orbital angular speed \(\omega_o = v/R\). This will give you \(\omega_o^2 = GM/R^3\).  
   *Relate angular speed to travel time:* the parcel must travel half an orbit to reach the opposite side. The period of a circular orbit (or any uniform circular motion) is \(T_o = 2\pi/\omega_o\) (see reference’s period–angular frequency relation in the simple harmonic motion section). The time for half an orbit is therefore \(t_o = \pi/\omega_o\).

2. **Drop into the hole (oscillatory motion inside the asteroid):**  
   If the parcel is dropped into the diametric hole, it will move under gravity through the asteroid’s interior.  
   *Determine the force inside a uniform sphere:* from reference’s treatment of the gravitational force of a sphere, you know that a uniform spherical shell exerts no net force on a particle inside it, and a particle outside feels the force as if all mass were at the center. For a uniform solid sphere, the inner point at distance \(r\) from the center is acted upon only by the mass interior to a sphere of radius \(r\); the outer shells contribute zero. Assuming the asteroid has uniform density and total mass \(M\) and radius \(R\), this leads to a force \(F = - (GMm/R^3) \, r\) directed toward the center. Notice that this force is proportional to the displacement from the center and always opposite to the motion – exactly a Hooke’s law restoring force.  
   *Recognize simple harmonic motion:* the spring-like force can be written as \(F = -k_{\text{eff}} r\) with effective spring constant \(k_{\text{eff}} = GMm/R^3\). reference’s worked example on small oscillations (diatomic molecule) demonstrates that for a system obeying \(\ddot{x} = -(k/m) x\), the angular frequency is \(\omega = \sqrt{k/m}\). By analogy, the parcel’s radial motion will be simple harmonic with \(\omega_h = \sqrt{k_{\text{eff}}/m} = \sqrt{GM/R^3}\).  
   *Find the travel time:* one full oscillation corresponds to a period \(T_h = 2\pi/\omega_h\). The parcel needs to go from one surface of the asteroid (one extreme of the motion) to the opposite side (the other extreme), which is half a period: \(t_h = \pi/\omega_h\).

3. **Comparison:**  
   You now have two expressions: one for \(t_o\) and one for \(t_h\). Both contain \(\pi\) in the numerator and an angular frequency in the denominator. Compare the angular frequencies you derived for the orbital case and for the oscillatory case inside the sphere. Simplify the expressions until you can see whether \(t_o\) and \(t_h\) are different or identical. That will directly answer which way is faster.
