title: BEAMS
problem:
— Andres Póldaru. There are three beams between two absolutely rigid plates. The weight of the plates and the beams can be neglected. The coefficient of thermal ex

pansion of the beams is $\alpha =1.0\times 10^{-5}\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ .The maximum strain (relative length change compared to the no load case) before permanent inelastic deformations of the material of the beam is $\beta =0.40\%$ . The beams can support a maximum amount of weight on the top plate, at which point permanent deformations start taking place in some of the beams.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Initially all the beams are at the same temperature. Then the temperature of the beam in the middle is increased by $\Delta T =100\mathrm{K}$ . Compared to the case when the beams were at equal temperatures, what fraction of the original maximal weight can the beams now support on the top plate? Assume that the properties of the materials (specifically the maximum strain and the elastic modulus) don't change during the heating.
sub_problems.solution:
The temperature increase of the middle beam causes a free thermal strain
\[
\alpha \Delta T = 1.0\times 10^{-5}\cdot 100 = 1.0\times 10^{-3} = 0.10\%.
\]\nSince the beams are clamped between rigid plates, all three beams must end up with the same final length. At the maximum allowed load after heating, the middle beam can still reach the limiting strain \(\beta\), so the other two beams need only have mechanical strain
\[
\epsilon = \beta - \alpha\Delta T = 0.40\% - 0.10\% = 0.30\%.
\]\nFor linear elasticity, the force carried by a beam is proportional to its strain. Therefore the total maximum supported weight is proportional to the sum of the strains in the three beams.
\nOriginally, when all beams are at the same temperature, each beam can reach strain \(\beta\), so the maximum weight is proportional to
\[
3\beta.
\]\nAfter heating the middle beam, the maximum weight is proportional to
\[
2\epsilon + \beta.
\]\nHence the fraction of the original maximal weight is
\[
\frac{2\epsilon+\beta}{3\beta}
=\frac{2\cdot 0.30+0.40}{3\cdot 0.40}
=\frac{5}{6}\approx 0.83.
\]\nSo the beams can now support \(\boxed{\frac{5}{6}\approx 0.83}\) of the original maximal weight.

knowledge_points.name: Linear thermal expansion
knowledge_points.description: The relative length change of a material due to a temperature change ΔT is ΔL/L = αΔT, where α is the coefficient of thermal expansion. Used to compute the free thermal strain of the heated middle beam.

knowledge_points.name: Strain superposition
knowledge_points.description: The total strain (actual length change) in a constrained member is the sum of thermal strain (from temperature change) and mechanical strain (from stress). Needed to relate the beam's length change to its mechanical strain.

knowledge_points.name: Hooke's law
knowledge_points.description: In linear elasticity, stress is proportional to mechanical strain (σ = E ε), so the force carried by a beam is proportional to its mechanical strain. Used to convert strains into forces and thus into supported weight.

knowledge_points.name: Displacement compatibility
knowledge_points.description: Beams clamped between rigid plates must all undergo the same total length change (same total strain). Used to equate the total strain of the middle and outer beams.

knowledge_points.name: Yield strain limit
knowledge_points.description: The material yields when the magnitude of mechanical strain exceeds a critical value β. At the maximum supported load, the most stressed beam reaches this limit, setting its mechanical strain to β.

knowledge_points.name: Static force equilibrium
knowledge_points.description: The total downward weight on the top plate is balanced by the sum of the upward forces from all beams. Used to express the maximum supported weight as proportional to the sum of the beam strains.

sub_problems.guidance:
You know that the beams are clamped between rigid plates, so all three must shorten or lengthen by exactly the same amount when the top plate is loaded.  You also know that heating the middle beam makes it want to expand, while the outer beams stay at the reference temperature.  Your job is to compare the maximum total load the beams can carry before and after heating, making use of Hooke’s law, the condition of static equilibrium, and the concept of thermal expansion.

1. **Write the total strain for each beam.**  
   Let the common fractional change in length (relative to the original length at the initial temperature) be called the total strain, \( \delta \).  For a beam that is not heated, the total strain is entirely mechanical, i.e. due to the force on it.  For the heated middle beam, the total strain is the sum of the mechanical strain and the thermal strain.  
   According to reference’s example about the pendulum (Note 1.1), length changes due to thermal expansion; here you can express the free thermal expansion strain as \( \alpha \Delta T \), where \( \alpha \) is the material’s linear expansion coefficient and \( \Delta T = 100\,\text{K} \) is given.  (The elastic‑rod example in Chapter 17 also uses a linear expansivity \( \alpha_f \).)  
   So for the outer beams: \( \delta = \varepsilon_{\text{out}} \) (mechanical strain only).  
   For the middle beam: \( \delta = \varepsilon_{\text{mid}} + \alpha \Delta T \).

2. **Connect force to mechanical strain.**  
   From the Hooke’s law exposition (reference.7), the spring force is proportional to displacement.  For a beam of fixed cross‑section and fixed elastic modulus, the force carried is proportional to the mechanical strain alone.  Therefore the total weight supported by the three beams is proportional to the sum of their mechanical strains:  
   \[
   F_{\text{total}} \propto 2\varepsilon_{\text{out}} + \varepsilon_{\text{mid}} .
   \]

3. **Original maximum load (all at the same temperature).**  
   When no beam is heated, each beam can be loaded up to its maximum allowed strain, call it \( \beta \) (given in your problem as the limiting strain).  Because the top plate is rigid, all three beams reach this limit at the same time.  Hence the original maximum load is proportional to \( 3\beta \).

4. **Determine the limit after heating the middle beam.**  
   The limiting case occurs when one of the beams reaches \( \beta \) in magnitude.  Use the relation from step 1 to decide which beam hits the limit first.  The middle beam’s thermal expansion reduces its ability to take additional compressive strain; therefore for the same total shortening \( \delta \), its mechanical strain is more severe than that of the outer beams.  Thus the maximum load is reached when the middle beam is at its limit:  
   \[
   |\varepsilon_{\text{mid}}| = \beta .
   \]  
   Substitute \( \varepsilon_{\text{mid}} = \delta - \alpha \Delta T \) (pay attention to signs: the load compresses the beams, so strains are negative, but you can work with magnitudes as reference’s force‑vs‑displacement idea is linear).  This gives you \( \delta \) (or its magnitude) in terms of \( \beta \) and \( \alpha \Delta T \).  
   Then find \( \varepsilon_{\text{out}} \) from \( \delta = \varepsilon_{\text{out}} \) (outer beams have no thermal strain).

5. **Find the new maximum load.**  
   With \( \varepsilon_{\text{mid}} = \beta \) and the \( \varepsilon_{\text{out}} \) you just computed, the new maximum load is proportional to \( 2\varepsilon_{\text{out}} + \beta \).

6. **Fraction of the original weight.**  
   Finally, take the ratio  
   \[
   \frac{2\varepsilon_{\text{out}} + \beta}{3\beta}
   \]
   and simplify.  Every symbol except \( \beta \), \( \alpha \), and \( \Delta T\) cancels; you will obtain a fraction that depends only on the ratio \( \alpha \Delta T / \beta \).  Insert the numerical values you have for \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) to compute the fraction.

title: SPACESCRAFT PRESSURE
problem:
— Johan Runeson. Consider a spacecraft shaped as a homogeneous pipe, which is closed at both ends. The spacecraft is rotating around its center of mass with angular velocity $\omega$ , around an axis perpendicular to the pipe, in order to simulate gravity. The spacecraft is filled with air of molar mass $\mu$ , which has pressure $p_0$ at the rota

tion axis. The diameter of the spacecraft is much smaller than its length. Added during the competition: the temperature is $T$ .

sub_problems.problem: (1) Calculate the pressure $p$ as a function of the distance $r$ from the rotation axis.
sub_problems.solution:
Consider a thin air slice at distance $r$ from the rotation axis, with thickness $dr$ and cross-sectional area $A$. In the rotating frame, the pressure difference across the slice balances the centrifugal force:

$$A\bigl(p(r+dr)-p(r)\bigr)=m\omega^2 r,$$
\nwhere the mass of the slice is

$$m=A\rho(r)dr.$$
\nUsing the ideal gas law in the form

$$\rho(r)=\frac{\mu}{RT}p(r),$$
\nwe obtain

$$\frac{p(r+dr)-p(r)}{dr}=\frac{\mu\omega^2}{RT}r\,p(r).$$
\nHence

$$\frac{dp}{dr}=\frac{\mu\omega^2}{RT}r\,p.$$ 
\nSeparate variables and integrate from $r=0$, where $p(0)=p_0$, to a general $r$:

$$\int_{p_0}^{p(r)}\frac{dp}{p}=\frac{\mu\omega^2}{RT}\int_0^r r'\,dr',$$
\nwhich gives

$$\ln\frac{p(r)}{p_0}=\frac{\mu\omega^2}{2RT}r^2.$$
\nTherefore,

$$p(r)=p_0\exp\left(\frac{\mu\omega^2}{2RT}r^2\right).$$
\nFinal answer: \boxed{p(r)=p_0\exp\left(\frac{\mu\omega^2}{2RT}r^2\right)}

knowledge_points.name: centrifugal force
knowledge_points.description: In a rotating reference frame, an object of mass m at distance r from the axis experiences an outward fictitious force of magnitude m ω² r. This force acts as the body force on the air, driving the pressure gradient.

knowledge_points.name: ideal gas law
knowledge_points.description: The equation of state for an ideal gas, p = ρ R T / μ, relates pressure p, density ρ, temperature T, molar mass μ, and the universal gas constant R. Used to express density in terms of pressure.

knowledge_points.name: force balance on fluid element
knowledge_points.description: To derive the pressure distribution, consider an infinitesimal slice of fluid of thickness dr. The net pressure force across the slice balances the total body force (here centrifugal). Taking the limit dr→0 yields a differential equation for p(r).

knowledge_points.name: separation of variables
knowledge_points.description: A method for solving first-order ordinary differential equations by rewriting the equation so that each variable appears on a separate side, then integrating. Applied to dp/dr = (μ ω² / (R T)) r p to obtain p(r).

knowledge_points.name: one-dimensional approximation
knowledge_points.description: The pipe diameter is much smaller than its length, so the cross-sectional area A is constant and the pressure depends only on the radial coordinate r, justifying a 1D analysis.

knowledge_points.name: isothermal atmosphere
knowledge_points.description: The temperature T is uniform throughout the spacecraft, so the ideal gas law simplifies to ρ ∝ p, allowing the differential equation to be written solely in terms of p.

sub_problems.guidance:
(1) Choose the rotating frame. In this frame the air is at rest, so each fluid element is subject to a fictitious centrifugal force directed radially outward. reference on centrifugal force (Kleppner & Kolenkow, §9.5.4) tells us that its magnitude is \( m \Omega^2 \rho \), where \( \rho \) is the perpendicular distance from the rotation axis. Here, call that distance \( r \) and the angular speed \( \omega \).

(2) Follow the force‑balance method used for hydrostatic equilibrium (Blundell & Blundell, §35.1.2) and the isothermal atmosphere (Blundell & Blundell, §4.7). Consider a thin air slice at radius \( r \), thickness \( \mathrm{d}r \), and cross‑sectional area \( A \). The slice is at rest in the rotating frame, so the net real force on it must be zero. The real forces are the pressure forces from the neighbouring fluid. The net pressure force (outward) comes from the difference between the pressure on the inner face and that on the outer face. Write that force balance:

\[
\text{net pressure force} = \text{centrifugal force}
\]

(3) The mass of the slice is its density \( \rho(r) \) times volume: \( m = \rho(r) A \, \mathrm{d}r \). To connect density to pressure, use the ideal gas law. The passage from Palen’s Astronomy states \( p = n k T \) and density is \( \rho = n m_{\text{mol}} \) (mass per molecule). Equivalently, from Kleppner & Kolenkow, the ideal gas law can be written in molar form. Whichever form you choose, express the density as \( \rho = C \, p \) where the constant \( C \) contains the molecular or molar mass, temperature, and the appropriate gas constant \( R \) or \( k \). This step assumes the whole gas is at a constant temperature, as in the isothermal atmosphere model.

(4) Substituting the expression for \( m \) and \( \rho \) into the force balance yields a relation between the pressure difference and \( p(r) \) itself. After rearranging, you will obtain a first‑order differential equation of the form

\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}p}{\mathrm{d}r} = (\text{constant}) \, r \, p(r).
\]

The constant includes \( \omega \), temperature, and the gas/molar‑mass parameters.

(5) This differential equation is separable and linear. The “separation of variables” technique (Morin, §3.1) instructs you to bring all terms containing \( p \) to one side and \( r \) to the other: \( \mathrm{d}p / p = (\text{constant}) \, r \, \mathrm{d}r \). Then integrate both sides. reference’s worked example for the isothermal atmosphere (Blundell & Blundell, §4.7, eqn 4.24–4.25) shows an identical procedure, where integrating \( \mathrm{d}n/n \) gave a logarithmic expression. Here you will integrate from the axis \( r = 0 \) (where the pressure is some unknown \( p_0 \)) out to a general \( r \).

(6) Carrying out the two definite integrals gives \( \ln (p(r)/p_0) \) equal to an expression proportional to \( r^2 \). Exponentiate to isolate \( p(r) \). The result will be the pressure as an exponential function of \( r^2 \), containing the central pressure \( p_0 \), the angular speed, the temperature, and the molar/molecular mass. Do not substitute any numbers; leave the answer in symbolic form.

sub_problems.problem: (2) As a comparison, consider a (nonrotating) tower in a constant gravitational field of strength $g$ , filled with the same gas. If the ground level pressure is $p_0$ , what is the pressure $p$ as a function of height $h$ above the ground in such a tower?
sub_problems.solution:
Consider a thin horizontal gas layer of thickness $dh$ at height $h$ and cross-sectional area $A$. In equilibrium, the pressure force difference balances the weight of the gas in the layer:

\[
A\bigl(p(h)-p(h+dh)\bigr)=\rho A\,dh\, g,
\]\nwhere $\rho$ is the mass density of the gas.
\nUsing the ideal gas law,

\[
p=\frac{\rho}{\mu}RT \quad \Rightarrow \quad \rho=\frac{\mu p}{RT},
\]\nwe obtain

\[
\frac{dp}{dh}=-\rho g=-\frac{\mu g}{RT}p.
\]
\nThis differential equation has the solution

\[
p(h)=p_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{\mu g}{RT}h\right),
\]\nwhere $p_0$ is the pressure at ground level.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{p(h)=p_0\exp\!\left(-\frac{\mu g}{RT}h\right)}

title: BLACK BOX
problem: — Jaan Kalda, Siim Ainsaar. In a black box with three terminals (A, B and C) there is a resistor (resistance $R_{1}$ ), a capacitor (capacitance $C$ ), and a series connection of a battery (electromotive force $\mathcal{E}$ ) with another resistor $(R_{2})$ .

sub_problems.problem:
(2) Measure the electromotive force of the battery, the resistances of the resistors, and the capacitance of the capacitor. Estimate the uncertainties. Always indicate the circuit diagram and the multimeter settings you used for the measurements!

Equipment: black box, multimeter, stopwatch, wires, graph paper.
sub_problems.solution:
Let us identify the terminals as follows: one pair of terminals is connected through the resistor $R_1$, another pair through the series combination of the battery $\mathcal{E}$ and resistor $R_2$, and the third terminal is connected to the capacitor $C$. Since the internal wiring can be arranged in two equivalent ways, the measured values may correspond to either $R_1$ and $R_2$ or be exchanged; here we present one consistent assignment.
\nFirst measure the open-circuit voltage between the terminals that contain the battery branch. This gives the electromotive force directly:
\[
\mathcal{E} \approx 1.57\,\mathrm{V}.
\]
\nNext, fully charge or discharge the capacitor as needed and use the initial currents in two different terminal pairs. When a branch containing a resistor is connected to the battery branch, the initial current is determined by Ohm’s law. Measuring the initial current in one configuration gives
\[\nR_2 = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{I_2} \approx 51\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]\nMeasuring in the other configuration gives
\[\nR_1 = \frac{\mathcal{E}}{I_1} \approx 200\,\mathrm{k}\Omega.
\]
\nTo find the capacitance, use the exponential decay of the current or voltage in the RC circuit. For example, the time for the current to halve satisfies
\[
\frac{I(t_2)}{I(0)} = \frac12 = e^{-t_2/(R_2 C)},
\]\nso that
\[\nC = \frac{t_2}{R_2 \ln 2} \approx 330\,\mathrm{fF}.
\]\nEquivalent methods are to plot the current or voltage on semilogarithmic axes and extract the time constant, or to use the area under the current–time graph.
\nThus the measured parameters are
\[
\boxed{\mathcal{E} \approx 1.57\,\mathrm{V},\quad R_1 \approx 200\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\quad R_2 \approx 51\,\mathrm{k}\Omega,\quad C \approx 330\,\mathrm{fF}}.
\]

title: GRAVITATIONAL RACING
problem:
— Mate Vigh and Jaan Kalda. While in generic case, the dynamics of three gravitationally interacting bodies is complicated and chaotic, there are special cases when the dynamics is regular. In particular, there are cases when bodies perform periodic motion. The simplest case of such periodic motion is when all three bodies, positioned at the vertices of an equilateral triangle, rotate as a rigid body. In what follows we consider a more complicated periodic motion.

Relatively recently ${}^{1}$ ,it was discovered that three equal point masses can move periodically along a common 8-shaped trajectory shown in the figure (arrow denotes the direction of motion). This figure is based on a computer simulation and has a correct shape. If needed, you can measure distances from the enlarged version of the figure (on a separate sheet) using a ruler.

Let us enumerate the three bodies with numbers 1, 2, and 3, according to the order in which they pass the leftmost point $P$ shown in the figure. Let $O_2$ and $O_3$ denote the positions of the bodies 2 and 3, respectively at that moment when the body 1 is passing the middle point $O$ . Similarly, let $P_2$ and $P_3$ denote the positions of the bodies 2 and 3, respectively at that moment when the body 1 is passing the leftmost point $P$ . Let $T$ denote the full period of motion of each of the bodies along this 8-shaped trajectory.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Express the following travel times for one of the bodies: (a) from $O_2$ to $O$ ; (b) from $O_3$ to $P_2$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Because the three equal masses move on the same closed trajectory with equal time shifts, at any instant they are separated by one third of the period, i.e. by \(T/3\) in time along the motion.

(a) The body at \(O_2\) reaches \(O\) after one such time shift, so the travel time from \(O_2\) to \(O\) is
\[
\frac{T}{3}.
\]

(b) By symmetry of the 8-shaped orbit, the motion from \(P\) to \(O\) takes one quarter of the period:
\[P \to O = \frac{T}{4}.
\]
Also, since the bodies are separated by \(T/3\) in time, the travel times \(P_2\to P\) and \(O\to O_3\) are each \(T/3\). Therefore the time from \(P_2\) to \(O_3\) is
\[
\frac{T}{3}+\frac{T}{4}+\frac{T}{3}=\frac{11T}{12}.
\]
Hence the reverse travel time from \(O_3\) to \(P_2\) is
\[T-\frac{11T}{12}=\frac{T}{12}.
\]
Thus the answers are \(\boxed{\frac{T}{3}}\) and \(\boxed{\frac{T}{12}}\).

knowledge_points.description: By symmetry of the 8-shaped trajectory, the travel time from the leftmost point P to the center O is exactly T/4. This is used to segment the orbit into known time intervals.

knowledge_points.description: For periodic motion along a closed trajectory, the sum of the forward travel times from A to B and from B to A equals the period T. This is used to find the reverse travel time from O3 to P2 as T minus the forward time from P2 to O3.

sub_problems.problem:
(2) Let $\vec{v}_1, \vec{v}_2,$ and $\vec{v}_3$ denote the velocities of the three bodies at a certain moment

of time. Write down an equality relating these three vectors to each other.
sub_problems.solution:
Since there are no external forces, the center of mass of the three-body system remains at rest. By symmetry, the center of mass is located at $O$, so if $\vec r_1, \vec r_2, \vec r_3$ are the position vectors of the three bodies measured from $O$, then
\[
\vec r_1+\vec r_2+\vec r_3=0.
\]
Differentiating with respect to time gives
\[
\vec v_1+\vec v_2+\vec v_3=0.
\]
Therefore, the required relation is \boxed{\vec v_1+\vec v_2+\vec v_3=0}.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of linear momentum
knowledge_points.description: In an isolated system with no external forces, total linear momentum (sum of mass times velocity) is constant. Here the motion's symmetry and periodicity imply the constant is zero, yielding v1+v2+v3=0 for equal masses.

knowledge_points.name: center of mass
knowledge_points.description: The center of mass of a system of particles is the mass-weighted average of their positions. For equal masses and symmetric configurations, it coincides with the geometric center, here point O.

knowledge_points.name: three equal masses
knowledge_points.description: The problem states the three bodies are equal point masses, so the mass factors cancel when summing momenta, giving a direct relation among velocities.

knowledge_points.name: no external forces
knowledge_points.description: The three-body system interacts only through mutual gravity; no external forces act, so the system is isolated and its center of mass velocity is constant.

knowledge_points.name: center of mass at rest at O
knowledge_points.description: By the symmetry of the periodic 8-shaped trajectory and equal masses, the center of mass is located at the central point O and is stationary, making the total momentum zero.

sub_problems.guidance:
You have an isolated system of three bodies, so the total linear momentum of the system is conserved (see the discussion of collisions in your reference – momentum conservation is always available when no external forces act). The problem description mentions a special point \(O\) and implies a symmetry that fixes the center of mass at \(O\) (likely the bodies have equal masses and start from rest in a symmetric arrangement).

1. **Locate the center of mass (CM)**  
   In reference section on center of mass coordinates (Kleppner & Kolenkow), you learned that for a two‑particle system one can set the origin at the CM. Then the mass‑weighted position vectors satisfy \(m_1\mathbf{r}_1' + m_2\mathbf{r}_2' = \mathbf{0}\). Extend this to three particles: if \(O\) is the CM and the masses are equal, the **un‑weighted** sum of the position vectors relative to \(O\) is zero at any instant.

2. **Connect position to velocity**  
   Remember that velocity is the time derivative of position. Differentiating the position‑vector relation you just wrote gives a relation among the instantaneous velocities \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\).

3. **Alternatively, use the CM frame directly**  
   From the first reference passage on the center of mass frame (Morin, eqns 4.67–4.68), the CM frame moves such that the total momentum \(\mathbf{P}'\) in that frame is zero. If \(O\) is the CM and the bodies start from rest, the CM frame coincides with the lab frame and remains at rest – therefore the total momentum in the lab frame is also \(\mathbf{0}\).

Write the total momentum \(\mathbf{P} = m_1\mathbf{v}_1 + m_2\mathbf{v}_2 + m_3\mathbf{v}_3\). Since the masses are equal (by the symmetry that places the CM at \(O\) without mass factors), this simplifies to a vector sum involving the velocities.

4. **Write the required equality**  
   Both lines of reasoning lead to the same simple condition. Combine the idea that the CM remains at rest with the definition of the CM’s velocity, or simply differentiate the zero‑sum of position vectors. You should obtain an equation that directly links \(\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\) to one another *without* any masses appearing.

The key is to recognise that if \(O\) is the system’s center of mass and the total momentum is conserved (and initial conditions give zero), the vector sum of the three velocities must be the zero vector. Write down that sum.

history.llm_reason: The guidance explicitly states the final answer by saying "the vector sum of the three velocities must be the zero vector" and instructs the student to "Write down that sum."

sub_problems.problem: (3) Prove that the total angular momentum of this system is zero.
sub_problems.solution:
The total angular momentum is conserved, so it can be evaluated at any convenient instant. Choose the moment when body 1 passes the middle point $O$ of the 8-shaped trajectory.
By the symmetry of the motion at that instant, bodies 2 and 3 are located at opposite positions with equal velocities, so
\[
\vec r_2=-\vec r_3, \qquad \vec v_2=\vec v_3.
\]
The total angular momentum is
\[
\vec J = m\vec r_1\times\vec v_1 + m\vec r_2\times\vec v_2 + m\vec r_3\times\vec v_3.
\]
At the chosen instant, the contribution of body 1 vanishes by symmetry of the configuration about $O$, so
\[
\vec J = m\left(\vec r_2\times\vec v_2 + \vec r_3\times\vec v_3\right).
\]
Using $\vec r_3=-\vec r_2$ and $\vec v_3=\vec v_2$,
\[
\vec J = m\left(\vec r_2\times\vec v_2 + (-\vec r_2)\times\vec v_2\right)=\vec 0.
\]
Therefore, the total angular momentum of the system is zero.

\[
\boxed{\vec J=\vec 0}
\]

knowledge_points.description: Total angular momentum about a point is the vector sum over all particles of r_i × p_i, with p_i = m v_i for a point mass. Used here to write J = m(r1×v1 + r2×v2 + r3×v3).

sub_problems.guidance:
- Start by writing the definition of angular momentum for a single point particle:  
  \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{p} = m\,(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v})\).  
  (This is Eq. (7.1) of Kleppner & Kolenkow or Eq. (6.2) of Morin in your passages.)

- For the three‑body system, the total angular momentum \(\mathbf{J}\) is the vector sum of the individual angular momenta:  
  \(\mathbf{J} = \sum_{i=1}^{3} m\,\mathbf{r}_i \times \mathbf{v}_i\).

- Notice that the system is isolated — no external torques act on it, and the internal forces are central.  
  Therefore angular momentum is conserved, as explained in the Schaum’s passage (“angular momentum is a conserved quantity; changing it requires a net torque”).  
  Because \(\mathbf{J}\) is constant, you may evaluate it at any instant that simplifies the calculation.

- Choose the instant when body 1 passes through the central point \(O\) of its figure‑eight trajectory.  
  At that moment:
  - Body 1 is exactly at \(O\), so its position vector \(\mathbf{r}_1 = \mathbf{0}\); consequently its angular momentum \(\mathbf{L}_1 = m\,\mathbf{r}_1 \times \mathbf{v}_1\) vanishes.
  - By the symmetry of the motion, bodies 2 and 3 occupy opposite positions and have identical velocities. Write this as  
    \(\mathbf{r}_2 = -\mathbf{r}_3\)  and  \(\mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{v}_3\).

- Now express the total angular momentum at that chosen instant, keeping only the contributions of bodies 2 and 3:  
  \(\mathbf{J} = m\,\mathbf{r}_2 \times \mathbf{v}_2 + m\,\mathbf{r}_3 \times \mathbf{v}_3\).

title: SPEED CAMERA
problem: — Mibkel Kree. In this problem, we analyse the working principle of a speed camera. The transmitter of the speed camera emits an electromagnetic wave of frequency $f_0=24\mathrm{GHz}$ having waveform $\cos(2\pi f_0t)$ . The wave gets reflected from an approaching car moving with speed $v$ . The reflected wave is recorded by the receiver of the speed camera.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Express the frequency $f_{1}$ of the reflected wave.
sub_problems.solution:
The Doppler shift must be applied twice: once when the wave reaches the approaching car, and once when the reflected wave returns to the speed camera.
\nThe car first receives the wave with frequency

\[\nf' = f_0\left(1+\frac{v}{c}\right).
\]
\nSince the car reflects the wave, it acts like a moving source emitting this frequency back toward the camera. The camera then receives the reflected wave with frequency

\[\nf_1 = f'\left(1+\frac{v}{c}\right).
\]
\nTherefore,

\[\nf_1 = f_0\left(1+\frac{v}{c}\right)^2.
\]
\nFor \(v \ll c\), this can be approximated as

\[\nf_1 \approx f_0\left(1+\frac{2v}{c}\right).
\]
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{f_1 = f_0\left(1+\frac{v}{c}\right)^2 \approx f_0\left(1+\frac{2v}{c}\right)}\).

knowledge_points.name: speed of light in vacuum
knowledge_points.description: Electromagnetic waves travel at the constant speed c in vacuum, which is used to express the Doppler shift formulas as a function of v/c.

knowledge_points.name: Doppler shift for moving observer
knowledge_points.description: When an observer approaches a stationary source, the observed frequency (non-relativistic limit) is f' = f0(1 + v/c). Used for the car receiving the camera signal.

knowledge_points.name: Doppler shift for moving source
knowledge_points.description: When a source approaches a stationary observer, the observed frequency (non-relativistic limit) is f1 = f'(1 + v/c). Used for the camera receiving the reflected wave from the car.

knowledge_points.name: double Doppler shift for reflection
knowledge_points.description: A wave reflected from a moving object undergoes two Doppler shifts: first when received by the moving object (observer), then when re-emitted back toward the original source (moving source).

knowledge_points.name: non-relativistic speed v << c
knowledge_points.description: The car speed is much less than the speed of light, justifying the use of the simple linear Doppler shift formulas rather than the full relativistic expressions.

knowledge_points.name: binomial expansion for small argument
knowledge_points.description: For |x| << 1, (1+x)^2 ≈ 1+2x is used to simplify the exact expression f0(1+v/c)^2 to the approximate form f0(1+2v/c).

sub_problems.problem: (2) In the speed camera, the received waveform is multiplied with the original emitted waveform. Express all the frequency components present in the multiplied signal.
sub_problems.solution:
Using the trigonometric identity
\[
\cos(2\pi f_1 t)\cos(2\pi f_0 t)=\frac12\cos\bigl(2\pi(f_1+f_0)t\bigr)+\frac12\cos\bigl(2\pi(f_1-f_0)t\bigr),
\]\nthe multiplied signal contains two frequency components: the sum frequency and the difference frequency. Therefore, the frequencies present are \(f_1+f_0\) and \(|f_1-f_0|\). Final answer: \(\boxed{f_1+f_0}\) and \(\boxed{|f_1-f_0|}\).

knowledge_points.name: received waveform form
knowledge_points.description: The received waveform is a cosine wave with frequency f1, as derived in the previous sub-problem, i.e., cos(2π f1 t). This allows the multiplication with the emitted waveform.

knowledge_points.name: cosine product-to-sum identity
knowledge_points.description: The trigonometric identity cos(A)cos(B) = 1/2[cos(A+B) + cos(A-B)] is applied to the product of the two waveforms, yielding sum and difference frequency terms.

knowledge_points.name: frequency of sinusoidal wave
knowledge_points.description: For a waveform of the form cos(2π f t), the frequency is f, read directly from the coefficient of t inside the argument. This is used to identify f1+f0 and f1-f0 as the frequencies present.

knowledge_points.name: positive frequency convention
knowledge_points.description: Frequency components are conventionally expressed as non-negative quantities; therefore the difference frequency is written as |f1-f0|.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recall that a sinusoidal traveling wave (such as the emitted radar signal) can be described by a cosine function of time, as in Griffiths’ Eq. (9.12): \(f(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \text{constant})\).  The frequency \(\nu\) (in Hz) is related to the angular frequency by \(\omega = 2\pi \nu\) (Eqs. 9.10–9.11; also Georgi Eq. 1.13).  Thus you can write the emitted waveform as \(\cos(2\pi f_0 t)\) and the received, Doppler‑shifted waveform as \(\cos(2\pi f_1 t)\) — ignoring amplitude and phase constants, which do not affect the frequency content.

The speed camera multiplies these two signals.  To see what frequencies appear in the product, apply a standard trigonometric identity to the product \(\cos(2\pi f_1 t)\cos(2\pi f_0 t)\).  This identity converts the product into a sum of two cosines: one whose argument contains the sum of the two original frequencies, and one whose argument contains their difference.

Now, using the **positive frequency convention** — that is, expressing oscillation rates as positive numbers — the difference component should be taken as its absolute value.  (The textbook discussion of the sign of \(k\) in forced oscillations, where \(k_r>0\) is chosen, reinforces that frequencies and wave numbers are conventionally non‑negative.)  Therefore, the multiplied signal contains exactly two frequency components: the sum of the original frequencies and the absolute value of their difference.  Write down those two expressions (carry out the algebra yourself) to complete the answer.

sub_problems.problem:
(3) Given the lowest frequency component $f_{\mathrm{low}} =4.8\mathrm{kHz}$ present in the multiplied signal, calculate the speed of the car $v$ . Note: the speed of light $c =3.0\times 10^{8}\mathrm{m / s}$ and the following trigonometric identity might turn to be useful:

$$\cos \alpha \cos \beta = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \cos (\alpha + \beta) + \cos (\alpha - \beta) \right].$$
sub_problems.solution:
For a wave reflected from an approaching car, the reflected frequency is shifted twice by the Doppler effect. For speeds much smaller than the speed of light, the frequency difference between the transmitted and received waves is

\[\nf_{\mathrm{low}} = f_1 - f_0 = \frac{2 f_0 v}{c}.
\]
\nSolving for the car speed gives

\[\nv = \frac{f_{\mathrm{low}}}{2 f_0}c.
\]
\nSubstitute the given values:

\[\nv = \frac{4.8\times 10^3}{2\cdot 24\times 10^9}(3.0\times 10^8)
= 30\ \mathrm{m/s}.
\]
\nTherefore, the speed of the car is \(\boxed{30\ \mathrm{m/s}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Beat frequency extraction from product signal
knowledge_points.description: Using the provided trigonometric identity, the multiplied signal contains sum and difference frequencies; the lowest frequency component is identified as the beat frequency |f1 - f0|.

knowledge_points.name: Radar Doppler frequency shift
knowledge_points.description: For an electromagnetic wave reflected by an approaching target with speed v << c, the frequency difference between the transmitted and received signals is Δf = 2 f0 v / c.

knowledge_points.name: Non-relativistic speed approximation
knowledge_points.description: The car's speed is much smaller than the speed of light, allowing the first-order Doppler approximation to be used.

sub_problems.guidance:
The problem asks you to deduce the car’s speed \(v\) from the lowest frequency component \(f_{\rm low}=4.8\ \text{kHz}\) that appears after mixing (multiplying) the transmitted and reflected waves.  You already have the transmitted frequency \(f_0\) from the earlier parts of the problem, and you are given the speed of light \(c=3.0\times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}\) and the product‑to‑sum trigonometric identity.

1. **Recognise what the mixer output represents**  
   Using the identity  
   \[
   \cos\alpha\,\cos\beta = \frac12\bigl[\cos(\alpha+\beta)+\cos(\alpha-\beta)\bigr],
   \]  
   you should have already found that one of the terms oscillates at the **difference** between the transmitted and received frequencies.  Therefore the given \(f_{\rm low}\) is exactly that difference:  
   \[
   f_{\rm low} = f_{\rm received} - f_0 .
   \]

2. **Approximate the Doppler shift for the reflected wave**  
   The car’s speed is certainly much smaller than the speed of light (a typical highway speed gives \(v/c \ll 10^{-7}\)).  The textbook passages you studied (Kleppner & Kolenkow, and Taylor & Wheeler) make it clear that when \(v \ll c\) the relativistic corrections — which involve terms of order \(v^2/c^2\) — are utterly negligible.  This is the “non‑relativistic speed approximation” you have just learnt.  
   Because the wave undergoes a Doppler shift twice (once when received by the approaching car, and again when reflected back), the received frequency in the non‑relativistic limit is  
   \[
   f_{\rm received} \approx f_0\left(1 + \frac{2v}{c}\right).
   \]

   *(Note: the full relativistic double‑shift formula would be \(f_{\rm received}=f_0\sqrt{\frac{c+v}{c-v}}\); expanding it for \(v\ll c\) gives the same linear term, while the next correction is of order \(v^2/c^2\) — exactly the kind of correction illustrated in the Taylor & Wheeler excerpt with the \(E/m\) expansions.)*

3. **Relate the beat frequency to the speed**  
   Combine the two steps:  
   \[
   f_{\rm low} = f_{\rm received} - f_0 \approx f_0\frac{2v}{c}.
   \]

4. **Solve for \(v\)**  
   From the last expression you can isolate \(v\):  
   \[
   v = \frac{f_{\rm low}}{2f_0}\,c .
   \]  
   Here \(f_{\rm low}\) is given, \(c\) is given, and \(f_0\) is known from the problem setup (the original transmitted radar frequency).  Substitute the numbers — staying aware that \(f_{\rm low}\) is in kHz and \(f_0\) is in GHz — and compute the speed in m/s.  

The method relies entirely on the low‑velocity approximation; the textbook passages assure you that the relativistic corrections are far too tiny to matter for a car’s motion, so the simple linear formula is perfectly adequate.

title: MAGNETIC BILLIARD
problem: — Jaan Kalda. Consider two absolutely elastic dielectric balls of radius $r$ and mass $m$ one of which carries isotropically distributed charge $-q$ , and the other $+q$ . There is so strong homogeneous magnetic field $B$ , parallel to the axis $z$ , that electrostatic interaction of the two charges can be neglected; neglect also gravity and friction forces. The first ball (negatively charged) moves with speed $v$ and collides with the second ball which had been resting at the origin. The collision is central, and immediately before the impact, the velocity of the first ball was parallel to the $x$ -axis.

sub_problems.problem: (1) What is the speed of the second ball immediately after the collision?
sub_problems.solution:
Let the speeds of the two balls immediately after the collision be $v_1$ and $v_2$, respectively. Since the collision is absolutely elastic, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved:

\[
\frac{mv^2}{2}=\frac{mv_1^2}{2}+\frac{mv_2^2}{2},
\]
so
\[
v^2=v_1^2+v_2^2.
\]

Momentum conservation along the line of motion gives
\[
mv=mv_1+mv_2,
\]
so
\[
v=v_1+v_2.
\]

Substitute $v_1=v-v_2$ into the energy equation:
\[
v^2=(v-v_2)^2+v_2^2
= v^2-2vv_2+2v_2^2.
\]
Thus
\[
0=-2vv_2+2v_2^2=2v_2(v_2-v),
\]
so the mathematical possibilities are $v_2=0$ or $v_2=v$.
The solution $v_2=0$ corresponds to no collision, so the physical result is
\[
\boxed{v_2=v}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Elastic collision
knowledge_points.description: A collision in which the total kinetic energy of the system is conserved. The problem states the collision is absolutely elastic, so this conservation law is applied to relate the speeds before and after the impact.

knowledge_points.name: Conservation of momentum
knowledge_points.description: In the absence of net external impulse, the total momentum of a system remains constant. During the instantaneous collision, finite external forces (such as the magnetic Lorentz force) produce negligible impulse, so the momentum of the two-ball system is conserved along the line of impact.

knowledge_points.name: Central collision
knowledge_points.description: The collision is head-on, meaning the velocities before and after are directed along the line connecting the centers (the x-axis). This reduces the problem to one dimension.

knowledge_points.name: Equal masses
knowledge_points.description: Both balls have the same mass m, as given in the problem statement. This simplifies the conservation equations and leads to the velocity exchange result.

knowledge_points.name: Target at rest
knowledge_points.description: The second ball is initially at rest, so its initial velocity is zero. This is a given initial condition.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the speed of the second ball immediately after the collision, approach the problem step by step, grounding each step in the concepts from your textbook:

1. **Identify the type of collision and the relevant conservation laws.**  
   The problem describes an *elastic* collision (kinetic energy is unchanged, like the spring-equipped riders on the linear air track in [Kleppner & Kolenkow 6.5.2]), and the motion is one‑dimensional (a *central collision* [Kleppner & Kolenkow 6.5.3]). Because the collision is elastic, both **momentum** and **kinetic energy** are conserved. Momentum conservation follows from Newton’s second and third laws, as discussed in [Morin 4.5.1]; the total momentum of the isolated two‑ball system before the collision equals the total momentum after.

2. **Set up the conservation equations for this one‑dimensional, two‑body collision.**  
   Following the general forms in [Kleppner & Kolenkow 6.5.3] (with \(Q = 0\) for an elastic collision), you will write:

   - Momentum conservation: \((m)v = (m)v_1 + (m)v_2\), where \(v\) is the initial speed of the striking ball, and \(v_1, v_2\) are the final speeds of the first and second ball.
   - Kinetic energy conservation: \(\frac12 m v^{2} = \frac12 m v_1^{2} + \frac12 m v_2^{2}\).

3. **Simplify using the fact that the two balls have equal masses.**  
   Because the masses are identical, you can cancel \(m\) from the momentum equation and both \(\frac12\) and \(m\) from the energy equation. This will give you two simple algebraic relations connecting \(v, v_1,\) and \(v_2\). (The situation is exactly the same as the equal‑mass riders fitted with springs in [Kleppner & Kolenkow 6.5.2], so you already have an intuition for what should happen.)

4. **Solve for the unknown speed \(v_2\).**  
   - From the simplified momentum relation, express \(v_1\) in terms of \(v\) and \(v_2\).  
   - Substitute that expression into the simplified energy equation.  
   - Simplify the result; you should obtain a quadratic equation in \(v_2\).  
   - Solve the quadratic. You will find two mathematical solutions.

5. **Select the physically meaningful solution.**  
   One root corresponds to \(v_2 = 0\). This would mean no change occurred—the balls never interacted. Since the problem describes a real collision, discard that root. The other root gives the actual speed of the second ball after the elastic collision.

6. **Check consistency with what you know.**  
   Compare the final result you derived with the outcome of the equal‑mass, elastic air‑track experiment described in the textbook. If your derivation is correct, they should agree.

sub_problems.problem: (2) Sketch the trajectories of the centres of the both balls during the subsequent motion.
sub_problems.solution:
In a uniform magnetic field a charged ball experiences only the Lorentz force, so between collisions each ball moves in a circle. For speed \(v\) the magnetic force provides the centripetal force:
\[
\frac{mv^2}{R}=qvB,
\]
so the cyclotron radius and angular speed are
\[
R=\frac{mv}{qB},\qquad \omega=\frac{v}{R}=\frac{qB}{m}.
\]
Since the two balls carry opposite charges, their circular motions are in opposite senses.
The collision is central and elastic, and the masses are equal, so the two balls exchange velocities. Therefore, immediately after a collision the ball that was moving stops, while the other ball leaves with speed \(v\) along the same line.
After that, the moving ball again follows a circular arc of radius \(R\), but because its charge has the opposite sign, the curvature is opposite to that of the other ball. When it meets the resting ball again, the velocities are exchanged once more. Repeating this gives a sequence of circular arcs of the same radius, with opposite senses of rotation for the two charges.
Thus the centres move along alternating cyclotron arcs, and the successive collision points are shifted so that the pair drifts in one direction (along the initial direction of motion). The sketch is therefore a chain of equal-radius arcs for the two balls, winding in opposite senses and translated step by step.
Final answer: 
\boxed{\text{The centres follow alternating circular arcs of radius }R=\frac{mv}{qB}\text{ in opposite senses, with successive collisions producing a drift of the pair.}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{The centres follow alternating circular arcs of radius }R=\frac{mv}{qB}\text{ in opposite senses, with successive collisions producing a drift of the pair.}}

knowledge_points.name: velocity exchange in elastic collision of equal masses
knowledge_points.description: In a central elastic collision between two particles of equal mass, the particles exchange their velocities: the incoming particle stops and the target moves with the incoming velocity. This governs the state after each collision.

knowledge_points.name: central collision

knowledge_points.name: only Lorentz force acts

   The balls are identical and collide head‑on (central collision).  
   • Use the result for elastic collisions of equal masses given in your reference: when one mass is initially at rest and the other approaches, the incident mass stops and the target mass moves off with the same speed and direction (Kleppner & Kolenkow 6.5.2 or Taylor & Wheeler 8.2).

sub_problems.problem:
(4) Consider the same situation as before, except that the three differences in the assumptions: the both balls have now identical positive charge $+q$ ; electrostatic repulsion between the balls is no longer negligible; the collision is not necessarily central (but the balls move still at the same value of $z$ so that the collision will not induce any motion in the direction of the $z$ -axis). Let $P_{i}$ denote the point where the surfaces of the two balls are in contact during the $i$ -th collision. What is the maximal distance between $P_{i}$ and $P_{j}$ (maximize over all the values $i,j =1,\ldots ,\infty$ , and over all the impact parameters of the collisions for fixed values of $B$ ,

$m$ ,and $q)$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
Let the balls have velocities \(\vec v_1\) and \(\vec v_2\). The total external force on the two-ball system is the sum of the magnetic forces, while the electrostatic and elastic forces are internal and cancel in the equation for the center of mass (CM):

\[
2m\,\dot{\vec v}_{\rm CM}=q\vec v_1\times\vec B+q\vec v_2\times\vec B
= q(\vec v_1+\vec v_2)\times\vec B
=2q\,\vec v_{\rm CM}\times\vec B.
\]
Hence
\[
m\,\dot{\vec v}_{\rm CM}=q\,\vec v_{\rm CM}\times\vec B,
\]
so the CM moves in a circle in the plane perpendicular to \(\vec B\) with cyclotron radius
\[
R=\frac{m v_{\rm CM}}{qB}.
\]

Initially one ball moves with speed \(v\) and the other is at rest, so
\[
v_{\rm CM}=\frac{v}{2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
R=\frac{m v}{2qB}.
\]

For two identical balls, the contact point \(P_i\) in a collision is the midpoint of the centers, so it coincides with the CM position at that moment. Thus all contact points lie on the same circle of radius \(R\). The largest possible distance between any two such points is the diameter of this circle:
\[
\max_{i,j}|P_iP_j|=2R=\frac{mv}{qB}.
\]

Therefore the maximal distance is \(\boxed{\frac{mv}{qB}}\).

knowledge_points.name: Center-of-mass motion theorem
knowledge_points.description: The center of mass of a system moves as a point particle with mass equal to the total mass, acted upon by the net external force. Internal forces (here electrostatic repulsion and elastic collision forces) cancel and do not affect the CM acceleration. Used to derive the equation of motion for the CM.

knowledge_points.name: Cyclotron radius formula
knowledge_points.description: A particle of mass m and charge q moving with speed v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B undergoes uniform circular motion with radius R = mv/(qB). Applied to the CM after obtaining m a_CM = q v_CM × B.

knowledge_points.name: Center of mass velocity for equal masses
knowledge_points.description: For two particles of equal mass, the velocity of the center of mass is the average of their individual velocities: v_CM = (v1 + v2)/2. Used to find the initial CM speed v_CM = v/2 from the given initial velocities.

knowledge_points.name: Contact point of identical spheres
knowledge_points.description: For two identical spheres, the point of contact during a collision is the midpoint of their centers. Since the system's center of mass is also the midpoint (equal masses), the contact point P_i coincides with the CM position at that instant.

knowledge_points.name: Motion perpendicular to magnetic field
knowledge_points.description: The balls move at constant z (no motion along the magnetic field direction), so their velocities are always perpendicular to B. This ensures the cyclotron formula applies and the CM trajectory is a circle in the plane perpendicular to B.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the system and the forces. The two balls each carry charge \(+q\) and move in a uniform magnetic field \(B\). They interact via electrostatic repulsion and occasional elastic collisions, but both of these are internal forces. The only external force on the system is the magnetic (Lorentz) force. According to the center-of-mass motion theorem in reference, the motion of the center of mass behaves as if all the mass were concentrated there and only external forces act. Therefore, you can write the equation of motion for the center of mass using the total external force.

Apply the Lorentz force to each ball (reference introduces the magnetic force on a moving charge as \(\mathbf{F}_B = q \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{B}\)). Sum these forces to find the net external force on the system. Because the two balls have identical mass \(m\) and charge \(+q\), the sum simplifies to an expression involving the center-of-mass velocity. This will show that the center of mass obeys the same equation as a single particle of mass \(2m\) and charge \(2q\) in the magnetic field, or equivalently a single particle of mass \(m\) and charge \(q\) with the same velocity.

From the initial condition (one ball moving with speed \(v\), the other at rest), use the definition of center of mass velocity for equal masses (as in the worked example with two identical blocks) to find the initial speed of the center of mass. The center of mass then undergoes uniform circular motion in the plane perpendicular to \(\mathbf{B}\) with a cyclotron radius you can determine from the single-particle analogy.

Now relate the contact points \(P_i\) to the center of mass. The problem states the balls move at the same \(z\) so the collision is in the plane. The point \(P_i\) is where the surfaces touch. For identical balls, this contact point lies exactly halfway between their centers—which is precisely the location of the center of mass at that instant, as shown by the center-of-mass coordinate definition for equal masses (the worked example explicitly shows \(\mathbf{R} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{r}_a + \mathbf{r}_b)\)). Thus every collision point \(P_i\) is a point on the circular trajectory of the center of mass.

To maximize the distance between any two such points over all collisions and impact parameters, consider the geometry of that circle. The greatest possible separation between two points on a circle is its diameter. Therefore, the maximal distance is twice the cyclotron radius you computed. Substitute the center-of-mass speed into the radius formula, simplify, and you will obtain the answer in terms of \(m\), \(v\), \(q\), and \(B\).
