sub_problems.problem:
(3) Under the assumptions of the previous task, what is the speed of the ball $A$ at the moment $t = T$ ?
(iv) Now, at $t =0$ , the string forms a very small angle $\phi$ with the $x$ -axis. Similarly to the previous two tasks, at the moment $t = T'$ when the ball $A$ reaches $x = L$ , the string is parallel to the $x$ -axis. Find the string length $l$ assuming that $l > L$ . The answer to

this point should contain only $L$ and numerical constants.
sub_problems.solution:
Because the string is non-stretchable, and at the moment \(t=T\) it is parallel to the \(x\)-axis, the two balls must have the same \(x\)-coordinate. Since the string is still taut, their velocities must also be equal at that instant, so both balls move with the same speed \(v\).

The electric field does work only on the charges inside \(0<x<L\). Over the motion from the initial state to the moment \(t=T\), the total work done by the field is
\[W = 2qE_0L,\]
because each ball gains electric potential energy corresponding to traversing the field region of length \(L\).

Initially the kinetic energy is negligible compared with the gained energy, so energy conservation gives
\[2\cdot \frac12 mv^2 = 2qE_0L.\]
Thus
\[mv^2 = qE_0L,\]
so the speed of ball \(A\) at \(t=T\) is
\[\boxed{v=\sqrt{\frac{qE_0L}{m}}}.\]

knowledge_points.name: inextensible string constraint
knowledge_points.description: For a taut, inextensible string, the velocity components of the two ends along the string must be equal. At t=T the string is parallel to the x-axis, so both balls have the same x-velocity.

knowledge_points.name: work done by uniform electric field
knowledge_points.description: The work done on a charge q moving a distance d parallel to a uniform electric field E is W = qEd. Here each ball moves L inside the field, so work per ball is qE_0 L.

knowledge_points.name: work-energy theorem
knowledge_points.description: The net work done on a system equals the change in its kinetic energy. The total work 2qE_0 L is converted into kinetic energy of the two balls.

knowledge_points.name: negligible initial kinetic energy
knowledge_points.description: The initial speed v0 is very small compared to sqrt(qE_0 L/m), so the initial kinetic energy can be neglected relative to the work done by the field.

knowledge_points.name: each ball traverses full field length
knowledge_points.description: Due to the geometry and the condition that at t=T ball A is at x=L and the string is parallel to the x-axis, both balls have moved from x=0 to x=L inside the field region, so each traverses a distance L in the field.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the speed of ball \(A\) at the moment \(t=T\), you need to connect the work done by the electric field to the kinetic energy of the system.

First, think about the motion constraint from the inextensible string. The textbook passages on string constraints show that when a string does not stretch, connected objects must have the same acceleration (or, in certain configurations, related speeds). At the moment described, the string is parallel to the \(x\)-axis and taut. Use the idea from the worked example of the string pulling a block (Kleppner & Kolenkow, 3.4.2) and the pulley example (Morin, 2.2) to deduce the relationship between the velocities of ball \(A\) and ball \(B\) at \(t=T\). Because the string is taut and horizontal, what must be true about their \(x\)-components of velocity?

Next, consider energy. The problem states that the initial kinetic energy is negligible. The textbook example of the bead on a hoop (Kleppner & Kolenkow, 5.5) shows exactly how to handle a situation where an object starts with negligible speed: you set initial kinetic energy to zero and equate the final kinetic energy to the work done by forces, or to the change in potential energy.

The force doing work here is the uniform electric field. The Purcell & Morin passage (2.2) explains that the work per unit charge done by an external agency in moving a charge through a potential difference is related to the field. For a uniform field, the work done on a charge \(q\) moving a distance along the field is simply the force \(qE_0\) times the distance. Identify the total distance over which the electric field does work on each ball from the initial state until \(t=T\). This total work is the energy input to the system.

Now apply the work-energy theorem. The Kleppner & Kolenkow passage (5.3.5) states that the net work on a system equals its change in kinetic energy. Here, the electric force is an external force doing work on the system of the two balls. So, set the total work done by the field equal to the total final kinetic energy of the system (since initial kinetic energy is zero). Express this kinetic energy in terms of the speed of ball \(A\) at \(t=T\), using the constraint relationship you found earlier.

Finally, solve the energy equation for the speed of ball \(A\). The result will involve the given quantities \(q\), \(E_0\), \(L\), and \(m\).

For the second part (finding the string length \(l\) when the string starts at a small angle \(\phi\) and is parallel to the \(x\)-axis when ball \(A\) reaches \(x=L\)), you will apply the same principles—work, constraint, and energy—but now the geometry of the string’s initial angle introduces a dependence on \(l\). Use energy conservation again, but this time the work done by the field may depend on the path lengths, and the constraint will relate the motions of the balls in a way that involves \(l\). The goal is to isolate \(l\) in terms of \(L\) and numerical constants only.

title: SURFACE TENSION
problem:
- Jaan Kalda, Eero Uustalu.

Tools: a syringe, a small glass plate, a support for holding the glass plate horizontally at an adjustable height, a cup with water (coefficient of refraction of water $n_w =1.33$ ), a caliper, a sheet of graph paper. Your working room has ceiling lights at an approximate height of $3\mathrm{m}$ . The glass plate holder is a short piece of plastic pipe with a nut; put the glass plate on top of the nut and turn the nut to adjust the height. By turning the nut, one can change the holder height only by the thickness of the nut; there are also spare nuts that can be stacked to increase the total height of the pipe-nuts system, and a cap that fits into the pipe - use it if there is a need to make the distance between the glass plate and the surface beneath it smaller than the height of the pipe. NB! Hold the glass plate only from its matte part and do not touch the glossy (transparent) part as fingerprints will affect the value of the contact angle. If you accidentally do touch, ask organisers to clean the glass surface.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Put a small drop of water onto the glass plate; this will form a plano-convex lens. Determine the focal length of this lens and measure its diameter.
sub_problems.solution:
A small water drop on the glass plate acts as a plano-convex lens. To find its focal length, adjust the height of the glass-plate holder until a sharp image of the ceiling lights is formed on a screen below the lens, for example on a sheet of paper or on the surface of the cap inside the holder. The distance from the lens to the screen at sharp focus is the focal length. Since the ceiling lights are far away compared with the focal length, the incoming light can be treated as approximately parallel.
\nMeasure the focal-plane height with a caliper for good accuracy. The drop diameter can be measured either directly with the caliper or, more conveniently, by placing the glass plate on graph paper and reading the diameter from the millimeter grid.
\nA representative result is
\[
 f \approx 15.9\,\mathrm{mm}, \qquad d \approx 5.8\,\mathrm{mm}.
\]\nThus the lens has focal length \(\boxed{15.9\,\mathrm{mm}}\) and diameter \(\boxed{5.8\,\mathrm{mm}}\).

knowledge_points.name: plano-convex lens
knowledge_points.description: A lens with one flat and one convex surface that converges light. A small water drop on a glass plate naturally forms such a lens due to surface tension.

knowledge_points.name: focal length of a converging lens
knowledge_points.description: The distance from the lens to its focal point, where rays parallel to the optical axis converge to form a real image. For a thin lens, this is a fixed property.

knowledge_points.name: distant object approximation
knowledge_points.description: When an object is much farther from the lens than the focal length, light rays from a point on the object are approximately parallel when they reach the lens. The ceiling lights (at ~3 m) satisfy this condition for a small drop lens.

knowledge_points.name: focal length measurement by distant object method
knowledge_points.description: To measure the focal length of a converging lens, place a screen behind it and adjust the lens-screen distance until a sharp image of a distant object is formed. That distance equals the focal length because the object is effectively at infinity.

sub_problems.guidance:
To determine the focal length of the water-drop plano-convex lens, you will rely directly on the thin-lens formula given in your textbook (Equation 11.153):

\[
\frac{1}{d_1} + \frac{1}{d_2} = \frac{1}{f}
\]

where \(d_1\) is the distance from the object to the lens, \(d_2\) the distance from the lens to the image, and \(f\) the focal length. For a very distant object, such as ceiling lights, the incoming rays are essentially parallel, so \(d_1\) can be treated as infinite (or so large that \(\frac{1}{d_1}\approx 0\)). The formula then simplifies to \(d_2 \approx f\). This is the experimental principle: when you adjust the height of the glass plate to produce a sharp image of the overhead lights on a screen below, the measured distance from the lens to the screen is the focal length you seek.

Now carry out the measurement:
- Place a smooth screen (e.g., a sheet of paper) below the water drop.  
- Slowly change the vertical separation between the drop and the screen until a crisp image of the ceiling lights appears.  
- At that position, measure the perpendicular distance from the centre of the drop (where the lens is located) down to the screen. Because the lens is extremely thin, the small-angle approximations from the textbook (e.g., \( \sin\theta \approx \theta\)) remain valid, and the image distance indeed corresponds to \(f\). Use a caliper to obtain a precise reading.

To find the diameter of the drop, you have two straightforward options:
- Measure its lateral extent directly with the caliper, or  
- Place the glass plate on graph paper and read the diameter against the millimetre grid.

Record both quantities. The procedure is grounded in the lens behaviour described in Section 11.6: the water droplet forms a plano-convex lens because it is flat on one side (the glass plate) and curved on the other, similar to the geometry of Figure 11.27. There, the angular deflection is proportional to the distance from the axis, ultimately leading to the thin-lens formula used above. No radius-of-curvature calculation is required; you simply measure the focal length by letting the distant object set \(d_1\to\infty\).

kp_used: focal length of a converging lens

sub_problems.problem: (2) Calculate the curvature radius of the water surface and the water-glass contact angle $\alpha$ . The contact angle is defined as the angle under which the water surface (the air-water interface) meets the surface of the glass plate.
sub_problems.solution:
The curved water surface acts as a thin plano-convex lens in air. For a lens with one flat side and radius of curvature $R$ on the other side, the lensmaker’s formula gives
\[
\frac{1}{f}=(n_w-1)\frac{1}{R}.
\]\nHence
\[\nR=f(n_w-1).
\]\nUsing the measured focal length from the setup, this gives
\[\nR\approx 5.3\,\mathrm{mm}.
\]
\nTo find the contact angle, use the geometry of the spherical surface. If $d$ is the measured diameter of the circular contact region, then the radius to the contact point satisfies
\[
\cos(90^\circ-\alpha)=\frac{d}{2R}.
\]\nTherefore
\[
\alpha=90^\circ-\arccos\!\left(\frac{d}{2R}\right).
\]\nSubstituting the measured values yields
\[
\alpha\approx 33.2^\circ.
\]
\nFinal answer: $\boxed{R\approx 5.3\,\mathrm{mm}},\; \boxed{\alpha\approx 33.2^\circ}$

knowledge_points.name: Lensmaker's formula for plano-convex lens
knowledge_points.description: For a thin plano-convex lens in air, the focal length f, refractive index n, and radius of curvature R of the curved surface are related by 1/f = (n - 1)/R. Used to calculate R from the measured f and given n_w.

knowledge_points.name: Spherical cap contact angle geometry
knowledge_points.description: For a spherical drop, the contact angle α, the radius of curvature R, and the contact diameter d satisfy sin α = (d/2)/R (or equivalently cos(90°-α) = d/(2R)). This geometric relation is used to find α from the measured d and calculated R.

knowledge_points.name: Spherical drop shape
knowledge_points.description: The water drop is assumed to form a spherical cap, meaning its curved surface is a section of a sphere. This is implied by the 'plano-convex lens' description and is necessary to assign a single radius of curvature R and to apply the spherical geometry for the contact angle.

knowledge_points.name: Thin lens approximation
knowledge_points.description: The water drop lens is treated as a thin lens, allowing the use of the thin-lens form of the lensmaker's formula, which neglects the lens thickness.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, treat the curved water surface as a thin plano‑convex lens. The water sits on the flat glass plate, so one side of this water lens is flat and the other side is the curved water‑air interface. For a thin lens the lens‑maker’s formula (11.150) tells you

\[
\frac{1}{f} = (n-1)\left(\frac{1}{r_1} + \frac{1}{r_2}\right),
\]

where \(f\) is the focal length, \(n\) is the refractive index of the lens material (here water, \(n_w \approx 1.33\)), and \(r_1, r_2\) are the radii of curvature of the two surfaces. For a plano‑convex lens the flat surface has an infinite radius, so the corresponding \(1/r\) term is zero. Apply the formula to the water lens by setting one radius to infinity and the other to the unknown curvature radius \(R\) of the water‑air interface. That will give you \(1/f\) expressed in terms of \(R\) and \(n_w\). Solve for \(R\); the result involves only the measured focal length and the known refractive index of water.

Second, explain why the interface can be considered part of a sphere. The textbook discussion of water droplets (Section 11.5.2, “Gravity versus Surface Tension”) shows that for small dimensions surface tension dominates gravity, so a tiny drop is nearly spherical. The water meniscus at the edge of the glass therefore forms a spherical cap. This is the same “spherical drop shape” idea that allows you to treat the curved surface as part of a sphere of radius \(R\).

Finally, connect the geometry of the spherical cap to the contact angle \(\alpha\). The contact angle is the angle that the water surface makes with the glass plate. Equivalently, because the water surface is locally perpendicular to the sphere’s radius at the contact point, the angle between that radius and the normal to the glass (the vertical) is exactly \(\alpha\). Draw the cross‑section:
- Mark the centre of curvature \(C\) on the symmetry axis above the glass.
- Draw the radius \(R\) from \(C\) to a point on the circular contact line.
- The glass plate is horizontal, so the vertical line through \(C\) is perpendicular to it.
- The horizontal leg from the axis to the contact point is half the measured diameter of the wetted area, \(d/2\).

In the right triangle formed by the vertical, the horizontal, and the slant radius \(R\), the angle at \(C\) between the vertical and the radius is \(\alpha\) (because the normal to the surface meets the plate’s normal at that angle). Thus

\[
\sin\alpha = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{d/2}{R}.
\]

From this you can obtain \(\alpha\) using your measurement of \(d\) and the \(R\) you calculated in the first step. (The reference solution uses an equivalent form \(\alpha = 90^\circ - \arccos(d/(2R))\), which follows from \(\cos(90^\circ-\alpha)=\sin\alpha\).)

Carry out the two calculations with your measured values for \(f\) and \(d\); the lens‑maker’s formula will give you \(R\), and the spherical‑cap geometry will then give you \(\alpha\).

sub_problems.problem: (3) Now increase the amount of water on the glass plate so that it covers a big part of the glass plate so that its top surface becomes almost flat. Determine the thickness of the water layer.
sub_problems.solution:
Increase the area covered by water as much as possible so that edge effects are minimized. It is enough that the water almost fills the glossy part of the glass plate, but it should not extend over the whole perimeter of the plate, otherwise the surface near the edge can be distorted and the layer becomes effectively thicker.
\nMeasure the water volume and the area of the wetted part of the plate. Here the water volume is
\[\nV = 2.00\,\mathrm{ml}=2.00\,\mathrm{cm}^3,
\]\nand the covered area is
\[\nA = 12.7\,\mathrm{cm}^2.
\]\nThe thickness of the water layer is then
\[\nt=\frac{V}{A}.
\]\nThus
\[\nt=\frac{2.00\,\mathrm{cm}^3}{12.7\,\mathrm{cm}^2}\approx 0.157\,\mathrm{cm}=1.57\,\mathrm{mm}.
\]\nTherefore the thickness of the water layer is \(\boxed{1.57\,\mathrm{mm}}\).

knowledge_points.name: flat top surface
knowledge_points.description: The water layer is assumed to have an almost flat top surface, so its thickness is uniform and edge curvature does not dominate the volume‑area relationship.

knowledge_points.name: negligible edge effects
knowledge_points.description: By covering a large area of the plate, meniscus curvature at the perimeter is assumed to contribute negligibly to the average thickness, allowing a simple geometric calculation.

knowledge_points.name: volume‑area‑thickness relation
knowledge_points.description: For a layer of uniform thickness t, the volume V is the product of wetted area A and thickness, so t = V/A. This directly yields the water layer thickness from the measured volume and area.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, ensure that the water on the glass plate is spread to cover a large part of the plate so that the top surface becomes nearly flat, as the problem describes. This gives the water layer the geometry of a thin, uniform slab, which matches the models presented in your textbook readings.

Next, measure two quantities:
- the volume of water you placed on the plate,
- the area of the wetted region (the part of the plate covered by the water).

Now, relate these to the thickness. In the Kleppner & Kolenkow passage, the volume of a small rectangular element of a thin uniform plate is written as \(\Delta V = t\,\Delta x\,\Delta y\), and for the whole plate the total volume is \(V = A t\), where \(A\) is the area of the plate and \(t\) is its constant thickness. The same idea appears in the Blundell & Blundell passage: a thin slab of gas is characterized by a thickness \(\mathrm{d}z\) and an area \(A\), so the volume of that slab is \(A\,\mathrm{d}z\). In both cases, the volume equals area times thickness for a thin, flat object.

Your water layer, being thin and nearly flat, obeys the same relation. Therefore, you can find the thickness by rearranging the volume–area–thickness formula:

\[
\text{thickness} = \frac{\text{volume}}{\text{area}}.
\]

Insert your measured volume and area into this expression. Perform the division (using consistent units, such as cm³ for volume and cm² for area to get the thickness in cm), and you will obtain the thickness of the water layer.

sub_problems.problem: (4) Calculate the surface tension of water $\sigma$ . Hint: a given amount of water takes a shape which minimises its total potential energy. Use reasonable approximations. Keep in mind that the glass-water interface makes also a certain contribution $U_{gw}$ to the full surface energy, the magnitude of which is related to the contact angle: $U_{gw} = -\sigma \cos \alpha A$ , where $A$ denotes the surface area of the glass-water interface.
sub_problems.solution:
Let the water layer have area $A$ and thickness $t$, so that its volume is $V = At$. The total energy consists of three parts:

1. Surface energy of the water-air interface: $\sigma A$.
2. Contribution from the glass-water interface: $U_{gw} = -\sigma \cos\alpha\, A$.
3. Gravitational potential energy of the water layer: since its center of mass is at height $t/2$, this is $\frac12 V\rho g t$.
\nThus
\[\nU = \sigma A(1-\cos\alpha) + \frac12 V\rho g t.
\]\nUsing $A = V/t$, we get
\[\nU = V\left(\sigma\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{t} + \frac{\rho g t}{2}\right).
\]\nFor fixed $V$, equilibrium corresponds to minimum $U$, so
\[
\frac{\mathrm dU}{\mathrm dt}=0.
\]\nThis gives
\[
-\sigma\frac{1-\cos\alpha}{t^2} + \frac{\rho g}{2} = 0,
\]\nso
\[
\sigma = \frac{\rho g t^2}{2(1-\cos\alpha)}.
\]\nSubstituting the measured values from the experiment yields
\[
\boxed{\sigma \approx 0.077\ \mathrm{N/m}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: surface tension
knowledge_points.description: The energy per unit area of a liquid surface; needed to express the energy of the water-air interface as σA.

knowledge_points.name: glass-water interface energy
knowledge_points.description: The energy contribution from the glass-water interface is given by U_gw = -σ cos α A, as stated in the problem hint.

knowledge_points.name: gravitational potential energy
knowledge_points.description: The potential energy of the water layer in the Earth's gravity field, calculated as mgh with center of mass at height t/2.

knowledge_points.name: energy minimization
knowledge_points.description: The equilibrium shape minimizes total potential energy; setting dU/dt = 0 yields the condition for surface tension.

knowledge_points.name: uniform water layer
knowledge_points.description: The water layer is assumed to have constant thickness t and area A, so volume V = A t, and the top surface is nearly flat.

knowledge_points.name: constant water volume
knowledge_points.description: The volume V of the water drop is fixed during the energy minimization, allowing substitution A = V/t.

sub_problems.guidance:
To solve this problem, you need to combine three energy contributions for a water layer of fixed volume, then minimize the total energy with respect to the layer’s thickness.

**Step 1 – Express the geometry and gravitational potential energy.**  
Assume the water forms a uniform layer of area \(A\) and small thickness \(t\), so its volume is \(V = At\) (fixed). The center of mass of this layer is at a height \(t/2\) above the glass. From your reference, recall that for a mass \(m\) in a uniform gravitational field, the gravitational potential energy is \(mgh\). Here, the mass is \(\rho V\) (density × volume), and the height is \(t/2\). Write down \(U_g\) in terms of \(V, \rho, g, t\).

**Step 2 – Write the surface energy contributions.**  
There are two surface terms:  
- The water–air interface has area \(A\) and, according to the surface tension concept in reference, its energy is \(\sigma A\) (see reference.15, where work to change area is \(\gamma\,dA\)).  
- The glass–water interface contributes \(U_{gw} = -\sigma\cos\alpha\,A\), as given in the problem.

Combine these to get the total surface energy in terms of \(\sigma, A,\) and \(\cos\alpha\).

**Step 3 – Build the total energy as a function of thickness.**  
Add the gravitational term from Step 1 to the surface terms from Step 2. Then use \(A = V/t\) to express the total energy \(U\) entirely in terms of the fixed volume \(V\), the variable thickness \(t\), and the constants \(\sigma, \rho, g, \alpha\).

**Step 4 – Minimize the total energy.**  
The problem states that the water takes the shape that minimizes its total potential energy. This is the same principle used in reference to find the most stable size of an atom: differentiate the total energy with respect to the variable (here \(t\)) and set the derivative to zero.  
- Differentiate your expression for \(U(t)\) with respect to \(t\).  
- Set \(dU/dt = 0\) and solve for \(\sigma\).

You will obtain a formula for \(\sigma\) in terms of \(\rho, g, t,\) and \(\alpha\). This is the equation you need.

**Step 5 – Interpret and use the result.**  
The resulting expression shows how the surface tension can be determined from the equilibrium thickness, the contact angle, and known constants. If you have measured values for \(t\) and \(\alpha\) from an experiment, substitute them (along with \(\rho\) and \(g\)) to find the numerical value of \(\sigma\). The calculation is straightforward algebra once you have the correct formula.

history.llm_reason: The guidance reveals the key algebraic isolation by instructing to solve for σ after differentiation, which is the decisive step the student should perform themselves.

title: OKLO FISSION REACTOR
problem:
Topi Loytainen, Jaan Kalda. Based on the ratio of the uranium isotopes $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ , as well as the abundances of the isotopes produced by nuclear reactors, researchers have established that self-sustaining natural nuclear reactors operated in Oklo ca $T_{0} =1.8 \times 10^{9}$ years ago in Gabon, central Africa. For such reactors to exist, two conditions must be met: (a) presence of deposits with high enough concentration of uranium; (b) sufficiently high abundance of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ in natural uranium. Rich uranium ores were created by floods: scattered uranium was dissolved in oxygen-rich water and transported by it to underground pools. Significant concentration of oxygen appeared in the atmosphere only around 2.5 billion years ago, so the first condition was not met earlier than that. You will learn below that the abundance of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ decreases relatively fast in time,

so the second condition ceased to be satisfied soon after the operation of Oklo's reactor.

What made the operation of Oklo's reactor possible was a stable influx of ground water that kept the uranium deposits sufficiently wet. Water is the so-called moderator for the fission reactor: it slows down neutrons emerging from fission reactions, dramatically enhancing the chances of a neutron triggering the fission of a next $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nucleus.

In what follows, in addition to $T_{0}$ you can use the following numerical values. Energy released by the fission of a single $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ nucleus: $E_0=200\mathrm{MeV}$ . Half-life of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ : $\tau_{5} \approx 7 \times 10^{8}$ years. Half-life of $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ : $\tau_{8} \approx 4.5 \times 10^{9}$ years. Latent heat of evaporation of water: $L =2260\mathrm{kJkg^{-1}}$ .

Specific heat of water $c =4200 \, \mathrm{J} \, \mathrm{kg}^{-1} \, \mathrm{K}^{-1}$ . Abundance of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ in natural uranium today: $R =0.72\%$ . We define abundance as the number of atoms of the isotope, normalized to the number of atoms of the given element.

Average abundance of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ in the uranium from Oklo's uranium ore today: $R_O =0.62\%$ . The total amount of uranium in Oklo's mine today: $M =5 \times 10^{8}\mathrm{kg}$ .

The duration of the time period over which Oklo's reactor operated: $T\approx 1\times 10^{5}$ year.
Elementary charge: $e =1.6\times 10^{-19}\mathrm{C}$ Atomic mass unit: $u =1.66\times 10^{-27}\mathrm{kg}$

Avogadro's number: $N_{A}$ 6.02 × 10 $^{23}$ mol $^{-1}$ .

Note that: (a) the abundance of other isotopes of uranium besides $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ and $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ is negligibly small; (b) $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ is not among the decay products of $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ ; and (c) fission channels other than the fission of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ (e.g., synthesis and fission of plutonium) can be neglected.

sub_problems.problem: (1) What was the abundance of $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ in natural uranium when the Oklo's reactor operated?
sub_problems.solution:
Radioactive decay is exponential. For isotope $i$ with half-life \(\tau_i\), the number of atoms after time \(T_0\) satisfies
\[\nN_i(T_0)=N_i(0)\,2^{-T_0/\tau_i}.
\]\nTherefore, going backward in time by \(T_0\), the amount of each isotope was larger by the factor
\[
2^{T_0/\tau_i}.
\]
\nLet today’s natural uranium have abundances
\[\nR=\frac{N_5}{N_5+N_8},\qquad 1-R=\frac{N_8}{N_5+N_8}.
\]\nThus
\[
\frac{N_5}{N_8}=\frac{R}{1-R}.
\]
\nAt the time when Oklo’s reactor operated, the isotope numbers were
\[\nN_5' = N_5\,2^{T_0/\tau_5},\qquad N_8' = N_8\,2^{T_0/\tau_8}.
\]\nSo the abundance of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) then was
\[\nR_O^{(\text{then})}=\frac{N_5'}{N_5'+N_8'}
=\frac{\frac{N_5}{N_8}2^{T_0/\tau_5}}{\frac{N_5}{N_8}2^{T_0/\tau_5}+2^{T_0/\tau_8}}.
\]\nSubstituting \(N_5/N_8=R/(1-R)\), \(R=0.72\%\), \(T_0=1.8\times10^9\) years, \(\tau_5\approx7\times10^8\) years, and \(\tau_8\approx4.5\times10^9\) years gives
\[\nR_O^{(\text{then})}\approx 3.16\%.
\]\nHence the abundance of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) in natural uranium when Oklo’s reactor operated was \(\boxed{3.16\%}\).

knowledge_points.name: radioactive decay law (half-life form)
knowledge_points.description: The number of radioactive atoms decays exponentially as N(t)=N(0) 2^{-t/τ}, where τ is the half-life. Used to compute the number of 235U and 238U atoms at the time of the Oklo reactor by evolving backward from today's values.

knowledge_points.name: isotopic abundance
knowledge_points.description: The ratio of the number of atoms of a given isotope to the total number of atoms of the element. Needed to express the composition of natural uranium and to compute the past abundance from the past atom numbers.

knowledge_points.name: only two uranium isotopes
knowledge_points.description: Other uranium isotopes besides 235U and 238U have negligibly small abundance, so the total number of uranium atoms is simply the sum of 235U and 238U atoms.

knowledge_points.name: no 235U production from 238U
knowledge_points.description: 235U is not a decay product of 238U, so its abundance changes only via its own radioactive decay, independent of the decay of 238U.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the abundance of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) at the time when Oklo’s reactor operated, you need to trace the isotopic composition backward in time using the radioactive decay law. The relevant concept of isotopic abundance is introduced in Section 15‑4, where you learn that the abundance is the fraction of the total number of atoms that belong to a given isotope. Example 16‑2 in your textbook applies the same exponential decay law to the two uranium isotopes \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\) and \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\), and shows how to relate the present‑day abundance ratio to the time elapsed, assuming you know how the numbers change.

Your problem is the inverse of that example: you are given the present‑day abundances (and therefore the ratio \(N_{235}/N_{238}\)) and the age of the reactor, and you want the abundance at that past time. The method is:

1. **Express the present isotopic ratio.**  
   From the present fractional abundance of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\), write the ratio of the number of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) nuclei to the number of \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\) nuclei:
   \[
   \frac{N_{235}}{N_{238}} = \frac{(\text{present abundance})}{1-(\text{present abundance})}.
   \]

2. **Use the radioactive decay law to go backward in time.**  
   The textbook example writes the number of nuclei as a function of time with the exponential form \(N(t) = N(0) e^{-t/T}\), where \(T\) is the mean lifetime. Equivalently, if you are given half‑lives \(\tau\), you can write \(N(t) = N(0) 2^{-t/\tau}\).  
   For each isotope, to obtain the number that existed a time \(t\) ago (the Oklo operation age), you need the reverse operation: the past number is larger than the present number by the factor \(2^{t/\tau}\) (or \(e^{t/T}\)).  
   So, if \(N_{235}\) and \(N_{238}\) are the present numbers, the numbers at the time of the reactor were:
   \[
   N_{235}^{\text{past}} = N_{235} \, 2^{t/\tau_{235}}, \qquad
   N_{238}^{\text{past}} = N_{238} \, 2^{t/\tau_{238}}.
   \]
   (If you are using mean lifetimes \(T\) as in Example 16‑2, replace \(2^{…}\) with \(e^{t/T}\).)

3. **Form the past abundance.**  
   The abundance (fraction) of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) at that past time is
   \[
   \text{abundance}_{\text{past}} = \frac{N_{235}^{\text{past}}}{N_{235}^{\text{past}} + N_{238}^{\text{past}}}.
   \]
   Divide numerator and denominator by \(N_{238}^{\text{past}}\) to write it in terms of the present‑day ratio and the decay factors:
   \[
   \text{abundance}_{\text{past}} = \frac{ \left(\frac{N_{235}}{N_{238}}\right) 2^{t/\tau_{235}} }
   { \left(\frac{N_{235}}{N_{238}}\right) 2^{t/\tau_{235}} + 2^{t/\tau_{238}} }.
   \]
   This is the expression you need, and it directly follows the logic of Example 16‑2 – only now \(t\) is known and you are solving for the abundance instead of the other way around.

4. **Insert the data.**  
   Into that formula you will substitute the known present‑day abundance, the age \(t\) of the Oklo reactor (as given in your problem statement), and the half‑lives (or lifetimes) of the two uranium isotopes. The textbook provides these lifetimes in Example 16‑2; if your problem supplies values in years directly, use those.  

Carrying out the arithmetic with your given numbers will yield the fraction of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) in natural uranium when the reactor operated. Remember to keep consistent time units. The calculation itself is straightforward once you have correctly set up the ratio.

sub_problems.problem: (2) What was the average power of the Oklo's reactor?
sub_problems.solution:
Assume that before the Oklo reactor started operating, the uranium isotopic composition was the same as the natural one at that time, and that after the reactor stopped the remaining uranium isotopes continued to decay normally until today.
\nFirst find how much \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) remained after the reactor stopped. Since its half-life is \(\tau_5\), the mass today is related to the mass at the end of operation by
\[\nM_5' = M R_O \; 2^{T_0/\tau_5}.
\]\nUsing the given values gives
\[\nM_5' \approx 1.84\times 10^7\ \mathrm{kg}.
\]
\nNext find the amount of \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\) at the end of operation. Since today the total uranium mass is \(M\) and the present-day abundance of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) is \(R\), the mass of \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\) today is \(M(1-R)\). Rewinding by radioactive decay over time \(T_0\),
\[\nM_8' = M(1-R)\,2^{T_0/\tau_8}.
\]
\nAt the beginning of reactor operation, the isotopic ratio was the same as for natural uranium at that time, so
\[
\frac{M_0}{M_8'} = \frac{R_1}{1-R_1},
\]\nwhere \(R_1\) is the abundance of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) at the start. Hence
\[\nM_0 = \frac{R_1}{1-R_1}\, M(1-R)\,2^{T_0/\tau_8}
\approx 2.14\times 10^7\ \mathrm{kg}.
\]
\nThe mass of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) that underwent fission is therefore
\[
\Delta M = M_0 - M_5' \approx 3.0\times 10^6\ \mathrm{kg}.
\]\nThe number of fissioned nuclei is
\[\nN = \frac{\Delta M}{0.235\ \mathrm{kg/mol}}\,N_A
\approx 7.61\times 10^{30}.
\]
\nEach fission releases \(E_0 = 200\ \mathrm{MeV}\), so the total released energy is
\[\nE = N E_0.
\]\nUsing \(200\ \mathrm{MeV} = 200\times 10^6\times 1.6\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\),
\[\nE \approx 1.0\times 10^{20}\ \mathrm{J}.
\]
\nThe average power over the operating time \(T\approx 10^5\) years is
\[\nP = \frac{E}{T}
\approx 7.73\times 10^7\ \mathrm{W}.
\]\nTherefore the average power of the Oklo reactor was \(\boxed{7.7\times 10^7\ \mathrm{W}}\).

knowledge_points.name: radioactive decay law
knowledge_points.description: The number of radioactive nuclei decays exponentially with half-life τ: N(t) = N0·2^(-t/τ). Used to rewind the decay and find past masses of ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U from their present-day masses.

knowledge_points.name: isotopic abundance
knowledge_points.description: The fraction of atoms of a particular isotope in a sample, defined as number of isotope atoms divided by total number of element atoms. Needed to interpret the given percentages R, R_O and the result R₁ from part (1).

knowledge_points.name: mass-to-moles conversion
knowledge_points.description: Converting a mass of a pure isotope to number of atoms using molar mass (≈ mass number in g/mol) and Avogadro's number: N = (m / M_molar) · N_A. Used to find the number of fissioned ²³⁵U nuclei from the mass difference ΔM.

knowledge_points.name: nuclear fission energy
knowledge_points.description: Each fission of a ²³⁵U nucleus releases a characteristic energy (here 200 MeV). Total energy released equals number of fissions times energy per fission.

knowledge_points.name: average power
knowledge_points.description: Average power is total energy divided by the time interval: P = E / t. Used to compute the reactor's power over the operating duration T.

knowledge_points.name: electronvolt
knowledge_points.description: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron moving through 1 V, equal to e·1 V ≈ 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J. Used to convert 200 MeV into joules.

knowledge_points.name: mass ratio approximates number ratio
knowledge_points.description: For heavy isotopes like ²³⁵U and ²³⁸U the relative mass difference is small, so the mass ratio is taken as equal to the number ratio. This allows using the number abundance R₁ directly as a mass fraction when calculating the initial ²³⁵U mass.

knowledge_points.name: abundance at operation time known
knowledge_points.description: The abundance of ²³⁵U in natural uranium at the time the Oklo reactor operated, R₁, is known from the solution to sub-problem Q2(1).

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the average power of the Oklo reactor, you need to follow these steps in order, relying on the textbook passages you have studied.

**1. Average power from total energy and time**  
The average power is the total energy released divided by the total operating time, as in the definition of power (rate of work). You are given the total time the reactor operated; be careful to convert it into seconds if you want the power in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).

**2. Total energy from fission events**  
The energy released during operation comes from the fission of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\). According to Example 15‑6, the fission of a heavy nucleus like uranium releases about 200 MeV. That number per fission is typical. To use it in SI you must convert electronvolts to joules: the textbook shows conversions using \(1\,\mathrm{eV}=1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}\).

**3. How much \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) underwent fission?**  
You need the initial mass \(M_0\) of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) when the reactor started and the mass \(M_5'\) that remained when it stopped. Their difference is the mass that fissioned. Both quantities must be deduced from the present‑day uranium and its isotopic composition, together with the radioactive decay law.

**4. Radioactive decay: rewinding from today to the end of operation**  
The radioactive decay law (Eq. 15.10 or the exponential form in the radioactive dating section) says that the number of nuclei changes as \(N(t)=N_0 e^{-\lambda t}\), with \(\lambda = \ln 2 / \tau_{1/2}\). In practice you can use the equivalent form \(N_0 = N(t)\,2^{t/\tau_{1/2}}\), which is easier when you know the half‑lives.  
– Apply this to the present‑day masses of both \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) and \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\). First, calculate the present‑day masses from the given total uranium mass \(M\) and the present‑day abundance \(R\) of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\).  
– Then “rewind” by the time \(T_0\) that elapsed since the reactor stopped:  
 \(M_5' = (\text{present }^{235}\mathrm{U mass}) \times 2^{\,T_0/\tau_5}\),  
 \(M_8' = (\text{present }^{238}\mathrm{U mass}) \times 2^{\,T_0/\tau_8}\),  
where \(\tau_5\) and \(\tau_8\) are the half‑lives of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) and \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\) (given in Table 20.1).

**5. Initial \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) mass from the natural isotopic ratio**  
At the very beginning, before the reactor operated, the uranium had a natural isotopic composition; you are given the abundance \(R_1\) of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) at that time. Because \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\) does not fission in significant amounts, the mass of \(^{238}\mathrm{U}\) was effectively the same at the start and at the end of operation. Therefore the initial \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) mass follows from the ratio:  
 \(M_0 = \dfrac{R_1}{1 - R_1} \times M_8'\).  
This step uses the concept of isotopic abundance, as illustrated in Example 16‑2.

**6. Mass converted to number of fissioned nuclei**  
The mass that fissioned is \(\Delta M = M_0 - M_5'\). Convert this mass to a number of atoms using the mole definition (the mass‑to‑moles passage). The molar mass of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\) is \(0.235\,\mathrm{kg/mol}\), and the Avogadro number is \(N_A = 6.022\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\):  
 number of atoms = \((\Delta M / 0.235\,\mathrm{kg\,mol^{-1}}) \times N_A\).

**7. Total energy and average power**  
Multiply the number of fissioned nuclei by the energy per fission (converted to joules) to obtain the total released energy \(E\). Finally, divide \(E\) by the operating time (in seconds) to get the average power.

All the formulas you need are contained in the textbook passages: radioactive decay, fission energy per event, conversion of MeV to joules, mass‑to‑moles conversion, and the definition of average power. Proceed step by step, using the half‑lives, abundances, masses, and time intervals given in the problem, and leave the arithmetic for yourself.

sub_problems.problem:
(3) Qualitatively explain why was

Oklo's reactor operating in a stable regime and did not blow up. Water inflow rate varied over time; what happened to the reactor when the water inflow rate increased two times?
sub_problems.solution:
Neutrons emitted in $^{235}\mathrm{U}$ fission are initially too energetic to efficiently induce further fissions. Water acts as a moderator: it slows the neutrons down, increasing the probability that they trigger another fission. Thus the chain reaction can proceed only while enough water is present.
\nIf the reactor starts to produce too much heat, the water begins to boil away. Then moderation becomes weaker, the fission rate drops, and the power output decreases. This provides negative feedback, so the reactor was self-regulating and could not run away into an explosion.
\nWhen the water inflow rate increased by a factor of two, the reactor could remove heat more effectively and therefore sustain about twice the power. So the power approximately doubled.
\nFinal answer: \boxed{\text{The reactor was self-regulating because water moderated neutrons; doubling the water inflow doubled the reactor power.}}
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{The reactor was self-regulating because water moderated neutrons; doubling the water inflow doubled the reactor power.}}

knowledge_points.name: neutron moderation
knowledge_points.description: The process by which a moderator (here water) slows down fast fission neutrons via elastic scattering, dramatically increasing the probability of inducing further fissions in ²³⁵U.

knowledge_points.name: water as moderator
knowledge_points.description: The problem states and the solution uses that ground water serves as the neutron moderator; the chain reaction is sustained only when sufficient liquid water is present.

knowledge_points.name: negative feedback
knowledge_points.description: A self-regulating mechanism where an increase in power causes boiling of the moderator, which reduces moderation and thus lowers the fission rate, preventing a runaway reaction.

knowledge_points.name: power proportional to water inflow
knowledge_points.description: The solution assumes that the sustainable reactor power scales approximately linearly with the rate of water inflow, because water both moderates neutrons and removes heat.

sub_problems.guidance:
To explain the stable operation of Oklo’s reactor and what happens when the water inflow rate doubles, think step by step using the concept of neutron moderation from the Eisberg & Resnick passage. Do not jump to a conclusion—work through the reasoning yourself.

1. **First, recall the textbook’s description of the moderator’s purpose.** In a reactor, the moderator (such as water) scatters the fast neutrons from fission, rapidly lowering their speeds. This increases their de Broglie wavelengths and therefore the cross section for capture by \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\), making further fissions much more probable. In other words, the chain reaction strongly depends on having enough moderator present to slow the neutrons.

2. **Apply this to Oklo.** The reactor operated naturally, and water played the moderator role. So, a chain reaction could only proceed efficiently while liquid water was present to moderate the neutrons.

3. **Now reason about stability – why didn’t the reactor blow up?** Consider what happens when the chain reaction releases heat. How does a large rise in temperature affect water? If the water changes state (for example, boils), how would that change its effectiveness as a moderator? Then, link that back to the fission rate: if the moderator is reduced or removed, what happens to the probability that a neutron induces another fission? This should suggest a feedback loop that prevents runaway fission – explain the full loop in your own words using the moderator concept above.

4. **Finally, address the doubled inflow rate.** Suppose water is flowing into the reactor. The reactor’s power level determines how much heat is produced, which in turn influences whether water stays liquid or boils away. Water inflow replaces water that is lost or heated. If the inflow rate doubles, how does that alter the supply of moderator to the system? How might the balance between heat production and water loss change so that the reactor settles into a new, stable level of fissions? Use the moderator principle from the textbook to justify whether the sustained fission rate (power) increases, decreases, or remains the same.

By following these steps and always returning to the textbook’s message—that the chain reaction’s efficiency hinges on the moderator—you will arrive at a qualitative explanation grounded in physics.

sub_problems.problem: (4) Estimate the total mass of water that flowed into the Oklo's reactor during its operation period.
sub_problems.solution:
The reactor energy output was \(
u E_0\), where \(
u\) is the number of fissions of \(^{235}\mathrm{U}\). We assume that almost all this energy was absorbed by the inflowing water, which was heated from \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(100^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and then vaporized.

For \(1\,\mathrm{kg}\) of water, the absorbed energy is
\[
E_w = c\Delta T + L = 4200\cdot 100 + 2260	imes 10^3 \approx 2.68	imes 10^6\,\mathrm{J}.
\]

Thus the total mass of water that flowed through the reactor is
\[
m = \frac{
u E_0}{E_w} \approx 9.09	imes 10^{13}\,\mathrm{kg}.
\]

Final answer: \( oxed{9.09	imes 10^{13}\,\mathrm{kg}}\).

knowledge_points.name: energy absorbed by inflowing water
knowledge_points.description: The reference solution assumes that almost all the reactor's energy output is absorbed by the inflowing water, which is the basis for equating total fission energy to water heating and vaporization.

knowledge_points.name: water heated from 0°C to 100°C
knowledge_points.description: The solution assumes the inflowing water starts at 0°C and is heated to the boiling point of 100°C before vaporization, setting the temperature change for the specific heat calculation.

knowledge_points.name: specific heat formula
knowledge_points.description: The energy required to raise the temperature of a mass of water by ΔT is calculated using Q = m c ΔT, where c is the specific heat of water.

knowledge_points.name: latent heat of vaporization
knowledge_points.description: The energy required to vaporize a mass of water at its boiling point is calculated using Q = m L, where L is the latent heat of evaporation.

knowledge_points.name: total fission energy from previous part
knowledge_points.description: The solution uses the total number of fissions ν (or equivalently the total energy ν E₀) derived in sub-problem (2) as the total energy output of the reactor over its lifetime.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, recognize that the energy released by the reactor is absorbed by the inflowing water, raising its temperature and then vaporizing it. This is exactly the type of energy accounting used in reference kettle example (Blundell & Blundell, 28.1), where the energy required to heat water to boiling and then turn it into steam is computed stepwise.

From that reference passage you have the specific heat capacity of water (about \(4.2\, \text{kJ} \, \text{kg}^{-1} \, \text{K}^{-1}\)) and the latent heat of vaporization for water (\(2.26\, \text{MJ} \, \text{kg}^{-1}\)). These constants are the ones you need.

Now, decide on a plausible inflow temperature for the water. A natural assumption is that groundwater enters at something like \(0^\circ \text{C}\), and that it is heated to the boiling point (\(100^\circ \text{C}\)). The temperature change is then \(100\, \text{K}\) (since one degree Celsius change equals one kelvin change). The energy absorbed per kilogram of water is the sum of the heat required for the temperature rise plus the heat required for the phase change:

\[
\text{Energy per kg} = c \, \Delta T + L .
\]

Once you have that per‑kilogram energy, the total mass of water that flowed through the reactor is found from the total energy output of the reactor. That total energy should be available from an earlier part of the problem (for example, it is the product of the total number of fissions and the energy released per fission). Therefore,

\[
\text{mass of water} = \frac{\text{total energy released by reactor}}{\text{energy required per kg of water}} .
\]

Proceed by substituting the values for \(c\), \(\Delta T\), and \(L\) into the energy‑per‑kilogram expression, paying attention to unit consistency (convert \(2.26\, \text{MJ} \, \text{kg}^{-1}\) to \(2260\, \text{kJ} \, \text{kg}^{-1}\) if \(c\) is used in kJ). Then divide the reactor’s energy output by that result to obtain the estimated mass. Carry out the arithmetic yourself; the guidance stops here.

title: STICKY BALL
problem:
- Jaan Kalda.

A glass ball of radius $R$ rests on a flat glass plate. A tiny droplet of water (of surface tension $\sigma$ ) is injected with a syringe so that water forms a small thin neck between the ball and the plate. Both the ball and the plate are perfectly hydrophilic, i.e. the contact angle of water is $0^{\circ}$ . Find the increase of the normal force between the plate and the ball caused by the presence of the neck of water.
solution:
Let the neck of water have a small radius \(\rho\), with \(\rho \ll R\). Since the contact angle is zero, the liquid surface meets both solid surfaces tangentially, so the direct vertical contribution from surface tension at the contact line is negligible compared with the pressure effect.

The meniscus is approximately spherical near the neck, with curvature radius \(r\). From the geometry of the small neck between the sphere and the plane, the secant theorem gives
\[
2r\cdot 2R \approx \rho^2,
\]
so
\[
\frac{\rho^2}{r} \approx 4R.
\]

The Laplace pressure jump across the meniscus is
\[
\Delta p = \frac{\sigma}{r}.
\]
This pressure acts over the effective area \(S=\pi\rho^2\), so the increase in the normal force is
\[
\Delta F = S\,\Delta p = \pi\rho^2\frac{\sigma}{r}.
\]
Using \(\rho^2/r \approx 4R\), we obtain
\[
\Delta F \approx 4\pi\sigma R.
\]
Thus the water neck increases the normal force by
\[
\boxed{\Delta F = 4\pi\sigma R}.
\]

title: TOTALITY
problem:
— Taavet Kalda, Jaan Kalda. Total solar eclipses are a rare phenomenon which occur when the Moon completely covers the disk of the Sun for some parts of the Earth. This doesn't happen during every solar eclipse because the Moon's apparent size in the sky is sometimes too small to fully cover the Sun, but also because the Moon's shadow usually misses the Earth due its orbital inclination. As a result, total solar eclipses occur on average every 18 months.

Let us consider a total solar eclipse where during the peak, the centre-points of Earth, the Moon and the Sun lie on a line on the same plane as the equator. We measure that right before the total solar eclipse ends at latitude $\lambda =28.5^{\circ}$ , the totality lasts for $t_0=2\mathrm{min}$ . Earth's radius is $r_e =6370\mathrm{km}$ , Moon's radius is $r_m =1740\mathrm{km}$ , orbital period of the Moon $T_{m} =27.3\mathrm{d}$ , orbital radius of the Moon $R_{m} =384000\mathrm{km}$ . One day on Earth is $T_0=24\mathrm{hrs}$ .

sub_problems.problem: (1) For how long is there a place on Earth where the total solar eclipse is observable?
sub_problems.solution:
As the distance from the Moon to the Sun is much larger than the distance from the Moon to the Earth, we can approximate the speed of the Moon’s shadow on Earth by the Moon’s orbital speed.
\nThe Moon’s speed is
\[
 v_m=\frac{2\pi R_m}{T_m}.
\]\nSubstituting the given values,
\[
 v_m=\frac{2\pi\cdot 384000\,\text{km}}{27.3\,\text{d}}\approx 1.02\,\text{km/s}.
\]
\nDuring the central part of the eclipse, the shadow moves across Earth along a diameter, so the total distance over which totality can be observed somewhere on Earth is approximately
\[
2r_e.
\]\nHence the duration of the total solar eclipse at some place on Earth is
\[\nT_{\mathrm{ecl}}=\frac{2r_e}{v_m}=\frac{2\cdot 6370\,\text{km}}{1.02\,\text{km/s}}\approx 1.25\times 10^4\,\text{s}.
\]\nThis is about
\[
\boxed{3.46\,\text{h}}.
\]

knowledge_points.description: Because the Sun is much farther from Earth than the Moon, the Moon's shadow moves across Earth at approximately the same speed as the Moon's orbital speed.

knowledge_points.description: For a central eclipse where the centers of Earth, Moon, and Sun align, the shadow traverses a diameter of Earth, so the total distance the shadow travels across Earth is 2r_e.

sub_problems.guidance:
To solve this, think about what limits the time during which a total solar eclipse can be seen somewhere on Earth. The eclipse is caused by the Moon’s shadow falling on Earth, and that shadow moves because the Moon moves.

First, find the speed of the Moon’s shadow. reference explains that the Moon’s orbit can be treated as circular, and it gives the orbital speed as  
\[
v = \frac{2\pi r}{P}
\]  
where \(r\) is the Earth–Moon distance and \(P\) is the sidereal period (Example 2.2.2). Because the Sun is very far away, the shadow moves at roughly this same speed. Use the values from the passage for \(r\) and \(P\) to compute \(v\).

Next, consider the path of the shadow. For there to be *some* place on Earth where totality is visible, the shadow must sweep across the Earth. The longest possible path the shadow can take across the Earth is a full diameter, which is \(2R_\oplus\) (twice Earth’s radius).

The duration you are asked for is the time it takes the shadow to travel that distance. Relate distance, speed, and time using  
\[
\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}.
\]  
Combine the expression for the Moon’s orbital speed with the diameter of Earth to isolate the time. Substitute the known radius of Earth and the speed you found from the Moon’s orbit.

The structure of this calculation follows the same logic as Example 2.2.2: treat the motion as uniform circular motion, compute the speed from circumference and period, and then use it in a kinematic relation.

sub_problems.problem: (2) How many degrees in longitude on Earth does the total solar eclipse cover?
sub_problems.solution:
If the Earth did not rotate, the totality region on Earth would be about $\pi$ radians in longitude, i.e. $180^\circ$, because the Moon’s shadow sweeps across the Earth at the relative rate set by the Moon’s orbital motion.
\nDuring the totality time $t_0=2\,\mathrm{min}$, the Earth rotates by
\[
\Delta\varphi_E = 360^\circ \frac{t_0}{T_0}
=360^\circ\frac{2}{24\cdot 60}
=0.5^\circ.
\]\nThe Earth’s rotation is in the same direction as the apparent motion of the Moon’s shadow, so the longitudinal extent is reduced by twice this amount over the whole eclipse duration. Using the standard relation for the total longitudinal coverage,
\[
\Delta\lambda = 180^\circ\left(1-\frac{2t_0}{T_0}\right),
\]\nwe get
\[
\Delta\lambda = 180^\circ\left(1-\frac{2\cdot 2\,\mathrm{min}}{24\cdot 60\,\mathrm{min}}\right)
\approx 127.5^\circ.
\]\nThus the eclipse covers about \(\boxed{128^\circ}\) in longitude.

sub_problems.problem: (3) What is the width of the path of totality near the equator?
sub_problems.solution:
Right near the end of the eclipse, the Earth's rotation moves the surface under the Moon's shadow almost perpendicularly to the shadow motion. Therefore the local width of the totality path at latitude \(\lambda=28.5^\circ\) is the distance the shadow moves during the totality time:

\[
 w_{\lambda}=v_m t_0 = 2\pi R_m\frac{t_0}{T_m}.
\]
\nSubstituting the given values,

\[
 w_{\lambda}=2\pi\cdot 384000\,\text{km}\cdot \frac{2\,\text{min}}{27.3\,\text{d}}
\approx 123\,\text{km}.
\]
\nTo find the width near the equator, we must account for the fact that the Earth's surface there is closer to the Moon by about \(r_e\) compared with the eclipse-end point. The Moon's apparent angular diameter is approximately

\[
\alpha \approx \frac{2r_m}{R_m}.
\]
\nHence the shadow width increases by roughly

\[
\Delta w \approx \alpha r_e = \frac{2r_m}{R_m}r_e.
\]
\nNumerically,

\[
\Delta w \approx \frac{2\cdot 1740}{384000}\cdot 6370\,\text{km} \approx 57.7\,\text{km}.
\]
\nThus the width of the path of totality near the equator is

\[
 w_{\mathrm{eq}} \approx 123\,\text{km}+57.7\,\text{km} \approx 180\,\text{km}.
\]
\nFinal answer: \(\boxed{180\,\text{km}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
The path of totality width near the equator is found in two steps: first compute the width at a location where the Earth’s rotation moves the surface almost perpendicularly to the shadow’s motion, then correct that width for the fact that near the equator the Earth’s surface is closer to the Moon.

**Step 1 – Basic width from shadow motion**
The Moon’s orbital motion carries its shadow across the Earth. When the shadow motion is nearly perpendicular to the observer (as at the latitude given for the eclipse end), the width of the totality path is simply the distance the shadow travels during the totality duration.  
- Use the concept of circular orbital speed from the textbook: for a nearly circular orbit, speed is circumference divided by period, \(v = 2\pi R / T\).  
- Apply this to the Moon: from the Moon’s orbital radius and sidereal period you can compute the shadow speed \(v_m\).  
- Then the width at that latitude is \(w = v_m \times t_0\), where \(t_0\) is the duration of totality.  
This gives a width valid for the location where the Earth’s surface is at the same distance from the Moon as the eclipse‑end point.

**Step 2 – Correction for the equatorial region**
Near the equator, the surface is closer to the Moon by about one Earth radius. Because the Moon’s apparent angular size depends on its distance (small‑angle relation), this smaller distance makes the Moon look slightly larger, which broadens the shadow on the ground.  
- From the small‑angle formula in your textbook, the angular diameter \(\theta\) of an object of linear diameter \(D\) at distance \(d\) is \(\theta \approx D/d\) (or in arcseconds as given in Fig. 1‑9, but the proportional relation is what matters).  
- The Moon’s linear diameter is \(2 r_m\). Its angular diameter at the distance of the eclipse‑end point is \(\alpha \approx 2 r_m / R_m\).  
- If the Earth’s surface moves closer by a distance \(\Delta d \approx r_e\), the shadow width increases by roughly \(\Delta w \approx \alpha \times r_e\) (think of the triangle formed by the top of the Moon’s shadow cone).  
- Compute \(\alpha\) using the small‑angle relation with the given Moon radius and orbital distance. Then multiply by the Earth’s radius to get the extra width.

**Final step**  
Add the equatorial correction to the basic width from Step 1 to obtain the width of the path of totality near the equator.

*Hint:* When applying the formulas, be careful with units (convert minutes to days, or work with consistent units for speed). The textbook’s worked examples (e.g., Jupiter’s orbital speed from period and semimajor axis, or the Hohmann transfer circular speed) illustrate the same \(v = 2\pi a/P\) logic. The small‑angle relation is explicitly given as \(\theta(\,'') = 206\,265 \cdot D/d\) and also as \(d_A = D/\theta\), which are equivalent. Use whichever form is most convenient, but remember the correction only needs the angular diameter in radians if you directly multiply by a distance.

sub_problems.problem: (4) What is the longest amount of time the total eclipse is visible for a single location on Earth?
sub_problems.solution:
The total eclipse lasts longest where the Moon’s shadow moves most slowly relative to the ground, which is at the equator, because the Earth’s rotational speed is largest there.
\nFirst compute the Moon’s orbital speed:
\[
 v_m=\frac{2\pi R_m}{T_m}
 =\frac{2\pi\cdot 384000\ \mathrm{km}}{27.3\cdot 24\cdot 3600\ \mathrm{s}}
 \approx 1.02\ \mathrm{km/s}.
\]
\nThe speed of a point on Earth’s equator is
\[
 v_e=\frac{2\pi r_e}{T_0}
 =\frac{2\pi\cdot 6370\ \mathrm{km}}{24\cdot 3600\ \mathrm{s}}
 \approx 0.46\ \mathrm{km/s}.
\]
\nThe relative speed between the Moon’s shadow and the Earth’s surface is obtained by vector subtraction. The angle between the two velocities is \(\lambda=28.5^\circ\), so
\[
 v_{\mathrm{rel}}=\sqrt{v_m^2+v_e^2-2v_mv_e\cos\lambda}
 \approx 0.654\ \mathrm{km/s}.
\]
\nUsing the observed totality time \(t_0=2\,\mathrm{min}=120\,\mathrm{s}\), the corresponding shadow width is
\[
 w=v_{\mathrm{rel}}t_0\approx 0.654\times 120\approx 78.5\ \mathrm{km}.
\]
\nAt the equator the eclipse is longest, and the same shadow width is swept out with the maximal effective duration. This gives
\[
 t_{\max}=\frac{w_{\mathrm{eq}}}{v_{\mathrm{rel}}}\approx 276\ \mathrm{s}=4.6\ \mathrm{min}.
\]
\nTherefore the longest total eclipse visible from a single location on Earth lasts \(\boxed{4.6\ \mathrm{min}}\).

sub_problems.problem: (5) For how long is the total eclipse near the location described in iii), at the distance of $a =50\mathrm{km}$ from the centreline of the eclipse path?
sub_problems.solution:
Since \(a=50\,\mathrm{km}\ll R_e\), the relative velocity of the Moon’s shadow with respect to Earth is the same as in the previous part. The totality region at the equator has width \(w_{\rm eq}\), so at a distance \(a\) from the centreline the shadow crosses only a chord of length
\[
2\sqrt{\left(\frac{w_{\rm eq}}{2}\right)^2-a^2}=\sqrt{w_{\rm eq}^2-4a^2}.
\]\nDividing this distance by the shadow speed \(v_{\rm rel}\) gives the duration of totality:
\[\nt=\frac{\sqrt{w_{\rm eq}^2-4a^2}}{v_{\rm rel}}=230\,\mathrm{s}\approx 3.8\,\mathrm{min}.
\]\nThus the total eclipse lasts \(\boxed{230\,\mathrm{s}\approx 3.8\,\mathrm{min}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the duration of totality at a given offset from the centreline, start with the basic kinematic relation that connects distance, speed, and time. The excerpts you studied show exactly this: in the Taylor & Wheeler passage a trip time in a given frame is computed as the travelled distance \(L\) divided by the speed \(v\) ( \(t = L/v\) ). The Morin passage similarly computes a time interval as a distance divided by a relative speed — \( (L/\gamma)/(c+v) \). The same idea applies here.

Now identify the distance the Moon’s shadow must cover at your location. The shadow’s path on the ground is a band of total width \(w_{\text{eq}}\) (the width of the totality region at the equator, which you already know from earlier parts). Because you are at a perpendicular distance \(a = 50\,\text{km}\) from the centreline, the shadow does not cut across the full width but along a chord of that band. Using the geometry of a circle (or a strip of width \(w_{\text{eq}}\)), the length of a chord at distance \(a\) from the centre is found from the Pythagorean theorem: first note the half‑width \(w_{\text{eq}}/2\), then the half‑chord length is \(\sqrt{(w_{\text{eq}}/2)^2 - a^2}\). The full distance the shadow travels while you are in the umbra is twice that half‑chord, i.e. \(\sqrt{w_{\text{eq}}^2 - 4a^2}\).

Finally, combine this distance with the ground speed \(v_{\text{rel}}\) of the shadow (which, as stated in the problem, can be taken from the previous part because the offset is small compared to Earth’s radius). From \(t = \text{distance} / v_{\text{rel}}\) you obtain the duration. Carry out the algebraic steps and the arithmetic with your known values for \(w_{\text{eq}}\) and \(v_{\text{rel}}\) to reach the answer.

\]
\[
 w_{\rm eq} \approx 2\,\text{min}\times 1.02\,\text{km/s}\approx 122\,\text{km}.
\]\nBy the assumptions, the typical eclipse width is
\[
\frac{w_\lambda+w_{\rm eq}}{4}\approx \frac{171+122}{4}\approx 73\,\text{km}.
\]\nThe typical eclipse length is one half of a great circle, so
\[\nL\approx \pi r_e.
\]\nThus the area covered by one eclipse is approximately
\[\nA\approx \pi r_e\cdot \frac{w_\lambda+w_{\rm eq}}{4},
\]\nand the probability that a given point on Earth is inside the totality path for a randomly placed eclipse is
\[
 p=\frac{A}{4\pi r_e^2}=\frac{w_\lambda+w_{\rm eq}}{16r_e}.
\]\nSo the expected number of eclipses until a given location is hit is
\[
\frac{1}{p}=\frac{16r_e}{w_\lambda+w_{\rm eq}}\approx \frac{16\cdot 6370}{171+122}\approx 3.5\times 10^2.
\]\nSince total solar eclipses occur on average every 18 months, the average waiting time is
\[
\frac{16r_e}{w_\lambda+w_{\rm eq}}\cdot 18\,\text{months}
\approx 5.2\times 10^2\,\text{years}.
\]\nTherefore the average interval between two total solar eclipses at a given location is \(\boxed{5.2\times 10^2\ \text{years}}\).
