knowledge_points.description: The motion of a two-body system is separated into translation of the centre of mass and oscillation of the relative coordinate; an impulse on one ball shifts the CM velocity and excites the internal longitudinal mode.

knowledge_points.name: simple harmonic motion of a dumbbell
knowledge_points.description: The longitudinal relative motion of the dumbbell is simple harmonic with period T (from part (1)); for two equal masses, the velocity of each ball is sinusoidal with that same period when the CM is at rest.

knowledge_points.name: velocity superposition and sinc-function minimum
knowledge_points.description: After an oblique impact the front ball's x-velocity is a sum of a constant CM term and an oscillatory term; the critical angle is found by requiring the minimum of this velocity to vanish, leading to an equation that involves the minimum of (sin x)/x (given by the hint).

sub_problems.guidance:
For part (iii), start by analyzing the perpendicular collision with the wall. The wall is effectively a massive stationary object, so recall from the textbook: "If \(M \gg m\), then \(m\) bounces backward with speed \(\approx v\), and \(M\) hardly moves." This tells you that the front ball reverses its velocity from \(-v\) to \(+v\) instantly, while the rear ball (and the rest of the dumbbell) is momentarily unaffected. Because both balls have equal mass, after the impact the center of mass has zero velocity (the two balls have velocities \(+v\) and \(-v\)). The textbook states: "The motion of a system's center of mass behaves as if all the mass were concentrated there and all the external forces act at that point." Since after the impact there are no external forces along the axis, the center of mass remains at rest, and the only internal motion is the longitudinal oscillation of the dumbbell. The dumbbell is essentially two masses connected by a spring, which performs simple harmonic motion. Use the textbook results: "The equation of motion is \(m \ddot{x} = -k x\)" and "the solution may be written as \(x(t) = A \cos(\omega t + \varphi)\)", where \(\omega = \sqrt{k/m}\). Here \(k\) is the effective spring constant from part (1) and \(m\) is the mass of one ball. The relative motion of the two balls follows the same formichelor, and the velocity of the front ball relative to the center of mass is sinusoidal. Because at \(t=0\) (right after the impact) the front ball has velocity \(+v\) relative to the wall, and the rear ball has \(-v\), the relative velocity between the balls is \(2v\) and half of that is the velocity of each relative to the CM. Thus the front balls velocity as a function of time is \(v_x(t) = v \cos(\omega t)\) (with \(\omega = 2\pi/T\)). Sketch this from \(t=0\) to \(t=T/2\), when the front ball reaches velocity \(-v\) and hits the wall again.

For part (iv), the dumbbell approaches the wall at an angle \(\alpha\). The only external impulse from the wall acts along the \(x\)-direction (normal to the wall). This impulse changes the \(x\)-component of momentum of the front ball. However, because the rod transmits forces along its axis, the impulse has a component along the rod (proportional to \(\cos\alpha\)) and a perpendicular component (proportional to \(\sin\alpha\)). Use the concept of impulse: "The impulse (that is, the change in linear momentum) supplied to the whole system is \(\mathbf{P}\)" and "the velocity of the CM is \(V_{\mathrm{CM}} = \mathbf{P}/M\)". The total mass is \(2m\). The impulse changes the CM velocity in the \(x\)-direction. Additionally, the component of the impulse along the rod excites a longitudinal oscillation of the dumbbell. For the relative motion, treat the two balls as a harmonic oscillator with reduced mass \(\mu\) (the textbook defines "reduced mass, \(\mu\), is defined by \(1/\mu \equiv 1/m_1 + 1/m_2\)"). The equation for the relative displacement is the same SHM as before, but with the relative initial condition given by the impulse component along the rod. The resulting \(x\)-velocity of the front ball is the sum of the CM motion and the oscillatory relative motion. The oscillatory part is proportional to \(\sin\alpha\) (since the component along the rod scales as \(\sin\alpha\) in the \(x\)-direction after projection). The hint gives \(\min(\sin x / x) \approx -0.217\) as the minimum value of a certain function that appears in the oscillatory response. This minimum, when multiplied by the amplitude \(\sin\alpha\), can cancel the constant term \(\cos\alpha\) from the CM motion. The criterion for the transition from one regime (where the front ball hits the wall only once) to another (where it hits a second time) is that the total \(x\)-velocity of the front ball just becomes zero at some later time. Set the sum of the constant and oscillatory contributions to zero at the instant when the oscillatory part reaches its minimum: \(\cos\alpha_0 + \sin\alpha_0 \cdot (-0.217) = 0\). Solve this equation to find \(\alpha_0\). Then convert to degrees if needed.

sub_problems.problem: (5) Under the assumptions of the previous task, let $\alpha >\alpha_0$ .Additionally, assume that while steel is highly elastic, it is not infinitely so: any oscillations excited in the rod will decay by the time the rear ball collides with the wall. Determine the speed with which the centre of mass of the dumbbell departs from the wall.
sub_problems.solution:
Under the stated assumptions, after the first collision the dumbbell moves as a rigid body rotating about its centre of mass, and the longitudinal oscillations in the rod have already decayed by the time the rear ball reaches the wall.
\nFrom the geometry of the motion found in the previous part, the speed of each ball relative to the centre of mass is
\[
 v\sin\alpha.
\]\nThe velocity of a ball is tangent to its circular motion around the centre of mass, so its component along the wall normal is
\[
(v\sin\alpha)\sin\alpha = v\sin^2\alpha.
\]\nThe rear ball therefore collides with the wall with normal speed \(v\sin^2\alpha\). For a perfectly elastic collision, this normal component reverses sign while the tangential component is unchanged, so the centre of mass departs from the wall with the same speed.
\nThus the speed of the centre of mass after the collision is
\[
\boxed{v\sin^2\alpha}.
\]

knowledge_points.description: The problem states that any longitudinal oscillations in the rod decay before the rear ball hits the wall, so the dumbbell can be treated as a rigid body during the second collision.

knowledge_points.name: post-first-collision state
knowledge_points.description: From the previous part, for α > α0 the centre of mass is momentarily at rest normal to the wall and the balls rotate about it with relative speed v sin α. This gives the rear ball's pre-impact normal speed.

knowledge_points.name: centre of mass
knowledge_points.description: The problem asks for the speed of the centre of mass; the solution uses the centre of mass to relate the motion of the balls to the overall translation of the dumbbell.

knowledge_points.name: velocity direction in rigid body rotation
knowledge_points.description: For a point on a rigid body rotating about the centre of mass, its velocity is perpendicular to the line joining it to the centre of mass. This determines the direction of the ball's relative velocity and allows its normal component to be found.

knowledge_points.name: elastic collision with fixed wall
knowledge_points.description: In a perfectly elastic collision with a fixed wall, the normal component of the contact point's velocity reverses sign while the tangential component remains unchanged. Applied to the rear ball's impact.

knowledge_points.name: impulse-momentum theorem for centre of mass
knowledge_points.description: The change in velocity of the centre of mass of a system equals the total external impulse divided by the total mass. Used to deduce that the centre of mass departs with the same normal speed as the rear ball had before the collision.

knowledge_points.name: fixed infinitely massive wall
knowledge_points.description: The steel wall is assumed fixed and immovable, so its velocity does not change during the collision and the elastic collision condition applies in the lab frame.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the speed of the centre of mass after the rear ball collides with the wall, work step by step using the concepts of centre of mass, rigid-body rotation, and elastic collisions from your textbook.

1. **Recall the dumbbell’s motion before the rear ball hits the wall.**  
   From the earlier part of the problem (assumed solved), you know that after the first collision the dumbbell translates *and* rotates. The centre of mass moves with some speed, and each ball has a speed relative to the centre of mass. The problem states that any longitudinal oscillations have decayed, so treat the dumbbell as a rigid body rotating about its centre of mass.

2. **Find the velocity of the rear ball relative to the centre of mass.**  
   In rigid-body rotation about the centre of mass, every point moves in a circle around the CM. The speed of a point relative to the CM is given by the geometry of the motion (the previous task gives you the magnitude). The direction of this velocity is tangent to the circular path, as discussed in the *Rotation about a Fixed Point* passage (here the CM is the natural reference point for the rotational motion). Use that direction to work out the component of the ball’s velocity that is perpendicular to the wall. This component is what matters for the collision.

3. **Treat the collision of the rear ball with the wall as an elastic collision against a fixed, infinitely massive wall.**  
   The textbook’s worked example of a superball bouncing between walls shows how to handle such a collision: for an elastic bounce off a stationary wall, the normal component of velocity simply reverses sign, while the tangential component remains unchanged. The wall is fixed and infinitely massive, so its recoil is negligible — exactly the situation described in the *Bouncing and recoiling* problem statement.  
   Apply this rule to the normal component you found in step 2. The tangential component does not affect the departure speed of the centre of mass in the normal direction.

4. **Relate the ball’s velocity change to the centre-of-mass motion.**  
   According to the impulse–momentum theorem for a system of particles, the change in total momentum of the dumbbell equals the impulse from external forces. Here the only external impulse during the short collision comes from the wall on the rear ball. The centre of mass moves as if all mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted at that point (see the *Center of Mass* exposition).  
   The worked example *Motion after an impulsive blow* shows exactly this procedure: first find the impulse delivered, then use $\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{CM}} = \mathbf{P}/M$ to get the centre-of-mass velocity. Because the collision is elastic and the wall is fixed, the normal component of the ball’s velocity simply reverses; the resulting change in momentum of the ball translates directly into the change in momentum of the whole dumbbell.

5. **Combine the pieces.**  
   The normal impulse from the wall changes only the normal component of the centre-of-mass velocity. Since the wall is perpendicular to the original direction of the centre-of-mass motion, the tangential component of the CM velocity is unchanged and does not affect the departure speed. The magnitude of the CM velocity after the collision is therefore determined entirely by the reversed normal component you found in step 2. Apply the impulse–momentum relation for the centre of mass (using the total mass of the dumbbell) to express the final CM speed in terms of the known parameters $v$ and $\alpha$.  

Follow these steps in order, substituting the expressions from the previous task where needed, and you will arrive at the requested speed.

title: EVAPORATION
problem:
- Jaan Kalda.

For the subsequent tasks, the graph shows how the density of saturated water va

pour in $\mathrm{g}\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ depends on the temperature in

You may also use the following characteristics of water. Specific heat capacity $c =4200 \, \mathrm{J} \, \mathrm{kg}^{-1} \, \mathrm{K}^{-1}$ ; latent heat of vaporization $L =2260 \, \mathrm{kJ} \, \mathrm{kg}^{-1}$ ; density $\rho =1000 \, \mathrm{kg} \, \mathrm{m}^{-3}$ ; molar mass of water $\mu =18 \, \mathrm{g} \, \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ . You may also assume water vapour to behave as an ideal gas. The universal gas constant is $R =8.31 \, \mathrm{J} \, \mathrm{mol}^{-1} \, \mathrm{K}^{-1}$ .

sub_problems.problem:
(2) If the piston is pulled so that it shifts by $a =3 \, \mathrm{dm}$ , the water cools to a temperature of $T_{1} =89^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ ; what is the mass of the water under the piston?

Water evaporation has a cooling effect the intensity of which depends on the relative humidity and air convection intensity. It appears, however, that once a dynamical thermal equilibrium is reached, the equilibrium temperature of a wet surface depends only on the relative humidity and the temperature of air and does not depend on the convection speed (as long as the convection is not too weak). This is so because the two competing processes determining the equilibrium state both depend on the thickness of the laminar (non-turbulent) surface layer exactly in the same way. In what follows we shall use the following assumptions. (a)

Atop a wet surface (such as a sweating bare skin), there is a layer with a laminar flow of a certain thickness $d$ . (b) Atop the laminar layer, the surrounding turbulent flow keeps a constant temperature $T$ and relative humidity $r$ , both equal to the respective values in the bulk of the surrounding air. (c) Heat flux from beneath the wet surface (e.g. through the skin) can be neglected. (d) The heat conductivity of air $\kappa =30\mathrm{mW}\mathrm{m}^{-1}\mathrm{K}^{-1}$ at $T =70^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (neglect the temperature dependence), and the diffusivity of water molecules in air $D =26\mathrm{mm}^2\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ . Neglect the dependence of $D$ on the temperature. Note that the particle flux (net number of molecules passing a cross-section in $y-z$ -plane per second and per cross-sectional area) can be found as $J = D\frac{\mathrm{dn}}{\mathrm{dx}}$ , where $n$ denotes the number density (number of molecules per volume).
sub_problems.solution:
The piston is pulled by a distance $a$, so the gas volume increases by
\[V_{\text{new}}=Sa.
\]
To fill this extra volume, some water evaporates. At the final temperature $T_1=89^\circ\mathrm{C}$ the vapour density is read from the graph as
\[
\rho_1\approx 405\,\mathrm{g\,m^{-3}}.
\]
Hence the mass of evaporated water is
\[m_v=V_{\text{new}}\rho_1=Sa\rho_1.
\]
The energy needed for evaporation comes from cooling the remaining liquid water. Energy conservation gives
\[m_v L=(m-m_v)c(T_0-T_1),
\]
where $T_0$ is the initial temperature. Since $m_v\ll m$, we may neglect $m_v$ on the right-hand side and obtain
\[m\approx \frac{m_v L}{c(T_0-T_1)}=\frac{\rho_1SaL}{c(T_0-T_1)}.
\]
Substituting the given values yields
\[m\approx 6.5\times 10^2\,\mathrm{g}.
\]
Therefore the mass of water under the piston is \boxed{650\,\mathrm{g}}.

knowledge_points.name: saturated vapor density
knowledge_points.description: The density of water vapor in equilibrium with liquid water at a given temperature; used to find the mass of vapor from the added volume via the provided graph.

knowledge_points.name: latent heat of vaporization
knowledge_points.description: The energy required to evaporate a unit mass of liquid at constant pressure; used as Q = m L for the heat absorbed by the evaporated water.

knowledge_points.name: specific heat capacity
knowledge_points.description: The energy required to change the temperature of a unit mass by one degree; used as Q = m c ΔT for the heat lost by the cooling liquid water.

knowledge_points.name: conservation of energy
knowledge_points.description: Energy is conserved; here the heat lost by the liquid water equals the heat gained by the evaporated water, assuming no other energy transfers.

knowledge_points.name: calorimetric evaporation balance
knowledge_points.description: The energy balance is treated as a simple heat exchange: the latent heat absorbed by the evaporated water equals the sensible heat lost by the liquid water, neglecting work, vapor heat capacity, and external heat.

knowledge_points.name: negligible initial vapor volume and mass
knowledge_points.description: The piston initially rests on the water surface so initial vapor volume is zero; the mass of evaporated water is much smaller than the liquid water mass, so it can be neglected in the cooling term.

knowledge_points.name: known initial temperature
knowledge_points.description: The initial temperature T0 of the water is known from the problem setup (e.g., boiling point 100°C); needed to compute the temperature drop.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, determine the extra volume created by pulling the piston. This volume equals the cross‑sectional area \(S\) (known from the earlier setup) times the displacement \(a = 3\ \mathrm{dm}\). Because the space above the water is in direct contact with the liquid, the water vapour that fills this volume is saturated. Use the saturation vapour density curve provided in your problem sheet — the physics is hinted in Section 37.5, where it is explained that warmer air can “hold” more water vapour — to read off the saturated vapour density \(\rho(T_1)\) at the final temperature \(T_1 = 89^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\). The mass of evaporated water is then  
\(m_{\text{evap}} = \text{(extra volume)} \times \rho(T_1)\).

Now apply energy conservation. The liquid water cools from its initial temperature \(T_0\) (which you already have from the equilibrium condition of the starting configuration) down to \(T_1\). The lost thermal energy is absorbed to evaporate the water that filled the extra volume.  

The energy balance involves two quantities from the textbook:  
- The specific heat capacity of water, \(c = 4.184\ \mathrm{kJ\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}\), from the worked example in Section 2.2.  
- The specific latent heat of vaporization of water, \(L = 2.26\ \mathrm{MJ\,kg^{-1}}\), given in Section 28.1 (and used, for example, in the kettle‑boiling‑dry example).

Since the evaporated water leaves the liquid, the mass that actually cools is \(m - m_{\text{evap}}\). Energy conservation therefore gives  

\[
(m - m_{\text{evap}})\,c\,(T_0 - T_1) = m_{\text{evap}}\,L,
\]

which is a direct statement that the thermal energy lost by the remaining water equals the latent energy needed to vaporise the mass \(m_{\text{evap}}\) (the “chameleon” character of energy in the conservation‑laws excerpt reminds us that thermal and latent energies are just different forms of energy).

In this problem \(m_{\text{evap}}\) is typically much smaller than the total mass \(m\); you may therefore neglect \(m_{\text{evap}}\) on the left‑hand side as a reasonable approximation, obtaining  

\[
m \;\approx\; \frac{m_{\text{evap}}\,L}{c\,(T_0 - T_1)}.
\]

Substitute your \(m_{\text{evap}}\), the known constants \(L\) and \(c\), and the temperature difference. Use consistent SI units (metres, kilograms, joules) for all quantities. The result is the approximate mass of water originally under the piston. (If you wish, you can then solve the exact linear equation to check how good the approximation is, but the simple formula is sufficient for a quick estimate.)

title: NUCLEAR REACTORS
problem: - Topi Lind. In order to maintain a chain reaction in a modern thermal-neutron nuclear reactor one needs three things: 1. nuclear fuel (e.g. $\mathrm{U}^{235}$ ), 2. moderator (e.g. water) and 3. coolant. In most cases the moderator acts as the coolant as well. Neutrons released from a thermal fission of $\mathrm{U}^{235}$ have a mean kinetic energy of approximately $E_0=2\mathrm{MeV}$ . However, neutrons which are that fast are inefficient in triggering fission of $\mathrm{U}^{235}$ : neutrons need to be slowed down to an average kinetic energy of $E_{f} =0.025\mathrm{eV}$ . In what follows, justify why non-relativistic approximations can be used unless explicitly instructed otherwise.

sub_problems.problem: (1) The rest energy of neutrons $m_{\mathrm{n}}c^{2} =940\mathrm{MeV}$ , the Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}} =1.38\times 10^{-23}\mathrm{JK}^{-1}$ , and the elementary charge $e =1.602\times 10^{-19}\mathrm{C}$ . What is the required speed of neutrons, i.e. the speed of neutrons with kinetic energy $E_{f}$ ? What is the temperature $T_{f}$ of a neutron gas where the average kinetic energy of neutrons is $E_{f}$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
For a non-relativistic particle, the kinetic energy is
\[\nE_k=\frac12 m v^2.
\]\nSince \(E_f=0.025\,\mathrm{eV}\ll m_nc^2=940\,\mathrm{MeV}\), the non-relativistic approximation is well justified.
\nConvert the energy to joules:
\[\nE_f=0.025\times 1.602\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}=4.005\times 10^{-21}\,\mathrm{J}.
\]\nThen
\[
 v_f=\sqrt{\frac{2E_f}{m_n}}.
\]\nUsing \(m_nc^2=940\,\mathrm{MeV}\), one finds \(m_n\approx 1.675\times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\), so
\[
 v_f=\sqrt{\frac{2\cdot 4.005\times 10^{-21}}{1.675\times 10^{-27}}}
\approx 2.2\times 10^3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.
\]
\nFor a gas in thermal equilibrium, the average kinetic energy is
\[
\langle E\rangle=\frac32 k_B T.
\]\nSetting \(\langle E\rangle=E_f\) gives
\[\nT_f=\frac{2E_f}{3k_B}
=\frac{2\cdot 4.005\times 10^{-21}}{3\cdot 1.38\times 10^{-23}}
\approx 1.93\times 10^2\,\mathrm{K}.
\]
\nThus the required neutron speed is \(\boxed{2.2\times 10^3\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}\), and the corresponding neutron-gas temperature is \(\boxed{1.93\times 10^2\,\mathrm{K}}\).

knowledge_points.description: Non-relativistic formulas are valid when the kinetic energy is much smaller than the rest energy m c^2.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, confirm that the non-relativistic formula for kinetic energy is adequate here. Compare the given kinetic energy \(E_f = 0.025\,\mathrm{eV}\) with the neutron rest energy \(m_{\mathrm{n}}c^{2} = 940\,\mathrm{MeV}\). Because \(E_f\) is many orders of magnitude smaller than the rest energy, you can safely use the classical expression for kinetic energy, as discussed in the passage on non-relativistic kinetic energy where the Newtonian form \(K = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}\) is valid for low speeds.

To find the speed, you need the neutron’s mass in kilograms. The rest energy \(m_{\mathrm{n}}c^{2}\) is given in MeV. First convert that energy into joules using the electronvolt conversion factor \(1\,\mathrm{eV} = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}\) (see the electronvolt knowledge point in reference). After converting \(m_{\mathrm{n}}c^{2}\) to joules, obtain the mass \(m_{\mathrm{n}}\) by dividing by \(c^{2}\) (where \(c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}\)).  
Next, convert the given kinetic energy \(E_f\) from electronvolts to joules in the same way. Then use the non-relativistic kinetic energy formula \(E_f = \frac{1}{2} m_{\mathrm{n}} v^{2}\) to solve for the speed \(v\). Rearrange to \(v = \sqrt{2E_f / m_{\mathrm{n}}}\) and substitute the values you have in SI units.

For the temperature, apply the equipartition theorem. reference passages explain that for a classical system in thermal equilibrium the average kinetic energy per particle is \(\frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T\) (three translational degrees of freedom, each contributing \(\frac{1}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T\)). Set this average kinetic energy equal to the given \(E_f\): \(E_f = \frac{3}{2} k_{\mathrm{B}} T\). Solve for \(T\) using the value of \(E_f\) in joules and the given Boltzmann constant \(k_{\mathrm{B}}\). This yields the temperature of a neutron gas whose average kinetic energy matches \(E_f\).

Work step by step: check the non-relativistic condition, convert energies to joules, find the mass, compute the speed, then use equipartition to find the temperature.

The guidance explicitly states the kinetic energy value \(E_f = 0.025\,\mathrm{eV}\) which is not given in the problem, revealing a key intermediate numeric result.

sub_problems.problem: (2) What is the initial speed of neutrons, i.e. the speed of neutrons with energy $E_0$ ?
sub_problems.solution:
Use the non-relativistic kinetic energy formula
\[\nE_0=\frac12 mv_0^2,
\]\nwith the neutron mass \(m\approx 1.675\times 10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}\).
\nConvert the energy to joules:
\[\nE_0=2\,\mathrm{MeV}=2\times 10^6\,\mathrm{eV}
=2\times 10^6\times 1.602\times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}
\approx 3.20\times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}.
\]
\nThen
\[\nv_0=\sqrt{\frac{2E_0}{m}}
=\sqrt{\frac{2(3.20\times 10^{-13})}{1.675\times 10^{-27}}}
\approx 2.0\times 10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}.
\]
\nSo the initial speed of the neutrons is \(\boxed{2.0\times 10^7\,\mathrm{m/s}}\).

sub_problems.guidance:
- The neutron energy \(E_0\) given in the problem (likely expressed in MeV) is its **kinetic energy**.  First convert this energy into joules, because the standard kinetic‑energy formula uses SI units.  The textbook explains that one electron‑volt is the energy an electron gains through a one‑volt potential difference:  
  \(1\;\text{eV} = 1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\;\text{J}\).  Since \(1\;\text{MeV} = 10^{6}\;\text{eV}\), multiply your \(E_0\) (in MeV) by \(10^6\) and then by \(1.6022 \times 10^{-19}\) to obtain the energy in joules.

- Evaluate whether the neutron’s speed is non‑relativistic.  The Taylor & Wheeler passage reminds us that for **low speeds** the Newtonian kinetic energy  
  \(K_{\text{Newton}} = \tfrac12 m v^2\) is valid, while the total relativistic energy \(E = m\gamma\) reduces to rest energy plus kinetic energy.  A quick comparison shows that a neutron’s rest energy is about \(940\;\text{MeV}\), so an \(E_0\) of a few MeV is very small compared with \(mc^2\).  Therefore the non‑relativistic formula is perfectly adequate here.

- Set the kinetic energy in joules equal to \(\tfrac12 m v_0^2\), using the neutron mass \(m\) that has already been provided earlier in the problem (or that you know from standard tables).  The equation gives a direct relationship between \(E_0\) and the speed \(v_0\).

- Solve for \(v_0\):  
  \[
  v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2E_0}{m}}
  \]
  where \(E_0\) is now in joules and \(m\) in kilograms.  Substitute the numbers and carry out the arithmetic yourself.  If you wish, check the result by comparing \(v_0\) to the speed of light \(c \approx 3.0 \times 10^{8}\;\text{m/s}\); you should find that \(v_0/c \ll 1\), confirming that the non‑relativistic treatment was justified.

sub_problems.problem:
(3) From a completely non-

relativistic point of view, what should be the mass of the moderator's atoms to slow down the fast neutrons as efficiently as possible? If the mass of the moderator's atoms were to be $M =135m_{\mathrm{n}}$ , how many collisions with such atoms at a temperature much lower than $T_{f}$ would a fast neutron need to experience to slow down from $E_0$ to $E_{f}$ ? Assume that all collisions are elastic and central.
sub_problems.solution:
For a neutron of mass $m_n$ elastically colliding head-on with a moderator atom of mass $M$ initially at rest, conservation of momentum and kinetic energy gives the neutron’s final speed
\[
 v' = \left|\frac{m_n-M}{m_n+M}\right|v.
\]\nThe kinetic energy after one collision is therefore
\[
 E' = \left(\frac{m_n-M}{m_n+M}\right)^2 E.
\]\nThe fractional energy loss per collision is maximized when the masses are equal, so the most efficient moderator atoms have
\[
 M=m_n.
\]
\nIf instead $M=135m_n$ and the moderator atoms are essentially at rest, then each head-on collision reduces the neutron energy by the factor
\[
\left(\frac{M-m_n}{M+m_n}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{134}{136}\right)^2.
\]\nAfter $N$ collisions,
\[\nE_f = E_0\left(\frac{M-m_n}{M+m_n}\right)^{2N}.
\]\nSolving for $N$ gives
\[\nN=\frac{\ln(E_f/E_0)}{2\ln\big((M-m_n)/(M+m_n)\big)}.
\]\nUsing $E_0=2\,\mathrm{MeV}=2\times 10^6\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $E_f=0.025\,\mathrm{eV}$,
\[\nN=\frac{\ln(0.025/2\times 10^6)}{2\ln(134/136)}\approx 6.14\times 10^2.
\]\nThus the optimal moderator mass is $\boxed{m_n}$, and for $M=135m_n$ the neutron needs about $\boxed{614}$ collisions.

knowledge_points.name: elastic central collisions
knowledge_points.description: The problem assumes all collisions between neutrons and moderator atoms are elastic and head-on (central), so kinetic energy is conserved and the collision is one-dimensional.

knowledge_points.name: moderator atoms initially at rest
knowledge_points.description: The moderator atoms are at a temperature much lower than T_f, so they can be considered stationary before each collision, simplifying the collision dynamics.

knowledge_points.name: non-relativistic mechanics
knowledge_points.description: The sub-problem explicitly restricts to non-relativistic physics, so classical kinetic energy and momentum formulas are used.

knowledge_points.name: non-relativistic kinetic energy
knowledge_points.description: The kinetic energy of a particle is E = (1/2) m v^2, allowing conversion between speed and energy after each collision.

knowledge_points.name: head-on elastic collision velocity transfer
knowledge_points.description: For a 1D elastic collision between a moving particle of mass m and a stationary particle of mass M, the final speed of the incident particle is v' = |(m - M)/(m + M)| v, derived from conservation of momentum and kinetic energy.

knowledge_points.name: optimal mass matching for energy loss
knowledge_points.description: In elastic collisions, the fractional energy loss of the incident particle is maximized when the target mass equals the incident particle mass, because the factor ((m-M)/(m+M))^2 is minimized (zero) at M = m.

knowledge_points.name: iterative energy reduction factor
knowledge_points.description: After each identical collision, the neutron energy is multiplied by a constant factor; after N collisions, E_N = E_0 * (factor)^N. Solving for N involves taking logarithms of both sides.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, ground yourself in reference’s description of elastic collisions: the experiment with identical glass marbles (or the linear air‑track with springs) shows that when two equal masses collide head‑on and one is initially at rest, momentum and kinetic energy are both conserved, and the incoming object stops completely while the target moves away with the original speed. This is the most efficient transfer of kinetic energy.

For the neutron‑moderator collision, you need to generalise. Write down conservation of momentum and conservation of kinetic energy for a head‑on elastic collision between a neutron (mass \([final result intentionally omitted]\), incoming speed \(v\)) and a moderator atom initially at rest (mass \(M\)). Solve the two equations together to find the neutron’s speed \(v'\) after the collision in terms of \([final result intentionally omitted]\), \(M\) and \(v\). (The algebra will give you a simple rational expression.)

Because the kinetic energy in the non‑relativistic limit is \(K = \frac12 m v^2\), the neutron’s kinetic energy after one collision is the initial energy multiplied by \((v'/v)^2\). The fraction by which the energy is multiplied is therefore a function of the mass ratio \(M/[final result intentionally omitted]\) only.

**Most efficient moderator**: to slow the neutron as much as possible in one collision, you want that multiplying factor to be as small as possible. Look at your expression for \(v'/v\): for what value of \(M\) does it become zero? reference’s marble example gives you the clue – when the masses are equal, the incoming marble stops. Hence the optimal moderator mass is \(M = [final result intentionally omitted]\).

**Number of collisions for \(M = 135\,[final result intentionally omitted]\)**:  
Take the neutron’s speed‑ratio factor you derived, substitute \(M = 135\,[final result intentionally omitted]\), and square it to obtain the kinetic‑energy reduction factor per collision (call it \(f\)). After each central elastic collision the neutron’s energy is multiplied by this same \(f\), so after \(N\) collisions  
\[
E_f = E_0\, f^{\,N}.
\]  
To find \(N\), take the natural logarithm of both sides and solve for \(N\). You will need the given initial and final energies: \(E_0 = 2\,\mathrm{MeV} = 2\times10^6\,\mathrm{eV}\) and \(E_f = 0.025\,\mathrm{eV}\). Be sure to use the same energy units when you compute the ratio \(E_f/E_0\). Plug in your factor \(f\) and carry out the arithmetic.

Following these steps will give you the precise number of collisions needed.

title: BIRDS
problem:
- Jaan Kalda.

A long and thin homogenous beam with uniform thickness and square cross-section floats horizontally in water with its top surface parallel to the water surface. A bird lands on one end of the beam, and as a result, the beam sinks so that the edge of the upper face on the bird's side is exactly at the same height as the water surface, while at the other end of the beam the lower face does not rise above the water. What is the maximum number of such birds that this beam can hold above water?
solution:
Let the beam have length $L$ and mass $M$. Since it is long and thin, we may treat it as staying horizontal.
\nConsider the limiting situation with one bird on the end, when the beam is just at the stated sinking condition. Take moments about the beam’s center.
\nThe beam’s own weight acts at its center, so it gives no torque about that point.
\nFor buoyancy, write the upward buoyant force as if the whole beam were submerged, plus a correction from the part that is above water. The full-submersion part acts through the beam’s center, so it also gives no torque. The only torque comes from the “missing” buoyancy corresponding to the triangular portion above water on the bird’s side.
\nThe center of mass of a triangle lies at the intersection of the medians, i.e. at $2/3$ of the way from the vertex along the altitude. Therefore the line of action of this missing buoyant force is at a distance
$$
\left(\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\right)L=\frac{1}{6}L
$$\nfrom the beam’s center.
\nThe bird’s weight $mg$ acts at the end of the beam, a distance $L/2$ from the center. Torque balance gives
$$\nmg\cdot \frac{L}{2}=F\cdot \frac{L}{6},
$$\nwhere $F$ is the magnitude of the missing buoyant force. Hence
$$\nF=3mg.
$$\nSo the beam can support the original bird plus 3 additional birds before becoming fully submerged.
\nTherefore the maximum number of birds is \boxed{4}.

knowledge_points.name: Archimedes' principle
knowledge_points.description: The buoyant force equals the weight of the displaced fluid. Used to relate the missing buoyancy F to the weight of water displaced by the triangular above-water volume, and to determine the maximum load when the beam is fully submerged.

knowledge_points.name: Rotational equilibrium
knowledge_points.description: For a static floating object, the net torque about any point is zero. The solution takes torques about the beam's center to eliminate contributions from the beam's weight and symmetric buoyancy.

knowledge_points.name: Centroid of a triangle
knowledge_points.description: The centroid of a triangle lies at the intersection of the medians, 2/3 of the way from a vertex along the median. Used to locate the line of action of the missing buoyant force for the triangular above-water portion.

knowledge_points.name: Small-angle beam approximation
knowledge_points.description: Because the beam is long and thin, its tilt angle is small, allowing it to be treated as horizontal for the purpose of lever arms. This simplifies the torque calculation by using the beam's length directly for distances.

knowledge_points.name: Uniform beam symmetry
knowledge_points.description: The beam is homogeneous with uniform cross-section, so its weight and the buoyancy if fully submerged act at its geometric center, producing zero net torque about that point.

knowledge_points.name: Buoyancy decomposition
knowledge_points.description: Instead of integrating the actual buoyancy distribution, the solution considers the buoyancy as if the whole beam were submerged (uniform, acting at the center) and subtracts the missing buoyancy from the emerged part. This isolates the torque contribution to the emerged volume.

title: CHARGED ROD
problem:
— Jaan Kalda. A rod of mass $m$ carries a charge $q$ ; both the charge and the mass are homogeneously distributed over its entire length $l$ . The system is in homogeneous magnetic field of strength $B$ , parallel to the $z$ -axis whereas the rod is in the $x - y$ -plane. Neglect any forces except for the Lorentz force. One end of the rod is

painted red, and the other — blue.

sub_problems.problem: (1) Consider the case when the rod rotates around its centre of mass. What should be the angular speed $\omega$ for the mechanical tension force at the centre of the rod to be zero?
sub_problems.solution:
Consider an infinitesimal piece of the rod. Since the charge and mass are uniformly distributed, every piece has the same charge-to-mass ratio
\[
\frac{\mathrm d q}{\mathrm d m}=\frac{q}{m}.
\]\nIf the rod rotates rigidly with angular speed \(\omega\), a piece at distance \(r\) from the center moves with speed
\[\nv=\omega r.
\]\nFor the tension at the center to be zero, the magnetic Lorentz force on each piece must alone provide the needed centripetal force:
\[
\mathrm d q\,vB=\mathrm d m\,\omega^2 r.
\]\nSubstituting \(v=\omega r\) gives
\[
\mathrm d q\,\omega r B=\mathrm d m\,\omega^2 r.
\]\nFor \(r\neq 0\), this simplifies to
\[
\frac{\mathrm d q}{\mathrm d m}B=\omega.
\]\nUsing \(\mathrm d q/\mathrm d m=q/m\), we obtain
\[
\omega=\frac{qB}{m}.
\]\nTherefore, the rod can rotate with zero tension at the center only at the angular speed
\[
\boxed{\omega=\frac{qB}{m}}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Uniform charge and mass distribution
knowledge_points.description: The rod's charge and mass are homogeneously distributed along its length, giving a constant charge‑to‑mass ratio dq/dm = q/m. This ratio is needed to relate differential magnetic and inertial forces and to simplify the final expression for ω.

knowledge_points.name: Lorentz force law
knowledge_points.description: The force on a charge element dq moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B is dF = dq v × B; here B is perpendicular to v so the magnitude is dq v B and the direction is radial. This is the only external force considered.

knowledge_points.name: Centripetal acceleration for circular motion
knowledge_points.description: For uniform circular motion at angular speed ω and distance r from the centre, the centripetal acceleration is ω² r, so the required net radial force on a mass element dm is dm ω² r. Used to set the dynamics of each piece of the rod.

knowledge_points.name: Rigid body rotation kinematics
knowledge_points.description: For a rigidly rotating object, the tangential speed of a point at distance r from the rotation axis is v = ω r. Used here to express the speed of a rod element in terms of ω and its distance from the centre.

knowledge_points.name: Zero tension condition
knowledge_points.description: When the internal tension at a point is zero, the net internal force on an infinitesimal element at that point vanishes, so the external force alone must provide the centripetal acceleration. For the centre of the rod to be tension‑free, the magnetic Lorentz force on each element must equal the required centripetal force dF_mag = dm ω² r.

sub_problems.guidance:
1. **Model the motion as rigid-body rotation about the centre of mass.**  
   From the kinematics of fixed‑axis rotation (Section 7.3 of Kleppner & Kolenkow), every particle remains at a constant distance \(r\) from the axis and its speed is \(v=\omega r\), where \(\omega\) is the angular speed.

2. **Recall the centripetal requirement for circular motion.**  
   As shown in the polar‑coordinate treatment of acceleration (Sections 1.11.4 and 2.10), a particle moving on a circle of radius \(r\) experiences a radially inward centripetal acceleration of magnitude \(r\omega^{2}\). Therefore, to stay on the circle, the net radial force on the particle must be \(dm\cdot r\omega^{2}\) (directed toward the centre).

3. **Identify the radial force on an infinitesimal piece.**  
   The rod carries charge and mass uniformly, so a small segment has charge \(dq\) and mass \(dm\). It moves in a uniform magnetic field \(\mathbf{B}\) that is perpendicular to the plane of rotation. According to the Lorentz force law (Section 6.1 of Purcell & Morin), the magnetic force on the segment is \(dq\,\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{B}\). Because \(\mathbf{v}\) is tangent to the circle and \(\mathbf{B}\) is out of the plane, the cross product points radially. For the tension at the centre to be **zero**, this magnetic force must be the *only* radial force acting on the segment, so it must exactly provide the needed centripetal force.

4. **Write the radial force balance for a general segment.**  
   Equate the magnitude of the magnetic force to the centripetal requirement:
   \[
   dq\,v\,B = dm\; r\omega^{2}.
   \]
   (The direction is automatically satisfied if the charge and rotation sense match the field orientation – the problem asks for the \(\omega\) that makes this possible.)

5. **Eliminate the segment’s speed.**  
   Use the kinematic relation \(v = \omega r\) (from step 1). Substitute this into the force balance. Simplify the resulting equation; you will see that the distance \(r\) cancels out, leaving a relation that involves \(\omega\), \(B\), and the ratio \(dq/dm\).

6. **Use the uniform distribution of charge and mass.**  
   Because both charge and mass are spread uniformly along the rod, the ratio \(dq/dm\) is the same for every segment and equals the rod’s total charge \(q\) divided by its total mass \(m\). Replace \(dq/dm\) with \(q/m\) in your equation.

7. **Solve for the required angular speed.**  
   Rearrange the resulting relation to isolate \(\omega\). You will obtain an expression that depends only on the total charge \(q\), the total mass \(m\), and the magnetic field strength \(B\).

Once you have \(\omega\) in that form, you have the angular speed for which the tension at the centre vanishes.

sub_problems.problem: (2) Consider now a case when initially the blue end of the rod is at the origin $(x = y =0)$ , and the red end at $x = l$ . The blue end's initial speed is zero while the red end's speed is $v$ , parallel to the $y$ -axis. It turns out that after a certain time $t$ , the red end passes through the origin. Find the smallest possible value for $t$ and express the corresponding value of $v$ in terms of $m$ , $q$ and $l$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Let the rod have total mass $m$ and total charge $q$, uniformly distributed, so every element has the same charge-to-mass ratio $q/m$.
\nFor a system with a uniform charge-to-mass ratio in a homogeneous magnetic field, the total Lorentz force on the system is equivalent to the Lorentz force on a point particle with mass $m$ and charge $q$ located at the centre of mass (COM):

$$m\vec a_C = q\,\vec v_C\times \vec B.$$
\nHence the COM moves in a circle with cyclotron angular frequency

$$\omega = \frac{qB}{m}.$$
\nInitially, the blue end is at $(0,0)$ and the red end at $(l,0)$, so the COM is at $(l/2,0)$. The initial velocities are $0$ for the blue end and $v$ in the $y$-direction for the red end, so the COM speed is

$$v_C = \frac{v}{2}.$$
\nTherefore the COM circle has radius

$$R = \frac{v_C}{\omega} = \frac{mv}{2qB}.$$
\nBecause the rod is rigid, its rotation about the COM has constant angular speed. Since the relative speed of the ends is $v$, the angular speed of rotation is

$$\Omega = \frac{v}{l}.$$
\nNow ask when the red end can reach the origin. The origin is a point on the COM circle only if the COM is at distance $l/2$ from the origin. This can happen earlier than one cyclotron period only if

$$R = \frac{l}{2},$$
\ni.e.

$$\frac{mv}{2qB} = \frac{l}{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad v = \frac{qBl}{m}.$$
\nBut then

$$\Omega = \frac{v}{l} = \frac{qB}{m} = \omega,$$
\nso the rod rotates in step with the COM motion, and the blue end remains at the origin; the red end never reaches the origin in this case.
\nThus the earliest possible moment is after one full cyclotron period,

$$t_{\min} = T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}.$$
\nFor the red end to be at the origin after one period, the rod must have rotated by an odd multiple of $\pi$:

$$\Omega T = (2k+1)\pi, \qquad k\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}.$$
\nUsing $\Omega = v/l$ and taking the smallest $k=0$ gives

$$\frac{v}{l}\cdot \frac{2\pi m}{qB} = \pi,$$
\nso

$$v = \frac{qBl}{2m}.$$
\nTherefore the smallest possible time and the corresponding initial speed are

$$\boxed{t_{\min} = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}}, \qquad \boxed{v = \frac{qBl}{2m}}.$$

knowledge_points.name: centre of mass motion in uniform magnetic field
knowledge_points.description: For a system with uniform q/m in a homogeneous B field, the centre of mass moves like a point particle of total mass m and total charge q under the Lorentz force, executing circular motion with cyclotron frequency ω = qB/m.

knowledge_points.name: cyclotron frequency
knowledge_points.description: The angular frequency ω = qB/m of a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field; used to find the period of the COM circular motion.

knowledge_points.name: kinematic decomposition into COM and relative motion
knowledge_points.description: The motion of a rigid body is split into translation of the centre of mass and rotation about the centre of mass; used to relate the end velocities to v_C and the angular speed Ω.

knowledge_points.name: rigid rod
knowledge_points.description: The rod is treated as a rigid body, so its length is constant and the relative speed of the ends determines a constant angular rotation rate Ω = v/l.

title: PHASE SPIRAL
problem: - Taavet Kalda. Here we shall study the motion of Milky Way stars in the Solar neighbourhood in the direction of the $z$ -axis, i.e. perpendicular to the galactic plane. For our purposes, we can model the galactic gravity field as being created by a continuous mass density $\rho$ (that accounts for the masses of stars, dark matter, gas, interstellar dust, etc), and assume that this mass forms an infinite mirror-symmetric plate, i.e. $\rho \equiv \rho(z)$ and $\rho(z) = \rho(-z)$ is independent of $x$ and $y$ . Throughout the problem, you may assume that each star's total energy is conserved over the entire considered time period. Gravitational constant $G =6.67 \times 10^{-11} \mathrm{~m}^3 \mathrm{~kg}^{-1} \mathrm{~s}^{-2} =4.30 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{pcM}_{\odot}^{-1} (\mathrm{km/s})^2$ .

sub_problems.problem: (1) Assuming that the mass density is constant over the plate's thickness. i.e. $\rho(z) = \rho_0$ , what is the acceleration $a_z$ of a star at a distance $z$ from the mid-plane?
sub_problems.solution:
For an infinite mirror-symmetric mass distribution with constant density \(\rho_0\), the gravitational field must point only in the \(z\)-direction and be proportional to \(z\), with opposite directions above and below the mid-plane.
\nUse Gauss' law for gravity:
\[
\oint \mathbf{g}\cdot d\mathbf{A} = -4\pi G M_{
\text{enc}}.
\]\nChoose a thin cuboid of cross-sectional area \(A\) and half-height \(z\), symmetric about the mid-plane. The field is perpendicular to the two large faces, so the flux is
\[
\oint \mathbf{g}\cdot d\mathbf{A} = 2g_z A,
\]\nwhere the sign is negative because the field points toward the mid-plane.
\nThe enclosed mass is
\[\nM_{\text{enc}} = (2z)A\rho_0.
\]\nThus
\[
2g_zA = -4\pi G (2zA\rho_0).
\]\nCancelling \(2A\) gives
\[
 g_z = -4\pi G\rho_0 z.
\]\nTherefore the acceleration of a star at distance \(z\) from the mid-plane is
\[
\boxed{a_z = -4\pi G\rho_0 z}.
\]

knowledge_points.name: Gauss's law for gravity
knowledge_points.description: Relates the flux of the gravitational field through a closed surface to the enclosed mass: ∮ g·dA = -4π G M_enc. Used here to compute the field inside a uniform slab.

knowledge_points.name: planar symmetry of gravitational field
knowledge_points.description: For an infinite mirror-symmetric mass distribution, the gravitational field is perpendicular to the plane, depends only on distance from the mid-plane, and points toward the mid-plane. This symmetry justifies the direction and uniformity of the field on the Gaussian faces.

knowledge_points.name: Gaussian pillbox for planar symmetry
knowledge_points.description: Choosing a Gaussian surface in the shape of a pillbox (cuboid) with faces parallel to the plane and symmetric about the mid-plane, so that the field is uniform and perpendicular to the faces, making the flux integral trivial.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the acceleration \(a_z\) of a star at distance \(z\) from the mid-plane, you can adapt the method of a Gaussian pillbox for planar symmetry, which you have seen for the electric field of an infinite flat sheet of charge. Because gravity also follows an inverse-square law, Gauss's law for gravity works the same way, with the enclosed mass replacing the enclosed charge and the gravitational field \(\mathbf{g}\) (pointing toward the mid-plane) playing the role of \(\mathbf{E}\).

**Step 1 – Exploit planar symmetry.**
The problem states the plate has constant density and is effectively infinite and mirror-symmetric about the mid-plane. The textbook passage on the *Field of an infinite flat sheet of charge* explains that for such a planar geometry the field must be perpendicular to the plane, with equal magnitude and opposite direction at two points equidistant on opposite sides. By the same reasoning, the gravitational field \(\mathbf{g}\) here points only in the \(z\)-direction, toward the mid-plane, so \(g_z\) is a function of \(z\) only.

**Step 2 – Choose a Gaussian pillbox.**
The *Applications of Gauss’s Law* passage (Figure 2.20) describes how plane symmetry is handled: pick a Gaussian surface that straddles the plane, a “pillbox” with flat faces parallel to the mid-plane. For your problem, place the pillbox symmetrically about the mid-plane, with its two large faces of area \(A\) at \(\pm z\). The field is perpendicular to these faces, so the flux through the side is zero, exactly as in the flat-sheet derivation.

**Step 3 – Apply Gauss’s law for gravity.**
Gauss’s law for gravity states \(\oint \mathbf{g} \cdot d\mathbf{A} = -4\pi G M_{\text{enc}}\). The flux through the pillbox is \(2 g_z A\) (noting that the field points inward, so the sign will be negative). The enclosed mass \(M_{\text{enc}}\) is the mass within the pillbox: the volume is \((2z)A\) and the density is \(\rho_0\), so \(M_{\text{enc}} = 2z A \rho_0\).

**Step 4 – Relate \(g_z\) to \(z\) and then to \(a_z\).**
Insert the flux and enclosed mass into Gauss’s law. Cancel the common factor \(2A\) and solve for \(g_z\). The acceleration \(a_z\) of a star is simply the gravitational field at that location (Newton’s second law per unit mass), so \(a_z = g_z\). You will obtain a linear relationship between \(a_z\) and \(z\), with a constant prefactor that involves \(G\) and \(\rho_0\).

**Step 5 – Compare with a similar worked example.**
The *Through the hole* passage in the Morin textbook solves a gravitational problem with planar symmetry by integration and finds, for a sheet of surface density \(\sigma\), a force proportional to \(x\) for small \(x\). Although that example uses a thin sheet, the same \(z\)-proportionality emerges in your constant-density slab. Your result from Gauss’s law will confirm this simple harmonic form, which is why the remark in that passage notes that for a slab of thickness \(d\) and volume density \(\rho\), one can write \(\sigma = \rho d\) and obtain a frequency \(\omega = \sqrt{2\pi \rho d G / R}\). Your problem is the uniform-density infinite slab, so the acceleration is simply proportional to \(z\).

Now carry out the algebra: write Gauss’s law with the correct sign, cancel factors, and solve for \(a_z\). You should find an expression that depends only on \(G\), \(\rho_0\), and \(z\).

sub_problems.problem:
(2) Consider a star that starts with zero velocity at a distance of $z = a$ from the mid-plane. With what period does it start oscillating around the mid-plane?

In reality, density decreases with growing $|z|$ . Measuring density has been a great challenge because of contributions from dark and other difficult-to-see matter. Here, we consider a breakthrough method of doing it. Consider the distributions of the stars in our neighbourhood on the $z - v_{z}$ phase plane, where each star is a dot with coordinates $(v_{z}, z)$ ; $v_{z}$ denotes the $z$ -component the star's velocity, and $z$ - the vertical coordinate. Initially, these dots were distributed nearly ho

mogeneously, but some time ago, the Milky Way was perturbed externally, probably by a passing-by dwarf galaxy; this shuffled the positions and velocities of stars, creating a bar-shaped overdensity region. When moving within that bar-shaped region from the centre to the periphery, the total energy per mass of stars increased monotonously. Over time, this overdensity region started "winding up", due to the oscillation periods of stars in the vertical plane depending on their oscillation amplitude $z_{\mathrm{m}}$ , and evolved into a spiral pictured below (Antoja et al. 2018, Nature 561, 360). An observation that you need to exploit below is that the ordering of stars by energies along the spiral today remains the same as it was at the time of perturbation.

The oscillation period of stars depends on the amplitude $z_{\mathrm{m}}$ because the gravitational potential (the potential energy per mass) $\Phi(z)$ is not parabolic. In such a case, the period can be approximately found by substituting the real $\Phi(z)$ with a $kz^2$ matching $\Phi(z)$ at $z = z_{\mathrm{m}}$ , i.e. with $k = \Phi(z_{\mathrm{m}}) / z_{\mathrm{m}}^2$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For small vertical displacements the gravitational field of an infinite symmetric mass layer is linear in $z$, so the star executes simple harmonic motion. The oscillation period is
\[\nT=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{4\pi G\rho_0}}=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{G\rho_0}}.
\]
\nTherefore the period of oscillation is \(\boxed{T=\sqrt{\pi/(G\rho_0)}}\).

knowledge_points.description: The vertical acceleration of a star inside an infinite slab of constant mass density ρ₀ is a_z = -4πGρ₀ z, a result obtained in part (1) and used here as the restoring force.

knowledge_points.name: simple harmonic motion
knowledge_points.description: The equation of motion d²z/dt² = -ω²z describes simple harmonic oscillation; the star's motion follows this form with ω² = 4πGρ₀.

knowledge_points.name: period of simple harmonic oscillator
knowledge_points.description: For a simple harmonic oscillator with angular frequency ω, the period is T = 2π/ω, independent of amplitude.

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks you to find the oscillation period of a star that starts from rest at a vertical distance \(z = a\) from the mid-plane of the Galaxy. The textbook passages you have studied cover simple harmonic motion (SHM) and how to find its period. Here is the logical path to follow, using only those ideas.

**Step 1 – Recognize the type of motion from the force law**
The problem states that the star is near the mid-plane and that the gravitational field of an infinite symmetric mass layer is linear in \(z\) for small vertical displacements. A linear restoring force (force proportional to displacement) is exactly the condition for simple harmonic motion, as explained in the textbook: “The force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium” (Section 3.7). Therefore, the star behaves like a harmonic oscillator in the vertical direction.

**Step 2 – Write the equation of motion in standard SHM form**
From the textbook (Section 3.7 and Section 11.2), the equation of motion for a mass \(m\) under a linear restoring force \(F = -kz\) is
\[
m \frac{d^2 z}{dt^2} = -k z,
\]
which can be rearranged into the standard SHM form
\[
\frac{d^2 z}{dt^2} + \omega_0^2 z = 0,
\]
where the angular frequency is \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{k/m}\) (here \(m\) is the mass of the star).  
In our case, the “spring constant” \(k\) comes from the gravitational force law. You need to express the vertical restoring force per unit mass (acceleration) in the form \(-\text{(constant)} \times z\). The constant you obtain will play the role of \(k/m\) in the SHM equation, so you can identify \(\omega_0^2\) directly from the physics of the gravitational field.

**Step 3 – Relate the angular frequency to the period**
The textbook (Section 11.2.1) defines the period \(T\) of a simple harmonic oscillator as the time for one complete cycle:
\[
T = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}.
\]
Once you have found \(\omega_0\) from the equation of motion, the period follows immediately by substituting into this relation.

**Step 4 – Assemble the result**
The only remaining task is to compute \(\omega_0\) from the given information about the gravitational field. The problem statement implies that for an infinite symmetric mass layer the vertical gravitational acceleration is proportional to \(z\), with a proportionality constant involving the density \(\rho_0\) and Newton’s gravitational constant \(G\). Use that proportionality to write \(\omega_0^2\) in terms of \(G\) and \(\rho_0\), then apply \(T = 2\pi/\omega_0\) to obtain the period. The initial condition (starting at rest at \(z = a\)) does not affect the period; in SHM the period is independent of amplitude, as you can see from the derivation in the textbook passages.

Follow these steps carefully, carrying out the algebra yourself to arrive at the final expression for the period.

sub_problems.problem: (4) Assuming that the mass density is almost constant for $|z|\leq 0.3\mathrm{kpc}$ , what is the mass density near $z =0?$
sub_problems.solution:
For a nearly constant mass density near the mid-plane, the gravitational field is approximately that of an infinite uniform slab. Then the vertical acceleration is proportional to $z$ and the potential difference from the mid-plane is quadratic:

\[
\Phi(z)=\int_0^z a_z\,dz'=2\pi G\rho_0 z^2.
\]
\nUsing the first data point, $\Phi(z_1)=180\,\mathrm{km}^2/\mathrm{s}^2$, we solve for the density:

\[
\rho_0=\frac{\Phi(z_1)}{2\pi G z_1^2}.
\]
\nSubstituting the given values gives

\[
\rho_0=6.1\times 10^{-21}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}
=0.090\,M_\odot/\mathrm{pc}^3.
\]
\nTherefore, the mass density near $z=0$ is \boxed{0.090\,M_\odot/\mathrm{pc}^3}.

knowledge_points.description: Relates gravitational potential to mass density; for an infinite slab with constant density, it gives the vertical acceleration a_z = 2πGρ₀ z, which is integrated to obtain the quadratic potential Φ(z) = 2πGρ₀ z².

knowledge_points.name: mirror-symmetric mass distribution

knowledge_points.name: potential from acceleration integration
knowledge_points.description: The potential difference Φ(z) is obtained by integrating the vertical acceleration a_z from the mid-plane to height z, using Φ(z) = ∫₀ᶻ a_z dz′.

knowledge_points.description: The solution uses a numerical value Φ(z₁) = 180 km²/s² from a data point (presumably provided in the problem statement or figure) to solve for ρ₀.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the mass density near \(z=0\), you need to relate the given gravitational potential data to the density via a simplified model. The problem states that the mass density is nearly constant near the mid-plane. This is the key physical setup: a slab of uniform density, symmetric about \(z=0\). 

Here is how to proceed step-by-step, using only concepts from the textbook passages you have studied:

1. **Identify the gravitational acceleration for a uniform slab.**  
   For a mass distribution that is mirror-symmetric about the mid-plane and has nearly constant density \(\rho_0\) near \(z=0\), the vertical gravitational field is linear in \(z\), much like the field inside a uniform slab. The relevant relation (which you can derive from Poisson's equation in its spherically symmetric form, Eq. 10.109, adapted to a planar geometry) is:  
   \[
   a_z = 2\pi G \rho_0 z.
   \]  
   This comes from the idea that Poisson’s equation links the gravitational potential to the density, and for a constant density slab, the field grows linearly with distance from the mid-plane.

2. **Integrate the acceleration to get the potential difference.**  
   The potential \(\Phi(z)\) is related to the acceleration by \(a_z = -d\Phi/dz\). To find the potential near the mid-plane, integrate the acceleration from \(z=0\) (where you can set \(\Phi(0)=0\) by convention) up to some small height \(z\):  
   \[
   \Phi(z) = -\int_0^z a_z \, dz' = \int_0^z 2\pi G \rho_0 z' \, dz'.
   \]  
   This is exactly the method described in the Kleppner & Kolenkow passage on potential energy: the change in potential is the negative integral of the force (or acceleration per unit mass) over displacement. Here, you are integrating the vertical acceleration to get the gravitational potential per unit mass. Carry out this integration to find how \(\Phi(z)\) depends on \(z\).

3. **Apply the given data to solve for \(\rho_0\).**  
   The problem provides a data point: the potential at a specific height \(z_1\). Use the relation you just derived, \(\Phi(z) = 2\pi G \rho_0 z^2\), and plug in that data point. Rearrange to isolate \(\rho_0\). The calculation involves substituting the known values of \(G\), \(z_1\), and \(\Phi(z_1)\) into  
   \[
   \rho_0 = \frac{\Phi(z_1)}{2\pi G z_1^2},
   \]  
   and then evaluating. You will obtain the mass density in units of \(\text{kg/m}^3\), which you can then convert to the astronomical units requested.

The reasoning is grounded in the Poisson equation (Carroll & Ostlie, Eq. 10.109) adapted to the constant-density slab, and the integration of acceleration to potential (Kleppner & Kolenkow, Example 5.8). The mirror symmetry of the mass distribution (Carroll & Ostlie, Section 25.3) ensures the potential is symmetric about \(z=0\) and the field is antisymmetric, supporting the simple linear form. You are now ready to carry out the integration and substitution yourself.

sub_problems.problem:
(5) Dark matter is an "invisible" form of matter that only interacts by gravity. In general, it is found that dark matter forms

halos that extend significantly farther than visible matter structures. By assuming that the dark matter density doesn't vary significantly within the volume of interest and that it starts dominating far away from the galactic plane, from around $z =0.7\mathrm{kpc}$ , estimate the local dark matter density $\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}$ .
sub_problems.solution:
For a mirror-symmetric infinite mass layer, the surface density up to height \(z\) is
\[
\Sigma(z)=\int_0^z \rho(z')\,dz'.
\]\nIf the dark matter density is approximately constant in the region of interest, then for sufficiently large \(z\) we may write
\[
\Sigma(z)\approx \rho_{\mathrm{DM}} z.
\]\nThe vertical gravitational potential is related to the surface density by
\[
\Sigma(z)=\frac{\Phi(z)}{2\pi G z}.
\]\nTherefore, using two large heights \(z_5\) and \(z_6\) where dark matter dominates, the dark matter density can be estimated from the change in surface density:
\[
\Sigma(z_6)-\Sigma(z_5)=\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}(z_6-z_5),
\]\nso
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\approx \frac{1}{2\pi G (z_6-z_5)}\left(\frac{\Phi(z_6)}{z_6}-\frac{\Phi(z_5)}{z_5}\right).
\]\nUsing the data at the largest heights, around \(z\approx 0.7\,\mathrm{kpc}\), gives
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\approx 7.7\times 10^{-22}\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}\approx 0.011\,M_\odot/\mathrm{pc}^3.
\]\nThus the local dark matter density is \(\boxed{0.011\,M_\odot/\mathrm{pc}^3}\).

knowledge_points.name: surface density (column density)
knowledge_points.description: For a plane-symmetric mass distribution, the surface density up to height z is Σ(z) = ∫_0^z ρ(z') dz'. It is needed to relate the mass distribution to the gravitational potential.

knowledge_points.name: potential of uniform infinite slab
knowledge_points.description: For an infinite slab with constant mass density ρ, the gravitational potential (with Φ(0)=0) is Φ(z) = 2π G ρ z², giving Σ(z) = Φ(z)/(2π G z). This relation is used to extract the dark matter density from the measured potential.

knowledge_points.name: constant dark matter density
knowledge_points.description: The dark matter density is assumed to be approximately constant in the region of interest (z ≈ 0.7 kpc), so that ρ_DM can be treated as a constant in the derivation.

knowledge_points.name: dark matter dominance at large z
knowledge_points.description: At heights around z ≈ 0.7 kpc, the total mass density is dominated by dark matter, so ρ(z) ≈ ρ_DM, justifying the use of the constant-density slab potential relation.

sub_problems.guidance:
To estimate the local dark matter density \(\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\), you can use the relationship between the vertical gravitational potential \(\Phi(z)\) and the surface density \(\Sigma(z)\) of mass in the disk, combined with the assumption that the dark matter density is approximately constant in the region of interest (at heights around \(0.7\,\mathrm{kpc}\) and beyond, where the problem states dark matter starts to dominate).

**Step 1: Relate surface density to potential using the uniform infinite slab analogy.**
From the textbook’s treatment of the uniform infinite slab (see the Gauss’s-law and potential integration in the first worked example), a slab with constant volume density produces a gravitational field analogous to the electrostatic field in a uniformly charged slab. For a vertical slice of the Galaxy, the surface density up to height \(z\) is defined as \(\Sigma(z) = \int_0^z \rho(z')\, dz'\). In the regime where the dark matter density is roughly constant (\(\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\)), this simplifies to \(\Sigma(z) \approx \rho_{\mathrm{DM}} z\) when \(z\) is sufficiently large.

Moreover, for a system with planar symmetry, the vertical potential \(\Phi(z)\) and the surface density \(\Sigma(z)\) are related. You have seen in the slab examples that the potential varies quadratically with distance, and its second derivative is proportional to the density (Poisson’s equation, \(\nabla^2 \Phi = 4\pi G \rho\)). For an infinite slab, integrating the field (which is proportional to the enclosed surface density) to get the potential yields a relation that can be rearranged to give
\[
\Sigma(z) = \frac{\Phi(z)}{2\pi G z}.
\]
This is the gravitational analogue of the formula you would obtain from Gauss’s law for a mass sheet.

**Step 2: Use two heights where dark matter dominates to eliminate the contribution from the disk.**
Since the total surface density includes contributions from both visible matter and dark matter, but you are told that dark matter starts dominating far from the galactic plane (around \(z = 0.7\,\mathrm{kpc}\)), you should select two large heights \(z_5\) and \(z_6\) from the data you have (presumably from a table or graph of \(\Phi(z)\)). At these heights, the change in surface density between them is almost entirely due to the dark matter, because the visible matter is concentrated closer to the midplane.

Write the surface density at each height using the formula above:
\[
\Sigma(z_5) = \frac{\Phi(z_5)}{2\pi G z_5}, \quad
\Sigma(z_6) = \frac{\Phi(z_6)}{2\pi G z_6}.
\]
Then, using the assumption of constant dark matter density, the difference in surface density is
\[
\Sigma(z_6) - \Sigma(z_5) = \rho_{\mathrm{DM}} (z_6 - z_5).
\]

**Step 3: Combine the equations to solve for \(\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\).**
Substitute the expressions for \(\Sigma(z_5)\) and \(\Sigma(z_6)\) into the difference equation. You will obtain an equation where \(\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\) is the only unknown. Rearrange to isolate \(\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\):
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{DM}} \approx \frac{1}{2\pi G (z_6 - z_5)} \left( \frac{\Phi(z_6)}{z_6} - \frac{\Phi(z_5)}{z_5} \right).
\]

**Step 4: Perform the calculation.**
Now, plug in the values of \(\Phi(z)\) at the two largest heights you have (around \(0.7\,\mathrm{kpc}\)), the corresponding \(z\) values, and the gravitational constant \(G\). Remember to keep units consistent (e.g., convert kpc to meters if using SI, or use appropriate astronomical units). Compute the difference in the \(\Phi/z\) terms, divide by \(z_6 - z_5\), and then by \(2\pi G\). This will give you the local dark matter density \(\rho_{\mathrm{DM}}\) in \(\mathrm{kg/m^3}\). You may then convert to solar masses per cubic parsec (\(M_\odot/\mathrm{pc}^3\)) if the problem expects those units, using the conversion factors for mass and distance.

By following this method, you are effectively measuring how much additional mass (and therefore potential) is added as you move outward through the constant-density dark matter halo, which is exactly the strategy the reference solution uses.

title: HOT PLATE
problem:
- Jaan Kalda. Tools: a resistor with resistance $R =220\Omega$ mounted in one corner of a foam plastic plate (resistor's upper surface is painted black), a power supply (on the power supply, readings other than voltage are not reliable!), two identical $40\mathrm{mm} \times 40\mathrm{mm}$ aluminium plates that differ only in their coating: one is polished, the other is anodized black and can be assumed to be a black body, 4 silicone rubber pads of thickness $t =0.8\mathrm{mm}$ , a foam cup with hot water, tweezers, a stopwatch, an infrared thermometer (press the knob twice and take a reading), sheets of graph paper and paper tissues for cleaning. Note that for thermal radiation, water can be also assumed to be a black body.

Do not apply voltages higher than $U =15\mathrm{V}$ to the resistor as this will lead to a melting of the foam plastic! Please handle foam cups with care and do not break them (you will not get a spare one)!

sub_problems.problem: (1) Determine the emissivity (thermal radiation power relative to a black body) of the polished aluminium plate. Hint: infrared thermometers measure temperature via thermal radiation power (assume it is calibrated for objects of $100\%$ emissivity); within relevant temperature ranges, this relationship can be approximated as linear,
sub_problems.solution:
Both aluminium plates were heated together in hot water, so after drying they had the same actual temperature. The black plate can be treated as a black body, so its infrared thermometer reading gives the true plate temperature. The polished plate, however, reflects part of the surrounding thermal radiation, so the thermometer reading is a mixture of the plate’s own radiation and the ambient radiation.
\nIf the ambient temperature is $T_0$ and the plate’s actual temperature is $T$, then the IR thermometer, calibrated for a black body, reads
\[\nT_{\text{reading}}=\varepsilon T+(1-\varepsilon)T_0.
\]\nFor the black plate, $\varepsilon=1$, so its reading is the actual temperature $T_{\text{black}}$. Hence for the polished plate,
\[\nT_{\text{polished}}=\varepsilon T_{\text{black}}+(1-\varepsilon)T_0.
\]\nSolving for $\varepsilon$ gives
\[
\varepsilon=\frac{T_{\text{polished}}-T_0}{T_{\text{black}}-T_0}.
\]\nUsing the three measurements:
\[
\varepsilon_1=\frac{26.2-22.9}{70.9-22.9}\approx 0.069,
\qquad
\varepsilon_2=\frac{26.0-22.9}{70.7-22.9}\approx 0.065,
\qquad
\varepsilon_3=\frac{25.4-22.9}{70.2-22.9}\approx 0.053.
\]\nTheir mean value is about
\[
\varepsilon\approx 0.062\approx 0.06.
\]\nTherefore, the emissivity of the polished aluminium plate is \boxed{0.06\pm 0.01}.

knowledge_points.name: emissivity
knowledge_points.description: Need to know that emissivity is the ratio of thermal radiation power emitted by a surface to that of a blackbody at the same temperature, as this is the quantity the sub‑problem asks to determine.

knowledge_points.name: blackbody
knowledge_points.description: Must understand that a blackbody is a perfect absorber and emitter (emissivity = 1) and that the anodized black plate is assumed to be one, so its IR reading gives the true plate temperature.

knowledge_points.name: blackbody plate assumption
knowledge_points.description: The problem states the anodized black plate can be treated as a blackbody, so its emissivity is exactly 1 and its measured temperature equals its actual surface temperature.

knowledge_points.name: Kirchhoff's law of thermal radiation for opaque surfaces
knowledge_points.description: For the opaque polished plate, absorptivity equals emissivity and, since no transmission, reflectivity = 1 − emissivity. This justifies expressing the reflected ambient radiation as (1−ε)T₀ in the thermometer reading.

knowledge_points.name: linearized grey‑body IR thermometer reading
knowledge_points.description: The infrared thermometer, calibrated for a blackbody and assumed linear in the working range, gives a reading T_read = ε T_surface + (1−ε) T_ambient for an opaque grey surface. The sub‑problem solves this equation for emissivity ε.

sub_problems.guidance:
The polished aluminium plate is not a perfect blackbody, so its thermal radiation is weaker than that of a blackbody at the same temperature.  You will determine its **emissivity** – the factor that tells you by how much its emission falls short of a blackbody (see the excerpt in Carroll & Ostlie where an “efficiency factor” e is introduced for this purpose).

Both plates were heated together and then dried, so they share the same actual temperature.  The **black** plate is treated as a blackbody because its surface absorbs almost all incident radiation and thus, by Kirchhoff’s law (Example 1‑2 in Eisberg & Resnick), it is also a perfect emitter.  The infrared thermometer is calibrated to read the temperature of a blackbody directly, so the reading you get from the black plate gives you the true **actual temperature** of the plates.

The polished plate, however, reflects much of the ambient radiation – it is a poor absorber and therefore, by Kirchhoff’s law, a poor emitter.  The total radiation leaving its surface in the direction of the thermometer consists of two parts:  
- the plate’s own **emitted** radiation (scaled down by the emissivity ε), and  
- the **reflected** fraction of the ambient radiation (fraction 1 – ε, because the surface is opaque).  

The thermometer cannot tell these apart; it simply measures the combined infrared power and, assuming a blackbody, converts it to a temperature reading.  As the problem hint states, for the narrow temperature range here this relationship can be taken as **linear**, so the reading is a weighted average:

\[
T_{\text{reading}} = \varepsilon\,T_{\text{actual}} + (1-\varepsilon)\,T_{\text{ambient}}
\]

where \(T_{\text{ambient}}\) is the temperature of the surroundings.

Now follow this procedure:
1. From your data, note the ambient temperature \(T_0\).
2. For each measurement set, use the black‑plate reading as the actual plate temperature \(T\).
3. Write the linear equation above for the polished plate, inserting its reading and the values from step 1 and step 2.
4. Rearrange the equation symbolically to isolate the unknown emissivity \(\varepsilon\).  (You will obtain an expression that depends only on the three temperatures.)
5. Apply this expression to each of the three measurement sets you have.  The results give you individual estimates of ε.
6. Compute the **mean** of the three ε‑values and estimate its uncertainty (for example, from the spread or the standard error of the mean).

By carrying out these steps yourself with the numerical data, you will obtain the emissivity of the polished aluminium plate.  The idea that a good reflector is a poor emitter – and therefore has a low emissivity – is exactly what Kirchhoff’s law predicts, and you will see it confirmed in your final number.
