title: Bullet in Cylinder
problem: A hollow cylinder of mass $M$ and radius $R$ rests on a rough horizontal surface. A projectile of mass $m < M$ having a velocity $u$ directed horizontally exactly towards the middle of the cylinder as shown in the figure. The shell gets stuck in the cylinder wall, after which the shell starts to move, slipping on the surface. The coefficient of static and kinetic friction between the cylinder and the horizontal surface are the same, and are equal to $\mu < 2$ .

sub_problems.problem: (a) In which direction does the cylinder rotate? State your answers for different values of $\mu$ .
sub_problems.solution:
Combining both force equations in the vertical direction and our 'torque' equation and that $F_{0} = \mu N$ , we get

$$\alpha = \frac{g}{R} \cdot \frac{(\mu -1) m + \mu M}{(1- \mu) m + M}$$

$$N = \frac{(2 m + M) M g}{M + (1- \mu) m}$$

Note that $\alpha$ and $N$ tend to infinity as $\mu \rightarrow \mu_0=1+ \frac{M}{m}$ . This means that the normal force can even increase infinitely if a large impulse is provided by the bullet. For $m = M$ , $\mu_0=2$ , and since the problem says that $\mu < 2$ , we know that both $N$ and $\alpha$ are finite and always remain true.

Now, for the direction of rotation, let us observe when $\alpha$ changes parity. Notice that for $\mu < \mu_1= \frac{m}{M + m}$ , we have $\alpha < 0$ , meaning that the cylinder will rotate counterclockwise. Let us try to understand what could've caused such a situation? This could've been caused by a large impulse by the bullet, when it exceeded the impulse due to friction. Similarly, for $\mu > \mu_1$ , we have that the cylinder rotates clockwise. Note that since $m < M$ , $0 < \mu_1 < \frac{1}{2}$ . So are answers for the first part are

$$\text{Directionofrotation} = \left\{\begin{array}{c l} \text{Clockwise} & \text{if} \mu > \frac{m}{M + m} \\ \text{Counter - clockwise} & \text{if} \mu < \frac{m}{M + m} \end{array} \right.$$

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law (translation)
knowledge_points.description: Used to write the vertical force equation for the system's center of mass: net vertical force (normal minus total weight) equals total mass times vertical acceleration of the center of mass.

knowledge_points.name: Newton's second law (rotation)
knowledge_points.description: Used to write the torque equation about the cylinder's geometric center: net torque equals total moment of inertia times angular acceleration.

knowledge_points.name: Kinetic friction law
knowledge_points.description: The magnitude of kinetic friction is μN, and its direction opposes the relative motion at the slipping contact point. Used to express the friction force in terms of the normal force and to determine its direction in the torque equation.

knowledge_points.name: Center of mass acceleration
knowledge_points.description: The acceleration of the center of mass is the mass-weighted average of the accelerations of the system's parts. Used to relate the vertical acceleration of the center of mass to the bullet's vertical acceleration.

knowledge_points.name: Rigid body acceleration relation
knowledge_points.description: The acceleration of a point on a rigid body is the sum of the center's acceleration, tangential acceleration α×r, and centripetal acceleration. At the initial instant, the vertical component of the bullet's acceleration is αR (with sign depending on position and convention).

knowledge_points.name: Moment of inertia (hollow cylinder)
knowledge_points.description: The moment of inertia of a hollow cylinder about its central axis is MR²; a point mass on the rim adds mR². Used to compute the total moment of inertia I = (M+m)R² in the torque equation.

knowledge_points.name: Torque (moment of force)
knowledge_points.description: Torque about a point is r×F; in 2D, τ = xF_y − yF_x. Used to compute the torques from the bullet's weight and the friction force about the cylinder's center.

knowledge_points.name: Horizontal surface constraint
knowledge_points.description: The cylinder's geometric center remains at a constant height because it rests on a horizontal surface, so its vertical acceleration is zero. This simplifies the vertical kinematics.

knowledge_points.name: Initial translation direction
knowledge_points.description: Just after the collision, the cylinder translates in the direction of the bullet's initial velocity (to the right in the figure) and has negligible initial angular velocity. This determines that the contact point slips to the right, so kinetic friction acts to the left, giving a clockwise torque.

sub_problems.guidance:
To find how the cylinder rotates, you need to relate its translational and rotational motion using the laws you’ve studied. Here’s the logical sequence to follow, grounded in your textbook.

**Step 1 – Identify forces and their directions**
Sketch the cylinder and mark every force acting on it. From the problem context, you have the cylinder’s weight, a normal force from the surface, and kinetic friction. The textbook explains kinetic friction: its magnitude is \( F = \mu N \), where \( N \) is the normal force, and its direction opposes the relative motion of the two surfaces in contact. Decide carefully which way the cylinder would slide relative to the surface, so you can draw the friction force in the correct direction.

**Step 2 – Write the translational equation for the center of mass**
Apply Newton’s second law in its translational form, \( \mathbf{F} = M\mathbf{a} \), to the cylinder’s center of mass. As shown in the textbook’s discussion of force and acceleration, you need to sum the force components in each direction separately. Write the vertical force equation first: the normal force and weight appear here, and since the cylinder does not accelerate vertically, the net vertical force is zero. This gives you an expression relating \( N \) to the weight.

Then write the horizontal force equation. The only horizontal force is kinetic friction. Set the net horizontal force equal to the total mass (cylinder plus any other object that may be moving with it) times the acceleration \( a \) of the center of mass.

**Step 3 – Write the rotational equation about the center of mass**
The textbook shows that for rotation about the center of mass, even if the center of mass is accelerating, you can use \( \tau_0 = I_0 \alpha \). The torque \( \tau_0 \) is the torque around the center of mass due to external forces. Evaluate this torque: only friction produces a torque about the center of mass, because the weight and normal force act through the center of mass. Use the definition of torque, \( \tau = r \times F \), or its magnitude \( |\tau| = r_\perp F \), to compute the torque from friction. Pay attention to the sign (sense of rotation) as illustrated in the textbook’s torque exposition.

The moment of inertia \( I_0 \) for a cylinder about its central axis should be known from previous study; if not, it is a standard result you can look up. Set the net torque equal to \( I_0 \alpha \).

**Step 4 – Relate translation and rotation via the no-slip condition**
Because the cylinder rolls without slipping, the acceleration of its center of mass \( a \) and its angular acceleration \( \alpha \) are related. The textbook does not state this condition explicitly in the given passages, but from the geometry of rolling you know that \( a = R\alpha \) (with the sign depending on your chosen coordinate directions). Use this to eliminate \( a \) or \( \alpha \) from your equations.

**Step 5 – Combine equations to find \( \alpha \) in terms of \( \mu \)**
You now have three equations: vertical force balance, horizontal force equation, and the rotational equation, plus the rolling constraint. Combine them to express the angular acceleration \( \alpha \) as a function of \( \mu \) and the given masses. This step involves algebra; do it carefully.

**Step 6 – Determine the direction of rotation from the sign of \( \alpha \)**
Once you have \( \alpha \) as a function of \( \mu \), examine its sign. The sign of \( \alpha \) tells you the direction of rotation according to the coordinate system you chose. Find the critical value of \( \mu \) where \( \alpha \) changes sign (i.e., where the numerator of your expression becomes zero). For \( \mu \) larger than this critical value, \( \alpha \) has one sign; for \( \mu \) smaller, it has the opposite sign. State the direction of rotation (clockwise or counterclockwise) for each range of \( \mu \).

**Note on the textbook’s friction example**
The worked example on a block sliding down a wedge shows how to set up force equations with friction and how to interpret the sign of the acceleration for different \( \mu \). The same logical approach applies here: after finding the expression for \( \alpha \), analyze how its sign depends on \( \mu \) to decide the physical direction of motion.

sub_problems.problem: (b) Find its angular acceleration about the centre of the cylinder just after the impact.
sub_problems.solution:
Just after the impact the bullet is stuck to the wall of the cylinder, so the bullet+cylinder is a rigid body. Let $\alpha$ be the angular acceleration about the centre of the cylinder, $a$ the horizontal acceleration of the centre, and $N$, $F_{\rm fr} = \mu N$ the normal and kinetic friction forces from the ground. The vertical force balance and the horizontal Newton/torque equations for the system give
$$N = (M + m)g + m\alpha R,\qquad (M + m)\,a = -\mu N,\qquad I\,\alpha = -F_{\rm fr}\,R + m a R,$$
with the moment of inertia about the cylinder centre $I = MR^2 + mR^2$. (The bullet sits on the cylinder wall at radius $R$.) Eliminating $N$ and $a$ yields
$$\boxed{\alpha = \frac{g}{R}\,\frac{(\mu - 1)m + \mu M}{(1-\mu)m + M}}.$$
Note that $|\alpha|$ stays finite because the problem assumes $\mu < 2 \le 1 + M/m$, so the denominator does not vanish.

title: Mathematical Physics
problem:
The study of mathematics has almost always paved the way for the development of new ideas in physics. Newtonian mechanics could not be possible without first inventing calculus, and general relativity could not have existed without heavy development in tensors. However, there are numerous cases where physical insight have paved the way for mathematics.

Perhaps the most notable would be the Brachistochrone problem, which asks for the path that leads to the fastest descent influenced by gravity between two given points. While it is solvable through the calculus of variations, Newton proposed an easier solution by modelling the path of light through a medium with a variable index of refraction. You may read about this problem and the fascinating history behind it here.

We will not be dealing with this specific problem, but rather multiple short mathematics problems that can be can be represented with a physical analog. To receive points, you must use the suggested physical set-up.

sub_problems.problem:
(a) Show that for small values of $x$ , we have

$$\cos (x) =1- \frac{x^{2}}{2}.$$

Physical Setup: Consider a small object moving in a circle.
sub_problems.solution:
Consider a small particle starting from rest on a circular path. It quickly and uniformly accelerates to a speed $v$ in a very small time interval $\Delta t$ such that $\frac{v\Delta t}{R} \ll 1$ where $R$ is the radius of the circle.

Since this time interval is so small, the acceleration is directed inwards. Without loss of generality, let us define the inwards direction as the positive $+y$ direction. The displacement $\Delta y$ is given by $R(1- \cos \theta)$ which gives:

$$R \left(1- \cos \theta\right) = \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$$

At time $t$ , since the particle hasn't moved very far, the inwards acceleration is still pointed in the $+y$ direction and using equations for circular motion, it has a magnitude of:

$$a = \frac{v^{2}}{R}$$

Making the substituting, we can simplify:

$$1- \cos \theta = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{v t}{R}\right)^{2}$$

Since $vt = R\theta$ is the distance traveled, this simplifies to:

$$1- \cos \theta = \frac{1}{2} \theta^{2} \Longrightarrow \boxed{\cos \theta =1- \frac{1}{2} \theta^{2}}$$

knowledge_points.name: Small-angle radial motion approximation
knowledge_points.description: For a particle in uniform circular motion passing through the top of the circle, for small subsequent angles the centripetal acceleration direction remains approximately constant. This allows the radial displacement to be calculated using one-dimensional constant-acceleration kinematics with a = v^2/R and zero initial radial velocity.

knowledge_points.name: Centripetal acceleration formula
knowledge_points.description: For uniform circular motion of speed v and radius R, the acceleration is directed toward the center with magnitude a = v^2/R. Used to express the inward acceleration in the physical analog.

knowledge_points.name: Kinematic equation for constant acceleration from rest
knowledge_points.description: For motion with constant acceleration a and zero initial velocity in that direction, the displacement is Δy = 1/2 a t^2. Used to relate the inward displacement to time.

knowledge_points.name: Radial displacement from top of circle
knowledge_points.description: The vertical (radial) displacement from the top of a circle of radius R after moving through an angle θ along the circumference is R(1 - cos θ). Used to equate the geometric displacement to the kinematic expression.

knowledge_points.name: Arc length formula
knowledge_points.description: The distance traveled along a circular arc of radius R subtending angle θ is s = Rθ. With constant speed v, this gives vt = Rθ, relating time and angle. Used to eliminate t in favor of θ.

sub_problems.guidance:
First, identify the quantities you can relate from the known physics of circular motion. The object moves along a circle of radius \( R \) at constant speed \( v \). After a short time \( t \) the arc length travelled is \( s = vt \). Use the arc length formula from the textbook (Kleppner & Kolenkow Solution Manual — Rolling drum and Spinning loop examples) to write this arc length in terms of the angle \( \theta \) swept out: \( s = R\theta \). Therefore \( \theta = vt / R \); this connects the motion variables \( v \), \( t \) and the angle.

Second, consider the radial (centripetal) acceleration. The textbook passages (Morin 9.2.2, Kleppner 1.11.4) tell you that for uniform circular motion the acceleration is directed radially inward with magnitude \( a = v^2 / R \). For a very small angular displacement, the direction of this acceleration stays nearly unchanged (pointing, say, along the \( +y \)

(b) A ladder of length $\ell$ with a thickness of $0.3\mathrm{m}$ is transported around a right angled corner where the two hallways leading up to it have a width of $3\mathrm{m}$ and $5\mathrm{m}$ . What is the maximum length of the ladder such that it can be successfully transported across?

Physical Setup: Consider the ladder as a compressed spring that can freely expand in only its longitudinal direction. Do not explicitly take derivatives. Instead, consider a force/torque balance. You may or may not need to solve an equation numerically.
sub_problems.solution:
Treating the ladder as a spring, we see that its length is directly related to its potential energy. Determining the point at which the ladder's length is at a minimum is equivalent to determining the point at which the rigid spring's potential energy is at a minimum. Using the fact that:

$$F = - \frac{d U}{d x}$$

implies that when the potential energy is at a minimum, the net force must be equal to zero. Therefore, we can set up a force and torque balance in order to solve for the shortest length. There are three normal forces to take into account. Balancing forces give two equations, and a torque balance gives the third. Solving a system of three equations will allow us to solve the problem.

Perhaps a slicker way is to realize that these three forces must be concurrent. At least two of the normal force vectors will intersect, and performing a torque balance where the pivot is selected to be that intersection point, these two normal force vectors will not contribute to a torque. In order to satisfy $\sum \tau =0$ , the third normal force vector must also intersect at this same place. This turns it into a geometry problem.

Solving the problem geometrically or analytically, you end up solving the equation:

$$\frac{a \cos \theta - \ell}{\sin^{2} \theta} = \frac{b \sin \theta - \ell}{\cos^{2} \theta}$$

which is possible to be solved numerically (or solved through an approximation). This wasn't specified on the exam, so most teams who arrived at this equation would have received the marks.

Solving, we get $L \approx 10.6 \, \mathrm{m}$ .

Selecting a pivot at the intersection of two forces eliminates their torques, forcing the third force to pass through the same point and turning the problem into geometry.

title: Flat Earth
problem: In this problem, we will explore the true gravitational model of the earth, not the one that is claimed in most textbooks. Contrary to popular belief, the Earth is a flat circle of radius $R$ and has a uniform mass per unit area $\sigma$ . The Earth rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ .

sub_problems.problem:
(a) A pendulum of length $\ell$ that is constrained to only move in one plane is placed on the ground at the center of the Earth. The pendulum has more than one angular frequency of small oscillations. Find the value of each angular frequency of small oscillations $\Omega(0), \Omega_1(0), \ldots$ in terms of $\sigma, \omega, \ell$ , and physical constants and the equilibrium angle $\theta, \theta_1, \ldots$ that the frequency occurs at. Assume for all parts that $\ell \ll R$ .

An equilibrium angle corresponds to the angle with

respect to the vertical where there is an equilibrium point.
sub_problems.solution:
The first thing that we note is that the acceleration due to the gravitational force is different as compared to the one on Earth. Consider a cylindrical Gaussian surface that has its circular faces parallel to the Earth. From Gauss's Law of gravitation, we can calculate the acceleration due to gravity on a flat plane to be

$$4 \pi G m =2 \times \pi r^{2} g \Longrightarrow g =2 \pi G \sigma$$

by substituting $m = \sigma \pi r^2$ . Let us now consider a small displacement of the mass $m$ from the origin. We see that there are two forces involved: the centrifugal force, and the gravitational force. We now draw a free-body diagram as shown below:

Note that the gravitational force will be restoring and is given by $mg\sin \theta \approx mg\theta$ . The centrifugal force is directed outwards and is given by $m\omega^2\ell \sin \theta \cos \theta \approx m\omega^2\ell \theta$ . Writing Newton's Laws on the

pendulum now gives us

$$m \ell \ddot{\theta} = m \omega^{2} \ell \theta - m g \theta \Rightarrow \ddot{\theta} = - \left(\frac{g}{\ell} - \omega^{2}\right) \theta .$$

An equilibrium position occurs when $\ddot{\theta} =0$ . This tells us that the two equilibrium positions are defined by

$$\theta_{1} =0, \qquad \theta_{2} = \arccos \left(\frac{g}{\omega^{2} \ell}\right).$$

For oscillations near $\theta_{1} =0$ , we can use small-angle approximations gives us

$$\ddot{\theta} = - \left(\frac{g}{\ell} - \omega^{2}\right) \theta .$$

Therefore, we see $\Omega(0) = \sqrt{\frac{g}{\ell} - \omega^2} = \boxed{\sqrt{\frac{2\pi G\sigma}{\ell} - \omega^2}}$ .

For oscillations near $\theta_{2} = \arccos \left(\frac{g}{\omega^{2}\ell}\right)$ , we let $\theta = \theta_{1} + \varphi$ where $\varphi \ll \theta_{1}$ . Using a first order approximation tells us that

$$\ddot{\varphi} + \left(\frac{g}{\ell} + \omega^{2} \varphi \sin \theta_{1} - \omega^{2} \cos \theta_{1}\right) (\sin \theta_{1} + \varphi \cos \theta_{1}) =0.$$

Simplifying gives us

$$\ddot{\varphi} = - \left(\omega^{2} \sin^{2} \theta_{1}\right) \varphi .$$

This tells us that $\Omega_1(0) = \omega \sin \theta = \omega \sqrt{1- \frac{g^2}{\omega^4\ell^2}} = \boxed{\frac{1}{\omega\ell}\sqrt{\omega^4\ell^2-4\pi^2G^2\sigma^2}}$

Remark 1: We can find the gravitational acceleration on the planet by in fact another way of analyzing the force per each infinitesimal ring. We can split the flat Earth into many tiny rings as shown below

Each ring provides a force of $d\vec{F}$ . If each ring has a thickness $dR$ , our force will be given by

$$d F = \frac{G m \sigma}{h^{2} + R^{2}} \cos \theta \cdot (\pi (R + d R)^{2} - \pi R^{2}).$$

Using the fact that $\cos \theta = \frac{h}{\sqrt{h^2+ R^2}}$ , we then find that

$$d F = \frac{G m \sigma}{h^{2} + R^{2}} \frac{h}{\sqrt{h^{2} + R^{2}}} \cdot (\pi (R + d R)^{2} - \pi R^{2}).$$

Using a first order approximation gives us

$$(\pi (R + d R)^{2} - \pi R^{2}) \approx 2 R d R.$$

We then find by substituting that,

$$d F = \frac{2 G m R \sigma h}{\left(h^{2} + R^{2}\right)^{3/2}} d R.$$

Now, integrating this force $dF$ from 0 to $\infty$ gives us

$$F = \int_{0}^{\infty} d F =2 G m \sigma h \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{R}{\left(h^{2} + R^{2}\right)^{3/2}} d R =2 \pi G \sigma m.$$

The gravitational acceleration is then given by

$$g \equiv \frac{2 \pi G \sigma m}{m} =2 \pi G \sigma .$$

Remark 2: We can find the equation of motion with the Euler-Lagrange equations. Let us consider a rotating frame at the center of the Earth. The pendulum's coordinates are then given by

$$(x, y, z) = (\ell \sin \theta ,0, - \ell \cos \theta)$$

which implies that the velocity of the pendulum is given by

$$(\dot{x}, \dot{y}, \dot{z}) = (\ell \dot{\theta} \cos \theta ,0, \ell \dot{\theta} \sin \theta).$$

In the fixed frame, the pendulum has an additional velocity from the centrifugal force which is given by

$$\vec{\omega} \times \vec{r} = (0,0, \omega) \times (\ell \sin \theta ,0, - \ell \cos \theta) = (0, \omega \ell \sin \theta ,0).$$

We now write the lagrangian of the system as

$$\begin{array}{l} \mathcal{L} \equiv T - V \\ = \frac{1}{2} m \sqrt{\left(\ell \dot{\theta} \cos \theta\right)^{2} +0^{2} + \left(\ell \ddot{\theta} \sin \theta\right)^{2}} + \frac{1}{2} m \ell^{2} \omega^{2} \sin^{2} \theta + m g \ell \cos \theta \\ = \frac{1}{2} m \ell^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2} + \frac{1}{2} m \ell^{2} \omega^{2} \sin^{2} \theta + m g \ell \cos \theta . \\ \end{array}$$

Now, using the Euler-Lagrange equations gives us

$$\frac{d}{d t} \left(\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \dot{\theta}}\right) = \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta} \Longrightarrow \ddot{\theta} = - \left(\frac{g}{\ell} - \omega^{2} \cos \theta\right) \sin \theta .$$

We have two cases:

Case 1: (oscillations for $\Omega(0)$ ) If $\omega < \sqrt{\frac{g}{\ell}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\pi G\sigma}{\ell}}$ , we see that the oscillations are stable. The oscillations would follow the equation

$$\theta (t) = A_{1} \cos (\Omega (0) + \phi_{1})$$

where $A_{1}$ and $\phi_1$ are constants to be determined from initial conditions.

Case 2: (oscillations for $\Omega_1(0)$ ) If $\omega > \sqrt{\frac{2\pi G\sigma}{\ell}}$ we see that the oscillations are stable. The oscillations would follow the equation

$$\varphi (t) = A_{2} \cos (\Omega_{1} (0) + \phi_{2})$$

where $A_{2}$ and $\phi_{2}$ are constants to be determined from initial conditions.

If $\omega = \sqrt{\frac{2\pi G\sigma}{\ell}}$ the oscillations are neutrally stable but do not display stable small oscillations.

sub_problems.problem: (c) The entire pendulum is moved a horizontal distance $r \ll R$ away from the center of the Earth. It is oriented so that it is constrained to only move in the radial direction. Now, find the new angular frequency $\Omega(r)$ of small oscillations about the lowest equilibrium point in terms of the given parameters, assuming that $\omega^2 r$ is much less than the local gravitational acceleration.
sub_problems.solution:
We use the fact that, for small oscillations of an object subject to a potential $U(x)$ , the frequency of small oscillations will be defined as

$$\omega = \sqrt{\frac{U^{\prime \prime} (x)}{m_{\mathrm{eff}}}}.$$

The potential energy is due to the gravitational potential and the centrifugal potential:

$$U = - m g \ell \cos \theta - \frac{1}{2} m \omega^{2} (r + \ell \sin \theta)^{2}$$

We see that

$$\frac{d^{2} U}{d \theta^{2}} = m g \ell \cos \theta + m \omega^{2} r \ell \sin \theta + m \omega^{2} \ell^{2} (\sin^{2} \theta - \cos^{2} \theta)$$

When evaluated at $\theta = \theta_0$ , the equilibrium position,

$$U^{\prime \prime} (\theta_{0}) = m g \ell \cos \theta_{0} + m \omega^{2} r \ell \sin \theta_{0} + m \omega^{2} \ell^{2} (\sin^{2} \theta_{0} - \cos^{2} \theta_{0}) = k_{\mathrm{eff}}.$$

We now need to find the effective mass. Note that the kinetic energy is given by

$$\frac{1}{2} m \ell^{2} \dot{\theta}^{2} = \frac{1}{2} m_{\text{eff}} \dot{\theta}^{2} \Rightarrow m_{\text{eff}} = m \ell^{2}.$$

Thus, the frequency is given by

$$\Omega (r) = \sqrt{\frac{k_{\mathrm{eff}}}{m_{\mathrm{eff}}}} = \sqrt{\frac{g}{\ell} \cos \theta_{0} + \frac{\omega^{2} r}{\ell} \sin \theta_{0} + \omega^{2} (\sin^{2} \theta_{0} - \cos^{2} \theta_{0})}$$

Now, we have $\cos \theta_0= \frac{g}{\sqrt{\omega^4r^2+ g^2}}\approx 1- \frac{\omega^4r^2}{2g^2}$ and $\sin \theta_0\approx \frac{\omega^2r}{g}$ . Substituting,

$$\Omega (r) = \sqrt{\frac{g}{\ell} - \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{2 g \ell} + \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{g \ell} + \frac{\omega^{6} r^{2}}{g^{2}} - \omega^{2} + \frac{\omega^{6} r^{2}}{2 g^{2}}}$$

$$\Omega (r) = \sqrt{\Omega (0)^{2} + \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{2 g \ell} + \frac{3 \omega^{6} r^{2}}{2 g^{2}}} = \boxed{\sqrt{\Omega (0)^{2} + \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{4 \pi G \sigma \ell} + \frac{3 \omega^{6} r^{2}}{8 \pi^{2} G^{2} \sigma^{2}}}}$$

sub_problems.problem: (d) The angular frequencies $\Omega(0)$ and $\Omega(r)$ are both measured and the difference is found to be $\Delta \Omega$ . Assuming that $\Delta \Omega \ll \Omega(0)$ and $\omega^2 \ll \frac{g}{\ell}$ , determine $\sigma$ in terms of $\omega, r, \Omega(0), \Delta \Omega$ , and physical constants.
sub_problems.solution:
Note that we can write

$$\Omega (r) = \sqrt{\Omega (0)^{2} + \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{2 g^{2}} \left(\frac{g}{\ell} +3 \omega^{2}\right)} = \Omega (0) \sqrt{1+ \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{2 g^{2}} \left(\frac{\frac{g}{\ell} +3 \omega^{2}}{\frac{g}{\ell} - \omega^{2}}\right)}$$

Therefore, we have

$$\Omega (r) \approx \Omega (0) \sqrt{1+ \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{2 g^{2}}} \approx \Omega (0) \left(1+ \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2}}{4 g^{2}}\right)$$

Therefore, $\Delta \Omega = \frac{\omega^4r^2}{4g^2}\Omega (0)$ . This implies that

$$g^{2} =4 \pi^{2} G^{2} \sigma^{2} = \frac{\omega^{4} r^{2} \Omega (0)}{4 \Delta \Omega}$$

We can solve for $\sigma$ to get $\sigma = \boxed{\frac{\omega^2r}{4\pi G}\sqrt{\frac{\Omega(0)}{\Delta\Omega}}}$ .

title: Boltzmann Statistics
problem: In this problem, we will explore Boltzmann Statistics and using it to build similar models for quantum particles such as bosons and fermions.

sub_problems.problem:
(a) Consider a energy of a gaseous molecule in space is given by 5

$$E = E_{0} (| x |^{r} + | y |^{r} + | z |^{r})$$

where the coordinates of the molecule are represented by $(x,y,z)$ , $E_0$ is a constant with appropriate units, and $r$ is a non-negative real number. The system is in thermal equilibrium with a reservoir of temperature $T$ . Calculate explicitly using appropriate statistical methods, the average energy of a thermodynamic system consisting of such gaseous molecules, considering the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. Analyse your result and provide a qualitative argument to support it.

Hint: If you are not familiar with how to solve this part, try part (b) first.
sub_problems.solution:
In Maxwell-Boltzmann's distribution, the probability that an isolated particle occupies the point $A(x,y,z)$ is given by

$$\mathrm{d} \mathbb{P} (E) = \mathcal{P} (E) \mathrm{d} V = - \frac{e^{- \frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T}}}{Z}$$

where $Z$ denotes the partition function. Note that although we write the probability such that an isolated particle occupied the space, but for a system of $N$ particles, there would be an extra factor of $N!$ in the partition function, but since the particles are considered independent, this factor would cancel out in further calculation anyway. Now for the calculation of $Z$ , we normalize the probability $\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}(E)$ over all possible states; meaning that we convert the probability function to the probability density function by summing total probability as 1. This gives us

$$Z = \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} e^{- \beta \cdot E_{0} \cdot (| x |^{r} + | y |^{r} + | z |^{r})} d x d y d z$$

(More accurately, the partition function of a set of molecules would be found by summing, and not integrating over the space, but since it is a continuous function, the sum reduces to an integral.) From the statistical definition of average energy per unit particle, we have

$$\langle E \rangle = \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} E \cdot \mathrm{d} \mathbb{P} (E) = \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} E_{0} \left(| x |^{r} + | y |^{r} + | z |^{r}\right) \mathrm{d} \mathbb{P} (E)$$

Substituting the partition function from above, we obtain

$$\langle E \rangle = \frac{\iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} E_{0} (| x |^{r} + | y |^{r} + | z |^{r}) e^{\left(- \frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T} (| x |^{r} + | y |^{r} + | z |^{r})\right)} \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z}{\iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} e^{\left(- \frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T} (| x |^{r} + | y |^{r} + | z |^{r})\right)} \mathrm{d} x \mathrm{d} y \mathrm{d} z}$$

$$\langle E \rangle = \frac{\sum_{x_{i} \in (x , y , z)} \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k T}} E_{0} x_{i}^{r} \mathrm{d} x_{i}}{\sum_{x_{i} \in (x , y , z)} \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T}} \mathrm{d} x_{i}}$$

Now let us evaluate some integrals to obtain a closed form for $\langle E\rangle$ above. Applying by-parts, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T}} \mathrm{d} x_{i} = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{- \left(\left(\frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T}\right)^{\frac{1}{r}} x_{i}\right)^{r}} \mathrm{d} x_{i} \\ = x_{i} \left(\frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T}\right)^{1/ r} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T}} \Bigg |_{0}^{\infty} + r \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T}} \mathrm{d} \left(x_{i} \left(\frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T}\right)^{\frac{1}{r}}\right) \\ \end{array}$$

Note that after applying the bounds, $x_{i}\left(\frac{E_{0}}{k_{B}T}\right)^{1/ r}e^{-\frac{E_{0}x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B}T}}\Bigg|_{0}^{\infty}$ reduces to 0. This gives

$$\int_{0}^{\infty} e^{- \left(\left(\frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T}\right)^{\frac{1}{r}} x_{i}\right)^{r}} \mathrm{d} x_{i} = r \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T}} \mathrm{d} \left(x_{i} \left(\frac{E_{0}}{k_{B} T}\right)^{\frac{1}{r}}\right)$$

The same integral ratio appeared in our original average energy per unit particle expression. However, the above integral was performed across one-dimension. In three dimensions (the integral is nondegenerate across all three dimensions), our average energy per particle expression becomes

$$\langle E \rangle = \frac{\iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k T}} E_{0} x_{i}^{r} \mathrm{d} x_{i}}{\sum_{x_{i} \in (x , y , z)} \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^{3}} e^{- \frac{E_{0} x_{i}^{r}}{k_{B} T}} \mathrm{d} x_{i}} = E_{0} \times \frac{3 k_{B} T}{r E_{0}} = \frac{3 k_{B} T}{r}$$

Hence, the average energy of a thermodynamic system of $N$ such particles is

$$\langle E_{s} \rangle = \boxed{\frac{3 N k_{B} T}{r}}$$

As a sanity check, note that the average energy is independent of $E_0$ , which was expected. This is because for any quadratic function in space (specifically, here this is $r =2$ ) we have the "Law of Equipartition", which states that every degree of freedom has an average energy of $1/2k_{B}T$ , which is confirmed by the obtained expression.

Aliter: Consider the partition function:

$$Z = \sum e^{- \beta E} = \sum e^{- \beta E_{0} (x^{r} + y^{r} + z^{r})}$$

We can turn this into the integral form:

$$Z = \frac{1}{\delta x \delta y \delta z} \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} e^{- \beta E_{0} (x^{r} + y^{r} + z^{r})} d x d y d z$$

Letting $a = (\beta E_0)^{1/r} x$ , $b = (\beta E_0)^{1/r} y$ , and $c = (\beta E_0)^{1/r} z$ , we can rewrite this as:

$$Z = \frac{1}{\delta x \delta y \delta z (\beta E_{0})^{3/ r}} \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} \int_{- \infty}^{\infty} e^{- (a^{r} + b^{r} + c^{r})} d a d b d c = \frac{C}{\delta x \delta y \delta z (\beta E_{0})^{3/ r}}$$

where $C$ is a constant, equal to the integral. The average energy is given by:

$$\begin{array}{l} E_{\mathrm{avg}} = \frac{-1}{Z} \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \beta} \\ = \frac{- \delta x \delta y \delta z (\beta E_{0})^{3/ r}}{C} \frac{C}{\delta x \delta y \delta z} \left(\frac{-3}{r} E_{0} (\beta E_{0})^{\frac{-3- r}{r}}\right) \\ = \frac{3}{r \beta} \\ = \frac{3}{r} k_{B} T \\ \end{array}$$

sub_problems.guidance:
To find the average energy of a single gaseous molecule in this system, and then of the whole thermodynamic system, you need to follow a clear statistical mechanics path using the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, the canonical partition function, and the formula that links internal energy to the partition function. The textbook passages give you all the necessary tools.

**Step 1: Express the probability and the partition function.**
The energy of a single molecule is given by the expression in the problem. Because the gas is in thermal equilibrium with a reservoir at temperature T, the probability that a molecule occupies a particular state (with coordinates x, y, z) is proportional to the Boltzmann factor, \(e^{-\beta E}\). As described in the textbook passage on the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, we treat each molecule as a small system connected to a heat reservoir (the rest of the gas). Therefore, the probability density is proportional to \(e^{-\beta E(x,y,z)}\).

To turn this into a proper probability, you need to normalize it. The normalization constant is the canonical partition function Z, which the textbook defines as a sum over all states of the Boltzmann factors:
\[
Z = \sum_{\alpha} e^{-\beta E_{\alpha}}.
\]
Here, the states are continuous (the molecule can be at any position in space), so the sum becomes an integral over all space: \(Z = \iiint_{\mathbb{R}^3} e^{-\beta E(x,y,z)} \,dx\,dy\,dz\). (The hint in the reference solution about N! factors is not relevant for a single-particle average, as the problem states you are considering the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution; the continuous approximation to an integral is justified by the textbook’s discussion of the density of states and the transition from sums to integrals.)

**Step 2: Relate the average energy to Z.**
The textbook shows that the internal energy U (here the average energy of a single particle, \(\langle E \rangle\)) can be obtained directly from the partition function without computing the full probability integral:
\[
U = -\frac{d \ln Z}{d\beta}.
\]
This is far simpler than evaluating the ratio of two triple integrals directly. So, once you have Z as a function of \(\beta = 1/(k_B T)\), you can find \(\langle E \rangle\) by taking a derivative.

**Step 3: Simplify Z using symmetry and a change of variables.**
Because the energy \(E(x,y,z)\) is a sum of three independent terms, each depending on only one coordinate, the triple integral for Z factorizes into a product of three identical one-dimensional integrals. Each one-dimensional integral involves \(e^{-\beta E_0 |x_i|^r}\) (with \(x_i\) representing x, y, or z). Because the integrand is even, you can integrate from 0 to ∞ and multiply by 2.

Now introduce a dimensionless variable to simplify the one-dimensional integral. Look for a substitution of the form \(u = (\beta E_0)^{1/r} x_i\). This is exactly the technique used in the textbook when evaluating partition functions and average energies for systems where the energy depends on a power of a coordinate; it extracts all the \(\beta\) and \(E_0\) dependence out of the integral. After this substitution, the integral becomes some constant multiplied by \((\beta E_0)^{-3/r}\). The constant itself is an integral that does not depend on \(\beta\) or \(E_0\), and you do not need to evaluate it — it will cancel out when you compute \(\ln Z\) and differentiate.

**Step 4: Compute \(\langle E \rangle\) using \(-\frac{d \ln Z}{d\beta}\).**
Write \(\ln Z\) as \(\ln(\text{constant}) - \frac{3}{r} \ln(\beta E_0)\). Differentiating with respect to \(\beta\) (remember, \(E_0\) and the constant are independent of \(\beta\)) yields \(\langle E \rangle = \frac{3}{r} k_B T\). (The textbook’s example for the simple harmonic oscillator and the equipartition result both illustrate how internal energy is obtained from a partition function via differentiation and how the equipartition result emerges.)

**Step 4: Extend to a system of N molecules and provide qualitative analysis.**
For a thermodynamic system of N independent, non-interacting molecules (the textbook emphasizes that for non-interacting particles, the partition function of the whole system is simply the product of single-particle partition functions), the total average energy is just N times the single-particle average energy. Therefore, multiply your single-molecule result by N.

For the qualitative argument: note that the result is independent of \(E_0\) and depends only on N, T, and r. The textbook passage on the equipartition theorem states that for a classical system in thermal equilibrium, the average energy per quadratic degree of freedom (i.e., where the energy depends on a squared coordinate) is \(\frac{1}{2}k_B T\), leading to a total average kinetic energy of \(\frac{3}{2}k_B T\) for three translational degrees of freedom. Your result should reduce to this familiar equipartition value when \(r=2\), because then the energy is quadratic in the coordinates (like kinetic energy \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2\)). For general r, the energy per degree of freedom is not simply \(\frac{1}{2}k_B T\); instead, the power law changes the average energy to \(\frac{1}{r}k_B T\) per coordinate direction, which is why the total average energy becomes \(\frac{3}{r}k_B T\) per particle. The independence from \(E_0\) is expected because \(E_0\) just sets the energy scale, but the average energy at thermal equilibrium is determined solely by the temperature and the number of accessible degrees of freedom (the shape of the energy function), as the system explores higher-energy states with Boltzmann-weighted probabilities.

Now, carry out the variable substitution, perform the differentiation, and write down the final average energy for N particles.

sub_problems.problem:
(b) Consider a specific case in which

$$E = E_{0} (x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2})$$

except where $|x|, |y|, |z| < 2$ and particles can only exist at integer values of $x, y, z$ . If the system is still in thermal equilibrium at a temperature $T$ , calculate the average energy.
sub_problems.solution:
The energy of any given particle can be 0, 1, 2, 3 (working in units where $E_0=1$ ). We need to calculate the Boltzmann factor for each energy as well as how many ways each energy can be achieved.

- Energy 0: $e^{0\beta} =1 \rightarrow 1$ way.
- Energy 1: $e^{1\beta} \to 6$ ways.
- Energy 2: $e^{2\beta} \to 12$ ways.
- Energy 3: $e^{3\beta} \to 8$ ways.

In total, the partition function is:

$$Z =1+6 e^{\beta} +12 e^{2 \beta} +8 e^{3 \beta}$$

The average energy is thus:

$$\begin{array}{l} E_{\mathrm{avg}} = - \frac{1}{Z} \frac{\partial Z}{\partial \beta} \\ = - \frac{6 e^{- \beta} +24 e^{-2 \beta} +24 e^{-3 \beta}}{1+6 e^{- \beta} +12 e^{-2 \beta} +8 e^{-3 \beta}} \\ \end{array}$$

Note that this can be factored further.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{E_{\mathrm{avg}} = - \frac{6 e^{- \beta} +24 e^{-2 \beta} +24 e^{-3 \beta}}{1+6 e^{- \beta} +12 e^{-2 \beta} +8 e^{-3 \beta}}}

sub_problems.guidance:
This problem asks you to find the average energy of a single particle that can only sit at integer coordinates \(x, y, z\), with the restriction that \(|x|, |y|, |z| < 2\). The energy of a particle at a given location is \(E = E_0(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)\). Because the coordinates are discrete and limited, the particle has a finite set of possible energy values—this is a “discrete energy levels” situation, as described in your textbook when it introduces quantized states (see the discussion of atomic energy states and the idea that bound systems have discrete levels).

Your textbook tells you that when a system is in thermal equilibrium at temperature \(T\), the probability of finding it in a state with energy \(E_i\) is proportional to the Boltzmann factor \(e^{-\beta E_i}\), where \(\beta = 1/(k_B T)\) (see the chapter summary and the section on the Boltzmann distribution). To compute the average energy, you need the partition function \(Z\), which is the central tool introduced in Chapter 20. The “big idea” there is a two-step recipe: (1) write down \(Z = \sum_\alpha e^{-\beta E_\alpha}\), summing over all distinct microstates \(\alpha\); (2) use \(Z\) to find quantities like the internal energy \(U\) via \(U = -\frac{d \ln Z}{d\beta}\) (or equivalently \(U = -\frac{1}{Z}\frac{dZ}{d\beta}\)).

Here is the method you should follow, step by step.

**Step 1: Identify all possible microstates and their energies.**
The particle’s coordinates can only be integers satisfying \(|x|,|y|,|z| < 2\). This means each coordinate can take one of three values: \(-1, 0, 1\). Count how many distinct \((x,y,z)\) triplets exist. Each triplet is a microstate. For each microstate, compute its energy using \(E = E_0(x^2 + y^2 + z^2)\). You will find that many different microstates give the same energy; the number of microstates with a given energy is called the **degeneracy** of that energy level, a concept explained in your textbook in the context of rotational energy levels and atomic quantum numbers.

**Step 2: Construct the partition function.**
The partition function is the sum over all microstates, not just over distinct energy levels. However, because microstates with the same energy contribute equally, you can group them:  
\[
Z = \sum_{\text{all microstates}} e^{-\beta E} = \sum_{\text{energy levels } E} (\text{degeneracy of } E) \times e^{-\beta E}.
\]
For each distinct energy value you found in Step 1, multiply its Boltzmann factor by its degeneracy (the number of coordinate triplets that yield that energy). Sum these terms to get \(Z\) as a function of \(\beta\). This is exactly what the textbook does for the rotational energy levels, where each level \(J\) has a degeneracy factor \((2J+1)\) multiplying its Boltzmann factor.

**Step 3: Compute the average energy.**
Once you have \(Z\), the average energy (which the textbook calls the internal energy \(U\) for a single-particle system) is obtained from the formula  
\[
U = -\frac{1}{Z}\frac{dZ}{d\beta} \quad \text{or} \quad U = -\frac{d\ln Z}{d\beta}.
\]
The textbook derives this in Section 20.2 and illustrates it for the simple harmonic oscillator. Apply whichever form you find easier. Because your \(Z\) is a sum of exponentials, the derivative is straightforward: differentiate each term with respect to \(\beta\), then divide by \(Z\) and apply the minus sign.

**Step 4: Simplify (if desired).**
The resulting expression can be left as is, or you can factor it if you notice a common structure. The reference solution shows that the numerator and denominator can both be written in terms of powers of \(e^{-\beta E_0}\), but performing that algebra is your task.

Remember: the key physical ideas are all in your textbook—discrete levels lead to a sum over states, degeneracy accounts for multiple microstates with the same energy, and the partition function is the gateway to all thermodynamic averages. Work through the counting carefully, and then let the mathematics of \(Z\) do the rest.

sub_problems.problem:
(c) In this system, there are two particles. What is the probability that at least one of these particles will be in the ground state (energy is zero) if:

(i) The two particles are distinct.
(ii) The two particles are identical bosons.
(iii) The two particles are identical fermions (fermions follow Pauli exclusion principle).

For each of the parts, assume that there are no other interactions (e.g. electromagnetism) and focus mainly on a statistical argument.
sub_problems.solution:
The probability of at least one particle being in the ground state is equal to one minus the probability of no particles being in the ground state. The probability of having some energy $E_{i}$ is:

$$P_{i} = \frac{\left(\text{number of ways this can happen}\right) e^{- \beta E_{i}}}{Z}$$

Summing up all the probabilities for nonzero energies gives us:

$$P_{\mathrm{atleast 1 ingroundstate}} =1- \frac{Z_{\mathrm{restrictions}}}{Z_{\mathrm{norestrictions}}}$$

(i) If two particles are distinct, they can take on energies 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Similar to part (b), we list out all the possible ways to achieve these energies if there are no restrictions:

- Energy 0: $1^{2} =1$ way.
- Energy 1: $2(1 \cdot 6) =12$ ways.
- Energy 2: $2(1 \cdot 12) +6^2=60$ ways.
- Energy 3: $2(1 \cdot 8) +2(6 \cdot 12) =160$ ways.
- Energy 4: $2(6 \cdot 8) +12^{2} =240$ ways.
- Energy 5: $2(12 \cdot 8) =192$ ways.
- Energy 6: $8^{2} =64$ ways.

If no particles are in the ground state, then:

- Energy 2: $6^{2} =36$ ways.
- Energy 3: $2(6 \cdot 12) =144$ ways.
- Energy 4: $2(6 \cdot 8) +12^{2} =240$ ways.
- Energy 5: $2(12 \cdot 8) =192$ ways.
- Energy 6: $8^{2} =64$ ways.

The probability is thus:

$$P_{1} =1- \frac{36 e^{-2 \beta} +144 e^{-3 \beta} +240 e^{-4 \beta} +192 e^{-5 \beta} +64 e^{-6 \beta}}{1+12 e^{- \beta} +60 e^{-2 \beta} +160 e^{-3 \beta} +240 e^{-4 \beta} +192 e^{-5 \beta} +64 e^{-6 \beta}}$$

Perhaps an easier way to do this problem is to think of the partition functions as generating functions. The partition function for placing two particles with no restrictions is the square of placing a single particle:

$$Z_{2, \text{norestriction}} = Z_{1, \text{norestriction}}^{2} = \left(1+6 e^{- \beta} +12 e^{-2 \beta} +8 e^{-3 \beta}\right) \left(1+6 e^{- \beta} +12 e^{-2 \beta} +8 e^{-3 \beta}\right)$$

Any combination of two terms will yield a different distinct possibility. Therefore, it is possible to express the answer in terms of

$$Z \equiv \left(1+6 e^{- \beta} +12 e^{-2 \beta} +8 e^{-3 \beta}\right)$$

but we will not be doing that here, time to bash away!

(ii) If two particles are identical bosons, they can take on the same energy, except we have to adjust for overcounting. With no restrictions:

- Energy 0: 1 way.
- Energy 1: $1 \cdot 6=6$ way.
- Energy 2: $1 \cdot 12+ \binom{6}{2} +6=33$ ways.
- Energy 3: $1 \cdot 8+6 \cdot 12=80$ ways.
- Energy 4: $6 \cdot 8+ \left(\binom{12}{2} +12\right) =126$ ways.
- Energy 5: ${12} \cdot 8= {96}$ ways.
- Energy 6: $\binom{8}{2} +8=36$ ways.

With restrictions:

- Energy 2: $\binom{6}{2} +6=21$ ways.
- Energy 3: $6 \cdot 12=72$ ways.
- Energy 4: $6 \cdot 8+ \left(\binom{12}{2} +12\right) =126$ ways.
- Energy 5: ${12} \cdot 8= {96}$ ways.
- Energy 6: $\binom{8}{2} +8=36$ ways.

So:

$$P_{2} =1- \frac{21 e^{-2 \beta} +72 e^{-3 \beta} +126 e^{-4 \beta} +96 e^{-5 \beta} +36 e^{-6 \beta}}{1+6 e^{- \beta} +33 e^{-2 \beta} +80 e^{-3 \beta} +126 e^{-4 \beta} +96 e^{-5 \beta} +36 e^{-6 \beta}}$$

(iii) If two particles are identical fermions, they can take on the same energy (except ground state), except they can't be in the same state.

- Energy 1: $1 \cdot 6=6$ ways.
- Energy 2: $1 \cdot 12+1 \cdot \binom{6}{2} =27$ ways.
- Energy 3: $1 \cdot 8+6 \cdot 12=80$ ways.
- Energy 4: $6 \cdot 8+ \left(\binom{12}{2}\right) =114$ ways.
- Energy 5: ${12} \cdot 8= {96}$ ways.

- Energy 6: $\binom{8}{2}=28$ ways.

With restrictions:

- Energy 2: $\cdot \binom{6}{2} =15$ ways.
- Energy 3: $6 \cdot 12=72$ ways.
- Energy 4: $6 \cdot 8+ \left(\binom{12}{2}\right) =114$ ways.
- Energy 5: $12 \cdot 8=96$ ways.
- Energy 6: $\binom{8}{2}=28$ ways.

$$P_{3} =1- \frac{15 e^{-2 \beta} +72 e^{-3 \beta} +114 e^{-4 \beta} +96 e^{-5 \beta} +28 e^{-6 \beta}}{6 e^{- \beta} +27 e^{-2 \beta} +80 e^{-3 \beta} +114 e^{-4 \beta} +96 e^{-5 \beta} +28 e^{-6 \beta}}$$

knowledge_points.name: distinguishable particles

knowledge_points.name: identical bosons

sub_problems.guidance:
Your goal is to find the probability that **at least one** particle is in the ground state. The most efficient route is to use the complement rule:  
\[
P(\text{at least one in ground}) = 1 - P(\text{no particle in ground})
\]

The probability of a specific arrangement (microstate) is proportional to the Boltzmann factor \(e^{-\beta E}\), and the normalized probability requires the partition function \(Z\). From the textbook,  
\[
Z = \sum_{\alpha} e^{-\beta E_\alpha}
\]  
where the sum runs over **all allowed states** of the two‑particle system.  
Therefore, for each particle type you can write  
\[
P(\text{at least one in ground}) = 1 - \frac{Z_{\text{no particle in ground}}}{Z_{\text{all allowed states}}}
\]  
where the restricted \(Z\) includes only those states in which neither particle is in the ground state.

The only difference among (i), (ii), and (iii) is **which two‑particle states are allowed** and **how they are weighted** (i.e., how you count microstates). The textbook explains that identical particles come in two classes: bosons can share a quantum state, fermions cannot (Pauli exclusion principle), and for distinguishable particles every labeling of the particles gives a distinct state.

To proceed, follow these steps in order for each case:

1. **List the single‑particle energy levels and their degeneracies** (the problem’s context gives these; you already have the numbers of ways a single particle can have a given energy).  
2. **Construct the set of two‑particle states** with total energy \(E_{\text{tot}}\).  
   - For **distinguishable particles** (case i): every ordered pair of single‑particle states is a distinct microstate. The textbook’s worked example for a two‑state system (Fig. 21.2b) shows exactly this counting: four states for two distinguishable particles.  
   - For **identical bosons** (case ii): symmetric combinations under particle exchange are the only allowed states. The example in Section 29.2 (“Anyons”) demonstrates how to form symmetric states: states where both particles are in the same single‑particle level are allowed (and count once), and states with particles in different levels are represented by the symmetric linear combination, which counts as one microstate.  
   - For **identical fermions** (case iii): the Pauli exclusion principle forbids both particles from occupying the same single‑particle state. Again the Section 29.2 example shows that only the antisymmetric combination of two different single‑particle states survives, so each unordered pair of distinct states contributes exactly one microstate.  
3. **Count the microstates for each total energy** twice: once with **no restriction** (all allowed states) and once with the **restriction that neither particle is in the ground state**. The ground state is the single‑particle level with energy zero, so in the restricted count you simply exclude that level from the single‑particle menu.  
4. **Form the two partition functions** by multiplying the number of microstates at each total energy by the Boltzmann factor \(e^{-\beta E_{\text{tot}}}\) and summing over all total energies.  
5. **Assemble the probability** using the complement formula above. The result will be a ratio of sums of the form  
   \[
   1 - \frac{\sum (\text{restricted degeneracy})\, e^{-\beta E}}{\sum (\text{full degeneracy})\, e^{-\beta E}} .
   \]

Do not plug in numbers yet. First, verify your counting for each case by comparing with the logic of the two‑state example in the textbook (distinguishable → 4 states, indistinguishable bosons → 3 symmetric states, indistinguishable fermions → 1 antisymmetric state). Once you are confident in the degeneracy factors, you can substitute them and the Boltzmann factors into the ratio. The algebra will simplify to the final expression; carry out that substitution yourself.

kp_used: identical fermions and Pauli exclusion principle

sub_problems.problem:
(d) Rank the probabilities in part (c) from highest to lowest when the temperature is

(i) high
(ii) low

For each, explain qualitatively why this must be true.
sub_problems.solution:
For high temperature: fermion $\mathcal{L}$ distinct $\mathcal{L}$ boson. As well as including the math, justification needs to be on the lines of every state having an equal probability, and thus we want the ratio between desired and total states.

For low temperatures, it's reversed. Particles will tend to settle in the lowest energy state (which is what we desire), and distinct particles have more ways to do it than identical bosons. Fermions cannot have two particles in the same state, further decreasing its chances.
sub_problems.answer: \boxed{\text{high: fermion } > \text{ distinct } > \text{ boson}}, \boxed{\text{low: boson } > \text{ distinct } > \text{ fermion}}

knowledge_points.name: high-temperature limit
knowledge_points.description: At high temperatures (kT much larger than energy level spacing), all accessible microstates become approximately equally probable, so probabilities reduce to ratios of state counts.

knowledge_points.name: low-temperature limit
knowledge_points.description: At low temperatures (kT much smaller than energy level spacing), the system is overwhelmingly likely to be found in its ground state(s).

knowledge_points.name: probability from microstate counting
knowledge_points.description: When all microstates are equally probable, the probability of an event equals the number of microstates satisfying the condition divided by the total number of microstates.

knowledge_points.name: Bose-Einstein bunching
knowledge_points.description: Identical bosons have a statistical tendency to occupy the same quantum state, enhancing the probability of multiple occupancy compared to distinguishable particles.

knowledge_points.name: Pauli exclusion principle
knowledge_points.description: Identical fermions cannot occupy the same quantum state, which reduces the probability of finding two fermions both in the ground state.

knowledge_points.name: distinguishable particles statistics
knowledge_points.description: Classical distinguishable particles have no quantum symmetry constraints; each particle independently occupies single-particle states, leading to intermediate probabilities between bosons and fermions in these rankings.

sub_problems.guidance:
To rank the probabilities from part (c) for high and low temperature, you need to think about how the particles (distinguishable, identical bosons, and identical fermions) occupy the available energy states under these two extreme conditions. The reasoning is qualitative, grounded in the statistical and quantum principles covered in your textbook passages.

**For the high-temperature limit:**

1.  First, recall what “high temperature” means for a system with discrete energy levels. From the discussion of the two-level system and the simple harmonic oscillator in the textbook (Blundell & Blundell, Sections 20.2(a) and 20.2(b)), at high temperature, the thermal energy $k_B T$ is much larger than the energy spacing. Consequently, all accessible energy states become roughly equally probable.
2.  The textbook passage on “probability from microstate counting” (Eisberg & Resnick, 11-2 and Appendix C) explains that the Boltzmann distribution is derived by assuming all possible divisions of the system’s energy occur with equal probability. At high temperatures, this classical limit is approached.
3.  Therefore, for all three types of particles, the probability of finding the system in the specific configuration from part (c) is simply proportional to the number of microstates corresponding to that configuration, divided by the total number of microstates. The total number of microstates becomes very large and similar for all three cases at high temperature.
4.  Now, focus on the number of ways to achieve the *desired* configuration. The textbook passage on “distinguishable particles statistics” (Eisberg & Resnick, 11-2) states that in the classical counting method, identical particles are treated as distinguishable. This means distinguishable particles have the maximum number of ways to be arranged into the given state configuration. For identical particles, quantum mechanics restricts this counting. The passage on the “Pauli exclusion principle” (Eisberg & Resnick, 9-3; Blundell & Blundell, 29) states that fermions cannot share the same quantum state, which restricts the number of allowed microstates for the desired configuration. Bosons, as stated in the same passage, *can* share quantum states, so their number of allowed microstates is intermediate between distinguishable particles and fermions.
5.  Qualitatively combine these ideas: since the probability is proportional to the number of ways to achieve the desired state, the system with the most ways (distinguishable) is the most probable, and the one with the fewest ways (fermions, due to the exclusion principle) is the least probable. Bosons, which can share states but are still identical, fall in the middle.

**For the low-temperature limit:**

1.  Now, consider what “low temperature” means. As described in the two-level system example (Blundell & Blundell, 20.2(a)), at low temperature, the system tends to settle into its lowest energy state to minimize its internal energy $U$. The entropy $S$ becomes $k_B \ln \Omega$, where $\Omega$ is the degeneracy of that ground state.
2.  The desired configuration from part (c) is very likely the ground state or a low-energy configuration. The probability ranking is now determined by how “easily” each type of particle can access this specific low-energy configuration relative to all other possibilities.
3.  For fermions, the Pauli exclusion principle (Eisberg & Resnick, 9-3) strictly forbids more than one particle from occupying the exact same quantum state. If the desired low-energy configuration requires particles to pile into the single lowest energy state, this is impossible for fermions. They must stack up into higher energy states, making this specific configuration forbidden or extremely less probable.
4.  For identical bosons, the phenomenon of “Bose-Einstein bunching” (suggested by the macroscopic occupation of the ground state in the BEC passage from Blundell & Blundell, 30.4) means they have an enhanced tendency to occupy the same quantum state, especially the lowest one. This makes the desired low-energy configuration more probable for bosons than for distinguishable particles, which lack this quantum “attraction” to the ground state.
5.  Distinguishable particles, which follow classical statistics (Eisberg & Resnick, 11-2), do not have the bosonic bunching enhancement. They can occupy the ground state, but they have many other ways to distribute themselves among the low-lying states. Thus, their probability for the specific desired configuration is lower than that of bosons, but higher than that of fermions (for which the configuration may be entirely Pauli-blocked).

In summary, for the high-temperature case, the ranking is determined by the number of microstates for the desired configuration (distinguishable > bosons > fermions). For the low-temperature case, the ranking is reversed due to bosonic bunching favoring the ground state and the Pauli exclusion principle suppressing it for fermions. Use these qualitative principles to order the three cases in each temperature limit.

title: Radiation
problem:
The Nobel Prize in Physics 2019 was awarded for providing a new understanding of the universe's structure and history, and the first discovery of a planet orbiting a solar-type star outside our solar system.

The Sun is one of several hundred billion stars in our home galaxy, the Milky Way, and there should be planets orbiting most of those stars. So far, astronomers have discovered over 4,000 planets around other stars and they are continuing their search in the area of space closest to us.

Since ancient times, humans have speculated whether there are worlds like our own, with points of views at the extremes expressed thousands of years ago. In modern times, the possibility of observing planets orbiting stars other than the Sun was proposed more than 50 years ago, and has grown into a vast and ever-expanding theory to make the evolution of the universe more clear to us than ever before. In 1995, the very first discovery of a planet outside our solar system, an exoplanet, orbiting a solar-type star was made. This discovery challenged our ideas about these strange worlds and led to a revolution in astronomy. The more than 4,000 known exoplanets are surprising in their richness of forms, as most of these planetary systems look nothing like our own, with the Sun and its planets. These discoveries have led researchers to develop new theories about the physical processes responsible for the birth of planets.

(Taken from the Nobel Prize in Physics 2019 summary, and the Laureates' popular science and scientific views.)

In this problem, we analyse and create a model for a system of two fictitious celestial bodies: an exoplanet and a solar-type star. Unless specified otherwise, consider the two bodies to be solely in each other's gravitational influence and rotate about their barycentre. In the three parts that follow, we will model the physics of a star, of the star-planet model, and the planet respectively.

# Part A

The star, with mass $M_{s} =2M_{\odot}$ (twice the mass of our Sun) and radius $R_{\odot}$ uses nuclear fusion reactions to provide pressure against gravity and electron degeneracy pressure, so as to maintain hydrostatic equilibrium in the star. As long as the hydrostatic equilibrium is preserved, the star is said to be in "main sequence". However, once the energy from the reactions taking place in its core starts running out, the star's outer layers swell out to form a red giant. The core of the star (having a radius $R_{c}$ ) starts to shrink, becoming hot and dense; the temperature of the core rises to over a 100 billion degrees, and the pressure from the proton-proton interactions in the core exceeds that of gravity, causing the core to recoil out from the heart of the star in an explosive shock wave. In one of the most spectacular events in the Universe, the shock propels the material away from the star in a tremendous explosion called a supernova. The material spews off into interstellar space.

Being solar-type, this star has the same proton-proton nuclear fusion chain reaction as our Sun: essentially, this is conversion of four protons (mass of a proton is $m_P$ ) into 1 He nucleus having mass $m_{\mathrm{He}}$ . The star is said to have a "stable lifetime" as long as it is in its "main sequence". The energy emitted by the star passing a sphere of radius $r$ per unit time is $P(r)$ , constant over time and the surface of the imaginary sphere of radius $r$ . The density of the exoplanet having radius $r_{\mathrm{E}}$ is a constant, $\rho$ , and it orbits around the star in a circular orbit of radius $r_{\mathrm{SE}}$ . Neglect any convection effects in the star.

sub_problems.solution:
Using Planck's distribution,

$$u (\nu) = \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{8 \pi h \nu^{3}}{c^{3}} \frac{\mathrm{d} \nu}{\left(e^{\frac{h \nu}{k T_{\odot}}} -1\right)}$$

This integration is well known and equal to $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/15$ .

Returning to our problem,

$$u (\nu) = \frac{8 \pi^{5} k T_{\odot}^{4}}{15 h^{3} c^{3}}$$

The energy flux onto the exoplanet is

$$J_{0} = c u \left(\frac{\Omega}{4 \pi}\right)$$

where $\Omega = \frac{\pi R_{\odot}^2}{r_{\mathrm{SE}}^2}$ . So

$$J_{0} = c \times \frac{8 \pi^{5} k T_{\odot}^{4}}{15 h^{3} c^{3}} \times \frac{\pi R_{\odot}^{2}}{4 \pi r_{\mathrm{SE}}^{2}} \Rightarrow \boxed{T_{\odot} = \left(\frac{60 J_{0}^{3} c^{2} r_{\mathrm{SE}}^{2}}{8 \pi^{5} k R_{\odot}^{2}}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}}}$$

We get the same result by applying Stefan-Boltzmann's radiation law for a black body, since this is how the law is derived.
